_childDocuments_.review: So I'm going to avoid comparing this game to Smash Bros. We all know that no game can match the absolute juggernaut that Nintendo, and the absolutely based Sakurai, created. What I wanted to see was if this game could stand on its own. And it ABSOLUTELY CAN.I gotta say, the developers over at Fair Play Labs absolutely COOKED. They took almost all of the criticisms with the first game and addressed them properly. When Thaddeus Crews said they rebuilt the game from the ground-up, they meant it. When compared to the first game, it's like night and day. You can tell that this was a labor of love, not a quick cash grab. Of course, the game is not without faults. Some of the supers could have been better, in my opinion. Though, the most glaring issue being some questionable cuts from the first game. Like, why is Leonardo and Michelangelo not playable in this installment? Why isn't CatDog in the game? Why is Lincoln Loud, the main protagonist of the Loud House, not playable while a supporting character is? WHERE IS TIMMY TURNER? Other than that, there are some bugs which I have no doubt will be patched out sooner rather than later.However, given at what was improved over the first... _childDocuments_.review: The TL:DR of this review is: Previously, I made a first impressions review after playing the game for 40 minutes. Now, it's time for an actual review.I'll start with the positive(s).+ The game runs fine on Linux. While I didn't test online play (too sweaty for my taste), offline play works amazing. The game worked right out of the box.Now for the negatives.- Many Inconsistencies [Ex: How is Korra bigger/taller than Jenny? Jenny is 6'6 (198.12 cm) WITHOUT her pigtails, and Korra is around 5'7 (170.18 cm) according to many sources.] Yes that is a small one, but sometimes small things can sometimes play major factors/roles in things.- Spongebob is "overpowered," no one can touch him. He's too powerful as a level 4 CPU, practically untouchable and unbeatable. Extremely annoying, infuriating, and enraging.- [Opinion:] I personally believe that the music was better in NASB1. Something just clicks for me with that soundtrack, but it doesn't do the same for this game. Especially with the title theme in NASB1, that one was great.- The moving platform in the Chum Bucket stage is glitchy.- There is no option to remove the time limit for stocks, which was something you could do in the first game.- The random character selection makes zero sense. In NASB1 you were able to choose a random character for the CPU only. In NASB2, attempting to choose a random character makes both you and the CPU as a random character.- There were incorrect character names in the credits. For example, Jenny was labeled as "" instead of Jenny XJ9 (Again, a small thing, but for people who do like Jenny, that is something that they will notice)- Game is not worth the asking price [$50 (USD)] [Purchase it on sale if you would like to play this game. Remember that Steam's refund policy (as of September 7th, 2024) is ]- As a sequel to a video game, it should have the same features as the original, with other features and/or mechanics added. There are features that are fundamentally missing, such as the replay function, which exists in NASB1.- NASB2 does not live up to the hype (if there was any to begin with. I know I was hyped when this game was announced, but this game was a huge let down for me)- The Hot Rod Jenny skin doesn't have the same look and feel as NASB1. In NASB1 the flames from Jenny with the Hot Rod skin were orange and (looked) cool, now they're blue and (look) boring.Neutral:~ Jenny's fist rockets aren't what they used to be in NASB1 (However, this could be considered as a nerf)Conclusion:As a fan of NASB1, I do not recommend NASB2. I believe this game is a waste of money, and I would've been extremely angry if I purchased this game at full price. So much so that I would've refunded the game after I made my original first impressions review.  Again, if you would like to give the game a shot, go ahead, but I would still recommend purchasing it on sale, so it's not as big of a blow to your wallet.  I've pretty much stopped playing this game as there are just way too many negatives for me to justify playing it again. It's just extremely sad when you're excited for a game, and it turns out to be worse than the original.Original Review:

_childDocuments_.review: Very clunky, a few characters have cheese moves. Especially Azula's lightning which makes CPU 1v1s so easy lmao. That betrays a bigger problem though: The CPUs are complete nonsense. They swing wildly between "needs 30 seconds to realize they need a double jump to clear an obstacle" and "understand your hitboxes so well that they can just walk into you to avoid being hit". No inbetween. Speaking of hitboxes, they also seem weird. Some moves that look like they should have quite the reach barely have any and others have laughably big hitboxes. My beloved Azula's lightning would not even be nearly as effective if the game had a sensible get-up. Instead, you have a strict get-up and it feels like there is a moment where you can't input anything. Most fighting games buffer inputs in those situations for a reason: it's gives a player a good opportunity to react in a disadvantage state. There are also minor things like some stage sounds not having any dedicated sound bar to adjust it. So it's always at the maximum that Master Volume allows.But all of this is as nothing in comparison to the deserted community, the broken campaign mode that takes way too long to let you switch off from the default button profile and the game apparently being comepletely abandoned already. Sadly, the game is so bad that I couldn't even pursuade my buddy who loves playing bad games to play with me.It's a damn shame, because a game where you can fight as Azula, Zuko, Danny, Jenny and the others is a cool idea. There are some good ideas in here (mostly stage options, which give a very nice spread for competitive versions and casual defaults). If this had the budget it needed, higher priority for the publisher and a better studio to develop it, this could've been a great game. Alas, it ain't.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved the first game a lot. I was honestly surprised a 2nd game came out so soon when the DLC run from the first felt like it just ended. It does seem a tad unfair to get us invested in a previous game only to release a better version but exclude so many characters we came to love. This game is vastly superior to the other in terms of mechanics, level design, characters, etc. But unfortunately because it's the second entry it's being compared to the first or other sequels from famous fighting games. In Smash Bros for instance, a game this is heavily based on, they don't add characters to then not include them in the next games. They understood people loved them, even if it was a small percentage of the fanbase. I honestly could deal with the lack of so many returning characters, it was odd, but I could deal with it. What I can't get behind is the online for this game. For the last couple of weeks, my game soft locks about 75% of the time when trying to form an online fight. At one time it seemed it was ranked play bugging out with quick play being fine, but then it proved to be both and I was just unlucky. This is a game I bought on PC to play online with others and if I can't do that, then my attention towards it will diminish as single player mode will only get me so far. If the online connections can improve, regardless of if the returning cast comes back I would give it a thumbs up only because I can't give it an inbetween score. And to be honest, there needs to be free DLC for people who own the first game who bought this one (especially with it costing more) for the levels and characters that got left behind. I had high expectations for this game, and it just narrowly missed the mark. I'll continue to play it but I expect to be done in about a week or so. What a shame. Clearly passionate developers.

_childDocuments_.review: Before someone has their conniption fit about the play time: the player base is SO dead just after launch that I couldn't find matches. I was lucky to find 2 in the time that I searched with 500 people on and gave up when the 5th attempt went on for 3 minutes.There are still major issues with this brawler. The movement feels stiff as hell and unresponsive. Some of the animations are ridiculously bad, like Azula's downward fall. She's just looks like a log falling, it's so jarringly dumb looking, like who saw that and said, "yeah, that looks good!". Reaction input still feels really, really bad but I guess because it's significantly better than the first game, it somehow means it is good?If they don't abandon this within 6 months like they did the first one, maybe they can adjust all these things. I say maybe, because it is certainly possible, but will they do it?They also need to drop that price tag. $49.99?! It's barely over a week and it's selling for 50% off on GMG and Humblebundle. Playerbase is dead as hell, 2v2s are always empty and so are Free for Alls. How about breathe life into your niche game by making the price not ridiculous? There's also the fact that by default, they give you the most stupid control options with no way to set the default option, only to make a profile...which you gotta select every time you start a match with people. What kind of brawler has jump by default not assigned to directional input? It's just such a bizarre decision...Overall, it has potential, more than the first, but given how the first was handled not too confident this will be handled any differently. Cash grab and go, or dedicated work? We will see.1.7/5

The future looks bright for this series, and patches are already fixing some minor issues that people along with adding control options like remapping keyboard movement (something everyone has been complaining about lately). _childDocuments_.review: Better than Rivals 2 or Smash Ultimate and (obviously) Multiversus. I only played the Arcade mode and online, but it managed to outshine those games. Still need to experience the Campaign mode and that sounds very promising. Character movesets are incredible, based largely on the best characters in Smash that were often underrated like Ness, Corrin, Mewtwo as well as staples like Peach, Fox/Falco, Captain Falcon... And this game is also does a great job of experimenting with zoning characters to make them actually cool and fun. Not to mention the great strong/light button system instead of Smash attacks. And I have not even learned how to use Slime mechanics (somewhat intentionally). It might be a bit hard to learn, but I think it is a lot easier than Smash Ultimate actually because most moves are great in this game whereas Smash and also Rivals 2 (can not speak for Multiversus since I never played it) have moves that can be very awkward and situational and others that you are basically supposed to use as a crutch in almost every situation. Nick basically lets you use multiple moves as a crutch, which makes it easy to learn. And the Slime mechanics have not felt super overpowered so not knowing them is not punishing, unlike Smash Ultimate where it feels like you need serious matchup knowledge to even hit some characters, or Rivals where it feels like you need to master the system mechanics to have a decent shot at winning after a certain rank even if you were great at Smash.I will say that voice acting is a bit of a weak spot. Only the bosses really shine with voices. I was never in the camp of people who thought these games needed voice acting and in this game everyone gets very short voicelines that make it feel like they do not have voices in most cases. Still I guess the voices do improve the game still with characters like Plankton, El Tigre and Jenny being pretty noticeable with them.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this in a bundle that I initially bought for another game in it, but this ended up being my surprise favorite from the pack. It's a surprisingly competent Smash clone with Nicktoons characters both classic and modern. It's great to see old favorites like Angry Beavers, Rocko's Modern Life, and My Life as a Teenage Robot represented alongside the newer shows, and there's something so satisfying about Ren and Stimpy inflicting their brand of slapstick on the other characters. It even has its own version of Smash's Break the Targets minigame that didn't return in Ultimate. All the characters are fully voiced by either their original VAs or very convincing sound-alikes (not sure which are which), and movesets are heavily based on their respective shows and personalities with countless references and homages.On top of the playable characters, there are also dozens of fully-voiced NPCs from the various shows appearing in the campaign mode, and they often have unique dialog interactions with the playable characters from their same shows. It adds greatly to the crossover feel of it.The only thing I don't like is that some of the character picks are a little odd (several series have side characters playable, but not the stars? And why only 2 of the 4 Ninja Turtles?), but that's not too big a deal.Worth a look if you like platform fighters and grew up watching Nickelodeon cartoons. Definitely far from the shovelware one might expect, especially with Game Mill's name being on it.

_childDocuments_.review: Nickelodeon All Star Brawl 2 as a game is an overall fun experience.Competitively I would say it's a bit of a mixed bag. Characters in this game are a mix of overtuned, perfectly balanced, or bugged. This would hopefully get fixed with patches in the future so I'll be looking forward to that. As of right now the playerbase has been decaying but you can still find matches in ranked relatively fast with crossplay on in North America, alongside with the games great rollback netcode. There is also a Grinders discord that has active players looking to play the game and tournament events that you could participate in. As for the casual experience you won't be finding much in comparison to that of Super Smash Brothers or the upcoming Multiversus, but from my own personal experience the game is very fun when getting together with a group of friends to mess around with. What really shines is the campaign that will keep any player occupied for a good amount of playtime with full voice acting of the cast and then some.I would recommend picking up this game at a good deal, for most people $50 is too much for this game not even including DLC.

_childDocuments_.review: I tried to get it honestly, but i think the game is just flawed.also this review is from a noob, i have little experience in the genre but i've played one other platform fighter so i can draw some comparisons and the issues listed there i didn't experience in that other title.1. bugs. including forcing you to alt F4 the game, lab tools not working, some parts of characters movesets becoming bugged randomly during a match (like phantom projectile refusing to work while on the ground but fine when in the air ?)2. many game mechanics that just don't seem to work properly your character rarely grabs the ledge even if the character is physically touching the ledge.controls are VERY wonky (at least on an xbox controller) with no option to customize things ? a moderate push to the left will send you dashing, which doesn't make much sense. sometimes my character will turn around when releasing the directional stick from a side input, which is obviously a huge issue.just let me set up a controller deadzone and customize the dash/tilt settings. even better let me bind tilt attacks specifically to my right stick.also there seems to be some heavy oversight on some character's kits, like azula's inability to hit grounded smaller opponents with her f.air and to a lesser degree n.air out of a short hop, hurting her neutral a lot.3. recovery options are pretty pathetic, but that impression might be mostly due to the fact that characters just refuse to grab the ledge. either way in my matches when someone was offstage he was probably dead, whether it be because the ledge trolled them or because they had to use their air dodge just to be able to get back on stage instead of, you know, dodging an attack or maybe because the specials recovery options in character's kit are so exploitable (given that it just won't snap to ledge giving you iframes).a platform fighter where everyone dies as soon as they're offstage is pretty bad in my opinion.4. slime mechanics, maybe good players enjoy it, maybe they don't but anyways that's a surefire way to overwhelm beginners even more in an already hard to learn game genre. ( plus I don't like these sort of "lemme change the rules of the game rq" buttons, neither do I think snowball mechanics are any good for any game but that's just me. )5. are you really asking 50 bucks for a low budget game, with some barely functional mechanics, some stuff outright bugged, bad visual presentation AND charging for DLC characters ?Hell no.

_childDocuments_.review: The game soft locks if you look at it wrong. Seriously, sometimes it'll just hang on the results screen with your character far in the distance. If someone quits out of a ranked match in between the ending and the results screen, you'll get soft locked. If you're playing arcade mode, it will soft lock. How these have escaped the devs for this long, yet they are pushing out single character DLC for $7 each is beyond me. To put that into perspective, you get 1 character for $7. Smash Ultimate gave you a character, a stage, and a bunch of music for $6. Call it shrinkflation I guess, but the quality of the game is just not there to justify charging that much for less than you'd get from a premium offering.The game does play well. I'm going to keep playing it throughout the free weekend. It is considerably better than the original. There's no way I'd buy it, though. It's way too frustrating to have to force quit the game at least once an hour. There is still a decent amount of jank here too, but again it is still better than the original.Even with the free weekend, I also have run into the same people several times in ranked. I don't think this game is going to have good staying power so if you're buying it, you should probably be buying it to play with some friends for a little bit as a party game and not taking it too seriously. Especially if these soft locking problems continue.Mr. Krabs also seems kind of cracked. I don't know too much about this game obviously, I've only played it for this free weekend, but I'm not so sure any character should have a mechanic that lets them kill you at 30 damage from a distance. It's not great form to have your paid character being one that is this good.Ranked is also not that great... no such thing as banning stages or counter picking. I actually ran into someone who seemed to be hacking because his character always showed as random in the character select screen, but when we got into the actual match it would always be one of two characters. One time, the VS screen image didn't even match up to their character. I can only assume this is to make sure that people can't counterpick him, but if it was baked into the game it'd eliminate that problem.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fun and has solid design, but has the glaring issue of being handcuffed to GameMill Entertainment. The same studio that brought you flops such as Avatar: Quest for Balance, Quest 64, Skull Island: Rise of Kong, and the infamously bad Big Rigs: Over the Road Racing.Yes, THAT Big Rigs, the one that has an 8/100 on Metacritic. Seriously, Viacom, please be willing to take your investments more seriously than this. NASB1 and 2 would have sold so many more copies and had better word of mouth if you went with literally any other publisher. One year of development time is not enough time for an outsourced dev team to ship out a $50 game--actually, it's $95 when you account for the costume pack and DLC.Edit: At the time of writing, the full game is $32 on sale, which is a much better ask for the kind of content and polish that this game has when comparing it to existing competitors such as Smash Ultimate, Rivals of Aether, Brawlhala, etc.Yet in spite of the circumstances, NASB2 is thought-out and genuinely enjoyable. The slime mechanic alone makes this game incredibly fun. I can even recommend this over Smash Ultimate given that I don't have to fight against the controls to do important techniques that are vital to how characters function, and because NASB2 has solid rollback netcode.Unfortunately, there are still a LOT of bugs that should have been patched  release, instead of treating the most loyal, day-1 purchasing fans as your unpaid beta testers. _childDocuments_.review: It is unfortunate, really.The original Nickelodeon All-Star Brawl was a game that was hyped up to be the "Smash Bros. killer." It didn't kill smash. Because, in my opinion, it is good, maybe even great. From just a few hours over this free weekend, I can confidently say NASB2 is superior to the first game in every way, adding new mechanics and refining the fast-paced, combo-centric gameplay that was already there in the original. The single player modes aren't outstanding, but are still far better than what was available in the first game. Everything is more polished and I have got a few laughs out of it.However...NASB2 is not polished enough to warrant a £40 (full-price base edition) asking price.For all of the developer's passion, it cannot compare to the publisher's greed. GameMill does not care about publishing quality, but rather, a large quantity of hilariously rushed steaming hot piles of ♥♥♥♥.A couple of examples:- Skull Island: Rise of Kong- Avatar: The Last Airbender - Quest for BalancelolIn all fairness, their Nickelodeon games are usually fine, but even still, you can tell they care more about making some quick money than giving the developers enough time to create something could've been even better.I'll likely buy this game for local play sessions (since I'm not too confident in the games longevity online) if it ever goes on offer for 95% off or something. _childDocuments_.review: A vast improvement on the original game in virtually every way. A huge boost to visuals, gameplay depth and single player content. While still rough in some areas, I'd heartily recommend this to anyone who is either a big fan of either Nickelodeon or platform fighters in general. Characters have a variety of mechanics and lovingly-crafted movesets to help them stand out from each other, and the Slime Meter gives players a ton of options both offensively and defensively. The campaign is a lot of fun with tons of dialogue and references, and a lot of natural replayability too. Roster has some kind of strange picks and omissions in some cases, but some deep cuts like El Tigre or the Angry Beavers, so I'll take what I can get. There is some lacking polish with some aspects like movement or hitboxes, and a fair few glitches however. Sometimes the game ignores my control profile, there's tons of minor visual or audio bugs at times like some music tracks playing over other music tracks, or characters falling through the floor. The campaign seems the most riddled with them.Considering the size of this team and the publish they have to work with, Fair Play Labs has done a lot of good here and created a major success story after the first game's mixed reception. With some patches for polish and extra DLC content, this will end up being a good package overall. Still a bit hard to stomach at full price on top of the costume AND character DLC though, so maybe consider a sale for some of those if you aren't convinced.

_childDocuments_.review: Is it weird to review a multiplayer online party fighting game, and focus primarily on the single player adventure mode? Is it proper? Because for better or worse, most of my feelings about this game are based on that adventure mode, and how I wish it was more fleshed out. Right now it's kind of an unbalanced mess, partly by design. There are certain power-ups in the adventure mode that are so powerful that they define the meta all on their own, and by "certain power-ups", I mean "the singular power-up that makes you invincible whenever you hit someone with an air attack". It's a roguelite game mode with only one "correct" build for every character, and that build is "get that one power-up that gives you complete invincibility and the perk that heals you every time you debuff an enemy".If you can look past that, though, the game's fun to play and super accessible to just about anyone willing. _childDocuments_.review: 8.5 / 10An incredibly good game that I can only recommend to those who plan on playing it a lot (which you should) (I'll explain). Things like the slime meter and the roguelite campaign are some of the most exciting things to happen to platform fighters in years, but there are lots and lots of little issues that can add up to a negative experience for some.Pros:-Character movesets & design are unique and so so so fun-Graphics are surprisingly good considering all the different source materials' art styles-Attention to detail is off the charts, every character is fully voice acted (including unique campaign dialog), stages and character animations are full of references to their respective shows, everything down to the names of moves and campaign perk icons are some kind of well-researched in-joke-Campaign can be really fun, some of the perks you can get are hilariously powerful like invincibility after landing air attacks, automatic homing projectiles, poison damage, etc.-Music consistently and aggressively slaps-Stage variations are excellent for casual / competitive play-Online is smooth 99% of the time, almost feels like playing offline-Seriously, slime is like the coolest thing ever, it never outright wins you a stock / match but it leads to some enjoyable strategies, combos, mixups, etc.Cons (as of this review):-Campaign runs don't offer a very large variety of perks, leading to a lot of repeated strategies-Campaign runs take a very long time, and can't be exited from the map screen-Campaign technically has a profile select option, but it is invisible-Arcade has so few match types, the same run will sometimes have the exact same match multiple times-Bosses are cool on paper, but aside from a few outliers almost every attack is too fast to react to and has deceptively large hitboxes, making aggressive play incredibly dangerous (shredder is especially bad, he spends twice as much time actively attacking as he does just being vulnerable)-When you select to begin a local or online battle, you can still accidentally change your character / costume while the announcer is counting down-Bugs bugs bugs, so many bugs, I couldn't possibly list all the different bugs I've experienced, let alone all the bugs in the game. I've seen infinite jumps, permanently flattened characters, characters phasing into each other on the results screen, endless loads, controllers not working in the menu, crashes, and more...The biggest takeaway for me is this: what brings this game down are little things that can be fixed, while what lifts the game up is its big features - the core gameplay and design. And for the record, I've had plenty more matches without any bugs than I've had with them, so it's hard to say they ruin the game outright. I'm hopeful that over time, the small bugs and issues will be patched out and the game will be able to shine more consistently, but that shine is already present here. If you're willing to put the time into the game to get better at it and get the most out of its strengths, then its weaknesses won't really matter in the long run.

_childDocuments_.review: Any platform fighter fan should give this a try. That the game received such a positive reception on launch despite the scuff and lack of polish in some areas is a testament to how fun and engaging the core fighting experience is. Despite not having the launch numbers of the first Nick All-Star Brawl, I expect this one to have a longer lasting playerbase down the line due to its higher skill ceiling and greater potential for self-expression (plus the game being about 700 times better in almost every way, besides not having Catdog). The meter mechanics that have formed the strategic backbone of the fighting game genre for the past couple decades slide in here surprisingly well, what impresses me most is the vast array of applications that the slime meter has, without feeling overwhelming to manage.For the rogue-lite single-player mode, it's alright. In my eyes it's a great idea for this genre, with infinite potential (platform fighters are often sorely lacking in the single-player content needed to build that broader casual fan-base), but the execution is lacking. After doing a few runs, enough to complete the story, it was already getting quite repetitive. Just not enough content or variation per-run to tap into the replayability that the rogue-lite genre can offer. Still, it's a novel concept for a platform fighter, and I can see other future platform fighters really taking this concept and running with it (maybe in NASB3). It is a shame that the circumstances of this game's creation have hindered its potential to really blow up. It was born from the ashes of a very lackluster game that was buyer's remorse for most, and only having like 1.5 years of development time led to many character cuts from the first - although this game launching with 25 characters is still a remarkable achievement, given how vastly different the gameplay design is. Not to mention having to spend its first week without the day 1 patch... if this game survives, it will be on the basis of simply being a good game. What we've seen so far seems to be a promising start.

_childDocuments_.review: Nick all stars brawl 2 is massive step up from the first one in every way. From the animations, move design, single player, and online content. With voice acting and cross play from the start as well, it really goes a long way in terms of quality. But the main highlight for me personally is the redesigns for almost every fighter in the game. Before this. most of the fighters from the first one had very samey up tilts, jabs, and down tilts. But here, every move is unique with a purpose and is completely different  from every other fighter.  Unique hitboxes, different status in knock back and more defined disjoints and such. The addition of side attacks and specials really help as well in better defining the fighters. Also as a quick side note, it helps you're enjoyment of the game if you are attached  to Nickelodeon in general, as if not it could be a bit degrading for you personally. The actual fighting gameplay is also pretty easy to grasp, but hard to master in all the right ways. You get very tight responsive controls that are snappy and butter smooth. I was kinda surprised personally with how easy it is to fall down from a platform after playing smash ultimate for so long, it threw me off guard for a good bit. Speaking of that, if you have been playing ultimate fort a while, you might be thrown off the loops for a good first few hours as you adjust to the feeling and movement of the game. But I still very like the tight control of it all. also something that threw me off loop was the end lag on some of the moves. Because in ultimate you SEE the animation play out and as soon you go back to you're idle animation, in both land and air, you can act again. But here it does the same thing, but you can't act out for a few frames, even with the animation of the move is done. One last thing from me about the gameplay is that I really dislike the hitstun in this game. You fly so far away from're you opponent for a few seconds in mid % but still can't act out of falling stun. It just looks like you can act out of it and do anything you want, but still can't perform any move, which makes the timing a bit awkward for me. The online experience is fantastic all around. The net code is really smooth and responsive as the local modes for me. As well the addition of cross play is great to see and being able to play with friends on different platforms is certainly a massive positive from me.  As well the online modes of competitive and quick play separation is great. Though I do not like the items being turned on for quick play though.  Should be a different mode for that.  But again, the online is awesome!The main campaign is really good too, but needs a bit of work though. My favourite thing about have got to be the different interactions  between you're selected fighter and the characters you meet and story beats. Watching their personality play out in this saving the world setting is pretty interesting  and the special back and forward lines between a few of them were great to hear. The rougue-like structure is also really addicting and fun to play as well. Slowly powering up, unlocking new core power ups and fighters is pretty expressive and a big list of em. The main problem for me here is that after a while, the fights and modes in every run gets a bit stale since you literally been there and done that. Same stages, with the same mobs, with the same board the platform and balloon stages. It never changes in terms of level design, but the order is different which is great but doesn't fix the problem. The fact that bosses are in the game is great too and it is fun to fight against them, but some of their animation movement and polish could be a bit more consistent with the fighters. Still like fighting against them and love that they are here, but I wish they were done a bit better with their own unique stages, more defined gimmicks and such. Overall Nick All stars brawl 2 is a blast to play. From all the different and unique fighters that everyone can find and play in their own way, to the awesome controls and online. And with a neat rougue-like campaign, the game truly delivers. If you are a fan of platform fighters and like to play online a lot, this is a great recommendation from me. Though if you prefer the single player side the story mode and bot fights, you might want to wait for a sale on this. If you still want to get into it, but the price is not working out for you, then defiantly wait for a sale. Otherwise, this is a great time to be had with plenty of hours to be skunked into online and local fights with you're friends. One final thing from me is that the regional pricing is really bad :( The stranded price for the game is eh for 50$ but the deluxe and ultimate versions are not worth it, as well the standalone prices of the fighters pass and costume pack. Would wait for a sale on these personally because I would not pay that price for so little content. Like for real, the season pass is 32$ CAD price. Add 18 more dollars to that and you would get the same price as the base game with the base roaster, features, and modes. Disappointing in that regard.

It's fun, feels good to play and perform combos in, and has a level of depth that I really appreciate in a platform fighter.With that said there are some issues that definitely plague the game right now, little inconsistencies where sometimes the same exact input wont grab ledge, or the game will register the input wrong sending you falling to your death while recovering, not common, but frustrating when it happens. _childDocuments_.review: Project M fans, this one's for you.Simply put, this game is incredible, and highly recommended for fans of Smash Bros or any platform fighter - and if you're a fan of Nickelodeon properties too, it is a *must have*. Every frame of this game is a fun reference or throwback to the original properties. The amount of love and due diligence to these properties is incredible, and the animation on the characters is vastly improved over the original. The controls are tight, movement is sublime, all of the best mechanics from across Smash Bros, its various fan-made mods, and other contemporaries is all here. It's almost entirely reworked from the original Nick All Stars, forgoing most of its bizarre mechanics for a much more pure Smash-like experience. As far as gameplay and gamefeel this is a downright achievement, and one that hardcore fans of the genre will immediately get a feel for. The Slime mechanic is a lot of fun - inspired by Guilty Gear's tension gauge and Roman Cancels, it lets players be creative and expressive with their attack strings and movement, cancelling essentially anything at any time and resetting back to a controllable state or saving it up all the way for a super attack. The training mode options let you view hitboxes, hurtboxes, trajectories, stage collisions, all right out of the gate. It's got lots of nerdy nuance for hardcore fans, but despite that, it's also easy to pick up and play for anyone even remotely familiar with Smash. Casual players can still have a great time throwing it on the tv, enabling items, and having some chaotic fun with a bunch of recognizable characters. The campaign is surprisingly fun too - a roguelite where you power up your character and only get one stock to make it to the end, with some fun pit stops to visit npc characters. Some have cute interactions depending on the character you play as. It has a good amount of replay value, and is a nice place to try out new characters.If I had to point out a few quirks or flaws, it's that it seems unpolished in some areas. Sound design could use some work - the sound effects and sense of impact can feel weak or flimsy. Super attacks sometimes lack sound effects completely, and the audio mixing on character voices is a little unbalanced. There are a few technical issues here and there, some players report crashing, and slime cancelling can lead to inconsistent behavior on attacks. The devs have addressed a lot of these issues for future patches, but it's worth mentioning. Overall it's a little rough around the edges in terms of presentation, and admittedly can look like a cheap game that isn't worth the $50 price tag - but don't let that fool you. Beneath it's appearance as a cheap GameMill licensed affair hides a rich and deep game. Even after two afternoons worth of labbing I feel like I'm only scratching the surface of it.

I'm glad to see that the voice acting is here from the beginning (and didn't feel like a last minute addition), the combos you can do with each character are mostly unique (especially with the slime mechanic letting you be more creative), and the single player has a lot more things to do with a campaign and mini games alongside traditional arcade mode.  Also, the addition of items and both casual and competitive stage layouts is a plus. Only real issue I have right now is the online isn't 100% perfect.  It works as intended most of the time but it's still buggy on rare occasions with some random glitches.  Also, I was confused on how to change controls originally so maybe an option on the main menu would be convenient.  If you like platform fighters like smash this is worth trying out (though I could understand waiting for a sale if you're skeptical you'll enjoy it).

_childDocuments_.review: I'd give the game an overall positive review at this point in time.GOOD:Huge step up from the first game in terms of content, graphics and readability imo. Much more appealing for casual gameplay with the roguelite campaign mode and having actual skins for characters is such a solid decision. Competitive-wise, the game is a bit slower than NASB1 at the moment, but it's much less of a single button spamfest than it was before. Slime meter is super fun albeit really tricky to use properly. At the moment, every character seems relatively balanced, of course this is super early on so things may change, but Slime being a universal mechanic does so much heavy lifting for the entire cast and it was a very wise decision to implement it on a balancing standpoint IMO.BAD:Once again, Nickelodeon seemingly pushed the devs to release a rushed product. A lot of things were addressed from last game like having voice acting at launch, the aforementioned character skins, etc. but now we have a slew of new gripes, such as online matchmaking liking to just break every hour or so (in my experience), and penalizing you for leaving matches that literally never start or for disconnects outside of your control. There are also simply not enough options in the controls menu for every player, which is an understandably missed feature considering all of the controller options, and will hopefully be addressed in an update. I'd personally like to see stick sensitivity options for people like me where my stick on my GCC doesn't quite reach all the way to the left, so I essentially can't dash without using double tap dash(gross). Rivals has this and it's a lifesaver.OVERALL:If you like Platform Fighters, this is a good one. Price point is a bit steep, but IMO it's way more worth it in this game for the whole package than it was for NASB1, even if I'm on the fence on which one I enjoy more mechanically at this moment. There's just more to it this time around.

_childDocuments_.review: This game takes everything that didn't work out in the first game and completely turns all of it around. The slime meter is an incredibly unique and interesting mechanic that not only adds so much to the potential of the game, but also differentiates this game from every other platform fighter. All of the complaints I have are minor, but I still do have a couple. The biggest one is the roster, I really dislike how they cut so many iconic characters from the cast of the original game. Although I do enjoy the cast of characters in this game more than the first game, I still think that they should have put more focus on bringing back iconic characters such as Sandy Cheeks and Catdog rather than introducing as many new characters at the beginning of this game, although this is mostly personal preference. The CPUs in this game are also very easy, although this is a minor complaint. While I hate to compare the game to Smash, the level 9 CPUs in this game are probably equivalent to a level 6 or 7 CPU in Smash, so you can't rely on facing CPUs very well to help you do much more than learn the fundamentals of the game. On the other hand, the online feature in this game is incredible and includes cross-play, and in my opinion that makes up for the sub-par CPUs. The single player modes in this game, mainly the campaign, are fun although they don't have too much replay-ability in my opinion. I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who enjoys platform fighters, as I believe it is the best one ever outside of Smash itself, but I would still recommend Smash first to a friend trying out the genre for the first time. I would give this game a 8.5/10 overall.

Neutral is a game of whiff punish chicken. Instead of buffing other characters to have safe moves on shield, they're just nerfing the characters that could actually pressure shield. I really really wanted this game to be good, and I can see the effort. The mechanics at their core just make for the lamest interactions in any platform fighter. Slime was executed beautifully, but it doesn't fix the issues core to the gameplay experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Well this came out of nowhere. This is a weird one. It's not a massive new mainline DQ game, but this game scratches a particular itch. If I had to say what it's like, this game feels a lot like Dragon Quest's version of Pokemon Legends Arceus, with a dash of Xenoblade-style landscapes and some hints of collectathon-ish platforming. You travel around, fighting and recruiting monsters, scouring every nook and cranny for new treasures. You take on various sidequests that sort of are just very loose broad guidelines that you'll fulfill as you continue to explore the world. The game is quite hands off and really does let you proceed at your own pace. The world is the real star here, with lots of evocative landscapes and biomes, side paths, pretty considered and interesting level design that at times can make use of the traversal abilities you bring alongside monsters you recruit. It's very colorful, very quaint, very cozy. Like an introduction to the idea of a JRPG and open world game rolled into one with a Dragon Quest skin.Combat is...fine. It's okay, but this was developed by Tose, who have made some really good action RPGs before. This is very simple in comparison. It's not the end of the world, and it lends the game a kind of laid back charm, but it feels like some potential was missed both in your main character combat and monster setup. Was also expecting there to be more puzzle solving where you swap off between the characters, but while there are sort of traversal puzzle environments and the like that I've seen so far, sibling puzzle solving seems to not be a thing.Music is good! It's mostly all old midi Dragon Quest stuff, but it's a much better showing than XI, for instance. It's also fun to just go around to encampments and the like and talk to NPCs because the game very much has that Dragon Quest localization flavor to it.Story is cute so far. It's not amazing by conventional standards, but it has that sort of DQ vignette fairytale feeling through and through. Wish there was more voice acting, but the major scenes are fully voiced.Also weird shoutout to the UI. It's extremely extremely clean, and gives perhaps, Kirby/Smash/Kid Icarus vibes? Very friendly-looking. Nice change of pace from the mainline titles which are kinda very window-heavy.As a PC version, this is very solid. No real UE4 stutters, runs extremely well. Some scenes are capped at 60 or 30 fps it seems like but the bulk of gameplay can be uncapped. It seems like if you're not hitting the framerate targer you set in settings though you can get some slowdown, so just make sure to pick an fps limit that you're able to hit. I can pretty comfortably do 120, and it looks night and day compared to the Switch. Better draw distance, resolution, and the like. Nothing like DLSS, but honestly the TAA here is decent enough and the game runs good enough already. Decent sampling of graphics and display settings, but no arbitrary aspect ratio unfortunately.For Steam Deck, in my experience you can get 30 fps for ~4 hours of battery with a 7-8w TDP cap, or you can get 2-3 hours of battery at 60 fps with uncapped TDP (capped to 12 or so also seems to work, but some drops here). Intermediate framerates like 40, 45 etc. produce slowdown.Price wise, maybe wait for a slightly larger discount, $30 or $35 or so. But I paid $40 and don't feel particularly ripped off, so far at least, ~5 hours in.

_childDocuments_.review: Wish I could give a neutral review.If you are a big fan of the series this game is more of what you want. If you are not, I don't think this entry will win you over. I spent around 5~ hours at the very start of the game grinding up a 'good' team. I spent another 5ish hours just cruising around and exploring the world and unlocking fast travel. The main story itself only took a couple hours to clear and wasn't very compelling. Post game is a random infinite scaling dungeon along with finishing your pokedex for monsters and treasures.Pokedex is another let down for me. There are 74 monsters total. Slime has half a dozen recolors. King slime has several. Dracky has like 6. Of the 74 I would guess maybe 15-20 are unique monsters that aren't just reskins. Dragon Warrior Monsters 2 has over 300. The original Joker game has 210. Of course there are some recolors like Slime and Metal Slime but the majority are not. Combat isn't too bad. It's all real time. Your character can hack and slash but honestly it does basically nothing. At around level 50 I hit for around 25 per swing. My attack monster does over 350. You have a sling shot like Monster Hunter World that has a ton of value. Ammo gets very annoying but it is well worth it. Dodge roll for i frames and telegraphed attacks make it a bit on the easy side. Only issue here is that the combat never changes. You do the same combo forever. You have no spells, only slingshot. Slingshot also doesn't really change. You go for small bomb shots to bigger bomb shots. A lot of the charm is in the base. I had 2 'hand' monsters that were doing what looked like rock, paper, scissors. I had two golems square up. King and Queen Slimes sleep next to each other. Little things like that were great and made it feel a lot more alive. Performance wise I had no issues and the game plays fine on MKB. Can rebind pretty much everything if you need to.All said and done, I think the game is incredibly ok. I do wish we could return to the older style. A Legends Arceus type game was a neat idea but feels very half baked. Would absolutely not recommend at 50 usd for anyone but die hard fans. I imagine most people clear the story in 10-15 hours tops. There is almost nothing to do short of endless grind after that. I don't see any real replay value either.

_childDocuments_.review: Just a super quick and dirty basic tech overview for things that I was looking for, not a "review":- Supports 30, 60, 120, 144 and uncapped FPS with a separate vsync toggle.- Supports resolutions up to 4k, but does not support ultrawide out of the box, you'll get black bars. Defaults to Borderless, but also has windowed and exclusive fullscreen.- A decent amount of graphics options, not super impressive but you can make it look significantly better than the Switch version in terms of actual graphical features, not just FPS/resolution, which is what I was worried about, as it looked bad on Switch and ran worse.- I had zero stutters in the 30 minutes or so I played, which was just me rushing through the beginning which I'd already done to at least get to some combat. Ran buttery smooth the entire time.- Rebindable controls (Can't remember if Switch had them, but always a welcome addition) + you can swap between Xbox/PS icons- While it's in an awkward spot, they remembered an exit button! Not too common for console devs to forget this anymore, but it still happens from time to time. In this case, you go to options and hit the start button or its equivalent depending on control scheme.The game defaults to medium settings, so if you're not on a potato, I recommend cranking those immediately. You can open the options very early on. It also defaults to a 60 FPS cap, so if you want to go higher, be sure to switch that as well. And while this might be more subjective, I found the default camera sensitivity to feel very weird and slow. Increasing the horizontal and vertical camera sensitivity by a single notch made it feel like a normal game.I wasn't paying too close attention to the cutscenes, but it seemed like some were locked to 30 and might've been pre-rendered videos since they had very low image quality. Not 100% on this though.Overall, the game feels tremendously more playable than the very compromised Switch version and looks far better to boot. It's not perfect, and I assume someone's working on an ultrawide fix if there isn't already one, but overall I'm pleased.

_childDocuments_.review: Had to edit my review because people are really underselling this game.I picked this up totally at random, saw the launch trailer for switch, forgot about it and then it appeared on steam, and i was looking for a chill, colorful and calm game.This game game what i was looking for, and then some more; right from the start you have Akira Toriyama iconic art style that i find nostalgic and fun, the young protagonists sense of adventure, braving a world full of treasure and monsters!The game has multiple open areas to explore, each with their biome, monsters and various treasure, tipically you have a forecast of what type of treasure you are going to find on the islands, that changes each expedition, so you have to pick wich monster you want to bring based on their affinity for treasure type, but also the monsters FORTE, like jumping, gliding and sprinting, that helps you explore.Going through the world with a party of 3 monsters, you are more of a support role when it comes to fight (you still have some cool moves tho), you can use a slingshot to deal different type of physical and elemental damage, but more importantly heal and buff your party of monsters, they do most of the damage, and have different skills based on their type and rarity; you can scout monsters by defeating them (to have a chance they'll join your gang!) When you go back to base the treasure gets appraised and your gang level increases based on the total value of your vault, you can then recruit monster you scouted giving them specific items (more rare monsters need rare items) and you can send monsters on dispatch missions to get you more resources for crafting (or even tresure), also in your base as you progress, new facilities and activities become available.The game creates a perfectly relaxed gameplay loop where you don't have to rush story missions but instead, you can pace them as you want between exploration and collecting treasure. (it's very addictive!)

_childDocuments_.review: Huge Dragon Quest fan here. The first hour is VERY rough and super childish. I almost gave up but the game kept sprinkling in small things here and there that I kept thinking "ok...that's cool" or "I've never seen this in a game before." I was very surprised to discover a gaming experience unlike anything I've played over the last 40 years. It has a little of everything. -Base building-Monster collecting/recruiting-Action combat where your monsters fight alongside you in real time (your monsters do the majority of the damage-Treasure hunting-Hiding treasure for other players to find-Appraising other player's treasure-Gang fights at base and in the field -Questing-Cooking-Several zones that are all free roam, with lots of hidden areas you can access if you have certain monster abilities with you -Monsters chatter (spoken) while you are wandering around in the field and some of it is pretty funny (though hard pass on the slimes making the slurping noise all the time)-More puns and pun names than you ever thought possible, even in a Dragon Quest game, which are known for punsIt's absolutely wild and I genuinely look forward to playing it each day just to see what new stuff is out there and how many other players viewed my treasures. The treasure hunting is so cool because you get items from other DQ games and they all have the history and lore behind them. Digging up other players items increases their value and also has the "Originally Discovered By..." data on it, like how trading Pokemon has the original trainer name.In the end, it's a damn shame that this came out on the Switch with it's abysmal performance of 720p and 20fps because on PC it's in glorious 4k with more graphics options than I expected and an uncapped frame rate. It looks amazing. My only gripe is that the music in some areas is just way too repetitive and I ended up switching it off here and there. Highly recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: A true completionist's trial. Casual players will be fine running through the story and a good chunk of content but people who 100% will have their mental fortitude greatly tested.All 777 treasures are RNG, finding each one does not remove them from the loot pool because you can find duplicates. Every time you pick up a treasure you can only see it's silhouette and type so you have to keep a spreadsheet on hand of every treasure you are still missing. You can only carry up to about 10 treasures per outing before returning to base. Your monsters can potentially drop their treasure every tick of damage requiring it to be picked back up. The worst RNG I have ever seen with even more handicaps to make it worse.Furthermore there's plenty of annoying sidequests that are ALSO RNG reliant. THEN even after you manage to do everything you still have to hit gold cap which is one of the most tedious mundane grinds I have ever endured. Gold Golems, a lot of them, and a lot of save & loading. I'd rather 100% a 200 hour long JRPG WITH MISSABLES than the 90 something hours I spent to 100% this collectathon. Good game.

_childDocuments_.review: I was hoping the game would be similar in quality to Dragon Quest Builders 2 for a DQ spin-off game, but it's not even close. This is an exploration game that does everything in it's power to make exploration less fun. The combat is almost entirely determined by your AI monster companions, who will spend the majority of a battle standing around not doing anything. When they finally do decide to attack you'll be lucky if they actually make contact with anything. In the meantime you can tickle enemies with your dagger or shoot pellets at them, both of which are wildly ineffective compared to the damage your monsters will do. Every few minutes while out exploring the screen will flash and tell you that you're getting tracked by a rival gang. This is probably the most annoying part of the game because the AI is so utterly braindead that your best bet is just to sit there and make sure you spawn the rival gang in an open and flat location so your monsters have easy access to them. Otherwise they'll spawn clipped through terrain or on uneven surfaces and your monsters won't be able to figure out how to get to them. There isn't much of a story which is a huge let-down especially after playing DQB2 which has a massive storyline to play through.Every time you return to your base the treasure forecast changes and I think the game expects you to constantly swap out your team to match the forecast, but the system is so annoying that it's best to just completely ignore it. You've got multiple teams of monsters that are sent out on missions that are unavailable to be put in your party and up to 10 equippable medal slots on every monster so changing them all around every time you come back to your base just isn't worth the hassle.The Forte system is an absolute mess. There are 5 Fortes: Scan, Sprint, Launch, Glide, and Stealth. You can only have 3 of them in your party at a time and Launch, Glide, and Stealth are absolutely necessary to fully explore maps. So if you wanted to bring a Scan monster for locating Recipe/Medal chests, it will be pointless since you'll likely be missing a required Forte to get to the chests anyway.The map designs are also a disaster. You'll be walking in an area and see a level 10 monster standing next to a level 40 because for whatever reason they designed the game so that you're exploring 1/4th of an island, then 1/4th of the next island, etc. instead of designing it so that you would complete 1 island before moving onto the next. This basically gets rid of any sense of progression in the game, especially combined with the lack of any sort of linear storyline.Tldr: An exploration game that lacks any sort of fun exploration

_childDocuments_.review: This game rekindled my love for Dragon Quest series, I've been a fan since the Dragon Warrior name era. If your childhood consisted of DQ franchise, then you will have a great time playing and reading about the items inside. One thing I hated is it took me 370 hours to 100% the game. QoL improvements are so needed and the small community it had paved the way too thin for completionist. There are no escalating odds in finding rare treasures and fulfilling 777 of them sounds challenging, which came as a torture during the final treasures. _childDocuments_.review: Dragon Quest Treasures is a spin off of DQ XI, which was an amazing game. It features younger versions of Erik and his sister on their quest to find treasure. The story is pretty simple, but the plot builds as you progress. The game is wonderfully colorful and vibrant. Enemies are classic DQ and the locations are varied and, at times, quite beautiful. The game features RPG-lite mechanics like leveling up and item usage, but it's more of an action/adventure game. You can roam an open world, accepting quests and tackling dungeons throughout. Battles are played out in real-time, with your monster allies helping you in battle. Your attacks are limited, but there's plenty of enemy variety to keep things fresh.The best part about the game is the collecting mechanic. You collect treasure, ingredients, monsters, and items and it's a blast. It can be quite addictive trying to find better and better treasure. And with more treasure comes more play mechanics like building up your base and opening up new features to play around with. This is an absolute blast to play and worth every penny. Don't let the childish visuals fool you, this game is fun and worth a purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: Once I got 9 hours in, that's when this game got boring. Not because of the music, not because of the story, because of the GAMEPLAY. 1. THE MONSTERS DON'T SHUT UP: I don't know what they were thinking where they decided to have your monster party members to say something literally EVERY 5 seconds. At first, its cute, its funny, I liked it. But after 30 mins to an hour, it gets old. And there is no option to turn it off. So while I look for treasure I am hearing the bat say "I like to SWOOOOOOOOP" every 5 seconds. Like I said, funny and cute at first, but after an hour, I am going insane. 2. AUTOSAVE: The autosave is not frequent enough, so if you are not actively saving every 15-20 mins or so, if you die you could lose TONS of progress. Because this game doesn't let you continue where you left off if you die, its straight up you go back to your last save. Very unforgiving for a game that is supposed to be relaxing and carefree lol. 3. REPETITIVE GAMEPLAY: When I got to the first island, it wants you to fix the other stations. I was like okay cool, then second island its the same thing, third island... same thing. Sure there is different quests on each island, but idk, wouldn't it be more engaging if there was a different reason or method to unlock the train stations on each island? Not just copy and paste the same dialogue for each train master. Also that's whats weird too, you get to a station that isn't up and running and the station master looks old and broken. Makes sense right? Then once you fix it, the station master STILL looks old and broken but when you talk to it it says its up and running, really? I couldn't tell! 4. LANDSCAPES: The islands are huge and beautiful, but so empty. It makes you want to run around and explore but there just really isn't much out there to find. It's too bland and too empty for how much area is offered to the player. 5. ENEMIES: Now this is a part where I don't really understand why they didn't put more guidance or advice for the player. When you have to unlock stations, there's usually very high level enemies at one of them. So I am guessing that means you just can't do it at the moment or you just gotta be careful and not die? Would be nice if the game told you, especially since the pig or cat talks to you constantly, even telling me "Are you sure you want to fight that?" when its a enemy that's like 10 levels below me. Like how about tell me that when its an actual high level enemy. Or they will randomly tell me "We can't talk to that monster right now" when I am fighting. What?? TALK TO WHO?6. THE CHARACTERS: I REALLY REALLY wish they would've done more with Mia and Erik. Like maybe make them look like actual treasure hunters? How come they dig up treasures with a KNIFE? How is that even realistic, it would be so cool if they had a shovel on their back and like a backpack so it LOOKS like they are out looking for treasure. Instead you just carry a knife around, which makes sense for killing enemies but when you are stabbing the ground over and over "digging" up treasure I am like what is this. CONCLUSION: The game play is just badly designed. I feel like it could be so much better if they had put more detail and experiences into the open world, and put thought behind the player experience such as thinking that maybe hearing a monster say something every 5 seconds could be annoying or how digging up treasure with a knife isn't that realistic. This game is definitely geared towards dragon quest fans, because all the treasures are items from other games. The music is great as always and the story isn't bad either. It just feels like a studio took unreal engine and used the characters and monsters of dragon quest and threw them into a badly designed unreal engine world. But since I still love anything dragon quest, I most likely will still play this game just to finish it for the story and music.

_childDocuments_.review: This is very much a game for the Dragon Quest diehards but as someone who very much is in that camp, this put a big smile on my face constantly while playing. The gameplay loop revolves around setting out from your hideout to explore various floating islands to find treasures based on items/characters from previous Dragon Quest games. You'll glide, ride monsters, and climb around various biomes filled with tons of trinkets and monsters littered all over. The ability to expand your moveset by taming monsters is a nice touch but the pool of monsters is rather small once you notice how many times they repeat them with a palette swap. The story and dialogue is purely kids stuff but to me the wholesome energy it brought was an asset and not a fault. _childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: For twenty bucks I'd grab it without regret, but for a full-priced game, I find it lacking.To preface, I'm a huge Dragon Quest series enjoyer, and this game has all the pros and cons the games usually do: It's charming, it's mechanically easy, the art is stylistically great, and the soundtrack is nostalgic. It has inexplicably unskippable repetitive features, it eventually boils down to a grind that makes your eyes glaze over and drains the initial joy out of the game. My primarily complaint here is that progressing in certain areas requires you to recruit X monster, which, aside from sometimes having to kill several dozen (buddy seeds included) to even get them scouted, will then send you on a goose chase to find the various recipes and ingredients that monster wants from you to sign on. Combined with your team's poor AI and the sluggish pace of travel, this honestly becomes actively un-fun in a short while, and the shallow exploration loses its charm quickly with the amount of forced repetition involved. I wanted to love this as I love every DQ game prior, but I really just find it boring.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could still refund this, but that aside, this game is only worth it on a deep sale, like under $20 or for very young children. Even then, it reminds me of the N64/PS era collect-a-thons, but with nothing interesting to keep you going.Story: It's your typical JRPG MacGuffin quest with some of the goofiness of DQ. Just a pinch. Your not missing anything, other than the vikings are portrayed more as adoptive parents than the cruel slave owners they're made out to be in DQ11. I think most people will be rolling their eyes or not reading anything. Kids under 7 will probably be fine with it.Visuals/Animation: Fair, nothing great. Animations are sparse, but what is there is okay. The visuals lack variety and look low budget. They're nicely shaded, but there just isn't a lot to see. Granted, this was originally a Swtich game, but this game is on par with games from PS3, like 2015's Dragon Quest Heroes. However, unlike that game, there are only about 20 unique monsters, recolored 5 or more times each (corner cutting is a reoccurring theme with this game).Gameplay: This is my biggest reason for wanting to return the game. Dragon Quest Heroes, while not my favorite gameplay style is at least fun for most of it's duration. The game is very easy and most of the combat is handled by your 3 party monsters. There is no difference between the games protagonist's Eric and Mia, other than visual and their voice. In addition to dagger attacks, there are slingshot attacks that do all the typical Dragon Quest spells. however it is a pain to use because your monsters and the enemy are running amok and even with a lock on, other monsters will be moving in and out of line of sight, blocking your target or you'll be getting attacked. Add to the ammo being limited and using the slingshot isn't fun. A cool down timer would've made this so much better. The other thing the game wants you to do is farms tons of materials for crafting and recruiting. It's incredibly tedious even though you can buy some. Just managing all the ingredients, realizing your missing one thing and having to go grind it for this or that. I mean this could work if there was less crafting and ingredients. Oh and if combat was fun.Your monsters have 5 different uses outside of battle depending on their type. The can be a mount, a short trampoline, a hang glider, a resource scanner, or  a stealth puddle. There's some very, very obvious little puzzles you solve with some of these. The mount is absolutely needed because Mia/Erik's base move speed is dreadful. Most go on overly long cool downs after using them. Even if you accidentally call the wrong monster, you get a long cool down. Ugh.There are also random "dungeon" portals you can discover. I use dungeons in quotes because they're just a series of 5-10 fights until you get to the boss. Then you might get a medal, which can be equipped give a stat boost. Not exciting, but that's equipment in this game. These medals can be obtained other ways, but they're relatively rare. They are the one semi exciting thing you can find (not as a treasure in the game's sense though).Then there's the "treasures". You dig these up (with your knife lol) after finding them in a little hot/cold mini game, often just by walking near their location. The animations is about 2 seconds too long and you will start to dread digging up treasure, especially because it doesn't have any immediate benefit. In fact it's a burden in some ways because your monsters have a chance to drop treasure when attacked, which you can then pick up again. It's not a huge deal, just incredibly tedious (notice a theme?). Treasure will respawn in the same places over and over again, even next to treasure hunting "gangs" (a la One Piece, but not as cool) which will hilariously make you question how these gangs are any threat to winning the treasure contest at all. Maybe they know these treasures suck too. Now you might be think, surely these treasures give you cool powers, equipment, or items like DQ games tend to do. No, no, and no. Treasure are past object from other DQ franchises, many of them never brought to the West. On top of that, they had the audacity to make generic things into treasures worth millions to whomever is evaluating the treasure. Things like a pointy hat or boxer shorts. There's even pieces of walls from various DQ dungeons for some reason. The only display as 2-D images in stand of sorts and you can only display 3 or so. They might get away with this in Japan, but here it looks like a lazy lack of creativity. Mia had an entire gold fortress in DQ 11. Why is a generic, very common ladder valued at millions to the games characters? There's also a bunch of cards from some DQ Hearthstone knockoff cell phone game with all Japanese text no one bothered to localize (no you can't use them to play a game either, missed opportunity). It's makes the treasures feel pointless and if the story didn't require you to acquire so much arbitrary wealth (that you can't spend, just for points), it would be.Sound and voice: Music consists of all the Dragon Quest songs you know. There may be some new tracks. There's this one track in a pirate camp with vocals and it's very obnoxious. Thankfully, you're not there long. The voices are good for Mia and Eric (though I think Eric has a different voice actor than in DQ11, sadly), but there is very little dialog outside the first 30 minutes. After that it's one of those games where they only say the first word of a sentence. The monsters are all varying degrees of annoying (looking at you, cute slime) and never shut up (you can't turn this off). The games sound mixing is poor, so mercifully some monsters are tough to hear.All in all DQ Treasures is a big let down. I'm not sure who this is for, outside of huge DQ Japanese fans who will apparently buy anything DQ branded. It's just painfully mediocre to slightly below average and to top it off, SquareEnix put very little budget other than the absolute bear minimum. They didn't even stop to play the game and ask themselves "Is this fun for more than 10 minutes?" Play Elden Ring, Tears of the Kingdom, Skyrim, God Of War Ragnarok; there are so many better ways to spend your time and money. And no, just because a game is aimed at kids (though I struggle to think of how kids today are even aware of DQ outside of Japan), it doesn't get a free pass to be below average, sorry.

_childDocuments_.review: Dragon Quest Treasures was originally released in 2022 exclusively for Nintendo Switch and it’s now finally available on PC (Steam). The game stars Eric and his sister Mia, two well-known characters from  (one of the best titles in the main JRPG series), and acts as a prequel, but can also be considered a spin-off since everything that happens here has no connection with the main title, so it can be played by anyone. After being raised by Viking pirates and encountering two bizarre creatures (Porcus and Purrsula), Erik and Mia decide to go treasure-hunting and discover two magical daggers that teleport them into a new world called Draconia. Here, the two are tasked with retrieving the Seven Dragonstones (exactly like in ) by exploring five different islands and collecting every hidden treasure on their way.As you can probably imagine at this point, the plot is just a narrative to justify the spin-off nature of the game. It’s a self-contained story in the lives of Erik and Mia that doesn’t get mentioned in DQXI, so it doesn’t add anything to the general plotline and even die-hard fans might find it not interesting enough, despite all the fan service present. The good news is that Treasures shares the same universe, artistically speaking. Akira Toriyama’s visual style is evident, with environments, monster design and even a couple soundtracks that seem to be taken straight from DQXI (and perhaps they are).Gameplay-wise, this is essentially a hack-and-slash RPG mixed with . You will have a long list of main and secondary missions (the latter being more like boring fetch quests) that will give you the chance to explore all the five islands of Draconia within a semi open world structure. You are free to explore them in any order, but it’s best to avoid some initially because of the high-level monsters, though nothing stops you from trying. Each island features different biomes and monsters, so there is certainly enough variety.The game is aimed at very young players, not only for the two young protagonists, but for the simplicity and easiness of the action RPG mechanics. During exploration and battle you can control either Erik or Mia and attack monsters in real time through a pretty shallow combat system that will make you spam the same buttons endlessly. After defeating them, you can recruit the monsters at your base by offering the required materials. Collecting and recruiting more monsters is essential to the gameplay, as each one has unique abilities that will make fighting, traversing the map and discovering treasures much easier, since you can directly sense the loot through their eyes. During battles, they are guided by the AI and deal even more damage than the two siblings. Plus, the monsters not included in your party can be sent on expeditions to retrieve more treasures for you. These will increase your treasure hunting rank and make the story progress further while also giving you the chance to expand your base.The PC port runs exceptionally well (despite the presence of Denuvo), with unlocked framerate and higher resolution options. Visually, it looks better than the Switch version of course, though understandably this is a game mainly designed for the Nintendo console, so don’t expect jaw dropping graphics. The game should also be playable on Steam Deck, which is awesome because it feels better to play it through multiple, but short, sessions instead of a few long runs (the grind can become quite annoying).Dragon Quest Treasures is a really fun spin-off with the same charming art style of the series. I think that those who have already played Dragon Quest XI will probably enjoy this one too, despite having simple mechanics and less story. The selling price is higher than expected though, considering it’s even higher than DQXI-S but the latter offers more content and quality overall. I would undoubtedly recommend it with a good discount, especially if you enjoy treasure-hunting and monster-collecting games.

_childDocuments_.review: A decent game, runs smooth as butter on the ROG Ally. It's not even a contest between this and the switch version, even if your machine is a toaster. The game itself can be fun, but only if you keep your expectations in check. It has almost nothing to do with the game it was spun off of and is clearly a very low budget project. It's an action RPG, but you're character is extremely weak and must play the roll of support for a party of AI controlled monsters you recruit to fight for you. The open world prioritizes scale over graphic fidelity, but is still pretty interesting to explore. The game also gives you an impressive amount of freedom to pursue different objectives and questlines as you see fit. The main quest is a bit short and half-baked, but the emphasis is clearly on the side content and building your gang through treasure hunting, which can be pretty addictive. This could have been a 100 hour game honestly, but you will likely tap out way earlier than that due to the lack of quality of life features. Fast travel back to home base is only possible through a consumable item that is only available in limited quantities until the post game. Exploration is severely hampered by your limited party size, as there are four essential traversal abilities, but only three slots for the monsters that have them. Item chests hidden throughout the world often contain essential recipes that you need in order to recruit new monsters, but there is no way to mark them on your map. All that sounds very negative, but in the end I did still enjoy my time with the game. I will say this though, $50 is way too much to ask for this one. Wait till it's 50% off and give it a shot.
