_childDocuments_.review: I'm gonna start off this review by saying I don't give a ♥♥♥♥ about the DQ series outside of respecting it for being a legacy series. I hate turn based combat so I could never get into them. However, if you, like me, have a loot goblin brain, then you will definitely enjoy this game. Collecting treasures and seeing your funny gold numbers go up is super fun. The game does get stale rather quickly, but if you just wanna play a bit here and there for the loot then it's a great time.Combat is still trash (though I prefer it to a turn based style) and you have very few options open to you. Your attacks are stiff and feel unnatural. The slingshot is the only viable method of attack. I really enjoy recruiting monsters and getting medals and hoping for the rainbow rarity, but getting it for medals is really hard, and getting it for monsters means it'll take you hours of grinding to find the materials you need to recruit them.I think that the game would be a lot more fun if you could attack with your monsters manually in battle kinda like Spectrobes. But implemented better. I'm around level 37 I think right now and I still do ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for damage with the dagger, so maybe having some sort of upgrade system for that would be nice. Also removing the material grinding aspect would be ideal since it's already grindy just to get monsters to the recruit station. Anyhow, if you just play the game for the loot elements then it doesn't matter too much.

_childDocuments_.review: Dragon Quest Treasures evokes nostalgic memories of Nintendo DS titles with its bite-sized gameplay sessions and charming art style. The game has a refreshing twist on traditional RPG mechanics. Instead of engaging in direct combat, your character strategically buffs your party of three monsters and debuffs enemies with a variety of pellets from your weapon, a slingshot, adding depth to each encounter.However, while the gameplay mechanics are novel, I couldn't overlook the game's tendency to feel repetitive, particularly in the later stages of my 40-hour journey. Additionally, the long cooldown on the monster forte, sprint, which allows you to mount one of your monsters, proved frustrating, extending travel times unnecessarily and disrupting the game's pacing.Despite these drawbacks, I had fun digging up treasures and the unique leveling system tied to collecting treasures instead of just battling other monsters, kept me engaged throughout. While Dragon Quest Treasures may not be without its flaws, its nostalgic charm and innovative gameplay mechanics ultimately made for a fun experience. If you are a fan of spin-off games from the Dragon Quest series, I recommend giving this game a try.
_childDocuments_.name: DRAGON QUEST TREASURES

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little side game in the Dragon Quest series. Story is interesting and gives insight into some of the things referenced in Dragon Quest XI, but isn't necessary to play to know what's going on. Loads of treasures that reference characters, items and locations from prior Dragon Quest games. The combat was probably the weakest element of the game to me, but that's personal preference more than anything.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, that was an amazing game!I read it was a mid game, so I was expecting that. That was not my experience though.The story is simple but fun, the characters are loveable and the gameplay is quite interesting.Speaking of the gameplay, it has lots of variety. Combat is a bit simplistic, you're more like a support character helping your monsters, but you can be more active and cause serious damage if you want to.There are some boss battles and they are interesting, specially the last boss.In general, I think the game is too big, specially if you want to 100%. I'm not a completionist though, so I am satisfied after beating the main quest in around 17h.I think my biggest (and only) complaint is in regards to its connection to DQ11. But anyway, super recommended, especially if you already like DQ and DQ11.

_childDocuments_.review: In some ways it plays a lot like what a modern pokemon game should play as if gamefreak didn't stop caring years ago; Using the monster's abilities to travel through a 3D world. Very fun when it all comes together. A treasure hunt full of anything dragon quest, from models to music.Major negatives include a very weak opening chapter, the game is trying to be simplistic because it thinks kids are retarded but if you make it too simple but still drag the story on like you would a normal dragon quest game then you just make the game boring. Imagine if minecraft didn't let you craft until 2 hours in.Other negatives include a lot of the design decisions. Why make the characters dig with a knife? It's a magic knife we get it but couldn't you give them a shovel or something?It's definitely worth it on sale if you know what you're getting into, this is the very definition of a spinoff game, don't buy this if you don't know that those are. This is for DQ fans only, I don't think anyone else would enjoy this.

_childDocuments_.review: It's amazing how the devs can use the same set of design, lore and location but make such masterpieces out of it with differing gameplay. This is just another one of them.DQ Builders 2 was honestly such a great game that put an emphasis on more world crafting/building.This one instead puts emphasis on more exploration and collections. Specifically, collections of monsters (Including special variants), collection of treasures, building infrastructures that help you perform collections more etc integrated with a myriad of puzzles and such.You can still come to expect all those various quality nuances that DQ series normally has (An example of this is the "Monster's vision" which ironically mimics literally what that monster would see, included warped or blocked visions). On top of that, a cast of same design monsters/people/ideas that are catered in a way to be unique specific to this game (Such as the forte system)Overall, this is another amazing game with unique game play mechanic/logic unrelated to the mainline series and i hope more people buy into it. The true down side is probably that price tag and hopefully this will not discourage the developers from making more spin offs from the main series.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is heavily flawed in every aspect HOWEVER those flaws are failure to pay attention to detail, neither game-breaking nor game-ruining. This is an amazing game. That being said...It sucks that you have to wait a full 5 seconds to claim any treasure including those dropped by allies. I understand the gameplay purpose of this timer, it just doesn't make the game any more fun having it in place.If an ally dies above or in water that causes your character to swim, you cannot revive them. If a treasure drops in or above water that causes your character to swim, you cannot retrieve it.The "safekeeping" score mechanic similarly adds nothing but annoyance to the game. It makes sense for treasures to drop when fighting rival gangs. It does not make sense for a Gigantes at level 30 to drop a treasure because they stepped on a Slime at level 1.There are areas where, barring interference from the game, you should be able to jump from point a to point b, but the game just teleports you back to point a as if you fell to your death,Enemies seem to spawn endlessly, which is great for grinding, but often means you'll clear a whole area, get ready to heal, and get stabbed in the back by the new spawn. Always. Heal. Constantly.A 5 level difference between your team and an enemy means your whole team dies if you don't pay attention, even though you might take 0 damage fighting that same enemy on your own.That's because the ally AI is absolute trash. They will walk into water, teleport back to where they were, and repeat until you summon them via forte. They will attack the high level enemies you tried to sneak past unless you use stealth forte to make them not-exist. They will get distracted by low level enemies you ignored. They don't pick up any drops. They have about 3 lines each and instead of using them in reference to activities, or otherwise purposefully using their voice lines, they just spam them every 3 seconds or so.That being said, the settings do allow you to kill all voices, but the lack of granularity means you lose all cutscene voices and all actual character lines including "we are near our destination." Dragon Quest Games typically have some of the most barebones settings possible, though, so I'll take it as a win.The game is set up almost like a gacha game, but without the real world money. At first it rewards you greatly, making you feel accomplished on every trip, but because you can get duplicate treasures, because those duplicates are worth (next to) nothing to the player, and because you can't see what treasures you have until you get home, that feeling of progress, of motion, is wholly replaced by frustration and stagnation in the mid to late game. By intentional design. Why? Just why?Tthe number of unique monsters is about 20. Dragon Warrior Monsters, a game boy color game, also had recolor monsters, but their monster cast added up to 300, not 70 someodd. I don't think a $50 game from today should have less than a quarter of the diversity that a gameboy color game from the same series 20 years ago had. They have chimaera wings as an item, but no chimaeras as monsters ffs.There are only 5 fortes and of them, you absolutely need 3 to explore, meaning those other two, Sprint and Scan, effectively prevent you from exploring if you use one of them instead of Stealth, High Jump, or Glide.Finally, the worst part of the game, at least for me, is that there is next to no skill in treasure hunting or combat or any other aspect of the game. Either you grind or you rely on rng. That alone would kill most games for me, but like I said at the beginning, despite all these flaws, this is a great game.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun little game.Not much in the way of backstory, a mini prequel to Dragon Quest XI's Erik & his sister Mia, As children, orphans & pretty much slaves on a Viking Ship, as was told in DQXI.They escape & free two magical creatures, which become their companions in their quest to become legendary treasure hunters. Your adventure is Erik & Mia Island hopping, recruiting monster allies, finding treasure, fighting rival gangs of treasure hunters, and fixing up their base and a dilapidated railway network, whilst also hunting for Legendary Stones for their magical pets.Honestly it is alot of fun and quite addicting. It is a great little bonus piece of nostalgia for Dragon Quest franchise fans finding the treasures, which are all figures and items from the extensive Dragon Quest games and spin offs.Very much recommended for a chill, fun game.

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic Dragon Quest spin off thats loads of fun. You explore a massive world with your monster friends looking for your treasure. This game gives you a huge amount of freedom allowing to explorer the wide world at your own pace. If you like either Dragon Quest or monster taming games, I highly reccemend.

_childDocuments_.review: Players take control of Erik and Mia as they explore a treasure hunter’s paradise where boundless adventure awaits. Loot can be hidden in the most fiendishly inaccessible locations, so players must recruit a variety of well-meaning monsters and make use of their unique treasure-hunting abilities. These charming creatures will help players to race over open fields, scale cliffs with a single bound, and glide over gaping chasms. They will even provide assistance in battles against rival treasure hunters! Collecting treasure will increase the player’s vault value, allowing them to expand their home base and further build up their brigade of friendly monsters.

name: Ara: History Untold
detailed_description: Edition comparison About the Game Build a nation and lead your people throughout history to the pinnacles of human achievement as you explore new lands, develop arts and culture, conduct diplomacy, and go head-to-head with your rivals to prove you are the greatest ruler ever known. It's Your World Now. Ara: History Untold is an evolution in historical grand strategy, featuring beloved classic PC strategy mechanics alongside innovative gameplay like a national crafting economy, true simultaneous turn resolution, a non-linear technology tree, and cloud-backed synchronous/asynchronous multiplayer - all with an expansive and vibrant presentation where you can zoom out from surveying the very edges of your empire all the way down to your citizens living their daily lives. In Ara, there are no pre-set paths to victory, leading to endless possibilities. Your choices will define the world you create, your experience, and your legacy. Join the Ara History: Untold Insider Program today! As an Insider you’ll join a passionate community of strategy game fans that receive exclusive updates, invitations to provide feedback, and opportunities to play the game before it is released. Sign up today at . Explore an Immersive Living World: Explore a dynamic living world filled with life and charm across sweeping landscapes ranging from tropical jungles to sand-swept deserts as you discover the resources you need to develop your nation. Witness the world come to life in vivid, realistic detail as citizens move throughout the world and react dynamically to times of health and sickness, war and peace, wealth and despair with unique biomes, cultures, and eras representing the diversity of the human experience. Build Your Nation: Serve your people and grow your prestige with numerous Improvements, from forges to libraries, citadels to cathedrals, public parks to industrial factories - as well as a global variety of the greatest architectural Triumphs ever conceived and built by human hands. Guide your people through the eras of human discovery: Nurture your people’s brilliance and invention as you progress your Nation through twelve  unique Technology Eras, making the hard choices about where to focus your Nation’s greatest minds. As you near the end of each Era, you’ll have to decide how fast to push your scientists along the path to the future - at the risk of the present. Oversee a rich and detailed national economy: Harvest the bounty of the natural world and deploy the labor of your people with a depth-filled National Crafting system. Will you manufacture Amenities - like lavish feasts - to provide your cities and citizens with powerful benefits, or invest in the creation of Equipment - the weapons of war - to prepare your Armies to defend your nation or conquer your rivals? Whatever paths you choose you’ll need to carefully optimize your resources and production to achieve the most efficient systems if you want to outpace your rivals to fortune and lasting glory. Rule Your Way: Choose from dozens of history's most influential figures to embody as you reshape the world through your choices. The unique and varied global Leaders and Nations in Ara emphasize a wide variety of different playstyles. Experiment with gameplay-impacting Traits and powerful Leader Abilities drawn from the effect they had on world history. Whether friend or foe, each Leader has a distinct personality based on their historical background that informs their AI behaviors. Experience True Simultaneous Turns: Every turn each nation's actions and choices resolve simultaneously, leading to suspense, anticipation, unique outcomes, and surprising twists on the classic turn-based formula. The fate of your people will be determined by your decisions and your ability to predict your opponent’s next move, putting your skill as a leader to the ultimate test. Defend your people by land, sea, and air: Warfare in Ara is presented in the Living World, as thousands of years of military conflict reflect the progress and martial prowess of your people. Develop technologies to advance your weaponry against your rivals, hone your wartime economy and industry to gain the edge, and outthink your opponent’s strategies as maneuvers resolve authentically at once thanks to the power of True Simultaneous Turns. Prove Your Worth in Online Multiplayer: Combining the speed and surprise of True Simultaneous Turns with the power of the cloud - multiplayer in Ara is fast, seamless, and able to be enjoyed asynchronously with a wide range of options to tailor you and your friend’s experience to the way you want to play together. A Microsoft Account is required to play online multiplayer.

_childDocuments_.review: After several more hours of play here is my updated review. I still hold to the fact this is one of the best civ games I have ever played. Pros:-Wares being produced individually such as tools, jewelry, medicine, etc and then applying them to your buildings and cities for bonuses is so much more immersive than simply grouping them together under "Consumer Goods"-The attention to detail is amazing, being able to zoom right down into the city and see the people walking around and working the fields, or your armies marching to the next province.  -The battles being more of a cinematic rather than just watching the avatars of giant spearmen the size of mountains clashing makes me drawn into each battle rather than just clicking away. I want to see what happens in the turn report. Cons:-The only giant con that needs to change is how armies are managed. Once you craft your said spearmen you then deploy them either as a singular squad or as a formation that has tactics grouped together with other units. Now, when you spend multiple turns crafting and then deploying, and then mustering said army it is permanent. You cannot add or switch units out of formation, you cannot change the units tactics, nor can you return them to the reserves to reduce maintenance cost. You have to disband the entire army and start all the way over. This is a huge oversight that needs fixed and it is absolutely no where near historically accurate.Minor issues:-Please turn off turn limits-add different speeds to how the game progresses. Id like to take my sweet time and enjoy being in the iron age and hate it when there is a rushed feeling. Wishlist:-Id love to see some form of internal politics take place. This is a game about the story of your people, well how about adding the will of the people. Senates, Parliaments, cabinets, assemblys for each government, various parties and laws that can be enacted. -Map Editor-larger maps & AI's not starting so close to player. Sugestions:-When progressing into the next act the "forgettable" civilizations are lost. This is interesting but it could be better. Maybe instead of them just going "oops i lost bye bye" you could add in something that is a massive crisis they face. For example they descend into civil war or there is the sea peoples invasion. Maybe a plague is sweeping across their empire and they must struggle to survive. So my suggestion is, instead of just eliminating players maybe give that civilization a chance to survive but it is a existential crisis they face. Just an idea. Overall I love this game so far, and I cant wait to see where the developers take it from here. I do recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Its a good base to work off, BUT.....Early Game- Enjoyable however there was a feeling of being rushed through the age.- AI is ridiculous at expanding even at low level difficulty- UI is pretty bad with too many individual clicks- Trade and diplomacy is lackluster Mid Game- Micro managing becomes painful- "Crafting" becomes complex- Tech to obtain required items for the 'wonders' becomes hard to follow- Trying to find a building to place within the list is awful (colour coding is just stupidly done - would be better to have sub menus ie Population / Amenity / Military)- AI becomes super aggressive at expansion whilst still having few "cities"- Game becomes a tech research race which is a shame- AI rulers become constantly needy and upset but permanently expand over the map- Delayed some settlement tasks only to discover i couldnt reactivate them resulting in an auto failLate Game (fail)- UI is impossible to find anything without scrolling endlessly to find a building that improves happiness for example (again no filter or sub menu)- Unlocked tech doesnt easily tell you what you got building wise unless you read thoroughly then write it down, then spend 4 hours finding it in the list when you lost your bit of paper- Micro managing crafting goes through the roof- Constant spam of "xxxx is idle"- Over 8 cities is just constant menu scrolling - Crafting is impossible to keep track of, having to click individual buildings - it desperately needs a production overview to set craft limits/priorities- Balance of units is questionable, had a group of samurai take out a fortified city with marines, rocket troops, flame throwers.- Tech to units, i can make bombers, sweet, no wait i need fuel for that and fuselage, no wait i need an airplane factory for that, no wait i need cement, no wait i need.............on and on and onUltimately i love what they are going for with the crafting aspect, it is a new take on an old genre. However, when you realise how many crafted items there are, and how many individual screens you have to click through to get things crafted its just a laborious and dull task. I ended up switching all cities to perma generate money and just went round the map declaring war to get it over with..... until the immortal samurai turned up!The game needs some love from the devs, it feels as though it makes total sense to them as they made it but for the average gamer its too much going on with too many windows mid to late game and not a great tutorial.If you love 4X, give it a go maybe on a sale or in 6 months time. It reminds me of my wife in that it wants to do everything, be involved in everything but sometimes its better to just take a breath and stick with what you are good at!Oh, and i also picked Elizabeth 1st and generated a heavy ocean based map to dominate the high seas with the British Navy. Made my first fleet began the maiden voyage only to discover i was in a lake..........win

_childDocuments_.review: This game could be my favorite game of all time. I am not being hyperbolic.At current, I would not recommend the game unless you catch it on sale and its really up your alley. My hopes is the developer and publisher see the promise in this game and continue to develop and iterate on it until it really clicks into place. I will update my review should this moment happen, and I am hopeful it will.Overall, the general idea of this game is a civ-like deep economic game. After about 40-60 turns of delivering on this promise, it will have gradually turned into a busywork game and lose its luster. Ill elaborate:-Industry- The main mechanic of this game is: buildings produce resources, and urban-style buildings will likely be able to produce more than one type of resource. Some resources require a node on the map, for example, elephants for ivory. Most buildings will have "supply" slots - one time costs to increase production as well as "ingredient" slots which provide ongoing increases to production. The resources themselves typically have multiple uses, so may be able to be used as a supply, ingredient, and/or as a luxury for the city. As you increase your tech, you unlock better things to build. Its a very integrated and deep the system and a solid core to the gameplay that gives you satisfaction very frequently of making your nation's industry a little bit more efficient each turn.HOWEVER, While the UI is not terrible and there was definitely some thought into it, each one of these changes is building-by-building. This isnt an issue at first, but as you get a few hours into the game, youll unlock a new resource and you have to manually check each building in each city - a few hundred supply and ingredient slots - to see if it is an upgrade for the building so you know how many to produce. Then, each turn you are scrolling through the 25 things you built this turn, to see if this is a turn you built that item and can slot it. It becomes exhausting.HOW CAN IT BE FIXED?UI upgrades are the easiest solution. The ability to look at ALL your Dwellings, for example, and click a single button to give them all baskets. An alternative is to set an "auto equip" process, but this is a major burden on AI. I think there may be some temptation to cut goods, slots, or mechanics, and I hope that is not the solution. -Resources-A bit of an extension on the above, but I wanted to point out a couple specific things with resources. First off, I think its absolutely lovely that some of the resources are rarer. You may have to trade, find alternatives, or go without elephants, silk, precious minerals, etc. It feels historical. I honestly think they could expand on this system with DLC because the unequal distribution of nature's goods is what fueled trade historically, and trade fueled everything else from wars to science to religion.HOWEVER,Resources obsolete, but there is nothing to do with them after they do outside of having them sit on your warehouse.HOW CAN IT BE FIXED?It would be great to recycle resources, target-export them for money, or have them be upscale-able (for example, using Lithic Tools to make Metal Tools produce faster).-City Statistics-This game has a really neat system of tracking your cities' Happiness, Health, Knowledge, etc. These are scales that, per city, provide benefits and negatives, and a significant portion of your industry will be dedicated to producing luxury goods to shove into your cities to boost these numbers and get those buffs.HOWEVER,These numbers go down over time with city size, gradually. And the same problem with graduality crops up; you dont notice it, its not really shown in a ledger anywhere, and youll just suddenly notice your capital's security is at 15 and your giving you a -20% force strength modifier. Whoops. Thats why my armies are losing.HOW CAN IT BE FIXED?This game has a significant notification problem already, so I dont think adding this to the bottom right helps. I think a ledger UI to see all your cities would help. An alternative would be to just remove maluses altogether, and instead have the values start on or near 0 and give you benefits for boosting it. Technically thats the same mechanic but its all about perspective, like the industry story of the WoW 'rest' mechanic.-Tech-The core idea behind tech is that they come in sets. In each set, you can research all the techs or you can skip a handful and advance early. You cant ever go back to those techs, but usually the items you unlock in that tech come back up in future techs, allowing you to say, for example, "I dont need rope for a while" and instead get to iron earlier. This is a brilliant, unique design and one of the better parts of the game, and couples well with the economics.HOWEVER,For one, techs come so fast that you very, very easily outpace the production of your cities. You might have finally built that building that can produce [x] for you, but now you are two turns away from [x+], or worse, you dont really need [x] anymore because [y] is better. One other small issue is that with so much depth to the system, its hard to know what you're really getting from each tech.HOW CAN IT BE FIXED?Slow down tech a moderate amount and speed up building production ever so slightly. I think if you focus on only the tech the game will move glacially, and you cant just make buildings build incredibly fast or youll fill up your cities too fast. This sometimes happens already in your capital and older cities. The small issue is resolved with a mixture of experience and tooltip research, but one thing that I would really love to see is what each good's potential ingredients are. When I unlock the ability to research "books" it tells me where I can produce it, what techs I can unlock it with, what they do as a supply, ingredient, and luxury - all great information - but strangely, not what this could have as ingredient. Since ingredients are a huge factor in production speed, this is a huge oversight that could be easily recitified.-Military-I love the idea behind the system. You build units and they go into an unmobilized pool. Then you unlock formations for your units to slot into, for example a Shield Wall needs 3 melee infantry and 1 archer. Then it gets certain abilities and benefits depending on the formation, and the unit itself is, for example, 2 swordsmen, a spearman, and an archer, known as "Shield Wall." Your Shield Wall formation itself levels up, not the units therein.HOWEVERYou cant ever upgrade the units themselves, which was a weird decision because its completely contrary to the rest of the design of the game. I cannot fathom why this choice was made.HOW CAN IT BE FIXED?Allow units to be upgraded, or at the very least, unslotted and replaced. Alternatively, rather than assigning unit experience, assign an overall nation military experience, so it isnt as painful to disband that unit of veteran archers that simply cant go toe-to-toe with knights. -Others-Graphics are 10/10. Very, very pretty game, especially for the genre. Im not usually a graphics guy within this genre but I did find myself zooming in and following the roads between my cities and other civs.Roadbuilding is a 8/10. The system is great and smart at a macro level but graphically on a micro level makes some weird decisions.Diplomacy is a 6/10. Pretty standard fare (okay, inoffensive) but the merchant system is nice; limiting the amount of imports you have access to. It would be great to see why a nation's baseline is where it isReligion is a 5/10. Leaders are 7/10. As of right now this collectively means I really, really enjoy the first 50 turns or so of the game, and lose interest once it feels like I need to do a nationwide audit every 5 turns. I hope to see some changes in the long term to bring this game to its ideal state. Ive never typed a review this long so thanks for sticking around and listening yall. I almost ran out of chara

_childDocuments_.review: PR team of Ara should be fired on the sport, because they've sold you the wrong game.Is it Civilization? Barely. Yes, it's 4x, camera overview is similar and you kinda expand across the map, but this is where the similarities end. I was actually very upset with my first attempt because of it.On my second (and current) run it has occured to me that Ara is Anno, only slower and more predictable. It's a game about production chains, resource balance and supplies. You will manage 5 cities max, because every city is a game withtin a game. You need to carefully plan a lot of things in a signle turn, and that's kinda refreshing. Turns are really long here. Your every decision matters in the long run.Even building mechanic is more in-depth and require quite a bit of planning from you. And wonders are finally wonder, you just can't randomly stack them in a single city.Ara has a very unique feel, pace and even genre. That's why diplomacy, war and even AI took a back seat and I'm not against it. Just note, that you won't quarrel a lot and soldiers here are more about clearing the obstacles, than conquering your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.I will ignore the tech state because after few hotfixes it is already working good in my rig, so devs will iron out bugs eventually.That all being said, Ara is not Civ (ignore this game if you're looking for Humankind or something along those lines) and it's not without some major flaws:- UI/UX is not even that bad, it's just clunky and too fragmented. At first you think that the resource management is diffucult, but in fact it's a breeze. UI is just riddled with needless clicks to get to the fabled menu- AI is very barebones, but on the other hand, it's not crazy or agressive- Diplomacy it a thing, I guess. Nothing I could add more here, though.- I love the general idea about troop gathering and forming armies, though at this moment it's complicated just for the sake of it- I don't think that the current nation roster is very representative and there is a lot of fragmented global cultures- Game must loudly update you with new resource developments and maybe notify you to add new stuff to the production roster, it's very easy to lost the plot on later stagesOne thing I wan to highlighy to the devs: for the love of God, please add the option for automatic resource assigment to the building type. It's fun to micromanage 4 farms, 2 mines and 4 housings. It's not fun with 20. It's just stupid work. Or create a button 'Assign upgrades for this building type'. Plus make it easier to upgrade your current buildings in the UI. That sort of stuff.In the end, I think that Ara will grow on on people, especially when they realize that this is whole another game. For now, I can strongly reconmend it for any Anno and The Guild fan, but Civ enjoyers should be really wary. It's not the game of simple domination, it's a game about careful planning with One More Turn flair.

_childDocuments_.review: It is another one of those "it has potential", but will that potential ever be realized? Oh well.Come back in 1-2 years to find out.Right now the UI and AI are better than they were during their playtest a couple of months ago, but they are still not working properly.I guess the AI is as confused as I am when it comes to wars. The unit strength constantly changes and armies can ambush you out of the fog of war. In most cases, wars end up as one giant moshpit that will decide the fate of your nation. Whoever wins that one battle has already succeded. Well unless you get kicked out of the war by the turn limit, which is decided by the attacker.The UI has gotten better since the playtest, at least you can now tell how much of a resource you produce per turn. Unfortunately, it still bombards you with loads of useless information while hiding the important things. To be honest I could rant on for ages about the UI, the balance and the needless complexity but I think it's better if you check out someone's stream while they are in the middle stages of a game.The early game looks fine and plays decent enough, but starting around turn 60-100 you will notice how tedious this game gets.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fine, detailed and well-designed 4x game. It's visually similar to civ-series, humankind, old world games. But under the surface it has neat mechanics and unique approach to the 4x genre. Its all about cute details, smartly designed systems and amazing graphics.The cons are currently a usual mix of freshly released 4x games from the last 10 years. I've played civ5, civ6, humankind, age of wonders3-4, old world, endless legend, endless space from the day one with more than 100 hours into each of them (3k hours in civ 5). These flaws are poor graphics optimisation, clunky UI, holes in design here and there and balance issues between the factions for MP. All of them currently (october 2024) is here, waiting to get fixed by devs and modders alike.With 4 patches released in 1st month already (and 5th patch coming this week) I have my hopes on this game. BTW the game has already a classic "one more turn" feeling I'd like to recommend ARA to all 4x fans, especially during X-mas sales when the game will be much polished and optimized.

_childDocuments_.review: This is primarily an economic management/chain supply game with 4X elements sprinkled along. This game has taken heavy elements out of the Anno 1800 mechanics and added classical CIV and Humankind elements in the mix. This is not an easy game to play; the learning curve is rather steep and during your first few games you might feel overwhelmed by the number of decisions that you have to make. This is more on a Paradox complexity level rather than a Firaxis one. This game wasn't easy for me to grasp in the first few hours and I'm a veteran of thousands of hours on Paradox titles as well as 4X games (started my gaming career with CIV II). Everything you gather matters. Everything you produce has at least a dual purpose. Buildings have many slotted items, can be upgraded and oftentimes have multiple production paths from which you must choose. Chains are difficult to set up, but once you manage, it feels extremely gratifying to witness your economy booming. Plus Items:- Non linear tech tree- Nearly everything is customizable with slotted items. Buildings, improvements, armies, great people, you name it. Crafting possibilities are mindboggling!- Cities and Units are limited (can be expanded by technology). Once you set up your economy turns begin to fly. Negative Items:- Diplomacy is really primitive and needs to be beefed up. You can't really interact with minor tribes except for random events. - UI needs to be decluttered and streamlined. As it stands right now, you need some time to understand how to best manage all those buildings and production chains. Also, it's extremely difficult to understand exactly how bonuses specifically impact production chains. - Army management needs to be improved. You can only merge units into formations while they're still in reserve. Combat close ups, while only optional, are a joke and need to be abolished.For me, this game is a yes, but I do understand that his is not everyone's cup of tea. This is a game which requires serious planning and has a steep learning curve. You need to like optimizing things to really enjoy this one. Is it worth 60 Euros? Well...I mean, for 60 Euros I did expect a better UI but I suppose that they'll be fixing this as the game moves forward.

_childDocuments_.review: I really, really wanted to give this a positive review.  There is so much to like.  The city building is great.  The economics are very satisfying, once you get used to them.  There is so much to love.  But, regrettably, the game feels woefully incomplete for a 1.0 release.  If this were some sort of early access with a roadmap, I'd accept it.  But this is not a game that was ready for full release.Combat is a hot mess.  Aside from some basic options that are just missing, but I believe will be patched in (upgrading units is a particular example), the entire way they're doing their simultaneous turns effectively means that everyone just teleports when you hit the end turn button.  Enemy armies will just vanish into the fog of war, and it's impossible to tell which direction they came from or went to.  This is especially bad on fast units (chariots are an early example) because you can only see one region around your units, but they can move multiple regions per turn-- so keeping track of them is borderline impossible, because you constantly have to guess where they went.Moreover, there's no transparency on what order the simultaneous actions play out in-- several times I have had an enemy army lead mine on a merry chase across my country because I wanted to kill them but they could somehow always move out of their tile before I moved into theirs and engaged.  The net result of all this is that, rather than feeling like a military commander, I feel like I need to put on Yakety Sax.Diplomacy is bare-bones, which is normally forgivable-- complex diplomacy is kind of a new trend in 4x, and it's understandable for them to go with an older interpretation.  However, whoever balanced it chose to make the AI relationship degrade from positive to neutral incredibly quickly, and negative to neutral incredibly slowly.  Further, AI opinion will just fluctuate at apparent random from turn to turn.  So, an AI that you leave at neutral will eventually have a bad day, decide to go to war over something petty, and then remain at the bottom edge of the opinion meter... forever.So, just make friends with people early on and it'll be fine, right?  Well, sure, but there's only a handful of positive diplomatic ties you can make with people (trade agreements, research agreements, and military alliances), and trade agreements are the only one that doesn't have a built-in expiration date.  The end result is that friendships can only last about 20 turns unless you bribe the AI significantly... But the AI will never bribe you back or try to maintain the friendship, because that's not how diplomacy is actually supposed to work.Religion exists in name only.  I have had missionaries spend multiple in-game ages trying to convert a single one of my neighbor's cities, to no avail.  There's not even any indication that they're making progress.  They just sit there, and send me a report every turn.  There's supposedly a whole complicated pressure system that you can kind of see in the religion overlay, except that it doesn't actually TELL you anything about cities other than your own, it just paints a pretty picture of how your religion is theoretically spreading.  Until I see a city flip to my religion, I'm deeming the system fundamentally broken, which means there's an entire line of buildings, technologies, and wonders that are actual traps, and complete wastes of time and resources.The economics, and the economics alone, are great.  I love planning out my regions and trying to optimize my layouts,  I have some quibbles about QoL improvements, but with the state of the game... I'm not even going to mention them, because they aren't anywhere near the significance of the other problems.I'm going to keep playing-- I want to finish my campaign, and maybe play another round or two just for toying with the economy.  Someday, I'd like to change this review.  But with the current state of the game... I can't really recommend it to anyone.  I wish developers would stop releasing incomplete products.

_childDocuments_.review: Take a meaty chunk of Anno, a splash of Civ, and some of the good parts of Humankind, mix them together, and you get Ara, something as whole very unique in the 4X genre and very much worth playing if you like complex games. While the main Civilization franchise has been repeatedly simplifying mechanics and streamlining to "appeal to a broader audience," Ara takes the complexity dial and turns it to 12, for a very refreshing experience once you wrap your head around it.A farm isn't just a farm anymore. Each individual farm in your empire is a multi tier upgradeable improvement, with three tiers and like a dozen different minor upgrades each of which are crafted by other facilities in your empire. Make a plow in your workshop, apply the plow to your farm and now the yields have permanently increased, repeat for things like fertilizer, electricity, and tractors at varying stages of the game. The main output for most farms is generic food, but if you build a farm on a barley resource node you get barley grain, which can be crafting into bread (among many other things), and that bread can be crafting into a fancy feast (among many other things) with some other ingredients, then you can apply that feast to your city as a consumable luxury resource to significantly boost population growth and happiness. This complexity repeats for most other improvements and resources, ore becomes metal bars which becomes metal tools which are used to enhance various buildings, furs become textiles which become clothes which become fancy clothes bundles as another luxury, etc., each step being handled by its own upgradeable building/improvement. Going through the ages and unlocking new uses and chains for resources for better luxury resources and building improvements I have found to be extremely satisfying. There's a lot of "management" here, I haven't found it to be very "tedious" for the most part, they are largely satisfying and rewarding mechanics to interact with, though there could be some UI improvements that make managing larger empires a little easier.Cities are huge. As cities grow they can claim regions, kind of at a similar rate to claiming tiles in like Civ, except each region is somewhat sizeable and has usually 4-5 slots for improvements/buildings (there are a few small/malformed regions with 2-3 slots). By the middleages your cities really feel like they are sprawling across the country side with like 50+ improvements, and by the end of the game this can hit 100+ (a city can claim up to 25 regions from what I can tell). The game starts with a fairly low city cap of 3, this does increase over the course of the game, easily up to 11+ cities, but each one has so much more going on it that managing 11 cities here doesn't feel like a small amount.The tech system has some pacing issues, but a tech speed slider has basically been confirmed in an early update. There are I think like 15 eras/ages in the game each with 8 techs, you need to research 5 of them to advance to the next era but you lose access to the techs you skip. There are techs in subsequent eras that will unlock some of the same things, so there is probably a path through where you only take 5 techs each era without missing anything important, but currently that's not really a concern with how fast research is. Without really putting any effort into it, research pretty quickly ramps up to the point where you are getting one tech every 3-4 turns, and you are inundated with new improvements, crafts, and resources that you aren't really in a position to interact with yet, resulting in your choice for the next tech you pick to research to be largely irrelevant. Currently this is not an interesting system and there's no choices or strategy involved with the tech system, hopefully that will be improved and I imagine a tech speed slider will help with it a lot.The game has some fairly gamey mechanics. I believe the only victory condition is score, which the game calls prestige, and prestige is a pretty central part of the game in a way that can be substantially immersion breaking. There are a number of mechanics where the only thing they really do is provide prestige, things like great works appear to be just prestige bumps, building a wonder first gives you a chunk of prestige, and certain buildings provide bonus prestige per turn when placed in a certain way, for example. The game is then split into "acts" which are different from eras, once a certain number of civs hit a certain era the world progresses to the next act, and a number of civilization at the bottom of the prestige ladder get removed from the game, just poof. There is a toggle to exempt players from getting kicked, but not AIs, though the devs have acknowledged feedback that many players want to disable this system entirely. I don't think it's a good system, I don't play these games to "win" I play for the journey and I want that to be immersive to the extent a game like this can be. This focus on score and arbitrarily kicking out "the weakest link" is just a constant reminder this is a game.I don't have a lot to say about the other aspects of the game. Diplomacy seems "functional" but not particularly interesting. Combat has a lot of complexity in army composition and formation, but is missing vital QoL features like upgrading units or reorganizing armies, the act of fighting an enemy unit is also extremely basic though I don't have an issue with that. Exploration is pretty meh, there are goodie huts with some basic resources and not much else, you'll automate it after uncovering your immediate surroundings and then basically forget your scouts exist (there are no real dangers on the map). There's a good variety of civs and leaders right from the start, and they have comparable individual bonuses to say a Civ game, but they could always be improved to be a bit more unique.Overall it's a decent game, the main strength is the economy/industry management and if that's not your cup of tea the game offers little else of note compared to other games in the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Ara: History Untold promises a deep and immersive historical strategy experience, but after spending time with it, it’s clear that the game’s mechanics, while initially intriguing, fall short of providing meaningful depth.Historical Choice: All Bark, No BiteThe game offers a wide array of historical nations and figures to choose from, giving the impression of diverse playstyles and unique strategies. However, this choice feels largely superficial. Despite the varied appearances and historical contexts, all nations play essentially the same, stripping the game of any real flavor or individuality. Whether you’re leading Rome or a minor civilization, the experience remains frustratingly uniform.Building Systems: A Tedious ChoreOne of the more interesting mechanics in Ara: History Untold is the ability to construct buildings that create items, which can then be used to boost other buildings or enable new units and structures. On paper, this sounds like a deep, tactical layer. In practice, though, it becomes a tedious checklist rather than a strategic consideration. Once you’ve built your umpteenth workshop or farm, the mechanic loses its luster. You quickly realize that you don’t even need to engage with half of these buildings because many become pointless as the game progresses. Worse yet, the game's pacing makes it feel like you don’t have time to explore or benefit from these options before it’s all over.Combat: Just Throw Them at Each OtherCombat in Ara: History Untold is as simplistic as it gets. You send units toward each other with no meaningful tactics or strategy involved. It’s a matter of numbers and brute force rather than any clever maneuvers or battle planning. If you’re looking for engaging or complex combat, this game won’t satisfy that itch.Choices That Don’t MatterOne of the game’s major selling points was that your choices would matter, but in reality, they don’t. Villages present you with the same set of dialogue options, and the outcome is always predictable: click the right button enough times or give them more stuff, and they’ll join you. The system feels like a grind rather than a meaningful interaction. Prestige, one of the core mechanics, is a random and often pointless value that you increase through arbitrary decisions. You can be the most powerful nation on the map, but if you don’t manage prestige, you can lose. It’s frustrating and nonsensical when, after conquering every nation, you still have less prestige than many others, and in one case, I intentionally culled myself by advancing technology too quickly and ignoring prestige—resulting in a baffling game over.Simultaneous Gameplay IssuesThe game suffers from the usual pitfalls of simultaneous turns. Managing nations and responding to real-time developments feels clunky, and the pacing often feels off as a result. The game feels more like a modern title in design than a well-thought-out strategy game. It was built to impress with its broad systems and historical scope but ultimately offers very little depth to sink your teeth into.ConclusionAra: History Untold tries to be a modern, expansive strategy game, but it falls flat in execution. It offers systems that look deep on the surface but are tedious and lack true tactical importance. The game’s combat is shallow, and the emphasis on prestige over strategy is baffling. Ultimately, it’s a game that’s wide as an ocean but shallow as a puddle. If you’re looking for a historical strategy game with meaningful depth, this isn’t it.
