_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I received a key from the  team to talk about Ara on the latest podcast.  Linked is a  by Rob from eXplorminate to help inform your decision!I recommend the game, HOWEVER there are three big issues that you should be aware of.  Before I get to those, here are the two biggest reasons I am going to keep playing this game.1.  I am a big Anno fan, and this has a similar feel.  It is no replacement for Anno, but it mixes Anno's production chain ideas with the 4X formula, and adds some new ideas in as well.  For example, if I manage to find some sheep, I can build a farm to harvest resources from them.  However, I have to choose what to harvest: wool or livestock.  Wool can be fed into other buildings that are part of a larger clothing production chain that will improve my citizens' living condition, thereby benefiting my cities' production and taxation rates.  Livestock can be given to a butcher to make cured meat so that my cities don't starve.  Now, if I have 2 sheep farms that each produce 0.8 of a chosen resource per turn, I am very close to being able to have one wool farm and one livestock farm.  One way to get there is to craft a plow and assign an expert farmer to increase farm efficiency.  Alternatively, I could import more wool/livestock via a trade route.  There are many layers to these systems that are very satisfying to manipulate.  2.  The way (1) is mixed in with 4X elements has me hooked.  I send out scouts to find key resources to fuel my production engines.  I base my research decisions on the resources I find.  Sometimes I am competing with other nations, which involves either being the first to claim a region or taking it by force.  This all ties back into how efficient my cities are at producing settler/military units, and whether I have access to the necessary resources either directly or via trade.  Now onto the three main issues:1.  The UI is bad.  I'm not talking slightly annoying.  Take this example: a farm has several item slots where crafted items can be inserted to increase the farm's efficiency.  Each slot has a specific set of items it can take.  For example, slot 1 can take a plow but slot 2 cannot.  There is no visual difference between these slots, so you have to click on each to see if you have an appropriate item for that slot.Now let's say you have 5 cities each with 3 farms, and you have 15 plows to place in them.  To do this, you have to click on City 1, switch the city menu to display all Harvester buildings, find Farm 1 (which could be somewhere on a long list), click on Farm 1, click on Slot 1 (if you remember that Slot 1 is for plows), click on Plow 1, close the Farm 1 menu, repeat for each farm in City 1, close City 1 menu, repeat for each City.  This is just one example, but these issues are present in every aspect of the UI.  The game also does not display important reminders and does a poor job of letting you know that entire windows (such as trade) exist.2.  The AI is not good, even on the 3rd highest difficulty.  It's hard to speak about the economy AI, although I suspect it has issues, but the military AI is practically non-existent.  In the 3 wars I've been in, the AI has sent 1 weak unit to attack me.  In the case where the AI had a powerful unit, they never moved it off their city, even though I had an undefended city RIGHT next to them.3.  Performance is bad.  I have a 2 year old gaming laptop with a RTX 3060 laptop GPU.  I can usually run any game on high/max settings at 1080p and get a stable 60fps.  I have to run Ara on low to get around 45 fps with frequent dips to 20 fps.Finally, on Ara's Discord server, the devs have said they have fixes close to ready for each of these issues, but I am always skeptical until I see results.  I really like Ara despite these issues, for the reasons I have mentioned.  That said, I want you to be aware of these issues in case they are deal-breakers for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Coming from someone who loves both Civ and Anno, and really wanted to love this game (and would have been inclined to make excuses for a reasonable number of flaws) - this game is just too flawed and too un-fun to excuse.The game somehow simultaneously has too little to do (in terms of fun empire management) and too much to do (in terms of tedious micromanagement). The visuals are simultaneously enchanting (terrain, cities) and cheap (unit icons, UI, battle animations). Resolving everything at the end of the turn also results in an ungratifying experience for exploration and combat.There are a lot of aspects about the game I think are smartly designed, but the core gameplay isn't strong. I did not, at any point, get the "just one more turn" feel from Ara. In fact, I split my playthrough across three sittings because I got too bored to continue, and eventually asked for a refund.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Way too much micro hindered by a horrible UI. I find it so hard to keep track of what I'm doing. There's too much UI clutter and it takes too much time to find out what I'm making, how much I'm making and how much I'm consuming + where is making it. Cultures do not feel unique, like in Civ or other 4X games - leaders have no personality either or unique soundtracks except for a little jingle in the diplomacy screen; they don't speak either. It is also further hindered by bad performance. I am a decent level ahead of the recommended specs but it still lags really bad on lowest settings.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a bad game. However some of the mechanical choices are either unclear or simply unappreciated by me. I like playing longer games. I like managing civs versus meeting win conditions. I like the mounting complexity that occurs late in 4x strategy games. It feels like ARA History Untold was designed against me - and that's ok. The culling system makes sense in PVP, less so in PVE. There's a dynamic that's lost when AI Civs leave the room. There's friction added when expansion into devoid territories is limited by city count. Agreements and relationships I've cultivated disappear, not because of my choices, but because a game system requires it. It's late in the game and the world feels more empty than ever. But no matter, diplomatic options are limited. No way to understand what the rest of the world is doing - how they are winning or losing. There's not even a map. This game asks you to spend time in all the wrong places. Wonderful ideas, perhaps executed in ways that tells me I'm not their target audience.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: A deep 4X game that takes a bit getting used to. It takes ideas from CIV, Humankind and Anno and merges them together in a satisfying blend with excellent visuals.What works well:+ Excellent Visuals+ Turns are fast!+ Lots of fun innovations that feel satisfying. For example: You need space in your land for wonders, you can't just magically build them and they take entire regions, taking the space of 4-5 other buildings.+ Every city has 5 quality of life stats you need to manage for success (Health, Happiness, Security etc. ) If you manage these well, your citizens are happy and you earn gold ages.+ Quality of life in your cities actually increase output of your cities (like in Stellaris)+ The only way to win is "PRESTIGE". This determines if you can survive the ages. Literally. It's a bit like civilization battle royale. There are 3 main acts and each act represents a milestone in history for example the  Middle Ages. If your prestige isn't enough when it's time to transition to the Middle Ages, you become lost to history, leaving the ashes of your cities to be scavenged by surviving nations.+ The amenities, crafting and supply chain buildings are a great idea but they're cumbersome to manage right now. Need a UI that shows ALL types of  Harvesters across your nation (only crafters available rn) instead of having to go through city by city.+ When you build a new army, they're in the reserves and don't cost any resources. If you want to deploy them, they take a few turns to muster and then become available in the map.What needs improvement:- UI needs overhauls to make crafting, managing your supply chains less cumbersome.- Pls let me search the map for a specific resource. - QOL improvements on micromanagement of your cities. - Performance optimization. - More robust UI for religion. I have no idea how my religion is doing outside of my cities. This makes it really hard for me to decide where to send my missionaries.- More and varied civilizations.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: This is a hard game to rate yes or no to, as I was extremely interested for the first 50-75 turns, but the game has quickly devolved into a micromanaging simulator focused on your crafting and production chain. I keep loading the game up, feeling like I should continue, but I play a turn or two and remember how bogged down I am with all my crafting and production issues that I wind up quitting out. I hope they continue working on this game and improve this aspect of it. I'd return to it, if they do, but doubt I will otherwise.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: I had high hopes for this game and I've been excited to play it for a long time. Unfortunately, it's a massive disappointment. Here are a few reasons why:1. The game is primarily focused on crafting and everything else about it is built around that. I knew there was a crafting system in place but I had no idea how convoluted and tedious it was. Constant crafting spam in a 4x strategy game is not a good time. It get's worse as the game goes on, to the point you don't even want to bother with it. The crafting system would be tolerable if it was streamlined and minimized significantly.2. There is no way to upgrade military units? So I'm forced to disband them periodically due to them becoming obsolete. What a huge waste and the game deserves a bad review just for this alone.3. Speaking of military units, once you deploy them from the reserves, there is no way to re-deploy them to a different formation, which again would force you to disband them and rebuild the units all over again in order to re-deploy to a different formation. Hopefully they patch that in later.4. There are no diplomatic relations details to show you exactly why any nation likes or dislikes you. Seeing the breakdown on positive and negative modifiers to relations on a tooltip or something is a basic quality of life feature that is not present in this game.On the positive side, there are some really fun 4x strategy game mechanics. I love how the Act and Era progress goes and I think it's interesting that nations get culled at the end of act 1 and act 2, but having the ability to disable that is important as well. The game is beautiful to behold, and you can't help but want to play it despite its flaws. I'm hoping that these issues get addressed, but the crafting system especially would require a massive overhaul to be more streamlined for me to enjoy the game. TLDR: Do not buy this game unless you want a strategy game built around a messy, complex, tedious crafting system.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: +-1000 hours on CIV VI and cumulatively +-1000 hours on other similar games, and many more gameplay hours with city-builders and all types of strategy games. My opinion is as follows:ARA is a disorganized, slow, unnecessarily complex, chaotic, infuriating, patience-demanding MESS!I will first give my score on a couple of factors that I took in mind and which I deem important for such a game, out of 10. Of course, the high cost of the game is something that largely affected my opinion in the analysis and score-giving of the following factors.Graphics and UI: 7/10 (randomly detailed, randomly not - UI/icons etc hide the charm... detailed icons, huge icons, many icons... I'd go for a colored AOE IV icon version)Performance: 4/10 (crashes; click-bugs; freezes; generally patience-demanding)Acts/ages/eras: 2/10 (horrible era system - eras are only namely mentioned and the game is 3 acts - eras; the most significant thing is research and it feels incomplete and sketchy - no immersion at all - bad copy of CIV)Maps: 3/10 (no real variety; I tried 4 randomly generated maps with different settings. Territories look dull and boring, the textures are detailed but there is no real variety, no real color, no real elevation and cliffs - mountains are simply impassable - Humankind maps look better, CIV VII maps more promising, too)Leaders: 1/10 (very cartoonishly out of context, like you put Mr. Bean in a SAW movie - they 100% copied CIV VI here, no doubt)Expansion: 8/10 (I do like the city cap, and territories)Wars: 5/10 (nothing special, the AI is super dumb and will just attack for expansion till you literally wanna go play something else or quit gaming altogether)Religion: 1/10 (no game-changer, it feels weird)It's an attempt to create a complex game that combines Sid Meier's Civilization games, Anno and Humankind without any utility to actually apply that complexity efficiently. Full of performance issues and bugs, sometimes you have to click 3 and 4 and even 10 times to get something done. The materials, products and the buildings that make them are all over the map and the tiny, hyper-realistic circular icons that appear together are VERY difficult to distinguish from each other, so you end up clicking everywhere to find the building that you need, hoping, with your intuition and on your patience limits, that it's the one you had been looking for.The difficulty settings are not clear. I am trying the easiest setting in an attempt to get familiar with the game while also being eager to reach the final era because I love future eras in these games. However, the easiest setting is weird. In one game, the AI was a potato, I suppose because the map was bigger so they didn't need to conquer me. In fact, I was 2 times stronger than the second AI. I gave the game up because I was overwhelmed by the production/building (and what not) UI chaos. Also, and I stress it - my device is pretty fast, the game has very annoying performance issues. No matter the settings I tried, ultra settings and lower settings give the exact same result in performance. It's just slow in average, with annoying bugs, like the game doesn't understand "left click" sometimes.I see people comparing it to CIV games, and I did mention it, because the basis of the idea is similar to CIV, of course. Despite that, it's nothing like CIV VI for example, but not in a good way, because although the idea is refreshing, you end up having to deal with production all the time instead of actually enjoying the game. It's like Old World, but more complex and broken/chaotic.There is no clear production line. There is no clear purpose. Everything revolves around "prestige", which is like oxygen for your empire-civ-town-village-cottage or whatever you managed to keep after being attacked 25 million times on "easiest". Am I an inexperienced player and should just suck up the wars thing? No, because it doesn't happen organically, the AI will attack you BY DEFAULT if they have no more space to expand, instead of making any attempt at trading (which is certainly not a game changer either). The graphics? Of course, pretty beautiful, but with ALL THE MENUS you are almost unable to see anything anyway, and you need to see the yields, the borders, the huge icons for units (that render them almost invisible as well), you end up with no actual space to see those "beautiful" graphics. Although mind you, I was looking at the buildings carefully and houses look very weird; some nice houses appear that follow the trends of each age, but then suddenly you see something like unfinished CONCRETE boxes with roofs all over the place, that make no sense at all - they look like slums, minus the high density (pun intended). To sum it up:The game is WAY too expensive for its current quality (day of release). It's a sugarcoated early-access game and we all had to pay them the money because they obviously invested a lot in it and people had to get paid, but it's NOT A FINISHED GAME. It's an early-access game, and we have been deceived. However, I do understand the developers/beneficiaries' side, because we live in modern capitalism. I think by giving it an early-access phase, the game would have gotten way better ratings. You can't make people expect a finished game and give THIS, because when you will want to invest more on it, people will turn their backs on you. There are so many developers making new games nowadays, you can't just go and release an unfinished game for 60 euros (in my case).Do I like the game? Yes, but it needs so much work. And start by firing whoever had the idea for this horrible UI, because the performance-killing detailed graphics aren't even visible anymore with that interface.Also, mind you, this game ends after all research is done, and you CAN'T CONTINUE playing after the prestige winner. This is the main reason I don't want to play this game anymore.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: The game is really cool. I normally prefer hexes, but I actually really enjoyed the way the game did its zones. The different currencies feel good and the goods management is fun. For the most part, I enjoy the combat; particularly the way units are deployed in formations that can give them bonuses. The tech tree and age system is well done. Even now I'm tempted to boot up the game. But there are so many issues that lead me to feeling frustrated or bored.Enemy scouts can run across my lands disrupting all my buildings because the game doesn't let me "attack" the region I think they're going to go to, nor does it let me tell my unit to chase the scout and attack whatever region it goes to. The game's performance isn't really where I need it to be on my machine. I end up losing out on a lot of the cool art because of that. And not being able to upgrade units is rough and feels bad.But the UI is the most frustrating and tedious part. Man, this game has so many cool things going for it. From a game design perspective, the systems are all really engaging. I guess I'm insane, because I'm probably going to start another run, despite all the evidence indicating that I'm going to quit out of frustration. I just hope the developers fix some of these issues so I can come back here and leave a positive review.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: The early game is great and to a certain degree is worth the purchase on its own. Very challenging especially on harder difficulties but the bar is high to survive the first cut off such that if you do you almost automatically go onto win. The other issue is that after the first act the computing power required is massive. To go much further feels very clunky and is beyond what I have available and I don't have an outdated computer. Not an absolute No. Maybe even a yes if optimisation allows me to play later stages of the game without the PC feeling like it is going into meltdown. Fix this and the balancing issue of first act vs 2nd and presumably 3rd and there is actually a really solid game here. Yes you micro manage, yes you have to really think about small tasks but it is the essence of the game which shouldn't ordinarily be deemed bad because its not Civ or EU or CK. The premise is fine just needs a fair amount of polish.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: This game is basically Micro managing Civ. It feels more like a city builder with a 4x game thrown on top. Ever aspect of your Civ can and will need to upgrade and buff. You will make sure that your Civ is not producing to little or wasting items. Everything has a menu for it so you will need to take you time learning every one of them and how to use them. That is the biggest issue with the game, that I have to spend so much time micro managing my civ in menus that I don't feel like I am managing a Civ in a fun way.Here is the Update- finally completed a play thur took me 3 attempt as first to game I was learning mechanics or made really bad mistakes. The graphics and overall Idea is good. However it still need work, first it seems that the AI will just declare war on you randomly especially if you have a touching border. So better have your military ready cause if not you will get steam rolled and lose the war maybe even the game. Generally the gameplay you have in the early game is the same in the late game just magnified.What it needs it away to streamline production.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: My high hopes about this game somewhat diminished in the second act. As I started to realise that this CIV killer was just a city management game. Lacking any real depth. I found myself spewing out  a variety of parts, food and furnishings from crafting zones, just keeping up with my ever growing populations and farms. At this stage I was beginning to regret my purchase. By act 3 i just wanted the game to end.  I was well in the lead but the initial fun and excitement I had in act 1 was a  just a distant foggy memory. But i had a long way to the finish line. The battles I had against my Arabian neighbour didn't add to my enjoyment either, as they lacked any decent mechanics and left me wondering how they could release the game with such bad battle mechanics. Well the team of devs really need to do a lot of work on this one before I come back. At $109.00 Australian dollars for the deluxe edition. Definitely not worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: It is a very interesting mix between Civ and Anno, but doesn't hit the spot.Too restrictive on having a huge empire and way too tedious on production chains. Almost every tech brings new types of items to gather of craft, up to the point that i lost patience at late game and just uninstalled it.Visualy it is beautiful, but you will end up most of the time zoomed out and the art won't matter anymore.As for nations.... it's a lackluster. All of them look the same, same units, same buildings, there is no individualization that will make you want to try nations except the leader  perks are different. But, at the end of the day, you will end up on the same route doing the samething. There is only one play style here, building tall. I belive Millenia does it alot better, in all aspects (except visual).Ara... is good to give it a try, but the price tag is extreme. I would recomend getting it at 75% discount. More than that i don't think it's worth.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Old World is where I set the bar for 4x experiences these days (let's see what Civ 7 brings to the table) and Ara: History Untold gets pretty darn close. Somehow, Oxide Games have managed to combine the minutiae of Anno 1800's dense supply chains with the high-level city/civ management of Civ 6 in a way that is neither too complex nor too mundane. Everything feels like this team wanted to take a novel approach to the classic Civ formula, and in my 90 mintues or so of play time it's really excellent. Frankly, Ara's replacing Civilization on my SSD until 7 comes out.Performance has been a bit of a sore spot on my 3070ti, but I'm otherwise extremely impressed with the depth, detail, and care put into Ara thus far.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: There is a diamond here, but it is very rough, and tangled within a sticky web of poorly-developed systems. Whoever decided to release the game in this state did a huge disservice to the game, the developers who love this game, and the players who want to love the game. Maybe it'll be good in a couple of years, but based on the vague-propaganda in the first few post-release updates, I don't currently have much hope.The UI is overall poor. There is lots of hidden information, absent information, and even some false information. Ex: There is a tab labelled "View and Manage your Masterpieces," which doesn't show my masterpieces.The Living World is absolutely beautiful to look at, but has little impact on gameplay. Terrain types have unclear effects on improvements (e.g. is a logging camp in a desert that much different than a logging camp in a forest? folks have argued over this in forums here.), and terrain has no effect on combat or movement. Biological resources (rice, wheat, horses) are fixed in place, and cannot be changed, added, expanded, or removed.Diplomacy is poor. There is no way to interact with tribes aside from random events. You cannot start a conversation, offer gifts, or send threats. You have to wait for those random events to trigger. Relationships with other civs aren't much better. You can offer gifts, but gifts have little impact on relations, and are often refused. As with tribes, the best way to interact with civs is to wait for those random events and then make the choice that suits your purpose. There is no way to trade or flip regions apart from war. Overall, diplomacy lacks agency. You just can't *do* much.Unnecessary rules are everywhere. Why are some improvements limited to X per nation or X per city? Obviously it's for balance reasons, but this could have been addressed by nerfing those improvements instead of adding random hard-to-remember one-of-a-kind rules. Ara says , but is it really my world if I can't go bonkers with wine or windmills? What if I just really like wine and windmills? Tough. You're only allowed so many of those improvements.And the crafting system. I love the concept. Love it! But it's so micromanagey that I can't stand one more turn. I've played a handful of part-games, each time going a little farther, but round about the end of Act 1, I just can't take it anymore. It's too fiddly and frustrating and limited.I want to see this game win, but it's not currently on a winning path. If I had a friend with spinach in their teeth, or an open fly, I'd tell them.Ara - get your act together. Be open about the problems. Be open about how you got here. Then make a commitment to doing better, engage the community, and make it happen - prioritizing openness and transparency all the way. Vague happy statements aren't helpful. Be real. Prove that you're trustworthy. Please.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: 9 hours in of slowly playing the game. Completed only 3 ages out of 12 so far. But since the game is fresh, it warrants a review.It's actually not bad.The graphics are a pleasure to look at. The level of detail is great - zoom in and see little citizens walking around. The buildings are also have a bit more realistic proportions than Civ. The camera can be fully rotated.The gameplay - essentially it's more or less Civ with some changes: a huge system of crafting items and materials, non-hexagonal division into zones. Some people don't like how much of a portion of the game the crafting takes, for me it has been fine.The UI feels a bit lacking in some places, you catch yourself thinking "would be nice if I could see or do this and that right now". Here's hoping to it being improved over time.The music is good. A variety of tunes intermingling with nature sound effects - doesn't get boring.The AIs seem to be fine while you are still learning the game. When you start to understand how to do things more optimally, they appear to gradually fall behind. Then again, so far in my game the distance in scores seems to not have continued growing, which means some challenge appears to be there.Additionally mentioning... How well it runs - on my older PC and 1080p it actually runs pretty fine so far (around 60 fps) - I've seen many people complain that it runs poorly on higher resolutions, then again the others have been saying to turn off vsync and tune down some of the settings like shadows.To sum it up... Is it fun? Yes. The management of the empire, seeing it grow and develop, technological advancement, and at certain points taking a breather, zooming in and enjoying the close-up look of it. For me it's been fun.P.S. If you play at 1080p, I suggest turning the UI scale down. 4k doesn't have this problem, but on 1080p by default the UI elements take too much space, don't look good, and leave too little space for the viewport.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a fairly casual player of these kinds of games, and generally prefer the civilization building to the military tabletop game that the newer Civ games have become. Civ 6 really didn't do it for me, since it became more about domination and the min/maxing that the more hardcore players love those games for. If you're more of a hardened expert at these things, I can't really speak to how the game plays in that regard and this review probably isn't for you.     For my tastes, though, this game is great. The leaders to choose from are diverse and interesting, with some of the usual cast you're used to seeing but also some intriguing new choices that aren't from the traditional historical military empire builders. Scientists and artists join monarchs and kings here, and I love the idea.      Turns are involved and do feel a little bit more micromanaged than current Civ games, and I was afraid the crafting would be onerous, but it's not. It's all pretty easy to manage and keep track of, and if you're already familiar with this genre of games it's surprisingly easy to pick up and play despite its complexity. For the things you need help with, there's the in-game Encarta (this game's Civilopedia) and it's managed to help with anything I've needed it for. The game has been designed to accomodate Civ players and cover all of the bases to get you into it... a lot of depth, and very complex, but it's still somehow fairly easy to learn and just play anyway. I found everything to be extremely intuitive, which is no easy task for a game with this many doodads to fiddle with. Even after hours of playing and hundreds of turns, the game doesn't bog down in waiting for AI to finish its moves; it handles it all as you play, without dragging things down. The military system is something new, but it's intuitive; you build units, create formations, and then deploy them into the field with a system meant to prevent two-turn army dumps. It takes a little getting used to, but aside from a lack of unit upgrading I like it pretty well.      Without getting into the minutiae of every aspect of the game, they've more or less thought of everything here; the game is complete in a way that usually takes Civ an expansion or two to get to. It's also running perfectly, without slowing down as turns progress and without any waits in between turns, no bugs or crashes that I've come across. A single game is lengthy, with plenty of expansion and room to grow and plan and the way that plays out will change your civ's progression fairly dramatically from game to game.      The only drawback I'd note at the moment is that it's tough to make sense of why diplomatic changes are happening. A rival civilization will go from loving you to hating you and back without much feedback as to why, and I haven't figured out what's causing it. It's not particularly hard to navigate or manage, but it is a little schizophrenic so plan accordingly. The other con is that resource management can be a bit fiddly, especially with food, so you need to manage it a little more closely than I'd like at times; just building farms and managing experts to utilize them sometimes isn't enough without also managing consumable items you craft at granaries, for example.  I do wish those items weren't quite as necessary, and you could rely more on just building for the resource more instead of having to manage both.      All said and done, though, I love the game. I was a little worried and skeptical when I picked it up, just hoping it would at least be a fun alternative to Civ6, but from what I've played... I actually like it a lot better. It has that same special sauce to it that makes you keep playing one more turn until you're writing a review at 3:30 in the morning.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Heads and shoulders above most 4x games on launch (remembering, most 4x games are trash and bare bones on launch, and need multiple DLCs to become halfway decent)Such a breath of fresh air compared to the stale, superficial, dumbed down path that Civ has taken. Really hopethe dev team gets the chance to build the game out further with DLCs
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Needs a little more time to cook in the oven in terms of UI, AI, and performance, but ultimately a very ambitious take on the 4X genre that holds great potential. Beyond those complaints, I would also hope to see more unique variation between different nations (give me unique improvements, unique units, or something that I believe is especially in-line with the game play, unique craftable, as currently the game lacks variation between the nations)
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: A Civ style game that actually has a proper pace for once. At turn 200, I was just entering the Early Medieval Era, and I was in the lead. I don't know how many hundreds of turns the game goes, but it's a long one for sure. The UI needs some work, there are many things that could be made better by simple improvements, though the devs have been patching the game very quickly.The game is slower than Civ, you really need to think about what you're building, it's not just fill the queue with all the stuff and let it go. The AI seems competent, and I like the way combat is handled. Two large armies can take several turns to wear each other down. Also, if a city has walls, you simply cannot attack it without siege equipment, definitely a welcome change from just spamming units at it. Force limits also mean you have to think about how you are deploying your troops, as well as their composition, because you need a good mix and units take a couple turns to mobilize from the reserves.I need to rethink my city building for the next time I play, but I'm excited to start another game.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: The game runs well and is an enjoyable civ-like. I enjoy the goods production mechanic, but it is begging for some kind of automation/UI ease in the late game. I ended up just ignoring the mechanic eventually because I didn't want to slot in items into the couple hundred farms in my nation. Additional automation as the game goes on could be interesting, maybe as an element of some kind of government or bureaucracy tech.I also really enjoyed that turns are resolved simultaneously, so combat kind of feels like the old board game 'diplomacy'.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: - performance is quite poor, but might be fixed overtime- requiring xboxlive for multiplayer should be part of the sys requirements instead of stealth installing it- the game itself looks like having potential but i'd wait a year or two before revisiting it- this is no civilisation, there is way more necessary micro management... so much that i don't see this game playable in multiplayer at all, as the game takes too long for that
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game because it's not trying to be a Civ killer/clone, it's trying to make it's own way in the historical 4X genre so DO NOT GO INTO THIS GAME EXPECTING A CIV CLONE.Kind of a TLDR of what has stood out  1. Settlement mechanic doesn't really exist so you and AI can settle right next to each other or deep within a pocket of the others empire with no penalty (SCREW YOU CAESAR THAT NATURAL GAS AND COAL SHOULD BE MINE!) 2. UI is ok enough but for the level of micro (especially later) it's pretty bad and needs lots of improvement3. Game optimization in terms of eating resources causing the game to slow when rapidly clicking certain UI elements4. Both military and building UI not having streamline elements as in older era troops/building not being dynamically replaced by the newer ones (Downgraded to the next highest tier if you don't have the resources to make the latest thing)5. Buildings should have some part of it's UI visual (as in you're going to build a new building in a region) show what type it is Economy, Industrial, Culture etc. without having to hover over it.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: More of an "EARLY ACCESS" Games, than a finished game!It lacks QoL features that are essential for that amount of micromanagement the game requires me to do. The game expects me to equip every farm etc. with tools individually. In order to do so you have to click through 3 menues. Multiple that with the amount of buildings you have. And then, when you want to upgrade to a better tool: have fun doing it all over again. A game, that wants to do things differently by introducing the player to some sort of supply chain build up, a good UI, good QoF are MANDATORY! How anyone developing this game wasnt aware of all the fundamental UI problems is not acceptable. Especially for a 60$ price tag.Its patchable, sure, but all of these things should be in the game on DAY ONE!

_childDocuments_.review: As an alpha tester, I had the joy of playing Ara: History Untold before its official release, and I absolutely adore it. It combines a civ-style turn based 4X with grand strategy and city builder-style production chains. But it's not just a remix of old ideas, it brings a lot of innovation to the table: * Instead of hexagons or squares, the map is built up of irregular regions following natural boundaries * A flexible scoring system which allows many different paths to victory * Truly simulataneous turns which enables large scale multiplayer * Giant maps for up to 36 players * A comprehensive crafting system allowing you to set up meaningful production chains to support your cities * The tech tree is non-linear with redundancies between techs, allowing many different ways to traverse it * A living world where you can zoom all the way from a nation-level strategic view, all the way in to watch your people walking around, going about their businessI've played most of the games in the genre, and Ara feels at the same time both familiar and different from other turnbased 4X games. Ara is a real competitor to the Civilization series. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: So far so good. You're in for a lot of pain if you can't adapt your thinking past Civ 5/6. Also, ignore the people complaining about losing 250 turns in. You can disable that. Ignore the people complaining about poorly explained systems/mechanics too, they have an entire tutorial that does that plus something like the Civilopedia that they call the Encarta.My only complaints so far are:- Game setup doesn't start with random appointments by default (I think they get 'randomized' when you select a leader, but it shouldn't work that way)- You can't disable the turn limit- Diplomatic relations go south dramatically for inexplicable reasons; one turn you're near-allied and the next they consider you an adversaryWill update review once I've completed at least one playthrough fully. So far I've been learning the early mechanics to master act 1.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a lot of good ideas, but it really fails to see any of them through. It has a diverse set of resources that are used to make an even more diverse set of goods. Supply chain management is interesting, but not overly complicated. It is, however, very tedious. There is no way to search for if your Empire has new resources if you discover them. There is no easy way to upgrade buildings that make your goods, and most production buildings have three upgrades. Combat attempts to offer some interesting decisions. You've got several types of units that you can arrange in formations of 1, 3, 4, 5, and 6 units. They can be arranged specific formations that gives them damage bonuses. However, combat is just slapping to portraits against one another where the biggest number wins most of the time. It attempts to introduce a rock, paper, scissors style of counter but it rarely mattered when I played. Once units are mustered they cannot be upgraded. I'm unsure if they can be upgraded once trained, but its a moot point. Finally, diplomacy isn't very impressive. I found myself mostly placating nearby AI so they wouldn't declare war on me while I juggled my supply chain. This game is in desperate need of some Quality of Life updates.

_childDocuments_.review: Its mid. Feels like the devs made the foundations of a gameplay system then forgot to add the flavor. Feels like youre eating tacos without seasoning. You can see what they were going for but god is it bland.in all seriousness. it lacks engaging gameplay loops. nothing i did actually felt like it made a difference. The maps even at their largest are shockingly small. All the leaders feel mostly the same with little distinction between them. by about 40-50ish turns in im jst hitting next turn without really thinking about anything.the crafting system is meh, mostly adding complexity for the sake of complexity it feels like. and most of the systems present are obtuse, not well explained, and you generally have very little control over them. I dont know what gives me more religious tennants when or why. I dont know what spawns paragons at all. And i am not entirely clear on the purpose of this games verion of great works of art.furthermore all the systems feel very isolated from eachother except maaaybe the economy. Religion felt disconected from the rest of the game. Diplomacy was so shallow so as to be meaningless. warefare was there i guess. and none of these systems had any interaction with any other systems it felt like. oh my religion has become dominant in rome? does this have any impact on diplomatic relations? trade relations? rates of hostility? as far as i could discern, no. nothing happened. in fact i couldnt even tell you what the point of spreading religion is. Maybe it gives more prestige? but if it does thats very poorly communicated and represented. _childDocuments_.review: An incredibly refreshing take on the 4X Civ genre. There are some confusing design choices, such as the inability to upgrade your units or pull them back into your draft pool, but the devs do appear to be listening and implementing user feedback so this may change over time.The crafting system, while a bit confusing at first, is the first breath of fresh air into this genre. Whereas most games have you capturing resources and that being the end of it, this game uses those resources as the building blocks for better and better commodities for your population to consume for bonuses, or construction supplies for new buildings and weapons for your troops. My only complaints here is the one-and-done resources, like tea being used only for herbal medicine, being very underpowered compared to other resources, and that some of the crafting costs are unbalanced to an almost comedic level.The con to this new system is that it's not first timer friendly to these types of games, and managing bonuses in the late game can be a bit unwieldy.The second breath of fresh air, albeit probably the more controversial one, is how this game sets up the win conditions. Your only objective in this game is to survive the test of time. You can -technically- win through a military victory as well, but really you're just winning the primary objective by default. How you go about winning the game isn't as linear as it sounds, as virtually everything you do in this game generates points and gets you closer to victory.The biggest loss I can say this game has for its genre is the combat system. It's incredibly simplistic compared to its rivals Civ and Humankind, even with the formation system, and feels like it was added more as an afterthought. Then there's the upgrading issue. You can't give your troops new weapons or pay for them to upgrade to the next tier, so once they're obsolete, you're basically treating your veteran divisions as cannon fodder if you didn't disband them already. This is something the devs said they're working on, but as of writing it has not been implemented. The only thing it seems to do right in regards to combat is that your units aren't being replaced with every single tech you unlock, so the impact/value of each troop is felt more than its rival games. If the combat had the depth that Humankind possesses, this would have honestly been GOTY for its genre, and earned the title of Civ killer that Humankind was striving to take.I honestly feel that, with the right QoL changes, this game would be phenomenal.

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend to do what I did.  Try this game out on Gamepass, that way you can get the full game, and not have to worry about a two hour limit.Let's say instead, you trust me.  My vote, after 20 hours on Gamepass is a thumbs down.  Mostly, the game tries but doesn't quite reach the level of Civ killer.  Much like Humankind and Millennia before it, what is different isn't worth it.  A good example is the era mechanic.  There are 'stages' you have to go through-but, if you aren't in the top 4 or so out of 10 players, you don't advance anymore-you go bye bye.  End of game.  Uncool in my book.  Another example is crafting.  While a novel idea, it turns into too much micromanaging that just isn't fun, it's tedious. _childDocuments_.review: When a game costs 60 USD and is sold as a full release, there are two expectations instead of just one.1. The game is itself feature complete2. The game runs without bugs, glitches, hang ups, and crashingWhen I first played on release day, the second made the first impossible to judge. With the patch released somehow reconciling the second for me, my short playtime doesn't merit much in the exploration of feature completion. But this far, it has remained coherent.So; does ARA meet the measure of a sixty dollar game? Well... -record scratch- -vhs rewind-Value propositions are VERY different than minimum expectations.Every game costs three things of its players; -Money; 60 dollars. Is this game worth skipping a trip to the grocery store?-Time; people only have a finite amount of it to spend on what they want.-Dedication; is this worth taking up your attention, hard drive space, and skill rather than an alternative?At a minimum I think ARA in its design is making an effort to push the genre of alt-history, culture-in-a-blender, turn-based grand strategy games forward. In the same vein that Humankind revolutionized the way Firaxis approached their seventh numbered title in the Sid Meier's Civ franchise, I believe ARA is trying to do something similar, taking inspiration from Paradox's Crusader Kings series with regional movement every turn rather than with an active-timer.I will stand by my initial critique; the tutorial exists less to onboard players and more to just exist as explanations for things.There are around four saves of the Byzantines I have where I would begin playing in a specific fashion only to discover a mechanic constraint that never got mentioned or explained and realized as well as I was doing, my time would be better spent starting over with that knowledge.Is it worth the dedication?Hard drive space, 32 GB isn't nothing, but it's not a burden these days either. Personal knowledge and skill, a lot of the game seems to be focused least on somehow perfect play and most on finding fires and putting them out before they explode in your face. But definitely a learning curve involved.Is it worth the time?There's plenty of satisfaction to be found in the game, and the music is good enough that I didn't swap over to my own playlist. As an experience it's very much a fun thing to see a vision and bring it forward because you learned how to understand what's going on.So... is all of that worth 60 USD?I don't regret spending sixty dollars on this at all, but I wouldn't have sold it at that price. I think forty better fits. There is a general lack of polish I would expect of sixty dollar quality, but if that's your barrier, it's also available on Xbox game pass so try it out there instead. I sincerely think this game would benefit from a free demo of the first hundred turns, maybe with three unique civs, multiplayer disabled, and the ability to restore demo saves after purchasing the full game. Just so you can try it and explore for yourself. But I will happily concede that ARA is not a bad game and change my review to positive.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: This is exactly what I wanted, a little more complex than civ but still not as hard as a grand strategy. It's biggest issue right now is the lack of simple QOL things- such as being able to easily search for buildings in the frankly massive build list- yes you can search for names but not effects. What if I want to see ALL buildings with "farm" anywhere in their name OR description- nothin; what if I want to set default products for particular buildings (highest level plow applied across the board farm wise etc); what if I want to simply see (and start) upgrades with a nice little green arrow on each building... Still nope. But these are all tiny problems, little niggling issues. The real issue is the performance, while it certainly isn't unplayable, even on my machine I would wildly see fluctuating frame rates from 15 to 45- I still can play and enjoy but it makes the game seem like something worth waiting on. Moreover, the maps seem tiny- random thing to add I know but it is true... and yet; I still said this was exactly what I wanted and that I recommend it. Why?Because I do love it;- I love the long crafting construction chains, building wonders via saving up crafting materials I may be better using elsewhere- I love that I can build my army anywhere- but deploy it to the front line. I love how many technologies there are, and the push and pull about if you get them all- or keep trying to jump ahead faster knowing that the key elements of most techs will still end up your way regardless. There is real choice and consequence, and with enough playing about and fiddling I can make everything work so much better. The AI, while not perfect, manages to take advantage of every time I leave an unprotected city- but then I can also take advantage of their wars on my allies to blindside them too! I really can't wait to see what mods, expansions and dlcs may do to the game. I am excited to see whatever gets added.Edit: I since found mass upgrading, it is under "improvements" but honestly I think it could have fit in the zones area too.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought Ara: History Untold the day after I found out Civ VII was going the Humankind route and changing empires with each "age". I've been playing Civ since the first game and could not dislike that more. So I got Ara as a protest purchase, but quickly fell in love with the truly organic way the cities grow. The dev team is plugged in and listening to feedback. I believe this game has a LONG lifetime ahead of it. If you're a jaded Civ player, and have also enjoyed titles like Anno 1800 in the past, you might love this one as much as I do.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: It needs some considerable tweaking and refining. The UI is clunky and opaque. Diplomacy is pretty skeletal and dull. The military and war fighting mechanics , while not without promise, are at this point extremely tedious (you can't upgrade units? Or send them back into reserves to reform into different formations? Really???). The game would also benefit considerably from additional content (which I have no doubt is coming in the form of free and paid DLC).All that said, the game is fun. It's got some interesting mechanics and features. To name just a few: The visuals are excellent. Silly as it is, I really enjoy being able to zoom in and see people walking around in the streets.The soundtrack and score create great ambiance.The numerous resources and amenities make the economy very interesting (although production management needs some work). The progress of the game through ages that not every civilization survives is a really interesting innovation that ups the ante and regularly shakes things up. Ara was clearly made by developers who have experience in and really enjoy the genre. With some additional development, I think it could become a major player in the genre. If you've played Civilization, a lot of things will feel very familiar but there are enough differences between the titles that this one has its own unique feel. Those who want a more refined product might want to wait a year or so but I absolutely do recommend the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Clunky, over-complicated and full of poor design decisions. It's very difficult to keep track of production - in order to tell which improvements are properly supplied you have to zoom right in, which you may have to do multiple times in order to add new tech supplies to existing buildings.You can't retreat from combat. At no point in history was it routine for whole armies to be annihilated, but in Ara, almost all combat ends with one side or the other completely destroyed. It takes too long to get a new army into action, meaning a war can be effectively over before it's started.There is no reminder that an amenity is about to expire, meaning changing amenity usually means wasting part of the old one.There's potential here, but it's a year or two from being worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR : "Better than Millenia, except for the combat system, which makes the game unplayable."So, this game is a mixed bag.  Basically, the economic side of the game is complicated and involved.  It will take a lot more play to unravel whether I think it's actually good, but it's definitely involved (and therein interesting, at least for the moment).  I've read some people saying it's like Anno.  I haven't played Anno, so I can't say, but I have played another so-so 4x that came out recently that was also described as having Anno-like economics, and it _is_ similar to that game, so...  Probably Anno-like?  Anyway, I'm calling that, overall, the good.  The other interesting tidbit I suppose is because you have discrete items you build (wheels, incense, candles, feasts, etc) as well as bulk resources (food, wood, material) these are not only used for construction, but also for example luxuries.  You have an actual stock, and you decide when and where to use them.  They have specific benefits when used ala.. I'll go with Endless Legend this time, just to shake things up.  Anyway, this part seems potentially fun.The bad is the military side of the game.  It's terrible.  Units are deployed as "armies" basically consisting of one or more units.  You can build them anywhere and deploy them at any city (and maybe military bases later, idk).  Once deployed, however, they can't be changed.  Because, restructuring your military is unheard of.  The military techs are poorly laid out, which is ironic since they are almost a carbon copy of Civ's.  Elephant troops seem to be worse than Chariots (I didn't build them, but the in game help says they're worse).  Horsemen lose to the starting warrior analog (probably because it's called a spearman).  And so on. This game has a very staid pace of things, so you build something then the next turn you deploy it and the turn after that, maybe, you can move it.  Once two "units" (armies, because remember they contain potentially multiple units) engage each other they are engaged to the death--a process that will take several turns.  You can't move them or withdraw, you just get to watch them slowly win or lose predicted with seeming 100% accuracy from the start of the battle for several turns.  3-5 for the battles I've seen thus far.  You also have force limits, so recognize that this is your entire force pool of "units" in this battle, generally speaking (depends how far into the game you are).  The other gotcha in this mess is they are using simultaneous turns with some hidden mechanics that are not explained--I've had military units "interrupted" by AI units stopping them from conducting their move orders, conversely I've spent a dozen rounds running in circles with an enemy unit I couldn't engage, even when they ran right through me (we swapped regions).  On the plus side, I have done this to AI as well, at this point, so, at least it's "fair"?   (it's bad).  Thus far, I've found the military conflict model in this game to be trash.The rest of the game is a mix of "hrm, ok"s and "that's fine"s.  The game is played on a map of voranoi regions, not hexes nor grids.  No, not like AoW's regions of hexes... Just regions.  Tech is sorted in ages, and otherwise works as you'd expect.  The only wrinkle here is that techs can overlap in what they unlock, and you can skip some techs if you want and potentially get all (or most?) of the unlocks later.  This probably has some optimizations to it if one felt like it, but I haven't studied the tree.  For example, you can get roads from the Wheel or from Trade.  Diplomacy seems to be the same as most of these games--not very interesting.  I have encountered a number of minor glitches and bugs, bad zooming, overlays not working properly, things like that.  There are wonders, they have a different name, they work like you expect.  They have craftable "masterpieces" which are like... the relics and stuff you could collect in Civ (I forget what they called them), except you craft them with your great people.  I mean your leaders?  Advisors?  idk, all these different terms for the same thing start to bleed together, I forget now what Ara calls them.  Anyway, yes, they have that too.  Religions?  Check, like civ, you found one (no faith required) and then can pick some verses (powers).  You start with two verses...  The set of options appears randomized.  Religious spread, yada yada.  All in all, it's a lot like Millenia.  Only with much worse combat, no natural wonders, and no special ages.  Their economic system is probably better, however, and their tech system looks, at first glance, a bit more involved (which I'll therefore describe as more interesting).  Also they have much better art assets, if that's important to you.  Finally, unlike Millenia, their features don't feel like someone was given a check list and said "how can I possibly do the absolute minimum to check off all these requirements?".  So... Better than Millenia, except for the combat system, which makes the game unplayable.  I'm going to go ahead and copy pasta that conclusion to the top ;).  (unless of course you can avoid all combat.  One game I was in, the AI couldn't figure out how to path to me or get around Belgium (the irony) and thus just stayed at war with me without ever going on offense.  Not sure I should count that as a positive).

_childDocuments_.review: Great game and definitely has that "one more turn" feeling. I've played the Civilization series from the original in the 90's through Civ VI as well as Humankind and Millennia. Ara brings to the table it's own design, concepts, and fun factor. _childDocuments_.review: Normally I am extremely reluctant to write a review for a game that I have played so little, especially when it comes to a game as complex as Ara History Untold. In this case, I'm doing it because in my opinion the game doesn't deserve the relatively poor ratings.Ara History Untold is basically a mix of 4X, Grand Strategy and City Builder. It's been hyped as a Civ competitor, but that's a bit short-sighted even though it was developed by former Civ V developers.It brings many fresh ideas to the table, such as:- There are now regions instead of hexes. These regions are further subdivided into smaller territories. This makes the map look extremely organic and natural.- Moves are executed simultaneously. This Wego principle, familiar from Wargaming, means that all players plan their moves first and then execute these plans together and simultaneously at the end of the round. This can lead to surprising constellations and means that my plan doesn't necessarily have to work, as the opponent may have executed something completely opposite at the same time. And in principle, a turn change is so quick that you can continue seamlessly after the end of the turn.- The game has strong City Builder components. This principle was already considered by Milennia, but is implemented more consistently and radically by Ara. There are a number of production chains, some of which are quite complex. There is also a large number of buildings, some of which can be upgraded several times.- Crafting is also a fairly new idea; the production of items to improve the quality of life in cities or to improve buildings.All these new ideas alone make Ara History Untold a good game in my eyes, as they have been implemented boldly and consistently.The pros and cons at a glance:Pros:- Many new ideas, most of them relatively well implemented (see above)- Incredibly pretty graphics, especially for a game of this genre. Ara looks really beautiful. You can zoom in very close and admire the attention to detail and the scurry factor.- Complexity. This is both a pro and a con (see below). I love getting to grips with games, but Ara might overwhelm newcomers to the genre. You really have to get to grips with the game (I'm currently doing so). For me, that's a plus (but I can understand anyone who says they don't want that)- Interesting military concept with formations and adjustable tactics, although you can't actively intervene in the battles yourself. Unfortunately, the terrain does not play a role in the outcome of the battle.- A variety of different leaders are available at the start of the game.Cons:- Some players suffer from significant performance issues, which I don't have. For me, the game runs smoothly and without glitches; I have a fairly high-performance system, maybe that's the reason.- The German translation is a bit of a problem in some places.- Complexity. Ara History Untold is a very sandbox-oriented game which can be quite overwhelming as the game progresses. The micromanagement can become excessive and degenerate into click work. Quality of Life improvements are still missing to make life easier. But you should know that before you get involved with Ara.- Absolutely rudimentary diplomacy options. The diplomatic options are extremely limited. Wars can be declared, trade agreements can be concluded, gifts can be given and borders can be opened or closed. That's it in principle. That is not a lot. In addition, the relationship between the AI opponents and the player seems to improve or deteriorate more or less randomly and, above all, for no reason. Ara's diplomacy system explains nothing. However, there are several types of wars. Explaining this now would go too far.- Some players, who have played much more than I have, complain about the poor AI, which is typical of the genre. But I can't say too much about that yet.Well, I think that some of the cons can be fixed with patches.So who is the game for?I think it's mainly for players who want to work their way into a game. I also think that someone who likes Paradox games is in good hands here. You definitely get that One More Turn feeling.Ultimately, my positive assessment is very subjective; I can understand anyone who says: I don't like it that much.I also wrote a positive review this early to trigger the positive review algorithm of Ara History Untold. Because the game deserves it in my eyes.

_childDocuments_.review: You ever play Civ or a Civ-like game and think, Ok let me count how many hex away from this city should I build this new city? Ara says "Thats not how city work"In ara Feel more connected to your city and your resourcesYou can't city spam because there is a City limit based on government type, so each city is important. You want them all to be successful, and you have to thoughtful place them near good resources, to get access to those resources. Also the City growth system isn't just 3 hex from city center. You can grow into all sorts of goofy snake shapes!Ever play Civ or Civ-like game and think, Oh look it's peppers I don't have duplicates of that, so I will build a city near it to get the + to happiness? Ara says "Thats not how Resources work"In Ara some resources are more valuable then others. This means that getting a duplicate of a grain resource can help you make more bread, which can be used as an amenity to increase growth of cities.Ever play a Civ or Civ-like game and think, Oh I guess the enemy is about to declare war on me, they have 10+ units stacked around my border? Ara says "Thats not how war works"In Ara you have a Force cap, meaning you can't just spam units and send them in a death line at your enemy. You build units that sit in the reserves, and when you need them you can muster the troops. It makes your military units more important so you don't want to waste them, since there is a delay in bringing the troops out. Plus them game wants you to build battalions (Unit stacks) that get bonus based on the composition of them.Ever play a Civ or Civ-like game and think, I have to  build all the wonders as fast as I can for the BONUS! My nation will have all the ancient world wonders! Ara says "Thats not how wonders work"In Ara a "Wonder" gives a nice unique bonus, but takes up an entire "Region" You don't just have infinite Regions. As a city grows you can add more regions to your city, each on gives somewhere between 2 to 5 districts. Each district can be used to build buildings that give very good bonuses. Building a "wonder" eats that entire region (thats 2-5 building slots) So you only want a "wonder" that benefits your current play style. Even then you have to balance is this wonder better than 2 to 5 buildings?

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a mixture of Anno, Civilisation and Total War though, the battles are automated unlike Total War. The game is very hard. I have been eliminated twice after only two ages advanced. Neither Spain nor Belgium survived into the early middle ages. I can build the largest city in the game even whilst behind everyone else but prestige gain is another matter entirely. The scope of the game is vast and I prefer this game to civilisation. I have barely touched the surface right now but I am keen to learn how to be a powerhouse. I did not realise we could be eliminated simply by lack of technological/prestige advancement which isn't an issue overall. The game is very beautiful and the game is going to be backed by Oxide into the future. This game is more like a mountain than a country walk. Having died twice in two games on easiest level makes me very happy to have the hardest levels which should actually be a very tough challenge. Overall 10/10 so far.

_childDocuments_.review: There is a lot to like about this game but at this time I cannot recommend it. The economic system is fun at first but as you progress through the game it becomes less fun and more tedious. After about three cities it is almost unbearable due to the amount of micromanagement needed and navigating the clumsy UI makes it even more difficult. It could easily be streamlined to make it more tolerable imo. If you are a hardcore economist, then this might be your game.Combat is incredibly bad. Units are placed into formations. Once placed, that's it. You cant upgrade them or restructure them.  Once in combat there is no retreat. It's all or nothing.  Wars can end without any notice. My opponent decalred war on me. I built a superior force and entered his city and war was ended and units teleported to my nearest city. I had no say in the matter. The whole combat/war system needs to be overhauled. Oh and the watch battle option is laughable.As for performance, I have had no issues and the game runs smooth. It looks good and there some nice touches if you zoon in on the regions. There is a lot to like about the game, but the combat and micro management just takes away the enjoyment. I hope they make some changes to these systems. Time will tell.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Not a bad game, also not worth the price. All the civs feel the same and the gameplay is the same every game. I like the multitude of resources and buildings, which unlike in Humankind is done decently in this game. The politics is really boring and the ai keeps declaring random wars when they're on the other side of the world.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Whoof. There's interesting stuff to like here? The *idea* of building up an economy that requires resources both feels more majestic as well as actually pushes you to compete for specific space on the map because that space has the thing you need to satisfy your people. But it suffers for three things:First, the balance between science and city production is out of whack. Even segregating industries and doing as little duplication as possible still leaves your cities massively behind as buildings take on average 10 turns to build while techs whiz by at 3-4 turns each. The sheer amount of stuff you can build becomes overwhelming, as the amount of stuff you actually build is paltry.Second, the combat is *weird*. No unit upgrading. Once units are tied to a formation, they exist there forever, so no breaking up an army to re-form it or add in more modern troops, you have to rebuild it from scratch. Spearmen vs. tanks are apparently the natural order of things.Finally, and the real deal-breaker, is that it's just so damned *tedious*. I've discovered how to make a workshop! Now, because it gives bonuses to things in the same region it is in, and because each city has ten or so regions, I'll need to open up my city, scroll through the list of regions, click on the potential site to build, and then scroll through the side menu of dozens and dozens of buildings (because nothing ever is obsolete) and click to build it. And then once I've built it, I need to scroll-click-scroll-click to build the next thing. But wait! My workshop isn't producing anything. So I need to scroll to find it again. Click to select it. Click 1 - 4 boxes to set up production, each of which opens a drop-down menu. And then click 1 - 4 boxes to add tools through a dropdown menu into the workshop to make it work better. So each turn is actually scroll-click-scroll-click-scroll-click-click-click-click-click-click-click-click. Ah, but now it's producing things that upgrade other buildings, so every turn it produces I also need to click on the separate menu to show buildings, scroll to find the building, click on the box, click on the drop down menu. So each new building is scroll-click-scroll-click-scroll-click-click-click-click-click-click-click-click that starts a chain of scroll-click-click every turn and of course you don't have just one workshop, you have six, so a single turn becomes  scroll-click-scroll-click-scroll-click-click-click-click-click-click-click-click-scroll-click-click-scroll-click-click-scroll-click-click-scroll-click-click-scroll-click-click-scroll-click-click to just deal with all of the production and you haven't made a *single ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ decision* in all of that. It's just exhausting. It's like one of those cheap phone Object Sorting games except the objects are pre-sorted and there's no time pressure, you just have to drag them to the boxes over and over and over and over again. And for every few minutes of that, you get to make a single strategic decision. I put a lot of time in trying to find fun in setting things up, and it's just not there.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: I don't remember the last time I had to play a game this long to figure out whether or not it's good or bad.Ara is poorly designed. It has all the pieces that need to be there for a good game, but they seem to just be thrown together in ways that only just barely hold together, and even that only sometimes.All of the details of how it looks and feels are exactly what you would want for a Civ competitor. It has a depth that Civ does not have. But it's like someone just took a bunch of game mechanics and put them in a big bag and shook it up real good.It's hard to imagine the design process that would have resulted in something like this. It is as if someone was given a list of everything that should be in the game, and put everything on the list into the game, and did not even once think about whether or not they would work together or how.Really something special that will be studied for a long time in game design classes, I think. But not good. Unfortunately.

_childDocuments_.review: Bought this game with my money!WARNING: THIS GAME IS TRASHPositives:1. At times, this games visuals make you really enjoy the game. 2. The music in the game is very good.3. I did not encounter any bugs or crashing4. The system they are implementing works as they intended.Negatives:1. The game seems unfinished. Much of the art or visuals at some places look amazing and other places look outdated or incomplete.2. The music may be very good but doesn't compare to Civ6 or other games that rope you into the country with music makes you embrace your civ.3. The system they have implemented does work as intended and that is my biggest issue. The game is quite detailed but at the same time too rushed. They claim you can create a civilization any way you like but if you do not do what they think is best your civilization falls behind and you lose. This is pretty stupid considering that some nations like the United States were not around until late in human history and have become a superpower quickly. So, why make me rush through history and not enjoy it? After several plays and attempts to balance what I want to do and what the system demands, I found that the way I want to play is contrary to the game, therefore, I lose. I shouldn't be forced to expand to early, go to war to early, etc. I should be able to focus on alot of many things, domination, expansion etc. Yet, if you focus on domination you are limited by the turns you can war. Your war ends right when you are on the cusp of victory and have to wait to declare war again to actually defeat your enemy as they start to rebuild an army to hold back your next wave of attackers. The combat system is too basic, boring and subpar compared to other games I have played. The politics are boring and it is the same exact actions by the enemy over and over. The event system is not random but sequential and every event happens every time in the same order depending on your choices etc. yet, there are so many things you have to do to maintain your country, your army, build resources and such that for a game that says i can be whom i want and develop the nation how I want i found that when I am aggressive, they don't give me military advisors, when i try to expand or grow, they don't provide me with advisors focused on growth, etc etc. Conclusion: I tried to like this game, but it is simply not very good. I tries to make you like it with a great intro and visuals that soon fall apart once you start the game. The game doesn't feel like a 2024 top notch civ game but something I would play about 10 years ago. It is clunky, unfinished, boring, too complex where things should be simplified and to simple where things should be complex. The event system is substandard and gets annoying every 5 turns when they ask you a question that they have asked you every game you have played and already know the answer for the best outcome. A little variety would be nice.  Everything I think the developers planned and wanted to do in this game they have accomplished with little effort in regards to quality and actual game testing. I regret buying this game after reading the reviews and giving them a chance. I held off originally waiting to see when Civ7 would release. However, after playing this game, I have found that not only do I hate this game with a passion due to all the dumb development decisions and the lack of execution on any part of this game that I now wonder if when CIV7 comes out that they will have the same problems as this game. I DID NOT FEEL LIKE I WAS THE ROMANS or ANY NATION WHILE PLAYINGI COULD NOT GET INTO THE GAME THEMATICALLYI FELT LIKE IT WAS BORING AND EXCESSIVELY COMPLEX IN ALL THE WRONG PLACESI FELT IS WAS SIMPLISTIC AND DRAB I ALL THE WRONG PLACES.Save your moneyThis is the first review on STEAM I can remember ever writing and that should tell you something. I actually went out of my way to write a review to warn you not to buy this incomplete and trash game.
