_childDocuments_.review: This game has been in my sight for a while, and now that I have finally beaten my first game, I can say without a doubt that it acomplishes the "one more turn" itch in ways few other Civ-influenced titles can reach. Just on that alone I can easily recommend it, but if you're browsing the reviews far enough to see mine, you could probably do with something more than "it's fun, I recommend it", so let me help you by giving you all the relevant information I can think of.Ara, at it's barest, is a non-fantasy civilization building 4X game not unlike other games such as, well, Civilization or Humankind. In it, you choose a leader that represents a group of people, after which you're dropped in a wild, untamed world with the task of making your nation the most memorable human civilization to ever exist. Each game is divided in three different acts that cover different eras of human history (prehistory - middle ages -  age of machining being the cutoff points), with the caveat that half of the nations at play removed from play permanently as their cities turn to ruin and their armies become bandits. You must earn enough prestige to make the pass to the next act - and hopefully, end up first. How you do it depends on what you do: military conquest, building monuments, spreading your religion, and having strong industries, among others, will all net you points, so you have a great deal of freedom to play around.First of all, of course, comes the very good question of "how does this game run?", and the answer is - it's finnicky. I'm not too good when it comes to the technical aspects of videogames, so I will share my experience - the game lagged horribly until I turned lighting and MSAA (I think that's the term) to the minimum settings avalaible. Once I did it, the game ran at a decent frame speed, even if it lagged whenever I flew over my capital at medium height late game. Hopefully the devs patch it eventually, but if you have issues, try doing that. First things first, you choose a leader. Like in Civ, the game is not limited to a single leader; Germany, for instance, has two possible choices for their leader, as does Greece if you buy in launch (unless they eventually make Alexander the Great a "normal" DLC). UNLIKE Civ, however, not all of these leaders are political leaders; among the cast of playable characters you have poets, scientists, activists for Indigenous rights, as the representative of the Cherokee; and for a more concrete example, as an alternative to Bismarck as the German character, you have Hildegard von Bingen, German prioress and Saint from the Middle Ages, as a research - and - religion alternative to good ol' "Blood and Iron". Each leader has different traits and specializations, so you might spend some time browsing to see which one suits your preffered playstyle better. Once you choose, you have an option to use a different color/model (with DLC) swap, and thus you start your first game.Once you start, you'll realize that, even with your city in it's infancy and barely any improvements, there's a lot going on; birds flying around, animals grazing, rivers moving, etc. This is part of the so touted "Living World" the developers promoted so much, and I am happy to report it lives up to it's name, as there is a lot of things going in both inside and outside cities; Wildlife moving around, flocks of birds, air vehicles (going from balloons to zeppelins to planes) flying over your cities, cargo ships leaving and entering your ports, citizens just walking around the cities in ridiculous groups of people, racoons and similar animals walking around, dogs (which you can pet by clicking on them, this earns you an achievement), and cars that change depending on what era you are in. This feel is helped by the fact that the game world is divided in regions and subregions rather than hexes, so as your cities grow, their shape changes to acclimate the regions they find themselves in. It's just a joy to see how much a place changes from a wild, untamed forest into a thriving, modern city full of modern farms, factories and skyscrapers, to see how cities change cosmetically as you survive the different acts. I do recommend spacing your cities quite apart, as by the end game I had an issue where most of my cities blocked eachother from attaining new regions. They can get quite big!At first, Ara's economy is very basic; you have food, wood, science, wealth and materials, which are used to build improvements that increase that specific region's yield (each region has a passive resource yield whenever you annex them to your cities; say, you annex a plain that produces four food per turn. If you build a farm on it, you increase the amount of food yields you get per turn), and dwellings that increase population caps for cities. However, the BIG thing that makes Ara different from it's competitors is the usage of consumer and strategic goods, and these are exploited via crafting improvements. Early on they are not that big - you can craft jewelry or "feasts" and use them to give buffs to your city's five stats (happiness, health, knowledge, wealth and security), and you can further spend materials to increase the speed at which these are produced (using precious stones you're getting from a mine to make jewel production go from six turns, for instance, to four). As the game goes on, however, you can unlock more recipes, and these recipes give DRAMATIC buffs to your buildings. It will get prohibitively to fund everything just with wealth (which is the most common option to increase crafting times), so you are encouraged to seek more resources. For example: a farm gives you 30 food per turn. Your city is generating -200 food per turn, so the population is stuck at that level, and thus you cannot annex new regions, which prevents you from both getting new resources you really REALLY need AND building space you're running out of, so you build a power plant, a vehicle factory, and a regular factory in a different city. You have access to natural gas, coal and rubber thanks to resource extractors you have in other cities, so you can invest coal and gas for the power plant to generate power faster (approximately +2000% faster) and the rubber to produce tractors faster at the vehicle factory; this reduces the output of resources of these extractors by 1 or more per turn, but now the power plant produces 2.5 electricity per turn and you get a tractor every three turns rather than six. After three turns, you equip a heavy plow, fertilizer, electricity and the tractor on the farm, boosting it's production to, let's see, 170 food per turn. While you were making these upgrades, however, you've redirected most of your steel output (which is also one such craftable) to fridge production at your factory. You have three fridges, which you equip in three of your city's dwelling upgrades, with each fridge providing a passive bonus of 50 food per turn. Now the city goes from -30 food per turn to 120 in the positive, giving you access to two regions in a single turn each. As you go on, a lot of your time in-between turns will be a careful balance between the resources you get per turn and where you invest them to craft materials and consumables you really need.These are the big things. I would like to go into more detail (like the military), but I have unfortunately run into Steam's character limits, so feel free to ask me anything in the comments you might be curious about. As a final point, a heads up for those who are like me: you cannot keep playing a save as a sanbox after winning or reaching the end. Here's hoping the devs eventually add an option to do so, but at the time of writing, it's my biggest issue with the game.

_childDocuments_.review: i wanted to like this game really much but i can t.The formula sound like something that was made for me. My focus in 4x games is economy and city building and i really love the concept of production lines. But nothing in this game seems to be really thought through. I like complexety and micromanagement but this has nothing to do with complexety. Its just tedious.i tried some rounds, got my ass beat till i settled on difficulty "prince" and played a game till round 240 (being in midage). And at this point i am just done.What do i like?- The production lines are a fresh system in this genre and on paper i really like the idea- They also found a way to have the goods being used into each other or consumed from the cities where it felt comfortable for me to use them even though they basically are consumables (and i am one of those guys who ends games with 99 potions because they could need them later...). ##To give an example... your city uses 1 Bread to give some buffs for 10 rounds. Therefore it consumes 0,1 bread per round. Now you can build a bakery that produces 1 bread out of thin air in 30 rounds. If you give them 1 corn per round and equip the bakery with tools it goes faster and manages to produce a bread every 8 rounds. So that city can sustain itself to have that buff forever and produces a surplus for other cities. I REALLY love that concept.##- also most shops and districts can be upgraded with different goods, that make them do their stuff faster or give boni to the cityBUTThe problem(s)- That concept is fun at the early game when you have 1 to 4 cities. But when you get up to 7+ Cities its unbearable. - Its not complexety, its just annoying when you have to klick through 2-3 windows for every building to check what its producing right now or change the goods it uses (there are regions for up to five buildings per region and my cities had mostly around 10 regions per city...)     - and yes, there are windows to summarise that but they too don t give you much more of a fast overview- The UI is horrible. Everything looks stale and has no real charakter. The windows are looking like they are from 2010. Everything is full of small text and looks just sterile (and i know... we are talking about microsoft here... they literally named their system after these things...) but it just looks horrible and doesn t help with the overview at all- and talking about looks. I know that maybe is a hot take but i think the graphic at all looks bad... I like to see the buildings and people wander around but everything looks kind of... cheap? Again no character in anything- especially everything regarding millitary     - arrows look like rain, all hitting exactly one spot and even that spot follows animals around while they walk    - Units just stand awkward in a square inside the region, not interacting or even colliding with anything    - the "battleview" is literally just a video you can start, that shows every unittype  repeating their fightanimation for     some seconds(i try to keep it shorter at this point)- Millitary at all isn t thought trough (no retreat, no unit upgrading, no way to change units inside a formation after its on the field ever again... you can only kill them so the slot is empty to build new ones- combat at all is dull- diplomacy isn t really a thing other than some events to chose one of 3 options (and war)- Leaders are boring (just different numbers and boni, no special buildings or units at all)- overall everything looks and feels cheap and clunky. It has cool ideas... but none feel like someone thought them to the end and how they actually playi really looked forward to this game... and i am sad to be this disappointed by it. I had fun... but its just not good and not ready to be played... sadly...

_childDocuments_.review: I hate to say it, but this game really disappointed me.I was hoping for a game to fill the void that Civ left when it started going full in on being awful with it's greedy monetization, and I got a game that ended up ruining all the hype I had for it, by just being a game about micromanagement. I like 4X games, and despise Economy games, and this game marketted itself as a 4X when it's really a City Building Economy game that pretends to be a 4X.Was hyped for weeks leading up to it's release hoping it would be able to learn from the failings & successes of the other 4X franchises like Old World, Endless Legend, Humankind & Civ. But it hardly feels like a 4X game, by turn 50 I was so bored I had started skipping turns waiting for things to build, and by 80 I just closed the game and did literally anything else. It's a game fit for people who want an economy simulator and not an actual 4X game, and it's not something I can enjoy.And it's not because the game is bad, There is a LOT to love here with how it has a uniquely human, the storytelling elements of the game, the actually extremely good leader selection & it's lovely graphics & watching the town be built overtime. But the good graphics really don't supplement the really poor gameplay. It's not a 4X or Grand Stategy, it's a micromanagement simulator, and not even one I can sink my teeth into for hours. Let's take the material Rope for instance, it's a crucial component for many recipes, and many triumphs. It takes 20 turns to build, you need 5 of them for most things... Immediately that seems problematic, so you can boost them for wool or silk, but guess what? You didn't spawn near wool or silk, and despite having 2 scouts scowering the map, you still can't find these basic materials within a reasonable distance to settle. So you can't make the crucial component fast enough to match the AI who somehow can make it quicker, without the boosting materials. So you end up falling behind to the point where the AI is moving on to the Iron Age, and you're about to be culled because you spawned in a bad spot, and the game did not put crucial materials even remotely nearby.The game also spams you with events extremely often, often times not being worth it to even read the storytelling & just look at the benefits vs the drawbacks. But these events happen so often that no one event ever feels significantly worthy of even giving a second thought, so it just makes the turn take longer than it already does. The UI is actually disgustingly bad, you can't find what you need, you constantly need to look at the city screen or click on an individual building just to find what you're looking for. You never know if what you are doing is actually effecting things since there's almost no information. And because you never have the information you need, you start to fall behind without ever truly knowing why or how, I've had to assume it was my bad spawn, but what if it wasn't? Well how would I know when the only thing visible to me is that I can't make a crucial component as fast as I need it without draining my wealth, or magically finding materials no one is trading.You just don't ever feel like you are in control of your nation, nor do you feel in control of it's economy, both of which are vital in these types of games. You have to feel like the choices & decisions you make matter, and yet 80 turns in I don't think a single choice of mine made any difference to how the game was going. I feel as if irrespective of my choices, I was always going to be culled due to the spawn I was given, and the economy, a vital aspect of the gameplay, being such an awful experience to actually play.This is a game with an expected turnaround of 800+ turns, while each turn's micromanagement, especially later on I imagine this gets worse, Each single turn could take take several minutes. This is not good at all, infact, it's the opposite of good, in multiplayer it's even worse if you play without turn timers. Because it took us an hour & a half to get to turn 30.If you wanted a game that finally addressed the pitfalls of the 4X genre, and actually took it to somewhere new, this just isn't it. If you want to pretend you're playing a strategy game while actually playing a micromanagement city builder, then well, this game fits that bill.I'm sorry, I really am, I can tell there's been an enormous amount of love & care poured into every part of this game. But I just cannot find this game fun at all as a longtime fan of other 4X games, It just fundementally takes the fun & enjoyment I get out of the genre & throws it away to make the actual managing of your empire so dull and boring.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that suffers from the comparison to Civilization.  Why?  Because it's a totally different game.It's mechanics are hugely different and take some time to understand. But once you forget about thinking you play some Civ clone and play the game in it's own right you will discover that it is a fantastic game with loads of underlying mechanics, focussed on production chains and city management. I personally love that.  One thing that annoys me though is the voice over who sounds like Opray Winfrey reading from the bible.  That was indeed a lot better in Civilization!! Appart from that I would really recommend Ara: History Untold to anyone who likes a complex city/empire- builder that is slow but really nice.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: The actual game play loop in my brief play through seems really fun and scratches that Civ itch.Now, while I do see a bright future for the game - I cannot recommend in it's current state until the performance issues get sorted out, it runs like utter garbage (even on low-medium settings with an an RTX 4070), probably one of the worst game, performance wise I have played in quite a while, it's unfortunate because everything else looks awesome.Ended up refunding, but I may come back in the future when I can see the performance issues have been ironed out. I hate to leave a negative review and I will change in time, but rather people have a heads up just in case!
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Game mix different genre (Anno, civ, paradox grand strategy) and it creates an addictive gameplay where the "just next turn" feeling is there.Crafting create interesting strategies and make exploiting map even more engaging.Does it need balancing, optimizations and expansions in specific sectors (diplomacy, warfare)? Absolutely, but the fundations of the game seem strong and the developers seem really open to players feedback.Big thumb up from me.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Shout-out to TactiCat and his "ARA: History Untold - Understanding Game Mechanics" video on Youtube. This really turned the game around for me, esp on how to get the information I wanted to find. There are still some issues like the procedural maps which all seem to be single continent no matter what you pick,  or the sameness feel of the all leaders, AI needs some tweaking, but I'd like to give the makers the benefit of the doubt to fix this down the line. CIV killer it is certainly not, but it has some very good ideas, and plays much, much better than Millennia.60.- is a bit steep for what it is, but after watching TactiCat I am actually having fun.

_childDocuments_.review: too much unnecessary micromanagement.  your factory has multiple slots in which you can put multiple upgrades to improve production. The factory can produce a multiple of stuff supported by a multiple of enhancements. Ofcourse when progressing one or more of all of those things need to be changed into other stuff.There is no screen where  you can easily do all this.. you have to click on the factory then again on the stuff you want to produce etc....Oh and this methode is ofcourse for all the buildings in the game...Not worth the price and way too much work.. if you like micromanagement and civ go play EU4.besides politics and trade are a bare minimum and the war mechanics are a hughe step back after playing Humankind.about the micro:1 city has around 18 provinces which contains around 4 zones to build stuff in which equals to 72 attention zones.Per zone you have to allocate around 4 supplies, 4 improvements and 3 consumables so about 12 different values  which all can change due to research and the amount of production you have.So 72 zones x 12 = 864 factors you need to watch and change per turn and not all on the same screen or easily grouped..oh wait do that 11 x the amont of cities you can have (more with the empire) x 864 = 9.504 changable and clickable options per turn...oh and I forgot about the Aminties, 15 per city :)

_childDocuments_.review: Tl;DR; A good 0.5 version of an Early Access game, a lot more polish, optimisation and balancing is needed to make it to a fully fledged game that could rival Civ. or anything else. Wait for update 10 before buying.City building: At start it is amazing but it devolves into playing with Excel sheets. Find free land, fill free land to make number go up (resource, material...). Wonders feel so underwhelming with only localised effects (except a few that give global "meh" bonuses). Once you get to a phase where you would like to re-arange your city, oh boy... No option to replace buildings (place on existing one) except to demolish it one turn and place on second (after you forget you demolished it last turn...). Oh and the building limits are a mess (one global GENERAL hospital?). Economy: Very good concept and mechanics, but... Have you ever had 30 fish with the capacity to process only 3 because the nation has, apparently, just a very limited number of butchers per capita? Same goes with meat and other crafting. Bakeries are the next obvious one. I need to be able to scale, why else would I need 60 grain(you cannot switch grain farms to anything else) and use 6 of it for bread... Please, give me the opportunity to truly exploit. Units and combat: Oh boy. Creating units? Nice and integrated with economy (need then wheels for my chariots). Mustering units and placing them on the maps? I like it, formations and different sizes are a good idea. But after the army is created and mustered, that is it. Only thing you dan is dismiss (e.g. delete) the unit. No option to adjust formation, add-remove units, upgrade units, nothing. Combat is a good idea, but you have to gamble where the enemy units will move so you can engage them. Missing zone of control or some kind of scouting? Diplomacy: Very basic and cumbersome. If I have a trade agreement, why does it expire? Or my aliance expires and I cannot propose a new one for 10 turns?  No depth here.Overall good start, but needs a lot of work based on feedback from community and further balancing

_childDocuments_.review: This is coming from a long time 4X/strategy game player who is bit bored with the "traditional" games play.I was hoping for something new or superior to the CIV series games that became too formulaic and every play session felt the same. If you are like me, you probably will be disappointed in with this game.Not a CIV killerTo get it out of the way, comparing this game with the CIV series is inevitable. Is it better or different enough? I would sadly say no. Sure the production chain is completely different from the CIV series, but as a 4X game, not really different. It's has bare bones diplomacy, warfare, religion, and so on.I think it's more closer to simplified turn based 4X Anno.It really feels like Humankind, interesting idea but basics are all trash.The GoodProduction chain is probably the only interesting part of this game. If you love more city building or crafting type of game, you might love it.The BadAs I mentioned earlier, all the systems you think of for a 4X games are there but all of them feel like a beta, unpolished and underwhelming. For some systems, they made some baffling choices. There are no fatal issues, may be the UI, but there are so many of them that make it not fun to play. I will list some notable issues.Terrible UI: Visuals are uninteresting but isn't bad. The issue is the navigation and presentation of information. It takes too much clicks to navigate and you aren't provided information you want.There are search box in lot of places but no concise presentation, tabs, etc. to make it user friendly. It may be due to the micro management system but it really need to be redesigned from the core game play to be intuitive and user friendly.Terrible music: I rarely care about music in a game but this one I turned it off. I can't put it in words but it gets on your way.Close up sound effects of the buildings are annoying too.Bare bones systems: Diplomacy has no character, AI is dumb, and UI doesn't present information well. Warfare is weird with units being card board cutouts, needing to deploy and cannot merge after that or go back to reserves or delete reserves. Three military units, which include catapults! can die to wild animals if they don't have hunting ability. Religion is is bare bones, nothing of note.Bad graphics/design: Overall graphics are nothing of note. It kind a looks like a generation late. Buildings and units are difficult to distinguish. Map and resources overlap and difficult to navigate or even just see.Very repetitive: Yes, 4X game can be repetitive but this game is very repetitive. Production chain system forces you to do mostly same thing every game and limits in number of buildings, tiles, and cities really limit variations. Focus on the production system really forces internal affairs and not really outwards that might change the game play. Although the dumb AI and lack of events won't impact the way you play any ways.SummaryIt's yet another 4X game that just checked the boxes but really looked into what makes them good.The game has nothing to offer other than the production chain system, and that system isn't polished.It's not satisfying to tweak with the production and it's tedious to micro manage with the game's UI.All the systems seem to be under cooked and are just  not enjoyable. I guess the overall balance is bad and make the game not fun to play.They would need a core level overhaul but I would not bet on the devs will go that far.Simply said, it does not have the polish to be a good 4X game and probably won't get that polish down the line.*Updated from initial thoughts

_childDocuments_.review: Early impressions are positive.The closest game I can think of for comparison is  or , aside obviously from not having the colonization theme. I'm playing on a mid-range CPU/GPU and having zero issues running the game at stable 60 fps - but it seems like many people with better computers are having performance issues. I'm the sort of person who sees it more as "micromanagement heaven", though. But it desperately needs some better UI and QOL improvements to better deal with that.

_childDocuments_.review: ARA: History Untold Review: A Surprising Contender in the 4X GenreI’ve enjoyed ARA: History Untold far more than I initially expected. In fact, it might be a serious contender to the long-standing Civilization series. Though I was apprehensive at first, once I got over the learning curve, I found immense enjoyment in the game.One of the highlights is the attention to detail. Zooming in on the map often reveals something special or unexpected—whether it’s people and vehicles going about their business or subtle variations in building designs, even among structures of the same type. Visually, the game is well done, with impressive graphical touches that add layers of immersion.The core of the game, however, is the economy simulation, which is its real "meat-and-potatoes." It sits somewhere between the complexity of Anno and Civilization, requiring enough micro-management to keep things interesting without overwhelming the player. While supply chains are essential to success, you don’t have to worry about logistics on a granular level. I found myself spending just the right amount of time tweaking my buildings to squeeze out extra production, which felt satisfying and rewarding.Despite the depth in economic management, the game doesn’t lose that addictive "one more turn" feeling at the macro level. When things are finely tuned, I’ve caught myself hitting the space bar a few times just to get to the next major decision. This pacing keeps the game engaging in the same way Civilization does, and I can easily see myself sinking a lot of hours into it.The military and warfare mechanics, while functional, are a bit opaque. There’s a basic rock-paper-scissors system involving infantry, archers, and cavalry, along with situational modifiers and some randomness that isn’t immediately apparent unless you dig into the tooltips. The health bars are divided into green, yellow, and red segments, indicating potential damage, though I’m still figuring out exactly how to predict the outcomes reliably. With time, I’ve developed a "vibe check" for battles, but I generally avoid military engagements, so I haven’t explored that aspect as deeply.Overall, ARA: History Untold is a satisfying alternative to the Civilization genre. It has a few rough edges—mostly related to quality of life and UI issues—but I’m optimistic that these will be polished over time. I wholeheartedly recommend it for fans of 4X strategy games, as it offers a fresh take with plenty of depth and enjoyment to uncover.

_childDocuments_.review: Really deep city/nation building game with 4X elements.  I have been a fan of the Civilization series for quite a while so was looking forward to this variant of the genre.  I enjoyed Humankind, but it never completely drew me in.  This, I find very absorbing and addictive indeed - it's a beautiful looking game (but requires good hardware to work at it's best), and you really get a sense of looking down (and zooming in) at a real living world.  I'm quite new to this kind of "cratfing" mechanic, but I found myself fairly quickly getting the hang of it.However, it's not all good - the tutorial could be deeper and more thorough; the Encarta is nice (I like to read through stuff), but it seems to have gaps.  I don't think the UI is as bad as others have said - but it's a little frustrating at times (e.g. having to click on a slot in an improvement to see what can actually go there (and if you have any!).  Annoyingly, there are also some graphical glitches (maybe only on Nvidia cards?), which is a shame on something so lovely to look at.  I hope they fix these soon - there have already been a few patches so I know the developers are working hard to improve things, and I appreciate that.As others have said elsewhere, the diplomacy and combat seem quite basic, but I'm happy to just dig into the tech trees and various improvements and goods that I can produce - and trying to keep the people healthy happy and wise :)  I usually lose horrendously on these kinds of games, but surprisingly I'm doing quite well on my first game.  I hate it when games are just too damn difficult; I want to just relax and have a bit of fun.  I love the way that playing this game just feels so absorbing and welcomes experimentation; it's like playing with a super complex and beautiful toy...I do wish diplomacy was a bit more nuanced though - the AI seems to randomly take a liking (or disliking) to you for no particular reason :)Overall, yes I can recommend this - it has its faults, but it's drawn me in like no other game in recent memory.

_childDocuments_.review: Purchased and played on launch day; EDIT: Completed two plays through on lowest and second lowest difficulties.I haven't had any performance issues or graphics issues at any point; I know there have been many people noting crashes or bugs, but I've not experienced any of those.  I am playing large size worlds with 8 civilizations.Beautiful game, with detail down to flocks of birds and herds of animals- that being said, camera zoom can go a bit wonky when switching between units and your regions tend to default to the "all jumbled together" setting when you click on a city.I like the prestige system- I don't feel like I have to lock in a single style of play from turn 2.  There are tons of ways to gain prestige so your particular play style shouldn't hinder you, even if you switch from militaristic to scientific goals. I always play new strategy games on the lowest difficulty first so it gives me a chance to learn the systems without much risk.  That being said, on the lowest setting of Ara I'm steamrolling everyone in the prestige department and it feels a bit TOO easy.  EDIT: Next lowest difficulty was a lot closer in early stages, but had significant separation starting in mid-game (the game even tells you this will happen though).The military system is a bit clunky- build units that go into formations.  You can activate them as an individual squad, but cannot later add multiple units together into a formation so plan your armies accordingly.  EDIT: If you move multiple units into the same region they will combine into one unit for movement purposes, which is handy. However, they do not get the "Formation" benefits. Units also cannot be upgraded, so your earlier units will have to be disbanded in order to build more modern troops without stressing the unit cap.  Yes, there's a unit cap based on government style and a few other factors. EDIT: Unit cap doesn't seem to be an issue; waged a war to try combat and wiped out another civilization with two catapults, two swordsmen, and two bowmen. The crafting aspect worried me when I first heard of it, but I've found that I like that level of customization- with multiple items able to be crafted at each center, you can build what your cities need.  There's not a good tutorial on how to craft other than "craft this" so spend some time playing with that system.I was also worried about the city cap- in Civ, I like HUGE sprawling empires so it was initially a potential negative.  I have changed my mind- there is so much to do with each city that I've got my hands full managing the 8 I have right now.EDIT: After two full games, I will say managing food for your cities / empire is a full-time task. Use your specialists, remember your crafted items that give bonuses (plows, fertilizer, etc.) and upgrade your farms when you can.Wishlist- a more involved tutorial that does more than give vague hints about things and actually shows how the complex systems interact. A more user friendly UI.  Unlike others, I don't mind the appearance of it, but whenever your mouse pointer goes over anything a pop-up appears explaining it.  Maybe give it a delay of a few seconds since casually drawing your mouse across the screen can cause an explosion of menus.  AI improvements- they were slightly better in the 2nd tier difficulty, but still not too bright.  Possibly some color to the different civilizations aside from their bonuses- the one complaint I've heard which I 100% agree with is there's no "flavor" to the different leaders.  Giving them some personality and maybe culturally appropriate units or architecture would do wonders for the game.Initial impressions are very positive- lots of things to like about this game and I hope there's strong support for it going forward.  EDIT: I'm still very heavily positive towards this game; though the city maintenance can be annoying at times, there are always solutions to your problems...whether you're in a position to capitalize on them is a different matter.

_childDocuments_.review: The production chain/economy stuff is definitely not going to be to everyone's taste. There is a real depth to production, resources, and building up cities, and some people are finding that to be tedious rather than inspired, which I think it is.It's just choosing to focus on some different stuff from Civ, and that's clearly throwing some people.In my opinion, the steam reviews for this one don't really reflect quality, they reflect personal taste. _childDocuments_.review: As someone who has spent thousands of hours in Civilization V multiplayer with historic speed mods, and after the disappointing flop of Humankind, I can confidently say that Ara is the perfect fit for strategy fans. It's not just another rehash of the same game, but instead brings its own unique touch to the genre.The game introduces so many different and new aspects, making it feel fresh and exciting. The UI might still need some refinement, and the overlay could use some smoothing out, but these improvements will likely come with time. The graphics are impressive, far superior to the underwhelming Millennia, which unfortunately couldn’t deliver on expectations.It’s worth noting that players with AMD graphics cards may experience some issues, while Nvidia seems to run the game flawlessly. This is something to keep in mind if you're considering jumping in. Despite these small hiccups, Ara delivers a complex, rewarding experience full of micro-management for those who love deep strategy. Overall, the game is an exciting and innovative addition to the genre, and I can’t thank the developers enough for bringing it to life!

_childDocuments_.review: Legitimately good game. A bit steeper of a learning curve than your typical Civ-esque game. Combines a lot of the complex production chains you'd see in an Anno game, and an interesting means for territory expansion with regions and building slots in regions. _childDocuments_.review: let me start by saying i really wanted to enjoy this game, i did. there are some really good things about it, the way the world tiles are laid out, the way you build up cities, the crafting, they really got that part pretty good. the biggest issue though, and the reason for the cant recommend is that the pacing of the game is terrible. there are a few things that go into this issue. 1. the only real win objective is prestige points, which makes the game essential a next turn clicker as you queue everything up and just wait for your next tech to unlock and reset your queues accordingly. the lack of diverse win objectives essentially makes the game boring as you really have no reason to really explore the game. 2. making and deploying units takes forever, which removes a lot of the interacting with the actual world. you also cant upgrade your units so it makes it wasted time spent and since the pacing is so bad to begin with, it really misses the mark badly. 3. there are so many different crafting options and then having to add crafted items to each building generally becomes a slogfest. having to click every box for every building to make sure you got the right item on it, the ui for that part is extremely unintuitive and grindy. you put this on top of the games only real objective to get to x turn to get your point total scored and it just feeds into the boringness. overall like alot of games nowadays, tons of potential but, its not worth the effort or money right now which is sad because there isnt really a good 4x game out right now. civ looks like a train wreck so ara was the real hope to be the one to go with.UPDATEim really trying to like this game, i really want to. i have put more hours in and so far what i have found is more negative. even on the largets map setting, i can see the left and right side of the map from my capital, the world is really really really small. havent made any boats yet because the absolutely tiny map has no need for them. really hard to grow and explore when you can see everything within 2 screens. game is getting duller by the moment, the lack of interaction with the world is the worst part of it. seeing now how small the world is, i can understand why they slogged down units. you could call it a city management game more then a 4x game and it would still be lacking as the crafting is tedious but mostly set it and forget it, with minimal effort i am outpacing the ai nations by double. (playing on middle difficulty as this is my first playthrough)unless oxide makes some big changes, i cant see this game being worth more then 80% off sale and even then it gets stale quickly.

_childDocuments_.review: Damn this game is pretty, and I like the removal of the lowest aspiring civs at certain points in the game. I just wish the game play was less tedious. Instead of focusing on geo politics and what neutral villages I was going to focus on, I was deciding should my workshop be building rope or chairs which inevitably becomes a decent amount of your game play. Another issue I noticed is that civs are mostly just diversified by number buffs instead of unique game play. I find that odd because apparently the devs came from Civ 5 which had some super unique civs to play as. It would be nice if each civ had something a bit more unique as far as units or playstyle. _childDocuments_.review: ARA is a very interesting fresh take on the classic historical 4x formula.  The living world is amazing your cities are full of people going about their daily lives and you can zoom in to an incredible level of detail.The core loop of crafting items to feed back into your cities and crafting buildings is very addictive.  For example your workshop crafts a tool which is then used as a supply to increase the crafting rate of the workshop.  Or another example a second workshop crafts baskets which is used as a supply for a dwelling which permanently increases production in the city, baskets can then be used by the city itself as a consumable that increases production for 10 turns.Combat is also interesting you can build formations that provide certain bonuses.  Also when you build units they go into your reserve but then they are deployed in formations from whatever city you want which provides a nice bit of flexibility.  The actual combat mechanics themselves are basic rock/paper/scissors type counters which is simple but effective.  Trade is interesting  each trade route (represented by merchants) allows you to import 1 good (either ingredients for crafting or a usable item) so for example if your not great at making pottery you can import pottery from other nations).The game just had a huge 1,1 update which dealt with some of main criticisms at launch mainly unable to upgrade military units and no overall crafting management screen.  Its also worth stating that the devs have stated that there will be 1 year of free significant updates.The core of the game is excellent there are area's for improvement (diplomacy and trade needs more depth and the civs need more asymmetry) however as stated above the devs have shown they are reacting quickly to player feedback and delivering on it so I would be confident these issues will be dealt with as part of the year of free updates (in fact they already have mentioned this).

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the many gripes I have with this game, I'm giving it a thumbs up. A dsiclaimer first: Civilization kind of spoiled me. I started my 4X journey with Civ 5, the Beyond Earth and then came Civ 6. Civ 6 is my favorite 4X game so far (and by far), due to its puzzly nature. Maybe that is the reason I've also become an avid board game enthusiast over the past couple of years (mostly medium und heavy games), who knows.Anyway, after 1000 hours of Civ 6 I was looking for some new 4X experiences, but neither Humankind, nor Endless Legend nor the most recent entry, Millennia, were able to fully meet my requirements.Ara, however, is a different beast. The efficiency puzzle it presents is one I really, REALLY enjoy and that design element alone will probably keep entertained until the much anticipated (at least by me) Civ 7 will release next year. The carfting system the whole "slot this here to increase production of item X to be able to supply it to this building and increase production of item Y, which I can then use for thing Z" is just *Chef's Kiss* Then there are some "meh" design choices in Ara that I wish were a little more fleshed out or just slightly tweaked. For one, the leaders and wonders are just super bland. Not in a graphical kind of way, but in design. I mean, I like flat bonuses and percentage increases as muh as the next guy, but the unique bonuses (you know, not the traits, those are fine) could have been way, way more interesting. Where are the leaders that let me break the game's rules? Where are the wonders that allow me to do stuff that I can only do when building that specific wonder? Come on guys, show a little more creativity. Combat also seems fairly uninteresting and uninspired. I haven't experimented much with it, though, take that with a grain of salt.And then...then there's the stuff that REALLY grinds my gears. Diplomacy is not only barebones asheck in Ara, it also super intransparent. I can't even tell, what reasons my AI rivals have for disliking me. Or why they go from "friendly" to "close" to "I'mma burn your empire to ground!", in that order, within a few turns. Or why their leader keeps giving me gifts evey other turn, while our relations keep going down in quality... None of that makes sense and diplomacy needs a big overhaul if Ara wants to rival the greats in this genre.Speaking of intransparent: some of the numbers the game calculates, like research for example, aren't well explained either. Oh, I'm getting this much research from this city. But how does that number come about? X research per y number of citizens, affected by modifiers? I don't know and the game doesn't tell me. Maybe I'm spoiled by Civ, where I could always tell how wxactly my income was composed...the prstige system, while interesting and reminiscent of accumulating victory points in board games, does have a bit of a runaway leader problem and takes any form of excitement out of the mid and late game. Maybe some tweaks could be done here to make for more enthralling third acts. So, overall, the game in its current state deserves its "Mixed" rating here on Steam. If you like complex puzzle solving and don't mind the challenge of super erratic AI competitors (or plan on exclusively playing this in MP), this game might be for you.I do hope, however, that Oxide will continue development and make the right tweaks to some of the aspects I mentioned here to make this a truly great 4X game.

_childDocuments_.review: I have kept a close eye on ARA since it was announced, and I am thoroughly impressed with the result that we received. There are still pitfalls, and I will mention them, but I'll be playing ARA for many months and years to come.This game **IS NOT** a Civilization clone or a Civilization killer. The pitfalls of that marketing, whether on purpose or by accident, are starting to show - and many players are not giving this game the fair shot it rightfully deserves because of it. This game is a mixture of 4X, City Builder, and Grand Strategy, and a far cry from what Civilization is. If you buy this game, go into it knowing that you won't only be managing your cities like you do in Civilization, but also its zones, economies, and industries at micro levels.I'm going to first hit on a couple of major points for both positives and negatives that I've experienced in my campaigns so far:+ Its immersion is amazing, and you can tell the development team put time and effort into every little detail to make the game map feel as alive as possible. Being able to click on people that are idle and them wave at you, being able to click on the dogs and pet them, are just some of the examples of minuscule details that set ARA apart from other games.- Performance can be a problem sometimes, namely when you first load into a game or zoom in on your settlements. With settings changes, especially on NVIDIA cards (both in-game and in the NVIDIA control panel), you can mitigate that and have a smooth experience. However, I hope to see the development team continue to push fixes and improve the game's performance.+ Industry, like that of ANNO 1800 for example, is a huge part of what sets ARA apart from the rest. Even the simple fact that they have managed to combine that micromanagement aspect with the high-level city management of many games in the 4X genre is impressive. Personally, I have loads of fun just learning about the industries and how to maximise their usefulness in your settlements. I understand that may not be for everyone, however.- While industry is a fun positive, and once you get used to it you can kind of just figure out what things you need to make, the UI for Crafting and Industry could use some work. It gets confusing sometimes, especially the more modifiers a building or zone has, to determine how or what to craft the items you need to improve those buildings/zones. If you play enough, you can get used to it, but obviously there is much more that can be done to make it more accessible right from the very beginning of a campaign.Some other positives that I personally enjoy that also set ARA apart from the rest in an increasingly competitive strategy genre are:+ Instead of being a hex grid, the map is made up of irregularly shaped zones. This makes the game much more immersive, and gives decisions on what buildings to place much more validity in the grand scheme of things.+ The scoring system is flexible, and allows many paths to victory - as well as the option to "cull" civilizations that aren't doing well at the end of each act. You can turn that off for human players in the Advanced Settings. Personally, I would like to see an option to turn it off completely, just to see how a game would go with everyone still in it at the beginning.+ The crafting system is comprehensive, and while it can be a bit much sometimes, it's much more fun and immersive than just bundling all of the goods into one resource like "Consumer Goods".+ Non-linear Tech Tree that you can choose what techs you want to research, in whatever order you want to research.+ Truly simultaneous turns, so (at least in singleplayer) you aren't waiting a long time for AI civilizations to finish their turns.To conclude, I've played a lot of strategy games and am a fan of most of the ones I play. However, most of them get played for a little bit, and maybe I'll come back to them with an update. ARA breaks that mold, however, and all I can think about when I'm playing is "one more turn", which very few turn-based strategy titles can do for me. I have had a huge blast with ARA thus far, and plan to play it for many hours to see what all I can accomplish. However, I would love to see Oxide continue to fix the performance and make it better. I love the game, but I don't like having to tweak video settings very often. I also would love to see them make the needed changes/improvements to that of the UI or crafting.Overall, ARA is a solid game that sets itself apart from the rest of the strategy genre. If I had to give it a number rating, I'd give it an 8/10. There's still room for improvement, and I imagine that in a year or two, ARA will be even better.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly on release day I tried it and wasn't super into it, but I decided to wait for another day when I felt in a better place to give it a chance.And I am glad I did. Made it through first 4 eras in my first run last night and into the second act. The crafting systems are insanely detailed and add a huge variety, the prestige system gives massive choice and many paths to work towards to win and less min maxing a very specific win condition like Civ series does. And the simulated living world is very cool. I actually really like the simultaneous turns system even in single player too.People need to be fair to the game, when Civ 6 launched it was a far inferior game to the current version. Millennia and Humankind had rough launches too and IMO in terms of a fun state, this game at launch is already way ahead of those 3 games at their launch state. It still needs work on it regarding the diplomacy system, a global crafting queue needs to bed implemented, and IMO more work needs to be done on the AI.In terms of the vibe of the game (not genre related) it honestly gives me empire earth vibes as much as it does Civ. And the crafting system and military systems evoke Anno as well as Paradox GSG titles.My advice is to try it on Gamepass and see if it's for you before buying here on steam, at least at the current launch state. It might not be for everyone and that is okay, no game is for everyone: GOTY as a concept is fundamentally flawed, there is no such thing as a perfect game for everyone, everyone has their own preference for their favorite game that launched that year, for example Elden Ring bored me away within first couple of hours with it. Following the masses/hive mind opinion is not a healthy mindset, you lose the ability to judge things based on your own opinion and instead base them off parroted "facts".I don't regret buying Ara at all. I'm gonna try and complete 2-3 games then will likely wait to see what near future patches add to address the issues. But a very promising start, well done devs!

_childDocuments_.review: I'd give this a neutral if steam had the option and will certainly say it's got the potential to swing to highly positive.  You'll see a lot of people dismissing negative reviews because the player was expecting another Civ game.  Well, I'd argue if you look at the game description, that's how it's being marketed which is honestly probably the games biggest problem.I want to stress even in it's current state, there's a lot of good.  The game visuals are solid.  Audio is solid.  The problem is once you start playing, it feels like they started building a Civ game, then shifted to building a city builder.  Most of the Civ aspects of the game aren't bad, but they are very basic.   After 20 hours it feels like the Civ aspect of the game is just filler for the city builder game.  Given it's being marketed as a grand strategy game, it falls flat in that regards which is why I'm going with the negative option on the review.In Ara, terrain can provide up to 4 resources.  Food, Timber, Materials, and Wealth. Here's where the first disconnect is.  How fast your city is able to build things is not affected by any of these.  Food indirectly affects it because you need food to grow.  But your city tier (aka city size) determines the base production output (meaning how fast your city builds things) and research output of your city.  While Timber and Materials are needed to make things, they have no direct impact on how fast your city builds things. This fundamentally makes no sense and means food basically trumps all.  The game has nice and distinct looking biomes but they're really largely irrelevant.Additionally this is what creates my pacing issue with the game.  Your research rate wildly outruns your ability to build things.  So your cities/improvements/buildings are forever an era or more behind your tech.  The vast bulk of city improvements are about building new resources/goods and how fast you can build those goods.  Very few of them actually buff the base output of your city so you don't really have much control over how fast your city can build improvements and how fast your empire can research tech.As a Civ style game, there's only one victory condition (prestige, basically score victory) and a set time limit.  This makes it feel like a fairly limited Civ style game.  It's got a unique 2 stage system for building and deploying troops (reserves) which is great in principle but let down but limitations and oversights.  You can build either a single troop or a formation.  Formation options vary depending on tech and limit the composition of the army but provide buffs.   That's all genuinely great.  But can't return troops to the reserves and can't make changes to deployed formations (IE upgrade or swap an archer with a crossbowman).  This includes not being able to upgrade troops.  Say you have a formation of 2 swordsman and an archer.  You've just unlocked crossbowman.  There is no way to upgrade that archer to a crossbowman.  You have to disband (destroy) the whole formation and build a whole new formation.  That's tedious when you're at peace and it's a major tactical limitation when you're at war.  You're also severely limited in how many you can have which further aggravates this.There is no espionage, diplomacy is your standard open/closed borders, alliance, research/trade agreement.  There is a religion system which includes spread, but in practice religion doesn't really seem to have any impact beyond giving you access to random buffs which don't scale based on the number of people following the religion.  If there's a benefit to spreading your religion to other nations, I haven't found it.That leads us to the production/city builder aspect.  I like both Civ style games and City Builders.  The concept here is great and to be fair is the primary thing that set it apart from other Civ style games.  The problem is how it's merged here.  Your top bar will tell you how much of a good you're producing, consuming, and your on-hand surplus.  Which again, doesn't really impact the Civ side of the game.  You also can't see from here where specifically they're being used.  Most improvements have one or more "supply" slots where you can slot a produced good of some sort to increase it's yield.  You can't see what the options are without clicking on each slot and you have to do this per improvement per city.  There's also a city level version of this as well.  This creates a micromanagement hell and the only thing saving you is the aforementioned city limit.In most city builders your production chains are purely based on buildings.  Building A produces Resource A.  Building B turns Resource A into Resource B.  Eventually you get buildings that need resources from multiple different buildings.Here you build building A and then have to choose which resource you want it to make.  You can feed the building certain resources to increase it's production output regardless what it's making.  You can also choose to feed the output resources (of varying types) to further increase.  What you can feed the building is static based on building type.  What you can feed the output depends on what you're producing.  These are again separate from how fast your city can build things.There is no automation options here, at least not that I've found.  There isn't a global policy that lets you choose "use plows on farms to increase yield" for example.  There's no global view to view/upgrade/edit buildings of various types.  None if this can be done the empire view level either.  At 4+ cities, you're either spending more time managing your production chains and consumption than exploring/fighting/civving or you're basically ignoring the production chains and trying to play a straight Civ game.  While this can largely be done, you're severely gimped doing so and at that point you'd probably be having more fun playing a straight Civ style game.To summarize I'd describe this as a city builder with an identity crisis.  It's not a BAD game but it's clearly marketed as grand strategy game.  It's not, not even a little bit.  It's a city builder with a thin empire building layer on top.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT (4th November 2024): After 108 hours, I have finally completed the game.The game is unpolished, it's more like in beta. It needs quite a lot of work in both basic patching and quality of life. It's playable, but the experiece will be suboptimal at this point. The bones are good. I hope they'll fix / actually finish the game until it dies completely. What they'll probably never bounce from are horrifyingly bad music (sound effects in general imo) and UI from 90s.Additional thoughs:Industry chains don't make sense. Manufacturing an item that would be used in another improvement as a catalyst is extremely ineffective as it adds increasingly negligible amounts of production. Example: 500 production to build a gear, that is worth 100 production acceleration. Endgame factory can either create 7,3 gears or 8,1 clocks per turn. It's simply much better to build clock directly without the gear as accelarator...Endgame improvements and experts are vastly underwhelming up to a point of uselesness, because of the city caps. Building them desn't increase the stat, because it's hard cappped. In patch notes they said they removed the caps, but I still have them in my game.Some improvement upgrades are nerfs. For example after unpgrading T2 harbor, you lose +20% general city production. That is HUGE. It affects EVERYTHING, including manufacturing, harvesting... ...everything. You just gimped your city by upgrading.EDIT (24th October 2024): Game doesn't have production overflow!!! O.o Neither in production nor in science. So many resources wasted... If you want to play optimally you need to micro per turn production according to what you are building. Plus you'll probably waste production anyway. This was solved back in 1990s... Wth...I am sorry, but I can't recommend this game at the moment.I have been trying to play this game, but at this point it's literally forcing myself. Didn't even get past medieval ages, and usually this is my favorite time.In a nutshell, the problem is the presentation.UI looks so bad I am constantly remineded of the old flop Master of Orion 3. Basic oversaturated unmatching colors, everything is blurry as hell, it's really tedious to get to the information you wan't need.Example: You make a new heavy plow. No you want to use it ofc. There is no simple way to display a list of all places where the plow would be useful (The plow field if empty or has inferior version). You need to go to each town and check all improvements there. This appiles to every action every turn.It's rather hard to determine what to build in the city and where to build it. The zones are hard to discern, especially in bigger cities so you have to kind of cross reference zones view with the bonuses on the map. It's slow and boring. A simple yields summery in each region would have sufficed.Basic formulas are obfuscated. For example you see City production but you don't see the derived three productions that are actually used to calculate stuff. Such as harvest producton, craft production and build production. This is definietely a niche game. You need to optimize as hell. And so we want to know how stuff works and what are the formulas. How much food will I get when I build a farm here? I managed to decipher it and posted the formula for others, but what the hell...Music... Oh, music... ...why... ...just why....??? /riverOfTearsBest I could do was to turn it off. Much preferable to that ...cacophony. Horrible. Horrible. Often a mix of several overlaying discordant tunes.Army. Why can't we send units back to reserves or upgrade them? This is such a bad design decision.Positives:The map iteslf is very nice. I love it. It's very alive. Regions and zones are asymmetric. Best I have seen.The production based economy is very interesting. In principle I like it a lot. It's just.. ...the presentation.Need to minmax so the choices matter.I don't think they can bouce back from the horrible UI and music. Another great game ruined by poor artiststs. Seems they were hired based on some political quota rather than on their merits...

On same settings, for few times I've got good amount of resources. For next attempt about 70% of sectors contained something. Next 3 times in hudge area around capitol ther was ~4 resources.6. Units movement is too slow. That mechanic to stop on boarder, use another turn to pick up resources or attack animal is just not. Even when having movement speed bonus it seems to do nothing.7. Production chain is very complex, but only way to find it out is to check description of every single item and remember all that mess.For such a high price I would expec AAA game, but got indie-ish beta production. _childDocuments_.review: This game shows a lot of promise and I will certainly have a go at it again after it has a year or so of polish. The complexity and innovation is great, and the developers deserve support. I hope this goes on to establish itself as a franchise and feel it is in a different lane from games it is inspired from like Civ, Anno etc.The principle reason I can't recommend this game is the UI and presentation. The game just doesn't present the things that are important well enough to make it playable or sufficiently graspable. If you are keen to really dig in and learn something complex without your hand being held at all then maybe this could be a plus for you. _childDocuments_.review: It's nice to have a fresh alternative to Civ, but I think this one needed a bit longer to cook. The abandonment of hexes was a great idea; it makes the map look much more interesting. But the crafting system really bogs everything down, making it an absolute slog trying to fight the UI and figure out what's crafting what, where, and what things need. Technologies getting abandoned when you advance to the next age can also really screw you over - late game my cities were constantly starving, because I missed the technology that granted the third-tier farm.The AI players were nonsensical; there was no way to get any gauge of personality from them, and I eventually gave up on trying to even interact with them when the relationship would decay so quickly that any benefits were lost within a handful of turns.After two games, I'm about ready to uninstall and wait a year or two to see if things have improved. But unfortunately, by then, Civ 7 will have released. So I'd have to say, give this one a pass.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: If you like Civilization and need something to slake your thirst until Civ 7 comes out, ignore this review and the game it's attached to, there is nothing for you here.Now to judge this game on its own merits, I just need to ask you one question: ; Skill issue on my part, I guess.Like every other game of this type (you know them all) the AI buckles under the weight of the mechanics.I danced with the tutorial for a bit before trying my first real game on the normal difficulty, and gave up some time shortly before Act 3 kicked in. I had more Win-The-Game Points (and almost every other stat, for that matter) than all the other players  and so it seemed pointless to continue teching up through the Atomic age while everyone else is still struggling to figure out what a Trebuchet is.With a bunch of friends all playing, you could probably find some enjoyment in the crafting system and the resource management aspects of the game (aka, the entire game), but if you want to duke it out with some buddies for land and resources, you'd be better off playing a Total War title, and if you want to Simcity your civilization to be the bestest thing ever amongst pals, just keep playing Civ.Playing this game solo is a good practice run for learning its mechanics, but even on the absolute hardest difficulty the AI can't do a damn thing right.  ~ For an example of how poor the AI is: One of the very first improvements you can build on a tile is a Farm, which generates more food on areas that  more food (obviously) as well as an additional boost for having multiple Farms being placed together in the same area. This was something I didn't do much on my first game, but on my second game I made sure to hit up those 4x Food tiles (the highest I've seen) with a bunch of farms all next to each other for the huge and easy bonus it gives. The AI, regardless of the difficulty setting, almost never does this, instead choosing to spread them out over multiple inefficient spots. I get that the AI shouldn't be perfect, but since the game's apparent entire point is resource management, you'd think they'd be able to handle something as basic as the first resource you start gaining. ~It is so unbelievably easy, a point that I stress because I see it as the most important.If a game is not providing a challenge, then why am I playing it?The graphics? They are okay at best, and lazy everywhere else.I'm sure it took a lot of patience to craft all those minor animations for the tiny people walking around your towns, and making sure they all have intelligent pathfinding, but then they skimped out on the leader animations by having around 10-ish stock body types that are recycled for the whole cast - Seeing Genghis Khan rubbing his hands together like Randall from Recess was particularly amusing.The music isn't memorable, the vibe doesn't evoke anything beyond what Civ does, and if you want to chill out and manage a town for a while, there are hundreds of other offerings on here that are much cheaper, and better.Also it will take you more than 2 hours to figure this out, so ignore this review at your peril - You won't get that refund~

_childDocuments_.review: I am SO disappointed in this game that I was really excited to try out. This game is not worth $60. This is maybe a $9 game at this stage. _childDocuments_.review: As a long-time fan of 4X strategy games like Civilization and Humankind, I was really excited to dive into Ara: History Untold, expecting a fresh take on the genre. Was wondering, why the marketing of the game was mostly silence. Unfortunately, my experience with the game left me deeply disappointed, primarily due to its abysmal performance, even at the lowest settings.I’m running a fairly powerful rig—nothing cutting-edge with 6700 XT, but more than capable of handling modern titles. Games like Civilization VI and Humankind run smoothly, providing decent smooth frame rates throughout entire playthroughs, no matter how large or complex the map gets. In stark contrast, Ara: History Untold struggled from the very first turn.On medium settings at 2K resolution, the game was crawling at a miserable 30-40 FPS, and that’s just at the start when there’s barely anything happening on the map. As soon as I began expanding and exploring, the frame rate continued to dip, making the gameplay feel choppy and unresponsive. The performance was so bad that I dropped to low settings just to make it somewhat playable—and even then, the experience was far from smooth. Playing at 2K on low settings should not be this painful in a game like this, where other 4X titles with much more intricate visuals and gameplay run flawlessly at the highest settings.To add insult to injury, while the game’s graphics might seem visually appealing at a glance, whatever artistic flair it has is completely ruined by the dreadful optimization. There’s nothing worse than trying to enjoy the detailed textures of your cities or admire the landscape, only for the game to stutter constantly and drag the immersion down with it. The pretty visuals, when you can actually appreciate them between the frame drops, just aren’t enough to save the experience when the performance is this terrible.Another thing is the narrator in Ara: History Untold that is not pleasant to listen to, often detracting from the overall experience with a tone that felt uninspired and monotonous. Rather than drawing me deeper into the game, the narration left me more disengaged.Moreover there are minor bugs that I encountered which are translations (lower and uppercase bugs), reporting a bug (which you can't, because Website is down), V-Sync problem (lowers your framerate by half). Overall, my excitement for Ara: History Untold has turned to frustration. The poor optimization severely hampers what could have been a decent addition to the 4X genre. Until the developers address these performance issues, I can’t recommend the game, especially to fans of Civilization and Humankind, who expect smooth and strategic gameplay, not a stuttering mess. At the moment it goes for a refund.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a nice game with some fresh ideas. Looks great.But it really needs a lot of QoL improvements and automation. And by a lot I mean A LOT.One example: You have to go through every improvement to see, if you have a better option to boost production. Every single time you produce/find/get - not unlock - a new one.Every. single. time. - every. single. improvement.Also, all the choices make those choices meaningless.You can produce everything you have unlocked and ingredients are just there to boost production.The result is, that you might think you're doing good because you have amenities and supplies and your production satisfies demand but in reality you don't produce at competitive rates or could improve by producing something else instead.If you don't constantly min/max you might end up wasting capacity and time to produce something you unlocked hours ago and had no ingredients to boosts production while in theory you have a way better option that you can boost.Or you got the ingegredients in the meantime but didn't see that you could use it somewhere to wastly increase output. It's just to much without any help/indicator from the game itself. And the fact, that related overviews about crafters, receipes and improvements are in totally different menues doesn't really help.Maybe wait until you see a big QoL patch in the update history and/or wait for content creators to actually recommend the latest version. It might become a really good game if the devs get this right quick enough, otherwise I'd not recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel for marketing and hype. It might be interesting. The 'living world' is entirely cosmetic. Extractive colonialism is still the normal sop. It's poorly optimized and often opaquely explained. A lot of the mechanics are passive. I do really like having good production chains - and that's the only polished mechanic. Combat has odd variables and the results can be inconsistent or down right incoherent. While 'balance' balance at launch has all the predictable complaints of any 4X including tedious questions about how to balance snowballing, this is partially because the AI's are also a disappointment. The supposed 'act goals' that would let you choose a way to play are just additional bonuses, that was a completely made up piece of marking. While game's events do seem more coached in specific history and occasionally feel like they nudge the game into a realm of alternate history unfolding on occasion they'res also a pretty small pool of events. The AI's do occasionally have events from their own character and culture's history which is a fun bit of interplay until you start to see the exact same events in the same order again and again. One thing that could have potentially limited the disappointment was a True Zone/Start map for people looking for that alt-history experience but it wasn't finished. Mostly what Ara has done is make me appreciate Humankind and Beyond Earth Rising Tide more than I have in years. Maybe in a few years Ara will impress me more than any other 4X game but the experience right now is that I'm playing an Early/Open Developers build. I will not the game's publishers are making an effort to remain engaged in their fan base and have planned for a year of continued development. _childDocuments_.review: So far loving this game, beautiful graphics, very detailed 4x kind of game and really cool to be able to zoom in close to watch the people working around your cities doing there thing.
