_childDocuments_.review: So, I just took a night and played Ara for 7,2 hours straight. I'll update this review probably once I have more experience.First of all: It definitely gives the "one more turn" feeling. The last 1,5 hours have just been due to "one more turn" xD People call it a child of Civ and Humankind, but tbh. it rather feels like a child of Civ and CK3 and it feels a lot better than Humankind. I have just started with normal settings, besides choosing the largest possible map size (such 12 civilations) on 4 continents map on normal difficulty. I watched many intervies about Ara beforehand, so I kinda knew what I should expect, but I had no idea, how much I'd like everything. For the most part I played Civ5 (over 1000 hours), Civ6 (over 400 hours), Humankind (over 60 hours).When I started the game there were two things I noted at first. I can barely see the flag behind every icon and barely recognize the leaders, so before starting a game I had to click on most of them to know what the game is offering me. All Leaders have one unique trait and a collection of non-personalized boni, which also other leaders can partly posess, but most likely in a different constellation.The second thing I noticed was the performance. i7 (10th gen) and RTX 2060 on a normal FullHD-Monitor here and I couldn't play on medium graphics without minor lags. I now turned most of the things on low and tbh the game still looks nice and at least I have for the most part around 45 fps, which is honestly enough for me on a 4x title. I also noticed that it lags in the beginning a lot more than a few minutes later. It feels like, he is still processing and loading stuff in the background, while you are already able to play. I don't know how much I like that, but as mentioned the graphics are still good even on low. I have yet seen no pixelized thing. Probably also the art style helps with this.The tutorial is optional and is done by little popups, which was a nice gentle way, which didn't feel like your hand is guided a linear path with no alternatives. It blends in and gives you the most basic information you need.For your cities there are no workers to send across the map or citizens to be placed on a tile (only specialists later to increase the bonus of a building), instead everything is done by your city production and its production queue. I still have no idea how the city production is calculated, though I could probably read it somewhere. I only know things that effect like the happiness of your city. Overall the micromanagement of workers doesn't feel like it's gone. It is instead moved to micromanaging the upgrades of your buildings. It's important for your empire to craft items. You need them for wonders (called triumphs), specific or higher tier units and also few for buildings. Some are just materials, others are consumables, which you want to have a somewhat reliant infinite production of, which is the standard setting. You can still give it a few urgent requests in between and the production further can be quickened by either investing income or otherwise using item specific ressources. And this is the most important depth of all the micromanagement.The micromanagement first seems sweet and then in midgame keeps you busy, when you have multiple cities, but thanks to the automatisation it keeps fun. Now by my mid game I know what items I want overall and need to optimize or which ressources to gather.Map and war is where I think of CK3. The map is devided into little segments, which for the most perform like hex, but not always are and definitely don't feel like them. It's fun to navigate around and also ruins or rather collectible randomly spawn even after the initial map generation. Also is the scout the only unit, which can collect them. These things for the most part are items, which again help you on the previously mentioned things. Usually every unit can move only one tile per turn, but with great personalities or roads you can increase this.On your way you find tribes, which can only be interacted with by random events. If you reach their highest opinion of you, they vanish and you get a citizen increase. If you decide to be on bad terms with them, you can eradicate them. I wish I could actively do something with them, but especially the assimilation feels rewarding, when you finally get the last random event you need to better your relationship.The combat feels good. It's not as tactical as the other games. It's rather like in CK3. You have a stack of units with different strengths and weaknesses and throw them against another stack, though ranged units can assist a fight without being involved. I have played a lot of CK3, thus I enjoy also this form of combat. I have no idea how close this is to Civ4. But it keeps things simple. Units can level, but it only and also automatically increases their stats. Surprisingly it doesn't seem like I can upgrade units and also depending on stuff in my empire I can only have a set amount of units on the map at the same time. I can build more and deploy them in a turn, but only until the cap is full. Every military unit can siege and the city has now way of resisting. Walls and such only gives the owner more time to react before the city falls and also walls require the enemy to have a siege unit, which can break them. Otherwise a city can't be sieged. A war also only lasts maximum for a set amount of rounds (usually 40 on said settings). For me this is still a good game, but if someone wants that tactical unit against unit combat, you won't probably enjoy the fighting aspect of Ara.Diplomacy feels okay. You can have as mentioned a trade agreement, but also a science agreement, a defense agreement and can have closed or open borders. You can denounce an enemy or declare war. It's basic and okay. The defense agreements works like in CK3. You can be asked to join your ally in a war, but you don't have to agree, which is cool. I only wish for more transparency in terms of relationship developments, since I have yet no idea what the AI likes and what not. I guess due to my actions I'm seen as a warmonger, but there is no indicator telling me that. Also I find it said, that the leaders have no voice, but at least their own music.The AI (on normal) doesn't seem to be too good in war. Among them a lot of things happen, but against me they only almost got two cities once, since I almost couldn't be there in time to challenge their armies, which had always been weaker than mine. I don't know how this changes on higher difficulty. In terms of winning, they are not bad, but also not that good. You win by having the most prestige at the end. You gain prestige by almost everything you do. (Yes, this sounds like Humankind, but it's better, because there are no milestones and a lot of factors.) To my knowledge none of AI civs have ever built a wonder or if so I didn't got a notification for it. (I could look it up.) There is one, who could potentially rival me, but I doubt it tbh. The others were quite far from each other in the beginning, but they grew quite close, so it often changed, who would be eradicated by entering the mid game age. And it really was a relief, when these civs vanished. All their lands become unoccupied, so there is again free room to grow and your scout can loot a lot of items. Now I'm with only 7 other nations and at least two of them are somewhat close to me technologically, though tbf. I focus on science.You get used to the simultaneous delayed turns. It's nice, if you want to redo stuff. It's a bit annoying in war, but it's okay overall and shortens the time you have to wait between turns.So overall I can remmond Ara so far, if you don't need that unit by unit fight. It's in my eyes better than Humankind and the prestige win feel right and not forced onto you. There are few things, which I'm missing and it rather has a city focus than a unit focus compared to Civ, but so far I enjoy it :D

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, Ara is a good game and I hope they take on board a lot of the feedback they’re getting to optimise it further with future updates and DLCs.As most people will cover the majority of pros, cons and issues/fixes, I just wanted to focus on an overlooked and underrated feature that could solve many issues for current and future 4X and grand strategy games in the micromanagement area.I’m not sure how often this comes up in discussions but, to prevent mid-late game fatigue and being overwhelmed by so many options, I think all these type of games (Ara, Civ, Humankind etc) should reintroduce automated cities and endless production queues.In Civ V you had the option to leave a captured city as a puppet state/city which would still be part of your empire, but would construct buildings on its own. You could then annex it and take control whenever you wanted (after a few turns of resistance on some occasions). And you could have endless production queues such as for research or gold, which was very useful towards the end of the game when you built every building available. These 2 options helped streamline my Civ V games on so many occasions and it always confused me as to why they were removed in Civ VI.With some sort of governor or mayor system (which some of these games already have), all the developers need to do is allow you to assign a simple mayor/governor to any city (doesn’t need to have a bonus but could do) at any time and let them take control of the city/production, with flexible options such as letting you take over whenever you want or letting you intervene for crucial choices such as where to place a district to expand. This way you can just focus on your capital city or certain key cities of your choice in your empire whilst letting the CPU/AI manage the other cities as mayors, especially as the game progresses and becomes more complex.This is also more authentic because in real life, even a king, president or dictator doesn’t micromanage every single part of their empire/nation, they have advisors, councils and other members who work with them to manage the nation.These options can be simple from just being assigned a default mayor slot each time you build or gain a new city, or more complex by allowing those mayors to have certain perks or negative traits etc, for more tactical variety.Micromanaging everything by yourself should be a thing of the past as these kind of games add more layers of complexity. There should always be even a simple option to have your cities automated or for endless production queue options to help streamline games and prevent late game fatigue or repetitive clicking of the same thing for every single city. If someone wants to keep micromanaging then that can be their choice by refusing to assign the mayors, but for other players who do not wish to micromanage, then these automated options should also be available so that gameplay can be accommodated for both types of players, as well as allowing the developers greater freedom to make their games even more complex without overwhelming players.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Its a game that feel familiar and fresh. The crafting system takes a bit of learning, I can see people getting upset when approaching it because its new and not presented in the easiest way to understand and once you "kinda get it" you can see the potential. The overall crafting UI could do with some work because it requires more attention on behalf of the player than it should (but also more memory work than most 4x's require). Performance apparently took a hit in an update just prior to release, its playable now but not amazing. Turn graphics down and its fine but the beautiful graphics are part of Ara's charm. I'm not bothered and contrary to some negative reviews had no bugs or crashes. I've seen complaints about redundancy in the tech tree as if that's an issue and I think that is ridiculous as its a feature designed to increase choice. Its a bit confusing as its new to 4x but I think its good as depending on the map you may choose to rush ahead and pick up stuff later, or research it earlier to take immediate advantage.If you're an old school 4x player that wants something with new mechanics then this is a good game. It feels like a blend of Civilisation IV Colonisation (but without the manually sending items between towns) and Civilisation VI, while also being its own thing. Honestly I think it'll upset some who will view it like Civ (which can be done as it is familiar) but then get frustrated it doesn't play like Civ. Like I said, if you want fresh new 4x mechanics and can persevere through a bit of a learning curve its worth a look.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately this game isn't very good, at least at this time.The performance is pretty bad, stuttering and even crashing to desktop at times.But really my problem stems from the fact that this was advertised as a Civ game but it really isn't. It's a micro-management game with heavy focus on doing a bunch of smaller supply chains. Like make a farm to get sheep, then do that to get fur, then get fur to do etc... If you like that stuff go for it, but it's just tedious to me. And worst is that everything is hidden within menus. You have to go to those farms within your city menu and then make the production and make sure you remember which farms are upgraded and what's producing what. It's just so much needless menu backtracking.And I will also mention just quick some of the baffling leader choices. Like I don't mind the whole not actually a leader but just a good person from that culture, that's fine. But then some of them are just odd. Like for Greece it's some random poet, not like a great philosopher like Plato but a poet, who was only chosen because she's a meme amongst the LGBT community. And the Cherokee, these great native people aren't represented by some of their actual leaders when they were a power but some random modern activist woman when the Cherokee were already under America for years, like isn't that kind of insulting?Anyways, it seems like if you like the micro management kind of city builder and understand that this is not a Civ game you may enjoy it. But honestly I think even in that regard it's just way too tedious and with way too many performance issues to recommend even people who like that stuff. This game was very disappointing. I may wait until it gets more expansions and goes on sale to try it again but really if you're thinking about it, hold off until a sale at least in its current state.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: 8 hours in , got to the end of act 1 after a couple of restarts.Firstly, had to change some settings to get the visuals smooth. By default felt like edge scrolling/ moving around map was a bit choppy. Once that was fixed I started to get into it.Huge learning curve. Really need to unlearn what you know in Civ and learn what Ara is all about. Its, got a different feel to it. I generally play peaceful in Civ, but in Ara I HAD to go to war. AI settling next to my capital? Nope thats not staying there! But I genuinely enjoyed the battles, even if they were simple to understand I think this is something that Civ 6 did wrong where battles and wars take a lot more micro management in Civ by bringing the units you need to the battle and shuffling around all the time, Ara gets you to preset your armies and give them formations and leaders and just put them up against the enemy. Less hassleI saw someone say politics plays no part in Ara, I strongly disagree. Having an ally for the set amount of time that you do really helps. And maintaining that relationship I thought was really important, especially toward the end of the act. I had two AI declare war on me and with my ally it felt like "teams" trying to keep their positions on the board before the next act starts. I love the trade contracts. Playing as victoria I start with an extra trade route. Plus adding more routes those trade agreements really did me well. It makes trade valuable because I was getting a lot of good things from my ally and possibly more than she was getting from me because I had a focus in trade.Im not sure about AI balancing though. When setting up the initial games, I tried a harder difficulty, when you mouse over the difficulties tool tip shows you some info, like "small bonuses, or no bonuses". I tried a much harder difficulty that said "no bonuses" but the AI were somehow constantly earning almost double prestige. Lowered to Prince and up to end of Act 1 I am winning mostly with 3200 prestige versus 2nd place of 3000 prestige. I might knock it up one level next game.The length of the act felt long, possibly 5-6 hours, felt almost like a whole game and could stop here just after act one and say I was satisfied, but of course Im looking forward to playing next act now. I can see why the culling mechanic was added too. Its refreshes the game, like theres new focus, not like when you play civ and its the same all the way through.Im not trying to crap all over Civ mind you. Civ is great, but Ara is fresh, its differentIts not for everyone. Need to be ready to learn a new game. Took me a while to get the grasp of the mechanics. Defo not as accessible or as familiar as Civ. But with some patience you certainly get your moneys worth. I suspect Im going to be putting hundreds of hours into this oneOn the negative all I can say is apart from that little change I had to do with game settings to get it running smoother, which possibly there could be some optimization here just to get that camera to be much smoother, the crafting mechanic.. this one is although a really really nice addition, also completely impossible to keep track of. Sure there are notifications when something is not building, but you will find yourself building crafting goods and not paying attention to what was built all the time, and then every now and again go through every single building to see what tools can be used and where. Its slow and laborious. Shouldnt be this awkward.Maybe I missed something in the menus that could list all the buildings and show their upgrades in a nice tidy list, but the tutorial hasnt told me anything that can be used to this effect. Also city planning just gets lost, theres so much info on screen and though you have a list to the right showing the different zones and an icon showing the building in a slot, there needs to be something where that list might have a better visual aid to see whats actually in those slots rather than having to mouse over each icon, but the clutter that is the main screen when you are trying to annex a zone or place a building is almost useless. I heard of complaints of the UI, and I get it.I suspect they will patch something here eventually, because it certainly has had a lot of love already. There is so much here and Im very happy with my purchase, just need a bit of patience to learn what it is.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: You know I really wanted to like this game. It was something new and had some mechanics that reminded me of other games I enjoy. The micromanagement reminded me of a sort of HoI4 or VC3 kind of play style while still having a humankind/civ over all feel. What brings this game way down is just the amount of bugs and outside systems that the game relies on to work. First I couldn't play it on my laptop. Seems like it might have been a problem with my AMD built in GPU confusing the game. Any other game seemed fine with running on my RTX 4070 on my laptop, but this game just decides that it wasn't going to do anything. What ever it at least will play on my desktop up until today.Today, now I can't get the xbox app to work within Windows. Which just means that the game is useless for wanting to play with friends all because of another company's app decides that it doesn't want to run in the background. I've looked up steps to try and fix the xbox app, but at this point I'm just fed up. This game is on Steam. Yes I know that in the description it says you have to have an Xbox network account to play, but why is it that you can't just use the resources available on the platform you are selling on to provide multiplayer? Sure I wouldn't be able to play with xbox players, but I find it hard to believe that many people will be playing an RTS on console. Heck even at this point I would be fine with simply allowing the two clients to connect using IP address like back in the old day. Why is it you can't do that?... Because of some vague mentioning that Azure is doing some of the processing. Nice, that means when ever Microsoft decides to cut losses or the developer can't pay for the servers anymore the game is just bricked. Stay away from this like the plague.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: way too much macro. you have to decide every single manufacturing plant, every single improvement to use what kind of tools they should use, what is the stock, how many tools you have left etc... after turn 40-50 it becomes a chore.events are useless, top one is always the best outcome, mid one is alright, bottom one is basically ignore. you dont even need to read.actual historical references to events IS AWESOME. you are not seeing a random event but you can learn about history and see that it actually happened as well.

_childDocuments_.review: I really really like this gameIn a TLDR this is like an Anno Civ game, extremely well polished, incredibly stable multiplayer and just a nice fun game.I'm not entirely sure where all the "political correct" reviews are coming from. Yeah it has a lot of women in it, but its no way the type of ♥♥♥♥ Humankind pulls off. And this is coming from a very conservative person who detests DEI woke trash. This is nothing like that. There's no multiculturalist washing, there's no weird liberal or pacifist agenda to it, it even adds Fascism (my beloved) as a government type you can choose which cements it as a non-liberal game by definition.For what you get, I would definitely say this was on par with Civ V first release. It had an incredible foundation that will keep being built on and I am hopeful for that.I see a lot about the UI and bad specs but I personally have no had these issues so this is a user bias that you'll have to figure out for yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: In first Act, crafting sounds fun but when you hit city limit of Ten, it takes forever to manage all the crafting.Too much Micro managing the crafting in later Act.  I spent about 85% of time in the supply chain system.It is a tedious chore.  I have so much foods and lumber at one time.  You quickly realize that you don’t even need to engage with half of these buildings because many become pointless as the game progresses. Worse yet, the game's pacing makes it feel like you don’t have time to explore or benefit from these options before it’s all over.Combat: I hate it when you can't upgrade units and reform them in different formation.You send units toward each other with no meaningful tactics or strategy involved. It’s a matter of numbers and brute force rather than any clever maneuvers or battle planning. If you’re looking for engaging or complex combat, this game won’t satisfy that itch.I am sad that there is no nuclear ICBM.  I want to build nuclear fallout shelter.  This game has 70/100 score.  It is not Civilization Killer.  It is not better than Civ 6.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: While the game definitely does have some issues with performance at the moment, it's honestly a really solid game.The crafting is quite extensive and you can tell they put a lot of love into it, and it's particularly satisfying to see your civilization grow and develop, as opposed to say the Civ series which while fun in its own right, doesn't really demonstrate that besides the occasional house popping up here and there along with the buildings changing depending on the technological age you're in.The diplomacy is very basic, and definitely leaves a lot to be desired, but it's not any worse than Civ VI's. The battles aren't Total-War complex, but the formations feature allowing you to put units into a battalion together is quite a nice touch, I was worried it was going to just be "craft a unit and then send it out or whatever) but there is a basic aspect of tactical planning involved there, which I definitely hope to see expanded on in the future as well.TL;DR It leaves a bit more to be desired in terms of complexity in other areas besides crafting, and is hampered by some launch day performance issues, but is overall a genuinely solid game.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: The game is very different from the CIV series. It is a mixture of ANNO and Humankind; however, this company does a GREAT job implementing the graphics, sounds, immersion and management to really give you the experience of leading a nation. I am just i awe of how much detail, options and choices you can do in the game on day 1! Imagine with the add DLC or when mods become active. In my opinion, I think Ara History Untold created a NEW experience for 4X, city building or grand strategy gamer's! A toast to you ARA, LONG MAY YOU LEAD! ;)

_childDocuments_.review: My Favorite Civ's are Civ 2 and Civ 5 with all the DLC's...Did not really like Humankind, and have honestly struggled to get into Old World...And I have a strong dislike for Civ 6...I have found this game far more enjoyable then many of the games in this Genre I have played recently...I love the added complexity too the civilization formula, lots of great supply chain management and its very micro intensive, all a plus for me.... _childDocuments_.review: This game has very solid foundation and I can see with further developments to address the shortfall in UI, performance and diplomacy, it will be at the same height as CIv. Currently, I can't recommend this game until they make enhancements to UI asap to manage mid/late game better. Right now, it's simply a nightmare to manage over 100 improvements.  It begs the question whether the developers themselves have played their own game till mid/late game.Once they fix the above, I will change change my recommendation to a "Yes".----------------------Updated my review to a "Recommended":Despite all the faults mentioned above, the developers have proved over the past two weeks they are committed to continuing making the game better and they're listening to players.  They are also responsive to players on the forum. The fact is, even with all the problems mentioned, I haven't had this fun with a 4X game in such a long time (and I've tried them all); last time I was this hooked was with EU4/Stellaris/Alpha Centauri/Civ 4.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: I'm only a few hours in but the crafting system, the gorgeous map and ability to zoom in on individual entities and cities, the large variety of leaders, the era system, the randomized research tree, and more shake up the formula just enough to make this my favorite civ-like in a long time. I wish it had a sprinkle of CK3/Old World and it would be perfect for me but it's great either way.My main complaints are optimization, a UI that doesn't explain or fullly show the details of the crafting system, and most of the events lead to just a basic flat percentage bonus and nothing that deep or meaningful. That said, the world and gameplay are strong enough to make me see past this and, as a base game, I'm excited to see how this ends up after some DLC and patches.I'll be playing this for a long time. My favorite 4x since Old World and it really does bring a lot new to the table while still feeling cozy and familiar. It's a great game that needs some TLC.Edit: This game does need a better UI, some optimization, and a stronger AI. That said, name a single 4x without those issues at the start. I am honestly having fun learning the systems in this game and it brings a lot of new things to the table while still looking gorgeous even when the game chugs. This game is revolutionary in my opinion. For me the greatest strategy games of the last decade that I've at least leaned into are Ara, Terra Invicta, and Old World. In my dreams this game and Old World have a baby. Fantastic game and I'll stick with it. Deserves better ratings IMO.Edit 2: I've completed two full campaigns and abandoned one. I'm starting to see some of the cracks in the UI and the AI but dude, that's all 4x games. I just hope this gets update. I like that Microsoft is behind it and that gives me hope but the overly crap impressions from civ gamers sucks. This game offers new stuff. Old World did the same but it had a year of polish before hitting steam. Let this game grow. There's nothing like it and I will keep playing it for a long time. Other than Oldworld this is my fave 4x in years. If they had a baby, it'd be a dream. Ara rocks.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Ara introduces some innovative ideas to the civ-style game, but its lack of answer for the genre's mid- and late-game problems (run away games, unwieldy micromanagement) and its uninspired art direction hold it back.I liked it well enough, though. Certainly scratched that civ-sim itch until that "other" civ game comes out next year. Maybe wait for a sale on this one?
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: I really like that you not only produce generic "food", "production" and "materials" but also real products like plows or wine that are either then used to boost the production of other products or to give bonuses to your city.It is a little bit more micro management than comparable games because of that. But it is something I always wanted in a 4x game.I really like it so far.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Decent game, new mechanic and play style which is a nice change but has major shortfalls.City growth and maintenance is a big one, AI with maybe 3 farms can grow cities to tier 15.But somehow when I have 10 farms My cities stagnate at Tier 8-9, even with amenities. 1 turn you have a surplus of +68 food, end turn and you're -30, and you navigate the stat bars as much as possible to try and understand why that happens, but a little hard to understand (I've always been bat at micro-management games). But you end turn and suddenly its +17, then a couple turns later its again at -22.Combat was a little odd, I got a war declared against me, a war of "expansion," which the result was that I lost a city with its territories. However as I observed the following took place;As I watched the health each turn as it depleted, I calculated 4 turns and had 2 turns left. Even though I had an army heading to defend, i Could see that I had 2 turns left for my army in the adjacent territory to get to my city (my city health was half reduced on the bar), the game cheated that turn and won the siege. I did the same to their city, my army of 3 swordsmen and 1 spearmen besieged their capital in a war of "retaliation."Battle rating of 24, they countered my siege with a spearmen of battle rating 8 (in the battle screen it said in 1 turn I will win this battle.) But nope, it dragged on for 5 turns. It managed to kill half my army, but I won eventually. 1 enemy spearmen against 4 of my units.Then I watched as I was about to win the siege, because they had nothing to defend with. So I watch the health bar going down and was almost at 0, where 98% was worn down. That turn before I ended turn, they spawn an army of 1 horsemen and 2 other units, swordsmen and spearmen. I figure, seeing as they won the last battle at my town which had half health, I should win this, they still need to move into the territory which takes 1 turn and then 1 more turn to attack. As i have them at less than half, that is at less than an 8th of their health I figured, well they still need at least 1 turn to counter my siege. But no, even though their army though at least 1 turn away, they counter that turn that is ended. So I end turn, and i didn't win the siege. Steep learning curve, i enjoy it, but when stuff like this happens it gets annoying.Also performance is a little clunky at this stage, especially on multiplayer, as it take sup to 1 minute or 2 to process the turns. But they announced an optimisation patch.

_childDocuments_.review: Whoever tries to compare this with a full fleshed CIV at the end of its lifecycle will be disappointed, and rightfully so. But the concept, as such, is truly beautiful. _childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for another Civ game, this isn't it. There are some aspects that are similar but it's closer to city manager game with multiple cities.  Combat and diplomacy are very light.  Even given all that, i'm enjoying the game.  I'm 9hrs into my first game, taking it slow and reading tooltips and doing the tutorial.  I was in last place through the first two ages but slowly worked my way up to first, mainly due to my heavy research focus.  I just hit Act II and once a couple more civs hit it, we'll have our first civ culling, which i'm excited for since one or two of them will be right on my borders.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10This game is a very fun and unique combination of traditional 4X games like Civilization and production chain management games like Anno. There is a lot of micro-management of the items your cities and buildings are consuming and also producing, which I find fun but is probably not for everyone. There is a huge variety of items to produce and learn how to best use though a decent number of them don't seem very useful to use and I tend to ignore them.I really enjoy how large and powerful your cities get. The game caps you on a relatively low number of cities between 5-10, but each individual city can grow over a much larger space than in other games. The cities end up feeling more like entire states or provinces within your nation which is a very cool way to handle things. You are incentivized to spread your cities out more to give them room to grow. Each individual map zone you expand into has 1-5 slots for buildings on top of the usual different combination of resources, providing more depth in how you grow your cities.Army management is also very unique. You can deploy units individually, but you unlock larger and larger combined-arms formations as you go later in the game which give bonuses for grouping specific unit types together. This reduces the unit spam games like Civ can suffer from. Combat itself is relatively basic and the city siege mechanic feels like it is over far too quickly, but combat is not the focus of this game so I think it good overall.The biggest issue I had with the game is the sheer volume of items, structures, and units to produce and use on a given turn. It is good to have variety, but it is an almost overwhelming volume of choice anytime you go into your cities' production menus. The game needs much better organization tools within those menus to group similar items together and hide outdated items that it no longer makes sense to see. For example, there is no reason to keep showing Spearmen as an option in my units production list when I'm in the late game trying to make a jet bomber. There are some powerful tools to reduce the micro-management of your nation. I especially liked the national industry menu where you can quickly check the status of every building in your nation of a specific type. You can set up rules to automatically add bonus items to your structures which really helps as your nation expands and you make more and more structures across your nation.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: No option for disabling AI culling during Act transition, but only for human players ?... really? I'm really pissed. I want to have the immersive of a great and huge world with many many nations from start to end. Civ isn't this anymore with 6 and 7. If i would want to play with all my 6 friends in a sandbox, i would have civilization 6/7 for. Give us an option for disabling all the nation culling as you promised. ... until then, here get your game back.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not good. I can honestly not reccomend this game.  I think they took some chances with things but everything about this game feels unfinished. Each nation feels the same. The architecture so far has looked the same across nations. I am not finding things like unique units or anything else, and the combat battle report thing is corny. Humankind took battle in the right direction but erred with their prestige system. Oldworld is too much like Civ 4 and is clunky in it's U.i. Millenia is bare, underfunded, and not the most accessible. Ara is what you get when you take all the worse parts of those games and mix it into one. I have requested a refund, I doubt I will get it because I do like to play more than two hours before I give up. But at 65 bucks it is way overpriced. At 65 bucks it is borderline abusive to have a game like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: I do not ever write reviews for any game. I'm writing one for this game because of I am a huge fan. I can understand why many people would be so-so about this game. It does require a lot more time investment for each turn, especially in the later parts of the game. It is complex for a beginner until you eventually figure out what works and what doesn't. But for me, It scratches my itch on so many different aspects, I have put more time in this game since it came out than any other game I have ever played. The good: I love the concept of city builders but there are some things that typically get in the way of me enjoying them. I have never been very good at designs of my city. This game takes that away. the regions and zones are already set. All I have to do is fill them in. I love the idea of 4x games. I only recently started playing Civilization this past year and I really enjoyed it. However, that game seemed limited to me and I became bored usually well before I made it to the modern times. Ara puts those two concepts and molds them into a beautiful game that I literally cannot stop playing. The not so good: The game could use some work. I really want a balanced, competitive game each time I play. As I climb up the ladder of difficulties, I cannot play many of them without human culling disabled. I really do not think culling should happen at all because nations should be lost just like in real life (captured, re-assimilated, etc.). I also believe the AI could use a little more help in general. The game has such a complex economic system that I love so much, yet the AI opponents are never able to compete with me for production strength in the late game. The military AI could also be better and perhaps expanded upon as this is in area that draws many people to 4x games. The tech "tree" should technically have pre-requisites. I have found myself missing training many military units as time can go by pretty fast late game( this happens in civilization to an effect too). It should be noted that the most recent update did help a lot at balancing the game and I am confidant the developers will continue to put the game on the right track as the best game that has ever been created.Overall, I have some gripes about this game, but the pros immediately overcame the cons for me right from the beginning. For people like me, this game is absolutely amazing. I hope the game can win over people over time as I want to play multiplayer with the proper settings so much. The latest update was great, slowing down the tech growth enough so we are not completely running over the competition. I look forward to the update in November with a better interface for the economic side of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: and now onto the short review//intro//Hello, MF Kraven here- and welcome to a less than 10 mins review. A YouTube series where I take a look at niche titles, hidden gems & often overlooked games & tell you whether or not you should buy it, in less than 10 mins. So if that is the type of content that you like, consider subscribing, & liking this video.Today I take a look at Ara History Untold, & extra special shout out to Xbox Games Studios for giving me a press copy to play. Ara History Untold is a Grand Strategy, 4X Alternate History game. Where you take notable people in history like George Washington, Benito Juarez, Haile Selassie, Catherine the Great & even Simón José Antonio de la Santísima Trinidad Bolívar Palacios Ponte y Blanco start from the beginning & race to become the greatest Civ- erm Nation of history, whether that be through science, arts, diplomacy, or conquest, it's your job to be the greatest ruler ever known. But is this Civilization esque game a contender? Or will Ara be another footnote in history? Let's find out.//Graphics, Sound & Artstyle//Starting off with the graphics, I'm running Ara on a 3070 & it looks great to me. In the first two acts, I like zooming in on my cities to see what my people are doing, I love exploring the land we're given & the sounds that accompany the game? Delightful. With the press copy I was also given access to the OST- it's 118 tracks, with all 12 ages having their specific tracks.//Gameplay//First you are given a choice, between 42 notable people in history. Each equipped with bonuses & flaws. You choose your difficulty & however many nations you want to face off against. You can edit the AI difficulty, map type (i suggest generating a new map just for each playthrough to feel fresh) AND the amount of turns. Keep in mind that there are 12 ages, divided into 3 erasThen starts Act 1, Turn 1. You're given a town on a random spot in the map, you dont get to pick where you will be. Clicking on your city you can see your summary, how many people are in the city, how much productivity, research food, income, wood & materials they are producing plus their quality of life. Making farms will increase your food, log camp will increase your wood, mines or deposits will increase your materials etc etc. As your population grows (with adequate housing & supplies) your city will generate a claim. Where you can take another portion of the map for your nation. They'll have icons with an apple, log, material & coin, depending on the amount will be how much you generate per turn- BUT ALSO when placing a farm on say a region that has 3 or 4 apples, you will generate MORE food and the same logic applies to all other resources. There are also random enemy spawns mainly wildlife AND supplies such as cows, grapes or other goods, and if you own the region they are in you will be supplied with a certain amount per turn (or building an appropriate building will generate EVEN more i.e. a farm for anything that can be farmed/ranched). After awhile Paragons will also come to your city, you can have them give you bonus points to certain aspects of your city or have them work on "masterpieces" that will give you coveted Prestige Points.Events will pop up from time to time, like "The Forest Fort" where you are given a scenario & depending on how you respond to it, you will receive/lose certain commodities or buffs to your city. This will start to happen more often as you come into contact with tribes scattered throughout the map as well as opposing nations. Events like this can better your relationships with other nations or have an adverse effect. There are 4 ages in each era, while in theory you or foe nations can advance through the ages faster than the rest, dependent on growth/research points. Once one player on the board is on the verge of advancing to the next Act or 5th era- the game will give all players a warning as the lowest ranking nati a Lisa" you can gain points, if you build the Taj Mahal, you get prestige, if you win a skirmish or war against another nation you gain points. If you reach the highest population you get points, etc etc.Ara also has a very creative religion system that gives your nation amazing buffs based on the reach of your religion. The more people come to your places of worship the better for you. Government is also another engine in game that can give you buffs. Dependent on what form of government you have, will affect all aspects of your ruling. Whether you think feudalism, Marxism, imperialism or any other modern government is the way for you, will allow you to tax the people a certain amount, have them be harder workers or rely more on government.  //Price//59.99 USD//How many hours estimated//I've played around 22+ hours of Ara, with one game taking me around 16 hours.//Is it Playable on Steamdeck?//While I had no issues playing the first Act, as more of the map gets exposed it does seem to stutter a lot after awhile. I also will strongly advise you to create your own key bindings for Ara if you wish to play on SD.//Final Thoughts//I pondered a lot about Ara. I'm not a seasoned Civ player like most people who will have even looked at this are, so I'm no help in that department. What I am is a casual player of strategy, simulation games of the sort- and there is a lot I love about Ara but a lot that has also left me largely underwhelmed.I want to start with the good, the historical landmarks look gorgeous, the sounds of the world in congruence with the soundtrack is a relaxing experience, the grind to be the first to build historical landmarks or to discover another nation is fun. I like sending my scout to just go out & explore. I love that Ara has a good variety of historical figures to choose from. I only wished we had more presidential or solid leaders. Hell, even dictators... On my first playthrough I did Benito Juarez, someone I admire & unbeknownst to me, the most OP leader in the game. See his ability is to gain an expert on day 1. Experts multiply certain buildings effects, so placing them in my Great Hearth will raise productivity in there by 150% to build amenities such as a feast that when used in my city will improve my food supply plus growth to level my city faster.Here lies the issues, see Act 2 and Act 3 quickly turn into a battle of production. Who can produce the most of a certain supply. Having to build workshops to build certain items will either drive you mad or make you feel totally engaged. Luckily I learned very quickly there is a screen i can go to, where I can see what everything that can craft an item is crafting what. Through research you can discover new buildings & amenities you can make but you need some of this or some of that, & you can improve anything that can be improved as long as it's researched but you may need certain tools so you must craft that. But what if a nation decides to attack you? Oxide Games give me much hope that Ara History Untold will be a game I will want to play in the future, we live in a time where CyberPunks & No Man's Sky can get their act together- we just need Ara to be in the oven for a little while more.Which is why I'm giving this a Wait for Sale. I feel like it's fair to say this is a niche title & some may be playing it to hold them over until Civ 7 comes out. Others genuinely love history & micromanagement. Theres fun to be had but for the full entry price of $60 USD, it feels too much like an Early Access title, one that has the bones to become a standout in the genre.(full review did not fit here but the Youtube link has it in it's entirety)

_childDocuments_.review: I am a veteran in 4x games and played civ 4 competitively, so I think I am quite capable to evaluate a 4x game within a few hours.I was interested in this game, but hesitant to buy it, mainly because of these points:1. It is quite expensive2. The reviews after launch showed issues with managing the resources and improvementsWhen I saw the news about patch 1.1, I was excited to see such huge improvements on the game.1. With the patch 1.1 they reduced the price (temporarily) by 20%2. The community was also positive about the changes and the UI improvements seems to be great.So I bought the game and played 18h since then.I did not regret it, as this game is really fun.Now about my impressions of the game:ECONOMY:I would say this game is a mix between Civ and Anno.I like to play "non casual" and try to improve each turn as much as possible.So that means, that you need to check your buildings regularly: If you made, discovered or traded new goods or resources, you might want to go into the buildings who use those and change the build orders or the tools that are being used in that building.You also have to take care about amenities a lot. They are consumed after 3-10 turns and you need a regular supply and need to assign the amenities you want  to the cities.That sounds like a lot, but you get reminders if you run out of amenities or resources.WARFARE:I did not play a lot of warfare, but for example in my last game Japan declared war to me shortly after meeting them.They had a much stronger military (you can always look up military strength), so I was in trouble.I was able to propose a peace treaty with the UI proposing to me to add 5 feasts as an incentive from my side. They agreed and now I have 20 turns of safety to prepare my military.Japan's stance is starting to get worse during that turns and I need to prepare my military.You can get huge bonuses to your military strength in your territory, so I think that there is a big defender's advantage in this game.PACING:You can change the research speed setting and a lot of people complained about normal speed being too fast. I also played with 2x research costs and I thought that is too slow.There are a lot of techs to research, so the games will take hundreds of turns. Quite long in my opinion, but I think everybody can find a suitable speed.I will stop here. Please feel free to comment and ask more questions.

_childDocuments_.review: Through slow but steady progression, this game guides your civilization across well-defined historical eras, such as the High Middle Ages and the Enlightenment. It claims to be a historical simulation, which it genuinely delivers on. The graphics are stunningly beautiful, though they demand high-performance specs to run smoothly. While there's room for improvement in the military aspects, it offers an alternative gameplay style to the renowned Civilization series. The only truly tiresome element emerges in the mid to late game with resource management, which desperately needs a user interface overhaul to enhance the player experience. Despite this, I'd say the game is well worth your time and money.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Updating this review as the 1.1 update fixes pretty much every major complaint I had about the initial release. I never had performance issues, but I know many others did and those were all fixed in patches shortly after release, the two major things that kept me from really getting into this game was the arduous micromanagement in the late game as well as a lack of a TSL Earth Map. Well, 1.1 brought both of those features and I ended up playing nonstop from the moment I got home until past midnight the day of the patches release. The game feels fantastic now and I know it is only going up from here. I highly recommend this game now.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: This is a begrudgingly 'Yes' review only because I cannot vote 'Kinda'.  There are so many excellent systems at play here that are held back by significant faults.  The way that products and materials weave together to add significant boons to your cities is marvelous... except that the UI does what it can to make the entire process of actually using them a chore.  The world is gorgeous and full of incredible small details... except that the performance is sub-par at the best of times and gameplay stutters for even just basic zooming and scrolling.  The nations available are a wide range from the 4x regulars (Rome, Japan, Aztec, etc.) to underrepresented (Cherokee, Ghana, Italy [sans Rome])... but the differences between nations feel negligible and diplomacy is a far cry from even Civ VI's lackluster affair.  Combat has epic multi-turn cinematic battles between legions of units... but deploying military forces locks them in and you can't upgrade, change or remove your choices for armies no matter how far the game advances.I like this game, despite its flaws.  But I would only recommend it in the current state to those looking willing to overlook some annoying flaws for a fresh take on the historical 4x that takes a lot of risks and manages to stick the landing on ... some of it?

_childDocuments_.review: DO NOT PLAY THIS EXPECTING CIVILIZATION At it's core, Ara is a production chain management game that uses a civThere are some really innovative ideas here, and most of them are executed well. First off, the region-based map system is a huge breath of fresh air. It makes city expansion feel much more deliberate and is a better fit for the spread-out 'district' system that Civ 6 popularized than a generic hex grid. Additionally, substitutions in the production management as you unlock new resources keeps even some of your earliest setups relevant and able to be repurposed. The game does have some notable flaws. While micromanagement itself is no issue, the UI is not well designed to reduce tedium. At minimum, there needs to be some sort of 'change all' button for improvements to reduce the clicking required when you get the next generation of tools available. Additionally, the pacing can feel a bit odd, especially in era 1 on large maps when nearly all space is filled rather quickly. Civilizations disappearing between era transitions helps, but then you have large areas deserted for a long time due to the inherent benefits of rushing your city cap as early as possible. Ultimately it feels like a respectable 7/10, that can become an 8/10 with some early patches. $60 is a bit much for the current state of the game, but I would recommend the game on sale to any production chain fans.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game, but I just can't. It's an interesting concept, but it's simply unplayable after the Enlightenment age. First let me say, this game has a feature that lets you set a number of turns when you have cities build science, which is terrific. Other games make it infinite, so you have to remember to switch out, which I never do. Being able to build science for seven turns, then I'll be ready to start another building is the best feature of this game.The most annoying thing about the game is the tool tips. They pop up as soon as your mouse moves over any icon, literally half a second. So most of the game is you looking around pop ups to see the actual game behind them. Half a second is the slowest you can make them, it defaults at a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ quarter of a second. Half the time you click to build something and it takes you to the encyclopedia page about that building because a tool tip popped up under your mouse before you could click. The second most annoying thing is no mini map. A lot of games do this, and I'll never understand why. That means you have to slowly scroll the screen inch by inch to whatever part of the map you're doing something in. The mini map is the most simple ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ QOL feature, allowing you click and instantly jump around the map, and so many games leave it out. Though this one would probably have a tool tip that instantly popped up and took you to their help page explaining what mini maps do. To compound that annoyance, only scouts have an auto explore. So when you eventually get boats that can traverse the ocean, you have to manually move them around to explore, to the far sides of the map, slowly scrolling out and back. Auto explore on every unit would be life changing. But mostly I can't like this game because it's unplayable after the Enlightenment. Switching your economy over in the industrial era is just a tedious headache. The patch made it so everything is one screen, but I still have to click on every structure one at a time, turn by turn, as I craft the things. Early on it's not a big deal, as I make farms and plows at about the same time, but by the late game when I have 30 farms and I'm slowing making fertilizer, it's just tedious. And it's that for every single structure. I want to be able to tell every workshop to switch to machine tools, and if I don't have enough to queue them up so as they're made they get switched. Because you spend 20 minutes every turn just click tools, click tools, click tools. And it's not worth it. And by the way, why do I have to slot in some of these things like plows? Plows are only used in farms, it's the only reason I'm making them. Of course I want them in my farms, that should be automatic. And if it the whole point of the game is crafting items for use in structures, and whole process of crafting items and putting them in structures is tedious, that tells you all you need to know about the game. It's like this game said "What if Civ had more clerical work?"I forced myself to actually finish a game recently, and got an achievement for reaching Act 3, the final act, which only 1 in 5 players have done. And less than 14 percent have won a game on any difficulty level. So the late game is clearly not just a me problem. Nobody can get through this game once you have to switch your economy over.

_childDocuments_.review: I’ll get straight to the point— it’s a game with organic and satisfying visuals… very fun to play and might be one of my favorite 4X of the recent past. But the game at this stage has serious performance issues. At at this stage the game chugs hard, even on “more recent” hardware. I would expect this mostly on multiplayer games I’ve experienced it playing SP as well. I heard from the devs that they released it a bit hastily but it has been in development for years, but, I will be patient and here’s why: The game was developed by a smaller studio, but I can tell that they have put a tremendous amount of time and effort into making a game that stands out from other mainstream 4X (most notably, Civilization which I have played for literally decades!) The crafting system and little details keep you engaged and entertained.. and allow for a vast amount of strategies and playstyles. I will be playing regularly over the coming weeks and I will edit my review once the game settles in!

_childDocuments_.review: In my eyes a very unique take on the 4X civilization builder, as it mixes classic empire and mixes it with production chain management. I find it very interesting, and I see plenty of potential for a very good game.Although, yes it is a turn based 4X game, I cant really put it as opponent of games such as Civilization.It more feels like a diversification on the genre. I only have limited playtime but in my experience the emphasis feels a lot more on growing your empire and managing supply lines. As your goal is to acquire "prestige", which is acquired through objectives, building, events, and masterpieces (The equivalence of great works in Civ)You do want to remain as high up as possible in the prestige leaderboard otherwise you get culled, forgotten, your civilization collapsed. Of course, military aspects are still present, you can attack other civilizations in your game to disrupt them, cripple them, or harm their plans, or raze a city since they build one right against your city.The military aspect does feel weird, because at the current state of the game you cant upgrade units to a more modern equivalence. And that personally bothers me.Another thing I noticed is that the game in its current state has inconsistencies, balancing issues and bugs.I do believe this game has potential, but it really needs a few hefty rounds of polishing up. But, with both compassionate devs that want to improve this game and the modding scene coming alive soon enough. I believe I will be sinking a lot of time into this game in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: "ARA History Untold" revolutionizes the 4X genre with its detailed economic gameplay. It features intricate supply chains and resource management, where your citizens and industries consume resources. Combining this with a Battle Royale concept makes it truly unique. While it might not appeal to everyone, fans of 4X and resource management games will find it captivating!
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: I am finishing my 2nd playthrough at Duke difficulty level (had a first attempt at Earl, but after first Act I decided to restart as I learnt few things).TL:DR - It is much more of a city management game than 4X. It is a good game, the "one more turn" syndrome is strong here. And it looks lovely. But I can understand how people who are used to Civ and Humankind (I played both and I really like Humankind a lot, more than Civ) won't like it and that's why I think it got mixed reviews. Because of wrong marketing/expectations. Haven't experienced any bugs or imbalances in gameplay. It's just not 4X, it's 4citiesManagemet+ Lovely style of miniature filming. I really do enjoy looking at the landscapes and my own little citizens going about their lives. It feels much more alive than any 4X game. But that's because it isn't really one...+ Flexible and overlapping technological paths. You can achieve same items/units/buildings from few different sources, so you research the optimal way for your current gameplay.+ Production, resources, zones, improvements - there are lessons you will need to learn to plan them well, but setting a supply chain that will be resilient is very satisfying.+ Multiple purpose resources - you decide what do you need them for and where.+ UI is very informative. With one or two exceptions - wherever you are, you can hover the mouse over the opened building, see what it produces, then hover of the material to see where it is used and how much you are producing and using. Very few times I had to check the "encyclopedia" for anything.+/- Combat. I don't mind it. It is not the focus of this game. I kind of enjoy it. If you find a stronger force, you have few turns to reinforce your army, but if you can't manage, they are pretty much dead. It's a bit of paper/rock scissors. Combat animations are cute, but unnecessary. Optimizing formation and units is the key as well as trying to be technologically ahead.+/- The culling. I like it. If you are really behind, you don't waste more time and can just start over. But you can also turn it off in advanced options of map setting, so I don't understand why people are so upset about it... Also... it seems really easy to be on the top - just build couple of Triumphs and you're golden (also, they are useful).- There isn't much of diplomacy to be honest. But in most games that is the weakest part. I found myself not engaging with other nations much.- Trade agreements are really weird. In my first playthrough I signed them. Which DOES give you access to all goods produced by other nation. And them to yours. Which means that if you produce 1 rope per 3 turns and they take it... you end up with no ropes that you need for your upgrade. There is no limitation that you can impose on them, quantity below which the resource becomes unavailable for trade or such... Trade needs to be definitely redesigned. In second playthrough I just refused any trade agreements and it didn't impact me negatively in any way. And at least allowed me to have 100% control of my inventory.- Not being able to raze your own city or abandon it. I produced an extra settler by accident and haven't noticed it until they settled next to my first one... And so (as I didn't want to change my government type) I had to suffer -10 to happiness in all cities.- Managing armies. Not being able to change anything after mustering can be a bit frustrating. You can always disband the formation and then replace them with a newly set army.TIPS: 1. Set zones for specific production - food, commerce and such. There are buildings that boost such groups.2. Always fill up starting city zone with Dwellings - extra housing is priceless.3. Remember that you can change some resource harvesting from those resources to base food. Very helpful.4. Remember about updating/adding new amenities to your cities AND residential areas.5. Regularly add production tools to your farms, mines etc. 6. I see people saying that food is always an issue. It wasn't for me so far. Just need to plan enough space for it. Plus, push technological progress towards it. Usually even if I'd have negative -800 on a city, overall I'd be on a plus. And then it would be just around the corner the moment I could upgrade my farms with new tools or the next level. Or sometimes because I forgot to add those tools I've already researched and manufactured.

_childDocuments_.review: Very cool unique game, it's essentially Anno meets Civ. Game focus is on production lines and beefing up your cities more than a focus on war. You can certainly war but at the end of the day your trade lines and production efficiency is the name of the game and I absolutely find this more enjoyable than Anno and look forward to how the game develops in time past launch. Very curious to see what they have in mind for expansions to bring more mechanics in the game down the line.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is incredibly deep. I've only scratched the surface so far--there is so much to this game that it can be difficult to explain. The crafting and production chain systems I think are its strongest attribute--diplomacy the weakest. I like the limitations tying the number of cities that can be founded to certain discoveries, buildings, or events. I also like the varied leader pool--so far I've dabbled with Washington, Sappho, and Zenobia and all three play differently. The game is by no means perfect--it can get overwhelming at times and, as I said, diplomacy is not the game's strong suit. The tendency to aggressively forward settle is especially irritating at times. More variation in maps would also be welcome and I wouldn't object to a huge map size. All in all, I give the game a solid 8.5 out of ten and hopefully the minor problems will be ironed out later. The game isn't a "Civ-killer" nor does it try to be. It's its own variation on the genre--and a welcome variation.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: The opening phases of this game are extremely good and there is an excellent vision of what this game is supposed to be. Unfortunately, the user interface is completely incapable of allowing the player to effectively manage the economy in the later stages of the game. Forcing the player to spend an egregious amount of time checking and microing and fine tuning the economy. At its core, this isn't a civilisation game and copying/pasting the civilisation UI was a massive mistake and not fit for purpose.There is a great game here. But the UI needs to be redone and the game needs *many* new tools and quality of life improvements for managing the economy. At this price point, this game simply cannot be recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: I love civlikes, from the best-of-breed SMAC to the Civ series to Humankind and Old World. It's great to see new entries in the genre. I'm glad Ara was made, although unfortunately it's not very good; it's worse than any of the above. It fails in a few ways.First: I was excited to hear about micromanaging; that's normally really my thing, but this game takes it too far; the micromanaging of production of specific tools to spend on boosts in certain districts is extremely fiddly and doesn't scale to more than one or two cities without becoming incredibly cumbersome. I didn't know that there was a level of micromanaging that's too much for me, but apparently there is and Ara gets there.Second, the UI is terrible. Fonts and dialogue boxes are way too big and cover too much of the screen (at 4k); they're always in the way. It's normal to need to get used to the interface with games in the genre, but Ara's UI is just bad. They may be able to fix this in later game versions.Third, they commit to this "moves during a turn just state intent, and things take effect at the end of the turn". That's just not fun; it feels detached.Fourth, and this is fairly minor (for me - for others it may be more annoying), the list of leaders makes no sense; while about a third are actual national leaders, the rest are just random historical figures who didn't control a nation. A medical doctor, some student activist who died in her 20s, a nun, these choices are bizarre.Did the game do anything remarkably well? Not really. The other games I mentioned up top all added some cool ideas to the genre. Humankind added a nomadic era and civ-changing, Old World added a lot of great narrative events. SMAC added tons of stuff. Ara? Nothing that I can think of.The music is decent. No complaints there.Even if you're into the genre, it makes sense to skip this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: I dont usually write reviews but between the negative comments which at times are baffling me to really enjoying this game, i am compelled to write a review.First and foremost, this game is a mix of a 4X and resource management game, something that is truly fresh and unique to the genre currently. Each play sassion i have struggled to put the game down it has the classic "wait one more turn" that i heve personaly only felt from Civ 5, Civ4, Empire at war and Stellaris. For me that is the highest praise, because although there are some problems and issues with the game, it keeps calling me back day after day.FIrstly, the issues i have are more then anything, with the AI.In my playthroughs, they tend to be the most unpredictable and nonsencical thing about the game, declaring wars they have no hope of winning, being your best friend with an alliance then 3 turns later hating you and opening up a second front on their pointless war, then ending the conflict they just opened up with you? A lot of what they do dosnt make the most sense, from building isolated city's in the middle of your territory to even some of the trade's and proposals, and what i personally think the biggest current issue with Ara is. they seam more there to fill out the space then provide legitimate competition in single player rouns, which though isnt nessisarily a bad thing, is verry limiting.Secondly, Combat can be a bit stiff, with things in most strategy games like terrain not playing any factors into a conflict, and raizing is interesting though i dont believe worth it currently. With some small tweaks under the hood, combat and the orginizations of troops could feel so so so much better, and its unfortunite that in its current state there was a focus on a "battle screen" which i can honestly say i have watched only once. If battles become deeper with either "moves"when in conflict, or at least things like a terrain bonus, it will quickly feel more impact and greater care will need to be taken when attacking/defending. The formations are good, they jsut dont currently do enough in the current state of the game. Besides that, i also thing some of the research/technology could be done better,, but as with all stratagy games they get better with DLC and time. I think my largest complaint is that sometimes if you are a reserch heavy civ, or built yourself that way, some tecnology is so very redundent. I get why its in the game, the whole ability to skip certian tech's is interesting and in some ways important, i jsut wish if you had 90% of the letherworking things unlocked it could give you a reduction on how long it takes to reserch or somthing like that, seeing as you have msot of the knowledge/unlocks prior.Ultimutly i am enjoying the game, and will continue to enjoy the game which i just know will get better with time.Take Ck3 or Stellaris, or even Civ for example, so i am confident my small gripes will be turned around. In the meantime its a great time, and it really feels like every city built, army used, and wonder constructed is a true achievement.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this. What little I have been able to play so far feels like a fun resource-management game (maybe not a Civ killer like others are saying, but fun in its own way).Problem is, the optimization is so bad the game is unplayable. _childDocuments_.review: Take this recommendation with a proverbial grain of salt; it might not be for everyone.  I came into Ara hoping it would be a refuge for me after leaning of the horrible direction Firaxis was taking Civilization VII.  It isn't.    Honestly, it has a lot of the crappy design choices that I hate the most about what's been revealed so far about Civ VII.  And I knew it before I bought the game, but wanted to try it anyway, because the overall package looked promising.  Ara is an enjoyable game - when you get rolling in the right direction.  The big problem is when you roll in the wrong direction, straight off a cliff.  I've already played several campaigns dozens, and even hundreds of turns only to realize I was going in too wrong of a direction to recover and just started all over again.  Obviously a lot of that is due to not being fully knowledgeable about this game and its mechanics yet, but that's my point:  You have to play Ara to learn how to play Ara, and when Ara teaches you that you've made a mistake, you need to be willing to learn the lesson.  I can see myself still learning stuff about this game after putting hundreds of hours into it.  PROS:-It is a well built game that works as intended.  Time between turns is nearly non-existent, and is as short at endgame as it is at the beginning.  That is a major feat considering how in games like Civilization (especially MY games) the time between turns can last for minutes.  -It looks really nice.  I love the organically shaped tiles and the dynamic way the game builds within said tiles.  Ara comes closer than any Civ-like game I've ever played to creating cities that look realistic.-It adds a lot of innovative systems to this genre and makes what could have been a simpler Civ-clone into something unique.-Tons of stuff to build....CONS:-Too much stuff to build....  I love having plenty of things to build in my cities, but Ara crosses over into the absurd.  And I'm not just talking about buildings; you have to worry about crafting components and goods that are used in multiple ways in your empire.  And you pretty much have to figure all this out on your own.  You'll need to have entire manufacturing chains running throughout your empire just to have the materials you need to build the majority of non-basic military units and many specialty buildings.-There is a STEEP learning curve, thanks to all the complex and innovative new systems that are in the game, like the one mentioned above.  Even after playing with the tutorial on you're left with an inadequate understanding of the more deeply-involved systems.-City caps.-Terrain generation is unkind toward your plight of trying to maximize the potential of each of your limited cities, leaving large swaths of the map as what I consider completely unusable.I could go a lot deeper with stuff I like and dislike, but this sums it up well enough to get my point across.  The game is designed well enough and I like it well enough that I'll recommend it, but it can be really befuddling at times.

_childDocuments_.review: Will I ever succeed in creating an immense world empire? I don't think so. Whether I will have a lot of hours of fun with Ara: History Untold? I'm sure I will! This is an ideal game to sit back and relax with a cup of coffee, plan some moves, keep up with your bookkeeping and enjoy that ambient atmosphere. The game is much more accessible than Civilization (which I personally find more hardcore), but of course, depending on your chosen difficulty, you can also crawl into the deepest layers of the game here. So the game has a lot to offer for everyone, newcomers to the genre as well as veterans. Is it a Civilization clone? Yes, because the formula is obviously very similar, and no because Oxide Games takes an entirely unique style and approach. And that deserves a big round of applause! My tip? You should play this game on PC, that's when (in my opinion) it comes out best. I am not a fan of the genre, but Ara managed to entice me anyway, and I appreciate that!Read More:

_childDocuments_.review: First of all : as of 26 September, if you have performances issues, I recommend switching the Graphic seeting of "Shading Quality' to either "Direct Shading Only" (100% perf improvement) or "Shading Low" (50% perf improvement). Visual impact is acceptable for the huge performance gains. Just know that the "Direct Shading only" option will make water surface completely bland and not display region borders on it : it's probably a bug that seems easily fixable though.Now about the game : it's an interesting 4x with very good new mechanics especially in terms of supply chain, but honestly it doesn't seem 100% feature complete for now. Diplomacy and Warfare are really barebone right now. Recommendation : while I recommended the game for the breath of fresh air it brings to the 4X genre, I would suggest trying it on gamepass first. If you like what you see and want to support the dev in their direction, then buy it on Steam. But otherwise just wait for the game to be fine-tuned before jumping in.
