_childDocuments_.review: Well this is my first game review, this game made me want to write a review since this is, my favorite genre. I've been playing civ games since civilization 2 and for the past two titles I felt like civ has been going backwards with a little added features. I feel like Ara is taking the direction civ should of taken after civ 5. The immersive environment is what I've been waiting for a long time. It makes you feel like its a living civilization. I would like to add that the crafting buildings are over kill. They should of had it to where only farms and towns were a on a land plot, maybe have a separate city window that adds more detail. It probably would of made the maps seem big if they went that route. Also have an option of automation for crafting, its just too much micro managing.  So far I haven't had any technical issues, I even downloaded the game on my HDD drive just to see what would happen because I had my doubts and didn't want to delete anything from my SSD for this. I don't have a powerful rig, I'm only running a RTX 4060 with a I7 9700F and I have everything running on max. I haven't reached an end game yet so we will see how that goes. The only issues I have personally, is that the maps are extremely small to cater to the immersive environment. A civilization could settle a city on another side of a continent with no penalties at all other than the high cost of constructing a road between cities at the start of the game. Two cities could utilize half a continent. The warfare was kind of misleading, I assumed from the game play that battles were real time like total war, another feature i believe should have been the answer to the stack of doom the civ series should have taken. Overall I love the game and highly recommend it, I just hope they don't drop the ball on updating the game and making it better. At least for now I could say this game made me not even care about civ 7 aka civ revolution 4. Side note I recommend civ 4 with either the rise of mankind mod or caveman to cosmos mod

_childDocuments_.review: Don't be misled by some of the reviews—while there are a few rough edges, Ara: History Untold stands out as one of the most promising entries I've seen in the 4X genre in years. The game offers a truly enjoyable experience with stunning visuals and advanced mechanics that remain accessible, no matter your skill level or play style. If you’re a fan of 4X games, Ara: History Untold is absolutely worth your time, and I highly recommend giving it a chance.

_childDocuments_.review: So the recent patches have mollified the performance issues of enabling the vsync, but optimization still seems like it has a way to go, that said, no longer unplayable.So speaking to the game, now that I've had a chance to play it through-Micromanaging resources in the early stage is VERY fun and you can really feel how effective paying attention to it is on how well you do. However, it quickly turns to tedium as soon as you have more than three or four cities, especially as the ages progress and the number of resources to create and manage and make sure are always supplied to your cities keeps increasing- all this with a very simple spreadsheet system I can only seem to hover over, I can't even pin it or add certain resources to my toolbar at the top. The problem with resources outside of the main four, Food, Gold, Wood, Material, is that they're treated as if they're just secondary luxuries but they're not, failing to keep a few of them supplied and crafted into greater luxuries can really slow you down, and managing the construction/acquisition of buildings that provide/feed on them IS the gameplay loop. It seems like it's trying to marry Anno and Civ, but it feels more like Victoria at a certain point, without the UI that makes that level of resource management intuitive.Nonetheless, snowballing is still fairly easy to fall into, I was far ahead of the AI before I reached the second act on normal, so even before reaching the final age I set most of my cities to gather money/knowledge and kept clicking next turn- not what I wanted to do, but I was getting really bored and wasn't really incentivized not to, if anything I was encouraged by the ridiculous level of micromanagement to be on autopilot as much as I could be just so I didn't screw up the fragile eco-system I'd built in early game that kept my cities from starving/suffering.There's a really fun game here, I'm not sure exactly how to fix/fine tune it, but somewhere between less resources or cities and a more intuitive UI there's a masterpiece waiting to be realized. Changing my review to yes because I'm not going to refund, I love the map and city building aspect of this game (turn off borders view on the lower right if you really want to see how natural the map looks as cities seem to organically reach out and connect along lines of resources and borders, it's so cool) and already feel an itch to replay it despite knowing it's flaws- I hope the team isn't discouraged and keeps trying to improve.

_childDocuments_.review: Really wanted to like this game and I don't often post negative reviews but it's a real mess. I've played Civ since the original (showing my age) and I've played the Anno games and loved both. Ara has tried to meld the two concepts which was why I purchased the game but unfortunately the concept has failed, especially when you get to the mid to late game. In Anno games you spend you time building the supply chains on a few cites and get invested in those cities. In Ara once you get too many cities you just can't keep track and there is no automation to help you, so you spend you time every few turns going through the improvements on each city and just adding the latest resources which is just soul destroying. Wars are also not enjoyable. The army logistics is like something out of a game 20 years ago, especially when you compare it to Humankind who IMO has the best 4X battles. The most annoying thing though is that wars automatically stop after a turn countdown which is just not realistic and extremely annoying when you've been attacked out of the blue and you've you're just about to take their city in revenge and the war just stops without giving me an option to continue or not. Wars don't work like that in any other game.... or real life. Both sides need to agree.Two major things to change that will improve the game are:1) Auto resource distribution, especially in mid to late game2) Remove war count down and just use war weariness as a penalty if they don't complete their war objective within the timeline.At the moment I couldn't even recommend this game on sale which is a shame.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely some kinks to be worked out here, but it's a fascinating and distinct entry into the genre. Lovely graphics are great, but I really enjoy the unique Improvement / crafting system. Managing this economy is central to the gameplay, and for someone who enjoys optimization games (like myself), this is a really fun addition to the 4X experience. I look forward to what they do with it in the future.Pros:  - Crafting system is intriguing, deep, and fun to manipulate. - I like having new military units go into a reserve for later use. - Graphics are quite beautiful for a 4x game, and the world feels very alive.Cons:  - Crafting UI is complex, requiring looks at lots of different screens, views, and reporting icons to understand. A streamlined view screen dedicated to understanding crafting chains and the flow of goods might be nice.  - Can't put military units back into reserves or upgrade them to more advanced versions. Just have to disband and build new ones.  - AI doesn't seem too smart when it comes to optimizing improvement placement or using its armies. Maybe I just need to try the higher difficulty levels?
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: It's an addictive game up to a certain stage of the game. It has a potential and so far I have thoroughly enjoyed it. I am really hoping they get the sales to product further content. The positives:- Very fresh approach to a 4X genre. It's just something new, and that's always exciting if executed to an acceptable level.- For people who enjoy micro management, it has a lot of moving parts. Multitude of resources, that have a meaningful use and are interlocked together.- Turn downtime is absolutely non-existent. Moment you press turn, your are in the next one. Probably because of the simultaneous turn system. - Different towns have a lot of meaning. You can specialise each town in production of different good and different resources. Hand pick which amenities they use.The negatives:- Late game is pretty much pointless. Not only it takes a lot of time, but gives very little reward, since there's just a handful of civilisations left, due to the battle royal system. And the map is empty. I think the idea felt good in dev's head but in the end it actually takes away from the engagement. - Army management is somewhat lacking. You can't upgrade your units, so them acquiring XP is pointless.- Battle system needs a lot of work. Once your army is engaged in a fight, you can't retreat. There is very little space for any tactics. You just hope you have better numbers. - Civilisations don't feel unique. You kind of always feel you play the same civilisation regardless of who you pick. It's the same play-trough, because leaders don't have unique buildings and unique units. - Diplomacy is non-existent. You just wait and see what other leaders decide to do with you. No way of influencing their decision. Whatever deal you propose, always get's rejected. So you can't really plan any alliances. - Performance. It's poorly optimised. - A lot of people will also say the game is tedious, but at the same time I like that aspect. So it just comes down to what you are looking in the game.Summary:A fun fresh approach to 4X. It's not a CIV contender. It's an empire management game with heavy 4X influence. It's in much better state than HUMANKIND was and it has a lot more potential than it did at the time. Price is on the higher end, but for me enough value for the money. If the devs start collecting the feedback and work on improvements, this could be something really good. I recommend the purchase, if you're not strapped for cash, it will fill the void as long as you like micromanagement.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Waiting for Civ 7? Try Ara. It's very similar but with interesting interactions around crafting items. This tedious but rewarding aspect gives you a reason to hunt out specific resources to fuel your empire compared to Civ's take that all luxuries are the same.Given a different set of resources around your country? Adapt by picking technologies that match up to what is around you... or consider invading your neighbor to get that material. No game should feel the same.Pros:- Civ Like Game, plays well, is gorgeous.- Unique and fun crafting and supply chain management aspect.- Game isn't dominated by conquer conquer conquer, having too many cities comes with penalties so choosing cities and locations is more important.- Combat leaves a lot of room for strategy and scouting. Plenty of chance to bait out an opponent, play mind games, etc.Notes:+- AI Cheats, but not at the 3-1 ratio of deity.+- Combat is fairly straight forward with troop compositions, but very poorly explained with how the numbers get there (or I'm not paying attention)Cons:- This game is tedious.- The combat is stacks of units similar to older Civ games.- Naval still isn't important for 90% of gameplay.- Being left behind an era is annoying after being delayed by aggressive wars.- Turns drag on at the 10 city + ages.

_childDocuments_.review: This game gets my mind buzzing with ideas on how to make the most of what I've got near me. Really fun! The time has been flying by for me, carefully considering what I can do to keep myself in the game, and just zooming in way further than I'd expect to see all my little guys running around. Real-time games can kind of stress me out, so the turn-based nature really appeals to me, and the turns can pass shockingly fast. Though you probably want to think before mashing next turn lolThe team at Oxide are really thoughtful and open to discussion, and they've gained my trust, so I'm super excited to see this foundation they've created get built on. Not to mention the extensive plans for modding. It's got me excited like Civ V all those years ago :) In the meantime, the gameplay is reeling me in and the interface is delightful for me. The music totally absorbs me into the game, it's super lovely.Also small thing, but I really enjoy how leaders have a unique trait and several more common traits, I always liked that common pool of traits like Civ IV used. _childDocuments_.review: To me civilization died a long time ago, when they increasingly decided that their games would be dioramas, and dumbed down the mechanics for casual console players instead of becoming more of a deep PC game; I found paradox games and never went back to civilization as it is "too simplistic", paradox games are all age specific, and the one alternative they do have (Millennia) goes on the opposite direction I would like these games to go. Millenia still looks like a diorama and is full of fantastical elements (no thanks). Ara picks up where civ 5 left off, expanding so much. I really like the more organic feel; I particularly love that EVERY SINGLE turn is important. You need to check things and make decisions instead of just clicking next turn because you're waiting for the one thing you're currently focusing on. In this game doing that is a mistake. It DOES get overwhelming, but I also remember having a steep learning curve when I discovered CK2, EU4 and Stellaris (the one that helped me understand the other two), but this amount of options allows for quite some flexibility and its about adaptation, which I also like.  Now, with the difficulty comes an issue: it obligates you to go for more optimal builds, especially at the beginning, but you still need to adapt to your starting conditions.The UI has been critizied a lot, It doesn't bother me, it is quite plain though, and of course I'm also waiting on QoL updates to the menus. Options are always good, but me being and oldschool strategy and rpg PC player, I'm used to those kind of menus.The other thing I really don't like about civilization is that no matter how much I tried (I have a mod called Ultra Marathon in civ 6), these games are not balanced for ages to feel full, it's about rushing everything to the end. Marathon doesn't change the techs, it changes everything, so what's the point? and even with my mod I was never able to fully fix this. Here in Ara, turn limits don't make things more expensive, and they are working on a pacing slider so you can change tech speed exclusively, That's the main feature I'll be waiting for until I replay the game, I really want to do here what I was never able to do in most civ games: play long sessions where each act feels like a whole game, where units are still cheap even if techs are expensive. At that point I'll probably re-review the game. The one negative thing I will say is that there is some obvious tokenization with the leaders, they even changed some certain historical character's biographies to make them seem more virtuous, it is such a small part of this game that it doesn't bother me much, and you can always choose which civs appear in your game. I just wish we would go back to an age in which corporations didn't pretend to care about such things, since in the long run they make more damage.

_childDocuments_.review: This game presents a fresh take on the CIV genre. There are new ideas and intricacies which makes it quite engaging for fans of the genre. There is a fair amount of micromanagement, but that isn't necessarily a bad thing if you enjoy managing small details. The tutorial and in-game help are not great, which means you have to feel your way around the mechanics of the game, but that's true for most games of this complexity. Complaints from players seem to be getting addressed by the dev so the game will likely continue to evolve and improve. For me it is quite enjoyable in its current state, and I have only had one recoverable crash in 24+ hours of play

_childDocuments_.review: Okay. I have no performance issues. Not sure if that is due to 32GB of fast memory or the RTX 3080, but my 10 year old CPU probably isn't helping.Positives:- Nice graphics and animations- New interesting crafting mechanics- Combat is functional (can't believe I need to state this, but with the broken nonsense in Old World, we have count it a plus).Bugs and UI- Can not select indivuals in the same regions- Tooltips often needs to be scrolled to show critical information, but also don't show they CAN be scrolled.- Some tooltip are almost impossible to trigger because there are more than one. For instance you can get one that shows how many of each type of believer there are in foreign cities, but is almost impossible to trigger.Negatives:- Crafting quickly turns into a chore- AI is braindead- Game systems force the diplomacy to be constantly changing and pseudo random- Poor connection between tech and their function.- Trade partners can buy anything our of your stores also strategic resources or things you need to stockpile for wonder (triumphs).With a few patches it might return to a recommend, but it needs to deal with UI, and could be better than Civ6 and Millenia, but at this stage the game is too frustrating, too boring, and too easy.

Opposite to civ they don't spawn in a corner equal distance between the others but around you. No diplomacy: I played as France, and Byzantium: the only way for you to have some positive diplo points is through events or by give a ♥♥♥♥ ton amount of highly valuable goods giving too less points, no other ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ways. So there is basically no diplomacy....Armies: No defenses of the most important aspect of the game, cities, you spend all the game micro managing all in the few cities you may build but nope it can be rased in a few turns or their pop simply killed fairly easily at range by AI, no REAL defense system. For the assault you can easily abuse this system by instant rasing a  city and winning a war.The other aspects of the game seems interesting, but this 3 ones just kill any future for that game, and makes it painfull to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Different than Civ which is good for the game. It's difficult to win a war against Civ - it's the king, for now at least. The game lacks some quality of life things I'm used to from Civ - automated end of turn, easily visible borders. UI is a little clunky and it's hard to keep track of things because of it. The pop ups are a little annoying - they clutter the map. Maybe it's just because I have the tutorial on. Combat seems like an afterthought. It just happens without even zooming in to the event or giving you really any notice. The graphics are nice but it seems a little too cluttered at times so it's hard to identify where free land is. The prestige system is pretty good. I like it. Some major problems:(1) Too much micromanagement for me. There are so many things happening at once and you have to make a decision about each one. It gets a little overwhelming. The UI makes this more difficult. (2) There are so many buildings and upgrades - not sure which ones to build or even making sense of their effects in the context of each city. May have been better to have fewer buildings but with more impactful effects for each one. (3) Diplomacy is pretty bland. I hope that gets an upgrade. The agreements have really no impact on the game. For me now, the game consists of just clicking next turn without any direction really to what my ultimate goal is other than gaining prestige points. Maybe that's the weakness of the prestige system - each game becomes generic since all you're working for is those points without any other victory goal. I have to give thumbs down for now. I may uninstall it and come back to it later once the game has had time to mature.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: I was originally concerned about the mixed reviews, but this turned out to be a great game. If you like 4x games and Anno-style 'supply and demand' management, you will enjoy this.The main aspects of the game that need some improvement are: - Deployed armies cannot be upgraded, placed back into reserves, or retroactively assigned to a paragon. - ARA would greatly benefit from a crafting material overview screen where all craft and production stations can be managed, without the user having to look around all your cities for specific buildings. - A city construction filter to search for improvements based on the type of bonus they provide (knowledge, happiness, etc.)The above are not in any way game breaking though and the game is still very enjoyable.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Takes a lot of time and effort to learn but still pretty fun. Graphics could be better and performance needs to be better. More customization for game creation (starting age, unlimited max number of turns, etc.) Game is very micro intensive. As someone who mainly plays civ 5 I appreciate the way the game does some things that are more like the older civ games but the micro is intense and could be automated to make the game better for new players.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: To put things in perspective, I played one full game in 51 hours (it is long, I played +/- 600 turns I think). I won this first game with 41,000 prestige, twice the amount the next two AIs had, and unlocked everything.What I like about the game:- It is peaceful and you don't have annoying natural disasters to make your life harder, like Civilization 6 felt compelled to introduce after they switched to a new game engine that came with beautiful graphics, but which made them go for a "script engine" for the AI unfortunately. The AI became absolutely stupid and useless, so they had to come up with something else for the difficulty: ruthless, constant attacks from neighbors and roaming barbarians, and natural disasters. Peace is a very welcome change, at least early.- I am tempted to say "no religion nuisance". it is a little bit more nuanced, but I won't get into that.- There aren't annoying things like pollution or global warming.So the game is designed to be peaceful and relaxing, which is really what I want from a video game. I don't need the crap of daily life when I play.For these reasons I am recommending the game. However, I wish it wasn't that binary; there are reasons to dislike the game, and I don't think I will play another game:- A lot of bugs and instability issues, the game crashes regularly.- The micro-management is overwhelming and tedious. The goal of the game is clearly to build an economy based on transformations of goods that becomes increasingly complex. So you build buildings that will allow to harvest or produce certain resources or goods, and themselves they typically require other resources or goods, and oh my God there are so many different resources and goods and buildings, it gets more and more complicated. Ensuring a steady supply of everything to enable the construction of the "next" things becomes tedious and obscure, especially when you can't see how much is produced where. And all of that is made more complicated by all sorts of limitations, like limit of cities, limit of regions, limits on types of buildings, etc.- The UI is terrible. I took me a long while to understand how things work because the UI does not tell you much. All you have to understand what's going on and what to do is essentially tooltips: you don't have windows to manage things and it is very complicated to figure how to do this or that. Many things are hidden from you, the UI is not clear and is clearly not succeeding at making management easy or intuitive. In the process of decision making, you want to have an overview of what you produce, how much, where, and how you can use it. You want grids in windows, not 1000 tooltips. If you don't have enough of something, you need to see at a glance how/where you could increase, where it is used, etc. You constantly have to go in every city, check the status of every building, every piece of land, the stats of the cities by looking at many different things all over the screen, or go through a long list of buildings. I'll give you a few silly examples: first, it is impossible to know where you produce a resource; if you have a shortage of something, good luck to find out how to solve the problem. And with some things, as they become obsolete (like baskets) you just can't produce them anymore. Second, there are limits on how many buildings of a given type you can build in a city and at the level of your civilization, but the UI never tells you. So buildings just disappear from building lists, you have no idea why you can't build them and no way to plan in advance. Another silly example: there is an obscure supply called "loom" that you can use only on tailors, and this supply increases by 200% the craft production of all buildings in the city. Go figure why. But, game changing !! It was fun to figure that on my own by pure chance ! Of course, you cannot build a tailor in every city, because of the buildings limits. But hey, it's better than nothing.- As cities keep growing, their "tier" increases and that constantly unbalances everything. From one instant to the other, a city that was doing great (because you just spent 10 minutes fixing everything) can suddenly have poor science, poor health, unhappiness, food shortages etc. The answer to that is adding supplies as amenities to the city and supplies to the individual buildings, if you can. But when you do that, you further unbalance your city as it starts growing again. Amazingly, food production seems to be constant problem, you do spend a lot of construction time and resources trying to cope with the needs. Even shortage of amenities is a problem ! If you produce grain in overabundance, don't think that adding 3 of them to a city will solve your problem... because you can add only 1, even if you have 50 of them. That's pretty silly. I am taking that example because it is very silly, I built granaries to improve food production; they also craft grain, but you end up with more than you can use because of the city cap and the limit of one amenity type per city.- In general, you are constantly in shortage of one thing or the other and you are rarely able to produce as much as you need of something. So there are a lot of things that you just don't build. For the lack of required resources/goods, and because a building can only build 1 thing (you cannot build several things in loop), and because of the many other limitations.- There is a problem with the end-game, when you unlock the last things it's basically game over, you win. So you will never build the latest things. The cool robots, and stealth planes, mech warriors and whatnot, you can forget. You will never build them nor use them. And the problem is actually present during the whole game, I discovered gun power in the high medieval era but I was able to produce it only several ages later, to give an example. Because that comes with complex requirements and I just didn't get what to do to build my musket men. But for many other things, you start building late because you are constantly using your production capacity to upgrade buildings and provide amenities to cope with constant food shortages and the needs of growing cities.- The fog of war that you have to refresh every time you load the game is annoying.- I said that the game is peaceful. Almost true. Everybody liked me... until I became first in score (highest prestige). Then suddenly they hated me (except 1) and the 2 highest contenders declared war. I was ready with 3-4 armies, it wasn't too hard to beat them. Then they understood the message and left me alone. One of them tried again later, but it was quickly over. All that to say that I basically went to the end game and won without ever upgrading my armies. I still had longbow men and catapults/trebuchets, and my military power was way higher than everybody else.- The commerce options are bad. A trade agreement offers access to all your resources. They can pick what they want, causing a shortage on your end sometimes.- Not enough uranium. On a huge map, I found only 3 places in the desert. Maximum chance to be unlucky.- The AI isn't very smart nor active. Other than attacking me when I took the first place, it never did anything other than proposing a research agreement every now and then. One of the civilizations liked me for some reason, and we were often allies. I say often because an alliance lasts only 10-20 turns or so, then you have to wait for a while before you can redo it. And usually you have to wait a little before you can ask for military assistance, so it is not very useful.In its current state, I don't think the game is replay-able.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, Its not for the casuals who like civ 6 or humankind , its not ez, its complicated, your doing a lot of supply chain management. If your bored with civ and humankind, you want something with a lot more depth , this is really good. and looks like the devs are gonna keep improving it. _childDocuments_.review: I love the graphics and the non-hex-based map (I hope for mods to enable even larger maps, as large is the bare minimum I like to play). Be aware that military has much less focus in this game than in Civ. as it's all about finetuning the economy, which  will lead to rather massive micromanagement. To such an extent, you can consider Ara a "planned economy" sim. With the recent patch, things got a bit easier to administer, though. If you enjoy this (e.g. Stellaris, Distant Worlds Universe), give it a go! If you just want to build cities, conquer, research the next tech and click "next round", it will not be for you, as you need to keep an eye on things.Ara has a lot of potential; like a gemstone that needs polishing. Patch 1.1 is a step into the right direction!

_childDocuments_.review: For me this is a winner. I wont delve into the details as much as other reviews: many reviewer have done a better job at it that I would.But I have to say that across most of reviews I have seen, I do think the negative comments are coming too early. _childDocuments_.review: TLDR: You see, son, when an Anno and a Civ love each other very much . . . Pros:The Region system. No hexes or grids and they look organic. They give the game a unique identity and I find it a very welcome change.It's a lovely looking game with lots of flourishes that show off the work the devs put in.A wild Deborah Wilson appeared! She's a very mellow narrator and they put the extra work in explaining who the heck the Paragons were.The crafting system. It's extensive and it gives your nation and its cities a kind of life. My capital has electric lights and IKEA while the city I built in the arctic to take that mineral deposit I wanted still has candles. Maybe that's just poor planning on my part but I find it adds to the choices I have to make.Is what it is:The units. Creating your own formations and armies sounds like a good idea. And it is, but it needs to be fleshed out more.Building upgrades. You can still build basic farms even after unlocking more advanced versions. It makes sense in context since advanced versions require crafted items you might not have or want to use, but a filter would be nice since there are a lot of buildings.Wonders, or rather Triumphs, take up a lot of space. An entire region. Which makes them a compromise to build. I personally like this, but you might not.The Crafting system. It's extensive and until you figure out all the menus and UI filters it can be a bit much. I also feel like I never have enough of certain things, but that might be intended.Cons:Not upgrading units. Upgrading units has been a thing since Civ 2, I think. It's such a basic mechanic that, even if intended, it represents a huge oversight in game design. What's the point of personalizing units if they can't keep up.Foreign relations feel really passive. The AI can offer treaties and deals I cannot offer them in return. It's frustrating.The relegation system. Sucky Civs dissapear at the end of an act. Just poof. Gone. It's really jarring. I get the intention, but too many Civs go all at once. Maybe one per stage of development after a certain point would work better?The Crafting system. It's extensive and It's hard to tell whats bugs and whats intended. I have steam engines and unlocked Black and Decker tools, but my tailors can't make bandages? Did I miss something? Are my tailors just dumb? So many questions.Certain mechanics are not explained well. At all. For instance, some buildings have empire wide limits, others city wide, others are unrestricted. This is not explained. Again, the mechanic makes sense, but a little warning would be nice.Recommendations to the developers:It's a solid game. This is coming from someone who has been playing these games since Civ 2. But Ara is still rough. Some more filters and UI improvements will help. More tooltips too. Expand on what makes the game unique. The region system and crafting are huge additions but you might want to lower, slightly, the time it takes to build things.

_childDocuments_.review: Ara: History Untold is a great foundation. For reference, I have only played Civ 5 and 6. My understanding of what these games are supposed to be stem from those instances of the genre and nothing more. Ara does a pretty good job at what it aims to do but still has a long way to go.I'd say almost everything that this game does differently is genuinely pretty good. I really like the dynamic tiles on the map,  the concept of live battles, and also the concept of item management among other things. I think it's amazing that the game's equivalent of barbarians don't need to be aggressive and that you can even assimilate them into your culture. There are a lot of different leaders that all seem pretty cool and spread out across the globe. A lot of other stuff. This is a good game that will have a lot of fun with. Despite this, I am going to discuss some of the problems plaguing it right now just because there's a lot of work for improvement.The elephant in the room right now is the insane micro management. As much as I initially liked the concept of items and managing them, it heavily degrades the experience in the long run. When you have so many different cities and tiles to take care of, you cannot be bothered to go back to a SINGLE structure in a random part of your nation to constantly change what it's producing. If you do, it's overwhelming and not fun. Not that you will, I mean I'm not sure how you could remember that a single workshop in a random part of the map was continuously making the same thing for about 100 turns. I think there really needs to be some sort of automation that allows for the automatic creation of items that you're lacking, at least for the casual player.Another thing I noticed is that city projects finish extremely quickly and it kinda sucks having to assign them pretty much every other turn. It makes the game way longer than it should be, and it feels super repetitive. I don't really know what the solution to this is, I guess making things take longer to build? The game is already super long though, so there needs to be some balance to not increase it. I just don't like having to babysit what the cities are doing so frequently, it becomes annoying and I just assign them random stuff at a certain point.One thing that I don't think I'm a huge fan of are how units are handled. I do like the concept of having units in your reserve. I don't like that it takes time to muster them. When you're under siege and can't just immediately spawn the knights you made 50 turns ago, it's definitely frustrating.A huge thing that I don't think enough people are discussing is the AI. In my experience so far, the AI is extremely aggressive and uncooperative, for some reason. They always shift towards disliking you and eventually declare war. When you send them gifts, their likeness of you depletes rapidly and just goes back to being negative within no time, so there isn't really a point in sending anything. Even when their relationship status is high, they don't want to trade, create alliances, open borders, or do anything cooperative. The AI always hates you. Speaking of other leaders, I think diplomacy could be a lot better. Your options are extremely limited with what you can do with other players. I think it'd be nice to trade with them or gift things that aren't items, such as wealth. Lastly, although I'm not gonna spend a lot of time on it because it will undoubtedly be fixed, the performance is kinda bad. It's not as bad as people make it out to be, but yeah this game shouldn't be 50-60fps on a 4070 super. It's being fixed though, so I don't really care.And in terms of general things, the graphics are pretty good. I do think there may be a rendering issue with the leader models. They look like the models themselves are high quality but could be rendered better, specifically with shading. The soundtrack is honestly a little annoying and I've found myself turning it off sometimes.I just talked pretty negatively about this game, but regardless of these flaws, it's very fun and addicting. It's a great foundation for a game that will ultimately improve and get better. The Civ games at launch are usually just as flawed if not way worse. It's good.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: The obvious inspiration gets mentioned too much, but as someone who has been burned out on Civ for ages, I am really enjoying this one. It took a little to get the hang of it, but there are interesting mechanics in this, a deep in-game wiki, and the game steadily develops as one plays. The cycle of ages with its culling of the lowest ranks means you have more of that early game exploration and settlement later on as well. The map opens up again. I enjoy the crafting system in all its detail, and the managing does not bore me at all. Indeed, it actually keeps me interested, instead of Civ which has had the same mechanics since the board game and early PC games and is death by lack of innovation. Give this one a fair chance, and I am sure it will flesh out even more. But right now? I already consider it worth my time.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: I was hesitant to buy, based on other reviews. As regular CIV player since 1991 I am very reluctant to like other 4x civ builders. And most propably I wont spend as many hours here as on the other franchise, but I recommend to give it a try.The micro management of the cities actually is less bad than I thought - on the contrary I actually like how you can speed up specific goals you have through a temporary focus on specific crafts. Some interesting mechanics in the military management. Buying Prestige Projects made it a bit too easy to excel on that front.What I do miss also here is a nice ending. I mean you play days and weeks on a game, and then it merely ends with a lame statistics screen. CIV also does that in its current editions so cannot count that as a negative...Gonna try a more peaceful winning condition now as I took over the planet shortly after entering Act 2.

_childDocuments_.review: To be honest I find this game potential fairly high as it definitely has some fresh and nice ideas.But for now I would not recommend buying it. (And not for that price 100%)It's incredibly buggy and not optimised at all. While graphics are not really good, game is lagging for some reason like hell.Gameplay also needs to be adjusted a lot. Starting from really strange wars and battles mechanics (cities after sieges are razed completely in a turn while some common battles can take more than 3 turns), proceeding with unbalanced usage requirements of resources, ending up with completely overwhelming interface where you cannot properly navigate through buildings in the city without any chance to filter them based on their abilities or specialities.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game for anyone who is interested in the exploitation and exploration aspects of the 4x model. I will give a quick review of X.Exploration: Scouts are extremely valuable. The maps are relatively large and the sheer number of resources, wildlife, and goodies creates an engaging environment for the early and mid game.Expand: There is a city cap which is limiting, but the cities themselves can expand and expand, and expand. Each city can build and build, build.Exploit: Resources, resources, and more resources. This game has an overwhelming amount of resources, crafted goods, and improvements. If anything, this game is a min/max, resource and goods management game. If you like micromanaging land, resources, crafted goods, and yields, this is your game.Exterminate: Military units are capped by formations and how many of each formation type you can muster. It isn't extremely limiting, but if your a warmonger, you will be frustrated by the system. This is the weakest and most wonky of the 4x's. From the simultaneous turns, to the unit strength adjusting with distance from your territory, to the muster process, no upgrading of units, this game is not for warmongers. No matter what you read anywhere, this is not a war game. Wars are turn limited and have objectives. This game is not like the 4x Goliath. Again, Resource management, building improvements/wonders, and exploration is what this game does well. War is just a small, complex, heavily structured, and limited part of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: I cant recommend the game for 60€/$ yet... some of the ideas like the management of troops in a "reserve-pool" from wich you can deploy troops in different formations any citiy, or the "acts" that get rid of the worst civs and make room for the remaining civs are nice, but the city-limit (max. 10 in an "empire" ?!) prevents expansion after the middle-ages and you get bored to death by extreme micromanagement (you have to craft hundreds of items for every city, farm, workshop, wonder etc.).
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: It's a really interesting take on 4X and I love the focus on collecting resources and managing manufacturing chains to produce goods that boost the Quality of Life for your population. Alot of the complaints about micromanagement being tedious and diplomacy being too simple are valid, but honestly I can see these easily being fixed in future updates and the devs already have a roadmap of improvements and features to be added in free updates based on what the playerbase has been saying and that makes me think this will come to be a great game.If you like trying different 4x games and maybe were let down by Humankind, I recommend trying this game out when its on sale and you'll see why I'm optimistic that the devs can flesh it out.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Game has a income bug, except it's not a bug, it's called rate. The game shows you have a income of, shows that you're bringing in resources and have resources going out, shows the income resulting, then lists rate the sometimes much lower rate. It then shows the income on the UI, but your reserves go up by the rate.Were you depending on your reserves going up by your income? Well ♥♥♥♥ you, I hope you enjoy floundering confused wondering what the ♥♥♥♥ rate is and where it's explained.Edit: To expand, game still has random bugs, some game breaking, some annoying. Tutorial's could use improving. After turn 200 the tedium expressed in other reviews occurs. Come back in a year unless you're a masochist who likes playing with the ideas in their rawer form.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: This game is quite good, and extremely detailed.   It's heavy on production chains (only other 4x I know of that does this is Millennia) and heavy on producing good to make other things.  It's really like a mix of a 4x and Anno, with 4x level of city building and the detailed production chains and goods production of Anno.  Combat looks to be fairly simple but you can stack units.  You can get bonuses by creating formations as well but the battles play out in an in-the-game-world combat animation.  It's not a seperate combat window like Millennia but is in the game world itself if you want to watch it (which is totally optional) and they look really nice.  Nothing like Millennia's ugly combat window.I haven't played more than 3 hours so far but there's seems to be a lot of depth to the game.  It's quite detailed in it's gameplay and graphically.  People go about their business in the cities you build and even have fun little animations when hovered over or clicked on.  But boy does it give your graphics card a workout.  I'm running a 4070 Super and on ultra settings with no limits on framerate it pegs the card.  Dropping it to a hard 60FPS sorted that out though.  CPU and memory are not heavily hit, just GPU.  No crashes so far, seems stable to me.  If you like a very detailed 4x experience this game may be for you.  I am certainly enjoying it thoroughly myself.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: If you like complex resource management games you will probably like this game.  If you don't, then it isn't for you.  It isn't 4X strategy game like Civilization.  It is a resource management game with Civilization elements.  I think many people watch the promos and make the mistake thinking this game will be like Civilization.  Hence the mixed reviews. I enjoyed this game, even thought it has its issues.  The biggest issue is balance.  Unfortunately I don't think there is a way to balance this game because it tries to mix complex resource management mechanics with civilization mechanics.  They should have not copied civilization so much and balancing might have been possible.  One example of the balance issues is that I was able to reach the Atomic age with longbows. This is because of a complex resource management mechanic and a simple Civilization research mechanic.  I had the tech, but I had to build the supply chains to maintain gunpowder units.  I couldn't produce the required amount of gunpowder to upgrade my units quickly enough.  Researching technology had no such requirement so I could easily just keep researching the next tech. They should have handled research differently.  For example the way Humankind did research would have worked better with this system.  To progress to the next era (and have access to the next tech) you need to meet other civilization requirements (not just research requirements).
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoying it alot! There are plenty of fine details that immerse you and progress is very satisfying. The crafting system is daunting, but really cool and impactful. Obviously with these games, you won't know how good it is exactly til like 50 hours in, but my first impressions are very good so far. There are people pointing out performance issues, but I haven't seen anything crazy with my high-end system. Maybe hold off if yours is mid-low tier. There's tons going on that the game needs to process
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: I preordered this game and I was so excited to play it. Unfortunately, it leaves lots to desire. The leaders are very much hard to differentiate (their powers are so minor). There is no voiceover in the leader's languages, which is a shame. The names that certain civs use for their cities start to run out pretty quickly and they start using names from other civilizations. This might seem like a minor issue but it kind of takes you away from the simulation. Research goes so much quicker than production, that you find yourself drowning in possibilities. Dealing with items is fun until nearly the end of Act 1, when you have to deal with tons of micromanagement. Overall, I have already purchased it and played for more than 2 hrs, so might have some fun with it until Civ VII is out but if I could not spend all this money on this game, I would.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Game does not value your time. To get an edge, you will need to do lots of micromangement by constantly changing what goods each crafting building creates and what inputs it should use to buff, and tweaking what amenities your cities will use (and as it automatically redoes the amenities, you will have to remeber to change an emenity on the last year of the ten year cycle if you don't want to waste an amenity when switching).
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Great game with a lot to do!The devs are active and patches are planned to come frequently.Don't expect a copy of civ or anno or a paradox game. While it's hardly groundbreaking (it's typical empire-building of the 4x kind), it's a different enough take on 4x and grand strategy. There's tons of economic systems in a grand scale, great if you are a nerd, like crunchiness, and like to think about alternate history and future. Some other typical 4x systems like diplomacy, marine resources, and religion... are quite light at the moment but that's not the biggest detriment because of how much there is to do with the economic chains. It's also cool to zoom in close to see what your people and animals are doing, even if it's largely cosmetic.I'm excited to see how this game grows, so consider trying it out if you have an open-enough mind and aren't going to go crazy over trying to optimize every nook and cranny.

_childDocuments_.review: First this is not civilization - it's more of Anno mixed with Humankind ( the latter to some degree ). The first play through will be a mess especially if you tackle it from the point of view of Civ , it wont work you will get bogged down in the supply chain and it will be to late and to frustrating to try an repair it. The game is not bad it has just been sold wrong - its a 4x but with a lot of micromanaging involved :   - each city by itself has its own economy and it does matter because it affects the development of that said city for example in order for it to grow you have to have food and dwellings , even if at a empire level your food is positive at a city level it can be negative which will stop the development aka growth , without growth you can t expand and annex new regions to the city and therefor solve the problem. The same with dwellings so either you plan in advance or you might find your self stuck. ( there are things you can craft like festival, medicine etc that you can assigned to a city to get you out of trouble for a short period of time, but those usually work for a pre-determined period like 10 turns , your city might need 12-15 to grow so again planning take a first role in Ara ). Not clear if you can trade between your cities like in Civilization in order to solve the food issue.  -battles : well this is interesting and frustrating at the same time - due to the turns being simultaneously it ends up being more of a chase than strategy ( mostly because the AI is pretty dumb ). Also you have a cap, not on units per say but more on the formations ( legion / wall shield / battalion ) etc that you can field - this can be increase by the number of cities and some research. Worth mentioning you can have as many units in reserves as you like ( reserves are units that are not on the field aka map ). Battles per say is automated you can look at a video sequence, looks good but gets stale quickly.  -diplomacy : from my point of you is bare-bones at this point nothing much to say here , the AI acts very irrational , and when you have an agreement with them when it expires you get a pop up that they broke the agreement dont want to continue and your standing with them goes down - based on what i have no idea.  -another system that is very strange is the culling - so Ara has 3 acts and i believe 4 eras per Act , when a certain amount of civilizations move to the second Act the Civs with the lower score from the previous Act are culled : they just disappear all the cities, units, agreements, population poof gone, just some ruins to explore are left. They could've implemented this better maybe they become barbarians or free cities etc.  -free tribes : very strange dynamic here  you get to increase or decrease your standings with them through random events ( give me 2 medicine cuz plague etc etc you get 20 rep with them or vice versa lose 20 rep and maybe some other effects towards your civ because ) - you cant declare war (or if you can i havent found how) / when they get assimilated you get the pop but not the province- its more like a migration. -crafting i like the idea and it makes supply chains and city dev very important but please either highlight which buildings could be improve or automate the system a bit - for example each building in the province can be upgraded with the right tech and the right tools which you need to craft but because there so many combinations and if you expand you have to manage so many provinces it becomes a very tedious job - and this is where most players will make mistakes and get frustrated cuz if you have 12+ farms you need to click manually on each one to assign it a plough which increases the yield. Again micromanaging is very important in Ara if you dont like it you wont like the game.In conclusion i believe Ara will have its own cult of players and with updates and if the devs listen to said community it will grow. I dont expect to be as popular as the Civ series but it will find its place and niche.

_childDocuments_.review: Combat is terrible in this game. Probably released too early. UI is non-informative and confusing. Replayability is "ok" but the game feels the same every time. Otherwise it's a great game but I can't recommend it for its $70 price. Maybe more of a $30 game, or even $20.Edit: After putting in more hours I have a few more things to say about this game:The game design sounds good on paper, but really is not fun for me in practice.1: Enemies seem to just show up out of nowhere, or maybe I am just not paying enough attention but because of the nature of the game you want to go through turns quickly because nothing is really happening. Your only warning is "enemy" sighted notifications that are buried in many many other notifications. Also you cannot set your ranged units to automatically fire so they just stand there and do nothing while your lands are being pillaged. 2: Crafting items sounds cool but I have literally zero desire to check every single city to see if its run out of supplies every single turn. Also the game forces you to build many buildings to make many things. I don't want to micromanage all this. They updated the crafting window but its still too much and does not add to the fun of the game in any way. It might be more fun of the citizens built these things automatically when they have the resources to do so, and maybe give you the OPTION to force them to make specific things.3: Nations will attack for no reason other than "they can". Diplomacy is too simple and there is not a lot you can do about it besides offer "gifts" they they can deny. Even if you are infinitely more powerful they will still annoyingly try to attack you and ninja you.4: Something specific: Archipilago isnt really an archipilago.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me first start by saying this is NOT a Civ killer by any stretch of the imagination. Just as Minecraft is not a 7Days to Die killer. They are different in so many ways. Yes the game looks pretty and the level of detail when zoomed in is extraordinary. It plays similar to Civ but building your empire is more than just plopping down a district and building certain buildings. The buildings you build in ARA can be built anywhere within your borders. You dont have to build a farm on pigs. Tho you wont get the bonus pigs if its not a farm but the choice is there. This game goes much deeper in the micromanagement side of things. For mr it is a welcome change from all the Civ clones.Combat is much deeper as well. It does not, in most instances, take one turn to resolve combat. It may take several turns depending on what forces you are attacking with versus what forces you are attacking. I personally have had combat last 5 turns or more. During this time you can add reinforcements. But so can your adversary. although you in most cases have no retreat options you better make sure that this combat you will win or do not do it.Ara is a unique take or spin if you will on the Civ genre without being a Civ killer.I have over 100 hours at the time of writing this and I will play it more than Civ 6 untill Civ 7 comes out. Many more hours more.

_childDocuments_.review: It's been a long time since Civ 6 came out. This year has seen both this game and Millenia release. While before that there was Humankind. This game can be summed up or rather down as a bland version of Millenia with more polished artwork. If how the game looks is the only point that matters. And you like the economic system of Millenia more than any other part of it's game play this might be the game for you. Otherwise I have to recommend against this game. I will go ahead and explain some of the main points as I see it:Pros:1) The economic system has great depth. There are many production chains to manage by the time you enter act 2. Otherwise known as the midpoint of the game. Or really the end game considering the AI doesn't seem to know what it's doing when things get more complex. I nearly tanked my empire entering into act 2 due to not managing the economic system correctly. If you really enjoy micromanaging production chains this game is worth considering. 2) The artwork is top notch for this type of game. It looks better than Civ 6 or Humankind overall. Has a "natrual grid" instead of plain hex tiles to give the map a more lifelike look. The only area it's lacking is that all units look the same. Where as in humankind there is some flavor depending on culture/civ your playing as. The mixed:1) The AI is rather poor compared to what the team making this game appeared to promise. I would rate this a con, but nearly every 4X on release has less than good AI. The options to interact with the AI are also very limited. Even Humankind had more choice here on release. Cons:1) War in this game is a total mess. Due to the punishing city cap it basically rewards players to burn city's to the ground. Since unlike in Millenia there is no real backlash to doing this. Late game warfare is totally broken. There are no nuclear weapons. Even if there were, air units have such extremely limited range they are only good for defense. Like picture a bomber from 2050 only able to strike 4 tiles away from home base. After you had gone though the grand trouble of a long grinding production chain it makes air units %100 worthless. This is by far the worst civ like game I've seen when it comes to end game warfare. Act 3 war basically plays the same as act 2 does due to all this. If you care about how fighting works at all in a 4X game. Just pass on this game period.2) The score victory system is very bland. It's marketed as letting you win many ways, but it's just a simple point system. Yes Humankind had the fame system that worked much like this game does. But Humankind at least had a space race victory that it put some actual effort into. This game is just about collecting points.  The game currently only has one speed setting and forces a game over when you finish the tech tree. Again this highlights the limits of how victory plays out in this game. The Civ games have a better victory system period.Bottomline buy Humankind if you want fun warfare, buy Millenia if you want deeper economy with interesting eras or simply buy Civ if you want a rounded game. This game for most people isn't worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Have about 9 hours into this game, playing a medium size map on slow speed.I have nothing but respect for this game, it has taken the good parts of other 4x civ games and stuck them together to make this.However like all games these days, they come out incomplete.I will put down what's wrong about the game.-UI: it could have been better and if these people were 4x fans themselves they should have seen this coming. having to click EACH building to check if i can put something in it to see if I can boost it. This is the same for crafting, sure it has a tab here you can check what making what but having to click it them zooms in so you can change the stuff there, then have to leave the settlement screen then do it to the NEXT building in that long tab list is just bad design.-Diplomacy: is bad, most the time it's luck that anything happens. have high relations with someone, ask for open borders, that's a no. don't have open borders but somehow they can suggest a trade deal, good to know they don't play but the same rules i do... Also speaking on diplomacy, speaking with tribes don't work at all. I decided to delay completing a deal and it was added to my goals, all they wanted was a spearman. I got a spearman and tried to complete the quest however i never got a pop up or even talk to the tribe.-Lack on information: Most of the items do have good amount of information, however it would be nice to know on the items screen where the item can be use as a supply to boost the building. Like rope, let us know on the item popup that is can be used in a building like workshop and other buildings. This will save time having to check each building if they take the item you found/made.Other than what I have down now, the game is very fun and it's worth the price.A good 4x civ game that has a chance to be a competitor in this often ignored market, I hope to see some QoL patches in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: This game is of the dangerous kind, the kind that gets you hooked fast mainly if you you're the kind of person that love strategic boardgamesREVIEWI must say that when i took the first look in the game i got a bit worried about how the gameplay was going to be. The first video i watched gave the impression that this was a clunked CIV 6. This wasn't entirelly wrong, but at the same time this is a different game with different objectives.If you like CIV 6 (which i really like), it isn't sure that you're going to like this game. It has a lot more of moving parts, deeper systems and a TON, trully A BUTTLOAD, of resources to track.Some people compared it to Anno, and i think it's a good compairison but at the same time, just like compairing to CIV 6, it's a unfair to think that they scratch the same itch.In the end I think this is a good hybrid between CIV 6, the Anno series and I would say with some Paradox DNA sprinkled in it. It's not going to be a game to everyone, but those that like these kind of games and crave to see a mixture of them will have a great time playing it.As a boardgamer myself, I think it gives a lot of "The Colonist", "Agricola" and "Eclipse" vibes. But of course, with a ton more to juggle between turns.What i liked:* City grow seems natural and i think is the best in any civilization game* Each region can be specialized into different focuses* A TON of resources to produce and use* It pays off to plan ahead* Trying to survive each era seems fresh vs other games* With players dropping off in each era, the map opens a lot for exploration and expansion* Exploration isn't something that you do only at the first erasWhat still has to improve:* Production management NEEDS a different UI. (developers: take a look at something like Imperator Rome)* Some overlays (ex: religion overlay) need more work.* Performance could be better, gets laggy sometimes

_childDocuments_.review: Ara: History Untold is an interesting game that I've enjoyed so far and expect to keep playing for a long time. I'm chiming in with a review far earlier than I would like to because so far, only two days after release, it has a "mixed" rating on Steam. I think that undersells the game and demonstrates the huge, fundamental problems with Steam's review system (i.e. incentivizing players to post reviews quickly, only allowing a thumbs up or thumbs down, and aggregating such that even 2/3rds thumbs up counts as "mixed").Like Millenia before it, Ara suffers in Steam reviews from being a niche game with Steam tags that push it to a wider audience than will likely enjoy it. It also suffers from the expectations that players of the Civilization series, in particular, bring to the 4X genre. Ara is not Civilization. It's not even all that similar to Civilization except in some very high level and superficial ways. And yet some reviews are full of comparisons to Civilization games (one wonders which Civ edition Ara is being compared to, because in many ways Civ 4 is as different from Civ 6 as Civ 6 is from Ara), including frustrations about aspects of the Civilization games that are "missing" from Ara (such as nuclear weapons). Ara is probably more similar to Millenia, but even that isn't a good comparison.Rather than evaluating Ara on the basis of other games that are more or less in its genre, broadly, I think it's better to evaluate Ara (or any game) on its own terms. Instead of asking the almost meaningless question "is it good?", the question is really "who is this for?" and "Will the people this game is for enjoy it?" So...WHO IS ARA FOR?Ara is for people who like intricate game systems. The production system is far more intricate than most other 4X or TBS games I've played, but in a way that is still highly abstracted. There is not a logistics simulation like in Shadow Empire, and the supply chains aren't quite as limited as in Millenia. Goods get produced, then can get either used as amenities, as aids to production in other buildings, and/or as inputs to other goods. There's little benefit (that I've found so far, anyway) in stockpiling goods, so the goal is to create throughput and efficiency - as you might in a puzzle game - rather than merely boosting production.The resource production and consumption system is at the heart of everything else that happens in the game. Research unlocks, above all, new goods to produce or new ways to use goods you already have. Not all technologies are necessary because most goods are gated behind multiple different techs. The raw resources in your surrounding area will have a far larger impact on the direction your Civilization takes than any traits your leader has (and most leader traits are relevant because of how they interact with certain resources). Even military units, as you get more advanced, are heavily dependent on your production chains.War (and thus, also, diplomacy) is very abstracted and, in my experience so far, of secondary importance in Ara. Unlike in many 4X games, the X-terminate X is de-emphasized here. It's a valid option, and some amount of military might seems essential, but this is not a war-game except inasmuch as war is an economic pursuit. Many 4X players will be used to the straightforward approach that most turn-based 4X games have taken of spam-units-win-war, but that's not what Ara is about. Again, that's not to say there is no war at all, or that military doesn't matter. Rather, it's to say that the production system shapes the way war works just like it shapes everything else.Another important way that this system shapes the game is in its pacing. In order to achieve the granularity the economic system demands, the game goes slowly. You will not be sending a spaceship to Alpha Centauri on turn 200 or whatever. I have not yet finished a game playing on normal speed, but it seems to me that just the first act (up to the Renaissance) alone can easily take 150-200 turns.In short, Ara is for people who want a slow-paced and micro-management intensive take on the genre.WILL YOU ENJOY IT?My answer is a qualified yes. As many reviews have pointed out, Ara still has some growing to do. I don't believe anything needs a fundamental rework, or that anything essential is missing from the game. I think it is doing exactly what it wants to do, and it is a wonderful game for its target audience.However, for a game built upon managing a detailed resource-based production system, it definitely becomes increasingly click-intensive to make changes to your setup as the game goes on. There are some queuing options that are missing (build this until you have X, or build X - build Y - build X again), and there is no good way to get a full overview of what is being produced and consumed where. While tooltip popups tell you a lot about individual buildings, they don't currently tell you what inputs those buildings take (even if you can guess most of the time). These are among the UI issues I think other reviews have mentioned (I've noticed that many say the UI is bad without saying why or how). I have noticed, however, that my own efficiency at managing my production has increased substantially as I've learned what resources are in the game and what feeds into what.I have a fairly powerful PC and haven't experienced the severity of performance issues others have pointed to, but even for me I wouldn't say Ara runs well. I have read that there were memory leak issues during the alpha or beta, and while those were theoretically resolved I did at one point have to restart the game in one of my first play sessions because it started to slow down. The game has also started to run a little more sluggishly as I reveal more and more of the map. Probably because there is a lot of eye candy in the game which is pretty, but to me feels a little superfluous. If you're the kind of 4X player who has sunk countless hours into games like Shadow Empire or Dominions, then Ara is almost obscene in its graphical beauty, but at the cost that it may not run so well.As for the AI, I don't feel as though I've gotten a good enough sense of how well it plays yet. I've noticed that some reviews have said the game is trivially easy and others have said its impossible to survive the first culling, so your experience will almost certainly vary. For my part, it does seem to me that the AI is pretty decent at walking the detailed production and resource tightrope (the kind of thing an AI should be good at!), but less good at broader strategic thinking and adaptation to changing game circumstances. Much as you'd expect. I'm sure a skilled player will find even the highest difficulty AI no real challenge, but that's true of basically every 4X game ever made because the incremental advantages humans have on a turn-by-turn basis adds up so quickly. For now, and for my part, I feel like the AI is relatively competent and not a barrier to my enjoyment of the game.CONCLUSIONI hope this review is helpful to folks who are seeing a lot of "I like/hate Ara because it's so similar to/different from Civilization!" reviews, and don't know what to do with that. I would write some sort of thoughtful summary, here, but instead I want to end with an non-exhaustive list of games that I think have more in common with Ara than Civilization does. Ara and Civilization share a general genre, but the systems they emphasize and the gameplay patterns they encourage are so different. Many of these games aren't even in the same genre as Ara, but my guess is if you like them you'll like Ara, and vice versa:MilleniaAnnoAgainst the StormVictoriaTerraformersThea & Thea 2Sid Meier's ColonizationBanishedReus 2At the Gates

_childDocuments_.review: Warning this is not your a typical civ type game... This will test your ability to maintain a mental calculation of needs and want on both social / economical balance, and keep your population fed throughout your empire. Housing and food play a major part of having growth within each individual city while the total of everything is used to maintain and grow your empire. Each city in itself can slow its growth due to it having not enough of one or more resources. Now for a few observations... 1. You do not have the ability to search for a favorable point to start your capital ( you are automatically pre-placed even in areas that are not indicative to the leader you choose)                        2. Roads are a helpful item to use for quicker transportation.                        3. Do not be in a quick hurry to build an army to quickly take land. Best to build a couple of squad level spearmen to use in clearing the wild creatures, and keep watch on them so you can pull them back with the heal option.                        4. Have not found a means to combine units into larger groups, although you can build multiple formations in a city and move the total as a single unit till you decide to separate them ( one  or more formations for ranged support).                        5. Do not build a Battalion level army and use it to attack wild creatures, as I found out the hard way that this then allows a greater amount of damage to the whole group compared to a single unit.                        6. Have also found that if you save the first turn, and then reload the first turn to look at different options the leaders of the other nations will randomly change. APPEARS TO HAVE BEEN FIXED...                        7. Land or naval builds always seem to come out of the capital even when the building city has a dock available, and you have to move the naval/military unit to the city originally it was slated to be built in. makes no strategic/tactical sense for this to happen.                        8. Have found that when building ships with a territory that connects to both a lake and coastal shore, that the ship is always launched into the lake even when your docks are located on coast.       YES I do recommend this game, but I can hope they who play this game are willing to take their time, and learn by diving in to the mechanics of the game. Definitely not your typical Civ game culture.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is still a rough gem that merges multiple genres (4X, city builder a la Anno and economic simulators a la Victoria 3). Seing the mixed reviews, I didn't know what to expect: I guess most of the negative review comes from the rough before gem. I was lucky to only have the time to try this one on the weekend (after some critical bugs were resolved) and can only recommend it to strategy game/similation fans as I can see the gem behind the rough! The positives- I really like the exploration and exploitation part of the game. The province based approach is really great for immersion and all provinces are not made equal, which adds a strategical though to expansion. I really like the production chains, where you use the ressources at your disposal to specialize and upgrade your buildings, while keeping your city-state productive and growing.- The expansion itself is also well made, as you need to balance the growth of your cities to keep their productivity up, while making sure you access basic ressources to keep their growth going (wood, food, materials etc.) and specific ones to specialize them and keep the production, growth etc up. While the expansion is not civ like (cities feel more like whole regions with sub provinces) choosing the right region to expand your city-state is really important and will give a direction to expansion for many turns (as each province usually have 2 to 5 areas to build). Religion, diplomacy can also be used to expand and of course, settling new cities in the right areas are essential to keep up in the prestige race.- While the ''exterminate'' area is weaker in this game, I like the approach of creating formations (legions, squares etc.) to bolster and specialized your armies. While war is not the main area of this game (a little bit like Victoria 3), it is still a viable stategy to gain prestige, grab well positionned cities from your neighbourg, or simply create space for expansion!On the positives, aside of being a complete and deep 4X, there is also well made concepts around the great people, that can become advisors, generals and other type of specialists. Wonders/great projects are also numerous and diversified enough to make a real difference in your expansion strategy. Finally, the fact that the game is won on prestige and not sheer specialization in 1 strategy (usually conquest in civ) is really well made. While I won solo games of civ by science/culture, I never survived long in MP games where everything relies on 'stacks of doom' and agression... in Ara, you need to carefully balance all aspects (science, military, production etc.) to stay on top.The rough gemWell, the game is far from perfect at this stage and most of these great concepts are in need of polishing and optimization, as the UI is really basic and the AI is not great at the moment. The game also suffers from a difficult access to holistic information to help you guide your strategy, which might repel some players.- The similation part of the game tends to be too much of micromanagement at this stage, mostly because of an unoptimized UI. Right now, at my knowledge, there is no way, for example, to identify which farm has a plow or not, which stone pits has tools etc. This means that, once in a while, you pretty much need to circle every single building one by one, in each of your city states, to check in what can be improved, especially after certain scientific milestones... This can sure be improved in the future with a new tab showing basic buildings and visual interface/pings to highlight potential upgrades to buildings.- AI can certainly be improved, especially on the diplomacy and miliary sides (it's erratic right now) and on some of it's economic choices. - A lot of information is hidden behind click walls and I am sure this can be polished in the future.- While I didn't notice major performance issues, it seems many players are living major performance issues. I am sure this will be fixed in the future and explains some of the negative reviews, especially at this price point.In conclusions, for me Ara is a must for any 4X fans even if it's still in a rough state in certain areas (UI, AI but also warfare, diplomacy and religion). I really get with this game a civilization feel, coupled with a rich simulation (Victoria 3/Anno) that makes me want to play that one more turn! I am also confident that most of the rough edges can be improved over time and that this game is maybe a year away of becoming a classic in the genre, after patches and DLCS.
