_childDocuments_.review: Now that the game actually runs smoother thanks to the second hotfix here are my first impressions:TDLR: After playing for ~5 hours I felt the desire to play another round of Stellaris or Civ 5 or 6. Unfortunately that means I will pbly give up on Ara for now. Sad. I was excited for this one.* The non-hex regions are great! I liked that already back in Endless Legend. However the boundaries could use some smoothing. The subdivision of regions feels a bit random. Why some regions have 5 small subregions and others only 2 - one small and a huge one? It would have made more sense maybe to associate that density with terrain prosperity?* However that leads to the two biggest problem of the game. Regions subdivision means you have to place 2-5 buildings per region AND micro-manage all of these improvements due to the crafting system. In the end it is all a huge pile of kind of identical mini tiles without any character. Every city is doing everything with very little incentive to specialize. If you have built one city you have built them all.* The idea behind the crafting system is great, but the implementation is quite bad. The GUI gets in the way of managing the 100 something production facilities you accumulate which all need to be constantly upgraded, equipped and balanced. I am not sure how someone thought: lets simplify combat and in turn create an even larger micro management horror.* Speaking about combat: It's quite bad unfortunately. The army management is a bit awkward and then you basically move around with your 5 stacks. When you engage an enemy you enter a multi-turn battle on which you have absolute no influence. You can "Watch the replay" to see a bunch of clones slap-stick beat up a bunch of more clones. You do that once and never again.* Great sound effects and while the music mostly fits in nicely it lacks a bit of impact.* The graphics are a bit generic lacking boldness to develop a unique visual style. Most of the units and buildings looks quite identical. There doesn't seem to be any variations between different cultures. It's quite nice that you can zoom in to see animals grazing, but there is no game mechanic associated to any of those details so you look at them once and never again.----Dear people with old laptops complaining about performance rest in peace that performance is also ♥♥♥♥ on a high-end desktop with 4090. I can barely zoom and rotate the camera getting what feels like 10 fps. I would call it "unplayable" in the current state. I really like this kind of game so will wait a few days for a hotfix, otherwise refund.

_childDocuments_.review: Ara: History Untold is a strategy game with a lot of potential, and I definitely recommend it for fans of grand strategy games.One of the standout features is the game’s intricate mechanics. Managing resources like wealth, food, timber and materials is critical, and every decision impacts your progress. The supply chain system is particularly interesting, though a better visualization of it would improve gameplay considerably. I love the graphics, which are detailed and immersive, making each era and city feel alive. However, I wish the game provided even more depth in its mechanics and historical accuracy, as it's mostly a mix-and-match of historical elements.The learning curve is steep, which may deter newcomers, but it offers rewarding depth for experienced players. As someone who enjoys complex strategy games, I find the region and zone system, along with the evolving mechanics through eras, quite engaging. However, the combat system feels too simplistic; it could benefit from more strategic layers, such as terrain advantages or tactical retreat options. Also I wish I had the chance to support troops in the course of an ongoing battle with further supply, weapons and so on.Diplomacy, too, leaves much to be desired. It feels thin and lacks the depth one would expect in a grand strategy game. With some AI-driven improvements, it could offer more engaging and meaningful interactions between nations, making the game much more dynamic. Also here I think a decent visualization of the diplomatic interactions can help. Diplomacy is always an n:n relationship, everybody with everybody, and this should be realized in the game.The crafting system in Ara: History Untold is another aspect I love for its depth and complexity. It requires thoughtful resource management, as every city produces and consumes different types of goods. The interconnectivity between the crafting of materials, building structures, and research progression adds layers of challenge to the gameplay. However, I believe the complexity could be taken even further by introducing a comprehensive visualization and statistics system for goods production and consumption across cities. This would provide a clearer overview of supply chains and allow for better strategic planning. A feature like this would enhance the game's existing depth, and create a more realistic scenario. One further idea could be to simulate also the transportation of goods between the cities. I think this could be a further very interesting aspect to set up the shipments and transport between the cities.In conclusion, Ara: History Untold is a game I genuinely enjoy and will keep playing. With updates focusing on refining combat, diplomacy, and the supply chain, it could become a top-tier game in the genre. Oxide Games should pay close attention to player feedback in the coming months to fully realize its potential.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's keep it simple: ARA is a distant cousin to Civ in the 4X space. So, It's differences, seem to have aroused strong differences among reviewers.If you: 1. expect a Civ clone; 2. are new to 4X; 3. hate games that aren't perfect on initial release; 4. trash games that don't play well/crash on your particular pc, regardless if it's working elsewhere; 5.expect perfection for $60; 6. are a generally trash poster on Steam....  then just return for your refund, post your toxic review, and leave the rest of us alone.OTOH, if you are an experienced 4X gamer, or seriously want to become one, this game is for you: 1. simultaneous turns- press enter and it's instantly your turn again; 2. vast supply chain management; 3. merge multiple units into higher organizations; 4. keep one national identity (via one leader) for the whole game; 5. areas and zones instead of hexes; 6. want the challenge of a game with many more knobs and dials than CIV; 7. just scratching the surface- see other reviews.Final rating: I don't know, it's a long game with a stiff learning curve, but I'm very pleased with my current experience thus far and feel I have received great value for the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

That being said they all suffer to at least a huge fall. I do not give two cents about any and all civilization after WWII. The modern era sucks in a historical standpoint and we don't really have a civilization sized event that is a mile stone to play with or prevent. Whoever develops a games that ends with WWII that being starting it, preventing it, ending it, or making it a hell of a lot worse will have actually have an end goal and at least have a guide to success.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely outstanding.The first civ-like game I've ever played where I genuinely feel like every map is playable; I have experienced *zero* feelings of wanting to restart a game because the map was terrible. _childDocuments_.review: Looks great, plays great. Very complex game which is going to turn a lot of people off. It's complex to the point a lot of people leaving reviews should probably try something easier... I recommend classics like Tetris or Pacman instead if your having trouble managing the resource chains.People want it to be CIV and it's similar but not the same. As a consequence, many franchise hopefuls fall into the same predictable misery people experience when they constantly compare their new partner to an X. So too many have fallen into that same trap. The good news is CIV is still out there if that's your preference, go back to what made you happy! Seriously, so done with people ruining the survival of a good game because THEY had the wrong expectations.For those that want to try a different take and love the genre, try it out! - Immersive, rich, teeming, great level of detail regardless of the zoom elevation. I play everything on ULTRA settings and no problems even after leaving the game on for hours. NVIDIA GeForce TX 4070 TI - matches the visuals, nice tribal themes at low tech you can tell they spent a lot of time with it. - Putting this as a plus overall if you pick up on a solid strategy. However the game is very punishing if you you don't maximize the resources your handed. You don't always have to focus on what's most convenient in terms of expansion regions sometimes there are resources that will give you an idea of what you might want to pour your production into. I find this really rewarding and well-tuned.  - Needs cleaning up a bit.  - Military seems to be tuned down a bit in this game but somewhat intention based on what we see in the developers blogs. I hope this changes a little bit since Exterminate is a big part of 4X experience. Overall not perfect but really enjoyable slower paced Civ game with a lot of potential. To the dev team: I wouldn't worry so much about balancing everything perfectly before making quality of life upgrades, balancing can be tweaked later.

_childDocuments_.review: Ara: History Untold is a true gem among 4X strategy games, bringing a fresh approach to the genre. The game impresses with its complex civilization-building system, allowing players to craft unique stories of nations across the ages. Every decision, from internal politics to choices on the global stage, has a tangible impact on your civilization’s destiny, making the gameplay deeply rewarding.The visual and artistic design is stunning – the world map is rich with details, and the diverse architectural styles and unit animations give the game a distinctive personality. The resource management and diplomacy systems are designed with flexibility in mind, encouraging players to experiment with different playstyles. The music and narration add a unique atmosphere, emphasizing the weight of historical events and the player’s decisions.Ara: History Untold also stands out for its depth, enabling players to build not just economic and military might but also a unique cultural legacy. The game offers vast opportunities for exploration and discovering new strategies, making every playthrough unique. It’s a remarkable experience that not only engages but also inspires. For strategy game enthusiasts, Ara: History Untold is an absolute must-play.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: A properly refreshing take on 4X games. It pulls ideas and inspiration from more traditional 4X games, grand strategy, and most importantly production-chain games like Anno into a very cohesive and addicting whole. I believe this makes the game more geared towards people who enjoy building and managing their empire, as opposed to the map painters out there.As stated in many other reviews, the UI in particular still needs a fair bit of work. Color-coding and naming the supplies slots in improvements would go a long way; taking inspiration from Victoria 3 and creating a "Buildings" window where all of our improvements are listed by type, and then by city would be so helpful. We need more alerts, for when Amenities are depleted, for when there is a new Amenity slot available, for when new crafting recipes are available in certain improvements, just to name a few things.All in all, though, I disagree with the sentiment from some other reviews that this is an "Early Access" game or that it wasn't ready for release. I am aware that some publishers out there have taken the habit of releasing blatantly incomplete games under a "1.0" disguise, because of the increasingly blurred lines between what is a complete release, what is Early Access, and of the possibility (or rather, expectations from gamers) that every game will keep being updated after launch. I don't think this is the case here, however. This is a solid game, well-balanced (perfectly? absolutely not - no game this complex can be, especially not at launch), and full of content. Will it be better in one year, after multiple updates? No doubt. There are a lot of areas of improvement, and a lot of areas where the game could be greatly expanded. But I am also unaware of any 4X or strategy game that peaked at launch.Having said all this, to me, this is one of the better 4X launch I've seen in quite some time. The bones of the game are absolutely great, the game is very fun as is and the future looks very, very promising indeed.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: I really like the way the developers approached the 4X concept and breathed life into it by focusing on eXploit. The long chains of production, resource management and economics fit perfectly with the other three X's. I found it interesting, even despite drowning in micromanagement as the developers didn't implement any automation. Horrible and ill-conceived interface, strange set of screens and trivial lack of mini-map (or eagle-eye view) spoil the experience, but the mechanics and game cycle are still interesting and can keep your attention.What I can't understand at all is the game balance. The numbers feel like they've been scattered around with randomization. The choice of leaders, which even a player unfamiliar with the mechanics can be horrified by. And further everything is even worse: troops of old epochs are stronger than new ones, dozens of useless formations, goods that are difficult to produce and lose to the starting ones, building improvements that only worsen the efficiency, technologies that literally give nothing, buildings that are not clear in what situation it makes sense to build..... I think this is the worst balance I've seen in strategy games in my entire gaming experience. It feels like the developers have never played their own game. But even more surprising was the first balance patch, which... fixed something that wasn't a problem at all, just simplified the economy beyond belief. And that...is...mind boggling.Despite the problems, I recommend the game. My first playthrough brought me many interesting hours. But I advise you to wait for a dozen patches.

_childDocuments_.review: The game looks beautiful, the city construction itself is enjoyable and the production chains are a great idea. Similarly, unit recruitment is divided into two stages, allowing you to produce ship parts in a city without a port and launch the ship in any city with a port. BUT ALL OF THIS DOESN'T MATTER!!! Cities established by the sea - in Civ, depending on the nation, this could be an advantage, in ARA it has only disadvantages, land provinces have from 2-6 zones for buildings, sea provinces always have 2 zones and only for fishing boats, which means that sea provinces cannot be compared to land one and every city on the water is doomed to lose to a continental city! (the real tragedy is a city on an island... basically you can only burn it down... but they didn't add the option either!). The game forces the end when we reach prestige dps or the turn limit has passed and there is nothing we can do about it. There are big problems with the smoothness of the game when you have 5 or more cities, especially on maps larger than normal!!! The combat and exploration mechanics are simply broken! - To attack an enemy unit that is moving, we have to guess where the enemy will move, ordering an attack is not enough, so what if we are standing next to it! If you don't guess, there will be no fight, and such a pedestrian will run away, even from cavalry, plundering you without consequences!!! Exploration, the ship sees in 2 fields and moves in 4, it means that it will hit the continent and you wasted movement points and turns - because each unit moves AFTER you click on the turn and not during it, as is the case in Civ, it means that it does not reveal map until you click turn - that is, you sail and chase enemy units blindly, counting on luck!!! I will add that the beautiful battles you saw in the ads are just graphic effects, you have no influence on what happens in the battle, only the composition of the units. Anyone who feels cheated after all this... I understand and share this opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: I have yet to play much, but I have to write this review as soon as possible due to the Mixed review rating currently. This game is not like Civilization my dear friends - this is more of an Anno. By no means I say this as a negative as I love both Civ and Anno, but a lot of people were probably confused... This is not a civ-killer. This is an excellent game that can stand beside Anno! This one is more of a city planner; managing supply chains, balancing it out, trading is quite simple, but you trade actual goods you make, and building a wonder is quite a decision with truly great rewards (as opposed to Civ, where you can stack 4 of them in a city). It's a slow game from what I have experienced, but I really enjoy this pace.I've seen a list of improvements coming in. Fingers crossed Oxide! I hope you can continue your work on this game, as it truly has a lot of potential. If you love Anno, you will truly enjoy this game. If you love Civilization, I would still invite you to try the game. However, you're better off waiting for Civilization VII if that is what you truly desire (domination, quicker gameplay, more of a board game feel etc.).Thus, I highly recommend this game! Cheers everyone :)(and yes, I will buy Civilization VII as well - I love strategy games!)

_childDocuments_.review: As an 'External Council' member for Oxide who has put a couple hundred hours into the game pre-release, I can safely say that what they've built here is a very strong foundation for a civ-like competitor. At launch the game is a fun, addicting and pleasing on the eyes civilization builder. The simultaneous turns means no waiting for things to process and that's even with up-to 36 players in a single game! It's admittedly lacking some depth in a few of its systems, religion and diplomacy come to mind, however its more unique features like the crafting offers a lot of options and setting up working production lines to supply your cities and armies is extremely satisfying. Because of its strong base I can see many ways for the developers to continue improving the game after launch and they've already committed to a years worth of free updates based on community feedback. Feedback which I know they'll be listening to as they have throughout the insider development period I was a part of. If the game doesn't quite do it for you here at launch, consider coming back in a few months to see how things are further down the line. I predict that ARA will 'stand the test of time' in the long run.

_childDocuments_.review: In this video I share my initial impression of the game, as well as gameplay of the first 100 turns.  It can also serve as a beginner guide for new players since I go over the game's mechanics.Basically, I have very much enjoyed Ara.  It's the best looking game in this genre, and it has fantastic performance, particularly when it comes to loading and AI turns.  The gameplay is quite fun for the most as well.  However, I do have some complaints.  The crafting becomes very micro-heavy and tedious in Act 2 and later.  I also wish there was more of a difference between leaders besides just some modifiers, such as unique buildings, units, and abilities.  The military system also isn't as fun as other games in the genre.  Finally, the narrator is terrible and she reads everything to you, including the entirety of event descriptions.  I simply turned her off by turning down the voice acting volume.  I'm looking forward to see how the developers expand on the gameplay.  Hopefully this doesn't get the same treatment as Humankind, which has seen so little improvement since launch.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: The game isn't Civ. Don't get it then be one of the many leaving a negative review because it isn't Civ. It's not Civ. Don't be a mouth breather.That being said I come from Civ 6 so naturally I made comparisons.The Good- Depth to the mechanics, "Thinking Man's Civ"- No cookie cutter tech rushes- Tech choices contextual to available resources leading to differing plays between games- High quantity of leaders out of the gate- None of the soy faces that modern Civ presents- Gameplay is genuinely engaging and tests ability to manage.- World and city graphics are excellentThe Bad- Poor Linux support, can't play multiplayer due to sloppy implementation of Xbox Live services- Still a few glitches- UI functionality is counter-intuitive and at times uninformative. Needs an overhaul.- UI aesthetic is bare bones and needs a facelift to add "style" to the game. Current one is offensively bland.- The Encarta could use more detailed information, such as what items can use in their crafting, building limits, etc.- Am I missing something or is there map view to see a breakdown of the zones in a region outside of having a settler or staking a claim?- Diplomacy is barebones and needs a massive expansion. The Ugly- Tainted by modern politics- Animated leaders have awful body language and too many of the male leaders look feminine. Not quite as soy-laden as Civ 6 but still bad.- Most leaders' animations are copy-paste even when it doesn't make sense (giving feminine animations to males, etc.)- Leader roster is questionable. Some of the leaders make sense (Bismarck, Charlemagne, Genghis Khan, Elizabeth, Washington, etc.), while others are civil rights figures (Native American nations are simply done dirty, Sappho?, Hildegard?). I understand they may have been important but they should have been paragons. They already had the perfect system for that set in place but didn't use it properly, for some reason. Being the Ruler of a nation should be reserved for actual rulers, preferably those who founded or redefined the nation *as a whole*. I question the dev's respect of history.Overall recommended. Love the gameplay and how it's deeper than modern, watered down Civ. City building far more engaging and skill-based. My gripes are mostly aesthetic, but they aren't bad enough to compete with the gameplay praises. I would rate it 3/5.The leftist politics are minor enough not to get in the way, but if it gets worse in future the review will be changed to a negative on principle.

_childDocuments_.review: This game adds something that I haven't seen in other historical games. It adds a deep and interesting crafting system to power your nation. I found it a lot of fun to balance the needs of my nation through creating goods and amenities while powering through a deep tech tree. Development of the game is ongoing with the first few patches significantly improving the game play with content based on community feedback. If you like historical games with maps, exploration, research, some light combat and very interesting and engaging crafting then you should try Ara: History Untold.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Finally something different then civilization but still good. The approach is a little bit different its more about production chains / supply then tiles, you have map divided on regions that you settle in (with settler). Then you build improvement (there are 3 - 4 sub regions in every region). Building  you can upgrade together with technological progress - and cities look huge. You have to produce materials that are used by buildings - quite interesting idea to boost production... In statistics you can see how many millions of citizens you have - game is not so hard, developers are working constantly with new updates - its great 4x if you want to try something different - just remember it is not civilization.  I would say its like a cross in between civilization + humankind and for example banished (city builder)...  It has a little bit from these 3 titles... Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: When Ara: History Untold launched in September, it felt pretty much as an Early Access game (but at full price). Too much micromanagement, too little fun. A couple of balance patches and especially update 1.1 made it enjoyable to play (at least in my opinion). It still is work in progress, but the devs have announced that major updates to Diplomacy and Warfare will come soon. I believe this will turn the game from good to great. I would recommend getting it during sale and enjoy the journey.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: I was a bit disappointed when Ara was released, but 1.1 update fixed a lot of things and addressed a lot of feedback. The core gameplay loop is amazing, but there are still supporting systems that are not as deep as I'd like them to be. If you like building your cities and providing for your citizens, you'll like Ara in it's current state. I hope that war mechanics, trade and diplomacy will be improved in future patches and/or DLCs.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Despite its flaws (and there are some) it's an overall enjoyable experience that I'm looking forward to seeing how it develops. The first point to remember is, this is not Civilization, it's the same genre, and there are shades of Civ in this game, but think of this as more detailed strokes rather than the broad brushes Civ games have. Graphics are healthy and updated, and the level of detail the player can zoom in on is refreshing, as are the battles that the player can witness play out before their eyes. I paid full price for the game and have no regrets.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: NOTE: For Linux users, it runs fine in Single player even on Nvidia cards with Proton Experimental (Tuxedo OS with KDE)TL;DR: If you set your expectations for this to be the same as Civilization games, you are doing disfavour to yourself. This  game does something different.I am puzzled why this game was not advertised more and seems like a hidden project, an experiment. And I see it as such: an experiment where there is a merge between Civilization and Victoria series. As such, it does things differently than both those mentioned games but then it is not so overwhelming like Victoria games, and not so pushy like Civilization game.In this game, player must balance city development more carefully and how to handle and channel resources (both harvested and produced). In my first game, I didn't do that properly and as a result, I had some issues with army maintenance and further production in the late game. But that is the learning process for us. Player needs to make best use of the region that contains 2 to 6 fields in it (6 is the max that I have found and it was very rare). Certain improvements on these fields have combo effect on the other fields (like grocer in combination with all the farms in the same region).For combat, it has these cutscenes which look nice and throw me back in time when game devs in the 90s would develop parts of the game which were not really necessary but it is there in attempt to enhance player experience. In essence, player doesn't have direct agency over the combat and thus reminds me of fights in Europa Universalis series - player makes composition of units (plural - as plauyer gan make divisions composing of multiple units) and as well as leader (general in Europa Universalis series). If units are powerful enough, the leader is an overkill but it can make a difference when units have similar power.Here, we build triumphs and not wonders which can be assigned to a player as a task to get extra prestige. Have in mind that building them is not as simple as in Civilization series - triumphs require certain resources. For example: it might require ceramics which player will have to produce beforehand. Triumphs give bonuses which last literally for entirety of the game which I do like.Prestige is THE most important stat in the game. It is a overall score that player race against other players/AI and can cut game short. Game is divided in 3 acts. At the end of the each act, those with the lowest amount of prestige are cut from the game. I have heard that some players complain about it but in the grand scheme - such lowly developed nations are just noise and fodder to be conquered so I do think that this is a good call to just remove them. They leave ruins behind them to be collected for additional resources.I like the UI a lot but I have 2 complaints:1) as game progress, player unlocks more improvements and some improvements are the same base. A fine example is the farm. While it is easy to find advanced version of the farm while the original prehistoric still exists in the modern age, it can be tedious to scroll this huge list of improvements to find grocer or well. It would be better to somehow have filtering that would add complementary imrpovements. If I type food in search, I would expect to have in response everything that is related to making food (including a butcher, grocer, inn...).2) assigning a specialist in the city screen is quite messy for the developed cities as circles for their slot are really too big and often overlap to other fields.All in all, I like the game, it is engaging, it has this 'just one more turn' feel to it. I recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: A Civ-like game with an interesting twist. The game places great importance on the production and supply of goods for your people. It had a rough start for me. In version 1.0, the production and assignment of goods quickly became a micromanagement nightmare. However, the developers took feedback seriously and  streamlined and fixed the problematic parts of the game. Since version 1.1, it’s a thumbs-up from me. I like this direction for Civ-like games.

_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game with some room to grow. It has that "just one more turn" magic for me that I haven't found since Civ. My favorite additions are the city regions and the economy and crafting system. These are a game changer for me. Yes, there are some flaws and some improvements that could be made mainly around UI and the level of micromanagement involved. Just before writing this review I saw the announcement of the first major update and I'm pumped. Sounds like they are addressing pretty much every concern I have with the game. Think the developers are very much in tune with the community in developing this game in the future. Can't wait to see what's available with the new modding support. I would highly recommend this game, but maybe wait for a sale??

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:Immersive gameplay: The game offers a deep and engaging experience where you can control civilizations and make meaningful decisions.Historical variety: You can explore different eras and civilizations, giving the game a rich, diverse feel.Strategic depth: Balancing diplomacy, resources, and military actions keeps things exciting and challenging.Great visuals: The game’s graphics are beautiful, making the world come to life in vibrant detail.Cons:Steep learning curve: It might take some time to get the hang of all the systems, especially for new players.Slow pacing: Some players may find the game’s pace a bit slow, especially in the early stages.Limited replay value: Once you've played through a few civilizations, the gameplay might start to feel a bit repetitive.Overall, Ara: History Untold is a solid choice for strategy fans who love history, but it might not be for everyone.

Only real complaints are the inability to upgrade military units, and the inability to go over the city cap, I know itll give me negatives but id like to be able to anyway, allow larger nations but give them penalties, should be a decision for the player if they can handle them or not.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: The UI needs a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ overhaul like, I need to lose weight. That said there's some phenomenal depth to this game and it really does have the potential to be a contender with Civ, establishing production chains is interesting, if in need of some streamlining (Again UI redesign when?), Interactions with other Civs is a little lacklustre so far, But as I'm still figuring out how to just survive the early stages of the Industrial Revolution It's not to much of a problem so far.One thing I really like about the game play loop in Ara: I can lose the game with out getting curbs tomped by my rivals. You must remain engaged with the systems in play or you will fall behind and your civilization will disappear into the ether.Overall this game is great. It just suffers from an Obtuse UI design and what I can only think may be the Devs assuming I'm a little bit brighter than I actually am.Ara's Early game is comparable to Civ V/VI or HUMANKIND. But where it differs as far as I can tell is the mid-game. Even as I climb the rankings and begin to outpace rival Civs There's a chance that I could wind up bottlenecking and getting my ass beat in a war. This forces me to actually consider my logistical situation. Line does not simply go up. Several lines must be going up in parallel if I want to maintain my pace. The mid game then becomes a balancing act of maintaining enough military to ward off the vultures. making the transition from muscle power, to steam power, to electricity. While also maintaining my outputs of Food and domestic good/amenities. Do you know what feels bad? Looking at my city I tucked away next to some Iron and Copper and realizing I didn't account for that cities pop growth as I expanded towards those resources. Forty turns later I realize FML that backwater has completely stagnated. Now My Steel production's bottlnecked and I'm like three turns away from Industrializing. You must stay engaged. You cannot afford to just coast and rapid press next turn the same way you can in HUMANKIND. I love this game. It makes me think. Just for the love of god it needs another UI pass.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Ara: History Untold is a complex game that I found surprisingly easy to learn. It makes extensive use of mouse-over to answer the ever popular question, "What the #*%@ does this do again?" In some places the mouse-overs are nested so you're following one link to the next. It sounds cumbersome but it really helps avoid closing one UI to open another and another to figure out what you need to know.The game is quite forgiving in Normal difficulty, my first game as Nefertiti I just played Economy, Research and Defense (while learning) and at turn 270 (ish?) I'm almost triple the Prestige of the next highest competitor.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Dear all,I rarely publish reviews - this is my first deep one.What I like:- It is complex, - it is beautifull- it is easy to learn - the Natural tiles - i love it - Battle royale :) love it - nice idea to dismiss the forgotten civsWhat I wish to be improved:- at regular difficulty the game is a little to easy and ai needs long time to also finish certain innovations- Why is there a cap for certain buildings that are reallyy neccessary (for example armory, Iron Production, etc.) - lift this cap - it really makes life difficult- The balancing for the economy when being attaced is really flipping the coins and suddenly all balances are red - this seems unlogic balanced- Allow a function to have more cities if needed - once 11 citiies are build you are no longer able to build additional onse even though you want and need this oil urgently :)- building near oceans really is no good idea - less fields on the tile and less output than on land area - this needs to be tweaked - building there is a true disadvantage- level up units / send them to training to level up - why not? why loose them?- more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for overview (difficult to keep track of what money, resources, etc. you put where in the production chain especially no overview on the mines and some other buildings. - allow additional museums to present the art (I had so much but wasn't able to present them)- I'm not sure - but system starts lagging at some point, even though RAM, CPU and Graphics are "bored"- one minor thing: the german translation is not really accurate - let me know where i can add appropriate translationsThe game is nice for those who love micro management - less nice for a quick run through - at the end I only wanted to urgently win and close the deal :) It took me 22hrs to finish my first game ^^. Still I like it - the approach to have sth. different from tiles is nice.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: So after some time with the game, honestly I have loved it.Now could it still use some work, yes. But I love the supply and demand aspects with the crafting system. It makes it feel like the world is working and aliveI wish there were some variability in some of the buildings, like a library and an art studio looking the same. But you are not always looking at them directly, so it’s easy to ignore. I find out of all the Civilization style games, I am coming back to this one WAY more than I did Humankind for example.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: The learning curve in "Ara History Untold" may seem slow if you play without tutorials or spoilers and initially skip crafting turns to quickly explore other game aspects. However, I've noticed significant progress compared to other games in this genre. The AI opponents are quick to engage in combat at normal difficulty when they sense weakness, which mirrors logical human behavior that the AI simulates through preprogrammed personalities. The one-city challenge isn't for me, so I opted to colonize parts of the map for lucrative resources. This strategy came at a high cost, losing a valuable city far from my capital, but I managed to save my second city and rebuild the fourth after it was burned down during an attempt to retake it. [No save reloads this time - iron man mode suits me better in such games.] SPOILER: It's beneficial to skip certain tech research to advance more quickly, as it appears you can still acquire those resources or buildings later through other technologies. I'll continue testing the game to see how it fares after the dust settles from two simultaneous wars and the war cooldowns. [No spoilers this time.]

_childDocuments_.review: I was reluctant to pay the full AAA price of 60€ for this, but in the end I am quite happy with my decision.As an (formerly) enthusiastic 4X player I was getting a bit tired of the lack of innovation in the genre. Humankind, Age of Wonders brought some, but were too shallow and the latest CIV installment is, I don't know, not for me. CIV5 was the last 4X game I played "for real" but it also was too unbalanced for me. It did not find a "sweet spot" in difficulty, being either too easy or too hard.Now this game brought back my enthusiasm. I am not very far into the 2nd act, so no lategame experience here, but it really drags me into the good old "one more turn" mechanic. The combination of CIV and Anno mechanics, the pace, the micromanagement, hard decision making in sheer endless possibilities, the balancing, the FUN. I am impressed of what they have achieved with this game.It lacks some quality of life improvements though. Without reminders you have to constantly check your cities "amenities" and it's quite and intransparent "in the numbers". Also: not being able to upgrade or regroup units is a bad design decision. But these are the only drawbacks for me and I hope they will improve that in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Good News, Everyone! History Now Told.Very nice game; similar of Old World combined with Civ.Easy to understand after a few turn with the tutorial then, pretty much common sense.I like having multiple Era, and the length of time it take to evolve to the next one (same as crusader king).Run really well, with nice graphic, and an enjoyable immersion.I was very skeptical from all the mix reviews and the high price, like most of us.Overall a well rounded game,I am happy and will spend lots of hrs in this journeys.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good game, the best way to describe it is Stellaris meet Civ (gameplay feels very different from Civ, but not as complex as Stellaris). It would be nice to have more civ specific perks.Good:- Graphics- Getting to know the complexity and subtleties of the game: tech tree, governments, ...- City cap and military cap forces you to play more strategicallyTo improve:- Simplify crafting: the menu with all the buildings helps, but should be possible to not have to micromanage every building- Have more civ specific features: buildings/military units, ...
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: I won't bother detailing the game play here, as others have done a great job of that below.What I will say is that it's worth sticking at the game and learning the nuances etc. I decided to play on an easy level, after a few re-starts because I was getting a lesson from my foes, so I could get familiar with the economics and tech progression; which I must say are detailed and certainly strategic. This allowed me to avoid being attacked by my unforgiving neighbours on higher levels, and,  I think the more you play, the more you will enjoy and appreciate the game for what it is.As a player of Civ II and up, I recommend this game, not as a replacement, but a blend of overarching strategy and micromanagement that's enjoyable: You'll have fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Nice game, though it needs fine tuning. It's a resource management game in a 4X jacket.Leaders, paragons and religion just feel like stacking bonuses or modifiers. Civs feel the same because they have no unique units or buildings.Also the music is weirdly lacking, like they didn't have the budget to hire a composer or something.Fun if you like resource management, you get to decide how things like grapes are turned into either food, wine or something else and use it to creat more and more complex products for you cities to function. However this becomes tedious on larger maps because nothing is auto-managed. Every city has to be planned and managed no matter how small. This makes is exhausting on larger scales and in the later game.All in all fun, but needs additions and changes to really be great and compete eith the dreaded CIV franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: This game deserves way higher than mixed reviews. Fresh, satisfying, original take on the 4x genre.I went in thinking it would be like Civ. It's not like Civ. I had to play part way through two different games before I got what the game was getting at, but once I understood "One more turn" syndrome did indeed set in. Give yourself some time with it to learn how the resource management and production works and keep an open mind. I grant it's rough around the edges, I mute ig music and play my own and the menus can be difficult to navigate, but the game will impress if you let it.

It takes up all the time going from one crafting improvement to the next, that it almost becomes irrelevant what goes on on the map. It's becoming too much. We need some better overview and empire-wide management screens. I don't need to manage every single tailoring shop, I want to be able to set some goals empire-wide instead. _childDocuments_.review: I've been super excited for this game since I first heard about it. So far the game has been amazing and fun, with a few twists. _childDocuments_.review: Another game in need of an average or middle-of-the-road option. It's always nice to see another entrant into the 4X/Civ-like space, as new titles can bring innovation and push the genre forward. Ara does some interesting things, but is ultimately bogged down by a lot of poor design decisions. The biggest change Ara makes is the city amenity and crafting system. Cities now have amenities that can be equipped into them for varying effects and there are accompanying production chains for everything from sandals to salted fish to telescopes and computers. What seems like a fun and interesting system at first unfortunately begins to sag under its own weight, collapsing into a nightmare of micromanagement as your cities grow and you advance through the eras. By even the end of act two, supply chains are long and cities can take a lot of these different amenities. Unfortunately, the game does not give you good ways to manage this, or even to see the information you really need. It's essentially a purely manual system that requires you to just know what's going on. And while the soft city cap may ostensibly limit this problem by lowering how many cities you'll even be managing, even just eight large cities is overwhelming when you need pots and glasses and bandages and books and paper and tools and a hundred other things. The game's manner for giving you information does it no favors, either. It adopts the right-hand pop-up system from Civ, which is fine, but fails to give you notifications that actually matter. Getting a notification about my first pot being crafted is maybe fun and useful, but by the time I'm getting fifty crafting notifications a turn it might as well be zero, because the amount of information conveyed is the same. Ara's other big change, splitting tiles into regions, is... fine. You'll want to cluster farms and similar improvements together to benefit each other, but generally it doesn't feel interesting enough to make a huge difference. The only exception to that is constructing wonders ("triumphs"), which require an entire region. This feels pretty punishing in some cases, and though I understand the intent is to force the player to think about trade-offs, this leaves (from my perspective) a whole category of wonders that will simply never be worth building because their bonuses are lousy. Water tiles, similarly, are a huge letdown. Unlike inland tiles, water tiles only ever have two regions. Fishing boats cannot be upgraded or enhances the way farms can, which just makes water tiles feel wildly underpowered. (Indeed, you cannot construct buildings on water tiles, not even water-based wonders, which is baffling.) Civ-like games have a long history of doing a poor job with naval/maritime aspects of games (one of the ways in which basically all the games in this genre are wildly ahistorical), and Ara continues that tradition with gusto. The civ/leader system also feels like a step backwards. While it is perhaps unfair to expect every game to have every feature, it does feel like simply giving flat bonuses to different civs is very dated as a mechanic. Gone are the unique units or buildings or whatever else you might expect, and here instead are mild tweaks around the edges for everyone, and an unchangeable color scheme. (The different outfits for the leaders are the only exception to this, and there are a couple of standouts for that.) Diplomacy and religion, similarly, are flat and uninteresting. Diplomacy is a particularly big offender here, as the system feels so shallow (and, frankly, like something the player has very little influence on) that you might as well ignore it. Civ games tend to get better as they get fleshed out over time with expansions, and I hope that is true of Ara. I wanted to like this game a lot more than I did, and I put about 20 hours into it when it first came out. But, once I put it down, I haven't felt a big pull to pick it up again. UI/UX changes to improve the managing of the crafting system would probably do the most good, but there are a lot of things that could use tweaking. I would wait on this for a while, to be honest, and see how it shakes out.

Would recommend if you like games where you micromanage a nation and build it up to overcome the other nations.

_childDocuments_.review: It's okay, it has a lot of bloat when it comes to crafting and production lines. _childDocuments_.review: I'm conflicted. I love the economic aspect to this game, and I love building up my civ. But the war system is really breaking my experience with this game. _childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Potentially interesting alternative to Civ, but as other people said, the game sorely needs better UI & UX to manage empire better. Right now, the biggest pain point is there's so much micro-management to modify buildings in each region of your cities.I'd still recommend the game, but maybe get it later once the dev has improved the UI and/or UX.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: The good: This is one of the most economically deep 4x games out there. It's gorgeous, engaging, and captures that "just one more turn" feel quite well. The developers are quite responsive and have promised, at minimum, 1 year of totally free updates.The bad: The complex economy can lead to some tedious micromanagement, and because of so much focus on the economy, other factors like warfare and diplomacy are a bit undercooked. That being said, they are aware of it, and the potential this game has to improve is huge.The game is already good, and is hopefully going to get much better. Buy it if you like 4x games or economy sims. Feels like a mixture of anno, civilization, and victoria.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Extra Casual 4X reviewer over here.My experience with 4X games has been CIV only because I appreciated being able to win without war (not a fan of managing armies) so when I heard of ARA I felt like it might be similar but without the hexagons plus it looked stunning and I like to make pretty things. So I got to give it a try! First game - I gave up near the end of Act 1 since I felt I did too much mistakes and I felt pretty lost. I decided to go for Game two but with acquired knowledge from content creators that explained stuff for me (not that the tutorial doesn't - I just hate to read). That game was much better! I started enjoying the crafting part quite a bit, I felt like I lucked out on a bunch of resources which feels super good and now I'm on Act 2 in second position. Bullet points: -I think the ''forgotten through time'' mechanic is really refreshing, I was sweating for a moment being in the lower ranks and it forced me to take decisions that were not part of my long term plan just to qualify for Act 2. -The graphic details are just amazing-The music is awesome-The crafting though becoming tedious as time goes on is a big difference with Civ and is an enjoyable one-The UI was scary at first but once you get used to it, it's fine. Maybe some QoL would be required to make micro managing become macro managing later in the game.I would recommend this game even if you are a casual like me. I have been enjoying these chill moments playing a few turns here and there and learning has been pleasant and satisfying. I definitely look forward to updates with new leaders and perhaps customizable leaders as well as more customizable maps where you could manipulate biomes (It might be there but I didn't see it at first glance).
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting twist on the 4X formula with features more at home in Anno than civ. Now that they have updated the leader traits to be more balanced and have included the national economy screen it is far less micro intensive and is a much more enjoyable experience that at launch. I can now confidently recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: I do play mainly strategy games since mid 80's and got through most of them, having thousands of hours put into games like CIV1-5, Hill Street Blues, all Paradox Games( except their latest ones, which i find  quite shallow & without soul ) , Gangsters Organized Crime, Total War games, Kaiser, Defender of the Crown etc........From the games mentioned i do  love the gameplay first of all. Though each of them got total different levels of complexity and amount of micromanagement with "Kaiser" being quite "low" in both terms while on the opposite Gangsters, EU4 or Distant Worlds being quite complex with alot of micromanagement. There are also games in between. They are all fun! How?A game is good if complexity matches gameplay, if micromanagement is adequate to gameplay. If ambience and flair excite. If the game keeps me curious for a long time. Ara does the job in it's game design and got into my list of good games. It went straight into my top 10 of all time, if not even Top 5.  In more detail it has exciting gameplay, also rousing through it's ambience and flair( eg with it's sounds, music and graphics ) . Theres a relativ high complexity given, especially in economics with it's crafting- and overall economy system. It's quite challenging, especially on the highest 3 levels. Also this game is in it's base version like a full game with lots of content, not like a "modern" game, quite empty with only DLC scaffolding.some critics: some systems could be more fleshed out like religion and military. Something like pro and cons effects of terrain in battle for military, or for religion more negative/positive effects for the presence of different religions in cities.There could also be more interaction with the city values like growth, happiness, health. Where are the diseases and riots....? Espionage could also a good way to give the game a further push. I do also wish more QoL for micromanagement.It can be even better...Good game!Go for it!
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: A refreshing if flawed new take on the 4x genre...The downside:It does need some polish. I actually wouldn't recommend buying this as it is now, at the moment... The micromanagement needed isn't great when the UI isn't helping as much as it should to keep track of everything as you play along. There is a LOT of stuff you need to remember i.e. Supply, Amenities, materials/goods intake and output. When you get to Act 3 it becomes quite the slog to keep track of everything. Also the A.I. is dumb. It doesn't know how to play the game. This is a game of efficiency and stats. The only time you're really in danger is during ACT 1 when it catches you with your pants down the first few turns cuz you didn't train a single unit to defend your self with.The Upside:There's a really, really fun game in here. It needs a few patches, maybe a couple of DLCs. It's potential is enormous. It can be a source of great stories specially in Multiplayer. Wishlist this and come back in a few months.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: A truly unique 4x, looking at empire building from a very different perspective.Some people will find it tedious but I love slowly and carefully managing the whole empire. The vast crafting and resource system makes every decision very important. Which region to claim, what improvements to build in zones/regions, which and how many items to craft at a given time, which technology to get next...etc. A very well thought out system indeed.The graphics look nice but pretty demanding, mind you I have a 4k monitor so most games are demanding at that resolution.My biggest issue (like many others) is the handling of military units. Can't be called back to redeploy and/or upgrade, Build it, deploy it, disband it. 36 leaders with unique bonuses, unusually high number of supported languages, truly unique gameplay, true simultaneous turns. I've experienced no bugs or crashes. All in all a very pleasant surprise. Not perfect but you can tell that it was made with passion and they wanted to create a unique experience.I've bought the base game then just now the delux upgrade to support the development.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Not as polished as Civ or other 4x games I've played. I love the maps looking realistic and alive by moving away from your typical hexagonal shapes. That being said, the map is too busy at times with the different buildings/units/resources all blending together and not distinguishing themselves enough from one another. I find the graphics, even on high-resolutions, not on par with what I would expect. My biggest pet peeve is the UI which is unintuitive to navigate to find what you need. But I am enjoying the crafting system and its unique take on building a civilization's interlocking economy. Overall, I recommend for its unique take on the genre. As well as the most important critique of all, I'm having fun with it.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Reviewing historical 4x games is a bit wonky, because it's arguably the genre that is most defined by a single series, and has been for the last 3+ decades.It's also important to note that the most recent entry into that series, Civ 6, took quite a while to achieve the same kind of regard that Civ 5 had. That game was pretty shallow and bare-bones long after launch.So expecting Ara to have the polish or depth straight out of the box that it took Civ 6 years to achieve is unrealistic. Right now, there are a lot of issues. But the game's bones are really solid. Gorgeous graphics. A supply chain system that Millennia tried (and woefully failed) to implement. A slew of leaders with many interesting perks, giving you a reason to try different playstyles. I think this is a game that would have benefited from an Early Access period, because A) some of the systems are threadbare, B) the AI is comically inept, and C) the late game is almost literally unplayable due to the amount of micromanagement required. But unlike Millennia, solving these problems won't require a complete re-think. I'd give this one a shot if you're waiting for Civ 7 and open to a different take on the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: You have something great here guys!  Great work!  There of course will need to be some adjustments to certain areas, but that is nothing that can't be achieved!I am putting the issues at the bottom as they are just issues I have right now and may change later and NOT A SERIOUS PROBLEM like others may indicate! My favorite feature improvements from past Civ features (no knock at the Civ guys) and the genre itself:1) The Military force and city count limitations is a good thing as the game progresses as that is a part of Civilization that was kind of an issue to me.2) Love not having to worry too much about city happiness as cities grow as you need to make improvements for that to happen which keeps that under control.3) It feels like a Civ-like game re-thought!4) The economic system itself, it is really interesting.5) The Rest of the game I LOVE!My Issues so far, but I know, there is always room for this future releases:1) Units are hard to manage and group together or know when they are grouped.  Maybe I am doing something wrong as I am still new. 2) The economic system is hard to keep track of later in the game.  There needs to be some way of seeing what is going on there from a higher level.3) Would like to see the detail of what each of the nations are doing good or bad or maybe a technology you need for it.  Maybe I haven't seen that yet, I am still just at Act 2 currently.4) I'm having a hard time understanding the Materials resource enough to improve it when it is low.  It is based on the crafted items from minerals and gathered resources from scouts for example, but I had a map location where there wasn't much of a mineral deposit anywhere and it was hard to manage that resource that well.  I am still learning though.5) Not sure yet if I like the Culling feature at each Act to qualify based on Prestige, but that can be turned off.  I think I may accept it later though as if it isn't going well, why continue anyways.6) It appears some nations can gain prestige and continue in the game even though they are starting to lose their cities.  Maybe they should lose some prestige for that when there is a Cassus Belli Retaliation War against them for example?
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Fun take on the 4X genre, stunning graphics, obsessed with the living world and (controversially) I think the combat is pretty good. Could definitely do with a few quality of life tweaks. UI does a decent job, but once you settle 6+ cities it can get pretty overwhelming. The more you play and get used to the resources, supply chains etc the easier it becomes, but definitely enjoying the learning curve so far!
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: I like the game.  It does have some gameplay flaws such as not being able to upgrade units or reorganize them after deployment.  Those are odd choices, but it looks like the developers are engaged and actively working on things like this.  It does have a good bit of micro, so if you hate micro, it is not for you.  If you like micro, you will love this.Basically, unlike in Civ (the obvious comparison), your improvements produce raw materials which can be further processed by other improvements as time goes on.  For example, if you plant wheat, you can turn it into bread.  If you farm sheep, you can harvest wool, and you can turn that wool into cloth.  You get the idea.The biggest weakness by far to me is war.  Not being able to upgrade units or reorganize is terrible.  I do like getting to watch battles play out, though.  Overall, I would give this a sideways thumb.  If they fixed military, I would give it a thumbs up.  It is more complex than Civ, but it is far more fun than Humankind.  Give it a try!Edit on 11/16/2024:  With the 1.1 patch, Ara fulfills its promise of a great 4x.  If you haven't bought it and you like a 4x, grab it now!
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: So You want to buy this game? Here's a quick few points worth considering:* At the point of writing this review, the game is largely unfinished. It's missing some key UI elements that are necessary to manage the improvements properly. Also bunch of bugs, like not being able to demolish things.* Probably best Civ game for multiplayer because of simulaneus turns.* The micromanagement at endgame is real! Not only You manage different improvements, You manage the improvements equipment and improvements production chains.* The difficulty feels solid, and AI will do things like, ferry an army of troops across the sea to your weakest city and declare a surprise expansion war on You. Which is awesome.* The game is really complex and I don't think it's possible to keep track of all the bonuses. No kidding You will get like 50 bonuses and debuffs to Your happiness stat at the end of the game.* I'm just playing on prince difficulty, and having experience with many Civ games, I keep on my toes. I just make it barely, at each age not to get dropped, and it feels awesome!* Expect 20h or more per game on a small map.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Compared to a strategy game, the graphics and visual appearance are something very cool!I think the historical explanations / presentations separately as you progress through the game was a very good idea on the part of the developers!I like how you can develop your city and your agriculture, many hours can be put into the game!From the peasant age to the modern age, you can go into the game and during that time you will kill a lot of hours!I have been waiting for a new strategy game for a very long time and this game more than met my expectations!I also really like the war design, you declare war, then when you besiege them and fight, you can watch the animated war in 3D, I really like it, and I've only seen it in mobile ads so far, but here they really did it!The game is very elaborate and detailed, so I won't go into too much detail.It is atmospheric, spectacular, historically correct and instructive.I can definitely recommend it to anyone who likes such games.As you progress through the game, it gets more complicated and difficult, so there's plenty of challenge!I can recommend it!
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: A 4X game with the typical rough start because games can't just be actually finished on release these days. This one has a solid foundation though, and at least a year of free improvements coming, so I'm optimistic. Even now at launch, it's already less buggy and more fun to play than Civ VI was at launch.
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: Tl;dr: it's a very good turn-based strategy game that does it's own thing and is by no means a "clone".The game is gorgeous-looking and very fun to play (the One More Turn Syndrome is strong with this one). The UI is fine and informative, but could use a few QoL improvements to make resource management easier. The true simultaneous turns  mean that all the actions are resolved once everyone ends their turns (no more "who clicks faster, takes the city"), which in turn means that you can undo all your actions (e.g. unit orders or rushing production). I really like the sprawling cities -- as they grow, they claim more regions and each region contains 2-5 zones on which you place all the improvements like farms, granaries, or workshops. The game is very stable and bug-free -- I've only encountered one small bug so far and it resolved itself (couldn't found a new city even though I was at 7/8 capacity), no crashes whatsoever.Don't believe the reviews complaining about micro -- it's really only present in the early game, when you have 1 or 2 cities, but soon enough you can just stick workshops to permanently produce only 1 thing and leave them at that. The goods storage is global so you don't have to worry about transporting goods or producing goods in specific cities.Apart from some UI QoL improvements, the only complaint I'd have is that army management could be better: there is no way to return a mustered army back to reserves, upgrade units, or to change the army composition (which could be easily done with some cost, e.g. taking a couple of turns to retrain or whatever).
_childDocuments_.name: Ara: History Untold

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing these 4X games for a while now; I'm not an expert in advanced mechanics and some other deep strategies, nevertheless, from the perspective of a person who loves the genre and tries to have a good time with them, I can CAUTIOUSLY recommend this title.It may indeed resemble a bit of a combination of anno and civ, but I would add something else here - great similarities to the Dominions series in some aspects. For me, this is a big plus. Unfortunately, the undeniable problem is the absolutely terrible optimisation and UI - it's not even about the difficulty of using it, but it just looks cheap and doesn't correspond to the theme of the game at all. The game runs fine on my PC, but on my laptop it's practically a slideshow (both devices very close in performance). Personally, I was positively surprised by how engaging and interesting this game is and at the same time disappointed by those flaws I mentioned above. I gave a positive rating because, despite everything, the disadvantages are few in relation to the advantages and the entertainment and visual value.It's worth keeping an eye on Ara until it's on promotion, because the game itself is really interesting and introduces a lot of fresh solutions to a well-known and well-liked convention. Elo

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of good ideas but sorely lacking in polish and balancing.When the game feels like a puzzle where you have to balance where to expand, what to research, and what resources you have it is a refreshing blend of 4X, city management, and factory game it is incredible. When they game fails it is a wild mess with hard to navigate UIs and the worst scaling you have ever seen. The game looks incredible and borders and rivers feel natural in way most 4x games don't. The trade-off is that the game runs worse on low than state of the art games on high for my machine.There are so many highs and lows to find here.In comparison to other 4X games, it offers a lot of things to think about and plan for society in peacetime. Production is a lot more than more hammers and more research is more better, as you need specific types of goods and supply chains to increase productivity and production in a way that feels natural and complex. There are various synergies between placing various buildings and staffing the right buildings with experts for your specific needs. The system is a lot more involved than districts in Civ6 but doesn't require planning from the start. The crafting makes you think as much about survival crafters and factory games as it does proper 4X gameplay.That is the concept however. In reality, the most relevant thing you want is "City production" and anything that stacks city production is going to be vastly better than anything else. Late game naval bases should never be built as they don't give you the production bonuses of earlier harbors. The game lets you build the old building however, so in-case you accidentally research them you don't brick your empire. This is far from the only issue with balancing and scaling however.Example 1: Coffee is a resource you slot into research labs, universities, etc to increase research. You make these in coffee houses that use coffee beans (among other things). This means that if you have 20 such slots by the end of the game, you will only ever need 20 coffee. Those 20 coffee are made with something like 2 beans each, so you need 40 beans. A coffee farm can make 20 beans *per turn* in normal conditions, and multiples of that by late game. So in an economic optimization sense you only ever need to run the farm 1-2 turns to supply the entire game's worth of coffee. After that you can bulldoze it over to make more houses or workshops or a monument to the forbidden beverage idk. Coffee houses give other benefits that make them very useful to keep around, and if you have the house the production itself has no upkeep. So you end up running coffee houses with no inputs for a hundred turns or more and end up with hundreds of thousands of coffee that you can't ever use.Example 2: A car is made with engines (among other things) and these have long supply chains. Instead of engines you can substitute with gold (like many inputs in the game), and this is for 10 gold. Most other industrial goods run into the 90-100 range, so this is probably a bug to get patched. Assuming they patch the 10 gold to 100, it still doesn't actually address the problem. An incense or tobacco farm when stacked with bonuses can make 200 or more gold, meaning that it is much more efficient to have plantation goods than the entire industrial era supply chain for cars. If your goal is to make cars, incense and tobacco nodes will get you there better than any number of iron nodes. You still want iron to make steel which late game buildings need, but that also means that the steel to make engines is very valuable for other things, further reducing your desire to supply engine factories with steel. You need 20 or so engines for the vehicle factories and after that it is always correct to stop making engines and instead substitute them in all factories. The only reason to ever make engines after that is if you are gold starved and they have patched them, otherwise the factory upkeep is actually going to be higher than substituting the entire factory.I think these illustrate what I mean by great ideas that completely fail due to how poorly balanced all the systems are combined. I don't think the bad diplomacy, completely irrelevant trade, and repetitive events really impact the overall good and bad of the game's core functions. I will however say that the tech tree is easily better than its peers in principle, though it suffers from how badly balanced the other pieces of the game work together.The game scratches the 4X itch, but it is undercooked and I only recommend it to 4X enthusiasts who want to try a brand new take with lots of potential. The potential is as of now however, quite unrealized.
