_childDocuments_.review: When I first pre-ordered the game I had my hopes up as well as a few concerns, but I was willing to give this game a chance.I wanted to like this game, i really did, and for parts I did, the game looks great and for the most part plays nicely, but there are just too many negatives to ignore, I want to go a little in-depth with my review here.This review obviously contains spoilers.- Story -It's a classic sonic game, you should never expect stellar story telling, but one thing I want to say is it feels, weird, Sonic 3 and Mania explained it's story through visual cues or short cut scenes, we have those here but some things seem unexplained, like how Robotnik can suddenly reverse time in the final stage, maybe he built the thing but lacks clarity. -Graphics -The game is very pretty and has a lot going for it, I thought some areas looked a little weird but I was able to ignore that for how stunning some places can be. The game runs amazingly too I only had 1 freeze and that was super early in the game after dying once.- Sound -I am very mixed with the sound design in this game, either there seems to be some sound lacking, or really weird choices, but for the most part the sound fits the scene, overall solid.- Music -I like some tracks but the others give me some serious Sonic 4 syndrome, at points I actually preferred Sonic 4s soundtrack, the music can go from really nice and catchy to just, messy and kind of headache inducing. Massive pass on the music in this game, such a shame considering Manias was so good. - Characters -It's always a joy to see Sonic Tails and Knuckles are an extra joy to see Amy, Robotnik of course rocking my preferred design for him, Fang was a big surprise and had a lot of cool moments, the new character though, Trip, I don't get. They are a cool character and have a cute design but other from that she does, nothing, just hangs around fang and appears sometimes. I like the touch that she is playable, but, I will get on that later.- Stages -The stages honestly were great but also not, some are nice to play and others no so, I thought we were ready to go past generic stage types for Sonic and for the most part we did, until you notice that the levels are pretty much just classic sonic levels but, slightly different, the games pacing even felt like Sonic Mania at times, it felt really uninspired.The final level too is both super creative but, kind of lazy, it's the same as Act 1 but you do it in reverse, in concept really cool but in execution, kinda lame. Also this game loves putting you in spots where you get hit, Cyber Station doing this a lot, not very clever design when it's for the most part unavoidable. - Bosses -They suck, 90% of the bosses suck. They are the worst part of the game easily, either hitting you with no telegraph or time for reaction, requiring super specific jumps to dodge, or, worst of all,  no clear indications on when you can hit things. When you hit a boss it flashes for a bit, showing you hit it, this also served as invincibility frames in the classic games, here it means nothing, you can hit a boss and then 10 seconds later you can try to hit it again and go right through it and die in a pit, which I want to also mention, this game relies WAY TOO MUCH ON, I rarely died to the boss itself but rather my going right through it into a pit, or given under a section to react to a attack which puts me in a pit, the Cyber Station Boss and the FINAL BOSS being a massive example of this, some of the worst bosses I have ever played hands down. I also want to add that they take too long to beat sometimes even if your perfect, you are not rewarded for playing it smart and getting many hits, you can only get 1 hit and you have to wait for the next opening, it's not fun.- Extras -I don't like the special stages, they are really unimaginative and boring, the bonus stages looked like it has a lot more work put into them, such a shame.Getting all the Chaos Emeralds feels meaningless, I THINK it's how you unlock Trip as a playable character but I was expecting a different ending, which it seems to just be the normal ending, again, a shame and also breaking the staple that started in Sonic 2 (Even though that ending was pretty minor), really weird.When I saw Trips story, I thought it was gonna be a new set of stages with Trip, perhaps to learn about her story, instead it's just the story mode again but with enemies spammed everywhere and the bosses having a lot more health, not worth getting the Chaos emeralds for.In conclusion, I don't recommend this game, at least right now, it's not well designed outside a couple of aspects, and got really annoying at the end. I am upset this game is not as poor as it is.Also, as a bonus, MASSIVELY overpriced for how much you get.

_childDocuments_.review: Sonic Superstars puts classic Sonic in the modern era of this franchise. It is pulled off in spectacular fashion. The graphics style really suit this game. 2.5D is a new frontier for the Sonic franchise that works surprisingly well. It truly feels like a classic Sonic The Hedgehog game. The new zones are exceptionally fun. Each zone brings in new mechanics and game play. There is even more enemies to fend off against in each zone. The designs for these said zones feel really refreshing, but kind of your typical Sonic zone selection. There's the green hill look alike, the desert zone, the water zone and lastly, another Eggman's fortress. Though, the zones differ heaps from one another which in a way redeems the titular format. Now, there are five different playable characters in Sonic Superstars. Sonic, Amy, Tails, Knuckles and Trip. Each character has its own special ability which are all very fun to use and adds a ton of variety to play through's. Being able to play cooperative is a nice touch that adds another layer of fun to Sonic Superstars. Customisation is great, with there being four skins for Sonic, while only one additional skin for the rest of the crew except Trip. There could've been some clever skin choices especially considering that there is an item shop. Though, the item shop is used for the battle mode robot. It allows the player to customise their own player for the battle mode and can make for some ludicrous combinations. There is a lot to choose from, whether its the characters you play as in the story, or a classic SEGA character (Nights). The battle mode is certainly very forgettable though. It would be played for a couple fun rounds than it becomes boring. One of the best parts of Sonic Superstars comes in the form of the new emerald powers never seen before in the Sonic franchise. Each emerald has a unique ability that offer fun game play. The powers do come with benefits, they may lead to a hidden area or to a gold medallion. It makes for great replay ability trying to find medallions or all of the gold enemies. Both the main story and Trip's story are fun, though Trip's story feels significantly harder. The boss fights have more health and there's always an Eggman robo chasing the player down. It can even get frustrating at times. Without Trip's awesome and overpowered super form, her story is a chore. Like any Sonic game, the music is always on par. Each zone has refreshing music that sets a perfect tone. The boss fights are quite good and fun. However some of them feel a little generic, simple and bland in design. There was some room for improvement. Some of them bosses are proven to be very challenging, especially the final boss from each story (Main story, Trip's story and the final story). Each one of them drag on for over six minutes each. With no checkpoints at all. So, if the player dies they have to go through the entire boss fight again. However, each final boss has a unique move set that have very fair attacks. Except for Fang's final boss, which has an instant kill attack which is confidently unfair in many ways. The music from each of these bosses is just perfect. It couldn't have felt more epic and climactic. Sonic Superstars reinvents the classic formula in exhilarating fashion and encompasses refreshing, new mechanics that have not been seen in previous entries. 8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: edit: I just finished the game in a little under five hours. The last third of the game is awful. Golden Palace looks & feels like an unfinished level and generally it's all unpolished... the bossfights get progressively worse too, until they're longer than the actual levels. Fang and the final boss are beyond bad. The final level's gimmick had me uttering to myself in disbelief. How they have the nerve to charge full price for this is beyond me. -----Given the price, it's impossible to give this game a positive review; it's not impossible to make a full-price 2D-style platformer, but this isn't it and even half the price would be pushing it a little. Denuvo inclusion is also a negative.On the other hand, the game itself seems pretty good so far. Sonic's physics aren't 100% perfect, but they're better than we've seen in any Sonic game for a long time sans Mania (which blows this away, obviously, even if Sega insists that we don't like Mania and don't want more of it). There's a nostalgic feeling while platforming using Sonic's momentum, something that the post-Mega Drive games eschewed but which feels close enough to the classics here. Level design is good and has plenty of inventive moments. Bosses are too slow for how simple they are, but otherwise they're executed well enough and can be clever.Performance is also very good: my ultra-thin laptop with a GTX 1650 (Max-Q ie. 35W-limited), i5-11300H and 8GB is capable, with overclocking (mem+core OC, obviously same power usage since it's hard-capped), of running the game at 2880x1620, V-sync-capped at 90FPS without dropping frames outside of some intensive set-piece moments. Without the overclock, it doesn't keep to the V-sync cap, but it does still stay above 60FPS which suggests that pretty much any desktop graphics card that isn't completely antiquated should be able to manage 1080p 60FPS gameplay (the minimum requirement of a GTX 750 seems reasonable). CPU performance also doesn't seem to be limiting.Everything they added outside of the levels themselves is bad though. Bad emerald special stages, a slightly better but still tedious version of Sonic 1's special stage (that thankfully only yields medals which can be collected more easily through other means), the stupid emerald powers that I assume 99% of players will ignore and which don't really mesh at all with the game mechanics.A quick note on the music. One of the boss themes had me convinced that it was reused from Sonic 4, so much so that I alt-tabbed the game and listened to the boss themes from those games to confirm that it wasn't. That should say enough about the quality of some of the music in this game. (Remember Ruby Delusion from Mania? What a sick boss theme.)I'd recommend this if it wasn't for the price. If you're a Sonic nerd and you have to play this game, at least go find the cheapest official game key retailer and pay a little less.

_childDocuments_.review: Sonic Superstars? A High-Speed Adventure with Ups and Downs! (ฅ'ω'ฅ)Sonic the Hedgehog has been a beloved gaming icon for decades, known for his lightning-fast speed and iconic blue quills. The latest addition to the franchise, Sonic Superstars, attempts to rekindle the magic of classic 2D Sonic adventures while introducing new elements. With its mix of positive and negative aspects, this game brings a rollercoaster of emotions for both long-time fans and newcomers.One of the standout features of Sonic Superstars is its revitalized take on classic 2D Sonic action. The game seamlessly combines 2D sidescrolling with stunning 3D graphics, offering a fresh perspective on the Sonic universe. Players can take control of Sonic, Tails, Knuckles, and Amy, each with their unique abilities, adding variety to the gameplay.The game introduces new powers and abilities, thanks to the Chaos Emeralds, allowing players to multiply, swim up waterfalls, and change forms. The addition of up to 4-player local co-op is a welcome feature, allowing friends to join in for some fast-paced fun. The Battle Mode, which supports up to 8 players, adds a competitive edge to the Sonic experience.Sonic Superstars falls short in some key areas, which have led to mixed reviews from players. Firstly, the game's integration with Epic Games and the presence of Denuvo DRM have drawn criticism. The game insists on an Epic Games account for online play, even on Steam, which feels unnecessary and intrusive for some users.The biggest letdown for many players seems to be the challenging and, at times, frustrating boss battles. Some describe these encounters as overly tedious and long, lacking the precise timing and rhythm that made classic Sonic bosses memorable. The absence of checkpoints during the final boss battle, coupled with instant death via pits, can lead to significant frustration.Additionally, despite its solid core gameplay, Sonic Superstars doesn't bring a unique identity of its own compared to fan-favorite titles like Sonic Mania. Some players feel that it lacks the same level of style and personality that made past Sonic titles shine. The game's music, a fundamental aspect of Sonic titles, also fails to impress, with some tracks reminiscent of the criticized soundtrack from Sonic the Hedgehog 4. This has left fans yearning for the high-quality, catchy tunes that the franchise is known for.Sonic Superstars is a mixed bag that captures the essence of classic Sonic action while introducing new elements. Its blend of 2D sidescrolling and 3D graphics, unique character abilities, and local co-op play provide some enjoyable moments. However, the game faces criticism for its intrusive integration with Epic Games, the inclusion of Denuvo DRM, and some frustrating boss battles. The absence of a distinctive identity and a lackluster soundtrack may leave some Sonic enthusiasts wanting more. While there are areas that could use improvement, Sonic Superstars manages to deliver a solid Sonic experience, albeit with some rough edges. For those willing to overlook the negatives, it offers a decent dose of fast-paced fun in the world of the Blue Blur.Interested in discovering great Steam games? _childDocuments_.review: Sonic Superstars is a massively mixed bag, and a game with massive amounts of potential, yet unfortunately fall short in various aspects which bring down the overall experience of the game in ways that can't be ignored. On the surface, it looks beautiful and offers plenty to both new and returning fans of the franchise, yet for the most part, it's outclassed by other games in the Classic Sonic series.Gameplay-wise, it presents the player with a vast array of enjoyable mechanics that are provided to the player throughout the game, keeping gameplay fresh across the game. Each new zone also mixes up the gameplay with gimmicks, and whilst many are fun and offer plenty of new experiences exclusive to this game in the series, it's significantly outweighed by other, more annoying gimmicks, many often making certain Acts drag on, with the most exciting part being the end, knowing you never have to return to it. It definitely has its merits, however I wouldn't recommend for those looking for a perfect platformer. Especially considering the fact that Classic Sonic as a series is fundamentally flawed as a platformer, when compared to competitors like Mario. Sonic has fast-paced movement, floaty physics, and a very small and zoomed in screen. All of these combined provide the potential needed for a fast-paced and exciting gameplay style, but mainly due to the zoomed in screen, you have such little reaction time that you will spend unnecessary amounts of time smashing into walls, or hitting enemies, bringing you to a complete halt. Other platformers, once again like Mario, have much more expanded field of visions, letting you have a much better idea of what is approaching and allows you to plan ahead and avoid oncoming threats, and yet the game that needs it the most, totally lacks this commonplace feature of game design.Another aspect of the game's design that is lacking in parts, is the incredibly inconsistent level design. Many Acts feature incredibly fun and enjoyable level design, however others are repetitive, annoying, and downright unfair to the player, such as jumping off cliff and ending up falling into a small hole below, with no indication on where you were intended to land. However, the most significant flaw in the game's design, and most certainly the game's most major downside is the incredibly tedious boss fights scattered throughout the game. They are unbearably long, prioritising long-winded animations that drag on, over actual content, with 90% of boss fights spent biding your time waiting for the endless flurry of attacks to end, only to realise its the same cycle of 3 attacks that you have to successfully counter 6 times over, making boss fights incredibly miserable. Worse of all, there are no boss fight checkpoints. Every death during a boss will put you to the very beginning of the fight, often putting you back upwards of 5 minutes and beyond, which will feel like an eternity when you're facing the same, repetitive patterns over and over again, and yet many feature a sense of unpredictability that leave you learning very little each death. In addition, various bosses have special one-hit death attacks, leaving your rings useless, and making the tiniest of mistakes often fatal. If it wasn't for these boss fights, this entire review would likely be much more positive, yet this one oversight has given me a much more realistic view of the game's issues, dragging the entire game down with it.Something that I'm less critical of, however, is the game's selection of playable characters. The 4 different characters each have different abilities that put them apart and give the game a level of replayability and puts it apart from other games in the Classic Sonic series. Additionally, the designs of the characters are fantastically made and are a perfect modern take of the classic artstyle that hasn't often been seen. The design of the rest of the game's environments is also beautiful, with backgrounds and areas each looking very appealing. Despite this, various textures in the game are low-resolution, and background textures can often be unpolished and clearly 2D textures pasted into the background, sometimes not even connected correctly, that can sometimes lead to the game's graphical design being dragged down slightly. Although, the games fast-paced style makes many of these issues less noticeable, but this shouldn't excuse these shortcuts taken by the developers. Something that does tie these environments together, however is the game's soundtrack. Whilst unfortunately not quite up to the standards of other games in the franchise, it is an incredibly high bar and despite not meeting it, there is still plenty to enjoy from the game.The game's battle mode is definitely very fun and whilst being limited in scale with only a few modes, can definitely provide people with a good deal of fun for a little while, however the online did not last long before becoming barren, so if you wish to get some time out of this versus mode, expect to be playing against many faceless, nameless bots. The additional character customization in the form of metal forms of all the characters, along with some extra customizable pieces, make the battle mode more fun and due to these being unlocked often through the main story, it does add an extra layer of replayability to the single-player as well.Skip this paragraph if you wish to avoid post-game spoilers.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------The additional Trip's Story that is unlocked following the main story, in which you play as the new character Trip the Sungazer, is definitely some fun additional content that keeps the game going and adds some playtime, however is almost entirely reused stages and enemies, with only small sections being reworked to fit Trip's abilities, and to add extra challenge to make this story a hard mode of sorts, which it does surprisingly well, yet it would have been interesting to see more new content in this story, however only the final boss has seen a real rework, which, as many people seem to agree, is for the worse. Whilst I will not ruin the experience, I'll let it do that itself, this fight demonstrates all my criticisms that I communicated earlier, tenfold. It is incredibly long, incredibly repetitive incredibly unfair with almost every attack being one hit, and not featuring a single checkpoint throughout, putting you back over 10 minutes at times, all over one minute mistake. This single fight is the worst part of the entire game and acts a roadblock for many players from ever seeing the game's true ending, and experiencing the real final fight. So, whilst this additional story is fun and adds extra play time, it does it in a way that doesn't make for a much more enjoyable experience, and I felt myself only playing it for the sake of the game finally being over.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Spoilers end here.Overall, this is not the best Sonic game to have been made, and if you wish for a more enjoyable and all around well-made game, play absolutely any other classic Sonic game. Sonic Mania is a good choice. Maybe not Sonic 4 though. But if you're happy to fight through its often infuriating flaws and sometimes boring gameplay, then you will definitely find yourself having some fun amongst everything else, but don't expect any long play-sessions. It's a game best played in brief bursts, as it's easy to become burnt out from. It's certainly not the best game in the series at all, but there is much worse out there, and whilst certain aspects of the game can be forgettable, there is still plenty to enjoy, especially in its graphics and features of its design, but only if you truly wish to endure its flaws, of which are plentiful and obnoxious.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: The first game I've ever refunded after many years on steam. Visually, great. Music, pretty good. Controls, okay. However... The camera is wayyy too close to Sonic/ other characters, to the point where you can't anticipate what is coming up ahead, where enemies are, etc. And more often than not, you'll just die or get hit by something which is seemingly unavoidable unless you know the level like the back of your hand. The camera needs zooming out 50% or more. There's also a few bugs such as changing your FPS to 120 means the spin dash won't boost as fast as it does at 60 frames, how this wasn't noticed during development I'm not sure, did everyone test the game with V-Sync on and a 60hz monitor? Overall, it could be a great game, but seems like it needed another 6 months in the oven to polish and eliminate some bugs. Hopefully these are resolved and if so, I'll pick up the game again during a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Annoying Epic online integration which could be forgiven if the game actually had online co-op. Played the game on the steamdeck and noticed ocassional stutters and  frameerate drops. The game is not unplayable but surpising it can't run smoothly on the deck given the nature of the game. Reoccurring issue when playing with the controller the game autopauses everytime you spawn. Gameplay is mixed bag. Some levels are good and others are middling. Music is average. Where the game is absolutely egregious is the boss design.While some of the levels have decent bosses with interesting gimmicks the final bosses have several one hit kill attacks, multiple phases and even if you learn the pattern they take far too long to kill owing to having to restart from phase one. Almost feels like the bosses were made annoying to pad out the playtime instead of making an actually engaging game with more levels. Boss fights should not be 7-14 minute slog fests which make you start over for making a single mistake.Unlockable character has decent gameplay but to balance for giving us a good thing the final boss for said character is hot garbage and a perfect example of the bad boss design present in the game. Buy it on sale if you are sonic fan starving for fresh content. Not worth the asking price of 60$.

_childDocuments_.review: Sonic Superstars is an amazing looking 2D platformer that not only feels like a new game but a classic as well. The visuals use aspects from the classics, honestly I'm impressed with how they manage to capture that and make it more detailed than other recent platformers. The level design is also reminiscent of classic Sonic games. I've seen people say the music is lame, and while I can agree about some tracks early on in the game, the rest of the level music is very good. Some use the Genesis soundfont like the original games and some have a new twist. It's a great feeling to have the fresh visuals with the Genesis sound effects and welcoming characters. There are also some pretty cool things after you beat the game. If I had to think about one thing negative about this game is that the boss battles are a bit hard and drawn out (which really could be said about any classic Sonic game), but not having to worry about lives makes it much more bearable. Anyway, highly recommended for anyone who enjoys the Classic Sonic series.

_childDocuments_.review: The controls feel great and the level design is decent for the most part, but oh my god.The bosses suck so bad and they legitimately do not value my time.- The bosses have long animations that play between attacks, with long drawn out cycles before you can even hit them again.- There are a handful of bosses where if you don't hit them quick enough, you have to repeat the entire cycle.- Most bosses take at least several hits, which means at least several cycles you have to sit through.- Some levels don't have bosses, but the vast majority DO. This is an issue you'll deal with NEARLY EVERY LEVEL.- I hope you like listening to a 20 second music loop on a multiple minute long fight.- There aren't any checkpoints on some of the longer bosses, so if you die, you'll have to redo the entire fight.- Did I mention some of the late game bosses have instant kill attacks?- You might figure out how to do some of the bosses quicker, maybe you learn that with a double jump or some emerald powers you can cheese them and it starts to become a bit more tolerable? I WANT to like this game, but this is an issue that makes me dread the end of every level. It's not just one or two bosses that suck, it's the entire philosophy around them that sucks the fun out of the rest of the game. Usually I like replaying Sonic games and getting better at them with each playthrough, but the way the bosses are designed in this game makes me not want to even bother.At least Time Attack is a thing.

_childDocuments_.review: Just as with Sonic Rush on Nintendo DS the stages feel like solid efforts by fans created within a mediocre level editor. The 7 out of 11 zones I have cleared before I decided to request a refund never felt like locations but more like mere assortments of platforms with different textures plastered on them. Compared to Sonic 3 & Knuckles or the 2D stages of Sonic Generations, the stages of Sonic Superstars thus have a very generic feel to them. To add insult to injury they recycle level themes, enemies, stage hazards, and even some melodies from the older games – but not in a good way as Sonic Generations did. They just cram them together with some new stuff and sell it as new zones.I would not mind the flaws as much if this game were 20 bucks, as there are some redeeming factors to be found: like some of the music or the new mechanics and abilities. The boss fights are okay as well. But considering the bold asking price of € 59.99 (or 69.99 for the deluxe edition) this just doesn't cut it for me, as I don't see myself replaying any of these stages. If you want some great Sonic, some great platforming and some great four-player co-op right now, save yourselves 10 bucks and buy Sonic Generations, Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed and Rayman Origins instead.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is being written after completing a single playthrough as Amy with all Chaos Emeralds collected. I don't know why Steam is bugging and saying I only have 30 minutes; at the time of writing, I've played roughly 6 hours.TL;DR: Game is quite enjoyable, but I'd wait to grab it on sale.2D Sonic is a tricky thing to get right. While Superstars is far from a perfect game, I'd say Arzest have done a fairly good job, especially given their spotty track record (read: Hey! Pikmin). The physics of the classic Sonic games are recreated extremely well, and I found I was able to consistently pull off platforming and stylish maneuvers just as I would in past 2D entries. While my initial playthrough was completed almost entirely as Amy, optional character-specific stages sprinkled throughout gave me the chance to try out everyone. Every character seems to play as they should. The game looks and sounds gorgeous. Particular praise in this regard has to go to the animation of the characters. The game's cutscenes lack dialogue, instead conveying the plot entirely through character expressions and motion. These are extremely well done, with each character's personality well displayed in the way they move and emote. Sonic's flippancy, Amy's compassion, Fang's foul temper, it's all communicated well. While I found the game to be enjoyable throughout, it has to be said that it's quite easy overall. Worse, there are a couple of disconcerting difficulty spikes. The Special Stages feel particularly undercooked; the concept for them has potential, but it doesn't quite come together the way I think they intended. The same could be said of the rewards for such; the Chaos Emerald powers are by and large not very useful, save for Ivy and the Super transformation. In addition, two boss fights I found to be irritating: the Fang battle at the end of Golden Capital Zone, and the final battle with Dr. Eggman. These two have the same general problem; they last for far too long, repeating the same or similar patterns too many times. This becomes boring, and can become extremely frustrating if the player dies toward the end and has to repeat most of the fight again. Technically speaking, the game ran smoothly and loading transitions were quick. I had no problems in this regard. I did encounter one visual bug, on the "Got A Chaos Emerald" screen, but it did not affect my gameplay experience. I'm a bit concerned about the depth of content for a $60 game. While I unlocked an additional story to play through, and the other characters offer valuable incentive to replay, the price still feels a bit steep. Overall, I enjoyed my first playthrough, but the game does have a few issues to be noted. I would recommend the game, but not at full price currently; I would wait for it to go on sale. Hopefully, if SEGA plans to continue working with Arzest, they can address these warts for future games.

name: Mato Anomalies
detailed_description: Mato Anomalies is a turn-based RPG that takes players on a journey across Mato, a fantasized neo-futuristic version of a bygone oriental city. Take control of the Dual Protagonists Doe and Gram to investigate strange anomalies around the city, or venture into rifts to battle demonic abominations determined to bring about the city's downfall. Team up with unlikely companions and unravel the dark secrets in this story of Duty, Hope and Justice. Dual Protagonists Take control of not just one, but two very distinct protagonists. Gather intel and knowledge to unravel the mystery behind the city of Mato as the private detective Doe, or venture into rifts and battle demonic abominations with your incisive arsenal as the resolute exorcist Gram. Anomalies Find clues throughout Mato by talking to NPCs, taking on missions and visiting shops to pinpoint Rifts, portals to the demonic creatures attacking the city. Enter at your peril and defeat them in battle and collect abundant rewards. Band of Misfits The enemy of your enemy is your friend. Difficult circumstances make for unlikely friendships. Find new allies during your investigations and gain their trust through conversation and shared experiences. Smart Combat Mato Anomalies provides a unique and challenging battle experience highlighted by shared health across all team members, gear matrix and dual-talent system. A unique combat strategy will be needed if you want to succeed! Dual Worlds Traverse across Mato, a neo-futuristic version of a bygone oriental city. Beneath its surface lies another world. Discover Rifts which act as portals into a place beyond space and time, filled with powerful enemies. Corrupt or Corrupted Insidious factions are somehow involved in the dark fate befalling Mato. Can our heroes find out what's going on? Or will they themselves fall victim to despair and corruption?

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, the 40 € price required a leap of faith, but it's everything I had hoped for: The insane text density and chill noir jazz music of Arrowiz' previous game, , but with less static gameplay. I was a bit sceptical if the step up from a visual novel (the aforementioned ) to "all game modes under the sun" (Adventure game! Dungeon crawling! Card battling!) could really work... and I think it does! Of course the battles are no Atlus spectacle, but they are comparable to  (and just as chatty), which this reminds me more of than , both in ambition and scope: It's no AAA production, but everything works, transitions in and out of battle mode are swift, and the game world is so WEIRD and interesting in the best way with everyone you meet acting shady as hell... I will expand this review over time, I just love Arrowiz' approach to games - so many informations and obscure cultural references in the text, you either swim or sink, read or die.One word of caution though:  features several translations. I would recommend non-Chinese players that maybe want to play in Japanese, Spanish, German, Italian or French to switch between the English script and their language a couple of times to see what they like better. The German translation for instance isn't bad, but a bit stiff, has some typos and and some lines simply made more sense in English. (Which seems to happen more often with the NPC lines than with the "main" dialogue, maybe they were translated by different people?)The "Metasphere" sections are clearly made from various building blocks you walk on, like Hot Wheels tracks hovering in a virtual void. Layouts are fixed, but not very exciting. Some very light puzzles involving switches. No random encounters at least! There are some attempts at visual theming (say, a stock market arrow graph pointing up a set of stairs for a dungeon about greed, and piles of cash on the ground, yeah, not very subtle), but for some reason that theme is used for a whole chapter, including all of the side missions, which IS confusing - when doing a side mission I often wondered "Am I right in this place? Haven't I been here before?"What makes the dungeons okay, and somewhat distinguishable: There are many little story beats thoughout a mission to prevent the obstacle course padding effect, a bit like flavour text in an old crawler where the text had to compensate for the basic graphics.One point I didn't like: The story has these big moments of drama, but very limited gameplay mechanics to support these, and whereas in a big budget game maybe a QTE sequence would have been used, here you sometimes get sent to a short dungeon section in the middle of a story beat, because this is the only "action mode" the game knows and it never really works.Generally, I don't like card games, analog and digital. Just not my thing. So naturally, the "mind hacking" parts are my least favourite, as not much happens during these sections, storywise. What's good though for a card game loser like me: I'm not expected to build my own deck. There are a couple of decks for different purposes pre-built. I'm not going to explain the rules here. Let me just say that brute force does  work. Which is a good thing, I guess, makes me engage more, read the card descriptions with care. The watch thief hack took me a good while, but in the end I had a strategy and won and it felt... rewarding? Pretty cool. It's all about playing your cards in the right order, using all of the stacking effects. And like I said, actually reading what's on the screen, haha.

_childDocuments_.review: This one is an absolute gem and I wish it would have more recognition. Sure there are some raw edges here and there - but this be a smaller team they make up perfectly with writing, story, characters, atmosphere and mood setting. The love poured into their world building and to share it with the player is felt all the way down. Merits- Great characters, they all are unique and different from each other from different areas with different background yet they manage to work together perfectly without feel any of them would be forced in the team.- Absolutely great background music, sound designs and voices. They all help a lot to upkeep the gloomy post apocalyptic Noir feeling the game was aiming for. - Great writing! It is entertaining and the characters all react on one another and comment on each other strength and weaknesses. Also  I think this was the first game where a new term surfaced us the player didn't encounter it before but our main character due of his background would be aware of it already. Instead of taking the main character a fool and re-explain the term it was explained to another character who had no idea about it and by no means he could know that either.  Small detail but I absolutely loved that. - Complex and very interesting story to explore and uncover it's secrets. - The art style is great, it is an interesting mixture between styles but carefully crafted together into a whole. It might be not everyone's cup of tea though.- Visible love of the developers for their world and building it up you can feel all that care they placed into it.Flaws- For the English VA the lip sync often wrong and it can be annoying in cutscenes. - The story and the game flow slow building takes a bit of time to pick it up but if you bypass the first chapter it becomes more intense after. - Lack of Intermissions. The story lead doesn't wrap up in a shiny paper it's content so sometimes some path or new characters joining the crew is raw. The story is very straight forward and heavily focusing the actual plot and investigation aspect without introducing arcs and smoother the flow a bit.- Illusion of a semi open world. It is not and gives no any room for exploring it is clear where you have to go to progress with the story. No on world treasures to find, all loot comes from merchants or dungeons/quest rewards only. - The card battle aspect might not be everyone's favourite element but the game offers skipping it so you won't stuck on it which is nice.- The lairs and enemies can feel a bit repetitive and 'boring' they only change with chapters. Though the dungeon's atmosphere with each chapter is amazing in return!Now my review not fully covering the whole game as I not yet finished it. But I am not disappoint and to me well worth the price and waiting for the actual release. I played the demo I loved the idea and was impatiently waiting for the launch. This so far absolutely my favourite Indie game of the year.

_childDocuments_.review: i came into this game on a recommendationat first the "budget" realy shows, gotta be real: my initial impressions weren't great.the lore and athmosphere just "felt" copied, the combat (design) kinda ripped from Soulhackers/Persona (minus the Pokemon elements).but boy was i wrong.yes: it's kinda sci-fic-cyberpunk mixed with "magic" and fantasy. after playing a lot the game reminds me most of Shadowrun (in all the best ways) when it comes to the lore and world.there's old wars, there's lots of technobabble, there's Shamans and whatnot. it's great, it just takes a while to build up.you can also clearly see the devs love for the cyberpunk genre (think Bladerunner), the easter eggs alone are pretty telling.backround art, character design, world design and even sudo-philosophical intermezzos, with their own audiotracks and ambience paint a very pretty picture after a while.i realy do hope they are working on a sequel, cause this is an IP i want to see continue.then there's the core gameplay. again it doesn't start out great.then you realize that there's basicaly a turnbased combat Diablo clone "under the hood". randomized dungeons to explore, with randomized loot. it's a whole side-system that realy grew on my. which is also supported by a very robust rpg-system-core.you get talent trees (classical leveling up); which are not just % increased, but also modifactions to existing skills (like added effects, reduced cd, etc.) for every character.you get a an equipment (weapon) system that works great with the dungeon-delving: weapons come in different rarities, which offer a different amount of possible affixes and not just increased damage/def. early on this won't matter much, but for later content you realy feel like you can build your team.then there's the amazing "perk" system ontop. you get kinda a sphere-board where board pieces are either quest rewards or found in dungeons (hunting for em also in the randomized loot dungeons is quite enjoyable).slots on this board are level locked. the board offers a fixed number of slots which you gradualy unlock while leveling. pieces come in stes and rarities. they also got sorta connections (random) which you will need to activate set-boni. sounds more complicated than it is. but it's a whole nother level of character/party building, loothunting and tinkering around.cooldown based special attacks (like taunts, aoe-damage, debuffs/buffs) ad another layer of tactics to the content and the idea to have a shared party-hp-pool also works to make the whole thing feel different.there's even "buff" shrines withing each dungeon (lair). these shrines offer you boni to select which apply then to your current run and often support also specific approaches to your party-build. then there's elite enemies, bosses, mini-bosses, little area-challenges (mostly in story/side story lairs).also like other good jrpg-dungeon-crawlers (again this is more or less side-content here, but enough to keep you busy for quite a while) you can easily skip most if not all animations or activate auto-combat.all these core-systems come together the longer you play. they work for motivating you to continue leveling and also hunting in rng dungeons and doing the sidequests. tbh. i found this much more enjoyable than it is in most "big" jrpgs.then there's the "mind hacking". it's kinda a card-based minigame you do sometimes during main- or sidequests. again you create decks and the system offers quite some options, but in general this was nothing special. it works, it's solid, but i wouldn't say it stands out. the presentation is nice though.the OST is also fantastic and so are most of the VO lines. in general the  plot is presented either in inengine animated cutscenes (which are pretty entertaining), kinda comic-book-like sequences or standart jrpg 2D art conversations. the athmosphere, tone and ambiance of the whole thing need a while to get going, but after a couple of hours i realy did enjoy exploring and learning more about this world and it's characters (Smoke is still the best...sorry). you realy need to get through the rough first impressions. areas are instanced and rather small, quest markers are shown on screen for everything (even not picked up side quest), npc conversation with randoms take place after a tiny loading interval, the U.I. is kinda clunky and early on neither exploration nor combat realy stand out. but stick to it...it's great. there are some minor issues i got: there's quite some spelling mistakes (english) and the shop U.I. is downright horrific.but none of that makes this a bad game.if you like complex jrpgs, noir or cyberpunk content or can live with a slightly more low-budget game which on the otherhand has clearly seen love and care from the dev: this is a save buy. also there's no artificial timelimit anywhere to be found.

_childDocuments_.review: Mato Anomalies is really three types of games fused together; Visual novel, Turn based JRPG and a card battler. In short, it has it's pros and cons but the developers were trying to squeeze in a bit too much. I lean more towards a maybe than a yes or no.First the main part of the game is a visual novel, and it is a very very long and detailed story that's not bad but I found it to be longer than normal. There's an option to speed up text and skip the voiced cut scenes (done in a comic book style). The English voice acting is mix of just ok and out right bad.Second, it's a JRPG and this is where I thought it shined. Turn based combat which also has an auto battle mode if you so happen to get bored of these battles. It's very Final Fantasy esque with some different mechanics. There's two unique mechanics that stand out. Firstly your team has one health bar. This actually keeps the fighting strategy a bit more simplistic. Also since you have one health bar, you only level as a team as well. You don't have to shuffle characters around in order to level them up like in other RPGs. Secondly there's the interesting gears system. Instead of weapons and armor you have weapons and gears that you collect in lairs or buy from vendors. You can use up to 9 gears in a layout. The gears have to be chained together by their set to get bonus team stats. The only thing I wish the game had is an option to save Gear layouts. It's annoying to test out gear sets and then have to figure out what order to put them in again and again. Layouts would of saved us some trouble. It took some getting use to but the gear system is pretty cool.Thirdly, there are card battles that are random and few. You collect various decks throughout the game. I thought the card battles were interesting but almost always they were way too difficult and depended on range more than anything to continue the game. They also don't matter except for a couple achievements. If you really hate the card battles, you do have the option to skip them. Just skip each turn until you die three times and you'll be able to continue the story. Annoying right?The world design is impressive, the dungeons system (lairs) are an interesting take on dungeons. It has the option to explore random lairs separate from the storyline for leveling and loot but I'm not sure if this randomly chooses a lair from a list of maps or maybe they are procedural? I don't know for sure here. The world and characters are cell shaded and the animations are ok. The special moves seem to be missing audio but it wasn't that bad.7/10 - Loses two points for trying too hard with card battles. Loses another point for not making the gear system stronger with management.

_childDocuments_.review: I have always liked games with anime aesthetics, as I consider myself a bit of a fan of the genre, and there was a time when I was very hooked on visual novels. However, despite this, I haven't had many opportunities to try some "detective" story novels, and this was one of the reasons why this title caught my attention, in addition to its graphic section that is. Mato Anomalies is a JRPG that is described as an enigmatic adventure in a neo-futuristic city, where strange events will drag Detective Doe into a paranormal conflict, being put at the center of the plot as its main actor. We will begin the  seeing our protagonist, the aforementioned private detective, Doe, being visited in his office by a group of characters of dubious origin, and who soon show their true intentions by covering his head with a bag and practically kidnapping him. Apparently, his services are required by an information trafficker known as Nightshade, who forces him to investigate some matters related to "Handouts": very coveted items in the underworld, shrouded in mystery for now.Without a say in the matter, our hero will set out to the harbor of Telosma, the city we’re at, and begin his investigation. In the course of the plot, he will be unexpectedly transported to a kind of alternate dimension, where he’ll encounter some horrid creatures straight out of a nightmare. It is then that another of the protagonists makes an appearance: a mysterious swordsman who will not only save his skin, but will also explain to him a little of what is happening around him.In between some turn-based combat tutorials, in classic JRPG style, we will learn that the creatures are known as "bane tide", monsters that feed on human emotions, and inhabit these sort of parallel worlds called lairs. But no worries, as our mysterious savior is quite skilled in combat, and will help us get back to the "real world", so to speak. After the level is over, we'll be told about our savior, who introduces himself as Gram, a shaman who is in charge of putting an end to the bane tide before they become more troublesome.As he goes along, Doe will become aware of a connection between the lairs and the Handout traffickers, and he will gradually become embroiled in this situation that seems to be much bigger than it appeared at first glance. With Gram and other companions by his side, our hero will enter this new world that is presented to him, without knowing where this dangerous investigation will lead him, all while a mysterious entity pulls the strings from the shadows. It's a pretty entertaining plot, with both suspenseful and comical moments, and I feel that it progresses quite well, and although some sections seemed a bit "rushed" to me, overall I enjoyed this story quite a bit.The  is divided into several parts: a visual novel mode where we can appreciate most of the dialogues, both story and side missions, and an "exploration" mode, where we will take control of our character to move through the city and its various locations, from the futuristic streets to the dark sewers. On our way we’ll find some NPCs offering their services as vendors, or looking for help with side quests, as well as cats or dogs to pet to pass the time. I want to add that the controls are quite simple, but the camera moves as long as we hold down the right mouse button. Sometimes it felt a bit stiff, but it wasn't too much of a problem. I read on the forums that the developers had the camera issue in mind, so maybe it will change in the future.We also have the exploration of dungeons, and combat. Contrary to investigating the city, the dungeons provide us with other interaction options, such as treasure chests, healing or mechanisms to open the way, as well as small books of information relevant to the location or entities related to it. We’ll move through the corridors, and sometimes several floors, of the dungeon in question, and we’ll fight enemies until we reach the boss and be able to finish our mission. It is a very entertaining part of the game, which reminded me quite a bit of Persona 4 for its design. It should be noted that in addition to the main and secondary dungeons, the title also has "random" dungeons, so we can have fun at our leisure, even after finishing the game. The combat is the classic JRPG turn-based, nothing too difficult to learn; but something that I found curious was that all characters share a single life bar, and I really liked its implementation. Our characters will have two possible "paths" for techniques, since each one can use two weapons, and depending on which one they have equipped, the skills they have will change. This gives rise to strategy, since different techniques affect different strengths and weaknesses; however, they will also have some techniques of their own, independent of the weapon. We’ll be able to make use of a skill tree to improve these techniques, organize equipment, and some other common mechanics of the genre.Finally, there is a card mini-game where we will be able to "convince" people to cooperate, making use of a glove that allows us to infiltrate the target's mind. As we recruit new characters, we will unlock new decks for this activity, which provides some variety from time to time; this mini-game is not "mandatory", since if you lose three times an encounter you can skip it without repercussions. Before continuing, I want to make a special mention to the diary menu: a sort of encyclopedia that covers from character profiles to guides, tutorials, and information about factions, among many other things. Very detailed and interesting to read.The  section is very curious and nice to appreciate, as it mixes several types of art for different situations. We have both 2D for portraits and conversations (mostly), 3D for exploration, combat and comic book style vignettes, and some scenes done as digital paintings that create beautiful and detailed environments. The dungeons’ styles are great, and besides the cool animations and interesting character designs, I really liked the color palette, especially how the shades change slightly depending on the lair (I know this is super specific but I loved the red tones of the attacks, they picked some nice colors!), and in this section Mato Anomalies left me very satisfied.As for the , I found it to be fantastic. It has several tunes from different musical genres, and uses a wide range of instruments ranging from harmonicas to classic guitars. There wasn't a moment in which the music wasn't a great accompaniment to the story, and adding to this a pleasant vocal repertoire, I must say that this section lends itself to enjoyment. I did experience that some of the cinematics occurred and/or ended very abruptly, and I don't know if it's because I was listening to the Japanese audio, but every now and then the voices weren't keeping up with the movement of the lips. This wasn't irritating or anything, but it was something I noticed and would like to add.In , Mato Anomalies is a new proposal in a fairly populated genre, talking about JRPGs of course, that entertained me a lot both with its story and characters as well as with the art and design of the lairs. It was a very enigmatic adventure, with the occasional plot twist and a bit of fourth wall punching. Without a doubt, I enjoyed this story, and although it has its quirks, I invite fans of the genre to give it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: The videos and screenshots make this game look like a mix of Code Vein, Persona and Scarlet Nexus with addition of your regular JRPG aroma.  Lol, it's nowhere near. What this game really is - is a Visual Novell that, for some unknown reason, also got some real time movement and interaction + JRPG style combat (sometimes) + deck-builder combat (also sometimes). First of all - everything in this game is linear as railroad track. I won't go much into details of the plot or combat systems, yet - you have a skill tree for each of your "battle characters", and once you level up you can Customize characters by assigning skill points. Sweet, eh? Except all your skills are mandatory and all you can affect is "this thing does 15% more damage" or "this dude will have 3% more HP from now on". You can't go exploring anywhere unless the game flow allows you. You can't make discoveries or level up in your own pace unless you are allowed to. And my favorite little cherry on top - at the starting location, there will be a settlement with a bar on higher ground. You'll have to run up and down occasionally for quests completion. And the only way to get there is an elevator. Which you have to use. You can't run up or down to make it quick. There is no location loading involved or whatsoever. It doesn't add to plot, atmosphere or anything at all. Just an elevator that makes you wait 5 seconds while your character goes up or down. Just... why?If this was advertised as a Visual Novel with combat elements for 20 bucks - I would be totally fine with that, but no, the game description says: "anime-inspired RPG experience". Yeah, so much experience, that I even can't.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, if only the game isn't priced at $40, I'd definitely recommend this game to anyone. Not to say the game is bad, it's that the price is a bit too high for what you're getting. $30 is what I'd be willing to pay for this game, or in my case, I bought the game while it had a 50% sale.My 40 hour playtime might suggest that I really enjoy the game, but in reality, I kind of want to get over the game quickly, because the repetitiveness of the game already starts to show up at around the 20 hour mark. New characters joining the party makes it lively for a while, but once you've figured out the best build for your party, you won't really need to switch parties for a very long time. A lot of the times enemies don't really pose a threat until you reach the very late of the game where debuffs can be very lethal. Crowd-control abilities are highly effective because not only you get to focus on taking out enemies one-by-one, you can also stall while waiting for cooldown to finish so you can repeat the same thing in the next encounter.The plot is unnecessarily long. Like, really. It starts pretty weak, then the game finally tells you the major plot points at Chapter 7 or 8, with Chapter 9 as the epilogue. The whole game would've been shorter if the earlier parts of the story isn't mostly just rescuing your buddies.Side quests, while adding to the world building a bit, aren't very rewarding. Their dungeons give green rarity items mostly, and after a while you'll probably just want to skim over their dungeons quickly.The thing that annoys me the most is the cutscenes. Sometimes the game presents cutscenes in a comic book style, and sometimes in a normal way that I don't even know at what point the game decides to go for comic book style or a normal one. The comic book style cutscenes are also jarring because the whole thing doesn't autoplay, and at times the character paused for a long time that you thought the character has finished talking so you press A to continue to the next panel, but nope, you skipped a dialogue.The occasional Slay the Spire minigame (called Mind/Hack in this game) does take you away from the dungeon crawling aspect for a while, but the developers definitely knew not a whole lot of people might be into this, so they made it so you can only choose from pre-determined decks, and there's a skip button if you lose enough times. In terms of the minigame itself, it's alright. You can't really brute force everything; you have to look at what the enemy is trying to do to be able to win. I had lots of close calls while playing through them, so it's something for someone that has been playing StS copies previously. Although the game provides you with 6 decks, I ended up playing with only 2 of them throughout the game, because the other decks has their own playstyle that requires the player to learn and adjust depending on the scenario, and honestly, it's a waste of time trying a different deck anyway.My final verdict is this game is a 7/10. While the game can be fun and interesting at times, a lot of the aspects of the game felt like it could have been done better if they decided to focus on fewer things instead.

_childDocuments_.review: is in part a dungeon crawling JRPG, a detective visual novel, and a card game, in other words it is overambitious. I enjoy this game; however, it has issues feeling both unfocused, and unpolished. I did not like the ending. the game has its moments and can be really fun, but it is about an average experience overall. With that said I will probably keep an eye on their future projects. The detective Doe has a few debts, and he is coerced into investigating a hot new commodity, but he quickly finds himself in over his head, and is nearly killed by a demon before an exorcist rescues him. They start working together, one trying to uncover a conspiracy, the other likes killing demons.The story is told through three ways, unvoiced dialogue, voiced in-engine comics, and cutscenes. These could work well together unfortunately the transitions between them feels very jarring and immersion breaking. The writing itself is fine and sometimes pretty great, during most of my playtime I was into it, though it has a few issues, there is a lot of terms, the phrasing can be stiff and awkward, and overall, it can fall into tropes. Some of this might have to do with the localisation, but I know nothing on that topic. It draws some inspiration from cyberpunk, and a few other places and does a good job at creating an atmosphere of downtrodden and exploited people. It is also very overambitious and tells a story that is larger than what is necessary, they should have kept the phrase “less is more” in mind, because the game feels very long. However, the story and ending they had planned would not work in a series (probably) and is best told at once, but personally I really disliked the last chapter and the epilogue, and frankly could have done without it.   features an impressive number of enemies, and a lot of them have interesting designs. They also belong to specific dungeons that have their own moods, music, and visuals which gives you some nice variety. However, some chapters feel a bit long, and so it can get repetitive. The music is good though, it has nice beats, different instruments and is an enjoyable listen, on the other hand we have the character designs that are a bit more varied in quality. Unimportant characters lack eyes, but there is also some trouble with shadows or the lighting which gives models a lack of depth even for anime designs. Another issue I had was with the city Mato, and its inhabitants. There are very few character models, and you often find herds of the same person walking around which is extremely immersion breaking. The city does not feel lived in outside of conversation, it is quiet, empty, and dead. The few NPCs you can talk with help little, ideally their dialogue would have changed after every chapter so we would have had something, but no, it only changes after a handful of specific events. One thing that I noticed quickly and noticed often was an issue with animations, they often end several frames too soon which stops any flow dead in its tracks as the characters goes from mid-attack to freezing in place. It looks very jarring, but luckily it is not an issue with every single attack.This problem is even worse during the comics since the animations finish before the voice lines, and sometimes you skip ahead thinking the panel was done, but no, surprise! There was actually another speech bubble for that panel which had not appeared yet, and which you had no way of knowing would exist. Despite being aware of this and waiting a few extra moments I  accidentally skipped over dialogue. If the dialogue and the animations were in sync this would not have been a problem. Doe is the first protagonist you encounter, and it is with him that you explore Mato and talk with all the different people and progress the quests. It is also with him where you play a card game.This game is framed as a way to acquire information people are not willing to share, and despite not liking card games I liked this one. It was pretty fun, and I enjoyed trying different decks to beat different situations. The only thing I disliked was having to die to restart since there is no manual restart, but if you hate card games there is also a skip feature. Unfortunately, I think the whole minigame is an unnecessary addition that the game would have been better without. I would have preferred if they instead focused more on Doe being a detective by giving us more dialogue options and giving us extra rewards or temporary buffs the more information we acquire. The buffs could be the exact same as the ones from the random lairs, but they would be applicable to the story or side lair in question.The second protagonist is Gram, an exorcist who can enter lairs to kill the demons within. As you progress through the story, he will be joined by one character per chapter for a total of six party members, but you can only bring four at a time which gives you some options to customise your setup. Personally, I had some issues choosing who to use since I found that they had fun and distinct playstyles that could complement each other well and in various ways. You are also able to build character in different ways on account of each weapon having their own unique skills and damage types, you could use Garm with a sword and do slash damage, but you could also use a spear and do pierce, it depends on what you need for your party.  One thing that keeps the game enjoyable is that each chapter has its own unique lair design, “mechanics”, and set of enemies. It is always cool to fight new enemies and sometimes it even felt like they went overboard, but I am all for overambition, if done well. However, there is a severe lack of bosses for side quests, fighting the same two bosses in every lair during an entire chapter does start to take its toll, especially since the different mechanics are only really utilized during the main story. It gets a bit samey on that front, and it is not helped by side quests having a formulaic structure. With that said I enjoyed the actual combat, I found that I liked it more the more I played which was surprising, but I really like the changes they made from a more typical JRPG. Your entire party shares a health pool which means healing is easy, and all abilities are on cool down rather than being MP dependent. This encourages you to use abilities frequently which makes combat encounters faster, while also eliminating some of the tedium. Yet fewer, more interesting encounters would have been nice. However, there is another problem. Having a shared health pool, and rechargeable abilities makes combat a lot easier and the game does not always account for that. Sure, it is fun to stomp my enemies and it is definitely satisfying, but some more challenge would have been nice. There is also an issue with the side quests, and that is that they are the easiest part of the game, they are often gated by story events that are of higher level and difficulty, so when you actually play a side lair you will face no challenge, and you will barely earn any experience whatsoever. That is kind of annoying. The larger issue is the length, I thought the gameplay was fun but even I was bored at the end, it is just too much and not enough changes across 40-hours. You only ever unlock three more skills! The rest are unlocked at the start or are dependent on your weapons!I am ending on a positive note since this is a recommendation. I like the  that they added post-release, it is not perfectly implemented, and the amount of loading is annoying, but it is really entertaining to stack bonuses and make your team ever more powerful as you destroy wave after wave of enemies. It was definitely the most fun I had with the gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: A bit of a hidden gem, in that if it were given more polish it could truly have sparkled. I enjoyed my time in the game, which is why I'm happy enough to recommend it, but I'd be hard pressed to name one single element that could be said to make it stand out. Probably what I liked the most was the cyberpunk setting and story, and yet even with that there is an obtuse nature to the storytelling which I suspect is compounded by the translation process that I felt kept me at bay from really soaking it all in. Equally, the world feels a bit lifeless at times, as though the budget couldn't  stretch to the vision they had, and the antagonists never get their chance to really shine, either.Let's be clear: it's not a AAA game. Expecting everything to be top notch is a little wishful thinking. Sometimes lesser budgeted games really excel at one thing, and they sacrifice other elements in order to perfect it. This feels like they didn't want to do that, and so nothing really excelled. On the flip side, nothing - except maybe the UI at times - is bad either.This is one of those games that if you don't go into it expecting the world, you'll likely be pleasantly surprised. If you go into it with high expectations you'll be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like Mato Anomalies, but it just wasn't all that fun to play. It's a long game filled with cheaply generated dungeons, boring battles and a card minigame that is forced on you, but is very unbalanced and not all that fun.The game has a cool style and I loved Arrowiz' previous game I played, Heritage, which I found was a very cool visual novel. I couldn't get into this game, though. You play as a Detective who forms an unlikely alliance with a Bane Tide Hunter. You go through somewhat linear dungeons to quell the threat of Bane Tide, which can also be generated randomly for grinding, and hack yourself into people's minds to get information for your cases. The story is somewhat haphazardly told, but understandable. The main problem are the battles and the card game, though. They are both extremely repetitive, only rarely expand in any interesting way and only consist of spamming your strongest skills that enemies are not resistant to over and over.Even so, the battles get really difficult really fast, as enemies start to deal over 100 damage per attack while you have like 700 or 800 health. Every single item is obscenely expensive, including healing items, so the only way you can really progress at a certain point is grinding the random dungeons for money and gear to sell so you can afford healing potions (which only fill up a very small amount of your total health anyway as they use a flat HP value, not a percentage value). The balance is completely out of whack, so unless you just want to grind forever for better weapons and EXP, you will just be stuck at certain points in the game, which then forces you to fight more annoying, boring battles that can at least be automated, but are still time consuming and annoying nonetheless.Outside of the dungeons, you are sometimes forced to play the mind hack card game. It's also unbalanced, with some card decks being absolutely terrible while others are much stronger. Enemies constantly attack you with high damage values while you have to juggle attacking not only them, but also their demons which give them additional buffs. It gets out of hand very quickly and often it feels you can win these just through luck.The music and graphics are fine and serve their purpose, and I really like the aesthetic of everything, but the awful balance and repetitive gameplay quickly become a drag and with the game being apparently at least 25+ hours long, there is absolutely no way I could have pushed myself to grind it out to finish it. Some good ideas, but the game desperately needed a polishing and balancing pass before release. Even for the relatively cheap price, you can find much better RPGs on Steam.

_childDocuments_.review: Played this game for about 68 hours on xbox and am currently in a new playthrough on pc.This game is rather odd, in a good way. I'd say this would probably be like a 5.5/10 on an objective scale, but there are some things that made me like this game so much I bought it twice.The world itself is just very interesting. A city in noir-cyberpunk-anime style with some weirdly interesting things in it. Really hard to describe. The feeling it gives is similar to the Playstation exclusive Gravity Rush series, if you played that. In terms of that the setting is such a strange world that I was eager to learn more about it. So you run around in Mato as Doe, a detective that solves people's everyday problems. Generally, the plot is told in visual novel segments, none of which are voiced, sadly. Through rare, there are some really georgeous event CGs.Doe forms a team together with Gram, who saves him from a bad situation at the start of the game.Looking at it, it is as generic as it gets: Doe solves some problems running around town, and at the end of nearly every mission he finds out that these monsters - idk what they are called - are responsible for peoples problems. So Gram travels to another dimension to terminate them and thereby resolves the situation in the real world.Basic anime stuff you might say. Yes, but no. During these missions you get dropped many hints that make all this stuff weird. People in Mato lower class need to buy oxigen tanks to survive. Factory workers get scammed and then start a revolution against the greed company overlord. Weird government research projects. Weird death cults. And so on. not exactely befitting of the anime trope.On their adventures Doe and Gram gather a bunch of misfits to help them along: the master thief Butterfly, ptsd-soldier Smoker with a drinking problem, a paramilitary/mafia type boss Lady Edelweiss with a Deathwish, and more. A prettly likeable bunch.Maybe it is due to the translation, but it feels like characters always think three steps ahead, a conversation starts normal and then characters sometimes come to weird conclusions that can easily be missed if you just read the dialogue and dont think about the consequences between the lines.Not gonna lie, in the end the plot gets really weird introducing time travel shenanigans and other philosophical concepts. However. I really like that? It builds up to the end by escalating further and further. But enough about that.The dungeon crawling is similar to Soul Hackers 2. The main antagonists all have their persona-like palaces that are similar to the soul matrix in Soul Hackers 2, except less annoying because these dungeons are not overly complicated mazes. And they look prettier.In combat, the party draws from a single health pool, which is interesting. All characters have specific roles to fill, and every single one of them is useful with interesting skills. Gram is the typical swordsman, butterfly is a thief with poisoning, healing and trap abilities, Smoker is a defender/buffer type character and so on. The two biggest downsides I must admit are performance on pc with some strange frame drops (including on the steam deck; I recommend high settings with AA off and locking it to 30 fps, yet even then it will drop frames to like 22ish in some hub areas and maybe some endgame dungeons) and the monster design. The monsters are mostly just some wacky shapes, that's it. They could have been cooler.Regardless. This is a janky and overly ambituous game that only partly archieves what it sets out to do.But the good things really are good and refreshing. I recommend it for the philosophical, weird story and world, the aesthetic and the cool characters.

_childDocuments_.review: For now, this game doesn't really have anything going for it. The story, the gameplay, and the main character are all monotonous.Due to the game's increasing linearity and weariness after two hours, I started to nod off.Up until this point, there hasn't really been much investigation required; all you have to do is move around accepting tasks and side quests, then enter a subpar imitation of the Persona 3 FES labyrinth where you have to defeat weak monsters and a weak boss in set locations; these battles are so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ exhausting and boring. Also stated in the game's instructions."Use the auto-battle feature if you're sick of fighting!" Let me guess, oh. Is it possible to unlock it later? Great, because it's not in the features currently. Update: It was added in after a few missions, what? There is also some stupid deck builder game where you can use futuristic gadgets to hack people's brains for information in the main story, but why? It's suppose to be a visual novel, not a card game nor combat game intermingled. Having said that, the visual novel component is merely okay, nothing exceptional, and has a hard time evoking Doe's feelings in particular.Yes, sure. A lot of games do these things to break apart the pace and make things enjoyable for everyone, while the game itself isn't absolutely terrible or unplayable, it's sure as hell not worth 60 CAD (Taxes). Are you aware of the video games you could purchase for this amount of money? There are several games with excellent gameplay, such as the Detective Frog Collection, Ai Somnium Files, and the Danganronpa Collection, plenty more but these are a few that come to mind. Moreover, why the hell do some visual novels opt to have voices in very particular spots while having the entire game be a reading novel? Choose one or the other, and employ a respectable non-monotone voice actor for the main character instead of everyone else.Do not waste your money on this game. It's barely worth 20 dollars.There is nothing inherently special or groundbreaking here. It's all been done before but better.
