_childDocuments_.review: Good game with lots of content. The main story alone will probably take ~30 hours, but there are lots of side quests and mini-games which should double the amount depending on how much of a completionist you are.Story and characters are also interesting with good balance of seriousness and comedy. _childDocuments_.review: Very impressive game, story/character wise. I'd say it's on par with Yakuza 0 in that regard.Combat is not even close though. Not varied enough and when it comes to bosses (or most encounters) your pretty much stuck with Tiger style. I used (even on Legend) Crane stance probably 5-7 times during the whole playthrough. Rarely you need so much crowd control. On normal difficulty even more so.Mini games are there and for some reason devs added one of the most broken/idiotic ones in this title. Lockpicking. The "best" part about this mini game is that it bugs out with higher FPS. 60 frames? EZ mode. 120 FPS? Go and suffer.Money making is done through Paradise VR game. Throw virtual dice, move to a certain spot and collect your loot/fight enemies/do idiotic lockpicking. You don't need to reach the Goal to receive rewards but you do, if you are going for some of the achievements as Paradise VR has some various spots with Skill books.Visually the game is alright but it has some issues with Ambient Occlusion and Lighting in general.Sound design is great as always. But for some reason the music is too quiet during the whole game.As always with Yakuza games it has plenty of stupidly absurd and absurdly stupid side cases/stories. Even all time favourite mahjong has it's own quest here! Rejoice people who refuse to play it, you will need to now, as final quest is locked behind stupid mahjong. Neat, right?The grind in this game is pretty insane even by Yakuza series standards. Collect all drone parts? Go and look up a guide, you will need millions of dough and Yagami knows how many crafting materials to get this one stupid achievement.If you are going for 100% (Kaito-san have mercy on your soul), the grind will be pretty unbearable. Good luck, you will need it.Even despite some idiotic additions and useless grind, the game is still one of the best Yakuza titles. It's rather expensive at full price but during some sales it's certainly worth the money for the fans of the series (and probably for some of the newcomers too, as it's a spin-off).

_childDocuments_.review: after playing through every yakuza game, some of them more than once, this game is such a breath of fresh air. resetting everything about the characters while keeping the world intact is so refreshing to see, as it helps us see the light of kamurocho from a much grittier light, a civilian rather than a yakuza. the story is as compelling as it is entertaining, and there are no loose ends left in this story.in the world of detectives, very rarely is there a case of black and white.

_childDocuments_.review: + Massively improved combat over the previous Dragon Engine games (Yakuza 6/Kiwami 2)+ Characters don't have their IQ drop when a gun enters the room+ Smaller areas added to Kamurocho are cool+ Most of the antagonists are pretty fun+ The entire final chapter is cool as ♥♥♥♥+/- Plot is much more coherent than the average Yakuza plot but lacks character. Pacing also gets very ♥♥♥♥♥♥ around 2/3rds in due to a long period of plot where you make zero progress on getting literally any tangible evidence on the mystery, going mostly off assumptions and logic, which hurts the whole detective angle.+/- Very hit or miss side characters, Kaito's only thing is just being dumb, Higashi is alright but barely around, and Sugiura is cool.- Fighting styles are very unbalanced; Tiger is objectively just better than Crane and Crane literally just doesn't get upgrades while Tiger gets over a dozen?????- Tiger and Crane are alright but both movesets are meh compared to those in 5 and 0/K1- Yagami is only ever interesting when he's torturing people; He feels like a lame version of Tanimura- The detective minigames like lockpicking, tailing, searches, and chases are all very meh, especially tailing missions which go on for too long and typically lack any challenge to keep any tension.- Small amount of new minigames that are all very mediocre along with series staples like arcade, gambling, and mahjong/shogi, minus karaoke; results in a pretty poor selection of minigames.

_childDocuments_.review: Loved the game from start to finish, the story is rich and interesting, we are presented with a big handful of really lovable (and hateable) characters. Writers did a great job setting the whole story and closing it with a pretty intense finale that may push you to drop a couple tears down your face. The rest is pretty much RGG doing what they know best, capturing Kabukicho the best way possible, tons of friends and girlfriends you can make along the way, interesting and really smooth fight moves, GREAT soundtrack and a vast amount of fun activities to kill time inside the game. Can't wait to buy Lost Judgment! - Final score: 9/10Also, I had to add how thankful I am of being a fan of Sega and RGG, they always listen to their fans. It's crazy how overnight they announced 2 new games, 1 remaster and released the Judgment saga with no prior notice. Gotta love RGG.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like the Yakuza game series, most likely you'll like this game. In particular, I can praise the attention to details in the environment, and the beat-em-up gameplay is pretty tight. Personally I find the game series a bit boring, but I also understand the appeal.Focusing on this specific game: I think "sluggish" sums it up well. It feels like the story has been spread as thin as could be, with constant interruptions after each small scene. Every small story progress we make is followed by either having to go home for the night, go visit our ex-boss to say hi, or some other excuse to have us run through the place again and again. And again. There are regular dopamine hits, but at the end of the play session we can realise how most of it was not super engaging.The nail on the coffin: the protagonist is voiced by Takuya Kimura, whose acting range is close to being a single dot. The only thing he ever does is basically mumble and look bored. This might be enough when he can let his looks carry him, but as a voice actor in a video game this really pulls the game down imo. The rest of the cast is pretty good as far as I could see.
_childDocuments_.name: Judgment

_childDocuments_.review: Okay I have to admit of all RGG games I played (Y0-7 and Ishin) this one is overall the best.All new characters are different kind of crazy and aren't trying to copy Kiryu+Majima madness, in fact RGG went brave with almost no references to Y games.There are however references to pop culture, both wetern (interview with a detective - when an actor is a vampire) and eastern (Hentai Kamen manga/movie), I love it!Kamurocho had a facelift, people are more detailed, music fits a detective game.On top of it are some new nice gameplay additions like drone useable normally but also as racing, then there is some VR minigame.Datin sim got improved and is finally interesting, but bedding 4 girls at the same time feels kinda pathetic and is not in line with protagonist's character (he is not insecure nor needs to prove he can seduce everyone).Finally, the main story is basically dealing with sins of UNIT 731 in a modern day. If nothing, this bravery earned thumbup by itself alone.Sadly there are boring repetitive designs from older games (minigames like gambling, darts, etc, NPC removal during group fights so you are left solo in the end).Some new stuff is not good, mortal wound mechanics is only trolling the player to get a taxi to part sewers for no reason.Then some annoying tough fights on streets appear for absolutely no reason and cannot be permanently stopped (thank god can mainly be ignored as rewards are abysmal).But the biggest sin is the one thing I hated in Y games and is again here.Side stories locked behind minigames.Why. What is the reason to lock out friends (required to get sidequests) behind for example darts win.If people don't like playing darts, please don't discriminate them by not allowing them to solve all detective cases.It is a design crime not to let a player to find a missing cat just because OMG the player didn't recruit ninja by winning a darts game against him.This game is a musthave regardless of it's big or small annoyances (will they ever learn that M is map, not TAB?) because many stuff in it are so much fun and can't be seen anywhere else.Here is hope these annoyances won't be repeated in The Last Judgment.
_childDocuments_.name: Judgment

_childDocuments_.review: Quirky, fun and a great story.I've never played any of the other games from this dev. Took a chance with Judgement and it's been awesome.If you are on the fence like myself: Great fighting, somewhat like the Rocksteady Batman games. You search crime scenes, run around a town and complete various challenges and of course work through the main story.I'm all about a good narrative and Judgment doesn't disappoint. The main story is interesting and filled with twists and new characters. I haven't finished a GTA game since Vice City for this exact reason. There are a lot of quirky and weird things in the game, which only adds to it's uniqueness IMO.The voice acting is probably the best I have ever heard in a game. The vast majority is spoken with some side quest stuff being mainly text. I can't recommend this game enough. Try something different!

I have to say, this game has one of the best combat systems out of any Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio game that I've played. _childDocuments_.review: I mentioned in my review of Yakuza Kiwami 2 that games in this franchise supposedly don't start becoming really refined until Judgment. I can verify that this is this case. You have two: Tiger, which is good at one-on-ones and Crane, which  is meant to be good at crowds. Somehow, they completely forgot to give Crane any style-exclusive upgrades, so any abilities are either universal or Tiger-only.The story is definitely a high point for the series. In this spinoff, you're not Kiryu, but instead a citizen by the name of Takayuki Yagami, portrayed by a real person (Takuya Kimura). He's a detective, and ends up unraveling a massive conspiracy that goes back three years and is tied to the murder case that made him quit being a lawyer. Yagami has, and makes, a lot of friends throughout the game, all of them being complements or foils to his personality traits.The minigames are your standard fare, but there's no karaoke (likely because of Kimura's agency-at-the-time being weirdly draconian about what he can or can't do. _childDocuments_.review: TLDR this feels like the Yakuza 3 of the modern dragon engine. Get it only if you feel like you'd want to beat it to play lost judgement, or you're totally out of content from other RGG studio games and you just want a fun lil romp through a reused kamurocho again.4 main issuesThe story is both overly drawn out and rushed. So many things fall in place in the last 2 chapters that it's kind of insane how much still isn't captured. Characters and their stories are rushed so quickly that it's just impossible to care about the story. You'll also see a lot of the plot twists coming if you've played RGG studio games and/or have watched crime dramas, but the game spins its wheels for the first half so the pace is insanely numbing. The worse addition is the Keihin Gang, which does nothing but make the act of moving through the story even more bland, as you tackle group after group, and fight the same reused bosses over and over. On the other hand, since we're not Yakuza anymore, the need for self-righteousness is through the roof. The constant enforcement of one objective best morality means there's no gray area to discuss or look at. They're either all good people, redeemable bad people, or utter psychopaths, which is  It makes for a messy story with a lot of moral conveniences.Again, it kinda feels like they adapted some TV/Move plot and so the twists mean that sensitive issues are handled poorly or just brushed over to keep the plot moving. It really does have some high points, and the story does try to raise the tension and spectacle, and resolve some of the characters issues, it just does so gracelessly. The combat. It makes Yakuza 0/Kiwami feel like a flash in a pan, where RGG essentially reset their combat experience when moving to the dragon engine. Like Y6 and YK2, Physics and hitboxes are super janky, with really odd animations that feel like everyone's flailing around a lot. Almost every difficult "rage" attack your enemies do can be easily avoided, or is impossible to dodge since it either comes from off screen or in the middle of your attack string so you can't easily cancel out. It's simplistic and the upgrades you get are mostly EX actions. Extreme EX mode feels half baked, and I really don't like using it since it makes the combat incredibly spammy and easy, and I don't want to look at more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ EX actions. The EX actions are way too long, being long, elaborate, multi-camera angle shots of the attack, which is cool once, but quickly wears out since you do them so many times. Mortal wounds ends up just being an annoyance rather than an interesting addition that forces new choice dynamics on you. The 2 styles feel like a waste of time since there's so little depth to the whole scheme, and for the most part the same problems from Y6 are still here. Maybe it gets better in Lost Judgement, I'll find out soon. Also the extract system isn't fun and I used none of them aside from the mandatory one throughout my playthrough. They are unnecessary. The characters. For the most part, very good, but also an abundance of irritating, bland or stupid moments which make them look like  weird caricatures of people that end up making the story even more shallow. The core 4 members are mostly good, but the main problem is the way everyone doesn't seem to align with any form of power level. Characters that are seemingly strong/rich/smart/cunning whatever, have almost no impact on the story at its most crucial moments since it just seems to let Yagami do everything, except be a woman. Yagami is portrayed a bit too much like a bad TV protag, in the sense that Yagami's flaws or shortcomings are never an issue in the core story or gameplay that feel like you resolve when you play through the game. It just feels like it's there for drama, where Yagami mopes around a lil and someone cheers him on, then when yagami really needs to step up, it all falls in place. You wonder if they wanted to do a Y5 and have 4 campaigns, one for each core member. The genre. It feels constantly stuck between wanting to be a Detective game and a Yakuza game. The awful tailing and chasing sections just make me want to sleep. There's no challenge or even risk to most of these. You just have to wait and it's tedious. The other detective stuff like the drone and evidence searching feels half baked, and at one point I was stuck for 5 minutes not realising you have to choose the WRONG answer for time to progress and the real target to appear. Just bizarro ♥♥♥♥ like that.  A lot of the sidegames are underwhelming and reused from other RGG games anyway. Like the yakuza games, we have whacky sidequests, over-the-top combat and lots of goofball moments to resolve conflicts. I'm not really sure what RGG want from a detective game. It's tonally jarring, and Yagami seems so serious sometimes I honestly feel like i'm watching a body double when he pulls out a line saying "I'm all fished out" when he solves  case involving fish and sashimi. RGG studios clearly want to talk about justice, the law and morality, but the plot, tone and genre make it impossible to take it seriously. the idea of Morality isn't binary black and white would work with a darker, shadier character than Yagami to explore. It's not to say the core characters don't do bad things, it's just the framing makes it impossible to discuss the bad things they do, like when they entrap some dude by luring him with another character. It's all for the "truth and justice" ™. For example, something brought up multiple times is Yagami's rent. It's just jankily handled. I had over a million yen early on, and I wanted to pay it off, but I had to max out 2 friends, and  the rent thing is never really resolved, It ends up making one of Yagami's only flaws (that's he's a broke detective), into a non-issue for the story and gameplay.I see a lot of cool ideas, and if this was the first game from a studio, or with a lot less funding, I'd probably outright recommend a try. But it's not. It's unpolished, and the script needs a few more do-overs to fix the pacing. The gameplay feels like it's constantly kneecapping the story, and the other way around. It genuinely gets as boring as Yakuza 3 at points, and I just wanted to quit, but I finished the core story and did a bunch of the side content so that I could at least learn a bunch going into its sequel, but I don't think I'm ever going to replay this. Hey, maybe Lost:Judgement's combat will be incredible.

_childDocuments_.review: I dunno if I'd get crucified for this, but I loved Judgment's pacing and writing over any of the mainline Yakuza games I've played so far. There's even little moments in this that are incredibly brief, but do a great job in putting a player in someone's shoes that the main series up to this point hadn't done nearly as well. It's a spinoff of the Yakuza series, but you can absolutely play this without any knowledge of the Kiryu Saga or the Like A Dragon games that followed it, and not once feel lost. It's a self-contained story that just happens to be in the same universe (i.e. the fictional realm of Japan).Apart from the larger differences in terms of the story's genre, this being a detective crime thriller as opposed to Yakuza's criminal underworld drama, fans of the mainline series already know what to expect: fun, if sometimes rather jank Dragon Engine combat with entirely new fighting styles for the main character, great music, fantastic Japanese VA (far more believable than most of the Yakuza games, even, since those almost tend to be theatrical in their performances), and that familiar Kamurocho setting to make you wish you'd booked that discounted flight to Tokyo when you had the chance.There are some new mechanics both in the main story and the side cases (this game's counterpart to substories) that are focused on detective work. But don't get it twisted: this game's telling one story. So as far as I know from one playthrough, you can't really come to the wrong conclusion or present the wrong evidence and lose a case. You just lose some bonus experience points, and occasionally get some funny dialogue calling you out for getting something wrong. But that didn't take away from how the story unraveled into the insanity that it did by the end, and it's a great time all the way through.If you've never tried a Yakuza game, and are, say, hesitant considering how many games the mainline series already has, then well, I'd say you're missing out. Start with Zero, you won't regret it. BUT if you only got the time, budget, or patience to only get into a shorter, more self-contained experience, then Judgment  is one to grab for sure. Especially on a sale, considering I got this when it was at an insanely low price for such a fantastic high budget main story and a ton of stuff to do outside of it.And sure, if you're a dub enjoyer, this one's got a dub. Lotta folks say it's good, so it'll serve you well. But the Japanese VA is top notch, rivaling the cast RGG Studio had for the mainline games, which is for the most part already pretty stellar.Good game, 10/10, would bribe my cute lawyer friend with convenience store sweets to go undercover as a sexy hostess all over again.

_childDocuments_.review: Judgment is an action-adventure game developed by Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio and published by Sega. The game was released for the PlayStation 4 in 2018 in Japan and June 2019 for the worldwide release. The PC version was released on Steam in September 2022 as part of the Judgment series bundle. Judgment is the first game of the Judgment series, a spin-off to the Yakuza/Like a Dragon franchise. The story takes place in 2018 and the player play as Takayuki Yagami, a former attorney turned private detective whose past events haunted him while a series of killings took place in Kamurocho. Yagami confronts his past and solve the killings with legal courtroom dramas, investigations, and martial arts. Judgment has similarities and differences to the Yakuza/Like a Dragon series. Does Sega’s and RGG Studio’s new IP spin-off series got your intrigue?Like the main Yakuza franchise, Judgment has a strong story and voice acting. Judgment took the story element further and I found myself really invested on the story. Judgment is also more character driven and leans heavily on the acting performance. The protagonist, Takayuki Yagami, is played by Takuya Kimura. From what I read about the actor, he’s famous in Japan. The story in Judgment is interesting and has some neo-noir flair as the story is formatted like an TV mini-series. The gameplay is familiar to the mainline series, so I won’t review it further. However, there are some enhancements and subtle qualities of life.  One of the major differences are the combat styles: the Crane and Tiger. Crane is suited for fighting against multiple opponents while Tiger focuses on one target. However, the different fighting styles are not too tied up so you can still use either style on any fighting scenarios. I do find the fighting techniques somewhat in reminisce to the older, Hong Kong martial arts films from the 1970s and 1980s. Feels like a Jackie Chan or Donnie Yen film at times. The dynamic intros are cinematic and well choreograph. The soundtrack for the combat styles is addicting to listen to. Furthermore, I found the overall soundtrack for Judgment to be very memorable, catchy, and straight banging. The composers for RGG Studio have done themselves an outstanding job. The “side cases” are the same as substories, but the minor characters are involved in assisting the protagonist in certain situations. It’s like Yakuza Kiwami 2, but it’s expanded, and the minor characters are useful. Since the player is a private detective, there are investigation mechanics like trailing a suspected character, chasing, disguises, and search modes. In addition, there are new minigames like drone racing/customization and Dice & Cube courses at Paradise VR (an “VR” monopoly type game for the player to earn money).Judgment’s strengths are noteworthy and commendable, but there are some imperfections. Yagami’s investigations mechanics feels light and an experiment that didn’t expand further. The skill points are hard to earn and takes a while to get all the points to unlock all skills. There’s a certain “exploit” by purchasing a specific drink, consume, and grind the Paradise VR minigame. It’s really a detachment and does hinder the game for those who want a perfectionist run, like me. Doing the minigames, activities, combat encounters, and food/drink consumptions are not enough.Judgment is unique because there’s not a game where the player can play as a former attorney turned private detective who knows martial arts. There are some influences like Ace Attorney, various courtroom TV-drama series, and Hong Kong kung-fu films but RGG Studio puts a unique spin and learned the lessons on their experiences on the Yakuza/Like a Dragon series, applying on what can be considered as one of the unique games released. There are lots of established franchises in the video game industry and I commend the developers for doing something original. As the first title for the new spin-off series, I look forward on how future title(s) improve in Lost Judgment and possibly how it parallels the main series. The game has my recommendation for both newcomers and long-time fans.

_childDocuments_.review: RGG did not disappoint with Judgment.While they are mostly known for the Yakuza series, you should highly consider playing it if you liked the Yakuzas. While there are similarities between the two IPs, such as Kamurocho or the presence of the Tojo clan, they are also very different, so you don't feel like you're playing another Yakuza.The story was amazingly well-written, and got me hooked from the beginning to the very end. Rather easy to follow, while still being elaborate, but never far-fetched. It makes you truly feel like a detective trying to assemble puzzle pieces. All characters have a deep story that doesn't feel made up, making you appreciate how every single one of them is written.The combat is very satisfying. It's smooth and diverse, with Yagami's two different battle styles. Sheer force has been traded for agility, which gives some spectacular street fighting. The heat actions are beautiful and there are plenty of them. Acquiring various skills will make it all the more satisfying.The music is fantastic. It never feels repetitive, far from it. Everything got its own theme, and before you know, you get to listen to them even when not playing the game.The game itself is very beautiful, and fluid, thanks to the FSR. Also, even if I played most of the game with JP voices, the English voices felt very "natural" and well done.Outside the main story, we get to see more classic RGG content. The sides stories (friend events) are funny and silly, and the sides "missions" (side cases) involves different kinds of mechanics making them diverse. Minigames are cool as well, I really liked drone racing and dice&cube.However, I did notice a couple of flaws, that altered the overall experience:- The Keihin gang mechanic becomes more and more annoying in the long run. At some point, it feels like you just know they are going to spawn anytime soon. They also have some of the worst enemies in the game (in my opinion)- The mortal wounds mechanic is interesting, but can be frustrating considering the punishment can be quite harsh if you just happen to be unprepared.There are also some less noticeable things that, albeit not as infuriating/annoying as what I mentionned before, can still be a little disappointing. For instance, there were a little too many tailing missions while not so much for the other mechanics. While on the topic of tailing, I kind of wished that it could have offered a little more challenge.Overall, it's an incredible game worth its price (although I bought in on sale), with a masterful main story and side content. On sale, it's a steal!

_childDocuments_.review: Wow.Judgement story wise is as incredible as you can expect from the Yakuza series. Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio doesnt miss. This may be one of my favorites and possibly my favorite story in all the Yakuza Franchize. Its incredible. Some of the greatest characters and antagonists in this surrounding corrupt people, the corrupt medical field, and much more. I do feel certain parts dragged and in certain moments side missions were forced into the story. Beyond that, those are my only complaints story wise. So now for me to be slightly unfair but to say something for the rest of the game.Combat is what you'd expect for a Yakuza game with two stances, and a whole new fighting style of course. However, one thing felt strange and clunky. One Tak often wont lock on to enemies worth a ♥♥♥♥ which can be very frustrating. Two, as much as I love the new wall attack stuff (run up to a wall, spring board off for a devestating attack) I found it not that often to be used, and also made dodging awkward because you have to hold R1 to dodge. I felt this kinda made it awkward. A little one trick pony move that dont get me wrong has many options from grab to heavy and options out of it, I still felt didnt add to much and made that whole thing awkward.Mini games are lacking I found. (which is big for a Yakuza game, Id especially say in repeatability)  There is a dice roll type VR thing I did not find to be that great. Theres, the usually Mahjong and Like a Dragon like gambling, and drone racing. The drone racing is like an ariel go kart from Like a Dragon. The other parts of this game do feel like reuses of Yakuza 6, as well as parts that have just better versions in Like A Dragon.To finish this off my only big complaints I can attack this game on. stalking missions (which there are far too many of and its boring as hell) and investigation sections. My feeling towards the investigation sections are eh. Not a big deal honestly. They often were kinda interesting, but other wise frustrating and led to a few moments where I searched it up because sometimes what they expect you to do is ridiculous and without much intuition or direction. This will lead to you running around the room trying to find your little clue, which can time to time feel like a needle in a hay stack. Then theres the stalking missions, that there are far too many of. They are very crap missions where you follow someone without being spotted, going space to space to hide behind cover. They are boring, and sometimes straight up frustrating. They at times made me feel like it was a chore to get back to enjoying the game. The Investigation sections also sometimes had that effect too. Oh, and the "parkour." Yagami is very nimble and does a bit of stunts you see. Hes quite fast and can climb over things. This add a few additions in the map of construction areas allowing you to climb over them and run between them. It also allowed you to jump up on cars which also have there own little interaction take downs and such which I thought was nice. It was seemingly weird though and not a big deal to add these areas. I feel it kinda took away from parts of the map and was pointless. Also, theres smoking now, but its kinda useless. As is also eating and many other things now. It just kinda add to your health? I found it nice in Kiwami 2 that it seemingly almost made me want to eat at every location because it gives me skill points. Which speaking of skill points...  there isnt much variety here. it just a points system of stars. You open your phone and do a pretty linear upgrade tree. I was not that impressed with its skills either. It was a major downgrade from past games. I think it was even a major downgrade from Yakuza 6, but I cant recall certain parts of it well.Overall, Judgement is an incredible and amazing game. (imagine that, Ryu Ga Gotoku only makes amazing games? noooo)However, outside its incredible story adventure, feels like a downer in the series. This is me being a bit harsh because, well for Yakuza game standards its a step down and backwards in many directions. (let me mind you this being a spin off that came out after 6) IT FEELS LIKE IT WAS A SIDE PROJECT. Which I wouldnt be suprised if it was, and well idk if its because its just now coming out on steam and its older now, but it does hold a smaller price tag. This is irrelevant to the verdict however, and I am in no way saying this game is bad whatsoever, its just the opposite of the peak of the series in many areas and kinda feels like a small little spin off that did absolutely incredible in every other area that which being its story and a lot of its missions.GANG WARS ARE ♥♥♥♥ AND ANNOYING. Basically optional areas of purple show up and these annoying gangs want to always fight you. It feels like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ version of MR. BIG BUCKS or whatever their names were in the Kiwami's. Also, a turf war happens chapter to chapter basically. An old guy will annoyingly call you over and over again for help. This is the Yakuza of Fallout 4's "Another Settlement needs your help." I do NOT CARE. O.O9/10 - Better than Yakuza 4 & 6? Yes. That makes this the bottom of my favories, it also has like one of the best stories in the whole series.BUY IT NOW. I am being extremely hard on it for the sake of Yakuza franchise standards.

_childDocuments_.review: (Playtime was split between this account and my main account, BARBECUED KITTY)If you enjoy the Yakuza series, then look no further. This spinoff puts you in the roll of a disgraced attorney turned detective who, after taking whatever jobs come his way, gets sucked into the underground crime of Tokyo to solve a string of horrifying murders. With the signature Yakuza combat and 2 styles to fight, a giant city to explore, and the incredible story-telling the series is known for, Judgment is not a game to skip. The shakeup of working as a detective and emphasis on investigation instead of fighting is a lot of fun and brings a welcome change to the series known for being a hardened Yakuza member.Judgment runs significantly better than I expected on the Steam Deck. I assumed it would be a lot harder to optimize, but as soon as the game started, it was a welcome breath of fresh air. The game won't be a stable 60 FPS, unless you are okay draining your battery within 1.5 hours, but 40 FPS is not only achievable, but feels incredible with over 3 hours of battery life. There are some pockets of framerate drops when loading in new areas, but overall, it was worth it for the smoothness, battery life, and low temps.To my surprise, Judgment also has FSR 2.0 incorporated into it, which was really unexpected. FSR 2.0 is the 2nd generation of AMD's upscaling technology, which allows a game to run much better on lower end devices by upscaling from a lower resolution internally. FSR 2.0 is not turned on by default though, so you do need to go to settings and fiddle with it. The game also offers cloud saves which, as a desktop PC gamer, will be fantastic to go back and forth on.Overall, I was impressed with the performance. You can set the game down to 30 FPS to minimize all drops, though you can still feel them, but the upgraded smoothness of 40 FPS won me over. If you are hoping to play this game on the Steam Deck, then I have good news for you, it is DEFINITELY playable. Full detailed settings we used can be found on our website below.

_childDocuments_.review: This review contains no spoilers or secrets.With over 300 hours, I'm blown away at how much content you get for your money. Even at it's full price on release, the main story alone has to be the longest (and most engaging) campaign I've played in my 30+ years of gaming. Maybe that's more-so a comment towards AAA games nowadays or Western game development, but it's easy to recommend Judgement for your dollar's worth alone.Addressing the campaign, I was hooked from the start and could best be described as "an amazing movie and video game had a love child ... who grew up watching kung-fu movies". I've seen reviews that Judgement's storyline is darker when compared to Yakuza (which I've not played) and I think this is a plus. Without those elements, the story wouldn't be as gripping. Like any good game or movie, the story makes you feel invested in certain characters which is integral for keeping anyone's attention for an extended period of time. There's no shortage of twists, turns, secrets, and revelations as you progress and this is something you experience from the very start.I wanted to dedicate a section to the comedic elements in the game. I wasn't surprised to see both well-translated and genuinely funny comments from characters but I was impressed that the producers leaned into this. For a story that is, at times, described as dark or disturbing, they interlace it with comedy that isn't just added for the sake of it. When those opposing forces of dark and light are written well, it makes for particularly memorable moments and I applaud the team at tempering those elements so expertly.Finally, to round-out your experience in the game, you'll find not just the main campaign but a whole 10-course meal of extra content. There's side cases, which are bite-sized jobs offered to you that you'll investigate. There's an equal number of people who you can become "friends" with after you interact with them a certain amount. Those two elements are linked, side cases can unlock new potential friends and vice versa. There's also a wide range of mini games and the devs have cleverly designed systems that make you want to engage with them (unlike some games that offer meaningless "arcade games" etc that don't interact with any other part of the game).In conclusion, I wouldn't just recommend this game, I would implore people to try it out. I've not had such an enjoyable experience playing a game in many years and I'm excited to have found a new part of the gaming world that I didn't know existed. Thank you to the hundreds of people who evidently poured so much of themselves into building this amazing game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is genuinely the worst game in yakuza universe. The story is actually really bad. First it is way to long, the game feels like it should have been done in chapter 8 not 12, the main character could solve 90% of his problems by being 10% more aggressive. There are some many times in the game where main character needlessly presents what he knows with know real outcome in mind. The plot is essentially driven forward by the main character either getting surprised and ambushed for the 100th time, or by needlessly letting the person go after committing god knows how many crimes to get there. The story in all is a drawn out piece that just was needlessly long.  The story is the least of my problems with this game, the game play itself is the big issue. The game needlessly pad time with pointless mini game mechanics. Every time you want to open a door, play a mini game to pull out your key. Running through a burning building how about you lock-pick every door. These mechanics ruined the whole atmosphere. The worst offender was the tailing mini game, I was scared to do side missions out of the sheer dread of having to tail somebody. Nobody has ever asked for tailing missions ever, in fact it is the only component of black flag that people dislike. The investigation was actually fairly neat, and quite enjoyable. I enjoyed putting cases together, but my god did I need to be quizzed on everything that has happened every 5 minutes. It felt like a way for the game just to remind me for the 100th time what has happened. The game essentially was treating me like I was an idiot who couldn't follow the story.  The combat was really disappointing as well. I have played most of the yakuza games on the hardest difficulty. This game ruined my whole experience with the mortal wound system, it is so out of place. The enemy in heat up mode can suddenly one shoot you, or leave your max health at a sliver. However, your heat up mode is essentially useless in comparison to the one in yakuza 6. There really is never a point where it is possible to go toe to toe with people. In all the combat system was lacking the charm of the mainline yakuza games. The story was weak, with a boring villain and underwhelming main character. In all this is the first game that is part of the yakuza franchise I dislike.

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10 MASTERPIECE!I got to be honest with you guys. I would have never thought that this game or the Judgment series in general would ever come to PC (I'll exclude Google Stadia that no longer exist. RIP).There were some rumors and speculation e.g.: "Lost Judgment will be the last game in the series due to a disagreement between Sega and Johnny & Associates, the talent agency behind Takayuki Yagami actor Takuya Kimura. The fallout stems from Johnny & Associates not wanting the Judgment games to launch for PC, as it conflicts with its particularly strict likeness policy — essentially, the company doesn’t want Kimura’s face to be so readily accessible on the internet." (quote from The Gamer, published on Aug 23, 2021).When I read these articles, my hopes were shattered. Because the game was pretty good. And it would be a shame if the series becomes a lost medium in the future because it's tied to consoles and if the two big companies (Sony and Microsoft) don't support backwards compatibility, you're limited to old hardware. That's why I always write reviews in which I ask for new releases of old games. And then there was the day Sega casually dropped a trailer that Judgment and Lost Judgment (+ DLC) were available on Steam. You have no clue how happy I was. Just the fact that there's a game on PC that I'm interested in is a reason for me to buy it. Hell, even if it was released only on GOG I'd buy it on that platform, as long as it's not available on the Epic Games Store I'm good (EGS is still an empty Fortnite launcher for me).And if you are complaining about Denuvo, then just wait until Sega remove it. I hope that they will not delist Judgment and Lost Judgment because of the quote (about those rumors and speculation) above. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------Now, with all that being said, let me tell you how the game was for me.The gameplay, story mode, cutscenes, etc are great. Especially the action sequences. It feels like I'm watching a Hongkong martial arts movie with noir vibe. XDI almost forgot that Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio is a AA studio and not AAA. They are well-known for recycling assets and using the same map again (except for the new games). As long as they tell good stories, I have no problem with that.If you don't like Judgment, you can still play these arcade games: Virtua Fighter 5 Final Showdown, PuyoPuyo, Fantasy Zone, Fighting Vipers, Kamuro of the Dead (similar to House of the Dead), Motor Raid, Space Harrier and Outrun.  So there are many ways to enjoy this game.Total and a message to Sega:Sega, I want to thank you again from the bottom of my heart for releasing this game on Steam. This game is now one of my favorite games of all-time. ^^I really hope that you will release more of your old games on Steam, especially Fist of the North Star: Lost Paradise and Skies of Arcadia. ^^

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a big fan of that studio who produces the Yakuza series and I decided to buy this serie because it was on sale, love that studio, a beat'em up, and story rich. It didn't disappoint me. I certainly felt there was some weaknesses but there weren't numerous. For me, the Drone race was not interesting. It's not something I enjoyed. And so the OG SEGA arcade game or for me the arcade itself, which was a copy-paste of Yakuza felt lukewarm at best. Each game they produce have the 1 thing that helps you produce the much needs money. Casino is up there but in this game it's the VR Game which is essentially a game of cat and mice in with a parkour you ultimately wanna finish with as much rewards as possible which produces a ton of money. The investment app was a fun way to unlock unique abilities/side mission/ items. So overall those things makes it feels like a proper unique game from of my favourite studio. The same thing can be said to the structure of Friends and Side Cases which add unique side stories, good way to make money and add some helpers that helps you get aggro from the street gangs you fight.  The main story is basically related to the Fate of the Yagami. It's difficult to not give spoiler but it's a thriller drame with lot of amazing cutscene, good side characters that are rich in back stories and that you love to get to know. The vilains are never one dimensional and have complex layers of story to explain why they are acting like they are. They are never absolutely evil - at least for the most part. It does take a stand against corruption and how deep it sinks in Japanese culture. I thought this was very interesting I would recommend, I cleared it with much ease with some decent but not excessive grinding in just over 100 hours. I feel if you focus on unlocking the skills by chapter 6 it gets much easier to get bigger fights with higher Exp and the main story itself it nowhere close to be enough to unlock the skills within rushing the main story. I do feel it could add a much higher level of difficulty as you're much weaker. In the last chapter finale, I feel this studio has been mostly hit or miss with games I've played. E.I. a most boss have 2 phases where you'll clear the first 50% in zero effort. at first you're familiarising yourself with the combat engine, clearly a CC: of Yakuza, so you kind of get some cheeky tricks that breaks any level of difficulty- Increasing your Heat Gauge, Using a Special combo when your have something in your hand that activate a mini infight cutscene that inflicts massive damage.So yeah, at the last fight, you get the boss fight pissed off, he goes hard on you, you run, pick up something and when close enough, juke him with zero effort, rinse and repeat and you clear the last fight with like almost getting untouched. _childDocuments_.review: At the time I reviewed this game, I had 88 hours of playtime on PS5.These are excellent games from RGG Studio - the developer behind the Yakuza series, which will be called the Like a Dragon series going forward. This series has a completely different cast of characters, but takes place in some of the same cities as the Yakuza/Like a Dragon series. These games introduce detective work and stealth, but otherwise are very similar to the Yakuza/Like a Dragon series, aside from the fact that these games include magical spells called "extracts" instead of equipable weapons. You can play Judgment whenever you want, but be aware that Lost Judgment contains a major spoiler for Yakuza: Like a Dragon, due to something major that happened in that game that affects the games' shared universe in a big way. I can't recommend this series more highly, and the bundle of both games + all DLC, including the Kaito Files, is the best deal you're going to get for the series on any platform, and obviously the Steam version is going to look better and allow you to use the input device of your choice. _childDocuments_.review: "Judgment" is an absolute masterpiece that showcases the best of Japanese game development. The game's storytelling is second to none, drawing you into a rich and intricate world filled with fascinating characters, twists, and turns. As you navigate through the game's immersive narrative, you'll encounter a plethora of diverse personalities, each with their own motivations and secrets to uncover.But what really sets "Judgment" apart from other games is its over-the-top Japanese weirdness. From its bizarre mini-games to its quirky side quests, this game has it all. Whether you're playing as a detective, beating up thugs with your fists, or just exploring the bustling streets of Kamurocho, you'll never know what kind of absurdity you'll stumble upon next.But even amidst all the craziness, "Judgment" never loses sight of its core values. The game's emphasis on justice, morality, and human connection is woven seamlessly into its storyline, providing a satisfying emotional payoff that will leave you feeling fulfilled.All in all, "Judgment" is an absolute triumph of game design. With its unparalleled storytelling and its infectious sense of Japanese weirdness, it's a game that no gamer should miss out on. So go ahead and give it a try – you won't be disappointed!

_childDocuments_.review: First, a video review My game streamsI love you Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio and Sega I am your biggest fan and I love your country Japan someday I will definitely leave Russia and go to your country forever  このようなクールなヤクザと判断ゲームのために非常にありがとうThe adventures of the indomitable Kazuma Kiryu ended in Yakuza 6: The Song of Life: The hero left for a well-deserved retirement, leaving the fans to pine for the former victories, and the developers to puzzle over how to properly continue the series. Well, while the new part of Yakuza is being developed, Sega decided to please us with an unusual spin-off.Judgment is not the next drama about the Japanese mafia's showdown. It's a thriller about the work of a private detective who has not only to fight, but also to investigate, interrogate witnesses and collect evidence. Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio mixed Yakuza formulas and Phoenix Wright novels, and the combination turned out to be unexpectedly successful.However, while the setting here is the same, the characters in it are new - there aren't even brief cameos or references to familiar characters in the game. And this detachment, oddly enough, is good for Judgment. Nagoshi Toshihiro not only managed to write an original story without any reference to the past events, but also experimented with the genre and tone. The epic story of Kazuma Kiryu was a kind of soap opera with plenty of Japanese humor, while Judgment, on the contrary, is a dark procedure closer to the Western viewer.The protagonist of the game is Takayuki Yagami, a private detective with a complicated fate. Recently, he was a successful lawyer and acquitted a guy everyone thought to be a murderer. Except that soon after the trial, Yagami's client stabbed his girlfriend to death. So the hero, unable to cope with guilt and glory of a maniac's accomplice, finished his career of a lawyer and became a detective. In this role Takayuki takes up catching the "mole" - the mysterious murderer, who brutally massacres the visiting yakuza. In order to get to him, the detective has to unravel a whole tangle of intrigue.VerdictJudgment is no hundred bucks, but just about everyone can enjoy it: from die-hard fans of "weird Japanese stuff" with its wild piling of mechanics to conservative fans of serious detectives and dramatic interactive cinematics. There is a great story, spectacular battles, and from the abundance of mini-games literally blurred in the eyes. The only thing left out is the puzzle fans: the game's investigations are very simple.Plus +exciting story;varied gameplay;A lot of mini-games.Minuses-They are not thereRating 10000 out of 10000

_childDocuments_.review: Judgment has been a very fresh and interesting new experience, given the new character cast, gameplay and stylistic elements of the game, even though its still based in the same universe as the more established Yakuza/Like A Dragon series franchise.Plot wise it was a nice tempo and really liked the chemistry between the various cast members, especially Yagami and Kaito, along with the rest of the new supporting cast.  The storytelling was superb as it was able to weave in back stories through out the narrative, whilst baking in various plot twists given it is a detective/mystery crime thriller.Combat wise it was definitely a stark difference from mainline Yakuza/Like A Dragon as Yagami is more of a technical fighter rather than a combatant relying just solely on brute force.  The initial fights at the beginning were tough to master, however once more SP skills were unlocked, the combat got noticeably easier which was a relief and interesting growth experience on its own.Particularly interesting and new are the observation and tailing missions.  I think it certainly fitted in well with the genre and as a first version in the first game I'm fine with it, though I hear from others it might be quite cumbersome.  Hopefully future renditions will fine tune this formula further, but was a good enough immersive experience for me.Side cases are the sub stories equivalent and have been just as wacky and serious.  I also really like the nice music that complements the overall game play through out the main and side quests.I also really enjoyed the uniquely new activities such as Drone Racing and Dice & Cube VR, which complemented the modern technology vibe brought about by a younger more tech savvy protagonist.However, some of the pain points include grinding a fair bit for cash to use in the Kickstarter App and to support unlocking all the SP skills for completion.Overall, it was a very fun time I had in this first spin-off in what I can imagine will be a successful new series by the RGG studio.  Looking forward to solving more detective mysteries with Yagami and Kaito in the next one.

_childDocuments_.review: Very safe purchase if you are familiar with any one of the games from this studio. It is also a good place to start, because it is a stand-alone story that is fairly well written, modern and sophisticated. The cutscenes are plentyful and have great cinematography. I also find the voice acting to be very convincing and the overall localisation is top-notch.This game has a lot of content in form of story missions, side quests and mini games. It is streamlined for those aiming for completion with its KamuroGo app. The missions you do can be very goofy but I believe this entire series of which this is a spin-off to manages its tonal shifts superply well.Some things I don't think are particularly strong include the key chain, tailing missions, looking around to find hot spots, lockpicking, putting on costumes (but only if the story needs it) and minor stuff like that. I totally get that they enhance the notion of you being a detective and that they help with the overall pacing, but I don't find them very engaging.The iteration of Kamurocho in this game is densely packed with detail and life, but somehow this micro-cosmos feels a little small. If only there were more locations. There's no rooftop or underground passage. To be honest, there isn't all that much you can do to screw around. Having played Yakuza 4 before as my introduction to the series, I'm missing several activities. You do have the opportunity to go to the arcades and enjoy some Sega classics, play Darts, Mahjong (in three different places), Shogi, traditional asian gambling (but only two), Poker, Black Jack, Drone Racing (which is a big one), go to the batting center and into VR (which is a recontextualization of everything you do otherwise). That list may seem extensive, but it is only half the stuff you could do in other games. Most of these things get introduced over time, so you need to advance the story considerbly to gain access to everything. But it's not like you ever run out of things to do. Also, I would have prefered if you had more to spend your items on. Once you are done with your drone and its upgrades, you only have brewing extracts left, which isn't all that useful, because this game isn't very difficult and the game grants you some overpowered ones that aren't consumed upon usage. At no point are you able to craft weapons or even have any outside combat unless an opponent brought one. It's good that you have no inventory restrictions, so no back and forth to move objects. But you also have no equipment whatsoever to adjust your playstyle.Some things I, personally, had some gripes with are the controls, for one thing. I swear, half of the time I performed an EX action was by accident, because it's the same button as the strong attack. I constantly bumbed into walls because the prompt to open a door didn't show up in time. Doing the thumb turn bypass with the controller is next to impossible, unless it's brand new. I had to disconnect my controller in VR everytime I had to open a safe, which made me avoid those spaces. Same goes for baseball and darts. You need to play all that with a mouse. I also hate the fact, that you cannot reload from within the game and have to return to the title screen and then reconfirm everything multiple times. But I guess then it would be easier to cheat, because you can save almost anywhere at any time.I don't think any one part of this whole game is bad. It just isn't perfect is all. The combat is still very satisfying, because of all that brutal stuff you can pull off. The graphics are great. The characters are well defined and memorable. The plot is a little hard to follow, but you can always look stuff up should you need to. This is a mature game with an intricate story and some dark themes, but it also has a cornucopia of ways to dissolve the tension and get you lost and immersed in this colorful world.

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve played everything that has been released in the Yakuza/Like a Dragon series from RGG Studio and enjoyed each one of them.  There were amazing games like Yakuza 0, weaker games like Yakuza 3, and different games like Yakuza: Like A Dragon (the most confusingly named one). Judgment isn’t technically part of that franchise, but it is from RGG Studio and is counted as a “Yakuza game” by most fans.  It’s the same universe, same city, and has similar interactions with the same Tojo Clan, even if only a side story character crosses over between the two games.   The engine the games run on and the style of the games is very similar.  In Judgment, you control Yagami, a former lawyer who is now a private investigator.  A simple early case, which involves you trying to assist in the defense of a Tojo Yakuza Captain named Hamura, pulls Yagami into a series of events at the core of the story.  Judgment’s main focus is telling a complex and intricate narrative that evolves throughout the story, though since unraveling is such a central part of the game, I’ll avoid mentioning much more about it. What I can say though is while the story in Judgment is interesting and unique,  with satisfying moments, it doesn’t feel as tight as previous Yakuza games and ultimately feels bloated.  It’s a fifteen-hour story told over twenty hours or more.  What’s worse is that the same is often true for the side cases.  Interesting and unique stories, like all side stories in these games, but told slowly. A lot of the game feels bogged down by dialogue or a need to remind people of the narrative, it’s unfortunate because it gets in the way of its own momentum, and rather than giving high-action moments, it draws out scenes or shows entirely too much detail when brevity could be better. That’s not to say it harms the story, but it does feel long-winded, and perhaps that’s also due to how Judgment is intended to be a detective story and so the game is mostly talking.  There are major moments to the story, but in the Yakuza series most chapters end with a major boss battle, in Judgment, there’s no major reason for the chapter changes, only a few chapters have a big boss battle.  It’s understandable as the enemies aren’t major Yakuza, but the pace makes the experience feel like more of a slog than it should be. The gameplay of Judgment works though.  With Yagami being a detective there are a few new mechanics at play.  Hunting through locations for clues in a first-person view is an interesting and unique idea that if anything is underutilized, as they’re some of the best moments of detective work.  On the other hand, the tailing missions where Yagami tails suspects are almost never fun, but that’s to be expected.  The good thing is those don’t happen too often, but they probably aren’t going to excite many people. The combat of Judgment is similar to the rest of the series as well, though with Yagami fighting with more of a Shaolin style with two different forms, one for large groups, and one for single enemies, but with enough upgrades it’s easy to use the latter for every battle.  The early hours make Yagami feel rather slow and weak, but a few skill point upgrades and Yagami will be able to take on almost every enemy without a challenge. There is one change to the combat that definitely stands out.  Yagami can take “Mortal Wounds”, which means the parts of his health bar are taken off.  This only happens when he’s shot or takes major damage from one of the “boss” characters.  This damage can’t be healed by eating and instead requires Yagami to get healed by a doctor or use a med kit.  The issue is there is just one location to heal up that I found, and the medkits, and fixing these wounds are decently expensive.  But as a mechanic, it just means players will have to go find the doctor, and once the money stops being a major issue in the game, it is simply a time-wasting chore, rather than an interesting gameplay mechanic.  Take that damage when you’re in one of the few battles where players can’t just free roam, and suddenly it changes a major story moment to a painful experience where players will have to struggle with a tiny life bar.   Of course, the Mortal Wounds can be mitigated with a few features, but rather than getting deep into it, it’s the most important part of the combat system, but also the one that never feels as good as the rest, and one that luckily was removed before the sequel, and hopefully will not return. There’s more to be said, with a lot of it being potentially spoilers, but at the end of the day, it’s a game where players should discover the story, side quests, missions, and experiences, and rest for themselves.  One other issue comes up in that there are a few DLC parts to Judgment.  I’m not sure if everyone gets those or if they were only for the initial launch, but these DLC bonuses range from pointless (An extra Staminan X?) to overpowered (an essence that lets you instantly kill almost every enemy or cause massive damage for bosses).  I’m not sure why DLC exist in Judgment, but it’s a shame because they unbalance the game and are no longer optional additions, they’ll sit in your mailbox outside your apartment but different parts of the game will leave bonuses in that mailbox so you’ll likely add them to your inventory at some point. The DLC isn’t a massive negative but definitely one that stands out and it’s something that RGG tends to do for all their games (DLC that unbalances the game). I just wish they had a way to lock it away for an authentic play-through because otherwise, it clutters up your inventory. Ultimately Judgment is another Yakuza game, with a different protagonist.  It has all the various Yakuza trapping with large side stories and interesting dialogue.  The story is solid but is told poorly at times, and the experience is long but still one I enjoyed.  After thirty-five hours I have to confess, they must have done something right, even if I was bored during a few chapters. Judgment is a slow burn but still one worth playing.  Though with that being said I don’t know if I would ever return to Judgment for a second playthrough due to the length of the story. Still, if you’re a fan of the work of the RGG Studio, I’d recommend checking this out at least for completion's sake and to learn more about the world of the Yakuza. 8/10 If you enjoyed this review, consider checking out my Youtube channel where I review games .

_childDocuments_.review: By this point the Ryū ga Gotoku franchise, formerly known internationally as Yakuza and from now on Like a Dragon, is extremely popular everywhere. We’ve come from having some spin-off titles having no international release and main titles in the franchise having the international release delayed by years, to getting almost day one releases worldwide and future announcements that get so many people excited it would’ve been hard to believe this just a few years ago.Judgment is the first game that is set in the same shared world as the rest of the Like a Dragon titles that has absolutely no “Like a Dragon” in its title. It was originally released on PS4 in 2018, has gotten an enhanced Remaster on current gen systems juts last year and now is finally available on PC, released the same day as its sequel Lost Judgement. And I have to be honest, even though I like these series in general, I truly loved only 2 Like a Dragon games so far and unfortunately, being extremely long titles, I did get somewhat tired of them last year when I finally wrapped things up with the PC port of Yakuza 6. Even though I’ve heard great things about Judgment, I was still afraid that it will tire me out. Instead, it has become the third game in the franchise that I consider exceptional.At its core, Judgment is a typical Like a Dragon game (apart from, you know, when it plays as a jRPG) – it’s a story-driven action adventure set in an open world that isn’t particularly large, but dense with details and stories. The combat is still somewhat jRPG-ish in how it happens, as during normal city roaming enemies just get randomly spawned to walk around and if they catch up with you, you enter combat that controls differently and the only ways to end this are to lose, win or try to escape. Combat itself remains, as it is in most titles, very beat ’em up/fighting game like, with combos, usage of weapons you find lying on the floor, visible health bars, special attacks and all of that stuff. Bosses that have more health and special abilities of their own are, of course, also still here and the big new addition for this whole system is that sometimes they can give you “permanent” damage, that cannot be healed normally.But despite the lack of big changes in the basics, there’s a lot of new ideas and approaches in Judgment to the point, where it feels unlike a Like a Dragon title. Sure, one of the fighting styles private detective Yagami (the main character) uses is reminiscent of the feet-heavy style Shun “Best character in the series” Akiyama has, but playing is Yagami is anything but playing like Akiyama. Being a detective, a lot of tasks Yagami-san has to accomplish required a new set of mechanics and Judgment does most of them well. You occasionally get to tail people, hiding behind corners and blending with people. You get access to two lockpicking minigames, one of which is really fun and the other is a big miss. The chase sequences return, being really well done this time around and a far cry from when they first appeared in the franchise and were terrible. You get to investigate scenes in first person mode, sometimes while using a drone for more advantageous perspective, and a lot of these are fun. There’s a disguise system that is criminally underutilized despite being really cool. And during some scenes and dialogues you get to perform some simple clue compiling and getting to the conclusion in the most efficient way possible.And the tone of the story and all of the side-stories is also expectedly fitting a detective tale, not a… whatever situation Kiryu, Majima or Ichiban often get into. What I especially loved was how a lot of these stories are now evolved to not just tell a nice story with memorable characters, but many of them often get a continuation or connection to other stories, creating the illusion of a real community in Kamurocho (the setting of the entire game, returning from previous titles). There’s even a really amazingly cool little epilogue story that happens when you’ve made all possible friends and helped people with lots of cases. And the “girlfriend” concept here too is finally feeling more like an interaction with a proper character, than just a mechanic for stats, with all available “girlfriends” getting genuinely interesting stories that you follow.That said, it still feels very… “girl is a prize”-ish and essentially stops any and all character nuance once you’ve succeeded and you can’t “just be friends” either. I wouldn’t have noticed or even cared if it wasn’t so far into becoming a genuinely great element of the story, instead of just a slightly more advanced and well written mechanic. Sadly, the aforementioned Friends and the rewarding epilogue story require you to grind a lot of stuff you might not be interested in. I mean – why do you need to play lots of poker to get a really wholesome side-story? Why lock it behind so much stuff most people will not enjoy?So yeah, Judgment isn’t entirely free of the usual faults of the Like a Dragon title. Fights do get more annoying than fun or challenging as the story goes on. Some systems and ideas become more convoluted for no reason, despite starting with a perfect balance of complexity. And the story isn’t free of occasional overtly dramatic moments that don’t really add anything to the storytelling.Yet. And yet. I couldn’t help but feel that Judgment might be the most “new player friendly” title in the franchise and, overall, the most… well… FUN. There’s no prerequisite story or world knowledge required, even if knowing the world of Like a Dragon adds to it. The combat system is very easy to understand and the skill system is very streamlined without too much extra stuff. We only get Kamurocho, which remains perfect as far as the size goes, so by the end of the game you will most likely understand where the street you need is without looking at a map or a goal pointer. And it hits all of the best story points you expect from a Like a Dragon title and a collection of really good characters. Personally, I’ve enjoyed this cast far more than that of Yakuza: Like a Dragon (now probably to be known as Like a Dragon 7: Like a Dragon?..) and Yagami-san is easily one of the best protagonists in the franchise so far.So, if you haven’t played a single Like a Dragon game before, I’d say – Judgment is the ideal starting point. I used to say Yakuza 0 or Yakuza 4 and I still consider those titles to be the other 2 best games in the series, but Judgment is just so much better as a jump off point for any series newcomer. And if you have played the series before… Well, if you like it, you’ve probably played Judgment already and know how great it is. And if you don’t – give Judgment a try as it might be the one that gets you hooked. PC port is fantastic, so now there’s no reason to not get this game anymore.

_childDocuments_.review: Ryu Ga Gotoku have got to be one of the most consistent developers of quality games today. This is another one of them, set in the same universe as the Yakuza series. However, you don't have to play any of them to enjoy Judgment. Like Yakuza 0, this title serves as a great starting point if you've ever wanted to get into these games. Beautifully crafted storytelling, it carries the game just fine on its own, but there's a LOT of other stuff you can choose to spend your time on in the at first - seemingly tiny district of Kamurochō. Considering the returning setting and similar gameplay, I'm amazed the developers manage to keep things fresh and fun across every new title they put out. Keep them coming.

_childDocuments_.review: It is without a doubt, a Yakuza game with a different character.There's a few extra mini games (from the Sega stores).Sub Stories and Main story are now called 'Cases' which isn't much. There's a lot of detective work you need to do. Sometimes the game hands you the hints on the map, sometimes you have to work it out based on what you know of Kamurocho. But at the end of the day, you're back in Kamurocho which hasn't changed all that much.You make friends now, with their own little quirks and requirements. Eat at this store X times. Introduce this character to another side character you meet (by making friends).Its fun. It's Yakuza. The combat feels a little, floaty? Delayed? I'm not sure how to state what it feels like. You will do a 2x combo of light attack, see the enemy ignore your attacks and throw a punch. You try to guard and it's delayed. 7 out of 10 times I will take damage from the first swing. Dodging also feels delayed. I will dodge during and attack and Yagami will either not dodge far enough, or the enemy will track your movement and hit you anyway. But it is still quite fun.Leveling up skills is now done via SP (skill points I think?). Eat a plate of food from a store, get ##SP per plate. Use that to level up the normal kind of stuff. Battle prowess, general 'life' skills or mini game skills (like drone flying or lock picking etc).If you liked Yakuza for the gameplay and quirky story/theatrics then I reckon you'll like Judgement. If you liked Yakuza for Kiryu as a character, I don't reckon you'll like Yagami too much. If we use Kiryu and Ichiban as a scale. Kiryu being a solid 10 in seriousness and Ichiban being a 1. Yagami is dead in the middle at 5. But its Yakuza. Its Kamurocho. Its all the normal shenanigans that we're familiar with and then some. Get it.

_childDocuments_.review: I have to admit for a spin off LaD game I wasnt expecting something of this quality. It took a very long time for this to come to PC and it was worth the wait. A fantastic in deep story viewing Kamurocho from another perspective and a ridiculous amount of side content which continues the RGG trend of being incredibly creative and hilarious. The combats pretty good but having two styles instead of three from the Yakuza games means you might enjoy this less. I personally liked the two styles, one is for crowd control and the other for quicker movements focused on a single enemy. heat system is much better in this because you get six charges at once instead of one so you can trigger heat moves with objects or the environment a lot more often, the pc version also comes with a bunch of items to refill your heat and health also. The main cast works really well together, the villains are terrifying and excude pressure in any scene they are in, the mo cap actors smashed it out of the park with this, the tiny movements in the faces at times add more depth to the characters which is rare to see.Only down side is the tailing missions, theres quite a lot of them to do and if you have played the old AC games you know what they are and hate them like everyone else. Overall this is honestly fantastic, it does enough to justify being different to LaD/Yakuza providing a ton of content in a well polished package.

The new characters are pretty good, the gameplay is a big step up from 6 and kiwami 2 being much more free flow. The lack of mini games (outside drone racing) will be a turn off for some, but the friend system makes the game have a lot of side stuff to pursue. _childDocuments_.review: For a Yakuza spin-off, Judgment is one of the series' best, with me clocking in at 54 hours having done a good 60% of the side missions. Building on the combat and graphics of the Yakuza 6 engine (no loading screens when you walk into a restaurant? WHAT?!) Judgment improves the combat of the dragon engine and you can switch between fighting styles again (though there are only two and the tiger style is by far the superior one). Great for newcomers to the series too as it is fairly disconnected from the main Yakuza storyline. So if you have never really tried Yakuza or played Yakuza 0 and didn't really like it all that much you should most definitely try Judgment with its better graphics and improved quality of life.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't finished the game yet, but this is hands down one of my favorite RGG games. Yagami is an awesome character, and I honestly think I am beginning to like him even more than Kiryu, despite playing every game in the Yakuza series. As usual, there are a ton of side activities and a unique "friend" mechanic that makes the side stories a lot more interesting than in the mainline Yakuza games. You can do side cases, fly drones, do investigations, lockpick, disguise yourself, and a bunch of other stuff that aren't in the Yakuza games. _childDocuments_.review: this review of Judgement is a part of my series of reviews on the Yakuza games, attempting to take them on chronologically. As such, reviewing this game is already somewhat of a failure of my original goal, as i have yet play more than an hour or so of Yakuza 3. So, for context, this review will use the context of my reviews of Yakuza 0, Kiwami, and Kiwami 2. if you find yourself confused, maybe look at those.Judgement was really the first time the Yakuza series stepped away from former Yakuza Leader and father Kazuma Kiryu. Kiryu was an awesome protagonist, but despite the fact that Kamurocho is a brilliant and believable setting, he himself can only do so much--enter Takayuki (I call him Light for obvious reasons) Yagami, an almost completely new character. He is smart and capable, being one of few attorneys to beat Japan's 99% rule, but his headlining victory is also a bullet in his heart: Taka's major win resulted in the acquitted murdering his girlfriend, causing the rookie lawyer to reconsider his career.Three years later, Taka has his own small Detective Agency, and aided by disgraced yakuza Kaito will work to figure out the next part of his life.Gameplay is almost exactly Kiwami 2 in terms of feel. Stores and buildings are all enterable and explorable, and the world is very detailed with no interruptions. Fights start automatically and in real time, and Takayuki has an almost entirely new set of moves separate from Kiryo or Goro Majima spread across two styles initially. Fighting has definitely also taken more of a back seat to other mechanics. In the first three hours, i had done 3 or 4 fights, whereas in the Yakuza games, you could probably multiply that by 5-10. Taka's clearly capable of fighting, but the devs have seemingly re-balanced it for a new story/character.The major new additions are mechanics that are incredibly similar to the Ace Attorney series. Taka, being a lawyer/detective, will gather evidence and present it to suspects or a in a trial to pick apart a testimony and in conversation has to determine the best questions to ask when gaining information. Like Ace Attorney, its not that hard, but definitely requires some lateral thinking and careful consideration of evidence.minigames this time include Fighting Vipers, a relatively unknown Sega AM2 game based off Virtua Fighter 2, Virtua Fighter 2, darts, and a somewhat limited version of 2010's Virtua Fighter 5 Final Showdown as well as a rail-shooter recreation of Yakuza: Dead Souls (the zombie game spinoff of Y4), making this one of few games where you're also getting mutliple x360/PS3 games as well lol. Sadly, it definitely feels less fun to just wander around in.Like the rest of the games, the sounds are excellent, with the city atmosphere coming through convincingly and the Japanese voice over being downright excellent. For the first time since the original release of Yakuza 1 and paving the way for future games, Judgement also includes an excellent English dub. The dub here works really well despite some mixing issues, and character models have English lip syncing should you go that route. Overall, its very well done. my complaints are as such:-who knew detective work required so much tailing--it seriously feels like every side mission boils down to slowly tailing someone around Kamurocho.-intro too slow, it seriously takes hours before you've unlocked the open world-lack of evolution in combat.-sprint toggle only toggles on, to stop sprinting you have to stop moving entirely.-world is just less interesting as it is in other series games.
