_childDocuments_.review: It's real and I'm not crying, you are! - 14th of September 2022To explain the excitement felt at the time..We waited for years as Takuya Kimura(Yagami)'s agency having trouble with mods, among other things. 2017 this game came on console only to come 5 years later together with its sequel on pc with all dlcs included and it was so awesome!We have a completely new cast of characters and a new protagonist, Takayuki Yagami. We're no longer an ex-yakuza. Now we play as a guy who left the lawyer life behind after getting an acquittal for someone who later supposedly kills his own girlfriend.  He's now a private detective working with an ex-yakuza, Kaito, taking cases all the time ranging from investigating murders to finding a lost kitty. We do it all in gameplay.The story is very thrilling and keeps you at the edge of your seat all the time. Except you have 100 side cases put mid-story rather than being where they should be - on the side. It interrupts the flow constantly and I wish it wasn't a thing. Gameplay:Combat is as refined as they could make it at the time. You have two styles with one having a bit too limited uses and the other being quite awesome. It's better than Yakuza 6 but still flawed. It peaks in Lost Judgment, the sequel.As its meant to immerse us in the detective life they go a little.. too far on the minigames. 2 lockpicking minigames, tailing, chasing, evidence presentation and investigations. You even have a key holder to pick keys from when unlocking doors. It's immersive, yes, I wish it wasn't taken too far. I found tailing OK but many find it too slow and tedious. The lockpicking minigames, however, got too far and got too long and tedious at some point in the game. There's a new system in Kamurocho - invasions by the Keihin gang. They occupy the entire town getting you into fights every 3 seconds until you beat the bosses. Again, overdone. You can't disable the system and the only way you see it's end is to grind the friendship system to its cap that for regular players would be after finishing the story. You're basically required to do everything including getting lucky in mahjong so you can actually get the last friend.Great game overall with one of the best RGG stories. Many if not all of the issues listed are no more in Lost Judgment. It's one of those cases where I wish they'd patch the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Quite disappointed by this opus, that shares a lot of the qualities of the Yakuza games, but ultimately fails to become its own thing. While the detective case suffers from rythm issues, it's decent and will keep you playing until the end of the game. Fight choregraphy is very good.However, the game feels more like a spinoff to the Yakuza series than Isshin - what you'll remember from this game are moments and characters that feel like they belong to a different franchise. And the detective bits in between are not very fun - they feel more like chores you play to get to the next interesting moment. Knowing how these elements can click together in other Ryu Ga Gotoku games, it's hard not to be disappointed by Judgment.

_childDocuments_.review: Reminds me of  to some degree, except in Judgement you're not a high school student skipping school to find his fathers murderer. Instead, you're a former Lawyer now being a Local Detective trying to solve murder cases and such (totally cool). Nonetheless, I wouldn't be too surprised if this game were made by the same creator... like seriously, take for example the side comparison. yes.. practically with everyone, including ones not of any importance related to the main story. yes, but only with the ones you can befriend or are otherwise mission related (main story missions or side missions). yes, an ass ton of capsule toys to be collected in fact. yes, but not nearly as many compared to Shenmue. yes. yes, though very few are the same as the ones you can play in Shenmue (I wish the boxing one where you punch the target by timing the button press were in this game) Yes. Yes, but also easier imo. Yes; Slot Machines. Yes, but with Poker and Black Jack. Also other things perhaps. Yes. Yes. Yes, occasionally as part of the Story. yes, an ass ton, almost around every corner you get into a fight. yes. yes.Shenmue's fighting system is a bit more combo ish, with each skill having it's own mastery level, in which you can strengthen by training in a Parking Lot or Playground. Also new moves can be learned from Scrolls and certain NPC...   Judgement has Skills that can be bought and Obtained with SP that are gained from fighting Yakuza and such (no training in a Parking Lot, etc).In Judgement you can go to Bars and Liquor Stores, get drunk and even use the Drunken Boxing style Martial Arts (sorta), but you can't in Shenmue (there are Bars in Shenmue of course, but you can't drink Alcoholic beverages in that game).You can play Pool in Shenmue, but not in Judgment (in Judgement you can play Mahjong or some other type of board game).In Shenmue there's a kitten you can feed and pet... In Judgement there are Stray Cats you can search for during Inspections (what's up with that? also kinda gives me the "where's Waldo?" type vibe lol)In Shenmue you can get beverages from Vendor Machines and drink them (although pointless, since it doesn't restore health nor anything... but somehow oddly satisfying to watch Ryo Hazuki down a Soda in a few gulps); but not in Judgment, though in Judgement you can go into restaurants to buy food and beverages (in which actually does restore health).In Judgement you can fly a Drone, and can also do Drone Races (no Drones in Shenmue).You can smoke in Judgment, not in Shenmue (not a big deal to me of course, I don't give a rats behind about Cigs).You can go to the Batting Cage and hit Baseballs in Judgement, but not in Shenmue.There are perhaps other similarities and differences as well, but for the most part I'd say if you like Shenmue, then you'll probably really like this game too. that goes without saying of course, that in some aspects I think Shenmue is better, while also Judgement may even be better in other aspects.P.S. _childDocuments_.review: With Kiryu having concluded his story (well until you get to a certain recent game) in Yakuza 6 but fans still wanting the same Ryu Ga Gotoku goodness, it was time for a new story to take the mantle. Enter Yagami, former lawyer turned detective, he becomes embroiled in a conspiracy that will bring past events back to haunt him.While Judgment is its own game, its really hard to not compare it to the previous series and this shows that Judgment isn't quite the step forward one might hope.For one, the energy is lacking, at least compared to the Yakuza series that followed before it. And the sub-stories, while still very good, aren't nearly on the level of past games with many outcomes feeling forced. The new mini-games aren't as fun and the combat isn't as thrilling, especially with an annoying mechanic introduced involving gangs and the level up being simplified.That said, the graphics, once you get past this weird noir tint it seems to have, are excellent with character animations and facial responses no longer looking wooden (though there is still some derp here and there) the final chapter is really fantastic, with some awesome fight choreography, capping off a thrilling story. This is helped by a really engaging main cast and a cool, captivating antagonist. And while it may present more of a series face, there is still the odd goofy moments that you can't help but smile at.At the end of the day, this is still a very good game and is still very much worth playing for those wanting more adventure from Kamurocho, the city that never sleeps while still providing trouble and eating the weak.

_childDocuments_.review: I just found the game underwhelming.  I have loved the Yakuza series, with the exception of that like a dragon dumpster fire.  The main story was rather lack luster.  A former lawyer turned private eye, who gets on the wrong side of the yakuza.  Really made no sense that someone who was not really a fighter would be able to survive being hunted by two different clans at points.  When you have a cut scene where they are just going to shoot your eyes out and kill you, you have to be saved by a thief with a heart of gold.  Someone you can get away, but you constantly go back to your office, where they could kill you right away but don't because "story".The fight mechanics left a lot to be desired for me.  The fights grew to be very repetitive, with having to keep changing styles mid fight depending on the number of enemies left.  The combo system was just a large amount of button mashing, with no real coherent system of stringing combos together.  Coupled with the pathetic block system, lack of real dodge dynamics and the relentless "advice" on doing wall strikes, which you have to time just right or jump right past your target.The friend system was ok, and did provide something to do other then just the main quest.  The whole food/drink/smoking system was a different approach, but really fell short for me.  Not a fan of the QTE chase events, but at least they were something different.  Getting around the city was a pain, whether it was walking or running, it was annoying.  There were so many times I just wanted to punch the lights out of the pedestrians in the way, especially after a fight; when they all get into defensive stances after you walk away.  The chapters were very short, and before you know it you are deep into the game.  Spent a long time just running around trying to find side cases, or friend events, rather then just dropping deep into the story and not leveled up enough to have a chance.  The tailing mechanics of the game were ok at best, whether it was on foot or with your drone.  The "disguise" system seemed very lazy.  Oh he put a black hat on, I don't know who that guy wearing the same clothes is.Overall just didn't like the game, and sorry I spent the money on it.  I have tried going back a few times, but its just more of the same.

_childDocuments_.review: Judgment is a Yakuza game. Yagami is a detective/disgraced former lawyer, sure, but he was also pickup up off the streets by a yakuza family. His partner Kaito is ex-yakuza. He runs around the yakuza-filled Kamurocho beating up yakuza. He defends a yakuza in court. Besides that, the game takes place in Kiryu's old haunt of Kamurocho. There's bone-crunching melee combat with multiple styles (vastly improved here from Yakuza 6.) You take on a bunch of sidestories (sorry, side cases) where you interact with the seedy, weird, and almost always goofy side of the city. You participate in a variety of laid-back minigames. In every way that matters, this is as much a Yakuza game as one that stars Kiryu or Ichiban. The story here is top-notch, with some of the best villains the series has to offer. Captain Hamura is an incredibly deep, cruel yet conflicted antagonist, brought to life by some excellent mocap acting here. The story twists from a serial murder mystery to a (expected for this series) grand conspiracy involving some of the most powerful people in Japan. Unlike a typical Yakuza game, this one doesn't rely on too many grand twists or double-crosses. The yakuza soap opera has to take a backseat and let the story progress through simple, honest detective work. And that detective work is... kinda bland? It works fine to distinguish Yagami as a character from the larger-than-life yakuza in this series, but as gameplay, it falls flat. Tailing missions are direly boring, investigation is little more than hovering your view around a hidden object puzzle, and revealing evidence never gets challenging enough to really make you puzzle through a mystery. These are small parts of the overall package here, but it's disappointing that the most unique things Judgment brings to the table are its weakest. On the other hand, this has some of the best side content in the series. Part of interacting with Kamurocho is making friends now, in an very expanded spin on Yakuza 0's friendships. Typically this will involve doing a few tasks for someone or participating in an activity. Sometimes it's as simple as triggering a few conversations, other times you need to accumulate things over the course of the whole game to fill their friendship meters. Once you're besties, they may give you rare resources, aid you in combat, or just greet you on the street. There's not a ton of true depth here, but it feels good and genuinely does make you feel more like a part of Kamurocho. This doesn't quite hit the highs of Yakuza 0 or 5, but it does provide some of the best action combat in the series, and proves that RGG Studio's formula has a lot of life in it.

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished judgement after it released on PC. And I have to say, this game is top 3 games on my list, right next to MGS3 and DMC5. The story, the music, and all the things you can do in Kamurocho really solidifies the game to be called a masterpiece. Although I admit, the Dragon Engine is a bit wonky at times for the gameplay, next to Yakuza Kiwami 2 as a standard and could use a bit more polishing. And for the story, every chapter had me on the edge of wanting to know what appens next, and all the relationships between the characters felt real and natural (Kaito and Yamagi best bromance in fiction) and played their roles phenomenally. there are a ton of characters that you can love, and a lot you are suppose to hate for reason. The story had a really great plot twist that didn’t for once had me rolling my eyes at compared to some other Yakuza games with a bizarre plot twists. _childDocuments_.review: Judge Eyes is essentially a Yakuza game with a few sprinkles of Ace Attorney. The combat in Judge Eyes is very similar to its Yakuza counterparts. Yagami's two fighting styles are similar to Majima’s Breaker and Kiriyu’s Brawler or Dragon’s stances. The cinematics are smooth and filled with tons of action scenes that can get over the top at times, similar to other Yakuza games. When the story slows down, that is where the Ace Attorney-esque side of the game shows. In this part, Yagami has to do investigations, sometimes presenting evidence, or even going into the courtroom as a defense attorney. I only wished this portion was more difficult rather than making the tailing missions long, since they felt redundant at times. Furthermore, Aside from other Yakuza games, doing substories doesn't feel pointless because Yagami is a broke detective looking for work, whether it be for cash or for justice. Substories/side cases don’t feel like a drag to do because there is a sense of purpose behind them. I found this very refreshing for a Yakuza game, because Side Cases didn’t isolate you too much from the story, they were relevant most of the time. Lastly, the casts were very fun this time. While most of the characters have their charm, I really enjoyed seeing Higashi’s character build up since it was easy for me to relate to him. For anyone questioning whether they should play this game or not, don’t give it a second thought, Play this game!!! <3

_childDocuments_.review: Do you love Yakuza games? It's one of the best gaming series ever made. No one probably expected that the same developers will create another original game. But they did it. Same city, similar gameplay and it's not a cashgrab. Not even close.Judgment is like a Yakuza spinoff because it's so similar but it's a new IP with new story. What this studio has done with Judgment is phenomenal. Not only they managed to write a completely new story for completely new characters but they also managed to reinvent the combat and think of new mini-games and ridiculous sub stories.You play as an ex lawyer who works as a private investigator now and you solve...cases. Budumtsss!The main case has a big story behind it. Soon after the game starts you involve yourself in figuring out the crimes of course. The story is as good as Yakuza games, full of twists and turns, unexpected events and so on. It's presented in the same way as Yakuza games.You work together with a partner who has connections. You also have your tiny apartment where you have the fridge and can eat from it. Yes amazing I know! You customize your shelves by placing statuettes on it and another surprise – a cat. Also you can take on side cases from there.On top of that you have the law office you work at where you usually go for story events and chat with other characters.Gameplay is similar to Yakuza games. You roam the streets of Kamurocho and fight the enemies. But you have couple of new things. One of them is a drone and another one is a camera. You need to tail people and sometimes take photos of them as proof. You can use your camera and drone for that depending on situation. To make it more fun on each case you also look for hidden cats which work as collectibles. You also need to pay attention to things, find clues and make a conclusion.Oh almost forgot – there's lockpicking too.Skills and abilities are similar to Yakuza games but feel fresh and redesigned. There are plenty of them – from usual combat related ones to some less important ones and funny ones.Combat is excellent. It feels better than any Yakuza game. It's so fluid, dynamic and diverse that it feels extremely satisfying. You have two fighting styles and can switch them on the fly.Side cases are as hilarious if not more than Yakuza games. They are outstanding and will make you laugh out loud like an idiot. You have plenty of them to solve and all of them are good more or less.You can also date and have a girlfriend. It takes time. You invite a girl on a date and talk to her, eat together, spend time together. After some time you can propose to be something else than friends. Oh lala. The girls also their own story lines.Mini games? Oh yes. Aside from the usual Yakuza mini games we have couple of new ones. First the weird VR mini-game where you have to go from point A to point B by throwing a dice and fighting. It's a bit rng based but it's fun.Now another one is drone racing. It's tough but hella fun. You can customize your drone, buy and apply parts to it making it better and faster. Along with that there are plenty of cosmetic ugrades to make it look ridiculous. And then you race through the streets of Kamurocho and fly over the heads of its inhabitants.In general the game provides so much content and activities that it's crazy. While the world is tiny it delivers what Yakuza games always delivered – quality over quantity. You'll never be bored in this one.Graphically the game is excellent. Character models are highly detailed and city looks stunning. Facial animations are decent and everythign else in general looks very good.Performance is pretty good, the game runs smoothly at high framerate and highest gra[hics setting without any dips to unplayable framerates.Played on 5800x, rtx3080, 32gb @3440x1440.No native ulktrawide support for cut-scenes but there's a simple fix which makes it work without many flaws.Sound design also is good. It's an english voiced game which was unexpected and it isn't bad at all. _childDocuments_.review: Holy moly have I been sleeping on this one. I have heard phenomenal things about  over the years but I am so damn glad that I finally played through it. SEGA have created what is possibly one of the greatest spin offs in history and have given us a detective story that is genuinely satisfying to solve and gives you all the right bread crumbs you need to solve the murder mystery. The game manages to really surprise you though through its clever subversions of its character portrayals, noir cliches, and even subversions of the tropes in writing that this team has been known for for years now. If you want a satisfying noir detective story that isn't cynical and self fulfilling, and also allows you to kick the ♥♥♥♥ out of hundreds of yakuza thugs all across Tokyo you need to pick this game up.You play as Yagami a disgraced former lawyer turned hard-boiled detective trying to unravel a murder mystery in the dark underbelly of Tokyo's criminal underworld. RGG’s Signature character writing makes Yagami an immediately sympathetic and likable protagonist who you can clearly see is trying to redeem himself following a dark past that you slowly learn about and discover is connected to your core murder case. This isn't a typical noir story full of cliche characters and tropes. Every member of the cast has a clear motivation for what it is they're doing and their allegiances turn based on the political landscape of Kamurocho. You won't just be dealing with corrupt organized crime members, the depths of this mystery goes all the way to the top with sociopathic cops, mad scientists, and morose politicians. It is so satisfying to see this team known for their excellent writing and characterization tackle fresh themes that allow you to go up against a much more believable evil in the setting of  than in any previous Yakuza game.Combat in  is among the best in the series. Yagami has two fighting styles he can switch between at any moment. The wide attacking, horde focused Crane style, or the single target damaging Tiger style. You have just the right amount of upgrades to make these styles interesting, though admittedly there is a clear favorite in the tiger style and its unlockable moves. The bosses are honestly some of the best in the franchise with the final boss in particular being cinematic and a truly great note to cap the game off on.The only real complaints I have with judgment is the fact that there really is only one city district to explore in this game compared to multiple districts like in other games in the series, and the side quests in this particular game aren't that interesting. Also, it’s a testament to how good the story and combat is in this game that I managed to enjoy my time with it since there are a TON of tailing missions. If there is one thing that I despise more than timed missions, escort missions, or underwater levels it is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ tailing mission. Please for the love of God stop putting these in games I beg you.Overall, if you have not yet played , and you’re an RGG fan, now is the time to check this game out. A genuinely satisfying murder mystery from top to bottom that commands your respect.

_childDocuments_.review: Applebees is more than just a restaurant, it is an experience.When you step through the door of the restaurant your first time, you are transported into a world unlike any other. The low light of the restaurant casts shadows on the knick-knacks adorning the walls, and the translucent hum of the various screens through the restaurant create a sort of ethereal presence in the restaurant.Right off the bat, you know you are in for a dining experience like no other."Welcome to Applebees!" a cheerful host says to you. "How many are in your party?" You hold up two fingers. "Right this way!" She responds. As you walk to your table, you wonder how she can deal with so many customers, yet remain so chipper, but shrug it off as another wonderful mystery caused by the splendor of Applebees.The waitress takes your drink order and for a moment, your head is spinning. Do you want a soda? Do you want iced tea? You look at the drink menu and you see a litany of alcohol beverages you have only dreamed about - Bud Light, Coors Light, Miller Light...The waitress offers a helpful suggestion of an Oreo Shake, and you say that sounds great. She asks if you'd like a round of water for the table as well. You smile. This is the kind of attention to detail that you expect from Michelin Star rated restaurants, not a Neighborhood Bar & Grill!As the waitress goes to fetch your shake, you peruse the menu. The pages are jam-packed with the names of delicacies that you can only imagine. Fiesta Lime Chicken? Shrimp N' Parmesan Sirloin? You shift in your seat; you suddenly feel very self-aware that you do not belong in this restaurant. Your palatte does not feel sophisticated enough for these cuisines, and you worry that you will not do these delicacies justice when you enjoy them.Just at this moment, the waitress comes to your table and all your fears are dissuaded. You order the Chicken Tenders Platter (a local favorite). You take a sip from your Oreo Shake and breath a sigh of relief as liquified Oreos slide down your throat. You lean back in your booth and relax.Suddenly, you hear a chorus of heavenly voices rise from behind you. You turn around to see all of the Applebees wait staff coming towards you, singing and clapping their hands. "Happy happy birthday, from Applebees to you," they cheer. "We wish it was our birthday, so we could party too, hey!"As soon as they arrived, the employees scatter, leaving you to dwell on the beauty of it all; the fact that Applebees treats you with such precise, special attention, the five-star cuisine, the exotic decor, and the fact that the wait staff is so eager to share in your special moments with you.

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game on the PS5 before the pc port released today so my review will be talking about my experience on PS5 compared to my experience so far on PC.This game right here is one of the great RGG titles that everyone should at least check out. The combat is similar to Yakuza 0 with how you have styles that you can switch on the fly, that being the Crane Style and the Tiger Style, Crane is more used for crowd control while Tiger is more used for 1v1 fights, but that's what they want you to think, because you can use either style in different ways, even if Crane isn't as good as Tiger, you can start a juggle combo using Tiger and switch to Crane for the more wider and quicker kicks with EX Boost.The story is amazing, probably one of the best stories RGG has put out next to Yakuza 0, 7, and Lost Judgment. As this is the first game in the Judgment series to follow Yagami and his group, this is a fantastic start, with a captivating case, which originally starts as something small like a serial killing that leads to something even bigger than just a serial killing, without getting into spoilers.The amount of Side Content in this game also is amazing, 50 Side Cases, and 50 Friends, a huge completion list like how it was in other Yakuza games, my bane of existence the Keihin Gang (probably the only thing that sucks in the game though the bosses are cool), the Judgment games as much as it is serious in its main story, balances that out with the wackiness from the side cases it has, though I did wish that certain points in the main story didn't stop for a mandatory side case.The detective stuff in the game is alright, the tailing missions as much as i did like them, get boring after the 6th time doing one, especially with the last tailing mission in the main story which is drawn out so long that i wished that it was just a cutscene instead, search mode is a fine addition, especially with the amount of SP you get for just looking around your surroundings, also the cats :3. Can't wait to see how modders take this apart, especially on how johnny and associates have prevented us from getting this game on PC because of that reason.So, if your a Yakuza fan, then this is a must play, if you never played Yakuza game in your life, this is a great starting point to the world of Yakuza and its city Kamurocho.

_childDocuments_.review: While I do recommend this game, I feel it's best to summarise my time with it with a simple list of pros and cons. The good:• Fun combat. RGG Studio realised how much we love the Heat Actions in the Yakuza games and decided to give us a power fantasy here, so Yagami can unleash a dozen of them before needing to recharge the EX Gauge.  The two stances break up the monotony of the atypical "XXY to win" strategy so prevalent in past Yakuza entries.• A gripping story with great themes. I was glued to my seat, desperate to find out who The Mole was and found myself enthralled in Yagami's quest for vengeance and justice.• Great characters.  Whether it be Mafayu, Kaito, Yagami himself or Saori and the rest of the lawyers, Yakuza and corrupt officials that line the cast, there's very few characters here that I can call "bad". I enjoyed all of their performances (JP Audio) and found myself attached to them.• Lots of side-content. As is RGG Studio fare, this game is absolutely loaded with mini-games and side content to extend your playtime well beyond the main story.• Graphics and performance.  Played this in 1440p 60 with 0 drops, stutters or compatibility issues. A pretty much perfect PC port and the best part is Task Manager showed it was using barely 10% of my rig during the most intense moments.• Longer than the average Yakuza game. Maybe a bad thing to others but for me, I thought this was a meaty game with a lot of plot and world-building, so I found myself a lot more invested than in say, Yakuza Kiwami which was over before I knew it.• Some of the best fight choreography I've ever seen in any game, and up there with the highest highs of RGG Studio's other games.Now for the bad:• Repetitive tailing missions.  Most people who have heard about Judgment have heard horror stories about these and yes, they're that bad. Imagine the worst Ubisoft Assassin's Creed tailing mission and dial it to 11, and you have one of the worst interruptions ever.  After Chapter 7 these do stop being as frequent, but they'll show up to frustrate you in the later chapters.  Just boring, sadly.• Pacing is way, way off.  Prior to Chapter 7, the game insists on breaking up EVERY. SINGLE. CHAPTER. with a side quest that often times is completely unrelated to the overarching narrative.  Gone are the brief gameplay introduction missions of the Yakuza series, here's full-fledged missions where Yagami abandons his quest for justice to do menial tasks and chat up Hostesses.    The game frequently gives you the "wait around for XYZ to call" objective until the 7th chapter or so, leading you to just wander aimlessly until you can progress the story.  I get they wanted you to use that time to explore, but when you're enthralled in the narrative it just becomes a nuisance and is little more than arbitrary padding.Overall I'd give this game a 4/5 and despite its blemishes, would recommend it to anyone who either likes RGGs other games or just wants a thrilling crime story to experience. For a first game in a new franchise, it's understandably rough around the edges but if you stick with it, you will leave satisfied. Just don't trust how you feel about the game prior to chapter 6, because it gets so much better thereafter.

_childDocuments_.review: RGG studio doesn't make bad games (at least, not since Dead Souls). I was wondering how this would feel, without the strong personalities of the mainline games' protagonists. Instead, you play a pretty boy in skinny jeans, but Yagami feels like a natural fit in the setting, and is interesting for a totally different reason than Kiryu and company.The narrative here almost feels like a throwback to the neo-noir of Yakuza 4, but, at least so far, the story hasn't taken a big wet turd on itself (if you know, you know). Instead, it's a broody, sometimes shocking story filled with tension, surprise, and intrigue. The investigation stuff is pretty linear, in the style of a Danganrompa or Ace Attorney game, but the linearity doesn't really matter once you let it sweep you up. And while the tailing missions are a chore (yeah, I get why every review complains about them), they're also a great way to slow down the pace, get you to focus in a different way. If you played any other Dragon Engine game set in Tokyo (Yakuza 6, Kiwami 2), then you know how the exploration is going to go, and you can guess what minigames from earlier in the series return (mahjong, shogi, casino stuff), and which ones are still gone (bowling, we miss you). Add to that familiar stuff the new experiences of piloting a drone around, a slightly more fleshed out friendship system, the revamping of heat into the not-quite-exactly-the-same EX system, and the whole new cast, main and supporting, and this is a great addition if you're a fan of RGG's other games, as well as a wonderful entry point into the cracked-mirror version of Kabukicho that RGG has been building for the last two decades. Thumbs way up. I'm only in chapter 5, and it's already captivating.Edited to add: Oh, right, I forgot to mention the English dub, which RGG wasn't really doing prior to this (except Fist of the North Star). It's excellent. Sega and their subsidiaries tend to do great voice casting and direction, and this is no exception. So if the mainline Yakuza series' lack of English VA turned you off, this has that option (but also comes with the Japanese dub as well if you're a purist; the best of both worlds)

_childDocuments_.review: Upsides+Gameplay feels good. Initially battles felt clunky, but as you get more skills, they turn more interesting and fluid. Battles weren't necessarily as good as in Yakuzas, but still really good, especially when most of the random ones can be finished pretty quickly.+Just like Yakuza games, the characters look really good and the city feels lively. Animation and directing on main story are good, while on side quests they are often simple and low effort, but somehow it's kinda charming how comedic it looks at times.+Interesting story.+Alot to do from side quests to mini games, even dating.+Investigations are fun, looking for clues and presenting evidence.+Cats everywhere.Downers-Theres alot of filler in the main story. It felt that whenever theres some big movement in the main story, you need to spend as much time on completelly unrelated things to advance the story. Often this is for character development, which might have been better as side quests, but there are also points where you need to wait to hear from other characters and the filler is just something to make you feel like you are actually waiting.-Most of the tailing sequences are pretty boring. There are some that are more interesting later on, but mostly they are a pretty dull. Points where you are able to hide are pretty specific, so how you handle the tailing feels pretty scripted.-Chase sequences. All of them, and theres quite alot. Chases are basicly just QTE and they tend to follow same patterns, have a group on the right, followed by group on the left, finish with fallen bike, on to next segment, rinse and repeat. I personally feel QTE is lazy game design, and this is nothing but that.-Kim. He is merely the harbinger of pain, but every single text message makes me hate him more.-Side cases are locked behind community level, and to raise that, you need to make friends. The cases open every 5 levels, so you will be spending alot of time doing friend events, of which most are talk, go away, come back, type things or fetch quests. There are some fun and interesting ones, but most are pretty mundane, and few are downright grind (Ebisu, Batting center, Extract guy, Mahjong. Thank god shogi wasn't on the list). Worst part is spending an hour getting the community level up to unlock a new side case, which might take just 5 minutes to complete. Getting all 50 friends isn't huge undertaking in the end, especially if you use guide for the grindy ones, but still it feels kinda unbalanced what you get for the effort.-Mortal wound system and guns. They are kinda cheap shots to chip away your max health, they don't take much, but it's annoying regardless.

Except now, instead of a death at a contested land plot, it's a death implicating an exonerated client as a serial killer and calling professional judgment into question. _childDocuments_.review: So what I love about Judgment is that I'm here for the characters and the vibe. You're not here for the grand operatic story about love and honor, you're here watching a bunch of schlubs in way over their heads in a town that regularly chews up and spits out any schlub who doesn't find a bigger fish to help them. But they're human. It's all the silliness and drama I loved with Cabaret Club Royale/Grand Prix, but a whole game of it rather than just one part of it. It's watching human moments between these people, getting caught up in the personal drama and getting to know the city piece by piece before you watch them twist and turn, facing countless trials as they slowly deal with something far bigger than themselves, calling on all the help and every cheap shot at their disposal to survive. If the law of Kamurocho is "you don't fight, you don't survive," Judgment's answer to that is "there's more than just a single way to fight." Which brings me to the pacing. I've been rolling this around in my head, because the pacing of Judgment substantially changes once you get through the setup. (The setup is roughly a third of the game, I am sorry) Each chapter takes about a day and a night, roughly, with time in between, but the structure goes "daytime case, nighttime case." The daytime case is usually something more procedural and there's more humor. The nighttime case is the darker, more violent serial murder/corruption investigation. The two connect, and there's not a clear demarcation, but those are the lines....now as you might not know because I neither have a T-shirt referencing the show that I wear to every convention nor do I quote the show and its lead character endlessly, I am a huge fan of a short-lived long-impacting ABC television series called Twin Peaks, the only David Lynch TV series to last more than a single truncated season. And it had an interesting structure. Every episode was a single day within the town of Twin Peaks. You followed the residents through their daily lives, and there was soap opera and danger, but things were usually a little offbeat. That offbeatness turned more surreal and dangerous as the episode went from daytime to nighttime, eventually culminating in the supernatural heart of the show, the investigation into the bizarre and shadowy world of Twin Peaks after dark and the murder of prom queen and town sweetheart (and cocaine smuggler and hooker and literal trafficker of the physrep of human despair) Laura Palmer. Somehow I'm vibing with Judgment because it subconsciously tripped my Twin Peaks switch, but also because like that show, the heart isn't the murder investigation or The Plot, it's with the human moments using the plot kind of like an armature to hang things on. Sure, Kamurocho is a surreal and dangerous world with mad bombers, ghosts, masked phantom thieves, a pawnshop owner obsessed with abstract watercolors, and a cafe owner who drinks thirty cups of black coffee a day. But all those people are presented in the most human way possible. Not necessarily real, but with a certain heart and empathy at its core. And that's what Judgment is. It's you getting to know people, and then caring not due to some grand operatic plot, but due merely to the fact that you got to know them all.

_childDocuments_.review: All Like a Dragon(previously Yakuza) franchise games are peak and this entry was no exception. Characters: One thing I love about this franchise are the characters. Yagami is a well-written protagonist, with a strong sense of justice and morality. He might not be as strong as Kiryu, Majima, Saejima, but he can still hold his own against a horde of enemies with his own fighting style. He feels more realistic with how we see him getting hurt when he jumps from high places or getting mortal wounds(untreatable with usual healing items/foods) from bosses' charged up attacks and gunshots. It's a refreshing take.Then there are Yagami's bros, Kaito,  and . As the story went on I liked them more and more. Fighting alongside them felt so exciting, especially during .I could describe the antagonist characters too, but that is too much of a spoiler. All I can say is, the main antagonist is quite , really liked his boss fight.Plot: I had been waiting to play this game since its worldwide release back in 2019, so I had already managed to spoil most of the major details for myself. Nevertheless, I highly enjoyed experiencing the story firsthand and doing the long battles/boss fights. For new players, I would recommend going into the game blind as the game's main theme is uncovering the truth. There are several gripping and exciting moments throughout the whole game, would definitely recommend.Combat: The combat features 2 fighting styles. One is more suited for individual opponents, the other one for a horde of enemies. The more you unlock moves and heat actions and get better at them by practising on street thugs, the more satisfying it gets when you do the main story fights. The moves are easy to learn. Literally planned my battle choreos for the bosses, looked really flashy when I applied them, reminded me of DMC5 in a way. Generally, the combat is fun regardless of how good or bad you are, as long as you don't stick to pressing 1 button to attack.Side stuff: Most of the side missions involved tailing the target and those got really tedious. The rest of the minigames were what are usually present in each entry, like shogi, mahjong, blackjack etc. As usual, the menu options for each restaurant looked scrumptious, never failed to make me hungry. There were also 50 characters that you can befriend overall by doing little missions for them, though I only did 46. Doing them didn't feel as cumbersome as I would have expected it to be. The game also allows us to pursue 4 girls as potential girlfriends. The stories for them were good enough for me to care about the characters. Finally, per the Like a Dragon franchise tradition, there's the . I haven't unlocked it yet, so I cannot give my review on that part for now.Overall, Yakuza is my all-time favourite game franchise, so this might seem a bit biased, but this game is definitely a 9.5/10 .

_childDocuments_.review: In full honesty, this game is about what I expected as an RGG studio game - that is, high quality in basically every regard. I've been a little spoiled for animations and faces recently, so my usually high opinion of their face and movement animation work is less stellar than it has been in the past, but as a whole Judgment still looks very good. The music didn't really stand out to me, unfortunately, unlike in the mainline games. I liked the start-of-chapter review stuff a lot, it helped keep everything in focus when I had to take a few weeks off the game and return in the middle of chapter 10. The story was definitely less convoluted than in the LAD games, but this meant that some of the really goofy moments (highlights of the LAD series, imo) felt a little off-key. But the combat might be the best they've done in this engine, it's definitely superior to 6 and K2. It's fast, fluid, and fun, even if the positional stuff (like wall rebounds) take a minute to get adjusted to. There was one section, late in the game, where you were required to learn a certain mechanic of an area, and if you fought the boss of the area without utilizing the mechanic, you were (unfairly) punished by making your attacks miss. Also, as a hint: your strongest move, flux fissure, cannot be chained into bosses. They'll just stumble. I did not have a boss encounter where this was not true. This is maybe a 7/10 compared to the heights I know RGG can produce. Still a 100% worthwhile experience ("fun" does not begin to describe the drone racing, especially as you power it up). If you like the Yakuza games, you'll probably like this.

_childDocuments_.review: On 50% sale or more, I would recommend picking this up. On PC - particularly early on - there's a number of technical issues. First and foremost there was a lot of sound glitching within the game, audio cutting out, or faraway voices being a super high volume. For some reason these audio issues stopped occuring a few chapters in with no change/update to the game or my PC? I can only conclude that there's some state that is fixed/checked in later stagesThe same issue applies with sprinting, I'll hold or toggle sprint and sometimes I'll sprint flawlessly... other times I'll run a few steps, slow down, and then start running again. Sometimes getting into combat will fix this, but most times you'll have to rely on a major cutscene. But, again, after a few chapters this behavior stopped occuring so there's really something not quite right in the early gameAdditionally, if you're playing this on a Switch Pro controller forget about trying to use the Nintendo button layout; this thing runs on Xbox controls and that's the end of it -- I changed controls multiple times to see if I get it to be the Nintendo format and in spite of the game saying changes we're saved, they just never were. This gets frustrating when you're placed in a scene with quicktime events... and even more annoying when you play other games then let you use the Nintendo layoutIssues aside, on sale I think it's a decent buy. It's not quite as good as the Yakuza games in my opinion and the story isn't as outlandish or engaging as those games either. Also, many of the missions/side missions require you to do '''investigation''' type tasks suchs as scanning a room for a specific object in first person, or tailing someone. These missions are extremely painful and every single time I rushed through them as quickly as I could. They're absolutely not engaging whatsoever, if there was an autocomplete option I would have immediately selected that insteadOverall if you've played the Yakuza games.... Kamurocho is getting a little boring, but the overall story is just interesting enough to pull you through

_childDocuments_.review: 'Overwhelmingly Positive" is very appropriate. If you liked Lethal Weapon, Die Hard, Jack Reacher type moves or true crime youll love this game. It's a detective game with beat em up elements with some GTA-ness in the mix but the story, the story is amazing. It does mystery right by having just enough unknowns for the player to gauge the flow the story but not the details. The details and twists are so well done and very compelling. I love the story so much that I hated the mandatory side cases because I just wanted to know what was going to happen next. The mandatory side cases is probably the only issue I have with the game. Fortunately those side cases are short and sprinkled in the beginning to early middle. Theres nothing wrong with the side missions from a gameplay standpoint except they don't relate to the banger of the main story. The setting of the game is also high quality. I've been to Japan a couple times and city and atmosphere was very accurate to what I experienced. I loved the attention to detail to various shops, streets, and buildings. The minigames included are pretty sick as they are old school style arcade games, darts, casino games, shogi, and drone racing. Basically this is a "snap" recommend.

As you can not run in the game, or even take more than 10 steps or so before you are bombarded with some 'gang' that never seems to vanish.I give thumbs up because i like YAKUZA, and the fighting style, but there are some flaws and lazy work that i have noticed that will keep the game from ever being a real 'hit' with general gamers (as well as long-time YAKUZA fans)

_childDocuments_.review: Overall good but not as excellent as some of the other games from the same studio._There's the same quality in terms of graphics , characters, voice acting , story telling and mini games. Quite a bit of humor too. Like in any Yakuza games really.  Some good mechanics too, like lockpicking, Drone racing is okay but needs some changes.  I also played it entirely on mouse/keyboard, and there was only 2 annoying things with that, controlling the vertical axis of the drone, and dodging, which weren't a problem to finish the game on hard._On the other hand, the story felt disappointing, not much surprise there.I feel it is more about questioning the player's moral about what's going on during the story than the story itself : The perception of what is justice, and if the end justify the means.  The story also started to drag on a bit near the end, before the grand finale, but then we get a super short epilogue where we don't know what happened to most of the characters. Some content is locked behind a grind wall that is too high so i didn't bother, for example, of the 50 side jobs in the game, i am missing 2 because they are locked behind the 50 friends requirements, which i didn't do because of said grindwall.The combat system also didn't really feel great or fun, and for real, the Keihin gang constant invasion are an absolute unfun pain very quickly.I also want to mention that tailing missions are bad, and the Keyholder system is completely useless.So yes, overall good, but i hope Lost Judgement has a lot of improvements, because that still felt disappointing in the end when compared to Yakuza 0 or 7 for example.

_childDocuments_.review: From the makers of the acclaimed Yakuza series, Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio, Judgment is the dramatic tale of a disgraced lawyer seeking redemption in a world rife with corruption and despair. Investigate the seedy Red Light District of Kamurocho by stepping into the mind of private detective Takayuki Yagami and utilize innovative investigation systems to uncover the secrets that lie deep within Kamurocho's corrupt underbelly. Experience visceral combat with two unique combat styles. Take down groups of thugs with sweeping blows in Crane Style, then switch to Tiger to overwhelm a single foe with a series of powerful strikes. Practice mixing-and-matching styles in combat in conjunction with a wide variety of skills, weapons, and powerful (and hilarious) EX Actions to unlock a whole new dimension in combat.

name: Lost Judgment
detailed_description: When a convicted police officer discloses the murder of the student teacher who bullied his son to suicide, the dark secrets of a Yokohama high school rise to the surface. Fight for the truth as detective Takayuki Yagami and go undercover at a prestigious high school to solve a string of twisted bullying cases. But as victims pile up, caught in a cycle of bullying and revenge, will the scales of justice tip in favor of defending the law or enacting vengeance? Crack skulls to crack the case in this action-packed legal thriller. RGG Studio proudly presents Lost Judgment, the sequel to Judgment that weaves investigative sleuthing, noir narrative, and bone-crushing combat into a story like none other. INVESTIGATIVE ACTION Tap into Yagami’s arsenal of private eye tricks to gather clues. Use hi-tech gadgets like drones and listening devices as well as hardboiled gumshoe methods like scaling buildings and tailing suspects to uncover the truth. No stronger evidence than catching a suspect in the act. FREEFORM COMBAT Master Yagami’s three unique, combo-heavy martial arts styles to overcome any situation from group ambushes to single-target takedowns. Plus, expand your arsenal with street signs, bicycles, and more to pack an even bigger punch. DEEP UNDERCOVER Go undercover as a high school club advisor to get to the root of the mystery, and have some fun along the way. Join the Dance Club and groove to the rhythm with your students. Challenge your ingenuity at the Robotics Club. Test your moves against fierce opponents at the boxing gym. You can even join the biker gang, where underground racing is the only way to earn respect. HIT THE STREETS As you comb the cities of Kamurocho and Ijincho in pursuit of the truth, take a break and get to know the unique culture of each city through bars and other nightlife hotspots. It may be worth taking on a Side Case to lend your detective skills to residents in need—you never know what might come of it.

_childDocuments_.review: Where Judgement 1 is a proof of concept, Lost judgement is the ideas fully realized.Lost judgement is a lovely game for a variety of reasons that I dont even know where to start.Its such a vast improvement over the original, on top of being a phenomenal RGG game.I'll start with some basics,"Do I need to play judgement 1 in order to understand this one?"No. All returning character are treated as "just another day in life of yagami and friends! :)"you wont be feeling like theres spoonfuls of lore missing from the games core story, at most are a small number of side quests that have a returning character, whom are side quest characters themselves that don't matter in the grand scheme of things. Never mind, gameplay wise, judgement 1 isn't a good time if you play it solely for the story. You'd be better of jumping into Lost judgement blind with no prior knowledge."Do I need to play any of the yakuza games or vice versa to understand anything?"No. While both series are in the same universe, familiar faces from yakuza do not appear in either game. Meanwhile, the plots of both games are irrelevant to the greater yakuza universe as of writing. Aside from a single side quest in yakuza gaiden/ the man who erased his name having 2 characters fight alongside kiryu for 10 minutes, anything else meerly boiled down to cameo's you wouldn't notice in the first place."Is the kaito files necessary?"The kaito files, while enjoyable, aren't needed for the main game. its a single ~10 hour story of kaito that likely is to give the writers some breathing space, should they be unable to use Yagami, without completely altering his design due to some external factors of the game itself. Its fun, but you're not missing too much.Everything about lost judgements gameplay is a vast improvement over the original. The combat is much smoother and feels more in like with traditional yakuza while allowing it to do its own things, side content is much more focused and allows for players to access it at their own paced. Tedious features such as mortal damage, and the "police timer" are gone. The grocery list of improvements goes on.For guys who can't get enough of classic yakuza combat, this is notably one of the more difficult games the studio has put out for all the right reasons. Someone making this their first RGG game will likely struggle unless they spend ALOT of time doing side content and getting beefy through playing the game in large increments. Someone like myself whose more at home and finished majority of the franchise on the hardest difficulties, victory feels earned. the challenge is present, but it never felt genuinely unfair, or cheap.The only criticism I have is purely with a couple mini games, the main outlier. theres a "vr" game that returns from judgement 1 that works like an offshoot of mario party. beat your opponent, net yourself a surplus of cash. if you really like the minigame, its a great way to get money fast. problem is, the minigame itself eats a lot of time to play, and should you occasionally lose for any reason, you get nothing for your time and effort. More ridiculous still, is in order to play the game, you have to use a consumable currency exclusively for it that the game sprinkles out in very small portions. I played it on a couple times ever, and regardless of if i won or not, there were so many other things I liked doing in game more, that even when I did want to play it, half the time I couldn't so I ignored its existence for the bulk of the game.Final verdict: 9/10TLDR: the bar between judgement games was raised so high, I can't wait for another one.

_childDocuments_.review: Lost Judgment is a thrilling detective game that combines a gripping story, engaging characters, and diverse gameplay. You play as Takayuki Yagami, a former lawyer who now works as a private investigator in Tokyo. You are hired to solve a mysterious murder case that involves a high school bullying scandal, deepfake technology, and a powerful criminal organization. Along the way, you will explore the vibrant city of Yokohama, fight against various enemies using three different combat styles, and participate in a variety of side activities, such as skateboarding, dancing, and more.Lost Judgment excels at creating a realistic and immersive world that draws you in with its rich details, dynamic events, and lively NPCs. The main story is well-written and full of twists and turns that keep you hooked until the end. The characters are memorable and have their own personalities, motivations, and backgrounds. The voice acting and facial animations are superb and convey the emotions and expressions of the characters. The gameplay is varied and fun, offering you a lot of freedom and choice in how you approach each situation. You can stealthily infiltrate a building, chase down a suspect on foot or by car, brawl with thugs using martial arts, or use your detective skills to find clues and evidence. You can also enjoy the many side quests and mini-games that add humor, depth, and challenge to the game.Lost Judgment is a game that will appeal to fans of detective stories, action games, and Japanese culture. It is a game that will make you feel like a real detective, a badass fighter, and a curious explorer. It is a game that will make you laugh, cry, and think. It is a game that you will not regret playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly one of the best, if not, the best yakuza game ever. The story is not perfect but it does keep you on your toes without making the players confused on what is happening despite it being complicated at times (it's easy to follow imo). Gameplay is top tier, I honestly thought I would hate the idea of juggling since it seems "unrealistic" (started playing from 0 so I kinda fell in love with the old dragon engine) but I actually loved it and the fact that you can use your surroundings as well (not just talking about pickable weapons or items)! Side cases are ok, most of them are interesting and I didn't mind doing it since they give decent rewards + can be funny at times. School stories is where its at though, it's long yes but bear with it, the minigames that comes with it is fun (8 out of 10 of them at least in my opinion) and the story is also thought provoking! Lastly, the OST is a banger as usual, no brainer on this one.I heavily insist on buying it once you have finish judgment, just make sure it's on a huge sale to make it really worth the price!

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of the best games RGG Studio has put out. Judge Eyes/Judgement improved a hell of a lot on what was wrong with 6 and Kiwami 2 combat, and Lost Judgement perfects it. Makes me genuinely excited for 6.5, because we'll be able to play as Dragon Engine Kiryu in his prime. The story is another thing entirely. I can easily say it's up there with 0 and 2's. _childDocuments_.review: This might be the darkest of the RGG/Yakuza games yet, to the point where it gets somewhat uncomfortable to ignore the main story and go about doing wacky side quests  The main mystery is incredibly intriguing however, and the main side activity, the school stories, adds an extra layer of mystery, which works very well for this game  Other than that, it's classic Yakuza, just in a grand scale  Out of the realtime combat Yakuza games, this is easily the biggest, and is chock full of things to do all over the two towns of Kamurocho and Isezaki Ijincho (A criticism I made on the previous Judgment is that being limited to Kamurocho hampered the game, but this game counters that very well)  The all new Seiryo High School increases this a bit further  As of the time of writing this review, I haven't finished either story yet, but looking forward to finishing sometime soon   Editing after completing main story, school stories, and 28/42 side quests:   The main mystery was incredibly compelling and comes to a believable resolution, but once the core points of the mystery are solved, the main story falters.   Yagami's obsession over  turns him into a bona fide hypocrite who criticizes others for trying to invoke their own justice at the cost of others' sacrifices while he himself does the same thing. Ultimately, nothing is really settled, and Yagami's solution is to fall back on the very same broken system that caused everything to happen in the first place, with an assurance that he'll protect those who fall through the cracks, which is downright laughable.   The school stories storyline is the other major story content in this game, and is something fresh in the context of RGG Studio games. This storyline tries to tread the fine line between the craziness of the side stories and the seriousness of the main story, and the results of this are rather mixed. The climax has an anime-ish SEISHUN! POWER OF FRIENDSHIP! type of feel to it, and I'm not sure if that really works. Still, the mystery of it all is very compelling, and made me want to see it through to the end, playing through all the minigames to get to it. Dancing, robotics, street racing, boxing, it all adds up to a massive amount of variety, giving you so much to do in the course of this storyline.   Some of the minigames did feel boring, however, such as the Girls Bite minigame, and it felt like it had to be done too many times to get to the end of that particular questline. Still, it's a minor blemish, and you come across several rather colourful and entertaining characters through it all. It's a shame most of this story is unvoiced. Would've loved to hear Amasawa Kyoko talk a bit more.   Oh, and I missed something important when I first wrote this review: TAILING MISSIONS. This was a huge annoyance in the first game, and luckily, the gameplay itself has been improved slightly, but more than anything, the number and frequency of tailing missions have been reduced drastically. If there was criticism about this from players back then by any chance, the devs clearly listened.   In the end, Yakuza 7/LaD remains the best Yakuza/RGG Studio game to date in my mind.  Lost Judgment does quite a few things right and is an overall improvement over Judgment and older Yakuza games in general, but the main story falters in the end, and the characters of 7 are more entertaining in general, giving 7 an edge over it

_childDocuments_.review: I have spent more time playing Yakuza titles in the last few years than any other game franchise or series by a longshot. Every time I finish one, I tell myself, "that's it, there's no way they can make the next game as good as this." With the way most studios end up burning their own beloved IP into the ground, you would expect it to happen for the Yakuza universe too. However, instead of becoming an abject failure of a studio like some, RGG somehow manages to publish yet another amazing game in Lost Judgement. A few impressions for those who have yet to invest:Mechanics: the brawls are as chaotic and showy as ever, retaining and building on the highly enjoyable combat of previous titles. The mini games are more addicting than hard drugs. The character banter is witty, and the amount of explorable space and things to do is truly remarkable. I was just expecting Kamurocho plus maybe a small district to travel to, but they went all out and made it a lot of total playable space without running out of amusements and side tasks to fill it out. Story: the plot hits all the classic Yakuzaverse high notes--a strong protagonist with deep convictions about justice, and the importance in standing up for your personal code of honor. There's a lot of short, funny moments, juxtaposed against larger story themes that examine some of the really messed up ♥♥♥♥ in society. Without spoiling anything, one example that really got me was a depiction of some sociopathic kids that made a habit out of bullying someone. They didn't pull any punches in showing how life-ruining it can be to find yourself trapped in that situation with no one to turn to for help. The writers don't shy away from the harsh reality of it, which makes the story surprisingly emotional. General Vibe: One last thing I really enjoy--much as mainline Yakuza titles have overtones of the crime film genre, Lost Judgement is likewise wrapped in a veneer of film noir and classic detective movies. It gives the series its own distinct place in the RGG ecosystem and I like the alternate approaches both types of protagonists take to get to the same end result. Performance: For reference I'm using an RTX3070--at the launch of Yakuza: Like a Dragon it took a while to get the game playing smoothly on my setup  The team has really improved the games on PC--not sure about Lost Judgement at launch, but currently it runs flawlessly on my PC at 1440p. Have settings maxed, DLSS running and never see frame drops below 60FPS which is a big improvement over the somewhat variable performance I expected.Get it now while it's on sale, it's worth every dime in my book.Cheers and happy New Year, kyodais!

_childDocuments_.review: Another solid entry from RGG studios.  More of what you like, although the detective aspect seems to be less prevalent this time around.  Sure, you still tail people (which still sucks), go over evidence and such, but it's not nearly as often as it was in Judgement.  Combat I'd have to say feels like it has improved.  It still has that classic Yakuza/Judgement feel, but this outing, Yagami feels like he packs more of a punch.  The addition of the Snake style really steals the show in my opinion and really feels like all you need honestly.  Crane and Tiger are still viable, but Snake seems to outclass them in every way.  The boxing style is ok, but It didn't bring a lot to the table other than really quick dodges and punches.  Effective? Sure.  Fun? Not really.  It gets old quickly, and you'll probably find yourself going back to Snake. The game is jam packed full of extra stuff to do as per usual.  Your favorite mini games are still there, with some new additions as well.  The school stories require you to partake in the mini games which aren't all that bad, but they get repetitive very quickly.  The robotics mini game  is really cool in concept and works OK, but if fleshed out a little bit more, it would have been way more enjoyable.  It quickly starts to feel like the school stories mini games feel like a chore to progress though which is a negative in my book.  However, you do end up learning some helpful skills from them.The story is not one of the strongest outings from RGG.  Is it good? Not really.   It's not really bad either, though.  I'd say its about on par with Yakuza 3 or 4 as far as plot.  It isn't bad, but it doesn't stand out as special either.  Familiar faces return which is always a welcome sight in these games.  While I don't mind Yagami, I don't find him to be nearly as interesting as a main character compared to the other characters we've been introduced to in the Yakuza universe.  He can hold his own in a fight, and has character development, but personally, I don't find him as likeable as Kaito.  Speaking of Kaito, the DLC is pretty fun.  Again, not an amazing story, but it's decent enough.  There's 4 chapters to get though, and maybe adds an additional 6-8 hours of play time if you try to do all the extra stuff.  Kaito will bring you back to playing previous Yakuza titles, as he's essentially Kiryu with his brawler and beast styles.  Combat feels super fun as Kaito because you're once again a walking tank.  Overall, I recommend.  If you're a fan of these games, you know what you're in for and you'll get your money's worth.  If you are on the fence, then wait for the sale.  I'm confident most people will enjoy the game, just don't expect it to be Yakuza 0 good.

_childDocuments_.review: While a holistically giant leap in quality from Judgment, the game still has that clunky, grindy AA-budget charm that RGG is known for, despite being a very well-renowned and established studio at this point. While I don't necessarily consider this a negative—enough to leave a negative review alone—it feels like this spin-off really exposes just how buggy and unfun RGG's games can actually be, and how much they don't want to deviate from the main series. It also feels as though this series suffers from a lower budget and expectations.Lost Judgment starts off with a strong story that quickly becomes predictable and boring, and loses its edge due to RGG's ever-present desire to keep everything tethered to the Yakuza story experience. The supporting cast that helps in Yagami's journey barely develop at all as characters and feel hollow and incomplete in the presence of the main character's bland and neutral existence, especially in the presence of Kaito. This series was better off being a single game.

_childDocuments_.review: Like all the Ryu ga Gotoku games, Lost Judgment is good, and worth playing, but I'm sad to say that I think Lost Judgment is the first game in the extended series to really disappoint me.  I often put up with rough mechanics to watch an interesting story, or allow fun combat to carry me through a plodding arc, but Lost Judgment is the first of these games to just feel clumsy on all counts, and I hope it is not indicative of the direction of future games.  Compared to the games on either side of this one, Judgment and Like a Dragon: Ishin!, both of which I enjoyed, this one feels like a misstep,  Certainly, Like a Dragon: Gaiden is incredible, so hopefully they bring those developments to bear on the Judgment series as well.The story requires suspension of disbelief at essentially every turn.  I felt the same way about Judgment, but I chalked that up to my experience with the pharmaceutical industry, which most people wouldn't be expected to share.  That's fair.By comparison, I'm not an expert on Japanese jurisprudence -- maybe they really don't have clear laws against overt contempt of court or blatant criminal conspiracy in Japan -- but I found Lost Judgment's insistence upon the untouchability of its linchpin antagonist very hard to swallow.  Every chapter makes at least one substantial leap of logic, sometimes even contradicting an assumption that needed to be true for a previous leap to be accepted.It's also depressing.  Making a video game about bullying is a tough sell to begin with, but when your ethical dilemma is whether or not it is acceptable to /torture and murder/ bullies who drive others to suicide, you have to be real careful that your protagonists don't lose sight of the fact that IT IS NOT OKAY, and start treating the villains like they are worthy of admiration, which totally happens here.  By the end of this thing, I didn't want to be on /anybody's/ side.The combat just feels... incomplete.  They introduce the new Snake stance very early as a way to engage high school delinquents without injuring them, but it quickly becomes apparent that it is far superior to either Tiger or Crane stance in the vast majority of circumstances, at least without upgrades.  It deflects attacks from behind, disarms basic combatants with a free QTE, and turns enemies into projectile weapons at the end of almost every combo.  It is GREAT FUN, but it is so effective that I finished 90% of the game on Normal or Hard without ever spending a single point on a skill.  Eventually, I was getting one-shotted often enough by bosses that some health upgrades were a must.Street combat is always trivial, even on Hard, but boss combat is dangerously unpredictable on Easy, full of staggering interrupts, unblockable stun combos, and even instant-kill QTEs.  You can have a boss down to their magic pixel after a long fight, only for them to lock you into an unblockable that eats half your health and downs you, starting you over.  This happened to me often enough that I started to use extracts (magic potions) to cheese my way through boss fights on the second attempt, simply because I wasn't willing to put in the time again.You encounter bosses with four and five health bars quite early on.  It feels like the combat engine designers took this one off, and their B team throws the kitchen sink at you to keep you from realizing.  None of the big fights in this game feel challenging, they are just over-long and full of cheats and damage sponges.  The game pulls shenanigans like three back-to-back corridor fights against a boss with a hard counter against frontal assault, not to mention his regenerating entourage.  It just feels like punishment.The game also misuses its detective game mechanics; instead of having you find one thing in a room or choose one piece of evidence to reveal, on a number of occasions the game forces you to find all six elements of a parkour course in first-person before you can attempt it, or forces you to cycle through eight of the ten articles of evidence in your possession to have the plot re-explained to you so you can progress, but still laughs at you if you choose one of the remaining two equally irrelevant pieces of evidence.At one point, the game takes away your smartphone, and when combat starts you realize it really has, removing your character's ability to access your inventory, equipment, crafting, and settings menus.  That's not clever design, it's desperation.  To add insult to injury, pausing the game in this circumstance informs you, "You don't have a smartphone right now!" and upon unpausing, your character does a little pocket-patting dance that causes him to drop anything in his hands and become uncontrollable. Even considering all of this, there is still a fun game in Lost Judgment, but the one thing I really can't forgive is how often the game goes back to the well of snatching defeat from the jaws of victory -- on many, many occasions, you spend a ton of time and effort defeating a boss only for them to win anyway.  I understand that sometimes it is necessary to have an incomplete victory to progress the plot, but I mean, these are literal cases of the boss you just brought to zero health sucker punching you in a cutscene, and then utilizing that advantage to get one over on you, whether that means stealing a plot device, hurting you, or hurting someone you care about.  There are better ways to handle this.  I've played ten RGG games that handle it better.If the player wins, let them win.  If you can't afford to let the player win, don't let them fight.On a final point, I really enjoyed the high school framing of the major minigames and subplots, but choosing to organize it as an unlocking progress tree was a mistake.  You can still make progress on the side story if you are not good at the minigames, but man is it slow, and if you don't like one of the minigames, you're forced to do it over and over again anyway to get to the next one, which might also suck.The dance club rhythm game is fun.  Virtua Fighter 5 is Virtua Fighter 5.  The robotics club... 1990s edutainment... thing... is unthinkably terrible, in a game that also includes drone customization and real live third-person camera drone racing.Contrast Like a Dragon: Gaiden's Akame Network, which is there when you want it and completely unobtrusive otherwise.  I understand folks thinking that was too simplistic -- it probably was -- but I appreciated being able to do substories on my time and at my speed.A lot of development resources went into Seiryo High School, to the point that it is almost a third city destination, and I think I would have rathered a less anemic Kamurocho or Ijincho, both of which feel empty in comparison to earlier games.Bleh, I dunno.  It's fine, honestly; I was just led to expect better by this studio's track record.

_childDocuments_.review: Already having completed the game on PS4, I can say playing Lost Judgment on the PC offers pretty much superior experience, both in gameplay (60 FPS is NEEDED for this game's combat to truly shine) and graphical fidelity, you can even notice much more particles on the screen during combat power-ups compared to the past-gen version on PS4. In comparison to Judgment Remaster this game truly feels like a next-gen title and not just another "cross-gen" title to me.Only big problem as of now that "visual novel" scenes (there is a lot of these in this game) look very bad on "lower" resolutions as 1080p or when DLSS/FSR upscaling is enabled and I'm hoping for a fix.Music in Lost Judgment is of my favorite OSTs in whole Yakuza series, probably among the best RGG Studio ever done.Cons:Levelling up now feels too grindy compared to first game, good thing that combat is very enjoyable.Also it's got TOO MUCH side-content, it might be as well a plus to you if you have time and patience to complete it all. I felt some minigames like robot battles or motorcycle "bosozoku" racing game wasn't as enjoyable as other side-content in the game and they took a good chunk of my time compared to others on my first playtrough on PS4.I hope RGG Studio continues to make more great beat-em up games like Lost Judgment and not commit wholly to new JRPG direction they took, for me personally both Judgment games were way more enjoyable than Yakuza 7's clunky and slow turn-based combat.This is a must buy if you liked Yakuza games prior to Y7's genre change, Lost Judgment is Yakuza brawler combat at it's peak. But, I highly suggest playing the first game before jumping in LJ to get to know the main returning characters and their story. Without the first game, despite what marketing said at the release, it won't feel right and you probably wouldn't understand much of the references.8/10, the true GOTY 2021 in my eyes.Some technical issues still present on PC, unless you have a 3090 and can play at 4K with DLAA enabled to "fix" the jaggies in VN-style dialogues.
