_childDocuments_.review: After loving Judgment so much, I went into Lost Judgment with very high expectations. Yet, despite being, on a technical level, a more or less straight improvement on everything the previous game had, I couldn’t help but feel disinterested in most of its contents. Luckily, it’s still a very solid entry in the Like a Dragon series, at least mechanically. And it still has some good storytelling.Just like its direct predecessor, Lost Judgement is an attempt to slightly tweak the Like a Dragon formula of beat ’em up action adventure in an open world into something that feels more like an investigation game. It’s still clearly divided into the adventure and action elements, fights can still be challenging and combat with randomly spawning groups of enemies on the streets continues to play a big part. But the adventure parts have more detective-y things than the typical Like a Dragon game. And Lost Judgment improves on basically every mechanic from the previous game, while additionally introducing some new ones. For better and for worse.For example, detective Yagami still occasionally uses disguises and tails people, but tailing has been made far more freeform in the way it plays. I know some people disliked how the mechanic was overused in the original title, so the developers made it far more fun. Same goes for the chase sequences, how much more improved the sections of looking around in first person view are… You also get plenty new gadgets to play with in addition to the drone and even a dog that can be used to track smells. Oh and now we get stealth sequences too, which sound like something that fits the game perfectly… but mechanically they are some of the worst stealth segments I’ve played in the past 15 years, like they’re from the early 00s PS2 era of bad stealth titles. And unfortunately, the mechanical improvements that I’ve listed often feel pointless. There are barely any tailing tasks in the entire game, for example, despite the great improvements, but you still have skills you can unlock for this almost unused feature. The drone is now almost never used by Yagami himself, despite the fact that instead of introducing new gadgets (and a dog) it would’ve made far more sense to put all of those features into the drone and make it more interesting and integral to your arsenal. The Chatter that you used to talk to people all the time in the previous game is now used for 4 contacts in total, only one of them writes you often and you never have any choices or abilities to contact anyone yourself… You can now do the word filtering process yourself, though, which was just a cutscene thing in the previous game. And it’s an amazing concept, yet, more often than not it’s so automated it feels like it’s underutilized. Oh and disguises are still almost never needed and when they are, it doesn’t matter what you use.In general, Lost Judgment follows the same trend as a lot of Like a Dragon sequels in that it tries to do more of everything. You have more fighting styles, more locations, more mini-games, more skills, more stuff to do… And as it usually is with this approach, a lot of what made the previous game so great gets muddied and lost in the process. For example – the fantastic concept of Friends and getting to help the community from the first game, something that had a meaningful and awesome payoff in the end, is now entirely gone. Which ends up making the cities you explore almost irrelevant as locations. Apart from the school, all locations around Isezaki Ijincho (returning from Yakuza: Like a Dragon) and even Kamurocho have no meaningful interactions, form no emotional connections for the player. They’re just places to go to for stuff to happen. It doesn’t help that Isezaki Ijincho is a pretty plain location in itself, but if you didn’t play Yakuza: Like a Dragon previously, you’ll probably never remember anything about it apart from 3-4 landmark locations and even those barely. The school interactions are seemingly introduced to replace the whole emotional core of the side content, but they feel so disjointed and so completely unrelated to Yagami as a character, that it’s hard to understand what the developers were going for here. To the point, where most of Lost Judgement, as far as the storytelling, the mood, the characters and especially side content goes, feels like a collection of 5 separate game ideas that were combined into one game with Yagami filling in the role of many unrelated characters. And as a result not feeling like he belongs to most of the game. Even for the main story until the last third of the game apart from several key narrative beats, it’s like you’re playing as a Main Character of a Video Game here to do what plot requires, not Yagami and his friends.It does get better as far as the mood goes in the main story, but it still feels a bit too little, too late and somewhat bland at that. The topics that are brought up are impactful and there are good character moments and scenes. But again – it feels like this would’ve been better served as several unrelated games in Like a Dragon universe with separate focus and protagonists, rather than this one single title that ends up feeling shallow as a result. Because it cannot quite deliver on everything it opens up, while almost entirely losing all of the charm that the first game had.The story DLC Kaito Files feels, in many ways, like a far better take on what original Judgment established and follows a simpler, but still surprising short story, where players get to play as Kaito. It does feel as a DLC, as it’s far simpler in many ways to the main game, but it has enough content of its own to feel really fun, it tweaks mechanics in ways that feel great. And in some aspects it even “fixes” the problems that the main game created. Lost Judgment, despite being in many ways an improvement on the original game, is just so… disappointing. And, as I mentioned, it ends up feeling shallow and lacking a lot of the charm that the original game had. It has great moments, it is somewhat easier to play and even friendlier to newcomers than the original. And Kaito Files is a really cool short story. But I cannot recommend it to anyone who is not absolutely in love with the series and/or the first game. And even there, I feel like you might be disappointed as I was, depending on what you expect from a Judgment game. Of course, getting the title just for a DLC is also a silly idea, it’s not really worth it, unless you want to play the main game too. So, I can only hope the series do continue, but next time the game focuses on what made the first Judgement charming, wholesome, investigative and memorable in the first place, instead of trying to turn it into a jack of all trades. Unless, of course, we get to play as a different character who would fit that archetype.

_childDocuments_.review: Haven't finished the game but I don't think I'm jumping the gun in saying this is one of my absolute favorite RGG games I think I've ever played. On top of the electrifying combat and improved styles from the base game, this installment brings not one, but TWO (if you bought it with DLC like any normal person should) new styles that drastically switch up the gameplay in more ways than I can describe. This game's ludicrous amount of fighting styles is reminiscent of Yakuza 0, and it possesses the same versatility in combat with the added touch of Judgment's many trademark moves (the counterattacks are SOOOO AWESOME!!!). Maybe it's just that LAD left me craving the olden days of Yakuza combat, but this was certainly something I was missing for a long while. Years, probably.But there's more to love! And, surprisingly, it's the game's story! Having played through a total of 9 RGG titles with the same general setting, tone, and conspiracy plot, it's hard not to get a little disillusioned with every twist and turn they throw our way with every passing installment. I think the peak of my annoyance with the franchise's winding plots was Yakuza 4 (you all know what twist I mean), but the series gradually found ways to keep it fresh as it entered Ichiban's journey in Y7. Upon playing Judgment, a game lauded for its superior story to its sister franchise, I was a little unimpressed with its structure, finding it to have a pace comparable to that of a TV show, not a game. I went into Lost Judgment with lower expectations, considering how more people seemed to dislike this one's plot than the first. And yet, this game managed to blow those expectations away. A more focused narrative than the first, with every aspect of the main story mattering in uncovering a puzzle that's less concerned with the well-treaded ground of organized crime syndicates like the Yakuza, Jingweon, or Triads and more concerned with a simple, unifying topic: Bullying.It seems a little stupid, at first. Yagami and the gang solve bullying! But, oddly enough, this game takes no hard stances and throws no softballs dealing with the subject, as well as the nature of culpability, guilt, and (obviously) justice. In many ways, that makes this game's main idea seem more thematically relevant than its predecessor, with a complex issue in the case of right or wrong that can't be watered down to a simple conclusion. Characters on both sides of this debate are sympathetic, and don't (SPOILERS FOR JUDGMENT 1) have their character motivations chalked up to desiring power or fame in the final stretch of the story. Essentially, it's almost groundbreaking how mature this game handles its subject matter, especially considering how childish RGG can seem with some other installments and their quandaries of philosophy and morality.This game runs great on a LAPTOP too. What's not to love? I'll update my thoughts after finishing, but I have to say this is definitely up there.UPDATE: Yes. This is my favorite RGG game now. All-timer final boss. Legendary.

_childDocuments_.review: LOST JUDGMENT BEATS YAKUZA 0 GAMEPLAY.THE END OF THE REVIEW. BUY THE GAME.Haha... So anyway lets actually begin the review, though thats the biggest thing you need, other than dont worry, trailing missions were mostly removed, and actually made insanely better. They only appear like twice in the main story. However, stealth has now taken its place, but it only shows up like 3 or 4 times so, good job Lost Judgment.So, the biggest first thing to address are these new gimmicks, along with other things that made Judgment, Judgment.1. Investigation no longer is annoying and sucks. What did they change? Nothing. They just made it enjoyable by making it much more intuitve, unlike in Judgment, where you would be rubbing up against every wall and sliding your camera around annoyingly trying to find out what clue you are looking for, Lost Judgment one, makes this not happen every damn mission, and is much rarer, and ALSO always has direction in what you are looking for, this was just way better game design in its direction.2. Uncharted wall climb/parkour Yeah, Yakuza got it now. Welcome to Lost Judgment, its about what you expect but it can be slow when its not a swing or a wall run. I REALLY wish they did more with this.3. Lockpicking and the silly key ring thing was removed, and the trailing was made good, no longer having boxes to snap to you naturally in a very Assassins creed type way get behind any surface. VERY GOOD. Plus, you can now blend into the environement when under suspicion.4. Stealth. The new trailing missions of Judgment. They suck, seriously they are really dumb. Throw a coin to break away attention then stealth take down. OR THROW A SMOKE BOMB AT THEM. Problem being its super linear and basically forces you to throw it. It basically almost plays itself just you interact with it. Its SUPER BORING. though like I said, it happens like 3 or 4 times. It isnt plagued with it like traling was in Judgment. In fact, ALL THIS STUFF IS RARER IN LOST JUDGEMENT. VERY NICE!Lets cover stances, where Judgment in a way revived the concept after long wait since before DRAGON ENGINE, (0, K1)Now, we have them back, and 3 of them this time in Lost Judgment, as well as a 4th you can obtain called Boxer.Snake, and Boxer are two new stances. Snake is a defensive, quick, grapple style thats block parries enemies. Its smooth as butter and my favorite stance in the entire series. Boxer, similar to Rush from K1 and 0, but no grab and its all boxer rules. Its over powered because when upgraded allows you to basically make the enemy die for even daring to try to hurt you, its dodges and counters are absolutely insane. These two stances are the best in the series honestly, with how powerful they are, they are VERY VERY FUN.THIS IS PEAK COMBAT FOR THE YAKUZA SERIES, EVEN CRANE AND TIGER FEEL BETTER HERE.The side missons are amazing, and not just the files you get in Judgment. Since the story has links to a highschool, you get a lot of interaction with school clubs and school mysteries now that Yagami works part time there. These are super good and some of the deepest side quests EVER in the series. Some argue to feel like they could be main game. Another think I love is that Judgment had the audacity to do forced filler, which Lost Judgment got rid of. Beautiful once more Lost Judgment. You also are given tools like a listening tool, and a detection tool to locate situations in the world, this grows into all kinds of secrets and side content, on top of all of them the best "tool" or goodest boy.Beyond the point of  you can take him for walks, he will detect trouble afoot, and bring you to some more new mysteries. Its actually incredible how you seemingly investigate some side content, not just "take a case" or "run into an event." I LOOOOVE THIS CONCEPT! KEEP DOING THIS RYU GA GOTOKU ITS SOOO GOOD!There is also a skate board you are given to travel around, its basically the first vehicle in the series, its super fun even if a little jank, and I found it great for moments of getting somewhere that would be much necessary for a taxi, or just zooming around faster or EVEN doing tricks which were fun. there are even coins to collect that are all around as you ride around that can be grabbed for rewards.The only other thing I can pick at is that the skill tree still isn't as good as past games. Seriously, can we also please stop hiding EX's in the skill tree Ryu Ga Gotoku? It makes the game ooze less coolness when everyone will want to go for meta or abilities that make the game more fun, give more power, strategy, or abilities. Keep all of the EX moves open from the start.This game is an ABSOLUTELY STELLAR GAME IN THE SERIES, MY GOD.The only down side? Somewhat the story....Its REALLY good, don't get me wrong, but it feels like it under delivered compared to Judgment a little. Ill never forget Judgments finally and all its segments to get there. (Especially the ♥♥♥♥ ton of annoying investigation, and trailing missions...)Overall, Lost Judgment OOZES with perfection in every field, I still loved the story, even if it was a bit of a mess in my opinion, it undershot Judgment. 9.7/10 - Lost Judgment, is my third favorite in the series. I have found it to grow to be special to me, its the best combat the series has ever had, its what Yakuza 6 wanted to be, with the quality of Yakuza 0. It is the master class dream, its only downside being a story that could have been better. Beyond this, the game is nearly in most departments the peak of the series, absolutely do not miss Lost Judgment. If you didn't like Judgment, try this game still. Judgment, you stick around for the story among the annoyances in design with good combat. For Lost Judgment, you stick around for it all. The best combat of the series, (beating K1 and 0 which I think is the peak.) Insanely deep side content, a lot of mini games, and things to do and experience, drone racing is even back on top of all this new stuff! School cases and clubs, the two cities, the 4 stances, vehicle... dog.... WOW. It may not be perfect, it may not be the best in every angle. Though, I believe the Lost Judgment, is nearly the greatest in every department, and in a good amount THE BEST.DO NOT MISS LOST JUDGMENT, BUY THIS FRICKEN GAME! THERE IS THE FIRST DLC EVER ON TOP OF THIS YOU CAN PLAY A KAITO JUST GET THE GAME, PLAY AS KAITO, AND WALK TO DOG!

_childDocuments_.review: The new style, Snake, is very good for being defensive. The parry functions pretty much exactly like Tanimura's of Yakuza 4, even including being able to parry people into walls (although this being the Dragon Engine, they will ragdoll and most you might get to do is an EX Action). The original two styles, Crane and Tiger, have also been rebalanced in new ways and you're expected to use all three styles to get through the game.There is now a system similar to Yakuza 0's where doing as many different actions as possible will get you more bonus SP on top of the base SP you get for finishing a fight.If you intend on using cheat items in order to clear the gambling tasks for TownGO, it would be wise to wait until at least the latter half of the game so that you get more SP from fights and therefore get an easier time of buying them in the first place.Keep in mind that certain things are only available at certain times of day, such as the school's shop and cafeteria not being open during nighttime. This doesn't come up all that often, but it's still something to be aware of.There is no more Mortal Damage like there was in Judgment, but getting hit by a Mortal attack will still hurt a lot and may leave you open for a follow-up, so try not to let that happen anyway.In the case of school story triggers, sometimes they are gated by progress in the main plot or other school stories, sometimes by stats. The School Diary app will inform you of what you need.Lots of side cases are hidden behind things like girlfriends and collectables in this one if you ever wonder why so many are ??? foreverFor an easy Robotics Club time check the parts list against practise battle rewards and farm accordinglySpeaking of robotics club, the quickest way to win is to beeline for the enemy base; if you can plant a blue block that has at least one square within the enemy's base, you win immediately, it's much faster than trying to actually do the territory control game.

_childDocuments_.review: My goal in every Yakuza game, and I've played all of them (mostly on PS4, and except for Dead Souls) as of right now, is to fight the secret boss Amon. This game's Amon fight was more funny than he was difficult. He is not the easiest Amon fight, that honor goes to Ishin, but I did beat him in the Gauntlet on my first try. Also, lately, I've been playing on hard mode.Speaking of, I think the gauntlet in this game is my favorite it's ever been throughout the series and I don't say that lightly. It was adequately challenging and fun without leaving me thinking "oh please, you shouldn't have" at the prospect of the "challenge" it presented. For example, in Yakuza 4, one "challenge" was to beat someone without hitting them with Tanimura, so you needed to put your back to a wall, parry them into the wall so they take damage and spend the next 5 minutes repeating that bored bored bored bored bored until you win. This was as stupid and as boring as it sounds. Also, the difficulty in the gauntlet seems to be averaged for "normal" difficulty, so playing on hard mode made the gauntlet easier to complete even with the constraints.As for the combat, massive improvements from Judgement. In Judgement, Crane was kinda there. All the upgrades were for Tiger and Tiger did tons of damage and did enough of a job to dominate the entire game. Amon in Judgement was supposed to remind me that Crane exists with his gimmick but I beat him without it anyway because Crane is... just kinda there. So what does Lost Judgement do? It adds a third combat style and boy howdy how did they do it, I don't know but now we got an amazing balance where each fighting style specializes in something different. It reminds me of Yakuza 0 and it is great all for it. Also, the SP system, which is perhaps the best it has ever been, rewards you for varying your fighting style. Note: it's a shame that the fourth fighting style does NOT have any unique SP awards so I ended up disabling it until late game (which is also fitting as upgrading it requires you do a side-quest thing). Sure, it was a DLC thing (that comes with the base purchase of this game, I don't own the Kaito Files DLC but I still had it) but come on! Put some SP awards for it!Late game, I ran around fighting random dudes on the street for around 3,000 SP per fight (around 1,400 from SP gained via the reward system and 1,600 SP for winning the fight. It is incredibly easy and not very grindy to get all skills before you beat the game. Though, if you taxi all over town instead of running around town, then you're probably not the target audience for this game, and also you will feel the grind to get all the skills.Sure, each style has its unique attacks, finishers, tiger drops, heat actions, and even dodging, but in my opinion, one of the biggest accomplishments is the "secret" of each style. Dodging with Crane increases movement speed while parrying with Snake prevents you from being knocked down (from attacks) and landing a charged finisher (has to be charged despite the game not specifying, I checked) with Tiger increases your damage. All these effects are temporary and until you get an upgrade for each style, they go away if you style switch. When you unlocked these skills to keep the style switch, not only do you get to keep it, but activating the "secret" on another style resets the timer for the secret(s) from the previous style(s) so if you play well, you can be a faster-attacking, stronger-hitting and un-knock-down-able Yagami that tears through the enemies. Boxing style has this too where if you land a counter hit (like Tiger drop, which I think is a mistake because you may as well Tiger drop late game), the secret ability is your EX gain is increased (more counters = even faster charging). Even with all this, Tiger is still obscenely strong, so the strongest thing you can do is get crane and snake secrets, swap to tiger, EX Boost and just go ham. My personal favorite is two squares into fully charged triangle attacks. Also, they got rid of the "strong hits break max HP" gimmick from Judgement, that good too. If I have a complaint, it would be why do we swap between the styles with one button instead of using the full D-Pad like in Yakuza 0? Shortcut? I'm aware but I'd delete the thing while delegating the healing to the pause menu, like it has always been and everyone continues to do, and just let us enjoy Y0's style swapping. Someone made a mod for that please and thank you.While the combat is the center, take a look aside for the side stuff... which I had finished the lion's share of all the side stuff by chapter 4. Every possible thing I could do at that point, I did until it was completed or locked. This is how I enjoy these games and make sure I fight Amon. Arriving to the start of the final chapter, I only had one last side quest to do and Amon. Overall, the humor I like is when funny things happen to characters and they play along. Something that I really do not like it is when these characters, that we've learned about and grown to like, suddenly start acting as if there's a gas leak in the room. Thankfully, the instance where this does happen is fairly brief and works as a contrast to how heavy the plot gets when you first access this side quest, so I'll let it slide.With characters mentioned, Yagami is better fleshed out compared to how he was in Judgement. Then again, I used to be a teacher so putting him in that context and not screwing up went a long way to making me like him. Still... I'm quite mehhhhhhh on him but what I did early on was mod Mine (read: Mi-Ne, not "mine") from Yakuza 3 via Nexus to replace Yagami and that somehow made me enjoy the game quite a lot more. The only flaw with the mod occurs in Chapter 7 but not in any meaningful way. Also, no "in school shoes" texture of sorts, so invisible feet when in school... which is funny but not impactful.Trying to avoid any spoilers (except for Amon), I'll just say that the other characters also have their time in the spotlight adequately that I overall enjoyed the story. Watching them play rock paper scissors while the credits rolled was amusing.Finally, the extract system... It's there and I seldom remember its existence. I imagine it would've made any particular combat section a cake walk, based on the effects I read; like "get the ability to shoot energy balls" or "get a thunder sword that you can use to smite your foes" or whatever; and also the "DLC" that automatically comes with the game gives you a sample to use (a free one for most of them) but still... I never really used them. Even in the gauntlets, I only used one where it is *required* to win. Overall, amazing entry by RGG that I recommend. I sure hope they don't only make turn-based combat games now and I also hope they never use the Unreal Engine like Ishin. Cheers.

_childDocuments_.review: The combat is undoubtedly one of the best RGGS has to offer, but as fan of yakuza/judgment stories which IMO is still so much more important I have to say Lost Judgment's story is the absolute weakest I've experienced so far. Whereas in the first game Judgment it was incredibly interesting to learn about the "fallen" lawyer Yagami, his backstory and motivation, and experience his character growth, the sequel offers nowhere near as much character development time: Yagami stays the same from beginning to the end, his character story incredibly bland, frustratingly boring to watch.There are some major moments, where the game could have used them to make him more interesting, but no, after some tiny emotional outbursts or occasional brain fogs he returns back to the same old calm, wise character.The school setting of the main story is refreshing, the horrible problems of school bullying are handled well (shout out to Sawa-Sensei) but it just doesn't help when the protagonist remains so bland for the majority of the game.So what about the other returning characters? I liked... Kaito and Shirosaki, I guess, but what about the rest?You could delete Sugiura and replace his tiny parts with Kaito, absolutely nothing of value would be lost.Tsukumo aka "Hackerman", the typical boring plot device, to make some occasional discoveries.Hoshino? Laughable, I don't even want to talk about him.What they did to Genda hurt me, I liked the old mentor in judgment who never gave up on Yagami, influencing his character growth. Here? Nearly invisible. Mafuyu, fan favorite, the same treatment.Lost Judgment massacred so many cool characters from the first game, that I wonder if the writers were suffering from burnouts or were just simply replaced by worse ones.Oh, and don't get me started with the antagonists.There are so many repetitive, redundant moments in the story where Yagami and one of the main antagonists meet up, bicker about their motives, over and over again. Maybe trying to overcompensate for the lack of depths of the other antagonists?So what about the side stories?Oh boy. Ignoring the disgusting fact that SEGA or RGGS hid some of the better ones behind locked DLCs, the majority of the stories are a boring mess. I just finished the game, and for the love of God, I seriously can't remember most of them (besides the school side stuff) because how utterly bland they were.I liked the mystery club, boxing, and some others, one of the highlights of the side stories. But when you compare them to the rest, it's just... sad. Ryu Ga Gotoku can do so much better, they showed it over and over again.But maybe they should take a step back, and invest more time?

_childDocuments_.review: Summary:Better more fluid and faster combat compared to most game made by RGG studios, but the game suffers from too much of a focus on quantity instead of quality, with a story that has terrible pacing and an unsatisfying ending.Upgrading skills:1. Too big and drawn out, forcing you to grind a lot to become stronger and to unlock quality of life features.Combat problems:1. Getting stunned and knocked to the ground takes the player to gain control.2. Grabbing an enemy while they're attacking makes it so your grab goes through them. A problem that happened in Yakuza 3 and Yakuza 4.3. Hitboxes of enemies sometimes would hit you from far away, even hitting you when you're behind them.4. Badly balanced fighting styles, with Crane being very overpowered, Tiger being pretty good, Snake being alright and Boxing being pretty bad.5. They literally locked a fighting style (Boxing) behind a DLC.Characters:1. Yagami felt more of a stereotypical detective thant an actual character with depth to him like in Judgment.2. Most of the characters too me felt too uninteresting and bland.3. They ramble on for too long before finally mentioning information relevant to the story. They also love to bring back past events from the same game or from Judgment multiple times.Story:1. Too much expository dialogue.2. Pacing was too slow, a lot of the interesting parts of the story where just spoon fed to you via dialogue making the whole waiting unrewarding.3. The main mystery of the story was too obvious.4. A lot of the reveals revolve around someone giving you paragraphs of them admitting to the truth, while not showing you what happened through the use of cutscenes or flashbacks.5. Plot and conflict drags on for too long.6. Constantly being forced to go from point A to point B to progress the story and substories. A lot of the time it just revolves around talking to someone in person instead of through the phone, just to be forced to travel to another location again.Sub stories:1. Too serious and it has less of that iconic silly humor.Mechanics from Judgment:1. They brought back those unfun and extremely tedious mechanics, like lockpicking, chase, trailing missions, finding clues in first person (Revolves around moving your camera around until you spot something), parkour (Where it sends you back to the beginning EVERY time you fall, and it's very difficult to not accidentally fall off) and sneaking where the AI is either too stupid and slow, or they can spot you while having their backs to you.Robotics:1. It's just a rat race to on who can connect and place their blocks on the opponent's territory first.2. Being forced to grind to obtain materials that can only be obtained by specific levels from the robotics minigame.3. A lot of unskippable cutscenes. Building ONE part? unskippable cutscene. Starting the same level for the 10th+ time to obtain materials? unskippable cutscene.4. It mostly revolves around building your way as fast as you can into the opponent's territory, which get stale after doing the same thing more than 20 times.5. Near the end you start running out of funds to upgrade since it only gives you 30k yen every 5 games, which forces you to play the same levesl over and over just so you can finally upgrade after also grinding to obtain the materials.6. In the final fight, the game forces you to use a robot that is inferior to the ones you can build at that point of the game.7. Whenever you're tackled by a fortress robot you literally can't do anything until it stops pushing you.Dancing:1. More difficult thant Haruka's dance mini game in Yakuza 5, but has less depth and less fun overall.Boxing:1. Locks moves from a DLC fighting style behind it's tedious progress system.2. Annoying stamina system that constantly slows down the fights or makes it very difficult to win unless you grind the same opponents over and over.Mini-games:1. Even though there's a lot of minigames, most of them barely have any substance, it's more about quantity instead of quality.School stories mini-games:1. To unlock more you have to play the horrible ones like Robotics and Boxing.2. The game constantly interrupts your progress by forcing you go from point A to point B and back to talk to some random person.3. You also get interrupted because of the game forcing you to level up a specific stat from the "Yagami's leadership" stat pool which also forces you to play minigames you don't care about to be able to progress the ones you want.4. Dating:1. The dating aspect of the game has improved a little bit, but it's still very bland and it's now locked behind a pay wall (DLC), which is pretty greedy in my opinion since it was free in other games like Judgment and Like a Dragon.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, RGG, you've done it. You've actually developed a game to surpass my favourite game of all time, and that was also by you, in the form of Yakuza 0.Lost Judgment is the long-awaited sequel to Judgment, two games that I and probably many others thought would never see on Steam. But here they are and damn are they worth the wait. As good as Judgment is, it is a rough-around-the-edges mess with a good story and (in my opinion) an even better story hidden within in the form of School Stories. What do I mean by rough-around-the-edges? A lot of new 'features' from Judgment that makes the story borderline annoying to play through. Tailing missions have improved for the better in theory, allowing you to blend in at any time when your target looks back at you, and you can finally take cover anywhere. However, it is still tedious. Other new features include what I would call basic platform jumping and climbing segments, where you have a stamina meter. Oh, and the stealth missions, which I normally suck at and hate, but the game holds your hand a little too much, forcing you to take cover at certain areas and even where to throw distractions. All these half-baked ideas are mashed together and somehow... work? I can't really explain it, but every moment you have to do these is somehow understandable as to why and never feel like an uneccesary chore.Combat is, well, like an RGG game that isn't Like a Dragon 7. And there are three battle styles (+1 through dlc) and each feel fantastic, with the kind of crunch you expect from an RGG game. Absolutely terrific.As for the story, this is probably the best one I've played through. Despite an early warning that it would involve suicide and bullying, two things that went through my head in my teens, turning me off to the story  from the start, I was eventually drawn in to the intrigue and plot twists, and my favourite antagonist to date. Trust me, I won't spoil anything because the main story is great.The best part however, is the School Stories, as you investigate shenanigans involving the high school in Ijincho. Each part unlocks different minigames, and events, as well as a well-written if a bit sappy story.And now, the negatives, and none of them relate to the game itself.- Denuvo. Just because I play games with that piece of anticonsumer garbage in them doesn't mean I like it. And I will ALWAYS call out SEGA as long as they continue putting this garbage in their games.- DLC. Yes the master race gets all bar the Kaito Files with the base game, but it's still ridiculous that items that make minigames pathetically easy as well as locking THREE OF THE FOUR girlfriends behind a paywall for PS4/5 versions is insulting. And if you think PC's getting away with it remember that Ishin is coming out at the same time as consoles. It's coming.- Price. Come on SEGA, no way both games should cost over $100 SGD. And making the Kaito Files 'free' when it definitely isn't worth forty bucks with the bundle is still stupid.Still though, I absolutely recommend Lost Judgment. I enjoyed every minute of it and will continue to enjoy it a lot more.Like a Dragon/10

_childDocuments_.review: I bought a PS4 just to play the Judgment games, and I was not disappointed whatsoever.Purely cause of this one.The story is one of the best in the Yakuza series (Even though it's a spin off) purely cause it's grounded and tackles a problem that relates to many common folk.The combat is also the absolute best in the entire series.There are 3 styles in total (4 with a DLC, but that seems to be automatically given when you buy the game)Each of which are extremely useful in almost every situation (Compared to Judgment where Crane becomes obsolete halfway through the game).Crane: centered towards evasion and crowd control, but it's speed allows it to even be useful against bosses.Tiger: all about damage and heavy hitting strikes, nuff said.Snake: Perfect for when you're surrounded or up against enemies with weapons, useful against bosses as well.Boxer: The "DLC" style, think of it as a fleshed out far more unique and far more fun Rush style that Kiryu had.All of these are always usable from the very start till the credits roll and combined with juggling and fast style switching allows you to pull off stylish combos and decimate foes.It's clear that RGG saw what was popular and what was despised in Judgment, and decided to fix everything and all that was popular was doped up on enough cocaine to even make your average Miami citizen overdose.Here's hoping RGG implement this amount of options in combat and uniqueness in their other games that follow the usual real time combat. And here's hoping Like A Dragon 8 turn based combat follows in the footsteps of the Judgment series, 7 being the seed, and 8 being grown to such a degree that even people that don't like such combat in games are able to like it.

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve always had a middling opinion of the Judgment spin-offs. The combat is definitely nice, but some of their ideas show some flaws of the real time action combat. Characters & story are good, but Yagami is definitely my least favorite RGG protagonist to date. Side activities & “detective” gameplay are indeed different, but often feel half-baked like a prototype version of a better system they didn’t finish. I’ve always seen it instead as a small experimental space for RGG to test their newer ideas that perhaps may not have gelled with the Yakuza template, rather than a truly realized distinct series of games.With LJ, I honestly didn’t expect much, but I can safely say that depending on your opinion of the first game, . That being said, I still don't think this series holds a candle to the Yakuza series right now, especially in light of those games’ being rebooted with a new main cast and turn-based gameplay. Those games embellish their wackiness and seriousness, while the Judgment games still feel like an iteration off for the type of game they’re still trying to become, still aping the best parts of a Yakuza game with little significant additions of its own. I do hope they continue to improve things, but I definitely want that sooner rather than later.LJ has 3 main improvements: - I definitely found the overall plot more compelling here than the original. Maybe not better structured and definitely not paced as smoothly, but I felt this story had a bit more nuance to themes of self-determined justice and the Japanese legal system going for it, raising it up. However, I can’t say the same for the characters. Yagami and his crew felt more like punching mouthpieces than … characters, with flaws and personality. Just a lot of moralizing lectures and finger wagging that wore me down in some of the many dialogue blocks. I just can’t say I prefer these characters to any RGG protag I’ve gotten to play before: they just don’t have enough compelling depth for me to care. - The combat is definitely improved, and at its best, it really gets you into a “flow” state. Whipping crowds with Crane, pounding bosses with Tiger, jumping in and out with Snake to disarm and counter power attacks, it works very well. The terrible mortal wounds mechanic is gone, and countering boss moves are a bit more consistent to pull off. My only issue is they REALLY lay on the enemies by the end, almost soft-locking me into having to repeat large swathes of areas, which just became more tiresome than fun sometimes. (LAD Gaiden kinda repeated this as well) - They have definitely taken  feedback with the detective gameplay and side activities. Tailing is almost non-existent for the main plot, and even then, is improved. The school stories feel more appropriately distinct from Yakuza’s side activities, even if mechanically similar. However, the new parkour and stealth systems are just half-baked. I never felt challenged or even engaged by them, they were just hurdles to get over. Same thing with observation and interrogations, they just don’t have me engaged in the same way Ace Attorney or L.A. Noire had me, also narrative based stories about detectives. It’s serviceable, but not enough to sell this game’s identity in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: What. A. Game. Where the previous Judgement game (JUDGE EYES) is THE Yagami's case, this game is more of ONE of Yagami cases. The story in this game introduces a lot of moral grey areas, and the oversights of the law. Where the previous game is a victory lap to finish what's been started, this game is a grim, dark, and quiet affair. The "villain" of the story is insanely well-crafted and can be deeply empathised with. At the end of the game, I was sitting back in my chair going ".....dude this is so f*cked up man...". If you've been bullied before, this game will hit you. HARD.The beat-em-up combat system in this game is the BEST out of ALL the Ryu Ga Gotoku studios games, period (and I've played them all). It's not even a contest. The different stances all complement each other, encouraging a lot of stance switching during combat. The heat moves are rewarding, flashy, and effective. Combat upgrades feel impactful, and actually upgrades gameplay. The upgrade points (SP) are given generously, but not too much to be considered "OP". The boss fights are seriously really well made. I haven't had this much fun in boss battles since Yakuza Kiwami 1. I played on Hard difficulty and was sweating so damn much in the final few boss fight scenes, but they feel very rewarding.The sheer number of new mechanics and mini-games introduced in this game is also downright ridiculous. They expanded on the detective aspect of this game a LOT, and also the number of fun minigames are GREATLY increased. In the previous games, the extent of being a detective was quite limited. Tailing missions were done so much it kind of got boring. However, this game actually makes you feel like a PROPER detective. There's parkour, noise amplifiers, radio waves reader, using a dog to sniff out scents, etc. Some minigames they introduced are dancing (not the Yakuza 5 one, this one is better by a long shot), boxing, skateboarding, photography, and so so so many more I can't even name them. This game seriously feels like a damn theme park, I can't play them all!Finally, the new characters in this game is very well done and well fleshed out. At first, some side characters rubbed me the wrong way, but character development kicked me in the heart, and I love them all. One very minor gripe is that I don't see one of the characters more , I wish they could've expanded a little more on him. Hopefully we get to see him in the next Judgement game. I haven't played the Kaito Files DLC yet, but I've heard good things about it and I'm planning to play it soon. Overall, while the plot is slightly weaker compared to the previous game (but still great overall), the other aspects of the game are 10/10. Highly recommend this game with or without a sale.

You will find yourself never have to grab a weapon from the ground because Yagami can handle everything with his bare hands.In Lost Judgment, Ryu ga Gotoku studio replaced the side cases with school club management. You get to meet various students from clubs help them break through their struggles. It portrays a humane, friendly little society in a cruel world.There are a lot of minigames in Lost Judgment compared to the predecessor. Most of them are fun to play, except the bike racing minigame.Lost Judgment is probably one of the best games that Ryu ga Gotoku studio ever made. _childDocuments_.review: ◘ Before getting into either game I heard that Lost Judgment was just a strict upgrade to the first game. So, going into LJ, my expectations were really high. And while I can't say the game met those expectations, it wasn't bad by any stretch.◘ A lot of people herald it as having the best combat in the series, but my core gripe with that statement is the difficulty. Yes, the combat is deep, and cool, and flashy, and Yagami has a lot of tools to play with and it's very skill expressive. There's nothing in the game that can stand up to getting the Crane Hidden Art attack speed, and just spamming Tiger charged attacks, or going into Boxer EX Boost. Every enemy in the game except Amon just folds in the face of Yagami's most basic combat options, let alone the laundry list of more obscure mechanics he has as you delve deeper into the combat. Judgment on Legend was WAY harder T_T than Lost Judgment on the same difficulty. And to me, that's a huge disappointment.◘ In terms of the story, I struggle to articulate exactly how I'd compare the two, but at current the way I'll put it is something to the tune of; Judgment's story is more "solid", generally being higher quality from start to finish and being a great crime thriller, while Lost Judgment's story is more emotional, more compelling, and has a better villain/core ideological struggle. I wouldn't definitively say one is better than the other.One of my bigger gripes with Lost Judgment outside of the combat is the side content. Some of the side content is really, really good, like the Boxing☻ and Biking questlines (good but get to repetitive IMO). And some of it is really, really ♥♥♥♥, like how 10 of the game's 42 Substories are devoted to the completely ♥♥♥♥ "Dastardly Detective" plotline. Actually deplorable that so many Substory slots are taken up by that. I haven't gone back and reviewed all of them to properly form a final opinion, but currently I think the Substory content in the game is very poor, while the School Story content ranged from excellent to okay-ish, depending on the club.◘ Overall for me this game is solid 7/10 (+1 because they added dating girl from the Judment series (♥_♥) )

_childDocuments_.review: I like to think this game is like the Yakuza 5 of the Judgment games. It might not have 5 characters or 5 cities, but the sheer amount of fantastic content in this game packed on top of one of the best stories in across all the Ryu Ga Gotoku games makes me wholeheartedly say that this is the RGG's best game they've put out to date. I sung the praises of Judgment in my review of that, but Lost Judgment blows that out of the water somehow.For starters, without any spoilers, the story. It's fantastic. If you liked Judgment you'll get more of the same in this. You have your usual detective work as Yagami Detective Agency working in tandem with Genda Law Office once more with another intricate plot that slowly gives you more pieces to the puzzle, finally letting you put it together in the end. At times it can feel like it's being too complex for the sake of dramatic effect, but it usually quickly pulled away from those moments by giving you a big piece of the puzzle after all that exposition.The gameplay/combat is the best in the series bar none. The 3 (or 4 depending on your decisions) fighting styles complement each other so well. Although for reasons I won't say, snake was the clear-cut winner for me for a multitude of reasons. Having a skateboard to traverse around Ijincho and Kamurocho was a great addition, albeit kinda finicky with how you'd hop off it if you passed over a pedestrian area for more than a second. I do hope they'll keep it and open up more traversal options in future entries, like being able to do the parkour climbing freely instead of only in instances when it was required by the story/side missions.As for the actual side content itself, that is where this game shines in ways the other games have failed to, or at least haven't done to this standard. As expected from the previous entry, Drone Races are still here and are more or less unchanged, but have a new set of maps for Ijincho. I was disappointed that I couldn't access the Kamurocho maps in this game, but that's a minor gripe at best. As for the rest of the content present in this game, you have a dance club (this game's karaoke like rhythm mode), A skateboard freestyle competition and races, motorcycle races, a very well fleshed out boxing mode (I think it's the best side content in any of the games so far), robot territory claiming battles, and of course all the returning city activities like darts, batting cages, shogi, blackjack and poker, the arcades, golf, and probably a few other one's I'm forgetting to mention.In conclusion, play this game if you've ever mildly enjoyed a RGG game. And even if you haven't do yourself a favor and give this game an opportunity.  I truly think this is a 10/10 game, and I'll never get over the fact that this game didn't win game of the year for 2021

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best games from the Yakuza franchise, and from the ARPG/Beat'em up genre as a whole.Ryu Ga Gotoku studio has refined the Dragon Engine combat to its peak, dare I say this is the best combat any game in the franchise has ever had. 4 different styles you are free to mix to make you own combos, add moves that let you interact with your environment, equippable weapons and a ton of Ex actions and you are set for a game in which you will seek every opportunity to fight random thugs just for the sake of combat.In addition, there's a lot of side content, not only through side cases, but the School Stories as well, in which each minigame relates to a bigger storyline and makes the experience more enjoyable. You also have your usual shenanigans inherited from Judgment, such as: drone racing, VR games, etc.Finally, the story is really good. Some people talk it down because it's not as high stakes as Judgment's, which is true, but that doesn't make it any less exciting or slow paced. In fact, the last piece of the plot may as well be the strongest and most intense in the series. Sum up memorable characters and you find yourself with a very solid game. Also, the soundtrack is phenomenal as well (I.E. from the OST: "Final Destination", or "Unwavering Belief").Lost Judgment is one of a kind, and proof of what RGG Studios can do in the future. The true successor to Shenmue.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is easily the peak of Yakuza's beat em up combat system. The amount of options, air juggles, ground combos and wallbounce/bound combos are insane not to mention just the sheer amount of moves there are to use. This game takes the gameplay of the Yakuza series is known for and transforms it into something even better which is saying a lot because I've played and loved every game in the series outside of Isshin (Due to there being no english sub). Story is also very good, presentation is up there with Like a Dragon and Yakuza 0 in terms of direction, characters and writing. On top of that it has a lot more of the goofy charm the Yakuza series is known for, the first Judgment game (which is also very much worth a playthrough) took itself slightly more seriously than the rest of the series but this game goes back to and fully embraces the goofy, wackiness of the mainline Yakuza series.Side content in this one is super fleshed out and has some of the best presentation in the entire series, this game doesnt really have minigames so much as entirely fleshed out game modes. Theres skateboard competitions, Biker gang races where the goal is to knock the opponents gang off their bikes, and entire Fight Night style boxing game mode that genuinely fun and has some depth to it and thats just the tip of the iceburg when it comes to fun side stuff.I actually have to give this game my seal as favourite game in the Yakuza franchise, it has the same if not slightly higher level of presentation, writing, characters and story as the other best games in the franchise (Yakuza 0, Like a Dragon and Kiwami 2) but it beats those other entries out with its incredibly deep combat system and genuinely well presented and consistently fun side content.

It's far less interesting than what we got in Judgment. But it still has great characters, a hallmark of RGG. I liked  in particular as a villain. Really creepy with a cool soundtrack for your fights with him. There were some other standout music pieces here (love the Snake Style battle music); RGG has really stepped it up in that department in their recent games!My biggest complaint is that this game feels bloated in a bad way. RGG games give you a lot to do if you wish, but here a lot of it feels like a slog. Most of that slog comes from the School Stories. Ugh. They tried to do too many mini games at once; RGG should have cut out half of that "content".Completionists will feel discouraged by trying to do too much in the beginning at once, like I did. Even without the side stuff, this game starts too slowly. I was thinking this might be the first Yakuza franchise game I give a negative review... But RGG's charm shines through so that I can still recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: This is, with no doubt, one of the best games Ryu Ga Gotoku Studios has made, even if it is just a spin off of the Yakuza/Like A Dragon series and a sequel.The story, the characters, the mini-games (specifically the school stories) and the subcases are all phenomenal, one could say it does them all better than the last game. With or without modding the game, it's just really really fun. It's flashy, it's fast, it's brutal, and it's the best it has ever been. _childDocuments_.review: What makes a Yakuza game a Yakuza game?To me, it's three things: the heart-wrenching story, the silly mini-games, and the general sense of hopefulness and goodness in humanity. This game has it all and even more.Yakuza's main story has always have had serious tones, and this game is no different. The main theme of the game is bullying and how the law fails to protect and save the people it is designed to do so. You will feel despair, you will feel happiness, Yakuza games have never been shy from killing off both one-shot villains and characters that are important to the protagonist's growth.  Yakuza has always have had "good endings" for most of its side stories (you can also make the case that most main stories also have a good ending). This is what I mean by "a general sense of hopefulness and goodness in humanity," in that the side stories make you feel good and hopeful, if not often laugh out loud at the silliness of it. I like a good story and if the story calls for a sad ending, I understand if that is the logical conclusion for that story, but at the end of the day we play games to escape reality, and isn't it better to escape into a reality that makes us feel happy?The best thing this game did right are the School Stories: they have a satisfying conclusion that ties in all the individual steps made in-between, and they allow to live through that high-school experience one more time; for many folks, high school was the best time of their lives so I can see the appeal. I thought the advisor mechanism is a pretty smart story framing device in this respect.  Talking about finishing all sub-School Stories, the Robotics Club sub-story is extremely unbalanced; you will want a guide in order to finish it. Essentially, the strategy I went with was to ignore everything else and went straight for putting a block into opponent's home base. I got lucky with the final battle and finished it in only one try; for some of the previous battles, I had to try multiple times and got extremely angry when my own robots would block my path (I learnt to work around it), or when the opponents simply kept destroying my robot so I couldn't anything. Generally, when the game design takes the agency out of your hand due to RNG, it's not very fun.The Boxing Club sub-story is a blast. It is challenging but not unbalanced (like the Robotics Club), and I don't think you can cheese this very much. There is no difficulty level in this sub-story, unlike the Dance Club sub-story that replaces the dancing mini-games Yakuza games are famous for. If you're not good with rhythm games, you will still be able to make progress.

_childDocuments_.review: As a huge Yakuza/RGG Studio fan, I have to say that I don't really understand the hype behind Lost Judgment. I think it is way over-praised and sends a message that harms the first Judgment and other RGG games.Don't get me wrong, it's still an amazing game, however I don't think it's the best thing ever or think it's better than the previous Judgment. The places where I think Lost Judgment lacks is with the Story and Yagami.I personally don't like Yagami in this game both story-wise and gameplay-wise. Now this may be just me but I don’t like the change of two fighting styles to four. With the first Judgment you’d most likely use Tiger most of the time and that did not change with Lost Judgment for me. The other fighting styles don’t seem to serve a meaningful purpose with how I was playing.For Yagami in the story, I don’t really understand Yagami’s reasons for many things and feel like many points of the story do not make sense or are underserved. It’s easy to say “He is doing x because of y, in the name of justice”, but even then epic fights or emotional moments are only half impactful if there’s no meaning behind a scene. So with that, I just started to dislike Yagami and how he impacts the story.For the story as a whole, I just don’t think it fits an RGG Studio action game in my opinion. If you just want to have fun and don’t want to invest too much thought into this game then you will enjoy it, but as somebody who wants to be sucked into a story, this game did not do that. I’d say this game has three main plots that tie together and I like two of them but the one that the game invests the most in both screen time and action. That’s why before I said many things are undeserved. I was thinking “why does x character get all this attention and the undoubtedly two best themes in the entire series?” and also “why does y need to happen?”. I’m personally mad about the themes I just mentioned being tied to an undeserving character. I always imagine what if they were used for somebody else. The amount of lost emotion is too much and once again is undeserving and makes no sense to me both story-wise and gameplay-wise.For the most part, I just think there’s less ‘detective’ and building characters and more ‘we need to move the story forward’, that might be the easiest way of explaining this.For content outside of the story, I think this game has the most in any RGG game. I personally haven’t seen most of it but I’ve seen enough screenshots and gameplay clips of places I’ve never seen before to tell me you really need to spend time in this game world to get the most out of it. This game doesn’t add filler to the story to introduce all the side content. It also took me until the Finale of the story to realize I can enable the DLC fourth fighting style in the options menu, because I had no idea how to access it through the side content it is linked to.I first played this game without DLC on PS4 before it came to PC. I only focused on the story because I didn’t like the poor console performance. I bought this game on Steam in 2024 after finally waiting for the prices to be worth a second purchase and its expansion.In my PC playthrough I admit I could not stand playing as Yagami again, so after a few chapters I installed some mods to play as Kiryu with his styles and many outfits. That will annoy some fanboys of this game but Kiryu’s styles really work well in this game’s engine. This may ironically be the best Kiryu game in terms of gameplay lol. Normally I wouldn’t outright change a character like this but I was so uninvested with a second playthrough, I thought why not…I won’t write a review for the expansion but that was so much more fun than the main game in my opinion. It’s overpriced in terms of the hours you get so wait for a good sale to get it.I recommend this game just so you can experience it, but if I could I would give this game a 'mixed' review.

_childDocuments_.review: Before I dive into why I gave this a negative review, I'd like to point out that this is my replay of the game. I played it first when it launched in 2021 and actually finished it in one sitting (17 hours) and I wasn't a fan of it then. When the game finally released on PC I thought to myself let's give it another shot and see how I feel. Once again, I felt the same but let me make it clear, there's only one reason I disliked LJ and that is it's writing.Judgment (LJ's predecessor) was a masterpiece in it's writing, combat, incredible environments and movie-like cinematics. Pretty much just like any Yakuza/RGG game you've played. LJ on the other hand felt like such a huge downgrade in terms of it's writing and story. _childDocuments_.review: If you liked Like a Dragon you'll like this game. Probably.There are a ton of similarities between the two games and that makes sense given that it's the same genre, studio, locations, etc. However, there are quite a few differences, and they're not always positive. So let's start with those.Let me start by saying that in RGG games especially, connecting to the protagonist is important. In Like a Dragon you had Ichiban; a loveable goofball with a loud suit and a botched haircut that he eventually embraces (you can't change it in the game, ever). In other Yakuzas you had Kiryu; a stoic dreamer honor bound and allergic to smiling.Yagami is somewhere in the middle. The boring, weird, stupid middle. He's a middle-aged man wearing teen idol fashion (skinny jeans, wallet chain) with a haircut that looks like a feathered bird's nest. His personality is bland and predictable; a generic good guy with few defining characteristics or interesting idiosyncrasies. I've never given less of a ♥♥♥♥, basically. I don't care if he lives or dies, as long as I get my SP points so I can punch dudes harder. That's not a very immersive experience. I feel like I'm being forced to go on a really cool road trip with an excessively boring person going through a midlife crisis.Now let's talk about one of the game's main features; the detection. Detecting? Detectiving? Anyways.When you're "investigating" a scene you're just zoomed in a bit, and you move the cursor around until a button prompt and audio cue from Yagami ("oh!" "interesting!" etc) occurs. You hit the button and you receive more information on that object. Eventually you get a notification that you've found all the things and the investigation is complete.When speaking to someone, you can question them, and/or choose multiple prompts. Usually the player's choice doesn't matter; you just go through all of the options until the dialogue is exhausted. When it does matter, it still doesn't because choosing the wrong option whether presenting evidence or asking a question just leads to "yeah maybe I shouldn't have chosen that" and then you try again. No consequences. No branching dialogue. The game just mocks your decision a little and you try one of the other few options.You also have a handful of gadgets. One is a long range listening device that you use exactly the same way you investigate a scene but now you're looking for a sound source instead of evidence. Another is a device that finds signals coming from things like electronic bugs so you follow a beeping sound and why am I still talking about this. You also slowly and tediously tail suspects, wait for the right shot with your camera, and do other things I also don't care to get into.If anything, the detecting just cripples the fun. The world is explosive, combat is violent, and the activities are an ADHD wonderland (or nightmare). But when you throw in a "walk behind this suspect for 10 minutes" moment that happens quite often, it impedes the pacing and makes you want to just get it over with. When you're pixel hunting for a stupid hot spot or shambling through a parking lot listening for beeps it feels like someone ripped the controller out of your hand and replaced it with a book.And that's the end of the negatives. The cosmetics are subjective, and yeah I can be picky about my protagonist so take that with a grain of salt. As someone that plays protagonists as an extension of themselves (versus the puppet master mentality) I can't even play games like Ni No Kuni because I can't play as a 13 year old boy voiced by a 33 year old woman. I tried. It was weird.The detective stuff might bring you some immersion or maybe it was simply mandatory to include those mechanics to really drive home the whole "I'm literally a detective" thing, but I don't know why they couldn't just leave it to the writers to make you feel like one without mini games who were (spoiler alert) the real killer all along.Moving on.The combat is solid. It's polished, predictable Yakuza combat with beautifully garish visuals, absurd animations, and flawless sound design. There's enough diversity between combat styles, moves, and stat boosts to keep you chasing upgrades and experimenting in fights. There's an incremental reward system for doing specific things in a fight which can yield more skill points too, so mixing things up and making things weird is rewarded.The graphics are the Dragon Engine so obviously they're gorgeous. Environments are detailed, the lighting makes the city feel real and alive, and character models are detailed down to sewing patterns in their clothing and/or a subtle blemish on their cheek. But more importantly than any of that you can actually DISABLE AA so the game looks crisp, unlike the extremely popular forced TAA turning sharp, vibrant experiences into vaseline smeared fever dreams. I'm looking at you, Cyberpunk. And Playstation ports. Like, basically all of them.The writing is... something. Something pretty good, most of the time. I mean, I know there's a cultural divide here, and things literally get lost in translation but the game's tone and writing constantly fluctuates between melodramatic soap and cringe-comedy for kids. Sometimes swearing is done very well in games and it conveys a real emotion or emphasizes a point with elegance and tact. And sometimes it's just a bunch of bad words thrown together at random in rapid succession by an uncensored Speak & Spell in the hands of a 12 year old with a learning disability. Lost Judgement does that a lot. Like, a lot. Like too much.The main murder case is engaging and interesting with some unexpected twists and turns depending on whether or not you knew Bruce Willis was dead the whole time in that one movie with a young Keenan Feldspar.  It's not groundbreaking, but it's pretty damn good.Minigames and side activities including side stories (quests) are varied and mostly entertaining. Some are intentionally shallow and goofy while others have real depth and strategy. There's a VR board game, fully functional Sega Master System, Battle Bot simulator, Boxing, Drone Racing, and all the other things that already exist in most Yakuza games.Aside from that, the game is absolutely a recommend from someone that beat Like a Dragon three times but I'm told it doesn't count if you're just bored and drunk so take it from someone that beat Like a Dragon just one time this game will scratch the itch if you're reading reviews because you need that Yakuza itch scratched. The combat and RPG elements alone will keep you addicted, but maybe you'll stick around for the story. And maybe, just maybe, you'll find the detective mechanics kinda cool just kidding seriously they're terrible.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start this review off by saying I loved the first Judgment, and I had extremely high expectations going into Lost Judgment. It definitely didn't disappoint and excels at every aspect.Firstly, the story and characters. The story in Judgment was extremely interesting, revolving around government conspiracies and medical trials. Lost Judgment definitely does not disappoint in that aspect, and revolves around the murders of former high school bullies. The best part about Lost Judgment is that, as the tagline says, nothing is black and white. Every character in the story has understandable motivations and goals, and no one is just evil for the sake of being evil. In addition to the story, you have the main cast of characters. Most of which return from the previous game. All of the main cast have amazing chemistry and they're all likable, (or hateable for some of the villains) at some points making you feel like you're a part of Yagami Detective Agency/Yokohama 99. Secondly, the setting and side content. The first Judgment was set exclusively in Kamurocho, the city which has been a part of the Yakuza series since its debut on the PS2 in 2005. That's not inherently a bad thing, however, but it definitely made the game feel a bit stale if you played through it after playing through Yakuza games where you've explored the ins and outs of Kamurocho already. Lost Judgment expands this to Isezaki Ijincho, Yokohama, which was introduced in Yakuza: Like a Dragon. Ijincho is roughly three times the size of Kamurocho, which gives more opportunities for interesting side cases story beats. Speaking of side cases, the side content in this game is insane. Not only do you have the side cases (or substories as they're referred to in Yakuza) and regular minigames we're used to in the Yakuza/Judgment series, you also have the school stories, which are a set of brand new minigames each with their own storyline attached to them, with an overarching story relating to the Mystery Research Club. Finally, the combat. I'll start off by saying Lost Judgment has the best combat seen in the Yakuza/Judgment series ever. I can't begin to describe how fluid and fun everything feels but it's definitely the best. Lost Judgment includes 3 main fighting styles, Crane, Tiger, and Snake, with a fourth boxing style which can be progressed through one of the school stories. Crane and Tiger return from Judgment, and they feel so much better in this game. In Judgment, the only upgradable style was Tiger, with any upgrades that weren't explicitly for Tiger applying to both styles. In Lost Judgment each style has its own skill tree and pros and cons for each situation. While you can just use one style for the whole game, the game encourages you to switch it up, with the Hidden Arts buffs and SP bonuses. The Hidden Arts buffs essentially encourage you to use every style in your battle, as they give you specific benefits when you perform specific actions in a style. For example, if you successfully evade your enemy's attack while in Crane style, and have a fully upgraded Hidden Arts skill, you can boost your attack speed for 12 seconds. This might not sound like a huge improvement, but if you switch styles and activate the Hidden Arts for that style, it resets that timer, plus giving you an extra buff. This is extremely helpful, especially in boss fights, and encourages you to switch up your playstyle. Also included are SP bonuses, which return from Yakuza 0, which were money bonuses. They essentially work the same way as they did in that game, giving you SP for performing specific actions in a battle, one of which being to defeat an enemy in each of the three styles, so to level up faster, you'll need to incorporate all 3 main styles into your playstyle.Overall, Lost Judgment is without a doubt my favourite game in the Like a Dragon series, and I encourage anyone who is on the fence to check it out, as it is an amazing experience throughout the whole game.

_childDocuments_.review: I have always suggested the Judgement series to everyone, but I always get a bit sad how not everyone has access to them due to them being PS exclusive at the time. Now that they're finally on PC, the long-awaited dream of me suggesting this game to literally everyone has finally come. I have accumulated over 150+ hours on both Judgement(2 playthroughs) and Lost Judgement(4 playthroughs) on the PS5 in just 2 months of getting them, and now another playthrough of LJ on PC! I can never say this enough, but the gameplay and story of both games are simply fantastic. Not to mention the super stylish moves you can pull off(and of course juggling lol).A few complaints I do have for the PC port are that pre-rendered cutscenes are locked at 30 FPS and playing anything above 60 FPS will make certain things janky/weird. An example of that would be the Snake Style parry. It works normally on 60 FPS, but starts being weird at 120 (however still playable). Another issue that has plagued other Dragon Engine games would be how charged finishers(Tiger Style and maybe Snake Style specifically for LJ) would freeze the character in place if played at an uncapped framerate. So if you're having that problem, I suggest limiting your framerate to 120. Those issues aside, amazing game and story-writing. All around lovable and very well-written characters. Would definitely recommend to everyone and especially to people who enjoy stylish brawler combat set in the RGG world.
