_childDocuments_.review: First: Don't mind my low playtime, I've played this game basically every single day since it came out a year and change ago on my Xbox One.Second: I'm going to be using the Japanese names for the fighting styles in this review: Waltz is Crane, Flash is Tiger, and Flow is Snake.Now with that out of the way, the actual review: It's about ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ time. Lost Judgment is the best work RGG Studio has produced in a long time (and, given that Ichiban remains the main protagonist of Yakuza and Kiryu returning for Yakuza 8, that "long time" is starting to look an awful lot like "ever".) The music is top notch, likewise the fight choreography. The combat is the best in the studio's entire catalog. The writing is top-notch, bucking long-standing RGG trends that I'd always found insufferable. The minigames are fun with the high school they're linked to being about as fun as you can get a high school to be and an equally fun narrative surrounding its students. Lost Judgment is a complete package that's earned my 2021 GOTY spot and, thanks to both this Steam release and the Kaitou Files expansion releasing earlier this year, has very handily usurped Sifu and Midnight Fight Express for my 2022 GOTY. But... why? Why do I hold it in such high regard? Let's get into that!First of all: Yagami. This isn't his first outing, but it is the first I've been able to join him on and I love the guy; his dynamic with his buddies (whether it's the original crew from Judge Eyes or newcomer Kyouko Amasawa) is wildly enjoyable. Whether he's cheering up a bullied child and encouraging her not to give up on her dreams or being repeatedly thrown for a loop by Amasawa's, well, loopiness, Yagami's interactions are always a blast. He has the "Just Some Guy" charm of Kiryu-era Yakuza bosses down pat. His fighting styles are all graceful and well-designed with additions like vaulting and wall-jumping to shake up the combat and his choreography benefits greatly from the fact that Yagami has to actually avoid and defend against attacks.However, the biggest reason I like Yagami so much is that for once in their career, RGG Studio have managed to create a protagonist that isn't patently insufferable. Kazuma Kiryu  quickly establishes himself as a sanctimonious hypocrite who prefers to run away from his problems until someone close to him gets hurt or killed and is wholly uninterested in committing to his platitudes about confronting the past and who he is, while Ichiban Kasuga is essentially the Japanese Wade Watts: a loser with no personality beyond "lol video game references xD!" who drags the entire game down into Satan's wine cellar and whose status as hero and protagonist is facilitated purely by the creators violating the narrative to jack him off at every opportunity.Yagami, on the other hand, has  His ideals are consistent and he has no qualms with committing to them; joined Seiryo High's Mystery Research Club as guidance counselor so he can investigate the main case freely? He will gladly see that job to completion. Strongly disagrees with the main villain on the nature of the law? He will just as lief throw hands for his ideals.Likewise, while he's certainly more relaxed than Kiryu, he's not childish like Ichiban: He'll kill time at the arcade or on the Mega Drive he's got at his office, but when he's kidnapped and strapped to a chair the man with the chainsaw who's about to vivisect him doesn't abruptly transform into some lol so random xd enemy design with a terrible pun for a name. When one of his coworkers has their house besieged by gangsters, the building doesn't abruptly turn into a dungeon with turnbased enemy encounters because "OMG DAE it's just like Dragon Quest!!!1!1!"Next up, combat: With RGG Studio deciding that LAD's braindead ungabunga which number biggest "combat" is going to be the future of Yakuza, it's up to Lost Judgment to continue the tradition of beat 'em up combat that is very easy to learn and hard to master, and it does so with gusto. But, not content to simply reiterate on what Kiryu had or what Judge Eyes gave Yagami, Lost Judgment decides to take that combat and make it  so. Both Yakuza and Judge Eyes have always had had light RPG and fighting game elements, but they've always been just that--light. Lost Judgment leans much more heavily on both by introducing status effects and allowing you to cancel attacks outside of super mode and the results are . Juggling enemies is incredibly satisfying, and status effects are balanced just right to spice up the gameplay while keeping it intrinsic.Additionally, the fighting styles themselves are a blast: Waltz, your crowd-control style, is loaded with graceful kicks and sweeping multi-hit attacks that make it as effective against a single enemy as against a crowd. Flash, the dedicated "strike first, strike hard, no mercy" single-target style has elements of bajiquan and a hold-to-charge mechanic that succeeds at making you feel the oomph of the charged attacks, while also providing you with a potent counter in the form of the franchise's mainstay Tiger Drop. Flow, the new style introduced with LJ that focuses on defensive prowess and throwing enemies, has a parry mechanic and strong options against armed enemies, as well as drawing very heavy inspiration from Wing Chun.Boss battles are also some of the best in the franchise because they're where everything comes together, backed by some stellar boss design; a recurring boss in the game has a number of the same options Yagami does, bringing his fights as close to Yakuza PvP as we're likely ever gonna get. However, there's also some other neat tricks: Mortal Reversals, and QTE design.Judge Eyes' controversial Deadly Attacks return here, but they don't lock your health bar anymore and dodging out of the way and hitting 3 (B/Circle for you non-Tekken folks) at the right time performs a Mortal Reversal which does a massive amount of damage to the boss. On top of this, LJ breaks away from RGG's single-input QTE design to occasionally introduce multi-step QTEs often designed to evoke actions you can perform in gameplay that resemble what Yagami does if you succeed.And then there's the writing. Lost Judgment has what I consider to be the best writing of any game RGG has released so far. With the Tojo and Omi disbanded as part of LAD's campaign to make its protagonist as special as possible, LJ doesn't have the benefit of established lore; it has to build everything from scratch and it does so  The game moves with surprising speed given how much work it has to do in comparison to its predecessors, and the antagonist factions it introduces leverage that atrocious decision excellently. The mystery in the game is legitimately compelling, and the game's climax is one of the best I've ever seen; it gets the "TV legal thriller J-drama" thing it's going for absolutely DOWN, and that makes it all the more badass when Yagami clinches a court case in the coolest manner imaginable. The high schoolers and their stories are all intriguing and do an excellent job of getting you  more invested than you probably should be. The antagonists are absolute gigachads who break two of RGG's main molds: One is a genuinely morally gray antagonist who has just as much of a point as the protagonist and manages to break the pattern of RGG villains getting capped literally the second they show anything that vaguely looks like doubt and the other is an unapologetic villain who has zero interest in redemption and stays evil until the end--and, much like Lost Judgment as a whole, they are very much a breath of fresh air.In conclusion: Absolutely buy this game. It's RGG's best work yet and its mere presence on Steam alongside Judge Eyes is a good sign that there's more Yagami in our future--and I'll drink to that.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is set in the Yakuza franchise, but it is more or less a soft reboot. There are slight callbacks to earlier games in the franchise, but you don't need to have played all the Yakuza games or even the first Judgment to enjoy and understand Lost Judgment.Lost Judgment is, not in particular contrast to other Yakuza games, a beat em up, but this time with detective elements such as tailing and observation to pick out as evidence later on.-Excellent soundtrack. It feels modern and fitting to the game's period.-Graphics. The Dragon engine looks good, even if combat physics might leave a bit to be desired. However, performance might be an issue even on lower settings due to how demanding the game is.-Recycled as Kamurocho may be, it is still well updated.-New bigger city to roam around in. However, at times it might feel empty or less alive than Kamurocho. Still refreshing, especially having played through all mainline Yakuza games.-Combat is refreshingly done and felt nice, especially after the heavier combat of the earlier games. Way faster and encourages style-switch comboing.-The story is actually relatable, yet still manages to even at times feel like well-written horror.-Characters in the story feel like real characters. A clear antagonist who is obviously a sociopath and almost clearly in the wrong, can still feel like he has ground to stand on to justify his actions and as if he has a heart, haunted by his past who still owns up to his mistakes.>Two characters simply talking to eachother in a room could never have been better.-Availability and amount of side content.-May be a bit long-winded if you're not feeling patient. The game takes its' time with introductions to side content.-The detective-spot portions want you to spot everything. Boring and annoying.-Difficulty spikes at random. Some enemies do ridiculous damage - more damage than the level's actual boss.-Unlike previous Yakuza games, dying twice and lowering difficulty is  for your savefile.-Clichés and tropes as with previous Yakuza games.-At times plain unrealistic, taking leaps of faith (and logic) for the story to proceed as planned. I was purposefully picking the wrong, outlandish or otherwise stupid options in the "present your evidence" sections, and I accidentally picked the correct option. It's... a strange twist, to say the least.-AI allies, which you actually have in this game as opposed to every Yakuza game, are downright useless.Hand-to-hand combat based with detective aspects. Leveling system grants points per mobs killed / bosses beaten. However, you get barely anything unless you farm mobs or otherwise grind harder stuff for skill points.Very power-consuming and can make your computer a space heater if tuned too high. Far more realistic graphics with more detailing.Animations or poses can be clunky, though.One of the best I've heard in a game.It is grandstanding, but it succeeds at it.The game's main villain has, at first, a dark synth-esque fight track that lets you know there's something more lurking underneath, and the finale track for him is... something you should play the game for.Bosses in general have fitting tracks. A knife psycho has a track with Psycho (1960) callbacks and an elegant piano to fit his personality. A scrappy brawn-based boss has a suiting electronic track to go along with a Scarface-like personality and upbringing.Lost Judgment is a wonderful game and an excellent step away from the heavy-to-fill shoes of Yakuza's earlier protagonists. Despite it's story and gameplay shortcomings, it remains a very enjoyable experience you'll want to see through to the end and to see it's contributions to important societal questions as much as be able to do ridiculous heat actions on random Kamurocho inhabitants.

_childDocuments_.review: On replaying, Lost Judgment's story smashed a lot of my pre-conceptions from its release a year ago. Unfortunately the rest of it is as I remember. The side content and especially the music is a step down from the original,School Stories are very hit and miss and some take a while to open up, and they overshadow side cases/substories as the main side arcs on offer. But on the other hand again, it's the best iteration of combat in the entire series so far. Unlike in Yakuza 0 and Kiwami, the different styles actually have some overlap which means they aren't completely disjointed. Tiger and Snake to respectively take on singular or clusters of enemies is a much better and more practical idea than two balanced, a light but weak and a strong but heavy style. LJ also actively rewards you for switching up styles during encounters, and with the increased style switch speed and new Snake style for counter-offensive plays it makes for good fast-paced fun. Unfortunately the style themes are ungodly bland even without the comparison to JE's, but the rest of the soundtrack is about on par.The game takes place primarily in Ijincho and under the shadow of (Yakuza 7) , which is unfortunate given the game was announced with the promise that Yakuza and Judgment would be parallel. Instead, LJ has to pick apart the pieces Yakuza left behind while Yokoyama grasps at the bottom of the barrel for any excuse to quell his separation anxiety for Kazuma Kiryu and actually have the guts to say to the world "there was no way around him appearing in Yakuza 8. Honest." RGGS shot themselves in the feet with the Ijincho map; it's a confused map that's comprised of samples of districts and offers nothing of value. It's so big and lifeless and I guess they felt the need to justify the time and effort that went into making it by reusing it and... not actually improving it. In LJ you get a skateboard for quicker traversal, which would be great if either map were actually designed around this. Instead it's only really viable in a few long stretches of road in Ijincho,  Yagami doesn't decide to just get off the board whenever he feels like.Speaking of maps, Kamurocho returns but like in Yakuza 7, it's really only a formality. So little actually takes place in Kamurocho in this game that it may as well have been gutted, with taxi fares from Ijincho just directly taking you to Genda Law Office, given that it's the one place in Kamurocho you visit the most. Without Don Quijote, and given that many of the elements unique to Judgment like Paradise VR and Iyama's hermit den suspiciously all migrate to Ijincho, Yagami Detective Agency may as well up and move there already. RGGS are trying to move forward while desperately clinging onto the past and the end result is a sad Kamurocho with relatively nothing to do, in back to back games.The story is pretty interesting. It starts off very disjointed though, back and forth between sexual harassment and groping, and... high school bullying. Once it starts to tie itself together it does so nicely, and I lament all the pre-release reviews complaining about the perfectly fine handling of its sensitive content just  they're sensitive topics. I recall the story being far messier, but in actuality it wasn't as bad as I remembered. It's still messy in places, but I still enjoyed it more than any main series Yakuza stories.Overall, it does things better, and it does things worse compared to its predecessor. It's relatively a solid entry though (when are RGGS games not messy and rushed?) and one I also prefer to anything in the main series. It says a lot that Furuta can still write a good story even while running damage control for Yokoyama's main series stunts. If he had written LJ, the reason behind that video would be  As someone speaking out of love for Yakuza (believe it or not) but also with an ability to call out the low points of the series without any rose tints, it honestly baffles, and worries, me about RGGS' future output with him in charge. I can only pray that future Judgment titles remain in Furuta's hands and continue to have as little to do with Yokoyama as possible.

_childDocuments_.review: Lost Judgement : the sequel to one of the best games in the series, how would it go?If you look on the internet, you'll be kinda surprise to see it's pretty much mixed bag. Some would praise it to the point of being "better" than Judgement while some would criticize it to the point of being "boring" compared to Judgement.So what causing these reactions?Simple answer? Theme/settings and stretching too thin in other aspects.Judgement focuses a lot on law and justice side. It's the game that influenced by other games in the same genre like LA Noire or Ace Attorney. The story centered around the protagonist, Yagami, who was a defense attorney switched to detective due to his first and last defendant. So it's pretty much more "personal" story. His ups and downs. That's why it's regarded as one of the best from RGG studios.While Lost Judgement tells a story of Yagami 3 years later (cmiiw), he got asked to come to Ijincho to help his colleagues doing some works that some how evolved into something deep and darker. While his previous legal firm in Kamurocho is tasked to defend another defendant which at first is just another case of sexual battery but turns out to become another case of homicide which later connect to another deep darker story that connect to what Yagami is doing. So you can see this is much less "personal" to Yagami but as the story progress you'll find yourself into the gray zone of "justice".GameplayMuch improved from the previous installment.You got 2 more battle styles, Snake and boxing. Personally, I think Snake is a "counter" style while Boxing is similar to Kiryu's Rush in 0 and Kiwami but pretty underdeveloped even in premium adventure that you don't constrain with times and money.Improved QOL by simpler mobile apps and you can call taxi from anywhere (twice the price, though). Buzzword system is more refined.2 more gadgets to use/play around with : Eavesdropper and bug detector. However, I think both are pretty much too underdeveloped. I think I used the eavesdropper like once or twice. While there's a line of side quests for bug detector.Stretching too thin? Underdeveloped?I think this is pretty much the cons of this game.I know they want to make the game that has a lot of content to do and play that they missed in the first installment by a lot. I mean there's only very few things to do in postgame for Judgement.This is probably due to the issues with actor's agency themselves so they don't want to go all out.So they did in LJ and it shows.I clocked at 40hrs as I finished the main story and the school story, haven't touch Kaito Files yet.I think for the school story while it's intriguing to engage and complete the story, I think they don't have time or resources (or both) to make it, thus the later half of school story is pretty underdeveloped. They're too short compared to the another half like I'm certain that I dropped like 20 hrs into the first half and probably less than 5 into another.Plus, the first half that I spent 20 hrs on are way too different in difficulty. You can look that up in the guide section.Some are easy like dancing club (basically Karaoke but dancing).Some are hard, either by the gameplay (skateboard gang) or money (girl's bar. It's a school story, trust me) you have to sink in, or both (robotics, bike gang and boxing).Some are short (photo club and esport) and some are ridiculously short (gambling).I already mentioned the fighting styles. Boxing is one of them you can improve by playing through the school story as there's a boxing club.The problem here is it's back to Yakuza 0 where you have to pay money to learn more skill AND use skill points to learn it. Some skills are entirely limited to the boxing minigames and didn't carry through the fighting style but you have to learn it as it's pretty much impossible to complete the club's story if you don't put anything in it.I don't say it's a bad style (it's probably one of my main style to play in premium adventure) but it needs too much investment.So basically they tried to stretch it to have more and more content for players but probably too thin and some got neglected.Detective works are pushed to the second row. While you still have to investigate from here and there, I think there are less than 10 times you have to do that in the main story and some of them is just to find the way/route to go/climb.It's not like the first one that you're too close to become Wright from AA.So overall?The story isn't that bad. I understand that many people probably doesn't give two f about school bullying (the core theme of the game) but it's a big issue for us in Asia and we don't have a proper way to solve this yet. This game revolves around this theme.They toned down the legal and investigating but you still have to connect the dot from time to time (remember "present evidence" system?).While the story feels a bit rushed and plot devices are used here and there, I think it captured the whole thing about this issues, especially in Japan where it is still one of the worst.And you probably doubt yourself if you have done the "correct" thing at the end of the game.If you ask me? I think I'm on the opposite side of Yagami on this issue.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic sequel to Judgment. This story includes all your favorite characters from Judgment (Yagami, Kaito, Higashi, Saori, and many more) while also adding great characters to the cast in Kuwana and Soma. Being able to explore Ijincho alongside Kamurocho was a great addition. 50+ side cases, 10 school substories, and a dramatic main story involving murder and bullying make for a very thorough and intriguing game. Plenty of RGG mini games as well. The Kaito Files DLC is great too. Short but good story and fun to play as Kaito.OST is top tier as well. Brings in a lot of the best tracks from Judgment, but adds so many original scores. Yagami vs Kuwana warehouse fight song is cracked. Now we wait for the third installment in the Judgment series!

_childDocuments_.review: 7 hours in and thats enough for me. The story is hard to follow and real tedious, the fighting is ok but after all the Yakuza Games and the Judgment it's nothing new, even the mini games are losing their charm. Then theres the lack of voice acting in everything but the main story, I mean come on, How many of these games does the developer have to make before finally making a fully voiced one?. If I wanted to read a load of text I would buy a Kindle!. My opinion is that this style of game is getting stale and the developer needs to do something new rather than coming up with new stories to put with rehashed assets and calling it a new game.

_childDocuments_.review: Lost Judgment improves on almost every aspect from its previous entry. The combat and music are the best in the LAD/Judgment series by a fair margin. The side content was also massively improved upon by way of the school stories, which introduced great characters, such as Amasawa and Itokura, and awesome minigames like dancing, boxing, skateboarding, and robotics (yes, i actually liked that one). The main story was very strong as well, albeit I slightly prefer Judge Eyes's story. Lastly, there were a couple of quality of life improvements, but none bigger than cutting the number of tailing missions way down which makes the experience much better. I almost forgot to mention the Kaito Files DLC which is great in its own right. All in all, it's easily one of the best games RGG has released.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: Overall a really solid entry in the series. Story drags a bit towards the end but features some very well written characters.Gameplay wise it's mostly upgraded compared to Judgment, a lot less following random people around which I'm pretty happy about. The parkour and stealth mechanics feel a bit forced but I don't mind it that much since it's not too frequent. I won't comment too much on the combat system because I'm pretty bad at it but I think it's good enough.The story is also intriguing. I think it dragged a little bit here and there, and some arguments between characters feel like they are repeating themselves way too much. If I'm being honest I think the previous game had a better story arc. However, I think the villains / antagonists in this one are very well established, probably the best in the entire series imo. Definitely a must-buy if you're a fan of RGG games.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the strongest RGG stories for sure. Really liked the school setting. Liked the characters and drama as well. Even liked the professor sub plot. The bullying and revenge plot line felt personal to me and even helped me to deal with some of my own past encounters. If you’re here for a good main story and some light detective gameplay, it’s a really good game. Some of the gameplay mechanics were improved over it’s predecessor, but others dumbed down like the chasing, which feels just unsatisfying. Some of the school cases can be a major pain. They are often way too long and too repetitive and also come with terrible controls. It’s not impossible to power through them, but it can be rather frustrating at times. RGG Studios are very bad when it comes to vehicle controls. They have proven time and time again that they just can’t get them right, yet they will keep coming up with new ones that are even worse.I recommend the core story as it comes with mostly no flaws, but beware of the side and school cases.

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic title from the Ryu Ga Gotoku. The sequel to Judgment is just as entertaining and fascinating as the first, and if you love Yakuza games, this is another one to add to your collection. As in the Yakuza games, the main protagonist is Takayuki Yagami, a former lawyer turned freelance detective who now finds himself in another job assignment that goes far deeper than he first thought and brings him closer to some people in the government than he suspected. The game encourages and rewards exploration, and while it is not an entirely open world, there is enough exploration in the city and beyond to keep you entertained. Along the way, you can do side missions for clients or help people in the City, as well as play a few side games ranging from Dancing, Boxing, and Drone Racing  The school stories are a lot of fun, with interesting stories and characters, and I've found myself paying more attention to them than the main story, which isn't to say the main story is bad. The main plot is amazing. Once again, I found myself emotionally attached to the characters and eager to find out what happens next. There are parts that are shocking and parts that make me laugh. Overall, it's a Masterpiece game.===== 2nd RUN on Legend Difficulty =====I just wanted to let people know that the Legend difficulty now has full access to the checkpoints that other difficulties get, so you don't have to reload your save if you die or fail a section. The game is fairly easy if you play it on Normal Difficultly, thus I quite like this change. NO more Tiger Style Ex/ Crane Style EX and smashing the Y button on your controller. I'm focused on the main story on this run so I understand better what's happening there are parts that I get more and still mind-blown by the twist in the parts of some chapters, well gonna say it's still one of the best stories in single-player games that I play. Still a Masterpiece for me. 10/10 I wish to see more Judgment Sequels in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Damn, this is probably the best RGG game I’ve ever played.This game is much better in every category compared to its predecessor. The only thing that it’s a bit lacking is the side cases, but considering you have the school side stories, it’s understandable that they didn’t put much work into the side cases.Regarding the main story, I enjoyed it more than the Judgement one, I don’t know why people clown on it. Overall I recommend this game to everyone, even if you haven’t played Judgement or even other RGG games.

_childDocuments_.review: I finally got around to playing this game, and let me tell you, it’s seriously great, despite it’s issues. Let’s start with its biggest strength : The combat. Lost Judgment has by far the best combat in any Yakuza game. Yes, it’s better than Yakuza 5. Having 4 different combat styles with fast switching, wall bounding and juggling is a dream come true : You have so many options to approach enemies and bosses that the combat never gets boring even against regular street enemies, especially if you play on hard difficulty with Lv0 attack upgrades. Another excellent addition are the Hidden arts buffs, especially the crane one that boosts attack speed. And speaking of attack speed, now it’s always at max level. Thanks god. Grabs being nerfed to PS3 Yakuza level is pretty much the only complaint i have with the combat in this game. Kaito files also has good combat, even if it’s more limited with only 2 fighting styles, with quite a lot of moves being recycled from Kiryu’s brawler and beast styles. Another thing that Lost Judgment greatly improved upon is exploration. You can explore Ijincho from Yakuza 7 and Kamurocho, but you can now use a skateboard (even in battle!) which makes everything so much faster and more fluid.The amount of side content in Lost Judgment is staggering compared to previous entries : There is an insane amount of new and returning minigames, and most of them are pretty good. My favourite minifgames are Biker Gang, Boxing, that allows you to unlock new abilities for the boxing fighting styles and Skating. Drone racing also returns, now in Ijincho.The soundtrack is pretty good, but not as good as Judgment. Some standout tracks are Hydra, Fog, Tough Cuss, Vorarephilia, Viper, Lazy Daisy, Dig In Your Heels, Final Destination and Unwavering Belief. But like, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, Unwavering belief gotta be one of the best final boss themes in the entire series.The story is also pretty good, but doesn’t quite reach the same heights of the best ones in the series like Judgment, Yakuza 0, Yakuza 6 and Yakuza 7.=====STORY SPOILERS AHEAD=========END OF STORY SPOILERS=====However, Lost Judgement ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up one really important thing : The long battles. They just suck in this game (except for the final one which is really good.). They are forgettable, too easy, too short and slow paced. For some reason they decided to replace a lot of sections with parkour or stealth section, and i’m not against them, but they have been used way too much and poorly. Each time you defeat a pack of enemies, for some reason the victory animation plays, ruining the pacing. They also don’t have any cool QTEs or action quickscenes like in older games, which makes them even worse. I sure hope they won’t suck this bad in Judgment 3 (if it ever happens).Overall, Lost Judgment is in my opinion one of the best Yakuza games ever made and the best or second best dragon engine game, with the best gameplay in the entire series by a long shot. You have to play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Right from the get-go, you can tell you're in for one heck of a ride. The story's as solid as a concrete bunker, and they've thrown in school stories that'll make you feel like you're back in your high school drama days – minus the acne, of course. You'll be hooked for days, thanks to more side quests than you can shake a stick at.Now, let's talk about our main man, Yagami. This dude's got more personality switches than a light bulb factory. Sometimes he's channeling Batman, all dark and broody, and then, out of nowhere, he's as Zen as Buddha under the Bodhi tree. I mean, seriously, at times, it feels like as if he's on the verge of imparting profound wisdom to the adversaries he faces.But hold on to your gaming chairs, 'cause the combat in this game is smoother than a gravure idol's bottom. It's like they took the combat from the last game and gave it a steroid injection. And don't get me started on Ijincho, the new location – it's like they doubled the size of the game overnight. (Okay, fine, they might have borrowed a page -or the whole map- from Yakuza: Like a Dragon, but hey, why reinvent the wheel, right?)In summary, Lost Judgment is not just a game; it's an immersive journey that transcends the realm of pixels and screens. The narrative is so gripping it could inspire a bestselling novel and the combat mechanics are so finely tuned they allow you to temporarily forget the outside world. If you haven't embarked on this odyssey yet, I implore you to do so.

On top of this, it has some of the memorable side content in the series as well, both in terms of side cases, and mini-games. (albeit, a bit too long) Overall, as of now, probably my favorite game by RGG, and I pray for a Judgment 3 one day.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing as an undercover detective beating up gangsters with random objects in the China Town district is probably the closest thing I’m ever gonna get to a Sleeping Dogs sequel. While its world map is relatively small compared to other open world games, it’s densely packed with a lot interiors to explore and things to do.  It feels a lot more like you’re exploring an actual city.  The mini games, arcades games, and collectible playable roms alone make it worth a buy as a retro compilation.  The over the top combat system is fun, especially when combined with all the environmental interaction and destruction.  I’m still finding new ways to beat down high schoolers.

_childDocuments_.review: Lost Judgment is the 2nd game in the Judgment series. If you have played the first one: Judgment, then you will recognize several people and the gameplay. There will be some references to some people and to past decisions, but they are very rare and will not affect this story line.You play as a detective where you start by trying to solve a somewhat small case, which later unfolds to something much bigger. The storytelling and plot twists are great. The ending was little bit disappointed though. There are several people that you wished that they could say something about, but perhaps it is reserved for the third game in the series (?), Final Judgment (???).So, good story, plenty of side quests and funny bits, get ready for a long ride.Final note, I wish the developers would reduce or remove that incredibly annoying vibrating ringtone of the phone. _childDocuments_.review: Near the peak of RGG. Great setting, lots of side content, solid characters and an in-depth story. The only criticism I have is the main plot isn't as compelling as the first Judgment. Unlike the first, this one is more of a philosophical exploration of justice and its consequences. So it's toned down from the usual RGG thriller motif. The hand holding in this one was almost as bad as the first which I find to be mildly irritating. There's no room for allowing the mystery or story beats to settle on the player, everything is explained, re-explained, examined and explored in detail with chapter recaps as the cherry on top. Yagami is motivated in much the same way as Kiryu but motivated by the truth at all costs rather than a bushido morality. This becomes a fairly strange handicap for the story in Lost Judgment because more than once I found myself disagreeing with Yagami and not being persuaded by his arguments or actions. I think I enjoyed that aspect and it played well within the story even if it was a little strange but they tied it up neatly at the end. The highschool setting was great though and it had a lot of fun side activities to go along with it. Definitely much stronger being in Ijincho than Kamurocho like the first game. Although some things do play out in Kamurocho and having a 2nd city is a benefit to the story and gameplay. and thankfully, unlike some past titles in the Yakuza series, there's unique stuff in both cities so they didn't get lazy (or w/e the reason) like they did in Y7 (LAD) or Y6. Highly recommend for hours of fun and a much more chill Yakuza/LAD experience.

_childDocuments_.review: "Lost Judgment" is a compelling game with a rich story and well-defined characters that feel authentic and engaging. The protagonist, a real-life star, is impressively modeled, adding to the game's appeal. The death of a main character introduces deep emotional layers, while the high school storyline, though separate, ties in closely with the main narrative. Unlike the previous game, achievements are more balanced and rewarding, and the DLC offers an additional, enriching story that deepens character backgrounds. However, completing all achievements can be time-consuming, and some players find the task-solving to be straightforward and linear, lacking alternative outcomes.

_childDocuments_.review: I like the main plot, but it lacks the necessary weight as in Judge Eyes. The combat is very good (I like the Enhanced Reversal: Certain Death skill and the maximum attack) but there are very few side quests, although they are quite high quality and cause a lot of laughter. I don't like any school quests because they repeat about an hour after you introduce them to that club, and I'm not interested in the stories for each club. I like Yokohama, but it lacks vitality because Yagami hardly interacts with anyone, and only when friends from Judge Eyes appear did I realize how much I missed the Friends system in Judge Eyes - I care about them more than anyone in Yokohama. The graphics have improved a lot from the previous part, and I can say this is the game with graphics most similar to AC Unity, especially when you choose to visit Yokohama at noon, but you have to change the date and time by sleeping on the bed instead of through the settings like in AC Unity. I play the game at 36FPS, Motion Blur on, FPS CAP UNLIMITED IN GAME, FPS CAP 35.9976 through RivaTuner, on a 144hz screen, Shadow Low, Geo Low, AA Custom, and playing with a controller has given me a beautiful experience, rarely lagging on my GTX 1650 Laptop. There are many mods and they are interesting, but not suitable for playing the main story because you will get stuck in the Loading Screen, I advise you to install the Skip Intro mod and Turn Off DLC Banner (I accidentally clicked on it and Steam popped up, after closing it, both the controller and mouse stopped working, forcing me to ALT+F4). I really like this game 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: my favourite high schoolers beating up simulator  that's worth every single $ and the best judgment release so far.on a more serious note with spoilers ahead:The whole idea of setting the game story in a high school environment surrounded by a bullying-suicide related homicide case was briliant. Except the goofyness (as usual for a RGG game), this one shines some light on an actual problem we face in the modern world and turned out as a great and emotional story.Yoko Sawa death hit hard - she was a really wholesome character but I've seen some people complain about Yagami bringing her up EVERY single time during an argument with someone (which I agree, could've been quite laughable at one point when literally EACH argument was countered with "What about Sawa-Sensei?!") but it actually makes sense as she was the one in this whole mess that no one wanted to fight for and make her murderer face the justice. _childDocuments_.review: I am going to recommend this game for the portrayal of bullying and the consequences it has. I was bullied during my school years a lot and it let me a lot of scars and trauma for me to battle them. That aspect of the game was done wonderfully and accurately. I believe that in the rest of the game that it lacks good writing (or at least on-par with the first one).Gameplay-wise, this is really incredible. Very few slow tailing missions, almost none lockpicking (which is made easier) and more gadgets to play with. The combat is a big step up from Judgement. On the final chapters, when I unlocked many of his abilities, Yagami feels really good to control to. He may not be as powerful as Kiryu or Saejima, but I think he reached the level of fun that Akiyama had in Y4. I really liked how they nerfed Tiger and buffed Crane, as well as the new style Turtle. This is the only game in the whole Yakuza/LAD franchise that I used every style the same and I didn't prefer one.  Story-wise, in the early chapters and the school stories are really good. I didn't really like any of the side-cases, which is a bummer because I play this games to have some laugh with the sub-stories as much as to get sad with the main story. The latter chapters have a lot of bad pacing and a lot of stuff are repeated. I think I read the same dialogue up to five times in one hour. Some story-bits are even taken directly from the first game like . Some characters from the first game that returned didn't have the same charm they had, like Siguira and even Yagami. Yagami's whole character arc from the first game is almost forgotten in this one.That being said, I really enjoyed my time and I may have said that it's the series best brawler if I hadn't played The Man Who Erased His Name mid-way through my play through of this one. I haven't played Kaito's File as of the time of writing this review, but I will write a separate review there.

_childDocuments_.review: Lost Judgment is an action-adventure game developed by Ryu Ga Gotoku (RGG) Studio and published by Sega. The game was released for the consoles on September 24, 2021. The PC version was released on Steam on September 14, 2022, as part of the Judgment series bundle. Lost Judgment is the sequel to Judgment (2018/19). The story follows Takayuki Yagami, who investigates a criminal accused of both sexual harassment and murder. However, the investigation deepens into bullying and revenge against it, blinding legal justice versus what is necessary. Yagami confronts the serious disturbances with improved investigation mechanics, revamped martial arts, intense hand-to-hand combat sequences, moral and legal gray areas, and high school drama. Does the sequel to Judgment increases the stakes and your intrigue?Lost Judgment has one of the darkest and most serious stories established in the Yakuza/Like a Dragon - Judgment franchise by RGG Studio. The main menu already makes a hard impact to the player– a Blade Runner-esque melancholy, depressive tone with pouring rainfall. The player knows the game takes it seriously. One of the subject matters is about bullying, and the ability for a person to respond to it. Bullying is a universal problem in all societies, but Eastern societies have a “silent reaction” and indifference. There are other, subtle subject matters and social commentaries RGG implemented in Lost Judgment I won’t spoil on, and these were handled very well. The acting performances are top notch and story grips from beginning to end. In some ways, Lost Judgment feels more like Persona 5 Royal, but no restrictions on the subject matters RGG was trying to portray. It’s brutal, depressive, and understandably complex with a few characters’ motivations and justifications. Lost Judgment has the mixture of the themes from I Saw the Devil (2010) + Jet Li’s martial arts in Fist of Legend (1994) + Jackie Chan’s fight against Benny the Jet in Wheels on Meals (1984) + the ferocious fighting sequences in The Raid 2 (2014) + and Philip Seymour Hoffman’s menacing performance in Mission Impossible 3 (2006). The perfect summary about Lost Judgment.The gameplay is familiar to the previous entry, Judgment, but the combat is improved, fastened, and revamped. The combat system in Lost Judgment is, perhaps, the best – on par with Yakuza 0’s combat styles. Lost Judgment has a third combat style, the Snake, which is a parry and disarm Aikido-style. There is a fourth combat style, the Boxer – originated as part of a DLC. Much of its gameplay is like the previous entry, but Yagami can skateboard for easier travel and the skill points are more generous. There is a subplot where Yagami becomes a club advisor who investigates a high school academy. The subplot can be lengthy as if the subplot feels like a game within a game but is worth it when it comes to gather SP to unlock combat skills. Lost Judgment has notable improvements over Judgment (2018), but it’s not perfect. The story is great for the most part, but later sequences feel a bit “off”. I won’t go further details due to spoilers, but the arguments on what or who is “right or wrong” doesn’t really hold a lot of value. It one of those gray areas where RGG Studios should explore further but didn’t for some reason as if the developers were conflicted themselves on what/who’s right or wrong. Some clubs in the high school club advisor subplot doesn’t affect the subplot’s storyline and feels like fillers. The robotics club minigame isn’t hard, but the gameplay mechanics and explanations weren’t clarified (think of it like a capture-enemy-base Tetris). Lost Judgment was released in 2021 and I was surprised the game wasn’t nominated for a game award’s categories like best action game or best soundtrack, given how few games were released in that year due to the COVID pandemic. I forgot to mention on the game’s soundtrack and it’s arguably one of the best soundtracks I listen to up to the present time. I still use it for gym workouts and exercises. Some themes and subject matters in the game are not restrained to tell a grim and serious story. In some ways, I felt RGG Studio put a lot of effort into this game because it implies future titles for the Judgment spin-off series are not certain. As of typing this review, there is no confirmation of a third entry to the series. Lost Judgment is, arguably, the most serious and mature stories published by Sega and RGG Studio. While the game has a few ineffective parts in the story, RGG Studio has once again done an impressive job. The game has my high recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: ( full review with screenshots:  )Lost Judgment is the sequel to Judgment, and like that game is a Yakuza series spinoff focused on the private detective work of Yagami and friends. It primarily uses the same Ijincho map as Like a Dragon, but don't expect much in the way of references to that game. Outside of a very subtle cameo and a few nods to reused locations, there's almost nothing shared between the games and you can definitely get by here having only played Judgment. Almost all of the major characters are returning faces from that game, and while you might still be able to have a good time if you started here, you'd be missing out on both a great game and a ton of background. So, assuming you're already familiar with Judgment, what's different here? Far and away the biggest change, at least outside of the new map, is the focus on Seiryo High School. After a series of contrived and deeply awkward shenanigans a few hours into the game, Yagami ends up as a counselor at the school and will work with almost a dozen different clubs over the rest of the game if you want to complete the main side quest. Each club has its own minigame, which range wildly in content, depth, and quality. The eSports club is merely yet another way to access Virtua Fighter 5, for example, and the robotics club only looks deep until you realize how bad the AI is at it, but the boxing gym is a brand new 1v1 fighter with loads of different opponents and special moves. The good news is that the best of these are quite fun and most of the clubs have entertaining stories to go with the minigames. The bad news is that several of the clubs easily take 4-5 hours to complete and there's no choice but to do them unless you would rather give up on seeing the end of the entire school side story. It would've benefited greatly from having fewer minigames that got more dev time each, or from making the clubs just take less time. Speaking of systems that needed more time in the oven, the worst offender by far is the stealth. I am someone who loves stealth games and regularly plays them on the hardest settings, but the stealth in this game is so indefensibly awful that I started dropping the difficulty to "simple" every time it came up instead of bothering to engage with it. It's completely linear and provides zero player choice, so there's no satisfaction to overcoming a section, and worse than that it's insta-fail if you're ever spotted. Nevermind that the goons you're sneaking around can hardly scratch you in a normal fight, once you start sneaking they're suddenly capable of one hit KOs. These sections are at least only used a handful of times in a 60 hour game, but they are truly offensively bad. My other big problem is more subjective. Judgment mostly had you dealing with yakuza bosses and corrupt officials, so you never felt too bad about harassing them for your investigation. This time around, Yagami spends a lot of time being annoyingly persistent with teachers, teenagers, and other civilians who are a lot more sympathetic when they just want to be left alone. It can get uncomfortable. On top of that, while the story does end up somewhere satisfying, it suffers from some pacing issues in the middle and relies on one specific incident for Yagami's motivation so heavily and constantly that it starts to feel silly. This would've been on the edge of not earning a recommendation if it hadn't recovered in the last couple of chapters. All that out of the way, what you're left with is a lot of the same strengths as other games in this series. Combat is generally very satisfying, although it feels like the new Viper style completely outclasses the existing Tiger and Crane styles against a lot of the hardest enemies. It's full of quirky characters and silly moments that'll usually earn a laugh. The main antagonists, once you finally know who they are, create some great setpiece boss fights. The one strong point that's less familiar is the school stories, which mostly offer refreshingly lower stakes and more wholesome content than what you're probably used to. It's good to take a break from all the murders and conspiracies to just go coach a dance team for a bit. --------For more reviews, see

_childDocuments_.review: My favorite RGG Studios game.Lost Judgment was an amazing ride from start to finish, while it definitely doesn't have as deep a story as what Judgment offered, I still appreciated it touching more serious topics like bullying, and for that, this is my favourite game. The gameplay is also the best they have done in the dragon engine so far, 4 battle styles (or 3 if you don't count the now free dlc boxer style!) which all play amazingly and fluid, style changing feels faster, crane doesn't feel underpowered anymore and snake was a really, really fun addition.Leveling up in this game is weird, it's like they tried to compensate the lack of SP gain in judgment by giving hundreds per battle or activity, but obviously the catch is that it costs a lot more to buy a skill. I honestly didn't like this change, it feels way more grindy than before and easier to exploit.Kaito Files story was great but I didn't really like the fighting in that game, brawler and beast coming back was really nice but kaito has almost no ways to destroy someone's guard that isn't a finisher or pressing circle which doesn't even grab correctly, he just throws them.Overall, Lost Judgment is amazing, an overall improvement on the gameplay Judgment established and a really good story. Definitely recommended to everyone who has already played the original game.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like Lost Judgment more than Judgment 1. I really do. But I don't.The narrative in Lost Judgment is, in my opinion, much better than Judgment 1 because it doesn't try to make its stakes world-ending. Yes, there are high-level officials involved in Lost Judgment's plot, sure, but it starts off very grounded and generally stays that way. Yagami's story is very much Yagami's story and everything that he's involved in carries personal stakes first. And I am very much into that kind of story.The combat is stellar too, basically improving on Judgment 1's in every measurable way. Now having three styles a la Like a Dragon instead of two does wonders for how you like to play. Likewise, the expanded "detective" segments serve the game well, with a lot of what would have been tailing and chase segments from Judgment 1 being replaced with stealth and Parkour segments.But there are flaws, and they're pretty huge.The first and most egregious of these is the locking of the main side story, the School Stories, behind minigame completion. To complete the School Stories investigations, you have to fully complete each of their respective minigames to their ends. This isn't too much of a problem with something like the Dance minigame, but it's insanely frustrating for the Robotics minigame. When I discovered I had to fully complete the minigames, I just gave up on the School Stories entirely.Another flaw appears once the RK gang shows up. With every plot point that involves RK, the only fights you ever see are against hordes of RK members, that's it. The only two important characters within RK are the leaders, so there really isn't any variety in antagonists beyond those two and one other individual. One fight with RK in the middle of the game has you fighting the same RK leader boss three times in a row. Deplete their health bar, fight again. And then when you infiltrate a warehouse with them, you likely fight a hundred enemies in total over the course of the infiltration. It becomes incredibly boring.Finally, the game does not play nice with automatic cutscene triggers. I ran into this at the very end, when the game explicitly told me to prepare before leaving. I set a waypoint for the item shop and proceeded to run there, only to realize that getting close to the cutscene trigger would, with no warning, send me into the final battle arc.I still like Lost Judgment, and I'll be playing the Kaito Files at a later date. But I find Judgment 1 superior, mainly because it's less annoying.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start with the good. The story was interesting. It certainly was the main reason to keep playing, even if it were just the first half (after which I thought the game was over but it just kept going forever). Another good thing is that something about the environment, the atmosphere or whatever it was had some sort of appeal, which had me launch the game time after time despite the many times I got annoyed. Now, one of the main reasons I didn't like the game: The constant combat encounters. You know in Pokemon, how, when you walk through bushes, there is a good chance you encounter a pokemon? Often you don't want to fight, but it just keeps happening. Luckily, you can avoid these bushes and walk out. Well. Here it is kinda like that except you can't leave these bushes. There is encounter after encounter after encounter. You wanna go to building X? Oh, here is a random group of thugs. What, you dealt with them? Well here you go, a bunch of aggressive high schoolers. Done? Well there ya go, the next group is coming your way. It really was a choir for me. I just wanted to see the story and move through the main missions, but these constant fights forced me to use the taxi to go everywhere. Which is quite expensive, and still had you move to locations. Another really bothersome thing was the lack of a challenge. The game held your hand all the way til the very end. Combat was so simple, on the highest difficulty I couldn't be bothered trying to understand it remotely. You have different buttons, combos, stances... well I don't know what the stances were for, what they did, how to get them. I just mashed buttons and I won everything easily. There are many ways to grow stronger... well. I left that all aside. Button mashing and done. It wasn't just combat. You are a detective. Except you, as a player, do none of that. There is no thinking involved. Trying to find evidence just meant clicking on stuff in a room. A stealth mission was literally: Walk to a square, get a pop up with the button to press, press it, wait, and then walk to the next square. It felt insulting. The main reason why I wouldn't recommend the game: So the button mashing thing in combat was something I did in the first four hours or so. At that point, I finally encountered an opponent where I'd have to try a little. I died. And then I died again. So, I was like... okay. Not bad, I may have to try to understand the game a little now. And then came the pop up 'do you want to change the difficulty to normal'? Every time I'd die, the game would ask me that. I got annoyed so much that I just accepted in hopes it'd stop, but no. It did not. It'd then ask to change to simple and during simple it still asks that....

_childDocuments_.review: + Great graphics+ Fantastic new characters+ Great story+ Incredible combat; IMO the best in the series+ 3 (+1 DLC) polished styles of combat; massive improvement from its predecessor+ Say goodbye to the tedium of running; you can now call taxis from your smartphone and skateboard around town+ Side/school stories are phenomenal+ Wide array of side activities; robot wars, boxing, burnout bike racing, skateboarding, dancing, on top of the usual RGG ones+ You get a +/- Great direction towards parkour and stealth mechanics, but said mechanics are somewhat unpolished and occasionally buggy+/- Lack of upgradeable storage space; makes things more challenging, but also requires more trips to shops+/- Dialogue gets a little tiresome at times. Take a drink every time Yagami mentions "Sawa"- Drone racing and VR Dice & Cube are downgrades from the previous game- Ingredients for extracts are a tad tedious to farmLost Judgment is phenomenal and an upgrade from its predecessor in virtually every aspect. The combat system is exciting and buttery smooth. Dragon Engine combat was kinda rough in Y6 and YK2, with Judgment being a little boring. But combat in Lost Judgment hits all the sweet spots. You get 4 types of combat styles, and switching between them is seamless. While Crane Style was pretty bad in Judgment, this game makes it fantastic for dealing with crowds.Story-wise, this game impressed me with how it managed to develop a quality story around school bullying. Some parts of the story are also considerably darker than the RGG norm, which was definitely an interesting change. Most say that Judgment's story is superior, but I actually prefer this one for tackling real world issues and the subject of morality.But IMO, the best aspect of this game by far are the school stories. Yagami should give up being a detective and become a school guidance counselor instead. There are 10 different school stories (quest chains) in this, and a number of them have fantastic character development. I never thought I'd be so committed to overseeing the championship victory of a school's robotics club.School stories also introduces a real star in Amasawa Kyoko, and I would be  disappointed if she didn't return in a potential third game.Performance-wise, the game ran perfectly and not once crashed in my entire playthrough.I loved every moment of this game. Easily one of the best games in the RGG franchise, and I doubt anyone would leave feeling disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: A very good game and one of the best in the "extended" series (Yakuza+Judgment).First I am so happy to see the Dragon Engine finally deliver : the game is really beautiful and the fights finally both enjoyable and fair (Y3 to Kiwami system was enjoyable only but broken).Activities are generally of good quality and I appreciate the gameplay additions to make the game more modern and less clunky (the parkour for instance...yes it feels dated compared to real action/adventure games but this is a step in the right direction).  As always, you need like 2-4 hours to be drawn in the game and after that you cannot stop playing until the end. The story is a bit weak if you look at it coldly (as many Yakuza games to be fair), but they half succeeded to deliver their message with strong characters and emotionnal momentum. I cannot spoil but I would rate this part B, A being the best stories in the series. I cannot put the finger on the reason behind this feeling, maybe because Yagami looped over one event and used it every time in his discussions so that he locked the game instead of developping the numerous interesting characters and leads (the school for instance is abandoned quickly by the plot). To sum up, maybe Yagami and his single argument were too dominating in the plot (compared to other characters, story branches, etc.) and that is why the Kaito files DLC felt like a deliverance.Aside from that, the game has a huge content, to the point that in almost 40 hours I have never ecountered some. This is certainly here of the best points : we cannot feel bored in this game and the step in modernity for all these old minigames feels good even if the side quests by themselves are not really memorable.Now I have a huge gripe with this port and I'm tormented to leave a negative review for this alone : the DLC button in the smartophone makes you leave the game (as intended) and then, when you come back to it, the game is FROZEN. So if you did not save, you can lose a lot of playtime. This is even more frustrating when you have already purchased the DLC, so the button is absolutely useless. Considering the content for the price, the usual free additions and the quality, I will keep my positive review but I hoped that this matter would be fixed.========KAITO FILES DLCMy man, this has a bit of drama within but the story was satisfying as hell. It reminded me a bit of Y1 strings+grittiness mixed with the nostalgic/emotionnal vibe of Y3. Again, if I examine it coldly, there are many flaws in the plot but the stream of emotions and the main line are so strong that they are forgotten. In a way, this DLC had the (genuine) humanity lacking in main game which felt colder (despite the forced scenes, because the game was too centered around Yagami and his view). This is unfortunately not something that memorable because this is a DLC and not a full game but this was a welcomed addition. Mikiko was also one of the first female characters (if not the only one) that feel (and look) like a belivable mature woman and not the "cute/pure/cheesy" girl to protect. I'm not especially feminist but a real woman is a lot more charming (hell she is) and interesting. Plus 30-40 women in the other games acting like 18 princess from movies was a bit frustrating.

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay 5/7- Combat is fluid, very interesting with 4 different fighting styles (Tiger, Crane, Snake, Boxing), and a gratuitous use of scenery and local topography to rearrange facial structures.- Exploration is fun and with the addition of a skateboard less tedious in longer commutes.- Extremely diverse modes of play, be it side-missions, school stories, random encounters, emulated Sega classic videogames and boardgames such as shogi and mahjong. There is enough content here to last a good 50 hours, and a lot more if you're the completionist type.  Story: Meanders a bit and drags in places, but this is a Yakuza game at heart so it has all the drama, twists and turns you might expect from a yakuza/detective story-driven game. Dialogue-heavy but not overbearing and there's a pause and/or skip button for the less patient.Setting:Kamurocho and Yokohama. Both fun to navigate and big enough to not feel small. At first the game might feel a bit empty as substories and sidecontent is made available once you progress in the special "school stories" section of the game. Both locations are beautifully realized. There's a day/night cycle and various mission specific locations that are graphically impressive. Longevity:The game will last the average gamer at least 35 hours, whereas a fan will get a minimum of 50 hours out of the game. Highly recommended for fans of rpg/adventure gamers. Not recommended for the brodude crowd.

_childDocuments_.review: To keep this short and sweet, i have to say, when you buy a Ryu ga gotoku game, you know what to expect. In this regard, this game doesn disappoint. _childDocuments_.review: A worthy successor to the starting game and a FANTASTIC experience that has left me wanting for a third game to this magnificent sister series! As a big fan of the last game, I came in with high expectations and it most certainly delivered with the keen interest for a sequel to be made!Game-play wise had since upgraded from the previous game, where you have more freedom to run around and not be boxed in by civilians and forced to fight. You can pretty much run from an encounter now, but honestly, why would you? They added the snake style to the list of fighting stances you are given, as well as the Boxing style which you can get from purchasing the full game and it's DLC. The story itself was surrounded in mystery, just as the last game, each chapter left me with more questions than answers, a feeling I absolutely love experiencing when playing a game like this. It also challenges the justice system and what we believe is the right thing to do, giving us a deeper understanding as to why some of these characters have done what they done. One gripe I had was towards the DLC, the Kaito files. While it was nothing more than just a DLC featuring Kaito as the playable character, he was amazing btw. I couldn't help but notice a few similarities from Kiryu's fighting stances and as well as the story treatment he was received. The Kaito files honestly became quite predictable and that sadly spoiled a bit of the fun and mystery that Judgment  had with Yagami. But all in all, Kaito was a great playable protagonist and is definitely a keeper ;)Other than that, a HUGE recommendation and I pray we get a third game!!!

_childDocuments_.review: RGG does it again, they took the already excellent entry title, Judgment, and improved upon it in this sequel in just about every way. For one, the annoying Mortal Wounds from the first game have been removed and you can now perform a counter-attack (unique to each style) against Deadly Attacks called a Mortal Reversal, allowing Yagami to stay on the offensive with a well-timed quickstep. Crane and Tiger have been rebalanced to better compliment each other while the new Snake stance is a wet dream for those who love landing parries and grapples. The OP DLC-exclusive Boxer style combines power and evasion that will decimate bosses with a flurry of punches for those who prefer to literally throw hands. Neither style is objectively better than the other and the game encourages you to cycle through them frequently for their various movesets hence keeping the combat very dynamic and fluid.The story is, at the very least, on par with Judgment's. Once again Yagami is investigating yet another murder but this time, there's a very heavy dose of bullying centered around it so a good majority of the game's content features the new Seiryo High. I will say, it is immensely cathartic taking down school bullies, especially as someone who was once a victim to it. Returning side characters have been given more screen time to flesh them out more as individuals, particularly Sugiura and Tsukumo, while the newer ones are given strong introductions to make them instantly memorable. Even if the gameplay isn't to your liking, at least you get a compelling Japanese crime-thriller to experience.My only real complaints are some of the new school club minigames being somewhat wonky to play (looking at you Robo lab and Motorcycle club) and the mandatory scripted stealth segments. On Hard difficulty, enemies will be alerted near instantaneously and you must sit through a 5-10 second animation of Yagami being caught and knocked out with zero ways to escape--it's frustrating when this is the same guy who could walk into a club and comfortably take on a dozen street punks (this is thankfully fixed in the Kaito Files expansion).As a PC port, Lost Judgment runs buttery smooth with very little technical issues on my end. It seems RGG Studio has progressively gotten better with each new release on Steam and I hope they maintain this level of quality. It is a no-brainer $60 title and if you already have it on PlayStation, buy it again just for increased frames because it plays like an entirely new game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game improves on Judgment in almost every way. This series, with just two entries, won me over the mainline Yakuza games. The cast of characters, their bonds, their banter, is just so good. The gameplay, fighting styles, perks, gear to equip, consumables. The maps, being able to explore Ijincho and Kamurocho and both maps having content to do. The side content, the school arc with the Professor, the biker gang, school clubs, minigames, etc. The Kaito Files DLC, the story it brings to the table. Everything about this game really raised the bar for what RGG is capable of delivering.That isn't to say the game is perfect, there's definitely some stuff to criticize such as while the main storyline is good, it definitely does feel like Yagami grasps at straws at some points trying to connect what is happening to Sawa. Or the controls for the skateboard feel, or the bike races. Encountering roadblocks in that you must complete one story to progress through another with the school arc. Even then, however, these critiques are so little in comparison to the overall quality content this game delivers. A situation of pros outweigh the cons and in Lost Judgment's case, it's outweighed by a lot.This game is absolutely worth the $60 asking price so if you find this for 50, 40, 30 then it's just more bang for your buck. I really hope RGG can see the success of Judgment and consider making Judgment 3 at some point in time. This series and any future entries will now be a day one purchase for me. That's how good I think Judgment is.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid improvement over previous entry.If you liked the previous game, or Ryu Ga Gotoku studio (RGG) games in general this is not a miss.To speak in broad terms, this game, much like its predecessor is RGG's attempt at making a detective protagonist.Keyword is attempt, as at the end of the day this is still an RGG game, and as with all RGG games, the protagonist defeats a small army by the end of it.Final chapter in particular has him (along with 3 basically useless AIs) going against around 100 enemies + 2 tanky bosses.That's not to say that the story sucks, there is no mystery, or there is no sleuthing taking place.All of that is definitely present, and is at a more than acceptable level.There is a well-presented mystery, and what I found an interesting story.What I am trying to complain about is that this is not so much a "detective" game as it is an action brawler.At the end of the day, it is not the evidence you gather that brings you closer to the truth, but rather beating basically everyone into submission.It works as far as RGG games go, but if you are looking for a more "mystery solving" game, this is not it.I would say that I liked the story of this game more than its predecessor.As with previous title, I think that the protagonist does not deliver his point across strongly enough.Once again, I find that the antagonist is very relatable, even more so than Yagami (the protagonist) himself.Antagonist makes a clear point as to why he does what he does, and why he sees it as necessary.He has collaborators who agree with him, and the antagonist does his damn hardest to not compromise them.This is to the point where he stays steadfast in his conviction to not harm his (in his opinion most important) collaborator after being betrayed by them, and even crying when they decide to take Yagami's side and give themselves to the police.Meanwhile, Yagami's main argument seemed to have revolved around one bystander dying, which kinda begs the question if that's the only problem he had with the antagonist's actions.I do not have much to say about graphics and gameplay of this title.It runs on the modern RGG engine, and has gotten the same treatment as all RGG games.There are a lot of side activities to be had, definitely more than is necessary.Graphics look nice, game runs smoothly (even on linux).Compared to previous game, I would say there have been massive improvements.Combat got better compared to previous title.There is a new style (technically two), and it is an absolute pleasure to use.For once, I start to feel that the combat is not just a DPS race slugfest, but actually skill based.There were still a few annoyances that left it feeling like the dumb slugfest, but overall, an improvement.SP is much easier to procure in this game, I felt like there was barely enough for anything in previous game, whereas in this one I was swimming in it, and got basically all upgrades I wanted half-way in (though I did grind for a few hours out of personal volition).This entry also does away with the annoying "mortal wounds" mechanic of the previous game, there is no longer a need to deal with annoying health limitations.This is also probably the first game since Yakuza 0 that actually got me somewhat interested in its side content."School stories" is an interesting take, but ultimately I gave up because I could not be bothered to go through the dancing segments that you are forced to take.To summarize, this is a solid entry in RGG's lineup.People who are familiar with RGG's games can expect more of the same goodness.People who are unfamiliar are in for a pleasant trip to Kamurocho and Ijincho (though, perhaps grab and do the first game beforehand. It is not required, but would provide context)

_childDocuments_.review: Lost Judgment is a fantastic entry in the Judgment franchise, and probably RGG's magnum opus as of 2023. While not as tight as it's predecessor, Lost Judgment features a compelling mystery for Yagami and his friends to solve.One thing that really stood out to me were the phenomenal performances of Takuya Kimura (Takayuki Yagami) and Koji Yamamoto (Jin Kuwana). I'm a longtime fan of Kimura-san, from SMAP to his record-breaking dramas, and I'm glad that he's very enthusiastic about continuing in the role of Yagami. RGG Studio really gave him a lot more to work with in this title, especially in regards to both the fully-voiced main story and the humorous side-cases. Koji Yamamoto also has the honor of portraying the best written antagonist in a RGG title. Kuwana is a deeply complex character that serves as an excellent foil to Yagami, and it's so fun to see these two go head-to-head with eachother. Also helps that he has a sick-ass theme.While certain aspects like the reworked Detective Mode and Parkour could be improved, Lost Judgment has the best combat in any RGG title ever released, surpassing Yakuza Zero. Combat is fast, flashy, and fluid – with Yagami's expanded moveset making the high encounter rate a joy to contend with.If you’re a fan of thrilling adventures filled with dynamic twists and turns  – look no further than picking up this game right away. Highly recommended for anyone ready for a great time.(Played through Lost Judgment when it was released on PS5, replaying on Steam Deck. Performance on Deck is great.)

_childDocuments_.review: A strong contender to be the best RGG title so far. Like literally, this game took everything from first Judgment and made it better. Story? Dark. Darker than the first? Personal opinion. This game though shows corpses (game literally opens with a decomposing one) a lot, constant references to bullying and suicide. So if any of these topics trigger you, be warned. But the story is good. Like other titles it starts rather slow but speeds up about halfway (around chapter 7) The antagonist I think is the best the series got to offer so far. Final battle - epic, and with that music..The music is too one the top in the series. Like no joke - in a series well known for it's bangers.My complaints with the first game was the attrocious tailing and the Keihin Gang being a pain in the ass. Lost Judgment fixes those issues. The tailing is now more engaging, maybe it's not the best but it definetely is a step up from previous title. Keihin Gang is now a major part for a School Stories - a completly optional giant side quest that could be a standalone game in all fairness. It involves several minigames(they might get grindy a bit but nothing serious) and could get a good chunk of your playtime. The combat and gameplay is perfected in this game. We got 2 new styles - Snake and Boxer(i believe Boxer was a part of DLC earlier but we got it for free in PC version) Each of the four is reliable and you can mix them up for nice combos. The graphics is still the good old Dragon Engine. Yeah, it's been 7 years since Yakuza 6 and it's debut. The game looks okay, but I think it's finally time to give up on it. I didn't noticed any major bugs and the game is fairly stable, it ran well too on my not-so-great PC.Overall I place Lost Judgment in the same place as Yakuza 5 and Yakuza 0, being now my third contender to claim my personal TOP 1 in the series.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish there was a mixed option rather than just recommend or not. I have a lot of issues with this game. The story tackles a lot of serious issues, and sort of uses them as stepping stones rather than give them the proper attention that they probably deserve. Also some of the main driving points of the story make no sense to me at all. The combat system is also a mixed bag for me, Yagami feels incredible, and the combos you can pull off are amazing. That's only if the enemies let that happen though. The negatives with RGG combat stay here, the insane block strings and hyper armor (and lack of hyper armor for you), the really weak base enemies, the bosses that just don't really react to what you're doing, it's all here. So it sort of combines into this thing where I feel like the game wants me to experiment and do long, involved combos, but the enemies don't give me the space to do that bc the ones that I can combo die before the combo ends, and the ones that don't command grab me halfway through the combo. DMC5 is a game I've been thinking about while playing this, and it's because the combat systems make me want to do the same thing, the difference is that DMC5s enemies are designed for that, and also designed to challenge you in the middle of your strings, Lost Judgment feels like the enemies have the same skeleton from Yakuza 0. Lastly, and I think this is probably a bug, but during the last chapter every boss but the final one teleported me into their command grab, which was really annoying. On the second to last fight specifically I had just sent the boss flying and then I blinked and I was getting stabbed. It was just really jarring, didn't cause a game over or anything. I've spent this whole review griping about the problems I have with Lost Judgment, I don't think it's a bad game, I just think it stumbles at literally everything it was trying to do.
