_childDocuments_.review: Cavern of Dreams is like a blast from the past: A near perfect encapsulation of what made collectathon platformers of the 90's so damn good.  Is it a bit short?  Sure, but it doesn't overstay it's welcome, and keeps the game feeling fresh with new puzzles, mechanics, and challenges along the way.  If you're a fan of games like Banjo-Kazooie, Mario 64, etc., definitely pick this game up and give it go, you won't regret it!
_childDocuments_.name: Cavern of Dreams

_childDocuments_.review: A gem of a N64-inspired platformer that sees you saving the eggs of your dragon siblings scattered around a variety of interesting worlds. It just feels good to be in this world. One of the better recreations of the N64 era.It exudes joy in nearly every interaction, with my favorite being the lil' "good job" you get from the adorable Fynn whenever you grab an egg. It's got a great platforming toolset that evolves as you progress and each new tool feels like it actually matters and unlocks new ways to approach each level.
_childDocuments_.name: Cavern of Dreams

_childDocuments_.review: Solid little game, thoroughly enjoyed my time playing since it felt exactly like when I first played Spyro — just without any combat (but it makes up for that with clever puzzles!)Cavern of Dream's overall world is relatively small so you become quite familiar with each level pretty fast, but there are so many nooks and crannies to find and so many puzzles to solve that the gameplay doesn't get old, and the running back and forth between levels doesn't feel tiresome either. I actually found it really fun to understand the layout of each mini-world so thoroughly that I could almost speedrun the tasks I was completing. Just when you think you've found everything, you realise you're still missing four cards and an egg... and you could have sworn you'd already been everywhere...Was pleasantly surprised that this game scratched that itch of finding secret areas in places you can only access in the end-game that are otherwise hidden out of camera sight. I also had a lot of fun finding ways to break the usage of certain items to explore hidden areas in otherwise out of bounds regions. Jester Boots in Prismatic Palace was great, pretty sure I wasn't supposed to 100% that level the way I did by abusing the Boots outside their designated area but boy did I have fun doing so. Completely skipped the puzzle in the central palace up to the top and didn't realise until a few hours later that there even WAS a puzzle there. Whoops.Overall, really great and relaxing game to kill a good few hours in. As of this review I've just finished 100%ing everything, with the help of some pointers from online guides where finding items was a bit difficult. Thought I was going to wrap up my gameplay here, but I just realised there's an inaccessible area in the Prismatic Palace I was dying to get to that the end-game item will let me reach... so I guess it's back to secret hunting for me!
_childDocuments_.name: Cavern of Dreams

_childDocuments_.review: Got on sale for 7.79 dollers and i can honestly say im impressed. The game does feel like a classic collection game from the PS1/N64 Era of gaming. back when you didn't have to pay attention to deep stories and annoying combat mechanics. The Tuto rial is  nice and shows controls for at least the Xbox controller. The game ran perfect on my steam Deck which very much a good form factor for the game because the small screen makes the game look nicer then you think with the art style. I will also say this is most likely a youth friendly game as at least for the beginning it's not asking for massively complicated control inputs.I can really see this being one of those long weekend games you play because you want to start a game and play while not requiring 100 plus hours of grind or some long complicated in depth story you forget by the next time you play.Defently worth getting on sale. if you really, really like old retro Collection game it might be worth full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Cavern of Dreams

_childDocuments_.review: got me thinking, among other things, about the various priorities the 3d platformer can take on...been playing this a bit in tandem with what is shaping up to be my first full playthru of mario 64 (and with sephonie as the most recent 3d platformer ive returned to) and i feel like they all illustrate some kind of imaginary rubric that u can place most of not all 3d platformers on. mario 64 here represents games that prioritize the Player Character above all else, famously slaved over for total perfection before a single real level was ever made...i'd say games like Demon Turf and Pseudoregalia pick up this torch the most. sephonie is for me the undisputed peak of the focus being the world itself, in a physical geometrical way...every move in ur toolkit is about interacting with specifically the space, u cant accomplish nearly as much in an empty room as u can with games in that first category. cavern of dreams then is a herald for games that mainly prioritize the world, but as Context rather then Shapes. its super super refreshing tbh...the spaces are about as far from abstraction as u can get despite how surreal and impossible they are. thinking about places and objects as Themselves are essential for solving the puzzles, which are the main focus here and an absolute delight...so many moments of realization were paired with a joyful smile. also super adorable and crittery, and vaguely disquieting but not in a way where it feels like its secretly threatening...all the colors are right there to be appreciated, its just strange to walk thru such expressionist worlds. an incredibly worthy successor to rareware platformers, which in retro terms were the kings of this kind of context-heavy approach (and in a slightly different way, story-driven adventure games like psychonauts). many of these indie 3d platformers take from the rareware lineage, corn kidz 64 also gave me a lot of banjo vibes, but all the games turn out so different! wonderful stuff, and extremely comforting game...v little high stakes platforming, just vibes and exploration and cool puzzles. also even tho this was a fairly easy 100%, its one of my favorites ive probably ever done...half of it gives u one of the coolest rewards EVER, the other half contains one of the coolest puzzles in the game...which ended up being the final card i needed, so it rly went out on a high note. and ofc, the whole game Expertly makes u feel like a Little Guy
_childDocuments_.name: Cavern of Dreams

_childDocuments_.review: A solid little gem of a platformer with a lovely N64 aesthetic and fluid gameplay. My favorite thing about it has to be the tone set by the music and environmental storytelling, painting a cutesy yet unnerving phantasmagoria that kept me wondering what i'd find next. Exploration is fun and encouraged even after all the listed objectives are complete, and i'd definitely replay it again and again in the future just to experience this dream once more.
_childDocuments_.name: Cavern of Dreams

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely delightful little game. Tight controls, gorgeous environments full of secrets to find and a cast of delightful characters that you'd be hard pressed not to love. It's a nostalgic game, but not in the shallow, corporate way of a Hollywood remake. It's a game about growing up, dealing with the mistakes of your parents and confronting the darker aspects of life.Like a lot of real Nintendo 64 games, it's occasionally pretty creepy but it never goes full horror. It's a whimsical journey at heart, and I highly recommend it to fans of 3D platformers and the Anodyne games specifically.
_childDocuments_.name: Cavern of Dreams

_childDocuments_.review: A short but wholly satisfying 3D collectathon platformer. There are so many creative mechanics and visuals at play! Cavern of Dreams kept surprising me at every corner.This game also understands what the best reward possible for completing it could be: Without going into too much detail, if you like exploring everything a game's world has to offer and beyond, I recommend you play this one through to the very end. You'll get what I mean.
_childDocuments_.name: Cavern of Dreams

_childDocuments_.review: Very cute and likable characters, especially Fynn and his siblings. Movement is solid; nothing too fancy but what's there works and doesn't wind up being finicky like 3d platformers sometimes are. Even the swimming works well and is fun. Difficulty is definitely on the easy side, but there are collectibles that require enough thought/precision to keep things engaging. The atmosphere is consistently exceptional. And even though the game is pretty short, I still found it satisfying.
_childDocuments_.name: Cavern of Dreams

_childDocuments_.review: It's such a fun and beautiful game!! The visuals and music are amazing, and the puzzles are all really clever! Some of them are more difficult than others, but none of them feel overwhelming or anything. The story, too, is also really good! There's a lot of depth; a lot of environmental storytelling that makes you think about the world of this game. And well, the dragons are just so cute :}
_childDocuments_.name: Cavern of Dreams

_childDocuments_.review: Cavern of Dreams is a retro indie platformer that harkens back to the golden era of Nintendo 64 games like Super Mario 64 and Banjo-Kazooie. It emulates them almost to a fault, because it also has slippery/floaty controls and quirky camera angles. Nevertheless it offers a nostalgic journey for old-school gamers.What sets "Cavern of Dreams" apart is its overall low difficulty. There's minimal punishment for failing, allowing players to explore the vibrant world without fear of long setbacks. The absence of combat shifts the focus entirely to jumping challenges, exploration, and puzzles. Some are easy to figure out, others not so much.Just as you start having fun with Caven of Dreams, you get to the last stage and it is a huge tonal shift, now having some horror elements. It is also much more difficult than the rest of the game, which for me lead to some tedious, frustrating moments and cheap deaths.Recommended at a discount.
_childDocuments_.name: Cavern of Dreams

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent game. The mechanics are solid, as are the controls. The game sticks to its core and avoids mini-games and gimmicks, annoying the issues with a small number of collectables being gated behind nonsense. The visual and audio design are also excellent, and are used to great effect to establish a simultaneously cozy and foreboding atmosphere.
_childDocuments_.name: Cavern of Dreams

_childDocuments_.review: To start, the game ran TERRIBLY when I first launched and I almost gave up. Saw a comment that suggested locking to 60fps and that fixed everything! On Nvidia just open the control panel and lock the program to 60fps manually.Now. What a lovely game. I consider 3d platformers to be my favorite genre but I was never super wild about Banjo. I'd say this takes that formula and focuses more on exploration and puzzle solving. There isn't any combat despite enemies that will knock you away. As you play you unlock more and more abilities that allow new progression. I wouldn't quite say metroidvania style but almost there. It's got a nostalgic and comforting yet also occasionally creepy artstyle that I loved. And when you're done, if you're a completionist, you get a new ability which allows you to re-explore the game (not like ng+ but I don't want to spoil too much) that reminded me of playing games as a kid when I couldn't afford to get new games and just had to milk each game for what it was worth. There are so many hidden areas and secrets that just reward the player for exploring and thinking outside the box, not with anything that really does much to progress the game, but just kind of lets players know, "Hey, thanks for caring enough to play the game."I will say the controls take a bit to get used to, and as this is kind of physics-based, some of the bouncing felt a bit wonky at times. This is a game that honestly gets better as it goes and when I got to the very end I just wanted to keep going and couldn't wait to explore all the previous sections again. I feel like there are still secrets I haven't found and that makes it feel a bit more magical to me.Thanks for the fun :)
_childDocuments_.name: Cavern of Dreams

_childDocuments_.review: A cute little game that reminds me of the n64 days. good puzzles simple mechanics but lots to do and collect. games like these go to show you dont need all the fancy bells and whistles to make a good game, the game is very basic and even have plenty of visual glitches but it doesent matter. well worth 13$.
_childDocuments_.name: Cavern of Dreams

_childDocuments_.review: A great retro 3D platformer. Big fan of the visuals and N64 aesthetic. Game is a bit cryptic. Fell off of playing, came back and could not figure out what to do to proceed. Didn't really care to or feel like attempting to look it up, maybe I'll come back to finish it one day. That said, it's more of a me issue, game is pretty solid and fans of 3D platformers, especially ones that try to scratch the retro nostalgia itch, will enjoy it.
_childDocuments_.name: Cavern of Dreams

_childDocuments_.review: Surprisingly fleshed out for it's genre of retreaux n64 platformers. Not much immediate direction, but not difficult to figure out either. Did end up looking up a couple of things, but it's all good.It's kinda got that OoT charm where there's bright/colorful/happy but also "hey what in the creepshow did I just stumble into??" Final section gets pretty rough though.Outside of that, certifiably cozy little platformer that's worth its price :D
_childDocuments_.name: Cavern of Dreams

_childDocuments_.review: This game perfectly encapsulates the atmosphere of Nintendo 64 games. Down to the shifting music when you enter water or sub areas of levels. For some reason I was expecting 8 worlds but this game only had 4 worlds (with some micro worlds for one collectible.) My only gripe with the level design is the game is very confusing with some portions. and world 3 is hard to understand and required me to back track a lot. I was also not a fan of the jump mechanic. Too many platforms required that you used the extra height from double bounces and ground pounds to clear. Tons of ledges also wouldn't properly work and Fynn would just fall. World 4 also had these chain ropes you had to grab onto and platform to the next one. For the life of me I couldn't figure out why I couldn't climb to the top. The Hub world also confused me as I thought the layout was similar to Grunty's Lair from Banjo Kazooie. I thought more parts of the hub were accessible from the current segment. All four parts of the worlds are connected from the starting position. I also didn't think that the other siblings were required, I thought they were optional skinsEven with all the problems. I still enjoyed this a lot. hopefully this game get's bonus content and worlds.
_childDocuments_.name: Cavern of Dreams

_childDocuments_.review: Big Banjo & Kazooie fan, and I can say that this game has been the closest to that series in terms of atmosphere, music and overall vibes. Really loved all the in-game options, such as the blur effect you can toggle on/off (I had it on, made me feel like I was playing a CRT on my monitor). No notes really other then if you're a big fan of N64 platformers then this game is a no-brainer for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Cavern of Dreams

_childDocuments_.review: I originally bought this version, absolutely loved it, but then bought and played it on the Nintendo Switch due to having time away from home and super wanting to play this game. If you feel as though it may not be accurate due to the system on which I played please feel free to look away or disregard my opinion.----------------------- Super Interesting Speed/Jump Mechanics- Actual Weight to Jumps- Writing/Dialogue- The N64 era visuals are On Point- Sound Design is superb- Level Design/Variety- The Music- The Length (short) (could also be a positive depending on your lifestyle)----------------------Cavern of Dreams is absolutely a blast of a small game, if you've enjoyed the recent burst of small indie 3D platformer projects like Psuedoregalia, Corn Kidz, Orbo's Odyssey, Super Kiwi 64, Lunistice or others you will absolutely enjoy this game.Cavern of Dreams is a super simple story of a dragon named Fynn losing his baby brothers eggs to a strange bat girl named Luna and using the guidance of a mentor named Sage trying to get them back. You might not be playing for the story, but if you're interested please read the spoilersMore than Corn Kidz or any others in recent times Cavern of Dreams wears its inspirations on its sleeve, it feels more like Banjo Kazooie or Donkey Kong 64 more than any of the others and it's not a bad thing at all. It's a very straightforward collect-a-thon with plenty of goofy off the wall characters and writing beats and super interesting lands with super interesting visuals that feel as though classic RAREWARE never truly left us.While Cavern of Dreams takes a lot of inspiration from RAREWARE games of the past it also definitely does its own things that make it stand out and above those games. Especially in the area of movement, fluidity, and game mechanics. The use of all of the different parts between flying, rolling, jumping, speed gathering, horn and tail jumping make for some of the most rapid pace fun platforming to be had. At first I was absolutely wary with the slow movements of Fynn but once Sage starts doling out new upgrades you wind up with a full set of absolutely wacky moves that all seem to bounce off of one another in weird and interesting ways. Even though the stages are small and contained they each have interesting set pieces to utilize the new and old moves you are acquiring every few eggs gathered.As for minor downsides we have a few namely in the music area. There are so few areas in the game due to its length and that is nothing to hold against the game itself, but when there are so few areas the music selection for certain areas needs to pop as best as it can, and Cavern of Dreams holds itself up very strongly in this area. However, there are a few areas where the music just doesn't sit right with what the game seems to be conveying at that time. Particularly the paintings you enter into at the end of the game seem super phoned in with the desert theme and snake theme in particular not conveying the loneliness and desolation of a dreamlike creation the rest of the game wanted you to feel at that current point.The only major downside I have with the game is that for collect-a-thon fanatics like myself the game is not long enough, it's the same issue that a lot of these newer indie platformers invoking the spirit of the N64 suffer from. If you want an exploration/puzzle/platformer game that you can fully beat in 3-4 hours this absolutely fits that bill and it's perfect for a busy lifestyle because of that. I can definitely see the game being played on future Awesome Games Done Quick and would absolutely love to see what the speedrun community does with it because of its short length. Cavern of Dreams was done with love and care and passion and chutzpah and moxie and I don't fault the short length of it at all because, just like the other mentioned games above, making games is super hard work with sometimes very little payoff. I absolutely reccomend it for anyone of any ageThis game ABSOLUTELY will pull you even further in once you've gathered everything and simply start exploring. The last powerup that you get is the ability to fly throughout the worlds and break boundaries and nothing has had me more excited for a final powerup in a game in a while. Bynine absolutely takes the cake for doing this. It astounded me flying out into the voids to see all of the weird things that were there and activating different devices just to see screens shake or have replicas of characters fly in from the sides at high speeds suddenly. Cavern of Dreams is a fitting name for the last portion of the game because of how surreal it feels to just fly around and see all of the out of bounds wackiness in each area. Nearly everything in the game you see is reachable and it feels like a fever dream. It is absolutely something 11 year old me playing Ratchet and Clank wanted in any video game and seeing it in a modern day game now still puts a smile on my face.Beyond the exploration though reading each of the signs that Luna and Sage have left for you in impossible to reach areas leaves the story of an abandoned creative who turned to destruction for attention and anyone who is into the arts will likely feel this story super personally. I'm not sure what happened to Bynine, but dear lord you made me cry and happy and personally felt with all the little things scattered about. You've made me want to learn Blender so I can make my own 3D worlds. I cannot wait to see if Bynine does more stuff in the future you absolutely have sold me. Also if you end up reading this I see you are a gigantic Pokemon fan, I would love a creature collection game, just tossing that out there.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm always in the mood for a fun 3D platformer as a fan of the genre myself, and this game really scratched that itch for me. Fun for all age groups, this charming game is bound to put a smile on your face while you play as it did for me.The roll move did take a little while for me to get used to at first, but once I got it down, I really enjoyed using it to see how I could use it in various different situations and I can see some genuine speedrun potential out of this move if you're into that sort of experience. It is also needed for several eggs so it's a good idea to practice this, as well as the other moves you gradually learn along the way, as much as possible.This is a collect-a-thon, and a fun one at that, too. Levels are just the right size for what they are and feature just the right amount of collectables, making 100% feel nowhere near as tedious as other games. It also encourages exploration and self-discovery as the game barely tells you anything and never instructs you where to go, so finding everything in a level feels rewarding, especially if you manage to do so all on your own. Nothing in this game feels too cryptic as there are just enough visual and dialogue clues to help guide you along without giving away the entire solution.This game does not feature any combat whatsoever, and is actually something I can appreciate. Many other platformers I've played either have a very basic attack that lacks depth or force you to fight enemies to open the way forward in a game not built for it, so the lack of any form of combat in a platformer is nice to see for a change. This, combined with the very relaxing atmosphere and dreamy aesthetic, makes this a very cosy 3D platformer that feels so good to play when you're stressed out and need to relax.Fans of N64 era graphics will be delighted by this one! This game looks and feels like it was made for the N64. It really makes you feel like a young kid again, especially with the aforementioned cosy vibes it provides. Games like this also prove that you don't need cutting edge graphics to make a game fun or look appealing.I do have a couple of criticisms against this game, however - one of which would be that (much like many other N64 games) you're forced to use the analogue stick to navigate menus when it would work so much better with a directional pad. This makes menu navigation feel much less responsive than I would like, especially when another N64 inspired platformer I played, Corn Kidz 64, also lets you use the d-pad in menus. I used an XBOX One controller to play this game, so this may not be the case for you if you're using a keyboard.Another thing I wasn't a fan of was that pressing the B button to exit the pause menu also activates your tail/throw move, which has messed me up on a few occasions. Climbing up poles also feels a little bit jank, though this is only really a problem for when the game expects you to jump from one pole to another; this is especially noticeable in one section of the final world where it can be difficult to judge exactly which direction you need to face or when to jump off to connect to the other pole. Fortunately, climbing isn't something you do in this game very often.Even with these minor issues, I had a great time playing this. It's a bit on the shorter side of things for sure; there's only 4 levels total, 5 if you include the HUB area, as well as 3 bonus levels, and you can beat it in about 4-6 hours or 8 hours for 100%. However, this is a case of short and sweet, and you definitely get your money's worth out of it. Consider checking this game out if you're a fan of 3D platformers. :)

_childDocuments_.review: This is a wonderful game! It perfectly captures the charm and sense of mystery that I first felt when playing the original Banjo-Kazooie, while very much establishing a unique atmosphere and identity of its own too.The character and level designs are phenomenal, with gorgeous use of colour and so much personality. The game's worlds are full of vividly memorable set-pieces, and the adorable hero Fynn's imaginative suite of dragon-themed movement abilities makes navigating these spaces feel fun, fresh, fluid, and responsive.The game's packed with challenges, between collecting secret cards and rescuing all of Fynn's baby dragon siblings! At the same time, the number of collectibles is nicely balanced and each one feels placed with purpose - deftly avoiding that '90s platformer pitfall where a game can feel unsatisfyingly over-padded. It's a well-paced and carefully-crafted game that doesn't drag on (ho ho) too long!I would consider this a must-play if you're a fan of 3D platformers, and can't wait to see what the developer has in store for us (or Fynn) next!

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic, nostalgic, and adorable. It feels like revisiting my favorite N64 games, without emulating the dated controls or camera issues from that era.While there are environmental hazards, and things that can harm you, there's no fighting or killing. This game is 100% focused on exploring its charming world, solving puzzles, and finding secrets. That said, there's certainly tension, stakes, and even some spooky moments along the way. _childDocuments_.review: Fun little Platformer with plenty of challenge..  I will be honest. its been a few years since I dived deeply into these types.. _childDocuments_.review: My favorite game to release in 2023.I feel, as a speedrunner of the game, that perhaps I should put my thoughts on the gameplay first, but I think that does the game a disservice. While it is a joy to play and master the movement of, what really stands out to me about Cavern of Dreams is its ability to set an almost inscrutable but very well-crafted atmosphere. The exact tone shifts from area to area, but regardless of where you go, there is a baseline feeling of melancholy. The small cast of characters is almost universally warm and polite, in their own ways, but at the same time it all feels a bit lonely. Not in the sense of the game's areas having too little to do, but in the sense that these people are lonely, and that living in the Cavern is lonely.The story, while fairly understated, is heavy with its themes, and I'd encourage anyone who plays it to think on it for a while. It isn't particularly up-front about it, particularly at the start of the game, but it is a story about art, and about the pressure to create happy, uplifting art, and about how that conflicts with the ability of art to serve as a coping mechanism for loss, and-I could go on and on for a while, but it's about quite a few things, many of them related to art.But it's ALSO a game about giving you a variety of fun toys to move around the world with. Both basic movement techniques taught in-game and advanced ones you can discover on your own are incredibly versatile, allowing you to traverse both horizontal and vertical distances with satisfying ease once you master them. While there is a fairly clear progression to follow through the game on a standard playthrough, the order you can take things in is extremely flexible thanks to the tail upgrade - your first one, unlocked very shortly after starting the game - being central to several of those advanced movement options.On top of it all, Cavern of Dreams doesn't outstay its welcome. A casual, blind, 100% playthrough will probably last somewhere from 5 to 10 hours, depending on how much you mess around exploring areas where no collectibles are hidden. Non-completionist playthroughs are even shorter, and if you end up speedrunning the game, the Any% run (for those unfamiliar with speedrun categories, the objective here is to complete the game as quickly as possible, regardless of how many collectibles you pick up) takes under 20 minutes. It's not so short that I was left wanting more, but not so long that I grew tired of it.Overall, exceptionally good game in presentation, story (though more-so in its themes than any unique twists or structure), and gameplay. A perfect package.also you get to play as just the cutest dragon there ever was

_childDocuments_.review: The Cavern of dreams is a very cute 3D platformer.  You play as Fynn, and have to collect all of your sibling's eggs throughout the levels and overworld.  Overall, it's nice, not the most polished in the world, but nice.  Also, turn off blurring in the settings, the game looks much better without it.Fynn's movement is all over the place.  On his own, he's slow.  However, he can roll, which functions as the run once you got the hang of it.  The only flaw is that there's no way to go faster up hill.  This does become a problem.  Fynn's upgrades are a nice idea in theory.  In practice gameplay wise it's a fine system.  But it plays mind games with you.  Can you not get this collectible right now because you don't have the upgrade to get it?  Or is it from a lack of skill/exploration?  I got stuck for a half hour trying to find the next world because what I thought wasn't reachable yet, it was.  There's a button near the snow globe.  Fynn's normal jump is tiny.  In order to jump, it feels that you really have to be committed to it most of the time.  I got very used to using Fynn's bigger charge up jumps, that I got stuck in a timed section where Fynn's normal jumps could make it.  Though his normal jump is so small, there are a lot of places it can't reach.The levels themselves, they're nice.  Pretty much what one would expect from a retro platformer like this, each even coming with their own NPC you have to do a quest for to give it more life.  Though one major complaint I have about this game is that the levels just get more annoying as you go on.  It just feels like the further I got into the game, the more often I would get angry at not being able to do the thing.  This comes to a head in the final level.  There's this section where there are these jumps.  If you fail, you have to walk a minute back to them.  And then there's the final boss that really got on my nerves.  I recommend getting all 40 eggs, the reward is worth it.  Overall, while the Cavern of Dreams is charming, I feel like I spent about a third of my time being angry at Fynn's limited movement or the level design.  But I did come away liking it overall in the end.  If this game looks like it's something you would be interested in, I recommend giving it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: Cavern of Dreams is a fun, indie spiritual successor to 3D platform mascot collectathons of the N64/PSX era such as Banjo-Kazooie and Spyro. The genre holds a place in my heart and I've played many, many of them. It's a shame that it feels like a dying breed sometimes, with only a few games being made by big budget studios such as Mario Odyssey or the Ratchet and Clank games. Fortunately a vibrant indie scene for platformers has sprung up to fill this void, and Cavern of Dreams feels like homage, tribute and spiritual successor all at once. It very much wants to forge its own path but hasn't forgotten its roots. Positives:-Gorgeous graphics! This is the sort of game that perfectly encapsulated how people perceived N64/PSX graphics back in the day, similar to what Shovel Knight did for 8-bit graphics.-Level design and stages are a lot of fun. There are relatively few worlds (the hub world and four level worlds) given that this is an indie project without the production values you'd expect like Yooka-Laylee, but they're creative and fun to explore, especially the airship level.-Lots of fun ways to collect eggs and other collectibles. Levels are detailed and have lots of signposting for you to mark something you might want to come back to later.-Interconnectivity between the levels is cool and something none of the platformers of the N64/PSX era did.-Very accessible. $13 is extremely reasonable as a price point and just about anyone can play this game regardless of skill level. Spec-wise this game can run on a potato so don't worry about needing a beefy PC.-Without spoiling, the reward for getting all 40 eggs is a ton of fun.Neutral:-I'd have liked to see more emphasis on platforming. The platforming sections are some of the highlights of the game, and having as few of them as there are feels like missed potential.-The music isn't bad, but it's not particularly memorable either. It makes the game feel a little muted compared to games like Banjo-Kazooie but it's not a dealbreaker by any means.Negative:-Even for third party platformers the camera has a habit of being your worst enemy and will get you killed.-Controls are a little sticky, like the double jump ability seems to not trigger sometimes.-Some of the eggs are very difficult to find and hidden in really obscure places to the point of seeming unfair. -The final world felt a little padded and involved some backtracking to the point where it started to slog a little even with how relatively short the game is.-Really minor but achievements don't seem to trigger, or at least they didn't for med.Additional Details:As of this review I've cleared the game after finding all 40 eggs in about six hours. If you don't care about completion you can clear it in 3-5 hours. I do plan on going back and collecting the trivia cards. Graphics options are limited but as I mentioned earlier the game run on any kind of PC under the sun so don't even worry about compatibility. Final Verdict (Anyone Should Buy, Genre Fans Should Buy, Wait For Sale, Avoid): Anyone Should Buy. It may not be the most sophisticated 3D platformer but it's a wonderful way to get into the genre and I hope to see more from this developer!

_childDocuments_.review: Cute game.  its a 6 hour collectathon with some cute characters for not-much money.  I even got it in a bundle with some other platformers so its worth it.  Movement is fluid and you unlock a few new abilities as you play so it works well enough.  The bubble ability is a bit finicky at times but not much of a problem.  Worth noting I did get all 40 eggs in this.  If you're looking for a short fun collectathon, this will probably fit your needs.  Theres a select few times I think I skipped what they actually wanted me to do by using the ability at hand as well which is another plus for some people.I did have some issues.  Firstly, I did get completely stuck at a couple of points with no idea how to move forward.  I even got every single egg in the Prismatic Palace cause I didnt know where the next stage was; turns out it was in a room I had already cleared out without the ability I needed to move open the next area.  Some eggs will be a tad annoying to find, and more cause the puzzle wasnt explained well enough or the mechanism was hard to find.  This isnt a huge issue mind you, and what eggs you struggle with probably will change depending who you are.  The roadblock that annoyed me the most was the Final level where theres a portrait of Sage that said "Something was off?" and I thought that was a hint at some lore or something.  But no, it turns out thats a puzzle you have to solve in order to open the green and red doors in the foyer.However, One more kind of esoteric problem actually comes from the final boss.  Before you fight them, you get the message "This is the final battle, there is no return" which, to me, signalled that I should get every egg *BEFORE* this final fight.  So I gather all the eggs, get an OP ability, and it ends up breaking the boss.  Its not even that easy to just "not use it" because of what the ability is , so I feel like I kinda cheated around the boss fight.  I *WAS* gonna fight the boss before getting the ability but just having that message there told me "you have no return" so I decided to get them first.  And whats funny is that there actually was a return.  You go back to the cavern and get the option to explore again right after to finish up the egg hunt.  Maybe you cant fight the final boss again after this fight is done but if that one message wasnt there, I probably would've enjoyed the boss fight more just cause I fought them without the OP final ability.Those two points are pretty minor though; I just dont have much to say on the parts it did well cause...it does em well.  It has what you'd expect of a good, short collectathon.  Characters, movement, exploration, so I'd recommend it overall.  Just expect one or two "BS" eggs and fight the final boss BEFORE getting every egg.  You WILL be able to 100% after so dont worry.

_childDocuments_.review: If you'd shown me gameplay of Cavern of Dreams and told me it was a Nintendo 64 game, I would've believed you. There's barely anything that gives it away as being a game released in 2023. I could still believe it was a lost relic from a bygone era, ported to Steam out of the blue nearly 30 years after abandoned development.The only clue is how fluidly it controls. Functional controls for fully 3D platformers were doable on the N64 and its contemporaries, but few managed quite like Banjo-Kazooie, or competitors like Spyro the Dragon, the likes of which are obvious inspirations for this game. Fynn controls superbly well, however there are oftentimes where ledges require a very specific kind of distance to be leapt from, or the height is  off. Otherwise, Fynn feels like a capable protagonist with his ability to roll around the decently-sized maps and the handful of upgrades he'll see from restoring magic to the Cavern of Dreams by rescuing his siblings.There are two collectables, only one of which is mandatory: the dragon eggs, which can be hatched to release Fynn's siblings to be played with (or, at risk of a scolding, can even be beaten and made to feel awful); the other are encyclopedia cards which contain lore. It's quite a relief that the game doesn't overwhelm the player with lots of tat to sniff out, dragging the expected playtime beyond what it needs to be. Even so, these collectables can be challenging and require a lot of backtracking, and some may leave you stumped without a guide. Fortunately, if you collect enough of your siblings from one area, they'll give you cryptic clues when you return to the lobby.There's little challenge from the game itself. Enemies and level hazards are far and few between, and what damage they do is only meant to launch you away to reset your progress on a slippery climb, or into a bottomless chasm. With there being no lives and little need for more than a handful of checkpoints, Fynn can travel most levels without difficulty. The greatest challenge is figuring out how to reach the eggs tucked away behind walls, or cards in plain sight but ever so slightly out of reach.All the puzzles make sense and some are as simple as thwacking a wall that has an off-colour shade to the rest of it, revealing a hole you can travel through. Others are about rotating statues or bringing an item to a character without dropping it. Despite the abundance of tricks you've got to figure out, none of them feel spiteful or out to get you. There's no moments where you have to play mind games with the developers, and any that could be accused of that are resolved by unlocking the final ability after defeating the end boss: the ability to fly without restriction.The levels are, I'm afraid to say, fairly generic and familiar. Most are in some way an homage to Banjo-Kazooie; the title itself is not so much a nod as a headbang to the lobby of the Bear and Bird's first adventure. But they're not so large and packed with things that you'll get sick of them, except maybe for Prismic Palace, which I found to be the most challenging of levels. As you might guess, that's an icy-crystal world. Who would've thought a place called the Coils of Agony would be the most refreshing level?Speaking of which, there are some unsettling areas of this game. Disturbing paintings that pull Fynn toward them to drain him of his soul, a giant clown-baby homunculus, mummies starring at the moon in a lifeless wasteland, and there are on occasion fish floating beyond the walls if you manage to clip the camera behind them. It's not  bad, but it did inspire some ideas for creepypasta.Those moments were rare, however, and the rest of the game is a beauty to behold. The level and character designs, the repeated textures stretched out along sharp blocky assets are totally in line with the 32-bit visual style it's going for. The music as well is charming, well worth the purchase of the soundtrack without question. Much as I'd like to go on about the graphics and soundtrack, there's only so many ways I can say I love every bit of it.Cavern of Dreams is fairly short; you can easily get it done in under 10 hours, and there's little reason to come back to it barring revisiting its aesthetics. The game is fun once, and if you want to scratch the nostalgic itch of the days of yore, you may as well play the classics. However, you should still give this a go if you yearn for the return of the 90s platformer or are otherwise looking for a lesson in how to make an authentic game of that style.I hope so very much for a sequel. The developers should be commended for what has been nothing short of a pleasure the whole way through!

_childDocuments_.review: Out of all the new-age 3D platformers I've played, this comes the closest to the style, level design, puzzles, and great writing that I experienced with Banjo-Kazooie back in the day. It's very clear inspiration was taken from Banjo-Kazooie, Spyro, and I presume a touch of Earthbound for the latter half of the game, blended perfectly into their own well-fleshed out world and stories that leave room for speculation. I started off full of nostalgia and warmth with the first level, and ended up on the last level feeling quite perturbed by.... well.... probably best to leave some surprises for those curious! If there's any criticisms, the one floor puzzle in the ice level was a bit too specific with too little guidance, and the controls were a bit frustrating at times when they pushed too hard for the perfect speed and angle, but overall this was a very joyful romp full of surprises and secrets that reminded me of the old Rareware days. I look very forward to the team's future projects, and highly recommend you give this out a try!

_childDocuments_.review: Comparing new 3D platformers to ye classics of old is always fraught with disappointment, as these pastiches very rarely learn the lessons from their predecessors that they ought to have if they're really going to stand up on their own. Cavern of Dreams is one of those rare exceptions where even though it does take a lot from other games, it doesn't do so thoughtlessly and it also manages to have some neat ideas of its own. No, it's not Banjo-Kazooie for a number of reasons, but the game is perfectly digestible without ever being either under or overwhelming, you're given a great move-set that feels specifically designed to test your mastery of the controls and let you kind of set your own pace as you're playing, the world and level design is solid, and the game doesn't unnecessarily waste your time or patience. In other words, it all comes together to be a pretty good game that I very much enjoyed, which is really not something I can hardly ever say about modern 3D platformers that I've played (or rather, tried to play and usually quickly given up on because they're too mediocre and plain just not very interesting or fun).There is also room for improvement, particularly when it comes to memorable writing and characters - not that what's there is bad per se, but maybe a bit too simple, straightforward, and sparse - and also really honing in on your world design to make each one even more distinctive mechanically and thematically (visually and musically as well!). I think if the developer took what they did right from this game and then hit their few weaker-but-still-solid points out of the park in a new title, they could go from having a really quite good game to an actually legitimately great game. Also, the controls are so powerful that it feels like you can accomplish a number of tasks in not what seemed to be unintended ways, but I honestly thought that was part of the fun so you won't hear me complaining about it.Thanks for making a new 3D platformer that I enjoyed, it's the first time in a very long time for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Cavern of Dreams

_childDocuments_.review: A cute, short adventure game that would remind you a lot of old-school 3D Platformers, Cavern of Dreams is a wonderful game to experience as it just fills you with good emotions with how colorful, nice, and stylistic everything is.The movement feels good and rewarding, the platforming is enjoyable and fair, and while the game isn't very difficult it's still a great experience overall, especially with how the game is hands-off to let you mess around or solve things in multiple ways, and how the game rewards you with little secrets in hard-to-reach places.The finale could've been a little harder, , but that's fine.Side note: The blur effect present in the game is toggleable, though I persisted through having it enabled(which resulted in getting a headache when I played for longer than an hour) as I feel the effect is part of the entire point of the game in how "dream-like" everything looks with it.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, a bit disappointed in this one. To start with the good, it does capture the feeling of an N64 game very well. The graphics are cute and well made. It has some interesting ideas for movement, though I can't say much about their execution...I kind of started already with the not so good, huh. While I can appreciate a moveset that allows for creative approach and skill-based speed gain, it still leaves something to be desired. The controls feel pretty fiddly, more than some actual N64 games. Even though the game technically does provide you with several movement options, you are likely to heavily prefer those that work the best. You don't really get to use your full range of movement often. There's also a bit of jank when it comes to movement. You might bounce off the wall when you meant to speed up or ground pound. I also experienced a few bugs, one which even allowed me to sequence break a bit at the beginning of the game. On the note of bugs, the game did crash on me once for seemingly no reason, although the game thankfully autosaves.The game is split into a few worlds, and honestly I'm kind of shocked at how small the whole game is. I was expecting something on the smaller side, though perhaps not to this degree. The worlds are fairly compact and it felt like I was done with most in a matter of minutes. While the game promotes exploration, you'll find there's really not a lot of ground to cover. It doesn't help that the collectibles are pretty limited. There's 3 types of collectibles in total, and I wouldn't consider any of them particularly hard to get. The idea of having no combat is interesting, and it's executed alright, but there are moments when your character just feels useless, being unable to even hinder or stun enemies in your way.The music was alright, just not very catchy. Though I do appreciate any instance of dynamic music. (We should do more of that!) The sound effects were good, nothing too special. Although I did start getting annoyed with character voices towards the end of my playthrough.The story was pretty meh... You have to piece together a bunch of it, which is complimented by some secrets in-game and the encyclopedia. Honestly, I just didn't find it all that compelling or particularly important for the game. I do like the character designs, though like the story much of the character's personality or backstory just ends up feeling unimportant.I have mixed feelings about the game. While I did get that distinctive feel of playing an N64 platformer, I also experienced little but frequent bitter realizations that it just isn't the same... Call it nostalgia blindness, I guess. I don't know if I would call it superficial. It has it's charm and it's not a complete waste of time, but I don't think it's getting into my list of best games of the year.

_childDocuments_.review: Reviewed on Steamdeck: 7/10 - onle recommended for some.Cavern of Dreams attempted to capture the nostalgia of N64 titles of old and present something new in what is an enjoyable 5-8 hour journey with its protagonist Fynn. However, while Bynine Studio did an excellent job hitting some key elements of what made some of the classics great this debut N64-styled puzzle platformer will not be for everyone. If you’re like me then watching the trailer and looking at screenshots of this game reminded you of childhood favorites and had you immediately excited. When you start the game will instantly recognize all of the influences that went into this game when it comes to graphics, me,nus and art direction. It wastes no time giving you the classic “bad person did this go collect the things to make it right” story. Collect the eggs of your siblings that have been scattered by a bat for some reason, hatch them, feed them mushrooms that you collect to help them grow, become stronger from helping your siblings (strength is only used to access new places and not for combat), and make your way to the cavern of nightmares. Besides collectible cards that tell you about the different things in the world, there isn’t much of a story to be told.Of all the things that I enjoyed in this game I would have to say the music and sound design was my favorite. Benjamin Keckley, if you read this my hat is off to you. Even after I put the game down I still had its melodic tracks going through my head. The little grunts and sounds your character makes performing certain actions are cute and somehow hilarious at the same time. Everything from going through doors to new areas, death, and picking up collectibles had that same satisfying feeling I got from the games I used to play (for me namely Banjo-Kazooie). The controls and camera are tight and easy to master which is good because this game is almost all platforming. Only a couple of times did I find myself dying due to an odd camera angle that caused me to fall or miss my target. As you collect eggs you unlock abilities that make certain areas or challenges easier and progress the “story”. The move sets you unlock are plentiful, but not always necessary to solve a problem or get to a certain area which gives a well-rounded approach to many of the platforming challenges you will encounter and keeps the game moving forward at a nice pace. I found it satisfying to jump, fly, and swim my way through the four worlds you are given to explore. If platforming is one half of this game solving puzzles is the other. After playing it I was honestly surprised that it doesn’t include the fact that it's a puzzle game on its Steam page. They are plentiful, varied, and for the most part easy to solve with only a few making me sit there and scratch my head or backtrack to other worlds/ areas to find something to complete them. I appreciated that they weren't overly difficult as they kept the pace of the game moving nicely and I’m not a puzzle-solving kind of person. Exploration is another highlight in this game. Most worlds loop back into other worlds giving it a soft-souls exploration structure. The worlds themselves aren’t massive but are unique and I enjoyed making my way around them and discovering their many secrets. Again, much like those childhood favorites you will find a unique cast of characters in each world with quirky dialog, sounds, quests and puzzles to be solved.However, this game will not be for everyone and something that should be said now is that I realized almost immediately that I was expecting this title to be something that it wasn’t, comparing it, and ultimately that led me to like it less. It’s not a bad game, but it’s not the game I wanted it to be. For some, these will seem like unfair or minor gripes.First I want to talk about combat. There is none. And while it certainly doesn’t need to be in a game to make it good I realize I went into this game thinking there would be at least something to thwack with my tail as I moved about the world. There are enemies, but without a health meter for them to tick down all they do is shoot you across the map and royally screw whatever puzzle or platform you were attempting. This often leads to you falling to your death, but generous respawns don't have you backtracking much if at all. But I still wish there was something to fight in this world. I'm not saying the combat in Mario, Banjo-Kazooie, or even Spyro was complex, but it was fun and made going from place to place and the world lore more engaging. I think that many of the design decisions with enemies and environmental hazards had speedrunners in mind when being implemented. At least it feels that way. The world is cute. Almost too cute for my taste. And if you enjoyed the semi-dark themes of some of your favorite N64 titles (again such as Banjo-Kazooie for me) you might find this game a little obnoxious at times. While at first the protagonist Fynn not having much to say didn’t bother me I realized that his lack of things to say (he does say some things) left me unattached to him and the world he was in. And while the characters you meet in other worlds are unique his lack of vocal interaction with them was disappointing and as a result, I didn’t find that I cared for the world much or the minor lore within it. Aside from my tastes and expectations of N64-style games, there were a few things I just found downright annoying. For the most part, getting to areas in levels was straightforward, but each time I would save and quit the game it would send me back to the central hub instead of where I was in the world so I would have to navigate my way back to where I left off. A minor but still frustrating thing that I’m unsure why was included in the game. There is also a very odd issue where if you are holding an item and pause when you unpause you just throw the item you were carrying. This had me throw the item I was using over a ledge many a time if I backed out of the pause menu using the B button. Because of these things, the world eventually felt shallow to me. I could see the passion put into this game and was impressed by the dedication to releasing a finished product, but alas I didn’t feel much for it. By the end it was just something to beat for me.Overall the game was still enjoyable and I liked what I experienced once I came to terms that I wasn't going to be reliving my childhood. I hope that the developer continues to make titles of grander scope, including some sort of combat system, bigger worlds, and more engaging characters. The controls, camera, puzzles, platforming, and above all music/ sound design were on point. TL;DR: This is a puzzle platformer with great music, good exploration, and solid core mechanics, but if you want to enjoy it fully don’t do what I did and expect it to be like some of the games you used to play.
