_childDocuments_.review: In terms of puzzles, there is a huge variety spread out across the world which constantly draw your attention and keep you playing. As a single player puzzle game enjoyer, I really liked the open world aspect that adds exploration to the mix.The shy auras and morphic fractals can get annoying and don't really feel like puzzles, but otherwise there are a lot of cool concepts. I personally like finding the secret challenges. I accidentally found one while looking for a logic grid puzzle and it is incredibly satisfying, reminiscent of finding the first environment puzzle in the Witness.It can be a bit jarring to go from relaxing exploration mode to 5 STAR ULTRA DIFFICULT PUZZLE SOLVING, but that kinda comes with the territory of mixing the puzzles together in a bigger world. You can ignore certain types based on your mood but it feels a bit bad having to leave a puzzle undone because you weren't prepared to engage your brain at that exact moment.I would like to see maybe a puzzle location indicator for when you've  nearly completed an area. It can be difficult to find the last logic grid or whatever in the larger zones and I want to find all the things.It is a bit of a shame that some of the higher level puzzles don't spawn in the early areas because it reduces the desire to re-explore those sections later in the game.The sheer number of puzzles you need to solve to get all the unlockables per area seems extreme. I like stopping to complete random puzzles on my way to do other stuff, but I don't think I'll ever have time to max out everything.Obviously, more character customization options would be appreciated but that's a pretty minor thing. I did experience the bug where the glowing hair (unlocked by completing the main quest line) locked after I changed my character appearance and then I couldn't get it back which was sad.Islands of Insight is a compelling, almost addictive, single player puzzle game experience with great variety and fun puzzles when it works. When it doesn't work, you're out the money and 35 GB of storage space. If they ever get the issues fixed and I can play again, I'll update my review to be positive. (See update below) Seems like patch 1.0.13a fixed my issue and I'm able to play again! :DI'm not going to ask for a refund because I was really enjoying the gameplay (albeit on the lowest possible graphics settings because my computer is actually a potato) for the time I was able to play.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very chill puzzle game that has the air of a fantasy quest.  There's no combat or any real stakes.  It's also pretty to look at.  Some of the puzzle types don't make sense to me (like the Galaxy logic boxes), but maybe I'll get there.  All I know is that last night, it was 12:30am and I said I'll just finish up this grouping of puzzles, and then it was 2:30.  It's been a while since a game did that.  The controls can be a little clunky.  It's difficult to accurately move quickly, whether it's flying through a series of rings or sprinting to touch scattered orbs in a certain amount of time, but it can be done if you want.  There's also the ability to socialize in the game, but that's not something I'm interested in, really.  But it is fun to watch other players bounce and glide around this world with you.

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like puzzles?  Do you like the idea of having a whole bunch of different types of them in one game?  Does the idea of a seemingly inexhaustable supply of the loopy things get you excited?  How about the prospect of finding hidden puzzles under that rock you just tripped over?  Maybe add a bit of platforming and flight?If you said yes to these questions, then oh boy have I got the good time fun game for you.This game, I gotta say, is one wild experience.  At it's core it's rather similar to The Witness in that a huge part of it is exploring different areas, finding and solving puzzles as you go.  Though it lacks the rather pretentious elements that game has... it's not trying to get you to have a super deep philosophy meditation or something.  There's lore to find here, but it's not super complicated or anything... not too hard to piece together what's going on, and it never gets in the way of anything.No, the puzzles and exploration are the focus here.  This is an absolutely ENORMOUS world, with every square foot of it just full of puzzles.   So freaking many of them.  There are many types, too, of varying complexity.There's the "tile" ones, where you're dropping black & white tiles into a grid to fill it while following certain rules, there's the ... er... tower thing, where you stand on this big square with all these towers and you gotta find just the spot where you can connect with all of them, there's funky match-3 puzzles, and so on.But also, there's more than just those sorts.  The game's idea of what a puzzle is can be all over the place, in a good way, really.  For instance sometimes you might find these weird pointy spire things, poke it and it'll put out this huge field, and somewhere in there, is 5 hidden whatsits to find.  Or there's the green/red box things that are all about getting the right vantage point, once you manage to find both of them.  Or nearly invisible archways to find.  Floaty jumbled rings where you're trying to get a perfect line through them, weird ball things that want you to run after them and parkour your way to victory (read: jump wrong and fall off a cliff).  Or maybe those truly devious glass labyrinths, where you cant find the exit despite that you're staring directly at it because the walls are made of glass and then you fall in that accursed pit AGAIN because you forgot it was there just like the last 500 times you fell in it, and then you found a tile puzzle IN the labyrinth and solved it but got distracted and fell in that pit again afterwards-*ahem*  I think you get the idea.  Lots of puzzles.  Lots of things to find.  Lots of stuff to DO.  The difficulty of all these things varies wildly, too.  Any given puzzle can range from "so easy I can do it in seconds", to "why would you do this to me".  This is really good, because it ensures that there's something for everyone here, and stuff to do within each puzzle type even if you have trouble with that type.  Like, for me, I just cant grasp the pattern things.  I can do only the lowest difficulty of those.  But hey, that's okay.  There's still plenty of them that I can do because there's SO MANY (just like everything else), but there's also going to be just as many to challenge experts, too.And if you find you're getting stuck on something?  No reason to get frustrated or anything.  Just back out of it, and go find a different thing to do.  The game very rarely forces you to do specific puzzles.  Though, this changes a bit in the "enclaves", which are basically the game's dungeons where you unlock new puzzle types or whatever.  These can be much harder, and fully completing one is absolutely not easy.  But you dont have to 100% any of them, and in fact the game warns you that trying to do so could be a bit too much, particularly considering just how darned sneaky the devs can be in hiding some of the puzzles.  Be prepared to get lost and confused from time to time (while tripping over puzzles).Honestly what truly amazes me about this game is that none of this ever becomes tiresome.  However much I do, I always want to do more, and there always IS more.  These dont stop being fun, even when I fall into the glass holes of stupid.Not that it's perfect, mind you.  In particular, the fractal puzzles are likely to frustrate you, due to the weirdness of the controls.  As someone who is very enthusiastic about fractals, this part was disappointing to me.  I love that fractals are in the game, but the way that puzzle type is controlled makes me want to stab a clown.Then there's the other problem, the elephant in the room:  This game is always online.  The devs seem to have gone for an odd MMO-ish approach, for... some reason.  I cannot grasp why.  There's cosmetics to earn (with in-game currency only) and daily quests and so on, and you'll see other players running around doing things.  From a gameplay perspective, this doesnt at all impact what you are doing... other players cannot interfere with you, and if they walk up to some tile puzzle or whatever and do it, that puzzle wont be done on your end (and you can walk up and do it too at the same time, but in a separate instance.  You'll never have something solved FOR you).  The issue isnt in the gameplay, it's in the "online only" part.  You'll get some rubberbanding and server boots every now and then.  Not enough to ruin it, mind you.  Not even close.  It's been pretty rare for me.  But it's there, and... I dont know WHY.  It makes little sense to me.Fortunately, there IS an offline mode coming, so that's good.  Still, rather baffling.I have little else to complain about, though.  For such an utterly enormous game to have so few things for me to whine about... that's rare.  That's very rare.  Really everything is so darned GOOD here.  Seriously, I just adore this one.  I love everything about it, even if the controls on the fractals are made of crazy.  What an absolute gem this is.  It deserves so many more sales than it's getting, so be a dear and do pick it up, eh?

_childDocuments_.review: Islands of Insight is a phenomenal puzzle game with an unbelievably flexible logic grid system, but it's clear that the game had an identity crisis and was ultimately living on borrowed time. Why a mostly solo puzzle-solving experience had to be designed as an MMO is a mystery. As a result, the game suffered from technical issues (e.g. connectivity, rubber banding) where it really didn't need to suffer. For a niche genre, garnering a player count large enough to sustain the servers was always going to be a challenge. While the post-launch addition of an offline mode is great, it too suffers from bugs and performance issues. The servers will be shut down in the upcoming, final update due at the end of this month, and the developers have explicitly stated that this final update will not feature bug fixes (though there will be a change to reduce SSD wear).Now, I'd like to see Islands of Insight endure far beyond that, but I honestly cannot recommend it in good faith in its current shambolic state (at least for full price). One thing this game never lacked was potential. Even just the grid puzzles could make for an excellent standalone experience that could rival the likes of The Witness. The formula is already there, but it has been completely buried in the poor execution. That it will soon be abandoned is a shame.

_childDocuments_.review: I can recommend this game, with one caveat:Do NOT play this game if you have a below average gpu or cpu. It is a nightmare to run on my desktop with 16gb ram, a gtx 1070 and ryzen 5 3600. This is after I adjusted all graphics settings to low, resolution to 1440p and frame limit 60fps. It was using all of my CPU core, 60-80% of my GPU and most of my ram. My desktop's fans were in overdrive. So, even if you think "well I can just lower my settings" it unfortunately doesn't work that well. Yes, I could've gone with a lower resolution, but my setup ran the talos principle 2 very well and that has a similar (if not better at the settings I got) graphical fidelity. As a side note this game has server-side movement on a basically single-player experience. Ethernet and being in the right country (no Australia servers LOL) help with this.  The game's puzzle design is excellent, its world is well made and the enclaves, which are their own complete puzzle experience, are a great place to run around and find new puzzles. The main islands are much less interesting, mostly having puzzles that rotate around and aren't difficult to find or complete. There are areas that are static within the main island which function as a sort of "mini enclave" and have a linear set of puzzles for you to complete. Puzzle design has wide range of difficulties and enjoyment. Plenty are easy enough a 3 year old could do it, while the hardest are comparable to really difficult sudoku or minesweeper. All 100% logical but just really, REALLY difficult. And they can range from very enjoyable to frustrating or uninteresting. Skydrops are the least interesting, and easy, Armillary rings are easy but really fun, logic grids when difficult are fun but sometimes the difficulty comes from being unintuitive (rarely). This game has quantity and quality, so you can pick and choose which puzzles you play to avoid frustration. The multiplayer system is pretty much just emotes, skins and pings, which let me ping all of the most difficult hidden cubes I found to a new player :O. There are friend requests and the ability to block people too. Movement is fluid, and VERY quick. I went around the game without sprinting for my first 5 hours and it didnt make a big difference until I tried to find every hidden cube by circling around the same island 20 times. The game is completionist bait; do not try to complete every area you come across. It will make your experience with the game worse. The game never needs you to complete islands 100% for any rewards but it does have a puzzle counter, which includes hidden cubes, arguably the most frustrating/annoying things to find all of. They're near invisible, have a sound cue that only happens when you're practically snug with them, and can be found in some very unintuitive places. They're like if Koroks could be under any rock in botw.  If an island doesn't have these cubes it is much more fun to reach 100%

_childDocuments_.review: Let's get this out of the way: The game is good. It is true that multiplayer is pointless, and without any meaningful way to interact with others beyond emotes, the game is certainly no Uru Online. But that said, if you're a logic puzzle fan, this is heaven. So many logic grids!To this point there's only been one puzzle type I truly dislike; the fractal puzzles, which as far as I can tell, are universally disliked because of how finnicky they are to solve. I wouldn't be surprised if they got replaced at some point. I also question whether mazes truly are puzzles but I guess if they're in every point and click adventure game ever made, they have to be here.Optimization is definitely a problem they'll need to solve. This is a visually rich game but it comes at a significant performance cost. I have not tried it on my Steam Deck yet, but based on my gaming laptop's performance, I'm not expecting anything great. But this also is definitely more of a mouse & keyboard kind of game anyway.It definitely taps into the same kind of dopamine rush that Genshin Impact's open world puzzles do. Just running around constantly finding puzzles to solve, it's a similar feeling. The skills in the skill tree are decent ones for a puzzle game, and the constant rewards for leveling up and solving optional puzzles is nice, it keeps the drive going.The story orbs you come across are so generic and philosophical that they start to feel like eating a toast sandwich. They go in one ear and right out the other. I don't need stakes in my open world puzzle game, but I have no real incentive to seek out the lore orbs because I have such an inert apathy to what they say.Just treat this as a single-player logic puzzler with an open world like The Witness, and ignore the philosophy--- hey, just like The Witness! I guess there are more parallels than I thought.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has had a strange, rocky, and unfortunately short life. People reading this after October 2024 might never know what the game was like in its brief prime.An extremely important thing to understand about this game is that the elevator pitch was basically "what if you had an MMO that was centered around puzzles instead of combat?" So the entire point was to have many players running around a shared space and solving puzzles. The puzzles are varied and enjoyable, but unfortunately they're all necessarily single-player. While I personally like the puzzle MMO concept, there simply weren't any features that justified the always-online multiplayer framework. So it went from being an always-online game (with an anti-cheat which was eventually removed) to having an optional offline mode for people with connection issues, and finally as of Oct 2024 it became offline-only.IOI is an open world absolutely littered with bite-sized puzzles which periodically refresh. The activities and interactables vary in type ("puzzle" is a catchall for all types): hidden objects, ring-races, etc., and a lot of binary logic tile puzzles. A warning for people who are used to pure puzzle games: your control of the character within the environment is an important part of the game. Not only do you navigate the world-space to access the various puzzles, but there is some precise jumping, running, and gliding, some of which is used in time/precision trials (you get effectively unlimited tries in those challenges).You can choose to play in first- or third-person, but first-person is strongly recommended for several perspective-based puzzle types.Note that there is one puzzle type that is 100% dependent on your ability to hear audio (this can be brute-forced with rechargeable hints), and there's also a type of hidden interactable that is difficult to find (but not impossible) without audio cues.Most of the puzzles that are scattered around the open world are randomized from a vast pool and get cycled out periodically, so you're free to just wander around and do whatever grabs your attention.The game also contains a number of islands with a curated set of puzzles that don't refresh with new solutions. These islands ("enclaves") are used for progression. They'll be used to gradually introduce new puzzle types (which will subsequently become available in the open world) and to guide you toward new regions with more complex puzzle constraints. Enclaves are typically packed with puzzles themselves, but the quota to move on is a pretty low percentage (You'll be shown a minimum quota of solutions, followed by a bonus goal, and then eventually a 100% goal if you choose to go for a full-clear).Binary logic tile grids are the meat of this game (they're the only puzzle type that explicitly declares a difficulty rating on each puzzle), and they're very good. Some great setters contributed to the puzzle count, and even if you were to ignore other puzzle types, the logic grids would provide plenty of entertainment. I actively play all the puzzle types in the game, but the progress tracker shows that logic grids are far and away my highest XP level.As you solve puzzles, you'll earn a small amount of currency, as well as mastery (xp) toward a level-up. Level rewards vary between currency, cosmetics, and lore entries. Currency can be spent on cosmetics or used to unlock a variety of upgrades (including things like double-jump, increasing the number of hints you can use, or increasing the currency payout for quick or errorless solves).Character customization is a bit underwhelming, but it's not a character-driven game and there's not much occasion to really consider characters' appearance. If you play in first-person (as I do), you really only see your character in a brief camera cut that occurs when you receive a rare reward. With the removal of multiplayer, there's even less cause to care about your character's appearance.Ultimately it's a shame that this game didn't get the support it needed, but the offline-only mode should be close enough to the classic experience that puzzle lovers can still get what they're looking for from it.Matchbox / 10

_childDocuments_.review: This is a puzzle game which has the environmental vibes of Myst, but with none of the BS mind-reading* required for progression.  Some of the puzzles feel kind of like Professor Layton, but only the straightforward logic-y bits and the 3-D visualization bits, not the riddles where there's multiple perfectly reasonable answers and you have to guess which one they want.  Several of the others are more of a "find the out of the way corner where we put A Thing To Find" type of puzzle, which will appeal to players of 90s collectathons like Donkey Kong 64 or Spyro the Dragon.  However, the game seems to be very forgiving in terms of how much you have to actually find in each zone, although I'll come back and update this once I know what's actually required for credits.And the *amount* of content.  I have 7 hours in this game and I'm still in the first major area past the tutorial island -- looking at the world map, I fully expect this will be easily 100+ hours of gameplay.  There's also a lot of character customization options, which I've probably spent more time on than I should; it's something I enjoy (I also play Final Fantasy 14 and have fantasiaed no less than 4 times), and playing online means other people can see my character model too!  However, if you ever get fed up with other players (I've only occasionally even seen them in the wild, the world is by no means *crowded*), you can always download your progress to play the rest of the game offline.All told:  This is the game I always wanted when I first played Myst/Riven/etc.  A++.*one or two of the "complete the pattern" puzzles may be construed as requiring BS mind-reading, *however*, as far as I can tell, these puzzles are not themselves required for progression in the game overall.

_childDocuments_.review: I like it. Would I recommend it? Yeah, I would. But it's lacking in its core features. Namely, the multiplayer is a lost opportunity. For being online all the time, I would like to see more from the progression and community aspect. I would also like to see more a cohesive narrative. Whenever I run into a bit of dialogue in the game, I forget that there's even a story and how it all relates to what I'm doing.As far as the puzzles go, they're diverse enough in type and difficulty that I don't see myself getting bored any time soon. If you like puzzle games, this is one that you can sink hours into given that there are an endless amount of unique puzzles to solve in an open-world setting. And if you get tired of solving specific types of puzzles, you can just move onto something else. Though, even the hardest difficulty is not really all that difficult.All in all, it's a cool concept that needs work, but it's worth playing if you like hours of brain teasers.EDIT: Welp, I put about 100 hours into this before finding a game breaking bug. _childDocuments_.review: Despite the numerous frustrations that many have already articulated, if you are a fan of just solving puzzles this game rules. The graphics can be glitchy, perspective changes without warning, you fall off cliffs that you didn't know you were near and the lack of controller support is just plain bizarre. Then the weird reality that there are other players around you that you could care less about because you can't interact with them is truly strange. You can't help but wonder how much this game would absolutely blow you away as a single player game that focused on optimizing that game play instead of the strange focus on the multi-player non-experience. But if you just focus on the puzzles you enjoy instead of getting wrapped up in all of the other nonsense, the price of the game is still worth it. It is just too bad that the developers seemed intent on building something that was not necessary.

_childDocuments_.review: This game, like any other, has its pros and cons. The very concept of an MMO Puzzle game with little to no RPG elements is really interesting, though not executed super well as of writing this review (more on that later). The puzzles are pretty cool, and with a couple dozen different puzzle types, there's bound to be something for everyone who like puzzles.There are essentially 2 types of puzzles: Hand-crafted ones from the devs (e.g. most Cubes and Quest Islands), and procedurally generated ones (e.g. most Rings and Skydrops). The bulk of the 10,000+ puzzles the game claims to have will probably be the latter, though that's not inherently a bad thing! While they could become dull and burn you out super quick in their simplicity (just ask my friend who hit mastery lvl 99, the current max level for any one puzzle type, on Armillary Rings ), everything is spread out and mixed together enough that unless you are going out of your way, there will be plenty of variety between everything. Even the quest islands, while focusing on teaching you 1 or 2 new puzzles or concepts, have at least 2-3 other puzzle types on them to keep things from being too same-y.The always-online MMO aspect of the game, as mentioned by other reviewers, is a bit of a miss honestly, at least at launch. None of the puzzles are directly co-op. In fact, a lot of the environmental puzzles on the main islands are first come, first serve, as once someone solves the skydrops you were eyeing, you can no longer solve them yourself. There are some you could co-op, such as the glass mazes, but most everything else you'd have to solve separately despite being in a party. And even if your were to want to work on the same Logic Cube, you'd need external tools, such as Discord, to communicate as this game has neither text nor voice chat. The only interactions you get are pings and emotes. Also when you're wandering around, especially on the main islands, it's super rare to actually bump into someone, and even when you do, it's primarily gonna be just passing them by as you're each moving towards your next puzzle.And the final note on the forced-online aspect is for those with less than stellar internet connections. If you can't connect online, you're not solving a single puzzle, despite their singleplayer style. And if your ping frequently climbs above 100, rubberbanding becomes a , as the ping compensation on their servers is quite terrible. I'm hopeful that the devs will make improvements over time, but at this stage it's hard to say.Despite my long essay on the folly of the MMO, if you are someone who likes to just relax and solve puzzles, then I still highly recommend getting this game. Looking for a puzzle game to enjoy with friends? Then you could probably pass on this one for now. Though I should warn anyone who decides to get this game and has an addictive personality like myself: It's super easy to get into a flow state of jumping from one puzzle to the next, and the next thing you know, it's 3 am on a work night but you still say "I'll just finish this area before logging off" and then proceed to not log off.

_childDocuments_.review: Now that the devs have publicly announced on Twitter (check the Lunarch Studios account, I doubt the IOI account will mention it) that they no longer have the option of continuing development on this game, it feels appropriate to update my review. Everything I said below still stands - I still believe this is one of the finest puzzle games published this decade - but with the future of the game's servers now being in question, I can only solidly recommend you purchase this if you are confident you will play and enjoy it in the immediate future; 'purchase and put it in my backlog to play eventually' is no longer a feasible option. This is a terrific shame, and I hope eventually the game's publisher decides to reverse course and support the game further in the future, but I doubt this will happen. Fortunately, the demo has at least been brought back online, so you can try the game and see for yourself whether it is worth the purchase, with all of the above in mind.---I have about 100 hours in IOI, plus 40 or so in the demo and open playtest - that's been enough to 100% all main campaign content in the game, and make a pretty decent dent in the sandbox content (although I expect I've still got a lot of hours left in the latter before I get bored!). Even after having spent that much time in-game, I still find myself as enamoured with IOI as when I first began, and I can unequivocally recommend it to anybody interested in any of the puzzle types it offers.The standout of the puzzle types is of course the logic grids; these are all carefully handcrafted, and in particular, the sequences of logic grids in the game's 'enclaves' (the loose equivalent of 'dungeons' in a more traditional MMO, in a sense) are fantastically designed to teach interesting new logical deductions to players in engaging ways. The difficulty curve of the game is well-paced, such that even people who have no prior experience with these sorts of puzzles can learn how to solve them and have fun - but speaking as somebody who frequents sites like puzzlink, PuzSQ, and GMPuzzles, I can also confirm that there is ample content here suitable for more experienced logic puzzlers.The other puzzle types are also broadly good, with particular personal favourites being Shifting Mosaics (a sort of 'Rush Hour'/Klotski sliding block puzzle), Rolling Block (Bloxorz, essentially), and Phasic Dials (a generalised version of the classic 'Lights Out' puzzle). As you can tell, some of the puzzle types are not completely original to this game, but IOI offers interesting spins on the classics - even the Match Three puzzles have been very thoughtfully crafted to be genuinely tricky, elevating them above the standard mobile game fare that one might expect from the genre.Honestly, I would have been happy with IOI if it had just been a collection of logic puzzles and nothing more, but the set dressing surrounding everything else is of just as high a quality. The visuals are beautiful from start to finish; some of the settings, like the regions populated by Greco-Roman or Egyptian ruins, are standard puzzle game locales that will in particular call to mind The Talos Principle, but even in re-treading old ground, the game adds new visual interest by utilising unusual and fantastical combinations of architecture and flora, such as East Asian architecture mixed with Canadian trees and cliffs.The audio work on the game is also fantastic; the music is pleasant and appropriate for each area, while not being so busy as to distract one from focusing on the puzzles. The sound effects are inexplicably satisfying; every time I find a Hidden Archway or place a tile in a grid puzzle, it is accompanied by a pleasing and relaxing sound.There are some genuine complaints to be had about the game, which I hope the developers address in time. One of the most common is the confusion surrounding the game's multiplayer experience, and I will concede that this is incredibly lacking right now - it is essentially a singleplayer game that one has to play online anyway. Some people have suggested the multiplayer should be removed entirely, but personally my hope is the exact opposite; I think there's some really interesting and underexplored potential for multiplayer interactions here (in the open playtest, it seemed like there was going to be an option to collaborate with other players on solving logic grids, but this has sadly been removed, it seems).There have also been some complaints about performance; my personal experience from my own gameplay and from watching friends play is that these concerns are largely outdated, as performance seems to be greatly improved from the demo (when it was admittedly quite poor). However, even now, it can be quite demanding to play the game on the highest graphical settings, which is a shame when the visuals are such a selling point.Finally, while many of the puzzle types are excellent, there are a rare couple that are so unpleasant that I find it confusing they've made it to release at all. Many reviewers have mentioned that Morphic Fractals are both difficult to control and barely a puzzle at all; I would also personally complain a little about Shy Auras, which are repetitive and have a rather unpleasant sound effect associated with them. Additionally, Music Grids have tremendous potential, but the game's designers seem to think that a high-difficulty Music Grid should just be a random assortment of noises played at high speed, with little actual sense of musicality required for solving them. With all this said, however, one of the game's biggest strengths is the way it lets one pick and choose which puzzle types to engage with and how often, so it is not very difficult to avoid puzzle types one does not enjoy.As aforementioned, I am happy recommending IOI to pretty much anybody who has even a passing interest in any of its puzzle types; at the risk of being hyperbolic, I genuinely think that this is one of the finest puzzle games of my lifetime (even if sometimes held back by some strange decisions regarding multiplayer), and I say that as someone who pretty much  plays puzzle games.One thing I find rather baffling is that the developers/publishers have been quite quiet in their marketing about the pedigree of their puzzle designers; among the many talented individuals on the game's team are: the developer of Taiji Matthew Vandevander; puzzle YouTuber Icely Puzzles; USA Team A World Puzzle Championship competitor Jeffrey Bardon; and many other individuals who have written puzzles for the World Puzzle Championship and/or prestigious sites such as GMPuzzles before. If you're sufficiently into puzzles that any one of those names catches your eye, then you are absolutely the target demographic for this game, and I cannot implore you strongly enough to consider purchasing it.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't let the 10,000+ puzzles selling point fool you, as almost all of the game's puzzle types aren't logic-based, or even puzzles at all. Many fall into simple categories like coming across an invisible object or chasing an orb before it disappears. That isn't to say that the logic-based puzzles are bad, just that there isn't enough of them. It also has the bane of my existence: music puzzles.I'm not really sure what this game is trying to be. I'm not even sure the developers know. There's lore bits sporadically scattered throughout the world, detailing what I don't know. And I don't care to piece it all together, simply because I'm not sure there's any overarching stories of the world to discover. I never felt like there was. The multiplayer is a needless addition, serving no real value, and an argument can be made for it making the game worse due to latency-related issues. Accidental deaths are common when your character teleports all over the place.This really isn't a puzzle game. It's a collectathon. Mileage is going to vary depending on how much one enjoys that sort of thing. Even I, who love that particular sort of thing, probably won't see this game to completion. I probably won't get close. Especially when there are much better games that do the things found within Islands of Insight, such as Supraland and The Talos Principle games.

_childDocuments_.review: I was a bit hesitant to pick up this game after reading other reviews, and indeed I do agree that an offline option would be preferable, but I'm happy to say that I've enjoyed this game more than I expected.My main concern was actually not the forced online play, but the variety and quality of the puzzles in the game. I had some concerns that many of the puzzle types seemed to be hidden objects or simply stand here and click. These concerns were in some ways substantiated. There are many puzzle types (hidden arches, and cubes for example) that basically amount to "wander around until you find the hidden thing". Others simply require you to find the right place to stand, (looking at you yellow rings, floating orbs, pillars, and matching symbol cubes). However I have found these more enjoyable and relaxing than I expected, and the puzzles I don't enjoy I can simply skip. There are *plenty* of other puzzles to complete and these puzzles are rarely required to complete an area. In fact I often find them a nice break from the more difficult logic based puzzles.Where this game shines the most in my opinion is in the hand crafted (I assume) logic grids found in the enclaves. These are by far my favorite puzzle type, and they come with a wide variety of rule sets that make them interesting and difficult to solve. However there are many other logic based puzzles in the game I wasn't expecting. Rolling block puzzles, match three, rotating pattern puzzles (I have no idea what these are called) and others.I still am not sure if the puzzles in the main area are handcrafted or generated. I also find the amount of puzzles in the main area a bit overwhelming. I have been skipping most of these in favor of the enclaves which seem to have a much more thoughtful design and layout.The story / plot line has not engaged me, but I wasn't playing this for plot anyway.Overall while this game does have room for improvement, I love the variety of puzzles and ambition in this project. It has the potential to keep me entertained and solving puzzles for a long time.

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost, Islands of Insight is a game that stands out in a lot of ways. This, unfortunately, is not always a good thing. Starting with the almost outlandish tagline of 10000 handcrafted puzzles, it seemed almost unbelievable, but as you delve into the game you realize that that's probably the case. However, it very much is a quantity over quality claim and it shows - there's a ton of filler stuff, that while fun are not overly deep puzzles. This isn't to say the quality isn't there, there are hundreds of great puzzles, but probably 10 times as many filler puzzles. These aren't all bad, in fact I enjoy the almost junk food approach of wandering blindly around the area and just quickly solving whatever pops up.This brings me to the gameplay flow, there's kind of two aspects to it. The more traditional puzzle game design of themed puzzle segments and these are great, completing enclaves and trials is satisfying and reliable. Then there's the open world, which is just an endless sea of respawning activities to enjoy. This likely won't appeal to everyone and represents a major aspect of what sets the game apart from other puzzle games. It can be super addictive and fun, but even if that doesn't sound like your deal, you can absolutely play the game as a traditional puzzle game and easily make up the asking price.So, its a huge game with a ton of good (not necessarily great) content. Unfortunately, there is a bit of a dark side. The mutiplayer aspect is another one of those things that stands out and there are certainly positives (I played in the same world with a friend a lot of the time and we could see each other, what puzzles we're looking at and so on) and that was a bonus, but the sheer amount of technical issues was a huge detriment - especially for solo play where it feels unnecessary. The game probably crashed 100 times in my 100 hours playing, certain progression would fail to save (though nothing regarding puzzle completion atleast, just skill progression, customization, currency and cosmetics), as well as other issues such as getting stuck in load cycles or in the terrain, being forced to verify files probably about 10 times because otherwise the game wouldn't start and other such problems.Overall - its a very ambitious game and its definitely worth playing if you have the patience to put up with some problems, but for every couple things it does right, there is a major flaw along side it. It'll be interesting to see if it inspires anything similar, because the game definitely proves a concept works.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is puzzle crack. Stuff to do around every corner, almost to a fault. Something I haven't seen mentioned in other reviews as much, but I wanted to call out was the brilliant idea of the "Underclued" puzzles. Given a set of rules without enough info to fully solve the puzzle, you are tasked with only filling in the squares you can tell for sure are one way or another. This is something I haven't seen done in other puzzles games, and along with the "Insights" you gather as you solve puzzles, it seems like this would be a great way to get newer puzzle gamers comfortable with logical puzzle solving.As others mention, I haven't really engaged with the MMO aspect or the other players in the server. I generally don't care either way about the shared world aspect of the game, but it hasn't detracted from my enjoyment thus far.

_childDocuments_.review: On the surface, Islands of Insight looks like a dream come true for any puzzle game fan. The game gives the initial sensation of that of a child who has just emptied a massive tub of Legos, tons of potential for creativity and exploration. But as you start to chew through what Islands of Insight has to offer, it starts to feel more and more shallow, its environments empty, puzzles placed without rhyme or reason, and you feel like you're chasing a trail of breadcrumbs that leads nowhere satisfying.There were a lot of odd choices made by the developers, the progression system and always online gameplay are the most common complaints. Don't be fooled, there is absolutely nothing this game accomplishes by being an "mmo". Imagine if you went to the public library and sat in silence with twenty strangers while you're all penciling in sudoku books or crossword puzzles, that's what 'multiplayer' in Islands of Insight is like.There is also a lot of bugs and performance issues, you'll find yourself rubber banding, lagging, progression resetting, and more just due to the unstable online servers. Even if you wanted to play this game with friends, good luck having the game actually send invites or register a party and allow you to see each other.At the end of the day however I would still give the game a fair rating though. There's tons of puzzles with varying difficulty, and I did enjoy a lot of the special rules for the logic grids. That along with a decent price of only $30, Lunarch isn't asking too much for the experience.Tl;dr Buy if you enjoy logic and environmental puzzles, pass on if you're looking for any kind of co-operative gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: A rather disappointing experience, largely because there is good content here that I enjoy, like many others I find the logic puzzles to be very good, but many of the other puzzle types don't live up to the same quality, particularly the significant amount of perspective based puzzles, making them feel like filler.This is hurt further by the world design and how you encounter these puzzles, the game has 'enclaves' or islands/dungeons, that are separate from the open world, while both I would consider to suffer from bloat, I found the structuring of Enclaves to be much more rewarding and engaging, having them focus on around 2 or 3 types of puzzles that progressively get harder as you make your way through, with another 2 or 3 simpler types that felt more like filler.But ultimately what made these feel rewarding is their finite puzzles, and being able to fully check off an island, this is not a feature of the open world, in which when you solve puzzles in an area, the next time you log on they will be replaced by another set of puzzles in the same spaces that you had just done prior.Conversely this is extremely unrewarding, because it doesn't feel like I'm actually progressing whenever I do any puzzles in the open world. while there are completion markers that go up in the menu, seeing areas fully cleared out and completed satisfies an itch in my brain, and they designed the game to deliberately take that away, the reason being I assume they just had too many puzzles to cram into the map they made.I didn't originally have a problem with the map being filled by simpler puzzles, as they could give you something of a breather between more challenging puzzles, but their way of 'wiping' my prior progress soured me on the game as a whole, I don't need more sky pearls or match blocks cluttering my experience.There is more that could be said of their constantly crashing online experience, completely unnecessary skill tree, daily missions, and a grindy cosmetic shop, but those weren't my primary concern.

_childDocuments_.review: Why can't I stop playing this game? It happened multiple times now that I say "oh, I could hop on for a bit" and suddenly it's hours later and I'm trying to force my brain to pay attention to one thing and not get sidetracked.This is truly a great game, if you're a fan of puzzle games! It's puzzles range from dopamine-inducingly simple to mind-bogglingly difficult, and anything in between. Pair that with a beautiful and gorgeous world to explore that seemingly has something new to find around every corner, and you got yourself a great combination. There's a large amount of collectables and cosmetics to unlock as well, which is always a plus.The puzzle variety is great, and while you often run into the same ones, I haven't had any feelings of repetition in them, since even the same ones often have enough variance to them to keep things fresh.I think the main appeal to this game is the gameplay "loop", that consists of you looking at the map, deciding where to go next, and getting wholeheartedly sidetracked on the way there by a million different things/puzzles/secrets. This truly is a puzzle game for an incredibly short attention span.The cons for it aren't many, and for me they're definitely no deal breaker, but just in case:- I had the occasional disconnect or rubberbanding happening due to server stability, which makes the movement-based puzzles where you have to jump precisely impossible to do. It got resolved after a quick relog, so no big deal, and only happened twice Quick edit here that I since writing this review realized that some of the unlocks are only for specific body types/forms of the character, and since I only ever played as one, I didn't see the unlocks. There are still some progression unlocks that didn't carry over which I'm unsure why, and unlockables from the mastery system reset randomly, but it doesn't have a huge impact on the play experience- The narrative/lore of this game is very meh. _childDocuments_.review: In short: it's not bad, but it's not polished at this writing.First off, there's no co-op to speak of currently (at best, you solve puzzles side-by-side with other players).  As such, expect up front a mostly solo puzzle experience with other people vaguely there around you.For the puzzles and gameplay, this is mostly a mashup of the Talos Principle, The Witness, solving Korok puzzles everywhere in Breath of the Wild, and the open world puzzle experience of Warframe all housed under the same umbrella. The puzzles are varied, they're well-implemented, and they're presented in slowly expanding variety spread out over a Disney-park-esque few acres of in-game property. This is all connected via a thin story, mildly frustrating social tools, netcode that's right ♥♥♥♥ but likely to improve, and a free season pass level tracker to drive that good-ol'-engagement-model forward, with a very well-presented and familiar FPS interface that is somewhat lacking right now in terms of options and accessibility.The puzzles are varied and fun, the open world exploration is implemented well, and the scenery and ambiance of the game fit together well. Puzzles are swapped in and out of the world at a reasonable enough pace to keep previously-explored areas fresh, with light Metroidvania elements to entice you to come back as well.Less fun is the netcode for the game, which is fine during sparsely populated times of day, but stutters and chugs and teleports noticeably during higher traffic. Seeing other players solving puzzles in the world also generally feels good, except when they occasionally run by and snipe a perception puzzle you're working on preventing you from finishing it. It doesn't happen often, but when it does, it's annoying. (This might be a bug; most puzzles in your session otherwise do not seem to "solve" competitively by other players.)I also had a few puzzles despawn out from under me because they rotated out, but that seems to happen very infrequently. This is probably a bug that they'll fix, so I can't begrudge it too much.But these all have been infrequent frustrations overlapping an otherwise good experience so far. The puzzles remain fun after 10s of hours so far, flow together well, and the back half of the game adds creative meta-puzzles to the mix that are a joy to solve without hedging too far into pixel hunts or inscrutable puzzle developer logic.That said, with much of the current game tied to a live service instead of standalone presently, I expect this to eventually collapse under its own weight, limiting the value of a purchase. But for $30 for what it is right now, it's engrossing enough to recommend for a few dozen hours or so, more if you particularly enjoy games you can pick up and play and drop off just as easily during a coffee break.In short, again: the current game won't exactly thrill or inspire, but it's a relatively safe and fun puzzle game for folks with good spatial reasoning skills and comfort with FPS controls. Which is good enough for folks that enjoy this particular niche, but a less solid recommendation to puzzle fans generally.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was temporarily free on the Steam Store when I picked it up; I believe devs are trying to breathe fresh air into the playerbase because they are struggling financially and are hoping to get people to purchase it.. so in the hope their bold strategy works out for them, I'm throwing in this review.It is a gorgeous game. Really heavy on the machine though; I might need a new PC but I feel like it could have done with more optimization. The puzzles are fun, if a bit repetitive.. but with thousands of puzzles scattered throughout a gorgeous landscape, it shouldn't come as a surprise that at least some seem to have a more regenerative feel to them compared to the many that are more individually handcrafted. Even on the lowest of graphical settings, you need a pretty damn beefy machine. Sure, it looks slightly better than The Talos Principle, but the framerates and overall performance are abysmal in comparison. And this really is an issue, because the handling of your persona is something I can only describe as floaty and MMO-esque, while also liable to get stuck behind a lot of objects when you'd really expect the character to just 'slide off' and get beyond the minor obstacle without extra player input. It makes the few timed elements of the game incredibly frustrating to me, even if I can just choose to skip most of those puzzles. All in all, I feel it really could have done with a bit optimization and playtesting.Positives are that there are indeed a considerable variety of puzzles, but the negatives is that not all of them seem to have depth of scale to it. The environmental stuff just takes running around, for example. But the logic puzzles do seem to have many layers of depths and modifiers. Still, as a whole the overall experience (puzzling, world-building and narrative) seem to be a bit wanting when compared to the greats like Talos, Witness and Portal. I think it suffers under aspirations and a scope that were too grand for the production team of the developers to really do justice to, and instead got a lot of the scale and visual impressiveness at the cost of a refined quality puzzling experience and a wishywashy Talos/Witness-esque story that really isn't much of a story for as far I can tell at this point.But I still recommend it. It is not a bad game as long as you know what you are getting: a very zen-like puzzler that can still make you use your actual grey cells every so often. (The frequency of which completely depends on the puzzles you choose to do, honestly.) Throw in that the world is huge and has you literally tripping over puzzles left and right, and there is going to be plenty of content for those who enjoy the experience.And for the record: I do enjoy it. But much like ETS2, it is very likely going to turn into one of those games where I feel like playing it for a while  for the things it does offer rather than a super-engaged nightly play session I plan my evening around. I probably wouldn't have bought it at full price, but I likely would have gotten it at 66% or 50% off... so I just got lucky with their promotion. (I may have to see if I can support the devs some other way since I feel bad about getting it for free given that they are struggling under the bad sales figures...)

_childDocuments_.review: Islands of Insight features over 10,000+ puzzles and over 5,000+ hidden items waiting to be collected. The game categorizes them into 24 types of puzzles. Through as you might imagine with those numbers, some may stretch the definition of "puzzle" and vary in terms of effort (ranging from mostly handcrafted up to a few generated).The game features the "main island" which features the wide majority of the puzzles that are to be discovered. The puzzles rotates in a daily cycle as otherwise the world would be overloaded with the cheer amount of puzzles that can be interacted with. If you missed a puzzle you will always get an opportunity to try your luck again at some point, through this may take a few days or weeks if you are unlucky. Some exceptions are persistent or generated on demand. Smaller islands and areas called "Enclaves" or "Quests" feature curated selections of certain puzzles, often with the intention to teach a certain "insight" or two.The developers early on searched the community feedback with countless Playtests and Demos starting from September 2023 up to the game's release. This helped shaping the game in the right direction in terms of gameplay. Some critical issues during the latest Demos like Latency/Rubberbanding as well of Performance Issues and the use of Easy Anti-Cheat seem to be addressed.A previously critical bug which randomly prevented progress in the game to be tracked for players has been quickly addressed by the developers.There is not a lot remaining from the coop features that the developers initially intended to implement during the Playtest back in September 2023. Basic interaction with other players is available (pinging locations on the map, using emotes, party management), but actual "coop" gameplay is not available as in solving puzzles together, communication or similar.The game is split into several instance servers, probably to handle load and not flood the world with players. There is no real control over which instance you log into, and no ability to change it without closing the game entirely and trying your luck again. The instances seem to have synchronization issues for the puzzle circulation at times.A feature to join an ingame/steam friend's instance is currently broken.There is also the fear about what being dependent on servers means for the future of the game in case EOS is announced. In terms of videogame preservation, this is an absolute disaster.While the removal of Easy Anti-Cheat improved the performance of the game a lot, it is still kinda demanding. You will probably need a beefy computer to play this game.The game is officially still in "development". Whenever this is improvements to the MMO aspects or content expansions is not disclosed.At the other side we will have to see if this not threatens the funding of the game, causing early EOS and making the game unplayable. Eventually, assistance from their publisher or efforts to preserve the game might become mandatory.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not perfect, by any means, but it is very, very good. If you love puzzling at all, you're going to quickly get addicted. There is so much to explore, so many different puzzles to try out all bundled in a really beautiful open world. I appreciate the care put into each puzzle, you can tell these were all sculpted to either teach you a new lesson or test our your skills with some truly challenging puzzles.But, if you like multiplayer games, co-op, or really just very fleshed out games, this one isn't going to be for you. The multiplayer here is an afterthought, and honestly a negative. It isn't all the time, but you will find moments where the server will hiccup or in general your play experience will be  interrupted by the shared world around you.  These are problems every multiplayer game has, and they are forgivable in the context that the game is actually delivering you something to capitalize on that multiplayer aspect, this game does not. There is extremely limited co-op support (you have to dig through some menus just to TP to a friend, and you can't even do it ingame, it has to be from the main menu), no co-op puzzles, no clan guild or any other community aspect of any kind. Heck, this game doesn't even have an official discord  server!For $30, this game is a ridiculous steal. If you are okay just accepting this is a single player game that will occasionally hiccup because it's actually multiplayer, you'll get your money's worth in game time without question. I really worry for this game, I hope the developers can figure out a way to capitalize on the multipllayer aspect and grow the game. I honestly think this game released way too early,  had they come out the gate with everything fleshed out (or kept the early-access tag on with a cheaper price) this game would've hit overwhelmingly positive easily. I hope to see the game improve, and I encourage you to take the $30 plunge for yourself, but wouldn't fault anyone from walking away because of what's missing today.

_childDocuments_.review: It's sad to see the potential of this game wasted by the devs doing about everything wrong that they could. Releasing in a messy state with a too high pricetag, throwing people that bought it at full price off by giving out the game for free when they didn't hit the target player numbers, forcing an online aspect that doesn't add much value to the game but causes plenty of connection issues, and now shutting off the servers, leaving an offline mode behind that previously destroyed peoples drives by saving waaay too frequently.The game for me was a 9/10, besides tracking of already completed puzzles (not a thing) and the puzzle rotation (timegating content in a way) almost perfect. Everything surrounding it, from publishing to customer interaction, however, is a big, fat 0/10.Devs, you have one chance to redeem yourself here: Release the source code, allow the community to come up with their own fixes. _childDocuments_.review: The always-online "multiplayer" that doesn't seem to actually have any multiplayer functionality makes this game sluggish and laggy, and it really takes some doing to get those adjectives applied to a puzzle game. It also seems to cause severe issues with puzzle progress synchronisation - I have on multiple occasions reopened the game the next day and seen several of the puzzles I completed the previous night now displaying as if they were incomplete. In a game where actually  the puzzles you've not yet completed is half the conceit, things you've already done no longer being visually distinct from things you haven't makes for a very frustrating experience.But a puzzle game is mostly about the puzzles, and in this case the puzzles are not anywhere near good enough to compensate for it - some entire puzzle categories are awful, the movement-based puzzles are made intolerable because of the aforementioned performance and server issues and even the enjoyable puzzle types are merely what I'd expect from a $5-10 indie game that doesn't have the downsides of the baffling decision to mandate an always-online platform.Among the puzzle grids - the puzzle types least affected by the game's performance issues and most fitting what can actually be described as "puzzles", the quality is much higher than the rest of the game, but still not reaching the heights you'd expect from a full-price title. While the difficulty curve is going to be very shallow if you have any experience with pencil and paper puzzles, it's not so shallow that it's hugely problematic. The bigger issue is that difficulty seems to be based on "let's just make the puzzle bigger" - there's very little hugely advanced logic, only a small handful of puzzles actually incorporate complex solving techniques while the vast majority increase difficulty simply by either increasing the number of equally-simple deductions you have to make to fill the entire board, or by requiring a longer chain of inference/bifurcation to work out why one of two options doesn't work. There's been very few puzzles I've encountered that I would describe as genuinely great pieces of construction. It's very obvious that this game is trying to ride The Witness's coattails, and that's a comparison that goes very poorly for Islands of Insight in terms of puzzle quality.Solving the puzzle grids isn't unpleasant. You can have fun doing that. But it's not good enough to justify the premium price tag for the game, and all of the other aspects of gameplay that were intended to justify that price tag actually just bring the quality of the product down. The "multiplayer" is non-existent except as a way of eating up CPU cycles and rubber-banding you during movement challenges, the huge open world has loads of objects that you clip through and misplaced textures randomly floating in the air because its size meant the developers couldn't possibly give any one area the attention it deserved, the "10,000+ puzzles" being used for marketing means 9,000+ of them are uninteresting (many auto-generated perspective puzzles for which every one past the tenth is just busywork with no new insight), and certain puzzle types - particularly fractals, which barely even qualify as a puzzle when they're quicker to solve by randomly clicking than trying to analyse them - are simply annoying.I said that a puzzle game is mostly about the puzzles. And that's why just about any indie puzzle game that focuses on the puzzles above all else will be of higher quality.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not a puzzle enthusiast and or a seeker of tranquility in gaming, but the unique charm of Islands of Insight is not one to be overlooked. I had a mesmerizing journey through an open-world puzzle game that stands as a testament to serene gameplay and intellectual stimulation.The World Awaits with Puzzles GaloreIslands of Insight has surely triumphed in crafting an open world that harmoniously marries ancient wonders and natural splendor with a touch of human ingenuity in the form of complex, yet deeply satisfying puzzles. As you navigate the expansive floating archipelagos, the sense of discovery is palpable—each island holding its own secrets, cues, and thought-provoking challenges that inspire persistence rather than frustration.A Puzzle Experience That Respects the PlayerWhat stands out about Islands of Insight is its unwavering respect for the player. At no point does the game punish you for experimentation or failure, which is a refreshing departure from high-stakes, stressful gameplay that often permeates the puzzle genre. Instead, each solved puzzle leaves a lingering aftertaste of accomplishment, beckoning you onward to the next enigma with a rejuvenated appetite for more.Serenity in Shared DiscoveryThe defining experience of Islands of Insight is not just the self-indulgent pursuit of solving puzzles but the shared experience with others inhabiting the same swathes of virtual paradise. The interactions I’ve had with fellow players ranged from subtly cooperative to jovially competitive, adding a delightful social twist to what traditionally is a solitary affair.Personal Moments of ElationDuring my playthrough, I recall an intricate constellation puzzle that, upon solving, revealed a silhouetted narrative etched into the starlit sky. The satisfaction was immense and indicative of the care that developers poured into infusing each puzzle with meaning and wonder. This game captures those moments of elation that only pure puzzle-solving can provide.In conclusion, Islands of Insight transcends the conventional bounds of a puzzle game by offering a world where challenge meets tranquility. It's a must-play for anyone who cherishes the quiet delight of solving puzzles and is searching for an escape from the cacophony of day-to-day life.

_childDocuments_.review: My thought on this game are mixed, but give a binary option of "yes" or "no" for a recommendation, I'll have to go with a yes. The game has got some great elements to it. I really enjoyed the open world aspect and the ability to jump from puzzle to puzzle and as you progress, they introduce a constant stream of new puzzles. Some of them aren't really puzzles, like finding hidden arches, or hidden rings. Others are pretty trivial like the yellow rings where you just need to stand in the right spot. Actually, there are a fair number of puzzles around perspective. But there were a number of fun and challenging puzzles too, especially the logic grids. The visuals are  great and I found myself firing up the game just to have a  relaxing time wandering the islands and solving various puzzles as I came across them. It's a good way to relax and play at your own pace.On the cons side, the multi-player aspect doesn't make any sense at all. I guess they devs felt like they needed this, but the game really belongs as a single player stand-alone game.  And while the game had some fun puzzles, and a LOT of puzzles..none of them were especially challenging or ties into a cohesive story.  After a while, you are just doing the same puzzles over and over. Contrast that to a game like Talos principle that has a great over arching story and more indepth puzzles and it comes across  as a mile wide and an inch deep. In the end, I'd recommend watching a bit of gameplay and see if it appeals to you. I enjoyed the time I spent, but I'm ready for something with more depth and more compelling story.

_childDocuments_.review: First/third-person multiplayer puzzle game.  You are a Seeker, created to explore the world and work out its mysteries.  Find puzzles, solve puzzles, unlock the story and explore.FOGEY ALERT: Most of the text is very tiny, much of it too small to read unless you're awful damn close to the screen, and there's no setting for adjusting font size.  This is particularly true for the options menus, and some of the sidebars seem completely illegible.MOTION-SICKNESS ALERT: There's a lot of running and jumping (and eventually flying), and to find and solve puzzles one has to look in all directions.  The game itself has a flashing/seizure alert as well.  I got nauseous within an hour.When I first saw the trailer for this game I was extremely enthusiastic, and wishlisted it.  Then, out of the blue, I got an email alert that said the game was on sale for free, and I jumped at it.  I'm glad I did, because I don't know how much I'll be able to play it between the tiny fonts and the eye strain, and I'd've been unhappy for having paid significant money for this experience.It's impressive for the amount of work that's been put into it.  All the puzzles, all the maps, all the graphics effects do represent a ton of effort on their part.  It's a very pretty game.  And people do like this sort of thing, as demonstrated by The Witness, The Talos Principle and others, and the idea of being able to team up with others is great.But it was severely diluted when I first got into the game and couldn't read the options menu to find out how to do fullscreen.  It was further diluted when I found the mouse click point was somewhere above the actual mouse position.  Then I got into chargen and couldn't read the menus there either.  I had to move halfway to the screen to figure out the word "markings" because I was clicking on options and not seeing a visible result.The puzzles are interesting, but some are hard to understand because the instructions can't be read.  They also have the potential to be grindy, as in there may be a lot of the same sort of puzzle.  This is apparently intended, as one has a proficiency rating that goes up with the number of puzzles of a type that one does.Solving certain quantities of puzzles unlocks more map areas, and also powerups.  The first powerup you get is the Double Jump, handy for reaching places.  I knew that was the powerup I got because the powerup tutorial told me...I couldn't read the names or descriptions of other powerups.I'm recommending this game because I thought it was a very good experience to get for free.  It is probably even a very good experience to get for slightly more than free.  But for anything approaching their full price, I'd hold off until they do something about the godfersaken font size.

_childDocuments_.review: This game soothes my brain and arrived at the perfect time for me.The puzzles are excellent and truly have a wonderful range of difficulty. There's fun stuff to do everywhere, and I've spent entire evenings just wandering around solving stuff with no aim in particular. There's one puzzle type that's a bit weak imo (morphing fractals) but I honestly love engaging with all the others.Something that I think is underappreciated is that this game wants to teach you how to get better at solving puzzles, and does so in a genius way. When a puzzle requires a particular logical technique, the game will tutorialize you about it *after* you solve the puzzle. That way, you get to make the logical leap on your own, and *then* they game will say "hey, you figured out something important solving that one. Here's what it was, remember it for later!" It's really smart, and cultivates skills that will help you solve logic puzzles even outside this game!My only major complaint is that I wish performance was better. _childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game because i had a lot of fun playing it, but the game is very flawed. Here is my review taken from my :As a big fan of puzzle games, I was eagerly anticipating the release of Islands of Insight, but my initial excitement turned to disappointment as I delved into the game. While I initially found myself immersed in solving puzzles for hours on end, my enthusiasm waned when I discovered that puzzles were respawning. This revelation shattered my perception of progress and completion within the game, leaving me feeling betrayed, because I was tackling a lot of stupid and mundane puzzles thinking I was progressing.However, once I shifted my focus to the core puzzles within the enclaves and quests, I found a renewed sense of enjoyment. These puzzles were meticulously crafted and provided a satisfying challenge, unlike the repetitive fillers scattered throughout the game.Unlike games like The Witness, which strategically unlock late-game puzzles based on player knowledge, Islands of Insight simply gates puzzles behind enclave completion. Even more, while this approach is not inherently flawed, I can't help but feel it represents a missed opportunity and a lackluster implementation. The supposed knowledge "unlocked" throughout the game often felt superficial, rehashing concepts already encountered in earlier puzzles. While occasionally beneficial, it seldom provided significant depth to the gameplay experience.Unfortunately, the storytelling fell flat for me. The cryptic narrative, delivered through obscure dialogues with a seemingly random entity, failed to engage me. I found myself skipping through these interactions, feeling disconnected from the narrative experience.One significant frustration was the amount of time spent searching for puzzles rather than solving them, particularly when attempting to complete challenges. The lack of clear puzzle locations, compounded by the game's sprawling open world, often detracted from the gameplay experience.Speaking of the open world, it failed to leave a lasting impression. Despite featuring distinct themed islands, they all blurred together into a forgettable landscape. The minimal interaction between puzzles and the world further diminished the impact of exploration.The multiplayer component also missed the mark. Lacking meaningful interaction or tools for collaboration, it felt like a tacked-on feature that added little value to the experience.Ultimately, while Islands of Insight offers moments of enjoyment, particularly within its core puzzle enclaves, it falls short in several key areas. The repetitive nature of puzzles, lackluster storytelling, and disjointed open world detract from what could have been a more immersive experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely not worth your money. The way you control your character is a one big joke. Sometimes you wanna jump, and the character simply doesn't do that, sometimes you wanna do a double jump and your character plummets to the ground. When you wanna get somewhere, to where your normal double jump doesn't reach, you have to do a holding jump, which sends you off into space, and you gotta wait for a few seconds to come back down, while hoping that you're gonna land where you wanted. It might not seem that bad, but after hours of playing, and falling over and over you simply start to wonder was there at least one person that actually play-tested this. And it gets infinitely worse by the fact that 15 out of 24 different types of puzzles require you to move/glide/run/stand in a perfect postition. While on the topic of the puzzles themself, they range from kinda enjoyable at moments, to horribly tedious.Hidden cubes/archways/pentards/rings are the worst of all these "puzzles". I wouldn't care about the that much, just a filler, no big deal, but the absolute genious creators thought it's a great idea to shove these stupid cubes into every. Single. Flipping. EXCLAVE. So after solving all logic cubes, mosaics, match three's etc., you'll spend 5 times more looking for these little, stupid boxes, meandering around the island like an idiot, and praying that at least for a second you'll hear a quiet sound of a hidden cube nearby. And after spinning around the location of the sound like a fricking fan on it's highest rotations, Congratulations, you found it! Only 47 more to go :)Skydrops are a boring way to make the sky seem less empty, while the actual "solving" part of them is finding a single small one next to the ground and looking around for the rest that form a circle, wow, how inventiveLogic cubes are fine(for the most part),environmental cubes are interesting, I liked the music cubes, the memory cubes on the other hand. Showing a pattern one diagonal line after the other, and then asking the player to recreate it is like, not a puzzle at all? And you won't convince me that a single person had any kind of satisfaction or enjoyment out of "solving" these.Match three and shifting mozaic, are puzzle types you'd see in a billion phone apps, why add them here if you're not gonna change anything about how they work?The rest is of the puzzles are either terrible because of the god awful controls, or completly forgetable.If you wanna buy a puzzle game with and interactive world, go buy Taiji or The Witness. All 3 are roughly the same price but the two mentioned above are way more worth it than this piece of utter dog ****.Edit: The creators decided to remove online mode, meaning if you had any form of progress it's gone now. An amazing way to kill the remains of already dying audience

_childDocuments_.review: Many reviewers have noted that the inability to launch in offline mode is a dubious choice that excludes certain players for technical reasons. That's clearly a business decision that Lunarch has made.However, I think there is a more pernicious consequence that may make this a dealbreaker for some-- this can be a privacy issue. A rather high cost to pay for this, so at the very least this limitation should be advertised honestly and upfront as the requirement does not meet common expectations.(I'd honestly like to avoid making a binary recommendation judgment here, but it's required by the steam review form. Perhaps the best way to put my thoughts is that the implications of quietly slipping online requirements into a mechanically single player experience are fostering distrust of motivations for what is otherwise a fine game.)

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of the low reviews are from the game being inoperable, but fortunately I never had any issues with load times or crashing on my own PC, so I'm going to bypass that completely.You basically play a Valkyrie inspired character ((Character creation heavily reminiscent of the Aasimar race from DND)), who runs around different floating islands solving puzzles. That's basically it, so this game could have potentially been super repetitive and dull after 45 minutes or so, but the sheer quantity and diversity of the puzzles is absolutely a saving grace. They very in size, and difficulty, and some of them are even just finding invisible gates and cubes by happenstance. Completing puzzles and gaining xp helps you level up and invest in skills like double-jumping, and you can also put points into unlocking 4 or 5 different cosmetic sets ((Honestly, not much. Maybe they'll add more over time? Behavior usually doesn't do too much with their "side project" games though, so I won't hold my breath. ))The graphics are kind of meh to me. The way the characters move is pretty stiff, and while the areas are gorgeous and lean pretty heavily into Egyptian and Japanese architecture, the graphics seem low even when they're on high. They put a lot of effort into having moving tattoos, and flowing lights in the characters hairstyles, but it just ends up looking kind of muddled. They put so much different colors and bright light spectrums into the game that occasionally things just end up looking like a blurry rainbow mess, but the majority of the time I really do find it to be very pretty & satisfactory- Doesn't heavily distract from the gameplay.They're also bringing an offline mode which is EXCELLENT. The only reason I can think of it being an MMO in the first place is to maybe receive help on difficult puzzles from those around you? But with no chat feature, and emotes being limited to things like "Bow" and "Shrug", it is literally a mute point.All in all I love puzzle games, and while this game isn't groundbreaking by any means, it is really fun, and beautiful, and it's going to give me a lot to do.
