_childDocuments_.review: The game missed the spot just slightly. It almost became one of my favorite games, my dream game - but unfortunately, it failed my expectations and for me - it's a negative.It looks great. It scratches my itch for exploration. The world is huge, very complex, full of hidden, difficult to reach areas. The vistas are amazing.It has a variety of puzzles - from purely logical challenges, through ones that require a keen eye, to those depending on agility and speed. Some are pretty cool ideas, I haven't seen in other games.And it also looked like a heaven for completionists (such as me). Yet, it quickly turned into hell.You see, there is no real goal in this game, not much of a story. But, with such a rich world of different puzzles and areas to discover, the goal could just be to complete all the challenges, discover everything in the game. Simply, to 100% it.Yet, I have noticed with the 2nd or 3rd play session with a game - that previously finished puzzles disappeared and new ones took their place. Well, that changed everything drastically. That one, single reason to play and move forward with a game just disappeared. You can wander around, still doing puzzles here and there just to progress at each location fulfilling the quota of finished puzzles for each area, but it just not the same type of challenge. I've lost any motivation. Not to mention, even that would not be 100% possible, as the comments show that one of the areas is impossible to complete due to the error.This is a case of so many games - a few great ideas mixed with ones that completely destroy the game. It's purely single player game, yet they implemented online multiplayer for no reason. They introduced offline mode only when the players were complaining. They dropped the game, leaving it with bugs. And they're probably still clueless why it didn't turn into a financial success. Such a missed opportunity.

_childDocuments_.review: With the addition of offline play I have finally been able to dive into this game without being jerked back by the elastic bands. This game is insane. Countless times I have had to laugh just to control myself from getting overwhelmed by the sheer size of the playfield and the countless puzzles found within. I have never been to Egypt. I have never seen its pyramids, but I feel like my reaction if I were to go there would be on par with how I feel everytime I enter this game. The world is massive, filled with what feels like infinite puzzles. I could spend the next 10 years in this game and still leave things undiscovered. How did they make this game?  Ignoring the mechanical depth of each puzzle type, the sheer variety of puzzles to be found and how a beautifully cohesive world has been designed to bring them all together with a sense of progression is a wonder to behold. I feel like the designers of this game were looking at real life, saw an world where people were busily engaged in the puzzle of their choice, isolated from each other, and wanted to create a space where we could all gather together, have fun with the puzzles we love but also be challenged by and seek help with a type we would never have seen otherwise. Sucks that my shotty internet connection didn’t allow for the devs dream to come true. I have heard people say that this game is an ocean in variety but a puddle in depth and I fully agree and love it for that.

_childDocuments_.review: My recommendation has to come with a few caveats, but if you know what you are getting into and like the sound of it, it's a pretty easy recommend for me.Firstly, while there are lots of different puzzle types, I think some are a bit more compelling than others. To a point that's fine - I actually think it's nice that some are as simple as 'find the hidden thing' while some are fairly complex logic challenges. I like to run around the large play space, and just solve whatever puzzles happen to take my fancy, and there's things everywhere you look. But I think it's fair to say I enjoyed the logic grids a fair bit more than the rather fiddly fractal puzzles, say. Some of the smaller puzzles spawn and despawn, which is a bit annoying if it happens while you're in the middle of doing on, but it's only happened to me a couple of times.Secondly, the multiplayer aspect is, as other people have said very slight. There's some daily challenges, and you see other people running around and you can emote at them and that's about it really. I don't mind that really! But it does make me worry a bit, about what happens to this game once they can't afford to keep servers running. I hope they find a way to take it offline, for that. Otherwise I didn't mind seeing other people wandering around (I don't think it adds much to get a notification on the side whenever anyone in the game does basically anything though). Finally, I think the movement and animation feels a bit floaty and unpolished which is a shame because for some of the things you do have to race around the areas. It's a pretty game, a lot of the time, but its rough edges are noticeable. Basically, when this game works it works really well, and if you like puzzle games then the areas where it doesn't work so well are easily forgiven.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: this game suffers from feature bloat that makes engaging with the core content (puzzles) more trouble that it should be, for a dedicated puzzlerOn the surface, this seems like a fairly inoffensive (if average) puzzle game. However, it also suffers from a chronic illness I like to call "AAA-itis"What is AAA-itis? In short, it is everything that makes AAA games so grand yet so shallow: a bunch of mechanics that seemingly only exist to bloat the feature list. Skill-trees, character customization, multiplayer... the game would be just as good without any of these things. But, they got added, and the overall package suffers for it.As for the puzzles themselves, they range from "barely qualifies as puzzle" to "actually decent". The worst offenders are all the "find the hidden thing" puzzles, because they simply aren't puzzles; they're collectibles that wouldn't be out of place in a AAA open world action-adventure with RPG elements.The block puzzles where you connect coloured squares into groups based on rules that change every puzzle are good though, and if they were the only thing in the game then I would be much more likely to recommend itI am aware that I barely played the game though, so I will give it a second chance and update the review once I do so

_childDocuments_.review: This game has an incredible amount of great puzzles in a serene and beautiful world, and I think it is worth the purchase, but it has somewhat messy design structure and problems with communicating what it actually is. In the most concise way, Islands of Insight is essentially a single player game similar to the Witness with ten times the amount of puzzle tablets but slightly less interesting overworld and more mainstream presentation.You may think it is an mmo, or a co-op game, but in practice it's not true. The only thing that networking is used for is to show you other players running around on a server. There are no puzzles that require two or more players to solve, you can't work together on a single puzzle, and puzzle progress and completion is separate for each player. Thankfully, there is an offline mode now that doesn't require constant internet connection for barely existing multiplayer features.But even if you treat it as a single-player game, there are still design trappings left from a desire to make a MMO that can confuse you. The game consists of an open-world main island and many small "dungeons" around it called enclaves. Puzzles in enclaves are usually grouped by theme, placed deliberately and don't change during the game. You can complete an enclave and move on. You *can't* complete areas on the main island, because puzzles there are randomly picked from a much larger pool of potential puzzles and they change every day or so. The idea is to make fresh puzzles available on every login, but it can be confusing to see previously solved puzzles disappear and be replaced by new ones. If you are a completionist, it will be painful to see. In general, if something is marked on the map, it is unique and will stay solved forever, everything else will probably be replaced by new puzzles after a while.I recommend treating enclaves as the main progression path and puzzles on the main island as optional nice-to-have content. Solve the puzzle types that you enjoy, but don't try to "complete" the area, it is impossible to do so!  Even if you stick to enclaves and puzzles at map markers, the game has a huge amount of puzzles (I have 150 hours and played mostly enclaves and marked areas on the map).

_childDocuments_.review: The "10.000+ puzzles" claim that this game is advertised with is... Kind of misleading. There's indeed an enormous amount of puzzles, but of the 24 puzzle types in the game, several of them I'd argue don't deserve to be called "puzzles" at all (note: this review will thus contain spoilers for puzzle types).For starters, 3 types of puzzles are time-based movement challenges. Calling these "puzzles" is equivalent to calling a time trial in a racing game a puzzle: at most you'll have to figure out the route you need to take, but often this is so trivial that I struggle to call these puzzles.Then there are 3 types of puzzles that are simply "invisible" objects scattered across the world. These objects glitter slightly to make them visible and make a sound when you come close to them: you need to e.g. walk through them to "solve" them. There is barely any thought needed to "solve" these things, as again, they are barely puzzles. They are plentiful in the world, and of course scattering a bunch of these things across the entire map is a very easy way to inflate the game's puzzle count.One type of puzzle requires you to match a fractal to an example fractal by using your mouse. It's unpredictable- or at least very difficult to predict- how the fractal reacts to the movements of your mouse, and in my experience it was quicker to randomly wiggle my mouse about than to actually try to solve and match the two images.As for the other puzzle categories, some puzzle types are very simple and there is almost no depth to their mechanics.Several puzzle types are perspective puzzles, with all of those being a variant of "stand in a particular spot and look in the right direction". These are often not very difficult, with it immediately being obvious where you should stand to make the puzzle work. There is no depth to these puzzles: a "Matchbox" type puzzle in the first game area and a "Matchbox" type puzzle from a late game area are practically indistinguishable. The only times where the game throws you some more variations of the theme are in enclaves or specific trials, but don't expect any in-depth iteration on mechanics here.Arguably the strongest puzzle type of the game is found in the Logic Grids, which are sudoku-ish puzzles found across pretty much the entire world and have various rulesets. Solving one takes place on an entirely separate screen (think Witness puzzles): the vast, vast majority of them are completely detached from the world.Arguably there is no reason why the majority of the remaining puzzles had to be scattered across an online open world. In fact, I don't understand why this had to be an online multiplayer game, which caused a lot of issues (e.g. performance issues). An offline mode as has been added was desperately needed, and also shows that this game did not need to be multiplayer in the first place (which probably would have saved the devs a lot of headaches). However, arguably the biggest multiplayer-related issue that was present in the game was the live service element, in which the puzzles in the overworld (not in e.g. enclaves) are all swapped out on a daily basis (meaning that if you get stuck on a puzzle, when you come back the next day it's suddenly not there anymore). There's no way to tell which of these puzzles you already solved or not, and bafflingly, this element also made it into the offline version of the game.In general, if you like logic puzzles, you might like the logic grid puzzles, but for anyone looking for a more in depth puzzle experience I can't recommend this.

_childDocuments_.review: I usually wait until I finish a game before writing a review. However, Islands of Insight is a game I am not likely to finish. It is a game that I will play, take a break, and then play again. There is so much to see and do that I can't imagine growing tired of it or running out of things to accomplish. I love exploring beautiful environments and solving puzzles. Games like Witness, The Talos Principle (I and II), The Trials, Sensorium, and Syllogism make me happy. I enjoy the freedom of wandering and taking things in at my own pace. Give me a variety of puzzles and I will enter a time warp, playing until the wee hours of the morning with no sense of how long I've been sitting.Islands of Insight is huge with a staggering amount of things to pique my curiosity. You can walk, run, fly, jump, or fast-travel around a gorgeous landscape that expands as you move ahead. If you are so inclined, you can let the objectives lead you from area to area. Within each area you can meet a basic set of goals or go for bonus points. I am leveling up and adding skills as my puzzle solving proceeds.  At this point, I can jump higher and glide further now that I've built up some experience.The game is multi-player in that you see others in the game world. You can communicate with some basic symbols and poses, but not chat. This is similar to the multi-player feature in Journey, where you can travel together and chirp but never talk. Somehow the world feels more friendly seeing that there are others out there enjoying the same adventure. There have been complaints that you cannot play off-line. For me, this is not a deal breaker, as I play on a PC that I don't move around. There have also been complaints about lag and stuttering. I experienced some minor lag one time. Other than that, the game has run flawlessly. I should say that I am running a newer PC with a lot of RAM and video RAM so I am way above recommended system requirements. The puzzles are diverse. I am quite good at some (music grids) and totally suck at others (sky drops). But, I can usually avoid the puzzles I don't like. If some are required, I can do the minimum and move on to something else.The game only supports keyboard and mouse (no controllers) which is easy for me because that is what I am most familiar with. Navigation is flawless and I rarely miss jumps (which means the implementation is more forgiving than most). Gliding from high places and taking in the scenery is absolutely awesome. There is a detailed map with fast travel points, a catalog of lore discovered, a list of puzzle types with insights/hints, and a screen to customize your character. The game saves on exit and I've never lost progress or had a crash. If you do fall off the edge of the world, the game usually returns you very close to the place where you fell. In some cases, you are returned to the entry point of the area but all progress is saved.Finally, there are those who won't support a game without Steam Achievements. As an achievement junkie, I am finding the lack of achievements in Islands of Insight to be a plus. No pressure, no trying to figure out how to get 100%. I can just have fun and take pride in the incremental progress I am making within the game.So, to reiterate. I love this game.  At the current price, it is a good value because Islands of Insight will provide a huge number of hours of entertainment. At about 25 hours, I've barely dented the possibilities. And, since puzzles re-spawn and challenges change, I am not apt to get bored any time soon. I highly recommend this to anyone who loves thoughtful puzzling and exploration.An Added Note - Islands of Insight went off-line in October. Since I had not taken advantage of coop features, this was not an issue for me and has actually resulted in better game performance (no server lag). I did not pay attention and thus missed the window for saving my progress locally. I started the game over and am enjoying it as much (if not more) the second time through. I still highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys taking respite in a beautiful landscape and working puzzles at their leisure.

_childDocuments_.review: I kind of went into this game expecting to find things I don't like about it, but I think it wound up being a pretty good game for what it is. To start I should say that I played this game entirely offline, so I can't speak to the online functionality, though I can't imagine it adds too much, I feel like I had a pretty complete experience without it. The most I can imagine is you could get together with your friends and solve puzzles together, but that's something you could also accomplish with a discord server.So Islands of Insight is following in the footsteps of several beloved indie puzzle games, but goes about the basic concept in a far less indie way, it's a very big open world absolutely stuffed with puzzles. First thing you should know is that the majority of the puzzles you'll encounter aren't bespoke. There are a lot of loose puzzles strewn about the world between the more hand designed areas that I imagine are pulled from a pool and refresh at certain points. So know that before you get it in your head that you can 100% this game in a way that leaves you with nothing left to do or that you need to do every puzzle you come across. Second thing you should know is this game has a very loose definition of what a puzzle is. There's a wide variety of puzzle types that run the gambit from really solid logic puzzles to clicking on a kinda transparent cube. I don't mind it that much, cause the kind of stuff you actually want from a puzzle game is still there, I think the other stuff helps to pace the game. If you ever get burned out on the real puzzles you can decompress by clicking on floating circles for a bit. Just know that the touted "10,00+ puzzles" is a little generous. As for the quality of the puzzles, they're largely pretty good, I'd say they're about on par with similar games. Among all the puzzle types there's decidedly a main type, logic boxes, which are tiled puzzles kinda like Picross that you can color in black and white, and you need to follow certain rules. It's very reminiscent of The Witness. That said, there are some rougher puzzles. If you thought the sound based puzzles in The Witness were bad, this game's sound puzzles aren't even as creative. The worst offenders are these fractals that you morph by moving your mouse to match an example image. It's so imprecise and inscrutable. But the beauty of this game is that most of the time you can just ignore the puzzles you don't like. Beyond the puzzles there's some light mmo trappings, there's a skill tree that allows you to unlock a few extra mobility tools, some quality of life features- nothing essential enough that it feels egregious to lock it behind levelling- and bonuses to get you experience and currency faster. I liked the movement, getting around isn't trivial, but it also doesn't get in the way of just going from puzzle to puzzle. I think my biggest gripe with the game is just that it's visually very bland. It's that specific kind of overproduced look you'd expect from a mobile game that c-tier youtubers get sponsor deals with. It's clear that it's aping off of the likes of The Witness and The Talos Principle, idyllic vistas populated with ruins from various cultures and eras, but it's done with such a lack of style or intent. Likewise, the story is presented very poorly. I don't mean that it's poorly written or uninteresting, but it's told in a very uninteresting way to the point where I didn't even understand the format till about 25 hours deep. And a small nitpick, but this game takes a hot minute for the game to load when you launch, even running off an SSD. But to the game's credit that's presumably because it's loading in most of the open world at the start, and after that it's totally seamless, so it's excusable.I don't think this game quite matches up to the games it draws from, at least not in the same ways. I think Islands of Insight is best enjoyed as a kind of background noise, something you play when you're in a discord call, watching something on a second  monitor, or listening to a podcast. But to its credit, it's very good at that. The real puzzles are challenging and varied, the "puzzles" are enjoyable in their own way, and completing either treats you to a lot of numbers and lights that set off the ole dopamine receptors, and best of all, there's a LOT of content. I'm nearly 45 hours deep and there's still plenty left to see. Almost makes me feel guilty I got it for free. With all that in mind, I think it's worth the asking price. If you're like me and you're a big fan of the games this game draws from, don't expect that much from it, but this'll be more than enough to scratch the puzzle itch till something more substantial comes along.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the greatest puzzle game I have ever played, full stop. That being said, it still has its fair share of issues. Regardless, don't miss out on this!Positives:-Incredible puzzle and world design-Absolutely stunning visuals-Surprisingly good player customization for a game where you wouldn't really expect it-Essentially infinite replayability because puzzles circulate over time and you forget the solutions to many puzzlesDownsides:-To say what literally everyone has been saying: this game desperately needs an offline singleplayer mode. These puzzles are still... fine... but I find myself avoiding them at all costs because they don't feel enjoyable to solve. The puzzles in question are morphic fractals and shy auras.-Many "insights", this game's version of tutorials, seem to come up long after you would have likely figured them out already, rather than earlier in the game when it would be more useful to have them. The tutorial is basically spread out across the whole game, with each enclave providing a specific challenge for one or two puzzle types, usually introducing new mechanics. There are some occasions where I got an insight and thought to myself "I really wish I knew this 5 hours ago".-The build in quest system is underwhelming and doesn't provide any extra gameplay intrigue. I'd love it if some quests would lead you on a specific path to complete a string of puzzles.I don't see myself stopping playing this game any time soon. _childDocuments_.review: I really loved this game. I really, truly loved all the time I spent flying around the world, solving extraordinarily well made grid puzzles, optimizing movement to get near-perfect times on flow orb courses, spinning and matching dials, lining up overworld mosaics, all of it. Even the fractal puzzles I didn't really like initially, they added a new island in an update that added a super interesting new twist on them that I enjoyed the hell out of. And the meta Secrets, so many of those were ingenious. Going back to old puzzles and blatantly ignoring the rules to follow those cryptic whispers, only for the puzzle to solve itself, feels unbelievably satisfying. As well, the idea of a MMO puzzle game, though many people were apprehensive to it, and I agree that the offline mode should've existed from the start, the world being alive just made it all that much cooler to me. I spent hours doing puzzles with friends, and honestly much longer just silently solving positioning puzzles with random strangers, just crouch-spamming when we found the right spot to stand on, just felt magical.Which is why this hurts so much to say that I can't really recommend this game to new players. There was so much potential in this game, so much that could have been done with such a monumental foundation, that just wasn't. And from what it seems like, never will be. I hate to tell people that you shouldn't buy this game, because this is exactly the kind of game that I would always recommend to people, and I did when it came out, at least a dozen times. But the devs gave up on it. It was clear that at first, they were full on committed to keeping this game alive and fresh. Less than 6 months after launch, the servers are now dead, the game is offline only, and all potential for updates has been completely wiped out. I took a break from the game, waiting for a new big patch, and never even realized I had to convert my saves, so I lost 200 hours of progress by missing the 1 month window. This is just a depressing corpse of a game with endless potential, and devs who either didn't have the bandwidth, or worse, the care to keep it alive. I hate to say it, but don't buy this game, not anymore.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent feedback systems for puzzle solving. Makes it feel really rewardingTo elaborate a bit more on the mechanics there are multiple progression systems at play. You have exp towards your skill tree or cosmetics, exp toward that puzzle type for titles, exp for the world and its cosmetic tracks, and exp for a customization track. These combine for a nice show of progression after each completed puzzle no matter how minor. The online mechanics are a bonus in my eyes. Sometimes you get lucky and see another player and can copy their solution on the pillar puzzles which I find charming personally. I don't feel spoiled cause the pool of puzzles is so large and I get to reap the bonuses. Its mostly the perspective puzzles and mazes that people can spoil but I've only focused that much on another player to see if they were solving something a handful of times.Seeing other players on a puzzle then starting after them and finishing it before they back out of it is also provides satisfaction like you "beat them" but no ones really in competition. The visuals are gorgeous For completionist the game has puzzle dungeons as well as randomized puzzles. So the main island has random puzzles throughout, while there a themed puzzle dungeons that have static puzzles that you can work on with friends, and eventually complete the dungeon 100%. Some people had the idea that everything is randomized and there's no "completing the game" but you can 100% all the dungeons to your hearts content.

Lots of motion in the textures and effects.  It's also huge.  Like... truly massive.  Almost too big.  There's almost... too much content.  Like so much it boggles my mind.  Especially for the price point.Movement is fun if a bit imprecise.  Platforming can be a bit frustrating but not overly so.  Some of the platforming challenges are made to be more difficult than they needed to be due to this.  Proper controller support would be nice.  This game NEEDS to be updated with that.To that end, this game needs some optimization, too.  It should be able to handle lower hardware with some grace.  Honestly... the goal should be to get it Steam Deck optimized.  This game is BEGGING to be on the Deck and on the road with you in offline mode. _childDocuments_.review: EDIT: I am amending my review to make it positive after Islands of Insight is offline-only and has fixed the major issue I had with the game. Leaving the rest of the review up for posterity.--I really enjoyed the demo and my limited game time for Islands of Insight. The puzzles are fun, there's practically an infinite amount of them, and I loved wandering around the world discovering new stuff. The exploration scratched the same itch as a game like Breath of the Wild that kept me wanting to explore the next island or comb through the next ruin. I almost never buy games for full price anymore, and yet I did for this one to support the developers.My biggest reservation was that this was a shared world, online-only game. It has no reason to be one. All of the puzzles are single-player only. Communication with other players is super limited. It's like this game was pivoted late in development to be an online, live-service game because those are seen as having the potential to make more money by executives and investors.And that is the reason I cannot recommend this game. I've been trying to play for two days straight and the game immediately crashes upon launch, and won't connect me to the server on reload. If this game was a totally single-player experience that could be played offline, this wouldn't be an issue. And sure, this bug will probably be sorted out soon. But its the symptom of the larger problem that this game has no reason to be online-only, and it's only a detraction from the game it could've been.If that doesn't bother you, then this game is great. I had so much fun getting pulled into completing areas and solving puzzles. There's a ton of variation so you don't get tired of doing the same types of activities, and mixing in the open world exploration and movement adds to the experience. The Lunarch team created a great game with a very pretty world, but what I can only guess to be decisions from higher up soiled the experience for me. I'm sad for the game that Islands of Insight could've been.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Fun Puzzle game, it is not multiplayer. Server issues will likely cause you to lose puzzle progress and your patience. Runs poorly. I am in awe that this game is allowed to be listed for purchase in this state. If I wasn't being ask to play by a friend, I would have refunded. I would advise you not to buy this game until (if) the Offline Patch hits, and if you want to play expecting a multiplayer puzzle game, you are being misled. Also, game is likely abandoned so all issues mentioned probably will be there forever.It is listed as an MMO, there is zero reason to interact with another person. Every puzzle, At least that I have seen so far, is designed to be a single player interacting with it. There is a chat box, but it only tells you a player has completed a puzzle somewhere in the wold. You can not chat in the game. You communicate exclusively with an emote wheel of a handful of emotes, one of which is a request for help. How do you help someone with a puzzle that you can not see, nor can you effectively communicate with the person needing help? Stupid.Since the game is aspiring to be an MMO, that means it is ONLINE only. This game with 130 peak people playing it over the last 30 days has catastrophic server issues. In the time I have played, I have disconnected regularly from servers, multiple times an hour.If you do want to play with a friend, you are relying on luck to get into the same server as them. The friends list is cosmetic and you can not invite people to play through it, so unless your friend is on the same server as you, standing in front of you, you can not party. Couple this with the server disconnects, the annoying effort it of repeatedly relaunching the game and crossing your fingers, just to play with a friend is frankly laughable how they have the unbridled gall to even mention MMO in the same breath as Islands of Insight.Islands of Insight lists there is over 10,000 puzzles. I'n my handful of hours played I have already seen repeated puzzles, by that I mean exact duplicate logic puzzles with the same answer. Not sure how they got the metric of 10,000 puzzles, it certainly does not mean unique puzzles, and there is obviously a significant amount of padding in that claimed amount. I suspect the amount of "Find the hidden object" puzzles inflates this figure.In a Reddit post, linking to a now deleted tweet, it is said the Devs are looking for new work.So I expect the game to be in an abandoned state. I suspect offline mode is going to also bring the shutdown of the servers for the online MMO that struggles to be online, and is also not really multiplayer.Graphically the game is nice, but the performance and optimisation is poor, which, coupled with the above comment, will not be changing I suspect. For context I have a 5800x and 3070 and struggle to keep 60fps(1440p).Weirdly, I am not a "puzzle person", but I have found most of the puzzles engaging. The gameplay is good in that regard, but it in no way makes up for the enormous problems the game has.Overall, it is a good puzzle game build on a broken foundation of poor optimisation, broken servers, and pointless online features which are not going to be fixed. If this was an offline or LAN game, it would have been a banger. The tagged on MMO features literally killed the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game. It's great. I don't have a problem with it going free to keep for 24 hours. _childDocuments_.review: Islands of Insight offers a little bit for everyone. There's plenty of puzzles of every difficulty level, and plenty of paths forward in the single player campaign for people of every skill level. However, there's also a great layer of depth to the game, with tons of difficult challenges and hidden content for players that really take the time to dive deep into what is has to offer.Pros:+ Gorgeous landscapes, especially when you get into areas like Lucent Waters and Autumn Falls.+ Puzzles for every difficulty level.+ Campaign is gated behind solving puzzles, but not so difficult that you can't skip the more challenging ones.+ Hidden secrets. I won't spoil these, but there are extra mysteries and challenges awaiting those that search for them...+ Co-op means you can play with friends. This is useful for finding hidden objects or finding missing puzzles in Enclaves, but you cannot solve puzzles for other people (and people cannot interfere with your gameplay.)+ Dozens, if not hundreds, of hours of gameplay available. Easily worth the money if you're a big puzzle lover.Cons:- GPU / CPU tend to get a bit fried on initial boot-up. I've had the game crash if I'm trying to do anything else on the computer while it loads. Once I'm in, it runs fine though.- Co-op is a bit lacking in certain departments and could use some additions to help with puzzles that aren't just part of the environment.- Small bouts of lag when loading in to new zones / Enclaves. Issues with rubber banding have seemingly been solved, however!TL;DR: Islands of Insight is a beautiful, fleshed-out love letter to puzzle enthusiasts. Its co-op features are rather limited and people will bemoan the fact that it's online-only, but you'll easily get your money's worth out of the game in just a few days of play.

_childDocuments_.review: A shining exemplar of an entry-level puzzle game. Not *every* puzzle is super-satisfying to solve, but the vast majority of them are. The always-online aspect is also a point against it, but the game runs smooth as butter and I haven't experienced any game-play disruptions. There are multiple progression paths and so many different optional objectives to take on--truly a completionist's paradise. And it also helps that the sound and music presentation are also fantastic. Solving puzzles strikes your ears with satisfying tones and the music is ambient, yet atmospheric.I don't even play puzzle games. I think this is the first one I've picked up in over a decade. And I just can not put it down.

_childDocuments_.review: I am only in the first island after the starter area, haven't even gone for wings yet, so I can't speak to the long term experience.  But so far it is beautiful and relaxing.  Some puzzles are bone simple, others real mind benders.  There's a few where you need to be able to run quickly and precisely, others where you can't make mistakes (but can keep restarting), but overall it is very forgiving (so far).  I had a friend watch me for a while and he will probably be buying it now.I would like a little more camera control, as I find it awkward to have my view well to the right of my character in third person plus would like slightly more zoom out, but after hours of play my mouse hand may have been in pain but my motion sickness was not showing itself so it's workable.This is not action adventure (so far).  You can't fall to your death off an island, and there's no falling damage when jumping off cliffs.  It's just puzzle after puzzle, with some of the effort going into searching them out.  I love it.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay. UNlike my more recent reviews where I'll bullet a list of pros and cons, I feel like I can't really put words to paper about why I can't recommend this game, unless I talk about them all together.I really really wish I could block the story. It's one of those "trying to be profound/you're a special little snowflake" stories, and that's compounded by the amount of bits and bobs they put on your character that in the INITIAL character creator, they don't let you take off, but in customization later you can. I like the character customization menu, it's a nice reward that you can take once you've got all the movement from the skill tree. I hate that this puzzle game has a skill tree. Oh, and let's talk about ALL that movement that's on the skill tree. You get:A double jumpa super jump that you can only use 3 times every 5 minutesThese items would have been far better in the same way they handled the wings. Give us a puzzle enclave for double jumping, or a puzzle enclave for super jumping (and remove that stupid cooldown). The puzzle enclaves were such a good idea! Why waste them like this?Oh! and let's talk about the puzzles. When the puzzles are actually puzzles (Armillary rings, skydrops, sentinel stones, crystal labyrinths, grids, match boxes, hell, I'll even count the kaleidoscopes) they're really good!... maybe don't call "find the hidden thingus" a puzzle. A hidden kaizo block is not a puzzle unless it's hidden cleverly, which I'll give to the Hidden Archways most of the time. if they had used the hidden blocks and flight rings as platforming challenges the way they used the hidden archways, I would have much less to say here."Ah but this game has community puzzles" Yeah, cool, awesome. Can't wait to see them. Your reality is that you're going to be playing the official puzzles for a very long time before the community gets invovled beyond jumpscaring you with THEIR overdesigned characters the moment you leave a puzzle grid.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played around 10 hours so far (including the demo) and am loving it so far:- The logic grids are a highlight. There are so many unique mechanics, which are often introduced with well-designed sequences of easier puzzles to ramp you up, and the puzzles themselves often have cool visual or logical "themes" (you can really tell they were crafted by hand instead of churned out by an algorithm, which is especially impressive given how many there are). It's honestly insane how I keep discovering new mechanics or rulesets that feel completely different to solve.- Outside of the logic grids, I'm impressed by the sheer variety of puzzle types. Not all of them are hits (looking at you, morphic fractal), but everything contributes to making an experience that doesn't get repetitive.- Overall, it's really fun and relaxing just to explore the world while stumbling upon small puzzles everywhere.I do kind of wish there was more co-op functionality somehow - right now, the easiest way to play with friends is having one person stream to everyone else. But just in terms of the puzzles, I don't think I've ever experienced this combination of scale and variety (without compromising on puzzle quality) in any game I've seen, and I can see myself playing this for a long time.

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy puzzles, this is a great game! There are an absolutely insane amount to solve (10k +) and a few areas have infinite generation of more puzzles. From movement to logic puzzles. matching to quick solves, there is a huge variety. A puzzle isn't clicking for you? That's fine, move onto others! Speaking of moving, the game is pretty fluid and jumping/flying around is enjoyable.  All that said, if you need a "main quest" or are looking for a specific objective, this may not be as strong of a game for you.   Note: No combat, so don't come looking for the fanciest sword :P

_childDocuments_.review: Tl;dr: for 20h its a fun puzzle game. Beyond that annoying.There are many things to like in this game: * Enclaves are designed well. * Many cool puzzle types. * Moving through the world is fun.But having many puzzle types comes at the cost at some of them being unfun for any given player. I hate music puzzles, because I suck at listening. I dislike matchboxes because I don't want to search for the parts of the puzzle I want to solve. And I dislike hidden objects and the wobbly glass graphics, as they are confusing instead of mentally challenging to me.There are also puzzles you might consider badly designed. The fractals are atrocious.Beyond that, there are just some things I find bad design. But those started to annoy me hours into the game and it was well worth the discounted price.The "sandbox" area. (That is the open world puzzles not part of enclaves! The game calls it "sandbox" only in the item unlock description, with no real explanation, apparently it was the internal name for it?) feels more like randomly generated puzzles instead of well designed areas. Puzzles get added on a timer to keep you able to fulfil the infinite quest for puzzles. But they lack quality in my eyes.Obviously, this also means you can never clean any area up, there will always be more to do. There is no systematic way to go through an area to do all the puzzles. You will never see the world cleaned up of puzzles. Especially the visually obvious puzzles seem to generate often, skydrops and shy auras.This "inifite" puzzle aspect, also shows in the unlocks of sandbox items. The amount of puzzles required to unlock a set of cosmetics in an area is huge, but the number of interesting puzzles low. So it quickly feels like a grind with slow progress. Further, the game has quite a few annoying bugs. Using quicktravel has a 50% change for me to get the game stuck. Not the character, but the game itself: Menu won't open anymore, no more moving, nothing. Only a restart helps. But restarts reset some aspects of the game. Because even though it is always online, some challenges do not save (e.g. the skydrop speed challenge). There are more, but those are the most annoying, as they are consistent and unvoidable.The open world multiplayer aspects seems useless, bordering annoying. The lack of meaningful interactions with other people is good, it prevents spoilers and backseaters, but makes the whole feature questionable. It's not like I'll go logic puzzling with my friends in game - I'd rather stream to them and talk to them.A quick puzzle ra(n)ting: * Skydrops: easy, fun, but useless. Doesn't count to any of the exploration categories for unlocking cosmetics. * Shy auras: Repetetive, boring beyond the enclave, visually distracting. A puzzle that has a simple 3 step approach to solving it, is not much of a puzzle: Fly there (can I click it?), stop and wait 3 seconds (can I click it now?), go away and sneak to it backwards (now I have to be able to click it). But they are also inconsistent in sometimes reapearing even though your approach should have made them inaccessible. * Hidden objects: Archs are wayyyy too much everywhere and give no challenge, the cubes are annoying. The rings are cool. * Fractals: Are so bad people openly recommend just randomly clicking and moving. If they could at least be controlled using the keyboard, as the mouse it too rough for the sometimes pixel-perfect requirements. But I will stop playing before I'll ever solve one again. (Apparently they will be changed next patch.) * Moving a-rings: Standing next to a puzzle and having to wait until it is actually solveable is not fun.Most other puzzles beyond those are fine to good. The logic puzzles are by far my favorite, they are also the only ones with a sensible difficulty rating.Lastly, the game has a story. It seems pretentious and badly told, but I am here for the puzzles, not the story.Also the game doesn't work well with ultra wide screen monitors, some of the rolling block puzzles dont fit the screen.Final rating: Totally fine to play some puzzles for 20h, but beyond that it becomse a chore.

_childDocuments_.review: There are a lot of things I liked and disliked in this game.  They are amazing and diversified. Some require logic to solve them. For others, you either need to be observant of the world or just fast enough to reach a point before a timer stops. No matter what your mood is, there is a puzzle for you. It's beautiful. There are four main areas, each having a different theme, and no two buildings are alike. The map also complements many puzzles. For some puzzles (All-Seeing Monolith Fragments, Matchbox, Hidden archway, Hidden rings), the topography is used to hide things you need to find. With Mysteries and Sightseers, you need to explore the map and find a place corresponding to a riddle/image. The topography is used in other puzzles where you need to follow a path (Flight rings, Flow Orbs, Wandering Echo). I would change nothing of this world. You are forced to be online to play this game in a shared world where you are mostly alone. You can interact a little bit with other players but not much. I have seen once a player ask for help for a matchbox puzzle and I couldn't even help him because I forgot where the other one was. That was the biggest interaction I ever had with another player. Because you are online, you can get a lot of lag. This makes one type of puzzle almost impossible to do because you need to pass through a series of rings while flying and without touching the ground. Right now, having the multiplayer aspect in this game brings problems and nothing positive. The developers should either make it so you can play the game offline or add some puzzles requiring you to solve with other players.  What story? At first, I was reading through all of the lore fragments I found. After some time, they just became all similar without ever giving us real information. Now, I mostly find them to complete the game without even reading them. Since this game is focused on puzzle and the puzzles are great, I do recommend this game. But if you want to buy this game to solve puzzles with your friends, don't bother buying Islands of Insight.
_childDocuments_.name: Islands of Insight

_childDocuments_.review: Really, really good. The world is fun to explore and packed to the brim with puzzles that offer great variety, both in terms of their mechanics and difficulty. The multiplayer element is not by any means necessary to the game, but it does add a little bit of extra flavour. I do wish there was more in the way of purpose and means to interact with other players, as only a handful of the puzzle types really benefit from the help of another player, and the only means of communication are a very limited set of pings and emotes. That said, the very same restricted nature of the system has made the interactions I've had feel all the more meaningful. There is something truly special about learning to nonverbally communicate with a complete stranger, and just spending a couple of hours hanging out and solving puzzles with them. It's a kind of feeling that no other medium can ever really hope to inspire.

_childDocuments_.review: So the online mode is no more, the servers are shut down. The remaining devs managed to cobble together a much-requested offline mode just in time, though the feeling remains that the original intentions behind the game were perhaps somewhat misguided. A graphically demanding, MMO puzzle game which does not support co-op solving of puzzles in any way? Weird. All moot now of course.As it currently stands, is it still worth playing? I would say so, if nothing else for the sheer number, variety and quality of puzzles. That's the only thing that should really matter to fans of puzzle games, and it would be a shame for people to miss out on a truly colossal achievement in puzzle games.Graphics? Unnecessarily intensive, but pretty modern.Performance? Not bad, plenty of options to scale down if need be, though for some reason hardware likes to cook with this one. Make sure there are no hot-spots on your GPU!Gameplay? There's bound to be some puzzles you like given the different styles available (and possibly some you don't like, *cough* fractals), though the vast majority of the puzzles are logic grids. The setters for these puzzles are absolute geniuses, and there are plenty of warm-up puzzles to teach you the tricks necessary to solve the extra challenging ones. Very satisfying for the puzzle enthusiast.

_childDocuments_.review: Out front, I'd give this game a 4/5. It's a magnificent puzzle game with hard puzzles, plenty of randomly generated ones with proper solutions, and a beautiful world in which they all reside. There's a few issues with the performance of the game (even at lower settings, my computer acts more like a heater), and frames will occasionally drop. That would be tolerable if not for the single glaring flaw this game has.This is a puzzle game and an MMO. The MMO aspect is always online, and causes massive lagspikes if the server or your connection isn't doing too hot. Again, for a puzzle game, this ordinarily wouldn't be a problem, but it becomes EXTREMELY frustrating when attempting to do any of the movement-based "puzzles" or any of the time trials. It's questionable why an MMO was the choice for this game, given that interactions with players are completely minimal (you can't really jump into a puzzle to help someone out), there's no text chat, you end up with an endless stream of "x solved y puzzle" with no indication of how difficult the puzzle itself was (and is thus just a waste of bandwidth, since every insignificant puzzle gets the limelight there, even if you blast through them one after another in the span of 30 seconds), and frustrations set in when another player takes a puzzle you were aiming for (the number of times I found myself hunting down another Rings or Moondrop because a random player I didn't see snagged it right before I got there is extraordinary).All in all, it's a great puzzle game, highly immersive, but the MMO aspect of it is still (since open beta) a rather questionable decision with no real tangible benefits to anybody. I just hope that I don't lose this game when the servers inevitably shut down for one reason or another. The game is built in such a way that it's entirely unnecessary, but the fear is still there.

_childDocuments_.review: I put about 10 hours into the game now that I have a computer capable of running it, and all I can think is that I'm glad I got the game for free. I don't regret playing it, but I certainly wouldn't want to pay money for it. The experience overall just feels... mediocre.First of all the puzzles. Some of the puzzles are pretty great. Basically all of the logic grid style are good and the rings are pretty fun and quick. The rolling block puzzles, match three, and phasic dials are okay too, although not my favorites. But so many of the so-called puzzles are anything but. If you're feeling very generous, you could call some of the perspective games puzzles, I suppose the skydrops, sentinel stones, and light motifs could loosely be called puzzles. But matchblocks, hidden rings and archways, sightseers, hidden pentads, and wandering echos? Hide and seek is NOT a puzzle.The hide and seek "puzzles" can be fun for a little while, but they quickly become tedious and overly time consuming. And unfortunately, if you want to progress the game, doing some amount of each puzzle is mandatory, as you have to do enclaves to progress the main quest and open new areas, and each enclave has a set of puzzle types that you have to do a certain amount of for the game to consider the enclave complete. My breaking point was the first enclave in the 3rd major area (of 5, I believe), where 3 out of the 4 required "puzzles" were hide and seek style. I noped out of the game then and there.One other issue with the game lie with the platforming. It feels pretty janky, with your character having a lot of momentum which makes it hard to land precisely. It's not that big a deal most of the the time, but when you're doing flow orbs (basically platforming time trial, also not a puzzle), it can definitely hinder you.The last big issue that I was running into was difficulty. Now admittedly, I'm not a hardcore puzzler, so I usually quit puzzle games when the puzzles start taking long enough that I'm not having fun anymore. I don't hold that against puzzle games, and I don't hold it against this one. The issue I have is that the difficulty labelling they have for the puzzles is all over the place. I would continually find puzzles labeled 2-3 on the difficulty that were harder than some of the star rated puzzles I found earlier. For a game this long, they really needed a wider rating scale for puzzle difficulty, like 1-10, then 1 star to 10 star for the "grandmaster" difficulty puzzles or whatever they called them.Overall, I don't know that I'd recommend it, at least not as a pure puzzler. If the idea of some good puzzles mixed with an awful lot of hide and seek seems fun to you, it might be worth a shot, although I'd wait for a steep discount. Otherwise, probably just give it a miss.
_childDocuments_.name: Islands of Insight

_childDocuments_.review: If you like logic puzzles and the like, then . However, please be aware of the following:Initially, Islands of Insight was Online only. However, player interaction was incredibly minimal (you could emote and ping at each other, that's it), so people asked for an offline mode, which was eventually rolled out. Then, 3 months later, the devs announced that the servers would close and the game would be offline only, and no more update would be delivered.  Also, we had only one month to backup our save file, which is way too short. Was it because the game did not perform as well as they wanted and the server costs were too high? Did they just get bored of it and wanted to move on to something else? We don't know. Communication from the devs has been quite minimal. Personally, it is hard for me to put much trust in Lunarch Studios after this.Most of the puzzles are good. Like, really good. They range from bite-sized snacks to full-on feasts. Most enclaves are really fun to go through, and then to 100% afterwards (to a point where sometimes  the remaining puzzle is the reward in itself for the exploration).However,Again, if you think a beautiful puzzle game full of logic puzzles and exploration is right for you, then you will love this game. Just be aware of the above.Personally, I like it, and I will likely play more of it (even though I have to start from scratch since my save file is gone). But I don't know if I can recommend it anymore as it is now.
_childDocuments_.name: Islands of Insight

_childDocuments_.review: the game is a niche puzzle game, intriguing and entertaining, but with so many wrong pieces fixed into it. the game tried to be a multiplayer experience, but with everything about multiplayer done poorly: * the "multiplayer" aspect of this game is just you can watching people running around the world, solve their puzzle on their end.* you can't connect to your friend directly, you have to randomly exit and reenter, hope the game put you at the same server with your friend.* despite everything in the game can be done solo, due to the game forced you to play as multiplayer, you have to wait for your game connected to the server.* and because it is connected to the server, if server lag happen, the traveling in this game can get wonky. good luck climbing up that ledge when you need to chase the wisp.* even when the game offered singleplayer mode in recent update, all progress you have in multiplayer does not transfer to singleplayer. practically a insult to singleplayer.lastly, the game doesn't seems to optimize well, so many asset, lighting, rendering put into the game to make it look pretty -- and it is stunning to look at, if the game feels choppy to play, it doesn't matter how pretty it looks. the game is a nice puzzle game, but so many pieces upsetting me too much to recommend it to other people. i hope the game gets better in the future; i paid for this game, i am okay to continuously suffer all the nonsense just to see it get better.
_childDocuments_.name: Islands of Insight

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not much of a puzzler. The last puzzle game I played was probably Portal 2, but Islands of Insight sucked me right in. It's incredibly addicting, but in a good way. Hats off to Lunarch Studios!I should lead with the major caveat: only buy this if you are okay with a forced always-online product. I went ahead and purchased it on launch because my intention is to play it now while it's active. This game is a kind of nontraditional multiplayer that is fascinating to me, where communication is limited to the bare minimum. The titular  are not just the lush, exotic habitats, it's the players who explore them.This game is basically a giant playground already, and having the playground to yourself just isn't as fun in my experience. IOI reminds me of being a kid and joining random Garry's Mod servers running custom maps. I would click on something that sounded interesting, spend an eternity downloading all the custom assets, and load in. Often I would end up in strange surroundings, someone else's creation whose inspirations I could only guess at. HUD elements and buildings suggested unknown activities, parts of an often unfinished vision. Other players might be around, maybe other curious explorers or maybe seasoned residents of a space I found foreign. IOI has bottled those memories for me.However, I still almost didn't buy IOI on principle for one reason: always-online games are at risk of disappearing once the publisher stops paying for servers. The possibility that Lunarch's captivating playground might disappear just like those obscure Garry's Mod maps is sad. It's also inexcusable for an actual product with a price tag. I can only imagine it's a gross overstep from the publisher Behaviour Interactive, or a puzzling (pardon the pun) error of judgement from a developer studio that has otherwise done everything right.A timely patch with a true offline mode would be much more preferable. I understand there are reasons for online-only gaming, such as increasing server population and discouraging piracy. I don't think any and all of the reasons  even hold a candle to the reasons . Risk of deprecation, being unable to play when servers go down, lag, and the lack of real co-op or social interaction, to name a few. As neat as the multiplayer is, it's definitely not necessary to enjoy the game.It's such a shame that I don't have nearly as much to say about the  of this game, because there's plenty. It's just that I don't have much commentary besides "Wow!" and "Well done!"The world is beautiful. I wouldn't call it immersive; as I said above, IOI feels like and functions as a giant virtual playground. That applies to the visuals as well, it's just that in this case the playground was created by a god-being with a flair for grandiosity. I call it stunning, delightful, inspiring, and mesmerising.The puzzles are engaging. I haven't experienced all the puzzle types or levels of difficulty, but so far there's been plenty that make you feel smart and plenty that give you something to chew on for a while. Some "puzzles" really serve as brain candy, popcorn for snacking on in between the more cerebral stuff. It results in great pacing and a steady dripfeed of dopamine.The gamefeel is just right. Everything is fast, responsive, snappy. The movement doesn't hold anything back. You can superjump into the stratosphere and glide anywhere you want very early on. The effects and sounds involved when you solve puzzles are pure satisfaction.A list of other things I think deserve kudos:-thorough tutorialization without handholding-a staggering amount of content-true sandbox design; quest progression unlocks a lot of content but you're free to go where you please, even resulting in sequence breaks-character customization offers some unique options-the limited player interactions are just expressive enough to make memorable virtual interactions possible-solid but unobtrusive progression systems, including leveling, upgrades, cosmetics, collectibles, and titles-robust settings, including toggle sprint and crouch-motion blur was turned off by default-mouse sensitivity was actually usable by default-I didn't need to to do any first-time setup, even on my crusty but hardy GTX 1070. The auto-detect settings got me a relatively stable 60 fps while the game still looked great. I even tinkered with it anyway and ended up using exactly what it set me up with from the beginning. I don't know whether to credit Lunarch or the Unreal Engine for this, but it's impressive as it's the first time it's happened to me on PC in memory.A shorter list of things I want to improve. Not negatives, just opportunities:-toggleable and repositionable HUD elements, first and foremost.-visual seams on character models and markings customizations-character animations. This is borderline a negative, but once again only because always-online means other players might be on your screen all the time as opposed to choosing between first and third person.-I think the fractal puzzles need more feedback for how you control them. Then again I've also decided I just don't like crystal mazes, so I'm prepared to accept that not all puzzles are for everybody.I think Islands of Insight has the potential for mainstream success. It is an experience that is far easier to digest than its peers in the genre. And despite its limited in-game communication, it's the perfect game to play with your significant other or Discord friends. It's up to Behaviour to market the game for what it actually is.
_childDocuments_.name: Islands of Insight

_childDocuments_.review: While my PC screams for help, I can play! That is, after suffering through the 10 minute loading time it takes after selecting offline mode. Oh and even at lowest settings, I still get performance drops down to the seconds-per-frame region. And if I move too fast, performance tanks even further. But who cares, I CAN play, and that's the key part. And there's some bugs in offline, like sparks getting much lower between sessions, putting me in debt to the Mirabilis Mafia, but those are just minor issues. Puzzles are phenomenal, for the most part (looking at you, hidden cubes and memory grids), graphics are not something I care about, music and SFX are okay, movement system is workable, lore can be safely ignored. Good game, but can (and hopefully will) be better.

_childDocuments_.review: it's hard to recommend a game like this.on its face as a puzzle game it's kind of mid, it feels like half the puzzles are the kind of thing you'd "solve" in a batman arkham game "look at this spot from this position" "pick up this slightly hidden thing" "fly through these rings" the other half are pretty ok/good logic puzzles, which i like.the game is kind of catnip for people who enjoy collect-a-thons and puzzles because there are so many of them all over the place that you find yourself just tripping over them nonstop.the story and atmosphere reminds me a lot of the talos principle.all of this is... fine.edit: recent patches have removed the online mode entirely. this is now a single player game, as it probably always should have been.edit: recent patches seem to have resolved rubberbanding issues, which was really the straw that broke the camel's back on my negative review. i still wouldn't say this is a great game, the multiplayer is still pointless and dumb but the overall experience isn't bad. it's just mid.
_childDocuments_.name: Islands of Insight

_childDocuments_.review: A great game with tons of puzzles, that are of different styles of puzzles, It's very nice to be able to fly around and find a puzzle that you feel like doing hard/easy/music/slidey/logic/environmental. I weirdly like the choice they did by making it online, it adds a bit of life and makes it feel like you are not alone on the game, and have made friends in the moment when you help each other find hidden cubes, :) Would highly recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Islands of Insight

_childDocuments_.review: This game is advertised as having 10000+ puzzles, yet a vast majority of them can not in good conscience be called "puzzles". Many of them are as simple as walking through a randomly placed archway or touching a randomly placed ring.The multiplayer in this game functioned mostly reliably at launch but after trying to revisit it today, I have found that there is no way to play it without experiencing major issues like getting kicked back to the main menu or players moving erratically.I would also like to mention that there is no way to reset your online progress by yourself. You will have to contact their support team which takes 24 hours to respond to an email and does not read them properly, nor do they answer any questions, even simple ones.While the design of the actual puzzles is phenomenal and should by all means receive a recommendation from me, the gameplay experience, and the false advertising leave me rather wanting to cure my boredom by defenestrating myself.
_childDocuments_.name: Islands of Insight

_childDocuments_.review: Update: they handled this game very poorly. they deleted all save files unless you transferred it from the online version to the offline version, rather than doing that automatically themselves. i still recommend this game but you should know what you're getting into with it because it's no longer (and never really was to begin with) what the developers originally sold it as.I've put 30 hours into this game so I think it's about time to review it. I first played its demo from the steam next fest and absolutely loved the game. I refused to buy it, though, because it required players to be always online despite the game being single player. There are co-op abilities and you are in a large, shared world, but the multiplayer aspects in this game are nearly non-existent. I really do enjoy seeing other people flying around the world and interacting through emotes only but the always-online requirement ensured this would be lost media in a few years whenever the servers stopped running. The devs recently announced they're working on developing an offline mode so I bought the game immediately.The game is beautiful first and foremost, as can be seen from the game's screenshots. It has bright, vibrant colors and shows a lost civilization's ruins on top of a beautiful floating (in the sky) island. The story exists through text lore and while this certainly isn't a game I recommend because of its narrative, I do find myself really interested in the overall narrative that is slowly unraveling. There's a rift in the sky, and hundreds of essence orbs scattered around that you talk to which start to depict what happened to this dying world. It's quite beautiful and deeply philosophical actually. The gameplay is quite spectacular. The movement feels good, offering double jump, running, flying, jump pads, and a super jump ability. There's some parkour challenges/puzzles that are ever so slightly degraded by the rubber banding on the servers but honestly it's negligible and should become a defunct critique once the offline mode is implemented. The puzzles are brilliantly crafted and have a wide variety. Some of them are hidden objects, some of them require flying skills, some require you to consider perspective and angle yourself at the right position to see something in a different way. There's glass escape towers where it's difficult to tell which way to go. There's music puzzles which require (and will heighten) your ability to identify musical notes. There's logic grids that play partially into the logic of sudoku, with many various rules that can apply at times and not in others. There's mosaics you can decipher, tetris-style puzzles, ring puzzles, and much more. The puzzle variety is impressive in both its quantity and quality.The best thing about Islands of Insight is how casual yet engrossing it is. It's a casual game in which you can get up and grab a drink, take your dog for a walk, or make dinner and you don't need to worry about pausing, placing yourself in a specific zone or anything. It's a game that allows me to be busy taking care of my dog recovering from ACL surgery while still having a blast and not worrying about dying or getting to a good stopping point. In fact, you can fall off the map in this game in which the existential being that talks to you will catch you and place you right back where you were.Islands of Insight is very reminiscent of my time studying for the LSAT. Much of that was simply figuring out logic puzzles applied through words. Islands of Insight is much less stressful than the LSAT but just like with the LSAT preparation, I see myself progressing in my understanding in real time. It's very rewarding when it starts to click and you begin speeding through certain types of puzzles or certain rule types, only to come across something new to learn and master. This is one of the most beautiful and unique gaming experiences with surprisingly fantastic quality matching its absurd quantity. This is a game you can easily sink dozens or hundreds of hours into, but also one that you won't feel bad about if you only put 15 hours in.
_childDocuments_.name: Islands of Insight

_childDocuments_.review: Islands of Insight is an amazing game with some of the best puzzles I have ever experienced, with a large variety of puzzles and difficulties. It is also very fun to play with friends and help each other solve some of the more tedious puzzles like SMALL INVISIBLE CUBES. 9/10 would recommend it to everyone, from beginners to puzzle masters.

_childDocuments_.review: *Islands of Insight* is an enchanting puzzle adventure that takes players on a journey through beautifully crafted islands filled with intriguing challenges. This game seamlessly blends exploration and puzzle-solving, creating an immersive experience that encourages players to engage their minds while enjoying the stunning visuals. The gameplay focuses on a variety of puzzles that test players' logic and creativity. As players traverse different islands, they encounter unique challenges that require critical thinking and problem-solving skills. The controls are intuitive, allowing for smooth navigation through the richly detailed environments. The game also includes hidden secrets and collectibles that enhance replayability and encourage thorough exploration. Set in a captivating world, *Islands of Insight* offers a whimsical narrative that unfolds as players progress through the game. Each island has its own theme and story elements, contributing to an overarching adventure that keeps players engaged. The environments are lush and diverse, featuring vibrant flora and fauna that bring the world to life. Visually, the game is stunning, with artful graphics that create a vibrant and immersive atmosphere. Each island is distinct, showcasing a variety of artistic styles and colors that enhance the exploration experience. The sound design complements the visuals with a soothing soundtrack and ambient sounds that draw players deeper into the world, making every moment feel magical. *Islands of Insight* is a captivating puzzle adventure that combines engaging gameplay with beautiful visuals and an enchanting world. It's perfect for players looking for a thoughtful gaming experience filled with exploration and creativity.---With its enchanting world and engaging puzzles, *Islands of Insight* offers a delightful experience that invites players to explore and solve their way through a beautifully crafted adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: Lots of fun puzzles with varying degrees of challenge put together in a beautiful shared world where you can see everyone else. You can't share quest progress with people, but it wouldn't really make sense too since you'd just be completing each others game - you can however party up with people which makes it easier for you to keep track of where your friends are in the world and share the experience while still doing the puzzles yourself.
