_childDocuments_.review: I had a whole angry spiel here about how terrible the online mode was: how unnecessary it was and how poorly built it was, forcing constant jittering every couple of minutes that forced you off the map and made many of the exact location puzzles impossible. With the release of the offline mode, my number one biggest critique of the game has been solved, and all that's left is a bunch of really well put together puzzles. I can recommend it without issue now.
_childDocuments_.name: Islands of Insight

_childDocuments_.review: A puzzle paradise. I was skeptical when i first heard about this game. But wow! It has exceeded my expectations. Ranging from quick little puzzles to mazes and more. You unlock more involved puzzles as you progress through the beautiful areas. It has a really good match 3 puzzle and a sequel to that famous flash game Bloxorz!
_childDocuments_.name: Islands of Insight

_childDocuments_.review: Islands of Insight is by far one of the best puzzle games I've played. It has what seems to be infinite puzzles scattered across a massive landscape. The amount of variety here is very much key. Any puzzle game could go make infinite tile-matching puzzles (think bejeweled), but that gets boring eventually. This game really thrives in the variety of puzzle types, of which there are 24 types. Some puzzle types are exclusively sound based, some visual memory, others you just need to wonder upon the world and acquire the correct perspective. In any case, there are varying levels of puzzle difficulty among these various type (of which many I didn't even mention). Certain tactics and methods will make you much better at completing certain types of puzzles, but at the end of the day: if you just want a fun puzzle game without much effort, this is your game; If you want a puzzle game that can challenge you with very difficult puzzles, this is your game. If you want to find the hidden secrets of unlocks that you find late game, this is your game. There are enough goals within the game to make it very fun to progress to your own preferred level, my only true gripe is the lack of an achievement system within Steam.This game certainly won't suit everyone. Some people get annoyed by certain repetitive puzzle types, but this game doesn't force you to complete them. You can go about your day and do whatever puzzles you wish in whatever order you prefer. This if your adventure to write and you make your own fun out of it.I'm not going to speak to lore as I generally ignore lore in-game, so reference other reviewers for that information, although it is fun to try and collect all of the lore fragments in-game.Regarding online servers, while I have experienced some occasional network hiccups that have caused very noticeable lag, I would not say it is game breaking in most instances, but does lock things up on rare occasions. If you have spotty connection though, it may make the issue worse, but I feel most of the issues I've run into I believe are just server load and balancing issues. Of the 150 hours I have in-game, so little of it has been interrupted by network troubles overall. Now that the game has been out for weeks, the network generally has stabilized and I have had no recent issues to note.Hope this helps someone else that likes a good puzzle adventure. Happy puzzling!
_childDocuments_.name: Islands of Insight

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic! A lovely game, wonderful puzzle design which makes you feel more intelligent as it teaches you the mechanics. The vibe is very relaxing, putting you in a flow state, with a great density of puzzles everywhere you look. The MMO aspect is nice and chill - you see people running about solving puzzles but there's not tonnes of interaction. It just creates a sense of camaraderie as we all explore and master the puzzles. Hope there are expansions down the road as I'd definitely pay for more islands, new puzzle types, more puzzles, etc. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Islands of Insight

_childDocuments_.review: First off, as many others have said, this is not really a co-op or multiplayer game. Sure, you can see other people running around the world doing their thing. But you don't solve puzzles together, and interaction in general is pretty limited. If you go into this game planning to just play on your own while seeing other people in the world you will enjoy yourself a lot more.That said, if you like puzzles, this game will keep you busy for a LONG time. I'm over 12 hours in right now and feel like I've only barely scratched the surface. There is a nice variety of puzzles, and the different types of puzzles all range in difficulty from solving it immediately to real head-scratchers that will take you a while to figure out. That is what I think is one of the game's biggest strengths: if you hit a puzzle that's really giving you trouble, you can just wander off and do literally hundreds of others. You can come back to it later... or not. It's pretty much up to you. While the game guides you in a general direction, once the initial tutorial island is over, it opens up a ton, allowing you to wander off at your leisure if you feel like it.Solving the puzzles gives you points, and there's an interesting skill tree that you can spend those points on to unlock bonus traversal abilities (like diving while in flight) to puzzle QoL improvements (like filling entire sections in the logic grid with a single click) to getting bonus points for solving specific puzzle types or by not making any mistakes. I never thought a skill tree would make sense in a puzzle game, but this one actually works. Kudos to the devs on that one! It makes solving all the puzzles feel meaningful, even if the puzzle was extremely easy for you.There are also quests that direct you to specific areas and new puzzles types that help you to unlock new island areas to explore. If you get tired of the current type of puzzle you're doing just follow the quests, and a new puzzle type will be introduced shortly. In addition to this, the islands that introduce the new puzzle types also have other puzzle types sprinkled around on them so you aren't just doing the same kind over and over again. Variety is maintained even when the game is teaching you a new mechanic.The world is gorgeous and fun to traverse. A brief note to makers of other puzzle games: PLEASE implement a movement speed like this game. You can zip around this game and be in a completely different place in no time, and the gliding mechanic makes this even more fun. There are so many puzzle games that have you plodding along, even in much smaller environments than this one, and it can feel so tedious when you just want to get to the next puzzle. It's so refreshing to be able to zoom around and get to where you want to go in seconds.To summarize, while I think the multiplayer aspect of this game feels tacked on, I still highly recommend it as a puzzle game in its own right. The puzzle variety is solid, the world is gorgeous, it's fun to fly around in, and if you get stuck on a puzzle there is always another one just steps away. I'm sure I'll be playing this one for a long time to come, even if they don't end up adding any sort of DLC content. This game is just huge and well worth the money. If you love puzzles, I think you'll enjoy this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Islands of Insight

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very good game for Autistic gamers like myself. Puzzles for days! Lots of thingies to collect! Lots of beautiful areas to explore. Music is pleasing and not distracting. You can play online or offline. Online doesn't really have a negative affect, since there is no PVP and everyone seems to be very friendly. I really cannot get enough of this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Islands of Insight

_childDocuments_.review: Well, I guess the first puzzle is actually getting the game to work.I pressed Play on the menu screen and was taken to what I assume is a loading screen (no loading bar, flashing dots, etc.). I could move my mouse, but the loading screen never went away. I tried loading the game three separate times, each time waiting over 10 minutes on the loading screen to see if anything would happen. Nothing. Game would not load.It seems the current state of the game is not acceptable or playable for a lot of people. Hopefully they work on it and maybe release it with an offline mode. Having to connect to the server seems to be the biggest of issues right now.I can't recommend this game and will be asking for a refund.
_childDocuments_.name: Islands of Insight

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a grip on me and I did not expect that from a puzzle game. From the Metatron aesthetic to the general flow of the puzzles, it's actually a pretty relaxing environment to explore and work through the puzzles in. There's a good mix of stuff to just run around and collect, quick puzzles for short sessions, and some more complex items for longer sessions. It FELT like I did a lot in what little I've played so far but going by the map there's definitely a lot more. I will say, while yes the game COULD be an offline only experience if they wanted to design it that way, I do actually enjoy the "solving puzzles in a lobby" feel the game has. Having people flying around, emoting, showing up on the map, trying to work out puzzles around you; it gives the space a different "feel" than if it was just you and a big empty world of puzzles. I can understand if people want that isolated "me against the world of puzzles" feeling but they definitely wanted a more "community/social" oriented thing with the design here. If the fact that it's an online game isn't a dealbreaker then this is definitely worth checking out. It definitely scratches that itch if  you're the type that spends most of your time ignoring what you SHOULD be doing in other games and instead running around exploring the world for stuff.
_childDocuments_.name: Islands of Insight

_childDocuments_.review: Islands of Insight is a beautiful fantasy theme park full of puzzles hidden everywhere. Logic puzzles, perspective puzzles, egg hunts, mazes, and match games as far as the eye can see. There are so many puzzles you can't worry about doing them all—it's overwhelming.I freaking love it. I love getting my map out, going to check out a place that sounds interesting, and never making it because I get distracted by all the other puzzles on the way. I love how outrageously beautiful it didn't need to be, but is; the world is thoughtfully designed like a AAA fantasy RPG. I love the sense of progression—the little rewards you get for completing more that help compel you forward. And the puzzles are great, too. They're numerous and varied.For me, the only caveats are: the game lacks lockbox/contraption/locked-room type puzzles (as far as I know) and the puzzles are a bit on the smaller size, even when difficult—the game could use some real "centerpiece" puzzles, so to speak. And the MMO elements, while perfect in my opinion, are quite light—mostly just cosmetics and experience rank. I'm not sure if you even have the option to chat? (If so, I haven't seen or heard it in use). You might want to keep that in mind if the MMO aspect is what is appealing to you.Loads of content, good variety, stunning environments = a strong recommend for any puzzle-loving gamer, even at full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Islands of Insight

_childDocuments_.review: GOOD- Most of the puzzles are fun to solve.- Some of the puzzle types are pretty unique, I especially like under-clued grids, off by one grids, myopia arrows, and music grids- There is both online and offline mode:     - Online mode is fun because you can be with a bunch of other people who are all solving puzzles instead of just doing them alone     - If you don't like online or your PC can't handle it there is also an offline mode- A lot of the puzzles are handcrafted- It was fun to work through each area and complete all the enclaves- The mysteries were pretty fun to solve and I wish there were moreBAD- Various technical issues: getting booted in the middle of a puzzle, rubber-banding, lag when joining a server. But the devs do seem to be trying to fix these.- Some of the puzzles are kinda repetitive or annoying to solve, puzzles like morphic fractals, hidden objects, and glass mazes- There isn't really any communication between players other than pinging each other- Personally, the story isn't very interesting, but it is optional so you don't have to follow it if you don't want toEven though the technical issues somewhat diminish the experience, I would still highly recommend it to anyone who likes puzzles and I think most people would enjoy playing this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Islands of Insight

_childDocuments_.review: It seems like a fun idea - an open world puzzle game, something like The Witness or Talos Principle. However, the presentation is very uneven. You get upgrades to change your movement, but what exactly is the point of flying around when really what you want to do is get to the puzzles? And visually, there's just way too much going on. Every inch of the place looks like its trying to be as interesting as possible, which makes it impossible to set a goal for yourself in the landscape. Basically I don't really understand why there is so much movement tech in a game where you're just going puzzle to puzzle.
_childDocuments_.name: Islands of Insight

_childDocuments_.review: If this game was just the world and all the puzzles, it would be an instant recommend, because the puzzles are actually excellent, but it has a completely unnecessary multiplayer tacked on to it, with the pitfalls of connectivity and server issues included. The recent addition of offline play highlights the fact that the multiplayer aspects were not needed at all. I hope the devs listen to the feedback regarding this (as they seem to already have) and phase out the multiplayer entirely, because I'm sure with the sheer volume and quality of puzzles people would love to pay for this game even more than they are now.A shocking amount of issues and nitpicks I have with the player experience are directly caused by multiplayer, such as glitching out of ledges due to latency, long load times and crashes. Sometimes less is more.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great puzzle game, nice open world with almost too many puzzles left right and centre! The solving style feels like a better version of 'The Witness'. Loads of variety including logic, spatial awareness and colour co-ordination. They tend to start off quite easy and ramp up in difficulty but there are plenty of techniques which are explained as you go along. I've enjoyed searching for different angles and solutions around the different areas (with the exception of the glass maze which I hate!).Graphics are really nice, few FPS drops here and there. The multiplayer element doesn't really add much at all though I don't think it justifies some of the negative reviews! Plenty of progression but not much in the way of a story. I think some sort of 'Elohim' type voice acting would go a long way as the plot feels a bit pointless so far. Looking forward to getting into some of the harder puzzles later on! Would recommend for anyone who enjoyed Talos Principle or The Witness.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like puzzle games, you should probably grab this one. There is just ludicrous variety on display and lots of puzzles to enjoy, along with a few slightly more active activities like flying. The way it's set up, there's always something nearby and there are usually easier activities to space out the more complex puzzles. You just enter this flow state of more complex puzzles with smaller bite size activities in between.There's not much to the multiplayer component; you can show your cosmetics off to your friends (if you manage to get into the same game), but as far as I can tell there are only a few puzzle types where watching another player could help you solve it. It does make the environment feel a little more lively, but it's not a big part of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Great for puzzle fans! This beautiful world is filled to the brim with small puzzles. I still don't understand the purpose of forming a party though.Also, the puzzle types are limited and must be unlocked.What this game mostly lacks (and cost it its success) is a multitude of big world environment puzzles that players need to work together to solve, a bigger emphasis on the traditional RPG element and real engaging purpose to tie it all up. Currently, it feels more like a playground with lots of puzzle stations of the same limited types. There are also voices that you can find and later reconstruct some sort of story maybe... but it definitely lacks any appeal (too mysterious and lacking engagement).Definitely a good game for those who like small newspaper puzzles and smartphone puzzles though.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't even like puzzle games, unless they have a good story to string me along (Portal, Talos Princible, etc.).  Despite having only bits of lore rather than a story, I can't stop playing!  The adventuring feel of the game makes going from puzzle to puzzle a physiological addiction.  It would be perfect, but as I said, the story is a little light for my liking, and I can't talk to people despite seeing them.  I know it would make spoilers way more likely, but some of these puzzles are so complex I don't see how words alone could spoil them.  It ends up feeling like a social limitation, which does create a certain feeling like you see in Journey, but I don't think that's better than being able to hang out in general chat like you see in most shared world games.Graphics, sound, basically every technical aspect is superb.  It's limited by using UE4 instead of 5, but it's still better than you see in any other puzzle game.9.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: If you are into puzzle games and sick of ones that are easily completed then I suggest Islands of Insight.  You can wander for hours solving anything you come across, aside from the game progression quests.  There is a ton (literally) of puzzles; add in the relaxing music and the amazing graphics and this is as close to perfect as you get.  The only downside I have encountered so far, is the vague puzzle information when trying to complete an enclave.  To put this in simpler terms you have #/# total puzzles completed currently. _childDocuments_.review: If you have been looking for a puzzle game, a "chill vibes" game, or a game that has almost limitless content, then look no further - Islands of Insight is a joy to play for as long as you want. It has all types of puzzles, including logic, perspective, hidden object, movement, and overarching/mystery puzzles. From what I have heard, the developers include many well-regarded puzzle makers, and it really shows in the quality of the puzzles. There are certain areas to play in order to advance the story, and a few puzzle types are unlocked through this progression. Besides that, you can choose to solve or ignore whichever puzzles you want. Any puzzles hanging out on the world map outside of the story islands are on a rotation, and changed out daily. Ones you have solved on a previous day don't appear to stay solved when they are rotated back in, so they are farmable but it is perhaps impossible to truly know or track if you have solved every puzzle in the game (the story islands are static and 100% completion can easily be tracked for these). The Co-op tag has recently been removed from the game, but I still think it would not be inaccurate to describe this as an MMO, or at least similar to an MMO. There is no chat feature, and the servers are not terribly full (intentionally, I think, due to specific puzzle types), but there is a party system, and you can see and emote at the people you come across, or flag points of interest to other players. There is a lot of criticism that the always online aspect of the game is just a form of DRM, and doesn't add anything to the game, but I do think it improves the vibes of the game after playing it. Speaking of DRM, at one point the demo included EAC, a DRM tool. Due to player feedback, this was removed within the same week the demo was playable for. I take this as a great sign that the developer/publisher are so open to accepting feedback timely, and am looking forward to the changes they make after collecting more player feedback on gameplay. One criticism I have is that the game is somewhat buggy and unoptimized. Thankfully my computer still runs it despite being under the minimum specs for the CPU, but I do not see why the requirements need to be so high in the first place. There was rubberbanding in the demo, but I have not encountered it in the full version of the game. A not insignificant amount of people have had trouble with quests not progressing, which is currently being worked on. The location of some perspective puzzles makes them  frustrating to complete. I think the game is a complete steal at $30, and highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Islands of Insight

_childDocuments_.review: Very relaxing puzzle game under one condition:If you're not completionist (or 200 IQ + pro-gamer dexterity for some movement challenges)Otherwise, you'll be very frustrated by some puzzles and challenges.However, if you're not a compuslive completionist and just casually follow mission markers then eventually you'll earn enough points to unlock "final/ending mission" (the one in the north locked by 75 mirabilis).There are many very cool and fun challenges (e.g. Glass Temple, finding hidden objects, armilary rings, skydrops) and the whole world is very beaudifully made (flying islands full of Ancient architecture from Greece, Egypt, China and South America).The only bad things in this game: - some puzzles are not for my IQ- sometimes, there is one hidden challenge/puzzle left that you can't find despite searching intensly- I wish there would be an option to customize hints and add hints for some challenges
_childDocuments_.name: Islands of Insight

_childDocuments_.review: The game is great, and it's beautiful!And I'm definitely recommending this game because despite the issues it sometimes has, the game is incredibleThe areas are spectacular to look at and go through, not to mention the whole 10K puzzles thing is crazy!The puzzles themselves are incredible creative, and keeps being fun to solve the entire time: you get tired of looking at logic puzzles? Fly around, follow various orbs, even go sightseeing or something, I dunnoHaving the puzzles "reset" daily also makes for an extremely varied interchanging landscape that in a way renews itself constantly, and its pretty great (also considering the number of puzzles in the game, is really the only sensible way to make it look good lol)Not to mention my biggest gripe with the game (how unstable online is if your internet isn't perfect) is being addressed since they are actually adding an offline mode! The developers are awesome for this one, I love it^^The only 2 small annoying quirks now is that when puzzles reset, they will of course sometimes reset into puzzles you have already done. My issue with that however is the fact that they don't tell you if you have done the puzzle already, so you kinda have to go and look at your puzzle count over and over to see if it was a new one, if you care about that...Also personally a bigger mastery tree would be fabulous heh

_childDocuments_.review: This is basically a  grid-puzzle book, wrapped up in a Mario Odyssey style presentation of Little Things Hidden Everywhere.The perspective and environmental puzzles are cute and pretty and varied enough to not get old: they have like six different takes on "look at thing from correct angle", and it works!But the real key is whether "connect all the dark cells, and ensure all light cells have the correct area" sounds fun to you. If yes, the puzzles are super clever and well-paced, with smart twists and mechanical build-up, and there's a ton of them! If that sounds like a chore, you'll be wishing the environmental stuff had  more heft.I'm personally having a great time poking around the endgame secrets, they're hidden in cute fun ways! And there's just so much here, and it's all so stylish, I'm delighted.Update (Oct 2024): I'm sad to see this game abandoned, but honestly, it's being converted into the form it always should've been. There's a very strong game at the core here, but it struggled under poor direction, with much greater MMO ambitions than actual ideas. I'm taking some time to scroll through the credits page and follow some of the puzzle creators, because  did some truly excellent work, even if the studio as a company is… clearly not managed well. (Scummy move to provide a month's notice to transfer your save file, and announce it in messages with very vague titles!)

_childDocuments_.review: A world filled to the brim with an incredible variety of puzzles and challenges to explore. This game is addicting, and the amount of different styles of puzzles keeps one from burning out on any one type. Each style of puzzle comes with it's own mastery level; gaining experience by completing puzzles allows one to level up mastery of each type and gain cosmetics and other character upgrades.Every so often, certain puzzles in the world are cycled out and replaced with new ones, keeping areas fresh and exciting even after substantial exploration.With a stock of quickly regenerating hints, even the toughest of puzzles can be tackled by anyone; at the same time, the most challenging level of puzzles might stump even the most experienced logic gurus, so there is satisfying difficulty regardless of personal puzzle aptitude.An incredibly charming game, I can't wait to keep exploring and solving.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm unsure why everyone is *this* mad at the always online components. I do think it's silly for it to be always online, but I've really had no real issues, and my internet connection is not the best. I've had no performance issues either. And heck, I only see a loading screen when the game opens. While it's a no-brainer to me that they should add an offline-mode for people who prefer it (because why not, really?), it really doesn't impact things as much as people make it sound like.As for the actual game, it's a gem. So many puzzles, always something to do, always somewhere to go. For the most part, the puzzles are on the easier part of things, except when they're occasionally not. And I think that yields a pretty good gameplay experience; you roam around, solving puzzle after puzzle, feeling real clever until one specific puzzles whacks you on the head and you end up spending the entire day staring at squares. That balance between 'a sense of progress' and 'a sense of challenge' is really well done for the most part (though I'm now in the later game and I'm stuck in an area where everything is hard, hence why I'm procrastinating by writing this review, send help).I think, for me, it's really just the 'I want to play a puzzle game'-game, as I know I basically won't run out of content anytime soon. Which is impressive. I've never seen a game with this quantity of puzzles without them being auto-generated. It must have been a tonne of work.For the future, I hope to see more coop-puzzles. At the moment, I've interacted with a total of 0 individuals throughout my journey. I suspect it's the same for most people. Without a coop-region of some sort, like a 'puzzle dungeon' or something, or something like 'we were here together', 'don't stop talking or you'll explode' or 'myst uru live', there just won't be any real reason to interact with anyone ever. And that's a shame when it seems like they've build a heck of a lot of infrastructure up around the multiplayer feature.

_childDocuments_.review: Doing a reverse No Mans Sky is impressive, but not in a good way. This game started out with so much fun. Meeting up with people was still a gimmick, but it was fun and had potential. The puzzles were bit basic for 90% of it, and some 10% were interesting solves that felt rewarding. Now, less than a year after release, and without any big attempt to make the game live up to its full potential of an MMORPG Puzzler, it was turned OFFLINE and TERMINATED. Terminated in the sense no updates will be done, to an incomplete product, which has at maximum a 1 hour playtime if rushed to finish (which you should, since grinding levels was online purpose mostly).This is as close to being a scam, if not just a scam. _childDocuments_.review: I should preface and say that i'm not actually a puzzle gamerThis game is quite good, the world is fairly interesting and the environments are nice if you enjoy the theme. Performance could be better but nothing to really emphasise in a puzzle gameThe puzzles are really satisfying to complete and generally enjoyable to play through, however there is some lack of creativity, and almost ALL of them are just far too easy (and that's coming from someone who is braindead and doesn't play puzzle games). There is, consequently, not enough difficult puzzles eitherAlmost all of the higher difficulty ones are super fun to do, mostly because the board is just bigger, so you need more trial and error, planning, time investment etc. Out of idk, 800 puzzles that i've done i would say that probably just about all of them except for maybe 50 took less than a minute to completeEventually it just gets a bit exhausting, because if i'm gonna complete puzzles this fast, i'd rather just play a raw puzzles game where i don't have to move my character from puzzle to puzzle, forcing me to change my posture from chilling one-handed mouse gameplay to MKB movementThe environmental puzzles are also... Not ideal. Some are nice and can be a bit challenging like Mathboxes or Hidden Pentads, but Flow Orbs is literally you just following a wisp essentially, hidden cubes or archways are nice, Sentinel Stones are far too easy and needs a larger playing ground and maybe verticality tooThe environment itself could be used more too. They're islands, sometimes mountainous, with buildings on them, and that's about it. Not sure what one could do but if you're really going to add Flow Orbs, make me chase them in to a neat cave behind a waterfall or ivy at least, something a bit more unique than just the environment as isOverall the game feels a little bit like a fetch-quest type of experience of you going through a checklist of things to do. Solve X armillary rings, find all hidden cubes, solve X logic grids, and so onThe lack of difficulty is starting to bore me, while the amount of quantity is starting to exhaust meHowever, i'm willing to branch out in to some other puzzle games now and see what they got to offer. I've always been limited by the difficulty, and although i found this one too easy, it also allowed me to build up a knowledge base for how to approach various problems within puzzling that i can take with meAnd for that reason this game is probably great for anyone who isn't all that clever like me and just wants a nice relaxing experience with some satisfying puzzles. _childDocuments_.review: This game was incredibly disappointing from several perspectives. The two most damning were as a puzzle fan and as a game design analyst. To put it shortly, Islands of Insight is a good concept that was executed insanely poorly. Islands of Insight is an open world, always online, live service puzzle solving game. There are thousands of puzzles sprinkled out into the world for you to find and complete. This was what initially sold me on the game. The last part, not the live service or open world bits. I wasn't paying attention when I saw those and frankly, I wish I had.This game has many pros, so I'll cover a few of those first and why.- The puzzles: This is a massive pro as the puzzles, for the most part, are all incredibly well designed. They are deserving of attention and are borderline pieces of art. They test your test your critical thinking skills and your ability to reason creatively.- Designs: The world itself is beautiful. A lot of work was put into the way things look here and I only ever found one issue with it, which I'll cover later. At times it felt like the design team was given all the funding for the game with how intricate everything is. - Music/Sound: The music is samey, you do get tired of it, but it isn't bad. It goes well with the game itself and each track is a nice background piece while traversing and solving puzzles. The sound design is so nice as well. It is so satisfying to solve a puzzle or part of a logic box and hear a sound that says you did something right.And after that short list, here are the cons. I have many so be prepared. I will also have the game's execution of its ideas as it's own little segment after.- The Idea: The game itself struggles with identity. It is both a puzzle focused game and an open world, live service title. I feel like the designers were all in a room talking about the idea for the game and went "How has no one done this?" when they should've asked "Why has no one done this?" Both ideas are solid on paper, but in practice, they just fall apart. People who care about puzzle games aren't as interested in open world, live service. Additionally, people interested in open world, live service aren't really interested in logic puzzles and the progression the game offers. It feels like this game tried marketing to one group in the middle who cares about neither of the game's main focuses. It's not surprising that it didn't take off, especially at the asking price.- Price: I personally received my copy for free. When not on sale, this thing is $30. For what you get in game, I will say that is far too high of an asking price. I get that it's open world and all, but besides a bunch of repetition in the puzzles and campaign, there isn't much value for those $30. I feel like if I spent any more than ten bucks on this then I would've been depressed. - RPG/other random elements: This game features three very weird things that it really shouldn't have had at all. Those being an upgrade tree for abilities, unlock-able cosmetics, and lore. These three things, once again, are things that the target audience of puzzle solvers really don't care about that much. And they're all so poorly executed. The lore is the best of the three, but it's still really bland. Cosmetics are rigid and don't make a lot out of your character. Who is a pretty massive blank slate from the start. The abilities never made sense to have and I'm sure apart from the dive and super jump, wouldn't make any difference if they were in the game or not. - Exploration/movement: Islands of Insight has a campaign of sorts. Why? I don't really know. It's not great, not terrible. But it is mostly repetition. It serves primarily to introduce you to the world and its puzzles. The world you are in is small, but also still fairly large. Your options for movement are incredibly limited though and fast travel is one of the very last abilities you can unlock and even then it has severe limits. The movement from place to place is extremely boring. Even  small jaunts are so awful to make. It made exploration often feel terrible. - Bloat: Probably the single most bleak part of this game were the puzzle bloated segments. Areas with too many puzzles. Just too many. At first, it's cool to stop and solve a ton. Feeling like you get a nice rush of satisfaction from all these problems you're solving. You eventually burn out of this and realize that almost all of these are quick puzzles that take almost no effort to solve. These are usually generated and not hand crafted. Meaning that you end up with slop instead of what you got the game for. Which were actual puzzles. I liked hearing that there were 10,000 something puzzles. But even before getting the game, I wasn't expecting high quality all the time. I wasn't expecting super low quality either. - Skydrops: These are a particular nit pick of mine. I believe these things to have incredibly terrible design. You are introduced to them once at the start. If you never solve the first one or click the "tutorial" for it, then you'll never know what they are. Then you aren't required to do them until much later in an enclave. Skydrops themselves are so plentiful and operated on a proximity logic with your character. If you didn't know they were a puzzle, then they would fit in almost perfectly with the area design. That's what i thought they were for the first 6 hours of my playthrough. Set pieces, not puzzles. The "tutorial" for them as well sucked. It didn't give a great description and just eluded to lining them up in a circle. It's poor design and at times can be too much clutter for their own good. - Performance: it took me long enough, but here I am. Islands of Insight, as previously stated, is always online and open world. This means that you are always connected to a server and rendering a lot of effects, textures, and models. Many of which are complex. Lower end PC's will have trouble idling the game. Mine is pretty beefy and was stuttering for the first half hour of my experience. Poor internet connections will also have a hard time just staying in game. It is very easy to be suddenly booted off the server for little to no reason. I imagine this makes it almost impossible to play for those on laptops who are on college campuses or in areas with poor connection quality. It is abysmal how unoptimized this game is. Now for the execution. I think I've already explained enough of this. So I'll just briskly cover some final thoughts on the execution of the game. :: The execution of islands of insight was pretty bad. You have a great concept, but done as bad as possible. Too many target audiences and no idea how to properly put together an interesting game based on everything the game has to offer. As stated previously, those who care the most about the puzzles just want the puzzles, they don't want this beefy program always connected to a server that has upgrade trees, a campaign, and lore. The developers should've expected this going into it. But I feel like they pushed forward instead of going back to the drawing board. This was a huge fatal error that led to an online game that was practically dead on arrival. Only seeing some rise after a free 24 period and a sale. That is pretty bleak if you ask me. There was no need for abilities, upgrade trees, cosmetics, or any of that stuff. The open world was pretty but too cluttered. It was boring to traverse and often made me less excited to explore than more so.Anyways, these are my feelings about Islands of Insight. Probably one of the most disappointing games I've played in recent memory. Not as bad as my top worst for the year, but man. I wanted something so much better. It's such a shame too because that game I wanted is there, it just isn't formed properly. TL:DR - Puzzle game that is open world and live service. Does the puzzles well but not the other stuff. Makes for a pretty bleak experience past a certain point.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: Last edit didn't "take"? Cannot recommend until recent patch is fixed. Offline mode unplayable, online mode no longer tracks progress. A good puzzle game that could've been great.There is  of content here to keep you occupied, and plenty of challenging puzzles to solve. The music is unintrusive and calming, and I find myself using the game to relax, just run around and do stuff. There is a ton of variety, too. At first, I wasn't too enamored of the "find hidden stuff" puzzles, but they've grown on me - they help to break up the pure brain-effort of the logic puzzles and serve as a palate cleanser. I've spent days in the game just going around doing the not-so-challenging stuff because I just wanted to chill, then come back to the hard stuff when I'm up for it. There are so many environmental puzzles that it's easy to get distracted as you navigate the game world, and I find it satisfying to be able to get quick little "wins" along the way from one location to another.Regarding the challenge level, your mileage may vary. There are definitely plenty of thinkers. There are literal thousands of logic grids to solve, but only a portion of those are of high difficulty. If you're just not interested in the easy ones once you've progressed past learning the ropes, you may spend more time trying to find puzzles worth solving than actually solving them. I won't go deep on the types of puzzles and the logic rules, only mention that I find some of them to be majority-trivial (e.g. the shifting mosaics), and some to be painful (e.g. the morphic fractals, though I've developed strategies to alleviate most of the frustration there).The decision to make platforming a significant part of the game is in conflict with the gameplay experience. The platforming is bad; the game sometimes boosts you  rather than transition to "fly" mode, attempts to fly when you're on the ground pressing jump, seems insistent on pushing you  ledges instead of helping you stay on them, and rubber-bands because of the choice to involve the network and a server to track your position and movement. (This could very much have just been local state; this isn't a shooter where that's vital.) The height of the jump is not in harmony with the design of the levels: there are many small obstacles you can't jump over except with a double jump, even though they look low enough that they shouldn't get in your way. You'll be running forwards and hit jump, but the game will just reject you back to your position or you'll wind up vibrating in place. The choice to create many ledges and vertical areas that you have to navigate only makes the movement more frustrating. There are many movement puzzles, for example, that require you to quickly and accurately perform platforming / climbing movement, but the above-mentioned problems can throw a wrench in your plans and leave you falling into a deep ravine, spending a long time to get back to where you can start again. Fortunately the movement puzzles aren't so challenging that the problems are insurmountable.The game does give you a little help (in the form of a charged jump) to recover from either a mistake or one of the many times the game doesn't do what you expect it to, but it's limited: you can only use it three times and it recharges one jump per five minutes. Touch any wall while flying and your fly goes away, so of course there are movement puzzles that require you to fly through tight spaces. Tip: unlock recall, and set a recall point before attempting movement puzzles in vertical areas.The game lacks attention to detail in places. You'll find yourself seeing "under" the edge of a tree or a rock in places where the base doesn't fully connect to the ground. You'd never notice except the game incentivizes you to look closely at small things. I've encountered a handful of puzzles that are just impossible because something spawns in the terrain (I've found a shy aura that verifiably spawns in some stairs, a hidden cube that's almost certainly inside of a rock, and a hidden pentad where I'm pretty certain one of the relics was in a tree). Or, the position of one game element blocks another (I've had a hidden cube blocking the only access to a matchbox, or an enclave jump pad at the exact POV for solving a skydrop). It's hard to QA thousands of puzzles to make sure they all work, or work in combination with each other, so this is pretty forgiveable - but it does demonstrate that quantity won out over quality here a little. Regarding the "shared world" experience, I've found it pointless. I can understand the vibe of populating the world with activity so it feels less lonely, but the few times I've encountered players they're either moving through quickly, standing still solving a puzzle, or actively in my way. I myself am only really in one place when solving a puzzle, which takes over the UI - so when I hear chirps I can't see who did it or what they did, and don't really care anyway. You can attempt to disable chirps, but you have to do it every session and it doesn't seem to work - I've set "hear chirps from: party only", but still hear them. Luckily people don't seem to use it much. I don't really understand what the point would be to play with someone else, since there's very little in the way of available collaboration. I'm not sure if it's possible to go into the same server as a friend, but we'd be on a Discord call or something anyway, and the in-game communication tools are too limited to have utility. Netplay does, however, bring to the table the experience of regularly getting booted to the title screen, perhaps due to a server restart or deployment. I've had it happen ~8 times in a row. And of course, when I come back, whatever I was in the middle of doing needs to be done again - if it's even still there.If you're a completionist, know ahead of time that some of the puzzles are impossible to solve. Some puzzles that attribute an certain area are physically located in a nearby area. Puzzle progress in an area only counts  puzzle solves - so as you progress, you'll be solving many repeated puzzles as you search for the handful you haven't yet solved, if you can find them at all. I have 98/99 of the fractals in "Lucent Waters" for example, but the last remaining fractal hasn't spawned for me in many play sessions. Math suggests it has about a 14% chance? Or, I'll start a new day with "37/38" matchboxes solved, solve every matchbox I can see in the area, and still be at 37/38. It could be that last one is very trickily hidden, it could be in another area, or it could be inside some terrain, there's no way to tell really.With the announcement of an offline mode, I'm hoping that a lot of the network-related flaws become a non-issue. Perhaps the lack of server-tracked state will improve a lot of the random movement fails. If we're really lucky, the lack of a need to have the same set of puzzles for every player will allow the game to present you with only new puzzles when possible, removing one of the two exponential factors in area progression and making it significantly less of a grind.Overall, I'm still playing the heck out of the game. While I've written many words about the frustrations, those are mostly to inform the reader and, if I'm lucky, inspire some improvement from the developers. The things I like are "the experience of playing", or "the satisfaction of solving a puzzle", and it's hard to be concrete about that. The things I dislike have very specific details. I wouldn't have played 300+ hours if they were deal-breakers. I'm still playing the heck out of the game and expect to continue to do so - I've achieved 100% completion in all the enclaves (except the new archipelago of curiosities - still WIP), and am close to 100% on one of the five overworld areas, working on the others. Work has me burned out, and this game has served as a real boon to my day :)

_childDocuments_.review: My mother and I both love puzzles as well as MMOs, so we were incredibly excited to try out Islands of Insight together, and picked it up on the free sale day. I actually enjoy the world and puzzles very much, though the game is very system-intensive. This is not a game for casuals, but if you like puzzles, you will always find this game to provide ample challenge.Update now that I have completed the game's main content and poured in over 100 hours:Islands of Insight is a very mixed bag. On one hand you have lovingly handcrafted puzzles of master quality, and a beautiful open world of fantastic aesthetics. On the other hand you have incredibly poor programming optimization that feels like it came out of an "intro to CompSci" classroom, which causes the rest of the game when you aren't solving puzzles to be moderately unpleasant. The UX and UI are inconsistent at the best of times, and a laggy buggy mess at their worst, making the sandbox mode (what is supposed to set Islands of Insight apart from other puzzle games) just generally unfun. The game is *incredibly* good at being what it is (a puzzle game) and incredibly terrible at being what it wants to be (an MMO).I'll still recommend it for anyone who wants a nice 50+hour trip solving the main questline and static puzzles, because it IS a fantastic puzzle game.... but don't touch it with a hundred foot pole if you have a completionist mindset or are getting it for the MMO aspect, because completion is functionally impossible, and the MMO doesn't exist.Update of an update: Now that the online service has uncerimoniously ended, and the offline mode was not fixed before shutdown, there's not much to jump at with Islands of Insight. The one thing that was supposed to set it apart and failed to, doesn't even exist in its failed state now. The offline mode is an SSD-killer unless you feel like modding the game through the community discord. All around, it was an interesting experiment while it lasted, that deserved far better treatment and support than the coding team was willing to give it.

_childDocuments_.review: From what I thought to be a very "unassuming free puzzle game" that I accidentally got thanks to a discord bot's free games heads up, was actually a puzzle game heavily inspired by The Witness, with surprising depth, tons of content, and iterative mechanics that sometimes blew me away.I've been playing this game for more than 60 hours, and have a little more than half of its content done. For a puzzle game, this is an insane amount of content to do. I have only played in Offline Mode, ! (EDIT: the Online mode has now been discontinued, but Offline works as intended.)There's the main 5 "continents", which will house some hubs to teach certain rules, auto-generated puzzles to keep the world full of things to do, as well as jumps towards other smaller "Islands", which in turn will unlock new kinds of puzzles, and have a certain, limited amount of puzzles per island. 100%ing these islands will require you to explore extensively and think properly as to where puzzles can be.The puzzles in themselves range between... weird to extremely fun to play with. There are some puzzles which I kinda disagreed with as a "concept", but I think that may have happened 3 or 4 times in more than thousand puzzles I have now completed. There's also some "mysteries" to solve, which will require you to pay attention to everything you've done thus far!The star of the show is however the Logic Grids. These will keep on iterating constantly and consistently. You'll always find new rules, new blocks, new patterns, new "ways of thinking", and seeking these is a delight that you will enjoy very much if you enjoy those kinds of concepts.There are however a few things I'm a bit "meh" about on this game: the Story, the iteration on other puzzles than logic grids, some "mishaps in puzzle design/conveyance" (ie mazes), and the QoL for hidden items.The Story is... To be frank, quite forgettable. It's hard to determine who is what, what are either of their aspirations, other than the Auroral. You will get the gist of what's happening, but it'll be hard to be invested into what they were trying to go for.The iteration on other puzzles than Logic Grids is unfortunately... Kinda lacking. There are moments where I wished different kinds of puzzles interacted with one another more, like how the Witness does. Unfortunately most of the iteration is locked to the Logic Grids, or at least in the 60% I've played through for now. Will amend this if it changes on the 100% completion, but at least know that there's very little interactions between puzzles.There are also some mishaps in how certain rules are conveyed, as well as problems in design on said rules. Mazes are extremely problematic on that regard: The start of certain mazes don't have exits, and will require you to exit them to find the exit... Which sometimes aren't even exits, but a single pressure plate in a dead end maze. A rewriting of the rule to "Find the Finish Plate" rather than "Find the Exit" would help a lot in understanding the possibilities of the rule.As for hidden items, I really wish there was an upgrade to help more with hidden items. Cubes have a "hearing help" to them, but I really wish there was a "visual" upgrade as well. Something akin to "Hidden objects get a small glow when getting closer to them", something you could unlock at the very end of the ability tree. Either that, or an unlockable approximated compass (something like "Far" "Near", "Extremely Close") to nearest hidden items on smaller islands would help a lot for 100% completion.But even with these flaws, even with these issues, I'm very glad I took the time to play this game. There's so much to do, so much to solve, interesting mysteries and ways to solve puzzles. If you got this game for free like I did, you've gotten a pretty great game to play.For 30€, the price might seem a bit steep, but the sheer amount of things to do in this game will more than make up for it. I'll still recommend it even at this price. Go and grab it.

_childDocuments_.review: Another game that would benefit from a Neutral rating on Steam. This game has a lot of potential! I'm sure with a little more work it can be something special. It just needs a little bit of refinement.First criticism: it needs more puzzle variety. The majority of puzzles are perspective puzzles where you just need to find the right location in the environment to stand and look at something from the correct angle. There are multiple puzzle "types" that exercise this same skill: Skydrops, Sightseer, Light Motif, and Armillary Rings. My suggestion: come up with a few more puzzle types and replace some of the perspective puzzles.Second criticism: the most original puzzle is also the one that needs the most work - Morphic Fractal. I love the way this puzzle looks and it's a fascinating idea, but right now it can feel both aimless and finicky. The aimlessness is because the puzzle doesn't provide any clues or starting information, so you end up moving the puzzle around randomly until you happen to see something similar to the solution. It's finicky because you'll find a pattern that looks very close to the solution but you'll be just a few degrees or pixels off. My suggestion: add some kind of information, guidance, or clue that helps players orient themselves on the fractal. Perhaps that could be an unlockable upgrade.Third criticism: Islands of Insight's description is "Seek out and solve 10,000+ puzzles at your own pace" but there are a few timed events - Wandering Echo and Flow Orbs. I call these "events" because they aren't really puzzles, they're platforming & parkour challenges. Consequently, they feel very out of place. I wouldn't mind if they were 100% optional, but there are a few progression gates that require you to complete them (example: getting from Autumn Falls to Shady Wildwood). My suggestion: leave them in but remove them from progression requirements. (Additional suggestion: these would be more enjoyable if the game had native controller support.)

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, lets start with the things i didn't like:1. The main land puzzles are pretty much a "do as many as you want" kinda thing as they change both in which are currently available and in position every now and then. I dislike this as it kills my feeling of completing a part of the island as all new puzzles will forever spawn there, but as it's restricted to the main land and not to the very well thought out smaller islands, i am somewhat fine with it.2. The fractal "puzzles". Here you have a shader with 2 parameters which you control via the mouse which in turn change how the picture (the shader) looks. Goal is to replicate a given picture. The main reason why i hate these, is that two different sets of these parameters can look extremely similar. This means that you can fiddle and fine tune your supposed solution forever, as you are very far from the solution even though your picture looks very, very similar to the target one. This goes so far as to me having said out loud multiple times: "How is that not it?" To the point where i couldn't even distringuish the two pictures. Just to then randomly fling your mouse around and the solution to snap into place from something completely different. The bad part is, when this happens i usually go: "Oh thank god" instead of being sad that the game took this puzzle away from me, which is a really bad sign.And now onto the good parts: everything else.The world is great and really fun to explore, the puzzles are very diversified and you pretty much never do the same thing for very long. The Smaller Islands have super cool themes to them and the puzzles, especially the grandmaster ones, are just fun to do.If you like the witness or hexcells, you can't go wrong with this game. You also get a lot of content. The advertised 10k puzzles is a lie as some take literally one second to complete, but overall there is plenty of difficult puzzles and also fun exploration to keep you occupied for many hours.

_childDocuments_.review: Though I'm not terribly far into the game, I think I can safely catalog an opinion. I'll start by saying this game isn't for everyone. But I kind of feel like it is specifically for me.I often like the idea of playing MMOs, but mostly doing my own thing while other people just happen to be around. That's the vibe here: it's a mostly single-player MMO. You can see other players running around completing similar tasks, and you can sometimes infer a hint by what they're doing, but there is no actual communication. A lot of people felt misled by the fact that it was launched with a "co-op" tag; it kind of feels like the devs intended to have the ability to queue with friends, but so far they haven't figured out that functionality. We can hope.The gameplay itself is best summarized as The Witness, if it had about twenty types of puzzle. It has the same "color in a grid based on increasingly complex logical rules," but it also has "find the right place to stand to align distant objects for some particular goal," "navigate this glass funhouse maze on a timer," and "find hidden objects in the environment," among others. It's a beautiful, complex, chaotic landscape filled with this kind of thing, where you can wander (or fly) around and just pick some stuff to do, varying your behavior so you don't get bored. Many puzzles are semi-random, respawning occasionally across the huge open world, but some are curated zones.The game needs polish and some optimization, but overall it's already a decent product for the price, if this genre is what you're into.

_childDocuments_.review: I typically play online games with a focus on PvP. I love sweating my brains out trying to min-max my builds and beat other players. This game is the antithesis of that, which is exactly why I love it. This is one of the most relaxing, lighthearted and fun experiences I've had the pleasure of having in a game.Sometimes you just want to kick back with something that's low stakes, with no pressure, and this game has that in spades. It's gorgeous to look at (although somewhat unoptimized), has a variety of beautiful locales with different scenery, a surprisingly good character creator (that you can edit at any time, at will), and a great selection of simple.While the puzzles themselves are generally very straightforward, there's enough variety in both the types of puzzles and the difficulty to keep things interesting. It does an excellent job of introducing new mechanics to you in a way that feels very intuitive, while also explaining things if you're struggling. There's a very loose "main quest" that helps guide your progression, but you're fairly free to do whatever you want. Every time I thought about closing it, there would be another puzzle nearby that I told myself I'd solve first, and then another hour had passed.A truly lovely game.

_childDocuments_.review: I can all but guarantee that you’ve never played anything resembling Islands of Insight: a strange yet serene shared-world puzzle adventure game set across a massive floating archipelago stuffed full of ancient wonders, natural beauty, and puzzles, puzzles, SO many puzzles.   Really, there are logic puzzles, memory puzzles, jumping puzzles, flying puzzles, hidden objects to discover, labyrinths to escape, fractals to... frack? Twenty-four types of puzzles to be precise and over 10,000(!) of them, all of which despawn and are refreshed about once per day. They say in open world games that the player should find something interesting every 15 seconds or so. In Islands of Insight, it’s rare to walk for more than a few seconds without bumping into a puzzle. Not that you’ll be walking much. Because each time you complete a puzzle, which without exaggeration happens about once per minute, you’ll receive a handful of sparks that can be used to level up a variety of movement skills, from double jump, to super jump, to gliding. I gained the power to fall with style about an hour and a half into my ten-plus hours with the game, meaning most of my non-puzzle solving time in Islands of Insight was spent soaring amongst the clouds as I traveled about the game’s five distinct biomes and 20+ enclaves, each of which introduces a new puzzle type or key mechanic, like finding hidden rings you can fly through. Oh, and those with a fear of heights can rest easy—there's a convenient lack of fall damage in this absurdly vertical world.  So, if all that—the intricate and inventive world that’s so fun to explore thanks to often breathtaking visuals and, of course, the mindboggling number of puzzles, most of which strike the perfect balance between challenging, intuitive, and satisfying—is the great, and the rich soundtrack and high-quality sound effects are the very good, what’s the less good? Well, for starters, Islands of Insight is arguably the least multiplayery multiplayer game I have ever played. It presents you with an awesome world that’s teeming with strangers and begging to be explored with friends, but it lacks an even optional chat function, instead restricting players to unobtrusive emotes. This decision was an intentional one, as the developers have stated that they never wanted the game’s multiplayer elements to intrude upon what is ultimately a serene single-player adventure. Which is fine but I suppose begs the question of... why? Why go to all this trouble of creating multiplayer infrastructure for a massive, shared world game to then turn around and intentionally de-emphasize that core vision? It’s just an odd decision that by no means ruins the experience, but it does hurt the game’s overall value. Because, as anyone who plays MMOs will attest, the community and the gameplay, arguably in that order, are what keeps people logging back in day in day out.  Still, for $30, Islands of Insight is well worth the asking price due to its heaps of content that includes a generous, microtransaction-free cosmetic upgrade system that, with a little grinding, will turn you into a blinding solar flare of fashion.  As for playability, I did encounter occasional spurts of framerate lag and some rubberbanding, but most play sessions were pretty smooth.  That leaves us with Objectives and Story. Based on some light text-based lore building here and there, I’ve gathered that this archipelago is more dream than reality—forged from the jumbled up memory fragments of a spectral entity who once inhabited our world. This would explain why you might see lush tropical foliage sprouting up from otherwise arid desert sands adjacent ancient Egyptian monuments. Or hanging Chinese gardens in a Pacific Northwest forest. Still, lore tidbits considered, Islands of Insight is too narratively squishy for me to feel comfortable grading its Story micrometrics. This open-ended approach suits the game’s worldbuilding and mechanics just fine, but without a clear story you really just exist to solve puzzles—not much variety to the objectives. Overall, I personally enjoyed this relaxed approach, but I could see non-puzzle lovers losing interest after the initial wave of novelty wears off. So, after averaging up our micrometrics, Islands of Insight gets the strong aggregate MEGA score of 3.9/5, and I’m happy to answer any questions you have about the game or my review.

_childDocuments_.review: Game was fun to start, but quickly spotted a frustrating issue that made me give up.The first puzzle you resolve has you turning squares on a grid either black or white to fill a grid following certain rules. - A more advanced rendition of this requires you to fill in five of them in a row without making mistakes. - Meaning if the game wants a square to be white, and you click it black, that's one strike.Would this normally be a problem? No, trying to get flawless solves is fun, but for the love of God, either let me bind which mouse button makes the square white and which one makes it black, or put an indicator on the screen of which is which. - Even when I press H for the help window on the puzzle, the tutorial says "don't make mistakes", it doesn't remind me which click does what. - Nevermind if you got a bit of ADD or a twitchy finger and misclick.Is it petty to criticize a puzzle game for requiring a bit of memory? Maybe. But I'd argue this particular thing also lands in the park of muscle memory. - Those puzzles can either be insanely difficult or stupendously simple, all it comes down to is how your brain intuitively associates black and white to your index and middle finger. - Go on, give it a shot, look down at your hand, your middle and index finger, and decide which one is white and which one is black. - If you decided index finger is black and middle finger is white? Grats, you'll have fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Multiplayer puzzle game without any multiplayer puzzles. What are we even doing here. The devs made a singleplayer version, and in a few days, that will be the *only* version of the game. Why did they even try to do multiplayer in the first place? So they could sell you cosmetics?I can't even play the game because it crashes on my machine but I've seen it be played. There was no need to make it so heavy. The wide-open "islands" format, seemingly chosen to let you have a higher chance of seeing other players online, just makes it so you have to render additional geometry. Portal 2 had the right idea: the map is only as big as the current puzzle area. No need to render anything else, it'd just be distracting and make the game run worse. Making it so heavy just makes the puzzles, which should be the primary focus of a puzzle game, less accessible. This is only made more insulting by the fact that some of the puzzles are 2d affairs you could literally play in your browser, like a New York Times game.I guess when I upgrade my PC I'll have some 10k puzzles to work through. _childDocuments_.review: A promising premise with a moderately nice art direction.  The problem is the puzzles.  It feels like 50% of the puzzles are these extremely simplistic "attach black boxes without making a square" puzzles.  And those are the only ones it feels like there's any effort put into them.  The other puzzles are far, far too simplistic; mazes that can be completed in 10 seconds, multiple variations of standing in one place to align objects, and they're counting finding hidden collectibles as puzzles. In the first two hours, the basic introduction to the game, there's legitimately only one action I'd say is actually solving puzzles.  And there is very little actual difference in the puzzles, just different setups with the same rules.  With the boasts of multiplayer, I was coming in expecting/hoping for something along the lines of Talos Principle mixed with the coop from Portal 2.  Instead what I got was a game where I complete overly simple puzzles in a different screen only to pop out of the puzzle screen to have an uncanny valley face staring at me as another player stares into my soul while I'm doing puzzles.  It's not fun, it's not collaborative, and it feels half-baked.Reduce the number of puzzles, make them more complicated (either longer puzzles or more steps beyond basic pattern recognition), make some of them require two or more people to solve to truly take advantage of your multiplayer.  Until then, this is one of the few games I've ever been disappointed enough in to refund it.

_childDocuments_.review: Update: 188 hours played.Still love playing this game even as an offline game only now. I hope the developers will consider making it open source code so the community can continue to patch and expand on the original idea.Original post: Feb 14. 2024Overall I absolutely love this game and can see myself playing this for years to come on and off. I have wanted an open world puzzle game where exploring the map is just as fun as doing the puzzles, not since The witness have I enjoyed just walking around so much. I also like the shear variety of puzzles available, so you shouldn't get bored easily. The minor set backs for me are that I wish there was more character customization available at the start of the game, the story element is boring (which I love to read so that really says something) and if there was a way to toggle that on and off it would be great. I do hope that they continue to come up with puzzle types in the future and cycle out ones that are not as enjoyable. Overall would recommend to anyone who loves puzzles and/or exploration! Side note, I know that a lot of early demo review channels have compared it to Myst but to me that is apples and oranges, Myst is a series of steps to progress and open up more area, very story driven, this isn't that type of game play. So if you are looking for another Obduction or Myst series adjacent game, it's not like that at all.

_childDocuments_.review: People who want a massive multiplayer co-op puzzle game will be disappointed. I went into this game knowing very little about it aside from the hype of my friends. This is a singleplayer MMO puzzle game. I think people are fine to be upset that the multiplayer aspect is fairly negligible, but if you're focussing on that I think you're missing the forest for the trees. The actual game is fantastic, one of the most entrancing and addictive puzzle experiences I've played in years. The puzzle and world design are masterful, and if you liked The Talos Principle or The Witness this will be a great experience for you. The movement is also surprisingly good, and it's a very satisfying experience.There are some caveats. It runs very poorly. I have a 1050Ti, and it runs somewhere from 35-45 fps at low quality. Obviously I'm not expecting high-end performance with a 1050Ti, but Destiny 2 for instance runs at a way higher fidelity with smooth frames. I enjoy the game enough to look past this, but it doesn't look great for me. It even crashed my GPU once when I opened both it and a Discord stream. The few multiplayer aspects that are in the game (parties, friends) are a bit non-functional as of the time of writing this (2 days after release), though I suppose since these features are generally not impactful this doesn't feel like much of a negative. I do wish to see things get fixed, though.If they add more meaningful ways to collaborate with your friends and improve performance I don't think people will have much to complain about. If people feel misled, that's fine, but on its own terms it's something I will likely sink hundreds of hours into.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first MSOG (Massively Singleplayer Online Game) in existence. The gameplay is entirely singleplayer but the session still has to be hosted online. You can not play in offline mode. You can see avatars of other players around you but the game doesn't support any meaningful interaction. There is no coop, no competetive mode, no leaderboard, no chat, no voice, nothing. You cannot interfere with their gameplay and they cannot interfere with yours. _childDocuments_.review: Islands of Insight is as much an exploration game as a puzzle game; and it kinda nails both of those elements(though I'm early). On top of that it's built around a MMO-ish progress system that is pretty blatant in drip-feeding dopamine. That system does work in this game though; basically removing the completionist exercise most puzzle games devolve into and practically forcing/allowing the player to do what they want in the moment; not just the next puzzle in a row. I don't know how long this'll stay fresh but I have to say I really appreciate the attempt of mixing these game styles and for me it works really welll.

But in striving for the impossible, they made something worthwhile in its own right: an endless puzzle buffet.  They figured out what sort of puzzles that they can produce at scale while maintaining quality, and situated them in a big open world.  It’s basically non-stop running, jumping, and flying from puzzle to puzzle.

_childDocuments_.review: One hell of a mess ! Far from being relaxing, it's fun up to a certain point.I liked the idea of completing puzzles and moving forward in the world but since puzzles constantly repop out of nowhere and daily quest are seriously annoying, it's not fun !Another problem comes from certain puzzles which are timed (it's more stressing than anything else) and some other which constantly shift colors are hard as hell to reproduce because understanding what is actually happening is a nightmare, it's also very tiring for the eyes.Now the world is pretty, controls are okay but still clunky, music is relaxing and you do want to play but not knowing where you're exactly at and where you need to go is annoying.I had the most fun with the black and white squares puzzles which gets crazy challenging but that's pretty much it... Most puzzles are cool but do get repetitive like finding a circles of balls in the sky or finding the spot where you cross all golden circle without crossing the dark one. The glass labyrinth are pretty silly, the pattern finding quickly gets annoying too, finding objects is cool at first but gets tiring especially when they are timed, etc.Finding secrets is cool at first but it gets painful annoying.It's definitely not what I thought it could be. Also, the game is advertised as multiplayer / mmo while you can't play with other players, you can't resolve puzzles together, you can only set a ping visible to players nearby which is nothing of solving "together". You get need quite a lot of time to unlock the wings which don't really allow you fly but rather float which is also used for some puzzles.The game also gives you a useless "skill tree" which doesn't change much safe for some rare ones which are oddly specific. This tree is useless and frustrating.Well, all in all, I can't recommend this game unless you want to wander in a world full of time attack and full of puzzles laying around every meter which makes you feel like exploration is not really part of the game. You feel like you need to solve all puzzles to move forward but you quickly get lost not knowing what is what which makes you solve puzzles at the same place for what seems like forever.The idea is there, some puzzles are very good but eeeh, it's not what I expected.Finally, I will still say that the devs are talented, lots of great ideas, lots of talent for music, graphics and impressive puzzles but I think they killed their game with some bad decision like daily quest, weird useless multiplayer (if they wanted to make a real MMO, there were possibilities but you feel like the team is probably too small to create something interesting), weird skill tree (if they were at least really useful...) and some frustrating timed puzzles which made me ultimately rage quit the game. I really wanted to like this game, I tried as hard as I could.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best puzzle games ever released. What makes it stand out is the quality of the logic grid puzzles, with all of them being hand generated, and many clever twists on modern classics like nurikabe, yin-yang, numberlink etc. The game contains a number of quite challenging puzzles which are hard to solve without hints, even for an experienced puzzle game player. The logic grid rules are also varied and I've found all of the variants I've encountered so far (which covers most of the rules that are available in the game) to be fun to play.There are two main issues with the game for me:(1) It's hard to find consistent puzzle challenges in the game as puzzles are spread all over. Often when you enter a new area in the game you first have to go through a number of really simple tutorial puzzles, which kind of spoil the fun of coming up with some of the logic for solving them on your own. My 7-year-old will join me to play (which is cool) and she can solve many of the 1-2 star puzzles already, which makes the more or less trivial to me. (2) Most of the 24 (or more?) puzzle types are not that fun. Now, you can make 80-90% of the game about solving logic grids if you want, but since the progression system in the game more or less requires you to solve other puzzles as well, it's hard to make fast progressions if you only want to do the logic puzzles. Out of 24 types, there are really only 3 or 4 that I enjoy: Logic grids, Matchboxes, and shifting block puzzles. Several of the observation puzzles are tedious as they require you to walk around and explore a lot, which is very different from playing a puzzle game.As some people have pointed out, it's easy to burn out on a puzzle game as the puzzles become to similar, and to an extent, the game solves this by giving you a world to explore between the puzzles.
