_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: To me, Infinite Wealth is a sign of the times, and if I could give it a neutral rating, I would. Going into IW, I had a lot of high expectations. (It is worth noting that I'm a serial completionist when it comes to the series.) And, in pursuit of honesty, this game both exceeded and fell flat in a myriad of different ways. In terms of gameplay, the game improved many of the things I'd complained about in the past, such as the Table Talk counter and being able to vault over things smoothly now. The battles themselves are also far more enjoyable with the different abilities and combinations you're now allowed to do. However, when it comes to the story writing, IW did not achieve what I think it meant to do. There are many places  where the writing is sloppy and makes no sense. Additionally, how they  If I had to sum it up, it felt as if IW was riding on the nostalgia of Kiryu's "last game" and didn't bother to create the strong narrative that we've seen in the past with the previous RGG Studio games.  It is worth also noting that, since Ishin! and what I've seen others say Lost Judgment, the DLC is getting out of hand. The fact that the game launched with around $160 dollars of DLC, replacing grinding in case one rather buy levels, settled poorly. That, and the Ultimate Edition being as expensive as it is, as well as locking New Game+ behind a DLC. Instead of being for the players, IW gave me the impression that the only concern was making a profit. And until we see a different tune (which who knows of the probability) I can't say I recommend Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth.(PS: You'll be grinding for a very, very long time.)

_childDocuments_.review: There's a part of me that really wants to recommend Infinite Wealth, but at the same time I have a lot of problems with this game that really dragged the experience down for me, mostly in how Kiryu was included and handled in this sequel to 2020's Yakuza: Like a Dragon.For context, I've played the entire Yakuza series with the exception of the Japan exclusive games and Ishin. I've even played the two Judgment games as well as the Kaito Files expansion for Lost Judgment. I love this series, despite its ups and downs. I was hesitant going into Like a Dragon seeing that it ditched the staple beat em' up combat of the nine games I had played prior in favor of turn based combat (ew). To my surprise though, I clicked with the new combat system immediately and found myself loving it. I loved Ichiban and his crew because of just how funny and entertaining they were to watch, with Ichiban even beating Kiryu as my preferred protagonist. For all intents and purposes, I loved that game. Fast forward to when Infinite Wealth was inching closer and closer to release, I was so excited to see all that was new. I loved the idea of a Yakuza game taking place in America, I was excited to see Ichiban and his crew come back, and the improvements to the turn based systems looked really cool.The one area that I was concerned about when it came to Infinite Wealth however, was the inclusion of Kiryu as a main cast member again. I was very conflicted. On one hand, I disliked Yakuza 6: The Song of Life as a conclusion to Kiryu's story. Don't get me wrong, Yakuza 6 was a good game, but I couldn't help but feel like it was too disconnected from the rest of the series when it was meant to be the big conclusion to the story of the protagonist of many years. A whole new cast of characters were introduced and the original ones that have always played a big part in Kiryu's journey were shafted to the sidelines, and that just didn't sit right with me. So while I had my reservations about Kiryu coming back for a lead role since his story was supposed to be over as he passed the torch to Ichiban in the last game, I was still excited to see Infinite Wealth as a chance to rectify the unsatisfying conclusion that was Yakuza 6 and end Kiryu's story in a more cohesive way that utilized the characters and themes featured in the older games. As more and more promotional trailers were released for the game as it grew ever closer to release, I only grew more and more concerned. The trailers only featured two new party members, Chitose and Tomizawa. When I imagined a turn based Kiryu game, I imagined something like Yakuza 0 that split the two protagonists (in this case Ichiban and Kiryu) apart. I figured Ichiban would keep his party members from Like a Dragon, and that Kiryu would have his own set of party members consisting of series mainstays like Majima, Saejima and Daigo, as well as some other important characters like Date and Akiyama. I could totally see Akiyama being a secret party member locked behind the business minigame kind of like Eri in the last game. I thought it would be really cool to be able to play as those old characters again in a turn based style, especially with all of the huge improvements to the combat that were shown off in the trailers. Of course, only seeing two new party members be announced was a huge worry for me, as the memories of Yakuza 6 not featuring those old characters became flooding back, and I only grew more and more reserved toward Kiryu's inclusion in Infinite Wealth if they chose to not go the route I was imagining.Fast forward to the game's release, and it turns out I was right to worry. For a reason I cannot seem to comprehend, Kiryu splits from Ichiban's party about a quarter of the way through the game and returns to Yokohama, bringing some of Ichiban's party members with him instead of having his own crew of series mainstays. One of these characters that splits off from Ichiban is Nanba. NANBA!! OF ALL PEOPLE!!! Some of my best memories of Like a Dragon are the scenes between Ichiban, Nanba and Adachi. They were the three goats! Their dynamic was unbeatable! But now you're telling me that Nanba's going with Kiryu instead of staying with Ichiban and Adachi!!?! Instead of Nanba, we get Eric Tomizawa, and while he isn't a bad character, he just feels like a total knockoff Nanba. Same thing goes for Saeko, who is in Yokohama with Kiryu instead of in Hawaii with Ichiban, and she's replaced with Chitose Fujinomiya, who just feels like a knockoff Saeko. I cannot understand why the choice was once again made to give Kiryu a whole new party instead of having him fight alongside the old characters. The reason for this in the story feels extremely contrived and dumb.  If you ask me, this reasoning feels like a very contrived and dumb excuse to not have to program more than two new party members. Once again, the same mistake was made as in Yakuza 6, except this time it harms Ichiban's part of the game since he loses some of the dynamic between his party that was in Like a Dragon. Infinite Wealth has successfully made me come to the conclusion that Ryu Ga Gotoku studio All of these problems eventually reflect on Ichiban, who essentially takes the sidelines in the sequel to his one game. Pro tip for the writers at RGG Studios, don't soft reboot a series with a new protagonist and make everybody like said new protagonist if you aren't ready to let go of your other one yet. There is no good reason for Kiryu to once again take the spotlight and hurt Ichiban's story in the process when Ichiban has only had one other game to truly shine in. I can't write much more since the character limit is steadily approaching, but I ultimately found myself very disappointed in Infinite Wealth from a story perspective. It's clear that RGG isn't ready to let go of Kiryu and I feel like that came back around and hurt the focus on Ichiban. I hope the next mainline entry can put the focus back on my goat and tell a story that I'm more interested in this time around.

_childDocuments_.review: Another great installment of the Ryu ga Gotoku franchise from RGG studios. PIcking up where it left off from LaD7 and Gaiden, the gang travels beyond Japan to Hawaii to dives into more conspiracies and personal dramas.Visually the game looks impressive even without the support of ray-tracing, with first time in the series where the weather can change dynamically when you are outside.Voice acting is excellent though the too often NPC voice line gets repetitive very quickly. The BGM and karaoke songs are also top notch, somehow still fits the slower turn based gameplay and still makes you feel pumped.The gameplay was also much improved now that you can freely move your character during your turn. This tremendously increases the tactical gameplay for chaining attacks and skills or moving your characters away to a safer place. The improved job system also let you carry skills from different jobs over, while this does make the game slightly easier, it does increase the fun factor by a lot and makes the frequent battle less boring.Despite not including new game+ in the base game, there will still be enough content to get you 100+ hours on the first playthrough. There are simply too many mini-games, side quests, a pokemon game, an animal crossing game, and not to mention the whole Kiryu side story included in the game. So despite the much bigger world in Hawaii, you would never feel like you are walking in an empty street at all, with things happening every step of the way.Storywise it is a step down from the previous entry, despite having a longer story, having to split the focus between Ichiban and Kiryu does take away from the cohesiveness of the game. While this franchise is known for having multiple main characters in a game, this time with trying to tying down Kiryu's ending while moving Ichiban's story forward does make it feel like an imbalance in the story dynamics. It is still a very good story, but it is definitely not an amazing one like in 0 or 7.Overall, another must play game in the series, though I do recommend picking up 7 for cheap to start before playing this one at minimum.

_childDocuments_.review: The pinnacle of the franchise so far, in my opinion. Gameplay is strong, and the story is long and in depth. Everything has led up to this, and while the previous game (Yakuza: like a dragon) introduced Ichiban and the Yokohama crew, this game goes to pretty great lengths to reminisce on Kiryu's character, along with all the trials and tribulations that have led him to where we are now. While I don't think the writing in any of the games is perfect, they have definitely learned a lot since the earlier games in the series. I aimed for a pretty high degree of story completion from the getgo, well worth it as it affords you considerably better weapons. At the end of the credit roll I was a bit under 73 hours. A good 20 hours longer than yakuza: like a dragon. Overall, this is one of those series in gaming that the magic of cannot be overstated. Great characters with big personalities, and epic journeys and accomplishments. I'd personally recommend playing the previous games if you haven't, and capping it off with this one. Because it makes the payoff all that much better

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth, a near perfect sequel I got the chance to play Infinite Wealth, and really enjoyed my time throughout the entire game.If you are looking for a genuinely good franchise to start, I believe this playing this game gives the player even more reason to enjoy the story and invest in past games. Nothing is more rewarding than being able to laugh to your hearts content, and being moved to tears by the same game that wants you to embrace strong emotion towards the story crafting and game play.  In synopsis:- The combat was a major improvement, and added plenty of depth such as: movement in battle, more classes to choose from (including carrying abilities over to any class), and a better balance of progressing level/equipment from start to finish. Weapons, fighting styles, and team compositions are variable, and allow the player to choose how to play, even on the hardest difficulty, all you need is decent equipment and level to complete the game with any party of your choosing.- The sub-stories and the side-content is always a masterpiece in any yakuza game: especially bringing almost double the karaoke songs than last game, adding unique mini-games to side-quests, and a plethora of opportunity to keep you engaged throughout both maps of Japan and Hawaii. Completing some of the bigger side-content such as dondoko island or sujimon league actually offers decent rewards to help progress the main story. Pacing is the key to success, you don't ever have to do only part of the game at a time. Both protagonists have their own ventures that really make you feel like they really fleshed out Ichiban and Kiryu, and if you are a fan of character development, side stories are perfect for you to get to know them better outside of the main story.  - The story is a very strong sequel to Yakuza: Like a Dragon (Yakuza 7), including plenty of homage to previous yakuza titles, while still carrying the franchise in a new and unique direction. All main characters are involved and keep the plot moving in a really good direction. The villains are written decently in yakuza fashion, and offer a very menacing (and sometimes comical) element to the story, with some having unique outcomes and connections to the overall plot. Implementing key elements of Yakuza lore into the story, and offering nice treats for yakuza game veterans to actually enjoy the game was the best part in my honest opinion. I have run into very minor points in the game that I ran into, but overall did not heavily impact my gaming experience with Infinite Wealth, this includes:- A certain party member won't join the team until the second to last chapter of the game, which felt a little underwhelming because most of the game requests you take a long period in the game to steadily grow stronger bonds with your team, which is difficult to not feel rushed if this party member joins late; however in a normal run of the game, this character comes in at a decent level and equipment, nonetheless it felt a little too late to simply join the adventure. - The DLC of the game does make some parts of the game easier, but not enough to completely skew the entire game. I came into the game blind, and I only had pre-order bonuses of 2 extra jobs/classes and a few starter set items; all coming from standard edition. I decided it was right for me to obtain the DLC with a new dungeon and New Game+, but you can still enjoy the game without purchasing extra content, I feel its completely optional, and I only purchased it after I completed the game to make sure I wanted the DLC or not.Overall I really loved the game, it included Kasuga Ichiban and Kiryu Kazuma in very strong protagonist roles, and the writing for both characters really elevated this game to a whole new level. The interaction with party members and their part in the story felt very genuine, and made me want to complete all character bonding moments with them to get to know them better. I have a bias towards believing Yakuza 7 wrapped its own story up just a little stronger than this game, but it does not take away from how good this game is; it is definitely strong enough to stand on its own and provide a strong sense of wanting to continue with the franchise in the future. I'm very glad to to have joined this franchise back in 2021, and I can't wait to see the next game make it's future appearance, I'm ready to see Kasuga Ichiban continue his adventure with his team!Gameplay: 10/10Story: 9.5/10Replay-ability: 9/10Price (69.99 USD): 7.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Kill the past. Secure the future.This review contains minor spoilers for Yakuza 5, 6, 7 and Gaiden.Kiryu has to move on from his past mistakes. Put his trust in others for the first time.Ichiban has to secure the future for all the ex-Yakuza he helped tear down. They are human too.Ichiban has to use the past as a stepping stone to reach for even greater highs. If he got up from rock bottom, he is capable of dreaming of greater heights. His father’s footsteps. His failed confession. A brother he didn’t have the chance to change.Kiryu has to see a brighter tomorrow, secure what little future he has left. Even if he himself tries to deny this fact. Still too afraid to let others into his life.Wandering around the city with Kiryu, reminiscing on all the past events you and him have been through together. The hardships you have faced against the insurmountable foes behind the many multi-layered conspiracies. The laughs you had with the side characters. The infuriation you felt whilst fighting the near-immortal Amon, or the fun you had batting your stress away at the cages. Finally being able to see some of the long lost characters. This is the life Kiryu has lived. You have seen it all through. Reminisce on it one last time.But he can't wallow in despair. He has new friends to keep his chin up. You have been an empty, depressed shell of your former self since 2011. It’s time to gain back some of that old spark. Enjoy life whilst it lasts Kiryu. Gather some positivity, if anyone could tell you how to do that, it’d be Ichi and his gang.This is partially Ichiban’s story after all, and what is Ichiban’s story if not a spontaneous bundle of misfits reaching for the sky?Ichiban’s tale is always penned in the love he has for his friends. The pals he can always confide in, Adachi and Nanba. The person most unapproachable to him, Saeko. The unpredictable ex-mafia who can whip up a mean dim sum, Zhao. The initially cold, but ultimately human members of the Geomijul, Joongi and Seonhee.Joining Ichiban’s group of middle aged do-gooders are the helpful wheelchair-bound Eiji. The cabbie who tried to rob him at gunpoint, Tomizawa. The girl who knows more than she lets on, Chitose. Lastly, the brick-faced Yakuza legend, Kiryu Kazuma himself.Putting Kiryu in Ichibans crew was an interesting decision. These are people he has never had a heart to heart with before. Complete strangers as far as he is concerned. But it worked. The relationship between Kiryu and these people clicked. Ichiban’s cheerfulness can even tear down the greatest of walls. Kiryu quickly found that he had a lot more in common with this pick ‘n’ mix of Japan's (and Hawaii’s) most bold.What really, really helps the bonds you forge with the party is all of the gameplay additions surrounding it. Wandering around the map could trigger a conversation where Seonhee mentions Joongi watching videos of rubber bands blowing up watermelons. Or a discussion between Ichiban and Tomizawa about hermit-crab real estate. Every one of these conversations is as enamoring as the last.But it's not limited to just this, eat at restaurants and the crew might burn their tongues on sesame balls or talk about how their sensitive molars make the party weak to ice magic. Levelling up your bonds allows you to do tag team attacks, combo enemies with your allies, and unlock new skills and jobs to experiment with.Everything you do with your party increases their bond level, as you increase their bond you can go out and grab drinks, usually resulting in a small character arc for that party member. Unlike 7, the characters have plenty of good moments and screen time. So it's not like Zhao or Joongi get a particularly short end of the stick like they did previously. Most of these drink links have nice conclusions, or add particularly entertaining bits of depth to the characters.So all of this makes the party fantastic. But what's a good band of heroes without some ruthless masterminds?The majority of the villains are quite good. Together they form a super solid antagonistic cast, though individually they are a bit hit or miss.Yamai is the standout here. Solid design, fantastic arc, great boss fights and extremely memorable voicework to boot. You’ll be hard pressed to find someone among the fanbase who didn’t end up a fan.Ichiban’s final boss is not bad, but it definitely will not make it to the hall of fame of RGG’s greats like Aoki, Shishido or Mine. However, Ichiban’s story does not end there. His big moment comes afterwards. His final scene, helping up someone from rock bottom through a naive, one-sided love is just so… Ichiban. The dream present in this scene never came to fruition before. But he made it possible now.Kiryu’s final boss has a few minor issues. I really don't know why they felt the need to include a “we are not so different, he and I” moment, when I think that much was made clear. But at the same time,I…I APOLOGISE.This game is nothing short of fantastic, following up on every idea, every core concept in this 9-game series is nothing short of monumental work. To be able to do it in this fashion, and deliver it with this much purpose is stunning.Something as special as this does not come around often.

_childDocuments_.review: At the moment of this writing, I have finished the main story at about 100 hours, did the side underground dungeons,open world grinding, and spend a lot of time at Dondoko Island, main story alone I think is roughly 30 hour if you beeline itOverall, it's a very good game, definitely worth playing if you enjoyed Yakuza Like A Dragon (Yakuza 7). The story, characters and music are a bit...weak compared to the previous game, but the gameplay and side content more than makes up for it.The story I feel is a little weaker, but it's also different, in Yakuza 7, we're actively learning about Ichiban and his past, his story is part of the main story. Here in Infinite Wealth, he's an outsider going into a foreign conflict, but bringing his personal charm into it as well, it's different and I enjoy the story for what it is, I still think Yakuza 7 did it better.For characters, the 2 new member in your party (Tomizawa and Chitose), they're good, they do their job as part of the story well enough, I personally don't find their development as good as Adachi, Nanba and Saeko in Yakuza 7. Yamai is another ok character, he started off incredibly generic and one note, but halfway through the game he changes gear, becoming a more interesting character, but I still find him just ok.Speaking of Yakuza 7, everyone from that game returns here, only they don't have much further development either, largely because they're already well established from the previous game, and that's kind of the problem here, RGG introduces 2 new character with ok writing, and brings back all the established older cast, but the new members don't do enough to shine compared to the cast of Yakuza 7 in their own game.Ichiban is still a gigachad, that didn't change, in fact him and Kiryu are the 2 standouts (obviously), the rest plays the well-done support role.Music is a disappointment for me at least. Remember Warmaker, Brutality, Overcoming the Dragon, Receive You The Hyperactive, ism, these are the track I can remember by name because how much they feed into the moment. Here in Infinite Wealth, I honestly don't remember any of them, because none of them stand out to me.Oh speaking of Brutality, in Yakuza 0, Kuze was your grudge match boss, you fight him like 4 times throughout the game, and the story around them feels different everytime, the same in Yakuza 7, it was Sawashiro, you fight him 3 times. Infinite Wealth doesn't really have someone like that, if you count Dwight Mendez, whom you fight 3 times, but he doesn't have that grudge match villain to go with him, and to be honest, Dwight feels weak, they hired Danny Trejo and that's that best material they can give him? And Dwight also don't have a memorable music track to go with his fight. Yamai could be considered a grudge villain since you fight him like 5 times, I don't really find him to be a villain, he's more like the Majima to Kiryu.The bosses in this game are ok, besides the first Dwight fight, the pivotal Kiryu fight vs the 3, and Sawashiro fight, all of them feels like they have no impact, even the final boss.The rest of the game I really enjoyed, the gameplay is an improvement, it's always fun to ping pong an enemy between 2 team mates, then knock into 2 other enemies, followed up by a downed attack from another team mate.Side activities include the usual, mahjong, gambling, batting etc, new to Infinite Wealth is a crazy taxi inspired delivery game, where you work for Uber delivering food, Pokemon snap (sicko snap) and a Pokemon game (Sujimon), with an elite 4 and a champion, the mechanic isn't that deep, but the core is the same, you fight enemies, sometimes you get the chance to convince them to join you, you field 3 and 3 as back up in a turn-based match vs another Sujimon trainer, there's like 100 or so sujimon to collect, but don't come in expecting a full fledged Pokemon game with intricate stats and strategies.Overall I recommend it at full price, some parts isn't as good, but other parts are really good.

_childDocuments_.review: I really did enjoy this game. It was faithful to the original with the characters and story. It added on to the combat a lot, adding mobility instead of random chance positioning to utilize items to beat people up with like bicycles. On top of the mobility, it added close range damage bonuses, of which Kiryu took the greatest benefit. It was fun to watch kiryu do heat moves randomly in standard dragon blue mode. They also fixed the job/level balance. They made jobs way less impacting on your stats as well as they made jobs realistically need to be leveled less than the previous game for all the skills and benefits you want and need. The balancing on hard mode and legendary mode made sense level wise, though it sucks you don't get the hard+ achievement when you beat it on legend+ first.The game's story wasn't as compelling as the last game per se, but the cult aspect and underground ties made it really fun. There were still fun minigames/sub stories/events to mess around in, to take a break from the story, which is a staple of these type of games. The bosses didn't seem as hard, though the yokohama underground boss is going to be a challenge on the final floor no matter what difficulty you play on.Overall it's a great game and I love it. The game holds up with the last game and in many ways it improves on it while bringing back nostalgia. I would for sure recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: This game is fun and if you liked Y7, you'll enjoy the gameplay of Infinite Wealth too. That being said, the writing is noticeably worse than Y7 and some other Yakuza games, and it feels like the writers fundamentally misunderstand some of their own characters, which is frustrating. Pros: +Combat has had QoL improvements over 7, and the Desperado class is really funny 🤠+I never once had to go out of my way to level grind, I was always exactly at the threshold the game expected me to be for story moments. This is in contrast to the brick wall you could hit in Yakuza 7 with things like the Majima fight. +Dondoko Island is incredibly addicting and a very good side distraction that I've put at least 15+ hours into. Cons:-I did not like the writing in this game. Even when the stakes were high, they did not feel high. Certain things felt extremely unserious but were played straight. Even the substory writing felt weaker. -Returning characters from Y7 do things that feel wildly, WILDLY out of character, which left a bad taste in my mouth. -The only time this game got an emotional reaction out of me (aside from anger or disbelief at the writing) was when (spoiler for the VERY end of the game) . That made me gasp out loud. This is a massive contrast from previous games, which have often had emotional rollercoasters and gut punches. Basically, all of my cons can be summed up by the way the writing and characterization was handled. -Of course, the horrible predatory DLC practices from Sega (locking NG+ behind a paywall and numerous purchasable DLC packs)As a big fan of the Yakuza/Like a Dragon games, especially Y0 and Y7, Infinite Wealth was probably one of my most anticipated games of all time. Maybe it's on me for expecting too much from this game, but I was in disbelief at so many of the writing choices. I'm still recommending it because I got 95+ hours out of it (still haven't entirely finished Dondoko island but have otherwise completed all side content/drink links/memoirs of a dragon/etc) and I enjoyed playing the game, I just loathed many of the story elements. But if you can get past the writing, the gameplay is very fun!

_childDocuments_.review: (Minor spoilers could follow, although I tagged everything I think I should!) Look, I know that it very well could be the recency bias getting to me, but I feel that this is my favorite of the whole Like a Dragon series. While I 100% respect and understand the opinion of those who say the ending was botched and that the antagonists weren't in alignment thematically with the protagonists Ichi and Kiryu, I have to disagree. Ichiban is a compelling character precisely because he is a constant force for good in the face of varying degrees of hardship. How he chooses to  was initially something that I abhorred, but I truly believe that this is what a character like Ichiban would naturally do given all of his previous characterization.Let's talk about Kiryu's arc too, because holy balls I ate that stuff right up. My main internal criticism of the series as it existed before Infinite Wealth and Gaiden (disregard if this isn't true and I'm just media illiterate) was how earlier games almost seem to portray Kiryu, Daigo, and Majima as great men BECAUSE of the yakuza instead of their really being great IN SPITE of it. All the LaD games do a great job of humanizing those in the gray zones and saying that people are worthy of compassion and respect regardless of their occupation or social status, but I very much wanted to see somebody really acknowledge the hurt that regular people experience at the hands of criminal gangs. To see Kiryu say this and show such selflessness/emotion was gut-wrenching yet satisfying  and was a fantastic way to hopefully ! Other things, combat's great (too easy?) although I forgot to use poundmate summons for the entirety of the game... It completely slipped my mind, I probably missed some great cinematics. Further, this game improves on LaD 7 in every way, I even enjoyed the grinding this time. Suijmon battling is probs my favorite minigame in years, too. Only critique is that NY Hot Dog is still inaccessible (although they acknowledged this in the in-game podcast lmaoooooo), that and SEGA Bass Fishing is too hard. C'mon SEGA, I may have infinite wealth but I don't have unlimited quarters to spend on your stupid fish game within a game.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. I love every game in the Yakuza (or Like a Dragon, if you want) series. This is the only one I've bothered to write a review for.I'd argue Infinite Wealth has the best combat system of any JRPG to date, and any future developers working in the genre should attempt to surpass it. All the best elements of the Yakuza 7 system return, and the weaker aspects of that game have all been refined. You still have the basic turn-based combat with various menus to scroll through, allowing a variety of attacks and support skills, as well as enemy weaknesses to exploit.The most significant change is the movement in battle. In Yakuza 7, each character had a radius around their model they would meander around in, and timing an attack correctly could result in a combo maneuver with a nearby ally. In Infinite Wealth, the movement of your active character within that radius is fully under the player's control, allowing you to deliberately set up those combos, and the combat system is now heavily based around that. The radius for each party member also widens at certain level milestones.If you aren't chaining attacks with your allies, battles will be significantly more difficult for you. What was an unreliable chance for a damage boost in the previous game is now the core of any effective strategy for this game. Every basic attack should be set up to create a combo with another party member, and many skills can create a chain-attack through knockback as long as you make sure you're positioning your active character well.Mileage may vary as to the battles themselves; due to picking up the new combat mechanics quickly, as well as some early-game grinding to experiment with them, I found most of the main story battles to be fairly easy. The aforementioned grinding also meant I was over-leveled for most of the main story, so that was certainly a factor. That factor also highlights how absurdly difficult some of the optional battles can be; the final bosses of the Hawaiian Haunt and Yokohama Underground were both long, hard fights, despite both being taken on prior to the finale of the main story, and all party members being about 10 levels higher than the recommendation for the final boss rush.Regardless of its flaws, the combat is a ton of fun to play. It's a shame the job system is still bad. For the sake of experimenting, I kept both Kasuga and Kiryu in their default jobs, and used party members supporting them to experiment with the job system. I'm sure people who get off on optimizing playthroughs will have a lot of opinions on this, but for the average player, the job system can be ignored for the most part.There are some cool abilities you can get from leveling up any particular job, but there's very few that can't be easily replaced by another ability from a different job. The main appeal is unlocking the Ultimate Attack for each job, since those do massive damage, and all have a unique cutscene associated with them, but unlocking them means maxing out a job level. On top of that, the skill transfer system only allows you to transfer one Ultimate Attack when you change a character's job, and that's only if your bond level with that character is at level 100.Other skill transfer slots are unlocked at lower levels, but those are only for basic skills, and it's rare that you'll need to level up a job very much to get the only basic skills you'll need. The Samurai get a skill that inflicts bleed almost immediately, and even though most of the later skills are meant to stack with the bleed, it's rare an enemy lives long enough for one of those to be useful. The Surfer job gets a powerful AOE heal fairly early on, and that will serve you well through the final boss. In fact, every job I experimented with had one or two useful abilities unlocked at early levels, then a bunch of skills that had limited to no utility most of the time, and then the Ultimate much later.My advice would be to focus less on mixing and matching job skills, but to pick the job you like for each character early on, and supplement that job with one or two low-level skills from other jobs that fill in the weak points. The HP, defense, and damage boosts you get from leveling a job beyond the point of unlocking its Ultimate far outweigh the value of wasting a bunch of XP unlocking multiple skills you'll never use.I'll never bother to 100% one of these games, but this is the one I've come the closest to. It has some of the best side missions in the decades long history of this series; Kiryu's Life Links alone would prove that, but those are just the most obvious. Even Lost Judgment didn't wrap me in to its side content as well, and that had been my previous benchmark for best side stories. As an attempt to entice you; Kasuga will enlist an old friend to grant a woman's dying wish, Kiryu will have a chance to reunite with Haruka, and if you didn't hate Ono Michio before, you will now.Some of the minigames are polished to the point where I've spent more time on them than I would've spent on actual games designed around those mechanics; I've never played Animal Crossing, and I haven't played a Pokemon game since Ruby, but I devoted dozens of hours to the Dondoko Island and Sujimon minigames. I started those minigames because rewards for the main gameplay were tied to them, but ended up having fun working toward those rewards. I don't think I was supposed to turn Dondoko Island into a crowded hub of urban industry, but I certainly enjoyed doing it.This is a great game, and any time you've spent reading my rambling about it would've been more enjoyably spent playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: With the exception of Yakuza 6, I don't think I've ever been as disinterested in completing the side content of a Yakuza game as I am in this one.That aside. The key problem in the game is that a lot of it is wasted potential. Kiryu is the protagonist with a proper arc and he only explores it for 30% of the game. Ichiban has no actual arc in this game and basically goes around where the story tells him to go without much of a reason to do so beyond the game bringing him there. The main antagonist has a shallow reason for being the antagonist and no reason at all to be Kiryu's final boss. Also, for what's supposed to be an epic and ultimate final boss for Kiryu, they made the theme song about as meh as can be. Really says something when the mandatory Tojo Clan boss fight is the best fight in the game.There's a lot of superfluous story elements based around the writer's desire to comment on a contemporary issue without tying it to a central theme, which leaves the overall plot of the story somewhat aimless. It seems to have a lot of the proper elements that can make a Yakuza game great, but fails to capitalize on them and push itself. With just a few re-writes and changes to the overall plot structure, this game could've easily been a solid entry in the series but ultimately fails to beat even Gaiden, which should've otherwise been a relatively minor entry compared to the what should've been be the ultimate conclusion to Kiryu's story. The only thing this game does better than 7 is the gameplay changes, otherwise it has been to surpass its predecessor in any meaningful way. Top that off with the fact they're charging at least $10 more and another $20 for New Game+ and the secret dungeon, which should otherwise be expected to come with the completed game at minimum.Do not buy this at full price if you value your time and are a long time fan of the series, you will be sorely disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: Haven't enjoyed a JRPG this much since Octopath Traveller 2.I can't recommend it if you haven't played the rest of the series unfortunately, or atleast 7 + Gaiden (even still you'll be missing out on A LOT).The combat is a step up in every possible way from 7 and I absolutely love RGG for this. I got into every encounter I could just because of how much fun I was having with the combat.Some wonderful story beats and themes were explored, and it made me teary eyed a few times throughout.A few games touch me emotionally like this one did, even if you could argue that in the storytelling department, it's predecessor was better.In 9 days, I spent 65 hours playing it and I enjoyed every minute. _childDocuments_.review: Crying before I need to cry to prepare myself. SEGA SUCKS FOR THE DLC PRACTICES. But, I love Ichiban (and crew) and Kiryu too much to leave a negative review.UPDATE:Game is overall an improvement from 7 in the game-play department. They added a number of QoL fixes to the turn-based combat (granted it can still improve). Side activities are everywhere and as wacky as ever. Dondoku Island is a treat. The Sujimon stuff adds a new layer to Ichiban's schizophrenia. Side stories are funnier and more heartfelt than ever. Unfortunately, the main story is far weaker than 7 and several of the past few entries. And, I think Kiryu overshadows Ichiban which is disappointing as well. Optional dungeons used to grind levels are somehow more tedious than in 7. The procedural generation doesn't work very well in that department and it's kind of a slog. Kiryu's side activities were also a bit of a letdown and felt lacking. Overall, great game only let down by a very weak main story and a few minor things here and there. Definitely not the best Yakuza game in the franchise, but it's a good time.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the biggest and the longest game among its series and just like yakuza 0, the game is split between 2 mc and offers massive tons of contents and huge variety of mini games that doesnt feel like mini games at all since I feel like clearing the minigame itself consumed more times than the main story. You can find yourself hooked in several minigames for ages like playing sujimon which feels exactly like pokemon, even has their own elite 4 and its dex completing and leveling system is pretty similar. There's also an animal crossing-like minigames where you have to build your own resort island, reach certain milestones to reach 5 stars, catching the fish and insect for encyclopedia, and finding DIY recipes, there's also a minigame that feels like pokemon snap where you must take photos of several sujimons within time limited event, a food delivery minigame where you must perform attracting combos to multiply your score, a 'tinder-like' minigames to hook yourself with girls that will reward you with actual realistic hot pics of featuring girls, and still many returning minigames from sega arcade and collecting cans from like a dragon. Every single corner in this games has its own content that you may even feel overwhelmed to try all of it and I recommend to take it easy, try to not clear each in one swipe as you can easily burnout if you try to do so.The substories in this games also brings back lots of returning characters for their story continuation or maybe give closure for some of them, that if you've been following yakuza series for long and always keep in check with each games substories, trust me you'll feel grateful. Infinite wealth brings back literally almost the entire major substory characters from yakuza 0, kiwami 1 and 2, 3-5, 6, 7, and even some characters from judgment make a brief cameo in this game, and I feel like this is the biggest fanservice I've ever found in yakuza games, even the music used here is also the same music used from older games and if you notice, kiryu's kamurocho battle theme is the original 'Funk goes on' from its PS2 games!Now talking about gameplay, it still feels pretty similar like the latest game but with some improvements like now you can manually positioning your party in combat, the enemy now has knockback direction after receiving impact from your attack, whereas if the enemy is flying towards your other party members it will perform something like a chain combo that doesn't cost you a turn, you can now use anything scattered in the battlefield as a weapon to inflict ailments or huge AoE damage, and for kiryu specifically, he can enter the brawl mode for a brief period of time to ignore the turn based system and kick everything on his way, and this is what I enjoy the most when playing as kiryu XDMy only and big disappointment for this game is that they locked NG+  feature and 1 major dungeon behind a $25 DLC, I almost played every yakuza game for 100% achievement but can't do this in Infinite wealth due to that sole reason as the achievement require you to complete the game 3 times and clearing 1 major dungeon that is also included in the dlc, and $25 for just unlocking new game plus is just sucks

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR:Great game, the story has its ups and downs. Runs smooth and is definitely a good leap from the previous game when it comes to endgame-combat & dungeons.If you're a fan of the Yakuza series and enjoyed the previous game with Ichiban you'll probably like this one.Longer version:After I beat the whole game at 100% and another quick speed run for the last couple achievements, I feel the need to give my words of feedback on this game.What are the good things?- More satisfying combat than the predecessor- Story is good, but has its lows too- Insane amounts of side-missions and mini-games- You get very much playtime out of this game (~100-120h for 100%, 55-60h story only)- More jobs, better upgrade system- Old jobs & cross-jobs stats- Old & new friends combined- Two characters to play as group leader- Variety of outfits in combat- Some "back to the roots" combat system for one character- A whole island as side-story and to generate some money- The option to bench members of the party completelyWhat are the things I dislike about the game?- The grind (RNG) for gear (not weapons)- The limit on defensive gear makes a lot of fights very hard, weapons are a bit better but still have a pretty quick limit to reach- All characters aside from the "main" characters & antagonists are pretty generic looking with low effort made- Clothing (out of fights) can only be changed after the story is done- As usual, some side-missions are lame and/or dumb- Enemies become bullet-sponges (insane amounts of health points) really quick- Even normal difficulty becomes a chore when you're trying to beat all dungeons during and the extra dungeon after the story.- Same old mini-games and locations (aside from Hawaii)- Getting ran over by boats when you're pretty close to the beach, which are 24/7 out there- Lack of different weather- Early game money is tight, but mid to endgame money is pretty much useless- Pokémon rip-off side-storyline which is pretty lame- Pricing of the game (I got it for a reasonable price on a key site)- Paid DLCs, which should be obtainable in the game- The whole tatara channel garbage (introducing social media in games is a No-Go)

_childDocuments_.review: Another year, another Like a Dragon game. It’s been this way for a while now, to be fair, and playing these titles is not tiring, even if a bit routine. Yet I can’t help but feel that the RGG team itself is starting to get tired and for all of the cool ideas and elements they put in these games, they might be dreaming to make a bunch of non-Like a Dragon games instead.Infinite Wealth, or Like a Dragon 8, is the second jRPG entry in the series so far, focusing on party turn based combat instead of beat ’em up gameplay. And while it has a lot of really cool things and quality of life improvements over the Yakuza: Like a Dragon, I can’t say that I’ve enjoyed it much.This title, just like its direct predecessor, attempts to mix all of the ideas and mechanics of the previous titles in the franchise but frame them in the way as if it was a Dragon Quest game. And just like last time, the ideas here are novel and inventive. It’s a “realistic” setting, mixed with ridiculous and over the top elements where angry dudes on the street visually transform into over the top jRPG-like enemies and people cast “magic spells” using mops and coconuts. While the fights themselves have a lot more dynamic elements to it, based on the positions of the people, objects on the scene and quick inputs for blocking or increasing attack power.Infinite Wealth makes those systems even more exciting and fun with some characters getting abilities that break all jRPG conventions completely. Your party can now perform combo attacks if they stand close together, different kinds of follow up attacks, ability to automatically win a fight against low level enemies. The way enemies appear and get aggressive towards you have been tweaked to be less annoying, with almost no enemies chasing you across the map. The system of bonds between party members (that enables some of those new attack types) have been tweaked and feels more fun. Class system is updated to make it different “jobs” more balanced and also now allows you to transfer a limited amount of skills from class to class, similarly to the job system in Final Fantasy V.And yet… so many frustrating elements of the previous attempt are kept as is and even some of these new quality of life features feel deeply flawed. Attacks can still miss based on random geometry and ragdoll physics shenanigans. Which is even more frustrating since the game still refuses to kill enemies on low health, if the finishing attack is a combination and the final hit of the combination gets a miss for some silly reason. The auto-battle is as pointless as it used to be and won’t help neither those who are not as in love with turn based jRPG combat, nor those who are but want to grind for a bit at a relaxed pace. The ability to win against low level enemies still initializes the fight and shows the results screen, taking valuable time, unlike Dragon Quest XI. On top of that you may get stuck when doing it, because it requires all enemies to die or get hit by a three-hit combo from the party leader. Given that it plays automatically, the buggy pathfinding along with the already mentioned geometry and ragdolls, can lead to a soft lock. Team combos and weapon attacks can often get in the way or not trigger, as they are position sensitive, yet everyone is constantly moving during the fight. The game does provide a visual guidance of what your attack should result into, but what actually happens is never consistent. On top of that, it’s often hard to even see which enemy you are aiming at during the especially crowded fights, as you might want to be planning a specific attack with a knockdown to send a group of enemies flying, but instead accidentally select the farthest dude in the chain without realizing it.Still, the base system is rather solid and has a lot of fun elements to it. But maybe you’re here, like me, for the story. That’s where another problem of lies – nothing happens for the majority of the game’s chapters. The game opens with strong storytelling that isn’t really leading up to anything very interesting, but is at least entertaining. And the final couple of chapters are chock full of story. But during most of the game, chapters will come and go with some characters introduced and removed from the story and something happening, but none of it being of any real consequence to the story or being interesting. That is if you’re lucky and you get any story, because the game might instead spend most of the chapter introducing you to a yet another mini-game you probably won’t care about. Want Pokemon? Want Animal Crossing? I don’t, but tough luck, here’s several hours of unskippable tutorials on these mini-games I will ignore.The game does get back to the story and overcompensates for the lack of it during prior chapters, yet, even here it feels extremely weird. The strongest elements of the story (which is quite boring in general, actually) all have everything to do with Kiryu. Because you see – this is a yet another attempt to “give closure to Kiryu’s story”, for the third time now? Fourth? That did work for me, because of the constant nostalgia bait and “here’s how that character is doing” moments. But also feels cheap, unnecessary and extremely unfair to all of the cast of the last two games. They didn’t quite get a chance to truly shine in the previous title and are treated as supporting cast to Kiryu’s story in this one. Heck, one of the party members gets added to the story in the penultimate chapter of the game, when there’s basically no time or space to do anything interesting with them.This particular aspect influences the way all other stories work too. Ichiban gets a fair number of substories, but they’re mostly bland in comparison to all of the emotional member berries Kiryu gets. All of the gameplay locations aren’t particularly interesting either and don’t get any meaningful story to them. There is a lot of “shocking twists” and window dressing, but none of that feels memorable or interesting. It doesn’t help that the game also often looks quite bad. Dragon Engine never had a strong suit with the day time (and to be fair, real life tends to also look boring and even ugly at day time), but in this case it feels especially bad since one of the biggest selling points of the game seems to be the tropical mood of the Hawaii. I would also be remiss not to mention the SEGA’s greed with DLCs this time around, as they’ve decided to lock down New Game plus, a classic mechanic for the franchise, behind a paid DLC.I didn’t dislike Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth, even if I was utterly bored through the vast majority of its playtime. It does deliver on cool jRPG combat mechanics and by the end the story picks up, even if the main story itself is really stupid. But the title feels like a weird blockbuster made based on test audience feedback, rather than a game that the RGG studio really wanted to do. I’m fine with having played the game, but I also don’t see myself ever returning to it in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: I DO recommend this game, HOWEVER...This is one of the weakest entries, story-wise, in the series.  Ichiban gets sidelined about mid-way through and it becomes Kiryu's game, but even then the story and villains don't really compel you very much.  The battles also aren't super challenging so there's not much reason to go deep into the jobs system, because you'll just steamroll everything with zero effort.Bonus content isn't very compelling, and the dungeons at the end of the game are pretty one-dimensional and only offer limited challenge.  We needed another Millennium Tower post-game dungeon, but we didn't get it.WHAT MAKES IT WORTH IT is the size and scope of the game.  Pretty decent substories that make up for it, and honestly, even a BAD Yakuza game is still better than what most other studios are putting out.  The mini-games aren't very mini, which is a good thing:BUT, I think Sujimon were implemented poorly.  The battles were kind of a slog, and a good concept didn't really execute well.  I wasn't very compelled to complete that stuff.Dodonko Island AKA Animal Crossing: Yakuza is actually pretty fun, but it takes too long and in order to get to 5-stars, you have to make an ugly island because small decorations aren't very efficient at raising your score.I still recommend it because it's Yakuza, but I was sad that THE MUSIC ALSO MAKES UP FOR A LOT OF THE SHORTFALLS!  Like, seriously, this is some of the best game music produced EVER.6/10 (for a Yakuza game) /  9/10 compared to anything else

_childDocuments_.review: So I spent a pretty big chunk of time here. This game is a fantastic addition to the series, marred by stupid business practices, and blemished with some real odd VO in the original Japanese dub. The good: The turn-based gameplay was already quite good in Y:LaD, and IW improves it all quite well. Dondoko Island is a great side activity. Sujimon is something I did not expect to have a good time with. Crazy how a side mode felt just as fleshed out as the game it's based on.Hawaii is great to explore! Lots of fun mini games!The bad: Compared to Y:LaD, it feels much slower to get things started. I won't spoil any story, but toward the end of the game, there are some prompts involving points of no return that are a little misleading. There IS a premium adventure just like the previous games, but for some odd reason, the game treats the points of no return as just that: points of no return.If you play the Japanese dub, you will find some of the VO choices real odd. Dwight, Danny Trejo's character in particular, is real weird with the Japanese dub. Dwight speaks Japanese, and I get that Danny does not, but for some weird reason, they got a different actor to speak the English lines instead of just using Danny's audio for when Dwight speaks English.The price point. No game is worth $70. I got this game during the spring sale. DLC practicesPractices involving downloaded contentDownloadable content that is badMonetization involving features that should have been in the base gameDecisions involving the cutting of content and being sold as extra content in the form of DLC just to make a quick buckIn conclusion, I recommend this game, but I recommend it on sale. It's a great game, the story is pretty damn good, though I think it falls flat in a few areas. The gameplay is improved on from the previous mainline entry. It's a great entry.

_childDocuments_.review: As much as it pains me to say, I cannot recommend this game due to the fact that new game plus is locked as DLC content. This shouldn't become the norm for any company to follow. New game plus in LAD and IW makes it so you can experiment with many different classes due to the increase in class exp. You're also locked to normal mode without the dlc, so you miss out on the challenge the harder difficulties provide. This game is incredible, and I would recommend this game if it wasn't for this grimy, greedy gimmick.                    There are some nice battle mechanics added to the combat compared to LAD. The ability to be able to move and position yourself during your turn adds new strategies and possibilities. You can do more damage depending on your positioning and the ability being used by positioning the character correctly. It can also grant you the option for another party member to join in for a combo attack. Debuffing and buffing are also more prevalent compared to LAD, which adds more strategic approaches. Overall, I'm impressed by the improvements. I'm a little disappointed by some of the classes from LAD not returning. Can't complain too much though, the new classes are quite fun, unique, and hilarious. Desperado and Kiryu's signature class were the ones I had the most fun with.                                                                                                                                                    Story wise, its a little bit of a mixed bag for me. The beginning and the middle are great. The pacing was on point, letting you get emotionally invested in the story and characters. On the final stretch though, the pacing goes to crap. Everything feels very rushed, making you feel like you missed something, or if something was taken out. Personally, I feel the game needed at least 2 more chapters to keep the plot consistent. The ending leaves you a bit high and dry, with a lot of questions left unanswered. Other Yakuza games made sure to give you certain closure or at least an explanation to characters and important plot points that occur, so IW left me a bit confused with the things that were left unaddressed. What is great story wise was the Kiryu memories and bucket list. This took me through an emotional roller coaster the entire time. A character who I've come to love in the span of 10 games is facing the end of his days. He comes to terms with his regrets, people he's come to love and care for, and the realization that his entire life he's been dealt a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ hand. He realizes his entire life he's always done something for others, but never for himself. It's still heartbreaking to see what seemed like an immortal, unstoppable, tenacious being having to face his death due to cancer.                                                                                                                                                        Yakuza games have always been well known for their substories and minigames. IW delivers and doesn't disappoint. The two main minigames this time are Pokemon and Animal Crossing spinoffs. Both are quite fun and addicting. You "catch" and level up different Sujimon you find throughout the map. Theres also a gacha system within in the game to pull for specific Sujimon. You can also participate in "raids" that occur every so often like in POGO to get specific Sujimon. They range from being utterly hilarious and troll, to as serious as a giant menace swinging an axe around. You go around town and travel other trainers to level up, eventually to compete in the Sujimon tournament. As far as the Animal Crossing clone, I haven't spent much time on it. I will be doing it on my next playthrough. From the little I played it was quite fun. Lots of customizing options were available and really played out like Animal Crossing with Yakuza characters.  IW has some of the most ridiculous substories to date, which is quite the feat considering its competition from previous installments. Sometimes, it really seems like they gave a manic homeless man crack, and made him write down the plot for each substory. IW definitely has some of my favorite and most memorable substories to date.                              Overall, I really love this game. It made me laugh, smile, tear up, ball my eyes out, angry, upset, and just about every other emotion. It was quite enjoyable, and would highly recommend if Sega removes the absurd NG plus paywall. For new players trying to get into the series, I would highly recommend starting with The Man Who Erased his name, then LAD if you don't want to start from the beginning of the series. All in all, f##k you SEGA, you greedy b##ch.

_childDocuments_.review: I am going to be very honest about this review and I am not going to mention any shady DLC business that SEGA is doing. I pre-ordered the game way way back and I gotta say it's worth the money for me at least.Spoilers aheadThe game is really beautiful in every way and sense possible, everything was a major upgrade from the past game (maybe beside the two DLC Jobs from 7 that didn't appear), the story was indeed a little bit confusing at times but everything almost got tied up at the end, there are a lot of people saying that the story is weaker than the past games or like it's close to Yakuza 4 worst, which is a bad statement, this a 9/10 story for sure.The characters didn't feel bland at all, the new party member Chitose and Tomizawa were really great and each one of them had their own "arc" in the story, the antagonists were also pretty damn good, Yamai being the best character in this game and not forgetting Ebina which is clearly "What if Ichiban was a bad guy?" which is really good in contrast to everything else.But I gotta say the whole romance thingy between Saeko and Ichiban felt cringey and not great at all, it wasn't really comic relief to me at least, I used to ship them in the first game and now it felt forced and not that good, beside the scenes from the start of the final chapter. (Not the end because it was somehow good at first and then it ended being cringe)The only complaint that I have is how THEY STILL forget some old characters that were important in the story, like The Florist or Nakahara and at the same time I wanted the game to have at least some Kurohyou references (maybe beside the Asakura boxing champion) but it is what it is, we got a lot of other really amazing references that were quite forgotten.There is also the whole Hanawa thing but it wasn't too bad, they at least mentioned him in the last chapter and it was quite good in my opinion, at least it wasn't just a small slide show and that was all.The minigames were also really great, Sujimon was nearly perfect and I loved it but I hope the next installment is going to be even bigger on this premise, I would love to see all the Sujimons from the Sujidex (beside the main story characters) and maybe having randomly generated enemies with different types of sujimons.Ending it I wanted to say that the last game was named "Like a Dragon: The Man Who Erased his name" and the last achievement for this game is "The Man Who Regained His Name" which is a perfect ending.It's a 9.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: When I  I called it a game that “should please franchise veterans while simultaneously being worth a look for those who want to take a look at it for the first time” – it was a great new entry point to the long-running series, that didn’t only introduce a new protagonist with Kasuga Ichiban but also an entirely new gameplay style for the franchise with turn-based battles. Granted, the new turn-based direction had a lot of room for improvement, but it worked decently well for a first attempt.Following a  action-spinoff focused on Kazuma Kiryu,  is once again a turn-based affair – only this time focusing on two protagonists, with Ichiban and Kiryu both set to embark on a new adventure in Hawaii, which marks the first time that the series takes place outside Japan. But while the gameplay has seen massive improvements,  unfortunately struggles with a plot that’s trying to handle too many different things at once.In fact, I’d argue that that the basic premise of the game itself is already a questionable one: As a soft reboot,  was a great entry point for a series that - by this point - already consisted out of seven (!) mainline titles.  should have continued like that – but instead, it does not only feature the return of Kiryu as a protagonist but also a lot of story content that focusses on his past. Following the plot of  might not require the player to be familiar with all of the previous games – but it will have a lot less of an emotional impact if you “only” played  before.This is especially apparent during the side content that’s tied to developing Kiryu’s battle abilities. While it might be optional, quite a lot of it is also tied to various nostalgia trips, which - while certainly appreciated by series veterans like me – are just not a good fit for the sequel of a soft reboot. In my opinion, keeping Kiryu and his friends as side-characters and/or continuing their story through spin-offs would’ve been the better choice here.That said, aside from the debatable basic premise, the plot of  is suffering from additional problems as well. While the story starts off quite promising, it struggles the longer it goes on (not only in terms of pacing), ending on an especially questionable open-ended note. Some of the story choices are also really out there, even for a series where you fight two tigers with your bare hands (fighting ). Additionally, the “big” villains of the game feel underdeveloped despite the game’s length (and - oddly enough – like they should be switched around when it comes to who’s tacking them on in the end). Lastly, it’s disappointing to see how badly the game treats its connections to .On the bright side, the colourful cast of party members remains a joy to hang around with, including its new additions. I gladly took my time to once again build up a bond with them through optional content, even though some of them play a significantly larger role in the story while others are introduced way too late: the final party member only joins at the penultimate chapter! Despite the already great cast, it’s the protagonists who really carry the game, however. Kiryu definitely steals the show here with his presence, which turns him into the centre of attention in every scene he appears. Ichiban, while still the same old likeable hero, unfortunately struggles to compete: Not undergoing any significant character development throughout the whole game despite an initial setup that would allow it, he pales in comparison to Kiryu instead of growing alongside him.While the story might not be the series at its best thanks to the aforementioned issues, it’s still an enjoyable ride thanks to decent characters and the many twists and turns throughout the plot that are expected of the series by now.  certainly is a “it’s about the journey, not the destination” type of game and this is where I have to talk about the excellent turn-based gameplay.Simply put, the improvements to combat, traversal and general Quality of Life have been substantial and I had a lot of fun simply engaging with the various life qualities the game offers. In terms of content,  is simply massive – it took me 59h to finish the story as well as all story-related side content (life links, drink links, most substories) and there’s still a lot of minigames, challenges, (job) levelling, gear upgrades and even two randomly-generated optional dungeons I could potentially finish.On that note: Locking New Game+ as well as another bonus dungeon behind the purchase of the deluxe edition of the game is simply outrageous, same with selling additional combat jobs through other DLCs. This type of content should not be sold separately, especially not from day 1.That aside, in terms of gameplay,  is one of the best games RGG Studio has made. Thanks to fast travel options (unfortunately not useable inside buildings for some reason) and a Segway, you can easily cross the huge locations in little time. Combat is vastly more enjoyable now, as you’re allowed to move your character this time around – with positioning now playing a huge role, since it allows you to set up combo attacks, back attacks or even make use of the environment. Combined with an easy-to-understand system of mixing skills from various combat jobs and a decent gear progression, I had a fantastic time with the turn-based combat this time around.As usual for the series,  also comes with the usual minigames like darts or SEGA arcades, as well as two “big minigames” this time around: Dondoko Island, which is somewhat similar to Animal Crossing, and the Sujimon League, where you can used previously “captured” enemies to fight against other Sujimon trainers. While I personally didn’t stick with them, they allow for different gameplay experiences from the main game if you need a break – and are entirely optional, since  doesn’t have a huge “you need a large amount of money to continue” roadblock like the predecessor did, which basically forced you to do the management minigame.Lastly, I have to praise the music this time around:  offers some really great music pieces throughout it’s 6h long (!) OST, with some big fight themes in particular being exceptional. The game also looks great, although the quality differences between important and non-important characters is a bit too noticeable. The game also crashed on me once, so I recommend saving often even though an autosave feature exists.To conclude,  is a game with fantastic gameplay and an only “okay” story this time around. Still, it tells a tale that’s only really possible in a unique series like this one and I wouldn’t want to miss it. I’m certain that if RGG Studio can keep up the momentum and improve upon themselves once more, the next game in the franchise will be something truly special.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best games I've played, along with being the best Yakuza game I've played yet, of which I've played 0-8, Gaiden, Ishin, and Judgment. There are light but vague spoilers, possibly in this review.There's so much to do and so many characterizations that it's unreal. I had so much fun during my entire playthrough. The gameplay is much improved over 7's and is so fun. The plot, for the most part, is great. The character conversations with the party chat, bingo, table chat, and drink links are so good and interesting, though I wish they were spread out more throughout the game. I found myself just completing the bonds immediately, which I felt could be better. The substories are some of the best in the series, and I really enjoyed them. Honolulu was an interesting change of pace for the series, and I really enjoyed exploring it. Though I sort of missed the connection with characters, their locations, and the people and stories of the locations that is typical of the series.I do overall prefer some of the themes of 7, with that game's focus on the downtrodden, and while this game does have that, it's much less of a theme. The plot was ...it was... interesting, but I feel it kind of lost itself. Things just sort of wrapped themselves up in the end, and it kind of felt meaningless in a way. Plot holes and dumps are typical and expected; I honestly do not care about that sort of stuff. It's a soap crime drama, and thus I just have fun. The story through most of the game is very fun, and I loved it. I do despise time jumps where there is a plot that should be shown. I'm looking at the epilogue for that one. Show, not tell?I do really appreciate the whole concept of legacy, friendship, and just introspection on life as a whole that this game does, however. It's for sure the best Kiryu game, and it solidifies his position and legacy. I absolutely loved the game ending with Kiryu regaining his name, though I would've loved a DEFINITIVE break from the life that he's lead. I hope in future games Kiryu is no longer a part of the underworld due to the analysis he's done on his legacy over the course of this game.I loved the parts where Kiryu was contemplating the fact that being a living legacy ultimately leads people to get hurt, but at the same time reckoning with the fact that him being a martyr and running away has also just caused himself and the people he loves to get hurt. It's a complicated things that he has this draw to the the Yakuza and the underworld, and it's lead to all the complications that come from that. I appreciate the introspection, that he want's both worlds. Yet still allowing for the people around him to support him. I absolutely loved when they would remind him he's not alone and never has been. It's so good. The bucket list was such a fun and sad way to go through all the memories over Kiryu's 30+ years of being associated with the underworld. This whole game makes me dislike 6 even more than I already did because THIS is the send-off Kiryu deserves. It's a true reflection on his flaws, life, and everything.Ichiban took a back seat in this game. I'll be honest and say I thoroughly enjoyed the Kiryu Party sections after Kiryu went back to Japan more than the Ichiban Party. Maybe it's because it had Saeko and Seonhee in it; maybe it's because I felt Kiryu's additional story had more meaningful and interesting moments past that split (Ichi's was good, but it was better before...) It's hard because, obviously, in a game where it's a send-off to a huge part of the series in Kiryu, any protagonist would, but it sucks because I would've loved more Ichi characterizations than just the whole marriage debacle. Chitose was a bright spot, though. I remember feeling a similar way for 0, in which Majima's side of the story was much more interesting than Kiryu's.The whole marriage thing was, for sure, one of the weakest parts of the game. I just don't see why Ichi and Saeko have to have a romantic relationship when Saeko literally mentions that she enjoys that Ichi and the party treat her just like everyone else in both 7 and this game and that she's not interested. I'm really glad it didn't put the two of them together, but the ending is kind of ambiguous. Ichi, you idiot. I do understand the whole Eiji ending. I personally don't forgive him, but it's 100% Ichi's personality to reach out to him, so I get it.FINALLY Seonhee is playable! YES! I enjoyed the fact that there were three playable women with much more jobs and interesting storylines than before. I loved Chitose, Seonhee, and Saeko, but I still wish there was more to them, that there were more female characters, and that freaking jobs weren't gendered in this game, like 7. Why? I don't understand!? I did love that the women can and do enjoy things like the hostess clubs, finally! Better handling overall, but it's still a Yakuza game... Please, please, be even better with women in 9. I'm begging RGG.I finally got into Mahjong! I love Mahjong now! Karaoke is amazing as always. AWAKE and Honolulu City Lights are two of the best songs in the series. I love power metal and city pop. Baka Darou is fantastic and way better than Baka Mitai. Crazy Delivery was pretty fun. I didn't really do Dondoko Island, though. I am planning to, but it's not really my interest. I like Animal Crossing, but not really the building aspect... Miss Match shouldn't have been a thing. I don't like those types of minigames (though it's better than the previous similar minigames.)  Sujimon, I don't care for it, so I didn't do it.The music is SO good. When I first heard "Funk Goes On" when I went to Kamurocho, I lost my mind, and the remix of "Receive You" in the Millennium Tower was so good, along with so many of the other songs. The theme song "The Invaluable" was very good too; I added it to my playlist right after I finished. They even managed to turn the annoying Sujimaru song from 7 into such an amazing remix that I actually prolonged the fight this time! Many times through the whole game, I was prolonging fights just to hear the music, which is always a great thing about these games.It's ultimately a love letter to the series, and I thoroughly enjoyed that as a massive Yakuza fan. Everyone who worked on it, thank you for making this game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great sequel to 7 and concludes the loose ends of the story in a satisfactional manner. I fully recommend this game to anyone how enjoys a story-driven (J)RPG.(+) They improved on the turn-based combat of the previous game. There are more synergies and interaction with various debuffs/buffs and combos now. The new classes with Hawaii/vacation theme are fun and quirky - you can beat up goons with frozen tuna, squids and your surfboard as Aquanaut, The desperado is great as well. Having two seperate parties, one in Japan, one in Hawaii motivates you to experiment with different team composition. As does the skill inheritance system. The story is, for the most part, well thought out.(-) The fact that they have decided to put New Game + and two playable classes behind a paywall is very disappointing. The new minigames Sujimon (aka lame pokemon) and Dodonko Island (Animal Crossing). Aren't particular interesting, to me at least. Also, DLC rewards are unnecessary cheat codes for those modes and make them trivial. Combined with how the combat acutally breaks when you are too high leveled (spamming strong spells mindlessly) you should just get and play the base game. The additional big swell dungeon adds only small slice of life cutscenes that aren't even voiced in a boring, monotone dungeon package.All in all, I had a good time, I enjoyed the story and especially the characters. Kasuga is just a fun, goofy and good-hearted dude. I can't wait for the next game in the series. (9/10)

_childDocuments_.review: This game is such a masterpiece. The story is brilliantly written, the performance of the characters are quality, the world is bursting with stuff to do. I'm relatively new when it comes to the Yakuza/Like a Dragon world, having only played Yakuza: Like a Dragon, and Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth. I really enjoyed my first go on LaD and knew straight away I had to get this too. As of writing this review, I have just completed the main story. I cannot stress how engaged and hooked I have been on this since it was released.I am a massive fan of the turn-based style of gaming, and that's what brought me to the game in the first place. IW adds so much more to the way you fight from LaD, with the addition on the movement and ability to make use of the environment around you. Then on top of that, you have the follow up combat and the chance that party members will do extra attacks for you. There's so many jobs to choose from and by using the skill inheritance, you can cherry pick skills from other jobs to make your experience even better. Hawaii is captured so well, the people, streets, beaches. I think they handled changing the setting well and in played a major part in telling the story right. They made the dungeons a lot better in this game, there feels like more of a challenge on each floor and it now feels more rewarding. I will definitely continue playing this game now I have finished it. I bought the DLC (which I know everyone is hounding at them for due to NG+ being locked behind it) so there's even more I can be doing now the games done for me. This game is a 100% must buy, provided you have played the previous one first!
