_childDocuments_.review: As my playtime might suggest, I thoroughly enjoyed this game. As a huge fan of Y7, my expectations for this game were sky-high and it delivered. Pros:-Combat is vastly improved from Y7, and I already adored the combat in that game. Being able to move around and chain attacks is a game-changer.-Beautiful locations, and gone are the blurry textures from Y7 (taxis/ATMs for example)-Characters and dialogue are still second-to-none. -So much high quality content. I was shocked when I had passed my final playtime in Y7 and I wasn't even 3/4 done with the story. Dondoko Island is a major highlight. I spent over 30 hours on that alone.-One of the best soundtracks in any game I've played. "Bodybag" is one of the best fight songs to grace my ears.-The new jobs/classes are all fantastic and varied. You can play however you want and be successful with any party setup even into the late game.Cons:-The story is a big step down from Y7, which is a shame because it starts out so strong and ramps up from there. I was amped up for an explosive finale, but the last few chapters feel very rushed and unsatisfying. It feels like the writers were running out of time or something. After how wonderful and well-earned every emotional or tense moment in Y7 was, this was a major disappointment. I was left wanting much more.-Drink links (with a couple exceptions: ) are a step down in quality from Y7. -Combat is way easier than Y7, with the exception of the two optional boss fights and a couple street bosses, I rarely felt challenged or in danger. I only actually got a game over one time the entire game, and it was very early on. And I was very careful to not overlevel - I made sure to do every street boss and dungeon below or at the recommended/fair challenge level. Of course this meant I was overleveled for the story fights, but unfortunately you can't have it both ways.-It's far too easy to become overleveled without even trying. In future games I would prefer a system where any strong or story enemy you face (i.e. not random street mobs) never drops more than 2 levels below your party's average level. This would keep all story moments, street bosses and dungeon fights fresh and interesting no matter when you challenge them.-New Game+, an additional dungeon, and several achievements are locked behind a $20 DLC. Just like the last game, 2 jobs are also locked behind DLC.-This is a personal preference, but I preferred the handcrafted dungeons of Y7 over the randomized ones of this game. Although like I mentioned before, the final boss fights of these dungeons are excellent, especially if you go in underleveled. It's a fantastic and thrilling challenge, and the most fun fights I had the entire game.This may make it seem like I have more complaints than positives, but that's not the case at all, it's just easier to talk about the things you'd like to see improved in the future than it is to endlessly fawn over what you love. If you liked Y7. you'll love this game. If you like good RPGs, you'll love this game. Despite a few shortcomings compared to its predecessor, I still 100% recommend this experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this franchise and regardless of how good this game may be, I feel obligated to leave a negative review because of these absolutely obscene DLC practices. A total of $158 of day one DLC for a $70 single-player game, one of which being a $20 DLC for the post-game dungeon and something as basic as new game+, a feature that has been part of the franchise since 2006. What is wrong with you Sega? I thought you learned from the backlash when you pulled this in Japan for RGG 7 since it was included for free in the international release, but it seems I was wrong.I know I may seem like a bit of a hypocrite for buying the game anyway, but I couldn't just not play the next mainline entry in one of the favorite games series. I also only bought the base game and did not buy any of the DLC, and I never will because it genuinely disgusts me.Edit now that I've finally finished the game: Not gonna lie, this was probably one of the weakest entries in the entire series, and definitely the worst mainline game for me. Even without this egregious DLC, this would probably still be a thumbs down for me. I have no clue how this is the highest scored game in the series (according to critics, but who cares about critic scores anyway).The story is without a doubt one of the worst in the series. It had some initially interesting ideas, but they don't really amount to anything in the end and the overall plot was pretty boring, uninspired, and just poorly written. Ichiban wasn't exactly the smartest guy in Like a Dragon 7 but he wasn't a total idiot either and was a very likable character, but I feel like in this game he acts a lot dumber than he used to and acts way too forgiving for his own good.  The ending was also not satisfying at all, and most of the new characters were not very memorable or well developed, especially the antagonists.  Like a Dragon 7 had a FAR better story with much better characterization, and that's really saying something considering 7 had that ridiculous "mirror face" ass-pull. The Daidoji was alright in Gaiden, but in 8, it's one of the worst and most inconsistent plot devices I've ever seen. The combat is also still some of the most boring turn-based combat I've ever played.It still feels like the brawler combat of other dragon engine games, but with very basic turn-based JRPG mechanics just slapped onto it. This time you can move party members around a small circle during turns, but positioning in this combat system still sucks. The way all your enemies and allies randomly walk around between turns just makes things extremely inconsistent. Now that healing and support skills are just AoEs instead of directly affecting every party member, someone may just walk outside of range and refuse to come back. Or maybe an ally will walk in front of an enemy attacking someone else like an idiot and get themselves hit. It just creates a lot of inconsistency and contributes to why I think this game has bad turn-based combat. It feels like they wanted a grid-based combat system but forgot to actually implement the grid itself. It is also good to see QTEs return after their absence in Like a Dragon 7, but they are kinda jarring since the game is turn based now, and they really lack impact due to the extremely small damage you're rewarded with when succeeding at them.And just like in Like a Dragon 7, every single fight still just boils down to stat checks and spamming the most damaging attacks you have over and over and over again until you win. Nothing more is ever required, or even makes a noticeable difference. You never have to think about conserving MP either because of the sheer abundance of MP items you can have, free HP and MP refill locations during every dungeon, free MP refills every time a character levels up, and the fact that you get a sizable amount of MP back every time you perform a normal attack. Every fight was honestly just boring. Little to no thought is required for your party composition and battle strategy, no mechanics that act as double edged swords to keep things interesting such as the press turn system in several Megaten games or smirk from SMT IV, pretty much the only thing that matters is levels. Hard and legend difficulties further drive home the fact that the only thing that matters is levels. They don't actually increase difficulty and require you to be well-prepared and use smarter strategies like a good turn based game would; the only thing they do is increase enemy levels, and can only be chosen on new game+ because it would be impossible on a fresh save.Much of the side content just feels boring and bloated. There's a few good substories here and there, but the biggest ones, Dondoko Island and Sujimon battles, are quite bad. Dondoko Island's gameplay is unfulfilling busywork, and Sujimon battles are somehow even more boring than the main game's combat. The stories attached to them are basically rehashes of Like a Dragon 0's business and cabaret side stories that have lost all their charm and originality.It's also just laughable that they actually think $20 is a reasonable price for the "master vacation" DLC. The new dungeon is just a bunch of re-used enemies and bosses, and it's the only feasible way to get to level 70 for the last "base game" achievement, plus achievements for the "Big Swell" and new game+, so they're basically trying to force completionists to buy this overpriced trash that was cut from the base game to be sold as day one DLC. And I'm sure I don't need to go into detail again about how disgusting it is to lock new game+ behind this $20 paywall.I really hope whatever RGG makes next is better than their last few games. It's not a good sign when two out of their last three games are what I consider to be among the worst in the series, with the only decent one being Gaiden (which I also still have some issues with such as how piss easy it is and the complete absence of new game+)

_childDocuments_.review: This writing in this game is so good that it actually sures up some plot elements of Ichiban's previous adventure. Kiryu's story arc in learning to rely on his party members is touching and extremely well written. I had initially lost faith that the main story for the latest entries in the series could even be well-written after Yakuza 6 and Yakuza: Like A Dragon. And it's clear that the writing team has finally understood the qualities that actually make Ichiban a great character, his optimism and heartfeltness, bordering on naivete, is precisely what makes him so charming and lovable.The gameplay in this is a huge step forward from Yakuza: Like A Dragon. The changes they've made to it compared to the previous are incredibly useful for quality of life as well as adding strategy and depth to how the combat plays, whereas before it was pure luck whether you would happen to find yourself standing near a weapon to attack with or that enemies would align themselves in a way that's beneficial for your special attacks, now with the ability to reposition your units in a radius around where they decide to stand, the gameplay is much more tactical and rewarding. Which is precisely the change I wanted to see and even noted in my review of the previous entry.The changes to the job system are also very welcome, in the previous entry you had specific skills you could acquire from each job, now you're able to customise exactly which skills you would like from each job that you've levelled. It's a small change but one that makes a big difference to the things you decide to level and when you decide to switch jobs.Kiryu spends a lot of time in this game reminiscing about the events from prior games, and when I look back over the series with him, it inspired me to go back and re-play all of my favourites in the series to re-live the journey.

_childDocuments_.review: It's truly hard to review this game.It's fun while it lasts, the gameplay's rather decent and all the side activities are at least interesting timesinks. But story-wise, it's the most disappointed I've felt with a Yakuza game so far.Nothing you do ends up mattering in the long run, including the stuff that you'd really expect to. None of the characters really grow in any way. The story sets up some interesting plot points, all of which fall flat by the end, with huge plot holes being left open, and none of the things that would interest long-time fans end up getting resolved. After finishing it, I had never felt more empty and frustrated with a Yakuza game before.The balancing is quite terrible too if you engage in the side activities. It feels appropriate at first, with some enemies in some areas being too strong for you. However, optional dungeons become available like halfway through the game, and after playing them for a while and completing one, I levelled up so much that the rest of the game became a joke. I would finish most non-dungeon fights with a single area attack, and defeat bosses (including final ones) in like 3 turns max. At the same time, the game fully expects you to engage in those dungeons, as they're only way to make enough money to buy or upgrade the highest level gear.And with that in mind, I have no idea why it's called 'infinite wealth' other than because they wanted to do something cool with the '8'. There's no moneymaking business activity here like there was in 7, and I fail to see how any other meaning of the phrase would fit in with this game's story.So all in all, I'd say get this on a sale but don't bother giving it too much of your time. If you enjoy all the side stories in those games and the weird characters you meet in them, that part of the game will probably please you. But as far as the main story and character growth, it's probably the weakest the series has ever been.For those of you who have played the game, let me list my grievances.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth is one of the most ambitious games in the series. The game gives you so much content to enjoy and the story lasts long enough to keep you occupied for a very long time. I've recently finished the story after putting almost 70 hours into the game, with around 50-55 hours contributing to the main story alone.  This is my 2nd favorite Like a Dragon game overall and it is a major step up from the game's predecessor (Yakuza: Like a Dragon), which is definitely saying a lot. To start off, the story is simply amazing. Yes, it is the longest story the series which can be a turn off for many people, but I'm glad that the story never really felt boring at any point. Sure there are some tasks in the story that detour from the main premise, but there are only a few of them and only serve to quickly introduce you to other side objectives (the Dondoko Island side business is the exception). The twists and turns keep you on the edge of your seat and you keep wondering if everything will turn out fine for the heroes of this story.  Pretty much all of the games exhibit the same feeling out of the player, but I find that Infinite Wealth brings it to a much more significant degree, especially given the challenges and stakes leading up to the finale. Another reason why I enjoyed the story much more is because of how much it advances the character growth of our main protagonists, especially Ichiban. If YLAD helps to introduce the relatively new protagonist and face of the series, then Infinite Wealth is the game that solidifies Ichiban as a character worthy of being the main protagonist going forward. I really admire how much growth Ichiban gets throughout the story, especially his willingness to give people a chance to change for the better. It has helped me develop a deeper appreciation for the character. On the other hand, I also am satisfied with the ending Kiryu's arc and how RGG helped to give his journey a proper conclusion and closure. I've been playing through each Yakuza/Like a Dragon game for a few years at this point, and the game does a great job allowing you to reminisce on things that have happened in Kiryu's journey. I think it is also good to mention that you don't need to play through every Yakuza/Like a Dragon just to enjoy the game. However, those who have had the opportunity to experience every game are in for a nice treat when they begin Kiryu's section of the main story. Part of me would've wanted more from the reminiscing aspect of the game, but the game does a decent job giving Kiryu the spotlight one last time.   Combat is also an improvement over YLAD. It is still a turn based system, but they implemented new features to make this feel more active. This includes giving your character the ability to move around in battle and dealing slightly more damage, and of course, Kiryu's Dragons Resurgence ability. These new features help to put more strategy in the moves you choose. The only downside with the combat compared to YLAD is the fact that some ultimate moves have been nerfed. For example, in YLAD you can use an ultimate move that hits everyone while the same move in IW will only deal damage to those nearby. It's not a huge downside since you can move our character around, so I wouldn't call it a major complaint. For side content, there is simply so much you can do. From the substories, to the mini games, to Dondoko Island, to Sujimon, IW will spoil you with so much. In my playthrough, I managed to get almost all of the substories finished in one playthrough and I spent a surprising amount of time doing the Sujimon side quests. I never really gave Sujimon much thought in YLAD, but that changed in IW when they introduced the catching and battling mechanics. I don't have any complaints with the side content, and I am glad that they introduced new side content at a steady pace, something that I had problems with in YLAD. That sums up my main thoughts on the three core parts of each Yakuza/Like a Dragon game, and it is reasonable to conclude that this game delivers a very enjoyable experience. $70 is a big price for a video game and it is understandable if that is a steep price to experience this game. Personally, for the experience and the amount of time I spent playing this game, it is worth the price. However, a sale would definitely make this game much more worth it.

There are important and emotional scenes with Kiryu, but these aren't game-ruining compared to Ichiban's spoilers. (I love Kiryu-chan too, but... Based on what I've watched and played so far, this game is definitely one of the best games I've played in the past decade. _childDocuments_.review: I'd just like to give anyone who is thinking about buying this title some points to consider.But first: a warning for players. Real ... uh ... surfers use a game pad. The game doesn't really clarify that. It's much more enjoyable that way.A) Avoid spoilers! It is almost impossible to get any information about the game without receiving some massive spoilers for the plot, especially if you are a fan and already know most of the previous titles. And if you play games for the dramatic build-up, the intriguing story lines and the plot itself, you will have to be very careful.- Even the promotional material that RGG themselves put out openly tells us about one immensely important storyline and how it will develop (the video about the bucket-thing). I would have wanted to experience that while playing the game. Now it has already lost most of its emotional impact.- Also, steer clear of the discussion board. On Steam, it is filled with trolls and disgruntled players as well as some well-meaning idiots who openly discuss crucial plot points that they also put into the titles.- Look at the DLC at your own risk. If there is a costume set, the images and descriptions will inevitably tell you which characters will be (playable) in the game.B) I would not recommend playing this as your first RGG title. The main reason is that the game becomes much more enjoyable if you know the story so far.- The RGG games have a strong tendency to self-reference older titles and pick up old storylines. It will not be impossible to follow the game if you haven't played Y0-7, but many side-stories may not have any impact on you and may even seem a little pointless if you do not know the background and lore that is connected to it.- At least play "Yakuza 7: Like a Dragon". That title basically was to the rest of the series what the "Saints Row 3" was to that series. With the new protagonist, everything became much goofier and over the top, even in the mini games. And Ichiban is basically a joke character who developed a lot over the course of his first story. If you don't know that journey, you might find him to be an irritating character. It's a bit like a renowned comedian whom you know well making a risky joke versus a complete stranger opening your very first conversation with one.To really get the most "feels" for your buck, I'd recommend ...   - Y0 to learn about Kiryu's, Majima's and Nishikiyama's past (and some more basics).   - Y1 to learn why Haruka is so important to Kiryu.   - Y2 to learn about a love interest that has not come up in any of the other games yet (the title is really good for other reasons as well - some of the best mini-games and side-stories). Honestly, I guess that even some experienced players may scratch their heads if she comes up in this game.   - Y3 to experience the connection between Kiryu, the Morning Glory orphanage and his    relationship to the kids there.   - Y4 and 5 to get a bunch of exposition about a buttload of important characters.   - Y6 to find out how Kiryu ended up in his current situation.   - "The man who erased his name" to know what happened in the kind of big time jump between the events from Y6 and Y8.- It's better to actually play the games, but you can also read or watch a plot synopsis or playthrough.C) Keep in mind that there are quite a lot of very angry people around right now. Some are genuinely and rightfully aggravated fans, others are just trolls feeding from the frustration. I can understand those fans, actually.- This game has a lot of bridges to cross. It continues the story of a new protagonist who is a way different character from the mostly stern Kiryu. That means that the game itself has a tone that is vastly different from all the earlier titles. And many fans seem to have an issue with that. Though I think that they got a little tired of Kiryu's story, they would have preferred a successor whose character is similar, thus keeping up the same atmosphere.- This game uses Denuvo, an anti-cheat, anti-piracy software that does nothing for the players and very little for the developers, as can be seen in the abundance of mods and other tools readily available for other titles. What Denuvo does is invasively scanning your computer, using up your resources and potentially damaging some of your hardware over time (minor damage, apparently).- If you prefer the English dub to listen to ambient conversations or just to look at the action instead of constantly reading subtitles, you might want to mute the sound (or switch to another language) when you play the karaoke mini game. I do not think that the English voice actors in this game are bad, but most of them are horrible singers - and not even enjoyably bad, as you would expect in a karaoke game.D) Don't worry about the DLC for materials and stuff. Game is grindy, as most RPGs tend to be. But the grind is completely bearable. I was a little suspicious at first that you might not get to complete any weapon upgrades or building jobs and that you would crawl through level progression without that costly help. But I'm doing perfectly fine.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth (aka Yakuza 8) is an A++ JRPG masterpiece.It is somehow even better than the last Like a Dragon game, which is quite a feat.PROS- Excellent story, as usual for any Yakuza game.- The new characters especially grew on me. Tomizawa, Chitose, and Yamai were some of my favorite new characters in a while.- There is so much variety of minigames and gameplay, its unbelievable. This game goes above and beyond.. Aside from the usual golf, batting, cards, majongg, etc... there is a full featured Pokemon clone game, a full featured Animal Crossing clone game, and a random Dungeon Crawler. Each one of these can keep you entertained for many hours, and damn near could have been individual releases on their own outside of this game. - The job system has been improved on since the last game. More jobs and more combinations.- This game is loooooong. 150 hours if you do a majority of the content. Where most long games you at some point 'just want it to end', I never got to that point in this game. It was fun and captivating from start to end for me.CONS- Day one DLC... a cardinal sin. The DLC adds 2 jobs, an extra dungeon, extra pokemon, extra island visitors, as well as new game + and increased difficulty modes. Its quite a shame. At least the base game is so content rich that you probably won't miss the DLC if you chose not to partake. That and if you do choose to partake, the DLC is pretty substantial.- Hearing "iTs NoT a ShOw, ♥♥♥♥ HeAd" over and over and over again when you are detected by enemies.- You need a ton of items to upgrade weapons, and you need weapons for every job. Sometimes you are limited from trying new jobs simply because you don't have the needed items to prepare equipment for it.- - The camera in the dungeon crawler minigame made me motion sick on more than one occasion. Also in the Animal Crossing minigame, though to a lesser extent.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth initially was very interesting, however as the story played out, it began to become more and more predictable and the story did not seem coherent after some time. It seemed as if the story was just loosely conjoined ideas and having the crew go from point A to point B and reacting to whatever happened next.The actual gameplay is good, pretty much similar to Like a Dragon, I can't really recall any improvements to the mechanics besides some new classes and abilities.Having played all the mainline titles, the story for this game definitely is on the weaker side, which is incredibly disappointing considering all of the build up. The pieces were there for something great, but unfortunately it fell flat. The story became such a drag I unfortunately stopped playing during the climax of the game. It's strange considering JUDGEMENT and LOST JUDGEMENT probably have had the best stories in the series and the story for Gaiden was pretty good as well. Speaking of the JUDGEMENT series, some characters from that game make a cameo in Infinite Wealth...for absolutely no reason, I don't even think they say anything. They're just there for the fan bait and it felt pretty shoehorned in, incredibly distasteful and it was highly distracting from the game.My other problem with the game upon reflection is the overuse of re-using assets and animations. I get that it is funny to an extent, however Like a Dragon is now one of SEGA's flagship titles, I do not think there is any more excuse for re-using the amount of assets that they do. That being said, Hawaii was a great addition and was refreshing to explore a new worldspace.I unfortunately cannot recommend this game given the issues with the story, the $70 asking price for the BASE game, and the fact that NG+ is still locked behind an even more expensive version of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth aims to build upon the foundation set by Yakuza: Like a Dragon, and in some ways, it outdoes its predecessor. Ichiban and his party mostly retake center stage, and they're no less endearing here than back in 2020, accompanied by a few well fleshed-out newcomers. Kamurocho and Yokohama are still explorable, but the bulk of the game's action is set in Honolulu, one of the best cities the series has seen to date, a delightful and authentic but still warts-and-all depiction of Hawaii.  Combat sees a number of relatively simple changes that make it much more dynamic and flexible. On other hand, while it's very nice to bring Kiryu back for yet another "one last time," this time tying up several outlying loose ends, he does overshadow Ichiban in the game's final act to the story's detriment. In addition, Ichiban's own substories rely a little too heavily on returning bit characters just so happening to be in Honolulu at the same time Ichiban is, and most of these characters are less endearing this time around.Nonetheless, the series I insist on still calling Yakuza remains strong with this newest outing, and I hope Ryu Ga Gotuku Studio can continue to keep up the quality.

_childDocuments_.review: LAD: Infinite Wealth was a blast to play from beginning to end and it was what I hoped a sequel to LAD would be like. Its combat is far more engaging, the scope of the world is twice as big thanks to the addition of Hawaii, the new characters like Tomi and Chitose are easy to get behind, the side content is overwhelming, the music is outstanding, and we get satisfying payoffs from both Kiryu and Ichiban’s stories. Before I played this, I heard a lot of negativity about how the game is sold to us and how Kiryu is treated in this entry, but the latter is the best part of the game’s story for me. I remember how pissed people were that NG+ was locked behind $20 DLC when it was free in every other game in the series. I didn’t care about NG+ but when I reached the end of the game, I had completed all of the base game dungeons and I expected some post-game insanity like the True Final Millenium Tower in LAD. Well that’s behind the same paywall and there wasn’t nearly as much effort put into it. The entire game can be completed without ever entering the post-game, which left a sour taste in my mouth despite how much I loved the rest of this game. Overall, this is an incredible entry into the series as long as you reserve your expectations about endgame content. With that summary out of the way, I want to highlight what I liked most about LAD: Infinite Wealth.COMBATInfinite Wealth’s combat is easily the most engaging turn-based combat has ever been for me. You quickly learn the new mechanics, like positioning yourself to hit enemies into allies or other enemies or making the most out of hype attacks, and it nearly becomes instinctual. There is much less menu surfing and it is satisfying to pull off wacky combos thanks to this game’s physics. The best part of the combat is Kiryu’s playstyle where you switch between his iconic modes and pull off blazing heat actions. The reveal of his hype meter allowing him to fight as if he was in a standalone beat ‘em up entre was incredible and it was at its peak when fighting the three legends. His job-related special moves were awesome too. All of the Pound Mates are new and the most powerful ones are a joy to watch, Akiyama and the Hostesses especially. While I was overall satisfied by completing the 6 dungeon levels in both Ijincho and Hawaii, the journey of completing them was still very repetitive. Their final bosses, the Amon clan and the Michio Rangers, were difficult but not nearly as much as Amon was in the previous entry. The real highlight of this game is what we can do outside of the combat.SiDE CONTENTMost of Infinite Wealth’s new side content is in Hawaii. From substories, to drink links, to greeting everyone you see, to selfies, to photographing streakers, to using a dating app, to playing a Pokemon ripoff, to Yakuza Crossing, this game has an overwhelming amount of fun stuff to do. My favorite substories had me helping a kid with his lemonade stand, giving Nancy a mate, using diaper particles to replicate snowfall for a dying woman, and taking on the giant Roomba twice. There aren’t as many substories as there are in most Yakuza games but they make up for that with Dondoko Island and Sujimon battles. I was never a big Animal Crossing guy but Dondoko Island had me hooked. Funny story, I was watching the show Shogun at the time and Ichiban does the same war chant that Torinaga does, except it’s to hype up his co-workers, not to start a war. The Sujimon battles were less satisfying but I am still glad I pushed through them. Hawaii’s setting is a breath of fresh air and hearing English when I least expect it always made me uncomfortable. I also had a strange experience where now that I was using U.S. dollars, I was way more frugal since I knew exactly how much they were worth, unlike Japanese yen. Despite everything I said about Hawaii’s side content, Kiryu’s side content was far more impactful. At first, you can go around Ijincho and Kamurocho to find nostalgic settings players will recognize from all over the series. Then, Kiryu has substories with people from his past like the OG hostesses, Pocket Circuit Fighter, Kashiwagi, Komaki, and the Munan Chosept guy. Those were excellent, but the real stars of the show had Kiryu come across important characters from his past with Date’s help. Besides Akiyama, he cannot meet any of them, but hearing how he affected them was very emotionally stirring. I teared up a bit with Yuya and Kazuki’s visit. By the point you reach these in the main story, Kiryu doubts his past choices and thinks his presence in everyone’s lives harmed them in one way or another. For so long, his title as the Dragon of Dojima was depicted as a curse, but now we get to see how it was an inspiring symbol for many. The main story’s largest critique against Kiryu is that the Yakuza have harmed more than helped and he’s a huge part of that. He made selfish choices to help them through conflicts or to escape responsibility. He made mistakes, but that doesn’t mean he didn’t change people for the better. I’m glad this game highlighted that both the good and bad can be true. While there isn’t much gameplay in Kiryu’s side content, it fleshes him out more than most of his games even do. SOUNDTRACKLike always, there are plenty of bops in this game. Defiant Charn came out of nowhere and ever since, I have danced to it while making meals. Impregnable Triangle and The Four were hype as hell with a hint of finality to them. The remix of Brutality sounds like Unwavering Belief’s child. The return of Judgement sung with Kiryu’s new bro was so exciting see at last. On top of that, we got a sequel to Baka Mitai that no one even knew to ask for, Baka Darou. This song made me realize that Mame’s appearance in Yakuza 5’s Baka Mitai wasn’t for comedic effect but to represent Kiryu’s entire life as an adoptive father, as it is in Baka Darou. Receive and Believe You represents Kiryu’s change from being a lone wolf to wholeheartedly accepting his friends' help, and it was a great raid theme. Finally, the perfectly titled The End of Denial felt so right as a final boss theme for Kiryu. It sounds like a realization and a coherent looking back. I also have to give an honorable mention to the original version of Funk Goes On which plays during combat in Kamurocho. I never played the original Yakuza 1 but I still had nostalgia for this song so it hit me like a truck when I first heard it. STORYThe way I feel about Infinite Wealth’s story is a bit complicated. On one hand, Kiryu’s story is incredible, side content and all, but on the other, Ichiban’s story just feels like business as usual. This is not a bad thing, but I feel like there is some growth missing in this game. Despite this, the only part of the game that gave me chills was when Ichiban was taking punches from an angry mob to protect Eiji, and he made a genuine smile without ever throwing a punch back. Moments like this are why Ichiban is great as a static character, he just needs to have his values challenged a bit more. The same can’t be said about Kiryu’s side of the story. On top of what was already mentioned, he also struggles to accept help or relay responsibility to someone willingly. Even to the very end of the game, he struggles to see his life as his own or to accept help from his closest friends, which I appreciate as a difficult flaw for him to break from. That brief cutscene where the four yakuza legends all let loose in the Millennium Tower as Kiryu huffs and puffs while his bros pick up his slack was peak fiction. With all this said, it doesn’t seem like this is Kiryu’s ending, more like a hopeful window to his future. He is free in the mind and he finally took back his name in the small way he could. For once, I hope this isn’t the last we see of him. He is so close to getting over that insurmountable hill.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game from start to finish and it's an all-timer as far as the series is concerned. That said, it's not without its flaws. Some of which could have been easily avoided. Talking primarily about the combat here.They much improved that, but some of the same kinks that were in 7 are still in here. A common point of frustration was that enemies can move when it's not their turn, which makes planning difficult sometimes. There's some other snags here and there that all boil down to it being a little unpredictable in ways that aren't fun sometimes and probably not intended. It's much better than in 7, though, even if it's a little easy if you do a lot of the side content (which you should, it's a Yakuza game.)Speaking of which, as most people have realized by now, the side content is a hefty chunk of the game that a lot of care is put into in these games. This goes so far that some of them have storylines that are continued throughout the games. This game does some Pokemon and Animal Crossing type stuff for some reason. The sub-stories and the other activities are pretty fun in this, as they usually are. Karaoke has more songs than it ever did before. Unfortunately, they didn't bring bowling back yet, so I'm afraid, this entire game sucks, sorry everyone. Either way, you can play as much or as little as you want, but you clearly should engage with it.I'm not sure what they are doing but they seem to have hit a stride when it comes to writing stories. I loved The Man Who Erased His Name (and I recommend you play that before this.) Obviously, this is highly subjective, I heard people with opinions to the contrary. I think a lot of it hinges on how much you care about Kiryu, since he plays a big role in the story, at times taking away top billing from Ichiban to a point where you might as well consider them joint main characters. This didn't really bother me that much since I care about Kiryu and some of my favorite stuff in the game centers around him. I do have some more specific criticisms regarding even the handling of him, but since I want to keep this spoiler free I won't get into it. It's nothing that takes away from the story as a whole though, it just seems they missed an opportunity there, but I'm hopeful they won't botch it later.Whatever they do with 9, I hope they can improve the combat further and let Ichiban breathe a little more next time. And bring back bowling. I don't even care that much about bowling but if it's not in that's just giving me bad vibes, you know.

_childDocuments_.review: BE CAREFUL, THIS REVIEW CONTAINS SPOILERS ABOUT THE STORY.I really really wish Steam gave us an option to give a mixed review. Beware, I'm going to be very critic in this review, and a lot of people will surely disagree with me. But keep in mind I'm not saying all of this to be hateful, but rather to try and give better pointers to a series I hold dear to my heart.So I've been (and still proudly am) a huge Yakuza fan. I've played all the mainline games and most of the spinoffs (only missing the psp ones and Dead Souls) and I can say without a doubt this is my favorite videogame series along with the Souls lineup of games.Since I've yet to write a review for any of the Yakuza games, one might wonder "why this one in specific?"Well, I think it's because I've never been more disappointed with any other games in the series than this one.Let's start in order though. I want to start by saying that this review is meant for both veteran players like me and new players who might have played only a few of the more recent Yakuza titles.The good things first about this game. Yakuza 7 introduced the RPG combat system to the series, much to everyone's shock, and imagine the big surprise when we all found out how well balanced, fun and engaging the combat was. Luckily, they kept that same engaging formula about the combat, while adding some new mechanics such as movement and combo attacks that certainly give new twists to fighting bad guys on the streets. The graphics are simply spectacular, the Dragon Engine once again shines brighter than ever before and the character models (along with facial animations) look realistic and credible. Honolulu is a gem and it's been very fun (and relaxing at times) to take walks around the beach and the majestic buildings.Skills, weapons, classes and poundmates function the same way as in Yakuza 7, which is not a bad thing. Most of the new classes are very enjoyable (Kunoichi and Samurai are very fun to toy with) and offer good variety, same goes with the new poundmates (although I think they are a bit too expensive and too scarce).Now for the "mixed" part of the game: the side content. I'm mainly talking about the two big side stories (Sujimon Training and Dondoko Island) and the substories. All the rest such as Hawaii Photo Rally is kind of irrelevant honestly.My biggest gripe with the side stuff in this game is how badly it's spread out during the game. During the first few chapters you get basically nothing to do apart from following the story. Then you start getting into the main side stories a bit before Kiryu goes back to Japan and right there the game starts bombarding you with tutorials and side content while you try to wrap your head around the Sujimon basics (which boils down to a very, very, VERY gacha ripetitive fighting minigame) and Dondoko Island. Then once you reach the middle point of the story and start getting into the second half of the game there's basically nothing left for you to do (if you've finished both side stories and completed all substories available up to that point). One could argue that players can make their own decision to finish everything as soon as it's available or spread it out during the story, but I think the developers should have just followed Lost Judgement's way of doing a side story (basically by not making players binge-playing the entirety of the side content of the game in one single chapter).Now to get more into the two big side stories. Sujimon Trainer was pretty fun overall; repetitive as hell but short enough to not make you fall asleep. And the comedy skits were on point during cutscenes.As for Dondoko Island... good lord Sega never do this again I beg you. I get they wanted to pay homage to two pillars of japanese gaming, but I found Dondoko to be so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ boring and repetitive. I'm very biased since I'm not a fan of those games, but the game itself forces Ichiban to stay on the island for like 30 minutes before you're allowed to get back into the main quest. And since it's an Animal Crossing reference, guess what you have to do? Break rocks, trees and open up spaces, put stuff around, raise the island level, invite people etc. etc. etc.I feel like the game really didn't need Dondoko Island, especially if I start thinking about the extra time they could've gotten from scratching this idea and working on something else. People are gonna love this mode, I did for a while, then I realized how needlessly dragged out it is, and just wanted to move on.And here comes my biggest disappointment with this game. The story.This is straight up what makes me want to give the game a thumbs down. The story is terrible. But it's not the kind of terrible you immediately notice,no; it's that kind of story that keeps you interested for a while, until you realize how much potential it's missing.First of all, I might be delusional for saying this, but I have this feeling that they wanted to go for "anime" style storytelling and dialogue-writing with this game. The whole prologue makes me think so. They went with this long ass quest to find Ichiban the right suit and topics for his date with Saeko, only for him to botch it by proposing to her. The whole thing feels like a scene taken out of a slice of life anime. I totally get Yakuza 7 was going for that "best friends forever/nakama" feeling, but I feel like the dialogues were much more genuine there than here. And this pattern keeps being a plague for the whole game.The whole story itself is not even that bad, my main issue is how awfully they've handled the main antagonists. They literally pop out of nowhere and the game tries SO ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ HARD to turn them into Kiryu and Kasuga's nemesis. Ebina made some sense, although his backstory is only told at the end of the game but by then he was already the main villain so "oh well we just keep going with it i guess". Bryce is straight up absolutely garbage as a character. He has no motive other than "conquering the world and being the lord of the criminal underworld mwahahaha". He has no interesting trait, he doesn't even respect the Yakuza tradition of having amazingly strong and buffed final bosses, he's just an evil dude with two guns. His whole cult shenanigan could've been such an interesting plot point but they decided to water it down to just him and his stupid army of NPCs with no names and no characterization. Yamai is the only good villain of the game, and he's not even a real villain in the end!Finally, a question to whoever finished the game: who do you really think the main character is? Kasuga or Kiryu?When I finished the game (and during the second half of it) I realized how much importance the game gives to Kiryu and his past, the ties he wanted to close and the people he loved. His dreams and his hopes, and more importantly his regrets. Kiryu is a main character with actual depth. His story does actually come full circle at the end of Infinite Wealth.But Kasuga? What the ♥♥♥♥ does he do during the game apart from acting like a retarded shonen MC? Basically all he does is trying to keep up with Kiryu and not letting him down, then he can't keep up and ♥♥♥♥♥ up, feels like ♥♥♥♥ and only at the end manages to win thanks to the power of friendship. He meets his mother and has almost zero time with her, gets constantly tricked and manipulated by Eiji only to excuse everything at the end, looking like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ One Piece episode.Kiryu got much more attention from the writers than Kasuga did, and while I was happy to spend more time with Kiryu and put an end to his story, I can't let this slide. This is supposed to be Ichiban's game, his story and his development. And to me it felt like Kiryu's last chapter, with Ichiban as a side character.Also ♥♥♥♥ SEGA. It's criminal to lock NG+ and difficulty settings behind a 20 euro paywall. And the extra dungeon is a copypaste from the normal dungeons. Don't buy the DLC.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not great to lock NG+ behind an extra or higher purchase. That's in poor taste and Sega can suck a fat one over it. It's also not great for there to be Denuvo for seemingly no reason.So with that established, let me tell you how I'm, yet again, wholly confident that RGG is ripe for a blossoming future.Let's start with the bad: The main red line running through the story is... not amazing. And I'm talking about the core story here. My biggest gripe with it is that a V-tuber is being used as a device to spread insider info and misinformation. Problem is that this element is not explored or used in any interesting way. There's no delving in V-tuber culture, simply nothing interesting comes from that part, which is a shame, because the Yakuza series tends to never let an opportunity like that lie to immerse the viewer in something that they may be less-than-familiar with. So all in all, it seems that a V-tuber was used because... it was hip with the kids? The way it's being used here, you could literally replace it with someone wearing an Anonymous mask or a shadow in front of a camera with a voice changer. It feels cynical.The twists and turns in the main plot also only really happen because "X actually lied to your face and deceived you and you're an idiot." a couple of times. It's one thing for Ichiban to be gullible, but like... everything relied a little too hard on Kasuga taking everything in good faith. Not to mention some of the villain's motivations are... questionable. "I hate this thing so I actually joined it and worked my way up and destroyed it from the inside while really it was ready to up and die by itself anyway."That's it, that's the complaints, everything else is great. Kiryu's unquestionable significant arc is massive for anybody who's been through the wringer with this through his seven games. I mean, the fanservice (of the normal sorts) is . It's a great longwinded reward for anyone who's a fan of the series. It doesn't end in a tearjerker like it did in Gaiden, but it still felt bittersweet and beautiful how his arc ends in this game. Yeah no I'm not spoiling anything here, sorry bud.Ichiban's arc is... actually non-existent? It should be a complaint, but it's clear that Kasuga's role in the story has always been as a nexus, something where others wrap themselves around and grow from. He starts naïve, and ends naïve but with his familial matters resolved. He's not being played as the hero who needs to grow strongly and change, he has a surrounding cast for that. Some might not be super happy with that, but I feel it helps put the player in his shoes. You always know where Ichiban is at on a matter. He's hopeful and he has no quit, and he'll stick up for anyone. My guy even has that Goku perk to him where a good chunk of the enemies he starts out with eventually end up on his side. Tell me that's not admirable.Thankfully, for the lack of growth Ichiban has, his companions more than make up for it. We've already covered Kiryu, but even the old team all have their own things to grow through. Life didn't stand still for them, but no matter what they all have their devotion to Ichiban. Because with every game, granted you've gone through the wringer for them in their personal arcs, they become better people. The same goes for the new additions as well, who are no slouch either. If anything, Erik and Chitose are the main focus of the team. One gains a level of courage that almost matches Kasuga's, and the other grows a heart of a tremendous size. You see their growth, how Ichiban's unwavering trust and faith in them changes them, and it's really lovely to see. Seonhee barely has an arc to her, but it's still a rather adorable one. Who knew the Queen of Ijincho's underworld was such a fangirl?Mechanically, it's about what I expected. RGG never fails to improve on their formula. Just look at every Yakuza game in release order. Every game that had something less desireable about it, found it fixed or at least touched on.Y3 had enemies that blocked too much, while having a moveset that'd slowly grown a bit stale. Y4 has multiple protagonists with their own movesets and juggles start to become more of a thing, or in the very least you have answers to blocks. Eh, well, except for Saejima's first few fights, but we'll gloss over that now.Y5 became exhaustingly long, despite which the time to focus on the five protagonists felt too short for each. Y0 reduces it to two protagonists who are beautifully fleshed and written out.And Infinite Wealth's no stranger to these improvements. Y:LAD jobs made characters feel rather samey. A breaker on Ichiban felt similar to a breaker on Nanba. The only way to bring some skills from one job to another was to overlevel the job, and only the skills the game was set to enable for that. There was very little interaction on positioning and litte importance on  you hit the enemy.Now, any unlocked skill can be brought along to another, as long as you've got the slots for it, which increase with character bond. Some characters have a clear bias towards other jobs, and the UI makes very clear what job benefits what sort of playstyle, unlike Y:LAD where it was easy to miss. You can move your character around within a certain range, and basic attacks while the enemy is knocked down or close-by will do extra damage. And if your bond is high enough, being close to an ally can get you a free combo basic-attack, or even if you knock the enemy into an ally. You have so many more options to maximize on the sensible x-factor these character have over their enemies: their sense of team-work. Or something something power of friendship.All this to say, if you play quick, you will benefit with opportunistic base attacks. If you play slow, you can take a more tactical and methodical approach, with optimal positioning to boot. It feels good to manage these high damage maneuvers because of the effort and practice you put in.If I were to gripe, I'd say that the choice of weapon upgrades feels a bit too lineair for most of it until the the end, where you often end up with a choice between either the statistically strongest weapon, or one or two variations of a slightly weaker one with interesting side-effects. Even though you can invest materials in a weapon to raise its stats, generally nothing will come near the final weapons strength-wise. It discourages early experimentation when you know the weapons you invest in will become nigh-on useless after a time.The inverse sort of happens with gear. Armor pieces boost stats, but usually the ones you'll keep on are the ones that have interesting side-effects, even if they're four or five grades below the best you've got now. A mid-range helmet that prevents stun? Even grade seven pieces with no effects have a hard time beating that. The accessories have a somewhat easier time of it, as they're rather clear-cut and most of them are there for the effects, with only some just existing for their stat boosts, of which they tend to be interesting at least, but not all too exciting. There's no armor that makes you autoblock bullets. Boy, that sure was a fun one to have in YK2.Other than that, if you know the Yakuza series and you know the Like A Dragon series, there's really just one major question you have to ask yourself:Well, guess what.If that sounds like a good thing to you, and I know it does to me, then this game won't disappoint.

_childDocuments_.review: Ichiban and company are back, baby! If you liked Yakuza: Like a Dragon you'll probably really enjoy this.TL;DR - Other than the scummy NG+ issue, the game is phenomenal. 10/10The story isn't quite as good as the last game, but it's still very touching and has a lot of humor along the way. I do like what they did for Kiryu, but I know longtime fans of the series tend to be divided on this. Since I only came into the series with the last game, I don't have the attachment to him that die hard fans do. I really do miss the crazy pervy humor of the last game (there isn't as much this time around), but it's okay. It's not a deal breaker.The game runs very well at 4K and is well optimized. I didn't come across any bugs in my playthrough. No crashes to report. Combat is more or less the same as the last game, with a few added mechanics. Exploration operates the same way. You will play between Japan and Hawaii after a certain point in the game.Much like the last game, jobs return here. Some of the last game's jobs return while new jobs also enter the picture. The nice thing is the power creep isn't locked behind jobs this time around, but more behind character levels, so now there's a reason to try and play any job you choose other than just for the sake of grinding job levels to min/max (if that's your thing). You can also carry over any skill in the game so long as you've unlocked the job and the skill, and your party members' bond levels are high enough to hold slots. You can only carry over a few skills at a time, but these can be swapped whenever you visit a Alohappy booth.Now let's talk about that famous elephant in the room: NEW GAME PLUS. Yes, I agree that the way they handled this was very scummy. It should not be locked behind a paywall. To add insult to injury, it wasn't handled well in-game either. Not everything carries over right away, and part of that is your companions' gear. You may be locked into a fight that's extremely difficult because it's time to recruit your companions, but they're using entry level gear and can't do anything to bullet sponge enemies or take harder hits. Hopefully that will get patched out (or maybe it has been already? I haven't played in awhile) soon.Overall this game is really solid and I really enjoyed all 134 hours. I'm sure at some point I'll do another playthrough just because I love Ichiban and co. so much, but for now I've got other things waiting in my backlog. Highly recommended! 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon Infinite Wealth is a huge sprawling JRPG thats absolutely drowning in side content and things to do while also refining and enhancing the turn based combat system that was introduced in Yakuza 7. And while I had a great time with it and as much as I love Ichiban Kasuga and his wacky adventures, the plot of this one did leave a little to be desired for me at least.Pros first though: the game is absolutely massive with so many side activities and sub stories in the grand tradition of Yakuza games. And some of the new mini games introduced are great, like Sujimon league which is stripped down Pokemon game where you catch weirdos and make them fight other weirdos, its wonderful. Or Dondoko Island, which is basically Animal Crossing where you take over renovating a run down island and turning it into a five star resort. It's simple, enjoyable, a good moneymaking tool, and a smart use of reusing assets on the devs part. And other more traditional activities such as card games or randomized dungeons for grinding. So if you're concerned about length when buying games this one's got you covered, it'll keep you entertained for a long time.The plot continues on from Yakuza Like a Dragon where Ichiban and his friends are living their lives when things get turned upside down and are thrust into an international conspiracy spanning both Japan and Hawaii with Kazuma Kiryu coming along for the ride as well. The story is pretty typical Yakuza faire, fighting underground crime organizations, twists and betrayals, the fate of Japan hanging in the balance, etc. But it does give us the player an excuse to go to America for the first time ever which is a breath of fresh air for this series.And now for the cons, and following from the previous paragraph I did have some problems with the game's plot. Kiryu's arc I found to be well handled and the themes of finality and not having much time left were compelling and acted like a celebration of his entire saga up to this point. And without any spoilers the ending I think was handled very well and a nice sendoff to the Dragon of Dojima.As for Ichiban's side of the story though is where most of my problems lie. Ichi is the same lovable dork as he was before and he did have some nice emotional moments, but it did feel like a lot of the side cast got kind of sidelined. Aside from Saeko, who's relationship with Ichi is a prominent part of the narrative, Nanba, Adachi, and the others really don't get many good moments and are relegated to this game's equivalent of Social Links. And while I liked the new characters like Chitose and Tomizawa they didn't get quite as much play as I would've liked, primarily Tomi. Also I found the villains to be kind of meh as well, one of them being a generic charismatic cult leader type who was kinda boring. All in all the plot had a handful of good moments but did leave me wanting, idk where they're gonna go for LAD 9 but I'm still keen to see.And another negative is the rather scummy way Sega handled the deluxe editions of the game, such as locking NG+ to the more expensive editions. It sets a bad precident and should've been included in the base game and I feel like that's worth mentioning.But in conclusion Infinite Wealth is another banger from RGG and despite my criticisms is still very much worth playing for anyone who loves this series like I do, or wants another massive JRPG to consume their entire life

_childDocuments_.review: Worst Yakuza by farStory peaks at chapter 2, and gets worse with each chapter (There are 14 in total)The gameplay is boring beyond belief, heal->wait 3 minutes for your turn again-> repeatThis game throws SO MANY MULTI ENEMY FIGHTS AT YOU ITS ALL IT DOES, even the bossfights have like 8 minions you have to clear first.The story itself has so many plot holes and builds from the top down instead of bottom up, there's no foundation and you just get random info dumps and predictable plot twists. A side character who has 2 cutscenes crying made me chuckle and that was all the emotions this game made me feel. Gameplay:Like mentioned earlier, boring, time wasting out the ass, and no real advantage to perfect blocking you eat like 80% of the damage anyway and status effects still hit even with it.Weapons that are fit for the state of game you're at aren't easily provided, you have to literally open youtube or google and search for them, hidden in a tiny tiny shop for exorbitant prices and then you are forced to grind a overleveled dungeon because location enemies scale with your progression so if you're past a certain cutscene in the story EVERY ENEMY YOU WILL FIGHT WILL BE IN PINK STATE (above your level so get ready to heal and waste turns).Animations are great and all and feel powerful BUT YOU LOOK AT THE HEALTH BAR AND YOU DID LIKE 5% of their health.You also get locked out of the world mid-chapter fights so even if you can save, you cannot do anything except replay the entire segment if you feel you've gotten into the chapter early because again there's no obvious upgrade path like the other yakuza games.  So you have to either stick to eating simulator with one attack every 5 turns or say goodbye to like 90minutes of game progress so you can go upgrade your weapon.RPG was the worst thing to happen to this franchise even IF 7 did it really well. 8 just forces game hours by boring powerscale. And as mentioned earlier the animations are beautiful.Side content+stories: Only saving grace, this world is full of funny and well written stories and minigames, some which you expect from the franchise, some that you dont. Uber Eats crazy taxi is fun but i don't think its enough where you should pay full price for the game regardless.Overall rating 3/10 - DON'T PAY FULL PRICE. IF you skip this game you're not missing out

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, my favourite Yakuza game on par with Yakuza 1.The story is just so damn good, and it has been good in every single mainline Yakuza game.But it just felt so special this time and the stakes were so high.I do wish they did a bit more scenes (and pre-rendered some more), some better quality of life and stuff but I'm just nitpicking at this point.It truly felt like a love letter to Yakuza fans who have played since the beginning, through every single game.If you want to play this, highly recommending starting from Yakuza 0 all the way up to Infinite Wealth (Don't forget to play Like a Dragon Gaiden before Infinite Wealth if you decide to play every Yakuza game, it's pretty important and canon, even though it's technically a spin-off). It's worth it and every single game is a treat of it's own. I don't think there was a single mainline Yakuza game that I disliked. I liked Yakuza 3 as well, despite what others say about it.If not, at least play from Yakuza: Like a Dragon (Yakuza 7) so you at least can see things from Kasuga's perspective (New protagonist).But man, it felt like I was praised for every minute I spent enjoying all the previous Yakuza games.On top of that, they made the previous turn-based system even better. And Kiryu's ability to straight up break the turn-based system is incredible and super fun.Makes you feel like you're playing the old Yakuza again. (or I suppose, Yakuza 6)Alongside that they made the turn-based system feel a lot more active.There's a lot more opportunities to attack and a lot of fun & interesting ways to beat up your opponents.It felt like I was playing a Persona game, I'd say it was akin to that level of turn-based combat but with even more freedom with what you can do and how you can position yourself.I'll always miss the old action combat system, but if they sprinkle it in like this every now and then and let me taste the oh so sweet nectar of the gods, then I'm ok with it.Especially when the turn-based combat itself is this insanely good.Although, all the micro transactions are a bit much.. including locking some main content behind a paywall separate from paying for the game..A bit scummy on their end and they've been pushing it for the past few Yakuza games, but they keep delivering in such a ♥♥♥♥♥♥' awesome way that, you know what, ♥♥♥♥ you, and ♥♥♥♥ them.Take my money.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been a fan of the Yakuza Series ever since I first stepped foot into it with Yakuza 0 on console. With the transition of the name to Like a Dragon, I was honestly skeptical at first, but I knew i had to at least try it. Now with Infinite Wealth, this game is honestly a masterful sendoff to the Yakuza series name.The game-play is polished from the previous game with additional jobs, side-missions, side-jobs, and a plethora more.First and foremost, the story. I am absolutely impressed by how long and entertaining they kept this series going. This game in particular continues the story of Ichiban Kasuga while giving the chance to finish the story of Kazuma Kiryu. In my experience with games focusing on essentially two main characters, usually the focus is either extremely one-sided, or improperly balanced. However, with Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth, they had balanced the overarching stories masterfully. They balanced the seriousness of the story with the goofiness that we all know and love of the Yakuza series.Without spoiling too much of the story itself, this is essentially the last game we will ever see Kiryu in the main story ever again, given that he has cancer. This game properly gives him a standing ovation and sendoff later on within the story giving all of us a chance to reminisce and see almost everyone that Kiryu has affected in their lives.Additionally, I am amazed how they implemented Kiryu's fighting style that we are so used to as a game-play mechanic. It fits so well with his current condition. The story itself molds and mends wonderfully together with the game-play, which is an achievement in and of itself. Not a lot of games, let alone a whole series, can do that for as long as they did here.Onto the DLC... honestly, with how they implemented New Game+ behind a paywall/DLC was not the best look at all. It was honestly the possibly worst mistake they could have made as a whole. However, with the rest of the DLC, I can understand why they did this. The DLC itself has no story significance and can honestly be skipped without missing anything regarding the story as a whole. Most of the other DLC are either cosmetic items, items to help with crafting, items for the main side gigs, and music tracks, and a few other things. Most if not all of the DLC can be accessed during a single play-through, so I can understand why the implemented the New Game+ paywall. A New Game+ isn't really needed to experience this game to its fullest.Still, I will say that it was jarring to see that happen, especially from this series.However, overlooking that flaw, everything else is amazing. The voice acting is superb, the story is excellent, the game-play is phenomenal. Overall, it is a wonderful experience.I highly recommend this game to fans of the Yakuza series as well as newcomers who are on the fence about buying this game.If you want to wait a little longer until it is on sale, I would highly recommend that especially for any game.

_childDocuments_.review: ( full review with screenshots:  )At a whopping 127 hours by Steam playtime, Infinite Wealth is now the longest game I've ever played by a huge margin. It took me nearly 40 hours longer than its predecessor, and over 30 hours longer than it took to earn a platinum trophy in Persona 5 Royal. Whatever else you want to say about this game, you can't say that you're not getting your money's worth. The bigger question is whether this incredible level of time investment is worth it. Although this is in many ways a great game, it's harder than I'd like to say that it was 127 hours well spent. Let's start with the good news. The main story is well done, and you could probably get through it in a relatively normal amount of time for a JRPG if you're focused on it. It has some fun fights and a lot of callbacks that I'm sure are exciting and rewarding content if you've played Yakuza 0-6. The new characters are deeply integrated into the plot and have satisfying arcs. Honolulu is a fun city to explore and feels as different from Ijincho as you'd expect.A lot of the other things that were good in the last game remain fun. The battle system is still great, and made more so by new jobs. The music is great. There are some entertaining side quests, the minigames are gloriously stupid, and so on. You'd expect at least a few things that are horribly underdeveloped in a game this long, but everything is basically fine at a minimum. The bad news is that while nothing truly feels incomplete, many parts of the game would have benefited from more refinement. Although the minigames are fun, there are only a handful of new ones and there's nothing as crazy as kart racing or running a public company from the last game. Most of them, like the parodies of Crazy Taxi and Pokemon Snap are solid experiences that run out of new content after 20 minutes and don't have worthwhile rewards. The highlights are supposed to be Donodoko Island and Sujimon battling, which parody Animal Crossing and Pokemon respectively, but neither of them have the depth to reach their full potential. Dondoko island boils down to spamming buildings all over your island until you get the next cutscene, and Sujimon battling is almost entirely determined by who has the best rarity Sujimon at the highest level. Since each Sujimon only has one move and all moves do pretty much the same thing with different damage totals, there's little reason to anything other than mash A and occasionally swap for type matchups. You need to complete Dondoko Island and the Sujimon league if you want to complete all the quests, but they're each long enough that you could have finished an entirely different game instead. That was one thing in the last game when the minigames were as fun as many other full games, but in this case it really didn't feel worth the time. Sadly, the minigames aren't the only place where you get the feeling that the devs didn't get all the time they needed. The story rushes to make sure every major character returns, but several of them clearly have no reason to be back and barely play any role other than being present. The final battles at the end of the game are well made and difficult, but the evil monologues you're treated to reveal that the villains never really had any kind of coherent plan, which makes you wonder what the point of it all was and whether there was supposed to be more content that would have tied everything together better. It's all capped off by one of the main party characters not even being present for the epilogue and instead just getting a single sentence to explain what happened. It's not quite "and then everybody died, the end", but it's hard to imagine an explanation other than not having time to make another epilogue cutscene. At the end of the day, Infinite Wealth is a great game that just tries to do too much. RGG wanted to have a sendoff for Kiryu while also telling a new story on the scale of the last game, and they really should have picked one or the other. Although they do a better job of integrating those two very disparate goals than you might expect, trying to cram all of that into a game with anything resembling a normal runtime just means that nothing gets the time it deserved. It's still a good game, but I can't help but wonder if it would have been better as two separate games that each had a single goal. If nothing else, that would have prevented the need to break the cast up into two small parties and given you more flexibility to build your battle team. --------For more reviews, see

_childDocuments_.review: *I gloss over the combat and some elements which are retained from 7 to Infinite Wealth (Jobs, minigames), which are mostly refined, don't look if you don't want combat spoilers and the like (no story spoilers, besides a certain someone you'll know from previous entries getting only namedrops in regards to their combat functionality), I only go into some depth since I made this in just a few minutes, sorry if it seems a bit jumbled.*You must take more into consideration when it comes to your party members' positions, as there are now back attacks which you can only achieve while in the allocated perimeter of a party member and have them be behind an enemy. Perimeters can also determine whether alternate attacks for some "basic attacks" happen if you are shown "proximity bonus" (prime example is kiryu, applying to all of his styles, this is the case for back attacks too), with added combo attacks for mp gain on hits for involved members if you are near one when choosing to use a basic attack, granting more mp over a basic attack for BOTH party members rather than just one. Back attacks can stack with weapon attacks, causing every hit to be critical, there're also follow ups once opponents are in a ragdoll state, which don't stop at just a single follow up at times. Direction-based and area-of-effect attacks are displayed much better, allowing for more intricate approaches. Environments in story-based battles make use of barrels as weapons, exploding after use, and the like, all having their unique debuffs to apply when used on someone, or if they are rammed into by ragdolled enemies or attacks. Some poundmates can now also use multiple turns. Team members get their own super meters, combine all for a super attack, all coming with self-buffs. Equipment seems more diverse compared to 7, I had some fun mixing and matching. Jobs return with some changes when it comes to transferring abilities, as well as microtransaction-only jobs. Some previous minigames return, others don't. Fan Service is present as always, not being so outlandish in this case (at least in Kiryu's part), having also been tied to Kiryu's ability progression, I had no problem with this implementation, nor the new male party member and anti-hero, the other new party member to the franchise..? Not so much. Kiryu's functionality is certainly different from any other party member I've ever seen, even getting his extreme heat mode from Kiwami 2, 5, and 6 on top of his established styles, having their unique traits.The added depth onto the established Yakuza 7 framework makes it much more enjoyable, the story though, is a bit lackluster, although, however, is easily held up by the quality and meanings of the dynamic intros, not to mention the themes of the bosses. Easily one of the best turn-based games I've ever played, still don't support their recent decisions in Ishin and this with the transactions (paywalled difficulty achievements, seriously?), oh - substories not telling you what lvl you should be (should've added an indicator), I tried to fight some a bit too early, a 5 level difference is enough to make you quickly lose if you aren't planning for a relatively drawn-out battle fighting for your life every single turn. I shouldn't be punished for NOT rushing the story or grinding dungeons for every substory in the offset chance I happen to be underleveled for them, you'll probably run into this problem 4/5 times or so.
