_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Infinite Content. This is a perfect sequel to the last Yakuza. I like the idea of a Like a Dragon series that continues to focus on Ichiban while still creating games that feature Kiryu and Goro with their own playstyles. This game retains a lot of the same gameplay and features of the previous one, but with more depth and extras. Every 20 minutes you'll run into new gameplay mechanics teaching you about extra features and side stories. You can choose to complete them right away or come back to them when you feel ready. It can be overwhelming, but there's so much to do I feel that I'd get around to it eventually. Many of the issues I was concerned with in the last game are fixed here, and the area of movement during combat adds depth to the choices you can make in battle. The emotional moments feel well-earned and the dialogue is well-written. It's almost amazing to see a game like this still be made today. A 100+ hour, single-player, story-driven game with that bright Sega color palette, stuffed full of extra content and minigames - It feels like a relic from an age of gaming replaced by cut content made into DLC, microtransaction sales as a metric of success, live service titles, muted colors, and ultra-realism over cartoonishness. It's a game that puts fun first and gives you so many ways to enjoy the cities you're given to explore in.With that said, the recreation of Waikiki, Honolulu is incredible. I distinctly recognize hotels I have stayed at, beaches I have walked to, the Ala Moana shopping center I'd visit all the time. Walking down the street, especially by Waikiki Beach, there are so many high-end expensive businesses geared towards tourists. Most of the shirts I see are touristy Hawaiian shirts, and the one Ichiban wears is very closely similar to one I bought in Waikiki myself years ago, but I haven’t seen any traditional Aloha shirts yet. You can spot a good Aloha shirt by the shirt pattern matching across the front seam when it’s buttoned together. The food featured are perfect replicas of Hawaiian mainstays. And I'm learning more about the 1900s asian roots of Asian American Pacific Islanders. Both day and night feels so genuinely Honolulu. Fire spinning, luaus, surfing, all represented and embraced. It doesn't shy away from real issues of Hawaii like homelessness, inflation, and high cost of living.I know I'm going to be playing this one for a long time. I'm early into the game, but I feel like I've still only scratched the surface. If the last game took me 100 hours, this one will probably take longer. Only issue I have is maybe Kiryu's voice-acting, it doesn't feel as gruff and doesn't match his stoicism and sincerity. I know the VA is doing the best he can for Kiryu, but I don't think it's a good fit. I'd like it if there were more options for karaoke too, with the ability to switch between vocal language tracks without having to exit to the title screen. And maybe add a lot more animations and variety to NPC characters - I can never get over seeing two perfectly identical NPCs synchronize their movements with the exact same walk cycles and dances. There are also NPCs that disappear in the background of cutscenes which is unintentionally funny, but also distracting. With all the dialogue available it’s easy to miss important lines. There should be a Visual Novel-style log system that lets you view the last lines of text, like they have in Metaphor: Refantazio.So far it's a 10 for me, there aren't enough hard flaws I'm seeing to knock any points down from a perfect score. This is the most accurate recreation of Honolulu I’ve seen, which makes me think Yokohama and other cities featured may also be just as accurate. Funny enough I was sad to see Ichiban walking out of the airport without a lei. I didn't have very high hopes for this one going in, but I've been really pleasantly surprised. There are a lot of improvements under the hood from the previous game. I only hope they keep adding more polish. I wish they added a postgame setting to turn off encounters so I could walk around virtual tourist-style.Update: Having finished the game, the weakest part of the game is the story. It is very exciting, but there are plot threads that fall short and loose ends all over the place. Still, I hope the next mainline entry has a concise naming scheme so that I know which game is the direct sequel, and I hope that this next game continues to take us to new destinations with impressively accurate representation.

_childDocuments_.review: While I am vehemently opposed to and abhor the decision to sell NG+ as a DLC, I must acknowledge that Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth is among the best games I've played this year. The turn-based system has been expertly revamped, the traversal options enhanced to scale to the humongous map of Hawaii, and new 'jobs' (that determine the character's move set in the game) minigames added. We now have a fluid ‘combo attack’ system executed with a teammate, explicit ricochet mechanic, and back-attacks that provide 2x the damage when attacking an enemy facing the other side. There is some scope for movement, which can be used to align hits to leverage ricochets and back attacks. There is also a ‘smackdown’ feature to clean up low-level fights in a matter of seconds, saving us from the monotonous button mashing. The gameplay has been a major upgrade from 2020's Yakuza: Like a Dragon, and I congratulate RGG Studios for this feat.The story is great, as with most games of the franchise. Kiryu's stoicism and Ichiban's charisma present each other as Yin and Yang, with both characters alternating seamlessly and preserving the plot line across chapters. Ichiban's substories present the characteristic goofiness in each Yakuza game. At the same time, Kiryu's stories are an ode to the legendary character, reminiscing his life. Each interaction is masterfully executed, with the lack of words and inherent ambiguities lending a bittersweet and sublime quality. The ending is especially beautiful, and I thoroughly enjoyed it.I don't usually write reviews, but Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth has impressed me so much that I can't help but praise it for everything it did right. While the game occasionally felt like a chore to gain upgrade materials, progression was never overbearing and came naturally. Apart from the paid NG+ fiasco, lukewarm boss fights (especially compared to Like a Dragon: Gaiden - whose final boss was in a league of his own), and a few minor bugs encountered during combat, I loved this game through and through. It is a must-play for fans of this series, and it is still a great turn-based game that tries to do things differently than others.PS: I'd advise new players to at least go through the previous games' story before starting this one. While most of the story should follow from Y:LAD, certain side-stories, especially Kiryu’s, go way back (YK1 or Y0).

_childDocuments_.review: This game is easily my favorite of the entire series and the best game I've ever played. If you haven't picked up a game in this series and you enjoy simply just playing video games; you NEED to experience it. Preferably starting with Yakuza 0 and working your way to this point as it is extremely well worth experiencing everything prior to this game. The amount of improvements to the combat system from Yakuza: Like a Dragon is astounding. I was expecting about the same combat system in this game but they overhauled it tremendously for Infinite Wealth and it is an absolute blast to play; I didn't get tired / bored of it at any point. My final play time in the game after the finale was 107 hours (my highest yet in the entire series) and I thoroughly enjoyed every second of it; I'm not exaggerating. That includes me going through all of the side content in the game; and it was just extremely enjoyable to play, there legitimately was not a single thing in this game I did not enjoy. If I could give it a score I would give it a 10/10.It takes a LOT of hours of playtime in order to play every game in the series; however I genuinely would not take any of it back. I've never felt this strongly for any other game series / game I've ever played; it really stands out that much. Give Yakuza 0 a shot (it goes on sale pretty often) and I hope you enjoy the ride because it is very very well worth it to eventually arrive at this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 8 is a game that expands greatly upon it's prior entry, fixing and expanding upon the rpg combat and the available classes available to all characters. It's writing, characters, visuals, and gameplay satisfaction are some of my most enjoyed out of an RPG when it comes to releases within the last 10 or so years. Story cuts, as well as pacing face a number of issues at times. And it leads to small bouts of confusion, or even a sigh from you whilst you sit through a cutscene trying to figure out what's taken place outside of your vision. But if I'm being honest, I couldn't care less about those problems. In most games, I'd gripe and be upset about them to no end like any other unsatisfied consumer. But when I put over 200 hours into this game, and nearly every moment of it I wore a smile on my face because of Ichiban and his ridiculously hopeful worldview and attitude? Why should small problems cloud my feelings towards the product, I loved this game. I loved every moment of Ichiban forging new bonds with the people of Hawaii, and doing everything in his power to save every last person he's forged a bond with. Because he's lost so much already, that losing anything else. No matter how small, or unforgivable they may seem. Isn't even a consideration in his mind.It's idealistic, as well as foolish. Much like people enjoy calling Ichiban, but the reality is. If we could all be more forgiving, be more like Ichi with his unwavering hope, optimism and loyalty. I'm almost certain the world would be a better place. But, then again I'm talking in a review of a video game. Not some real life role model and hero. So, rather than continue to spout praise and how much I earnestly loved this game. Let's move on to my rating.Objectively, the game is a 8.8/10. For it's issues, pacing, and story cuts.But in my heart, it's a 10/10. The second that I've ever given to a game personally, and I only hope that my time playing Yakuza 8: Infinite Wealth has taught me to treasure the things I do have and do right by those I know so when they need a hand. They're willing to take mine, and come out the other side better for wear by my side.

_childDocuments_.review: Like others have said:Improved gameplay, slightly weaker story.What stands out most to me is that the difficulty feels better. The last game was pretty close to content tourism unless you ran straight over to the enemies marked as too high for your current level. Barring that, the fights that were supposed to be at-your-level were pretty easy and became more of a grind. Infinite Wealth seems to have changed that up, somewhat, and even the fights that are at your level sometimes throw a curve ball.The zaniness is also still present. Parodies and jokes around Crazy Taxi, Hawaii 5-0, Pokemon and more appear. Want to take part in a reality show at a mall? Engage in an underground Pokemon battle that uses real people? Sing Karaoke when you should be solving larger problems? It's all on the table for you.But the story is a bit disjointed. It kind of has to be, given that *you don't start immediately in Hawaii*. . Aside from that, the story also does, as others commented, shoe-horn-in a handful of characters that really don't make sense being present anymore. This was always going to be an issue when trying to have a more ambitious setting/game size, but it's also at times handled a bit clumsily, too.Beyond those things, yes, NewGame+ is in a DLC, though I feel like it's less of a problem given that the base-game is a bit more challenging.And further, there are certainly QoL changes, including the ability to skip/sim battles with enemies far below your level. That helps a great deal as you get further into the game, because you'll eventually be at a point where an entire zone is just  weak enemies that do nothing but halt your movement. So the skip/sim thing is a small but important addition.Overall, I think the gameplay is better, the setting/sandbox is bigger, and it's actually a bit more fun than the last game. But that's partly because I value gameplay over story for most games... if you are really attached to these characters at this point, and are here more for the story, then it's still a good game but be prepared to have a few moments of slight disappointment at times.

_childDocuments_.review: "This is a great game, just not a good yakuza game" part 2I love the franchise to pieces and I wish it was the best it could be, but god being a fan of it is frustrating nowadays.Long story short, if you like good games, ones that let you progress at your own pace, are wacky in a good way with a lot of really great moments, scenery, music - it's for you. Provided you like RPGs that is. Gameplay has been vastly improved over last RPG entry. Nobody can deny that the game is good and will give you a lot of bang for your buck, whether you're into tourist aspect, camaderie aspect or just storytelling of the franchise. Even the most lackluster yakuza story is a great story by triple A standards.If you're a Yakuza fan, there's a bunch of things that were incredibly frustrating or disappointing to witness. Some story elements, some things that weren't changed but definitely should have been and a bunch of missed opportunities to maybe right some wrongs that previous games neglected.I'll start with some positive things that I really appreciate about this title, including some that i could say about pretty much every game in the franchise:- Characters. They're always done extremely well, and this game is no exception. Yamai, Chitose, Tomizawa, Bryce, even lesser characters like freaking Gondawara of all people being actually a really great guy with a wholesome moment.- Music. They just never really miss. The credits theme was outright gorgeous.- General vibe. It's a yakuza game. Obviously just having a good time in whatever city you roam is practically guaranteed. There's many ways to interact with your own party and learn more about them as characters. The bond bingo boards were a good shout in that regard.- Remembering the franchise. For the most part, the whole "Bucket list" thing was honestly just wonderful. While the trailer already gave away some of the characters from the past that you get to see, the others were a very pleasant surprise, especially Yakuza 5 and Yakuza 6 reps. This is also a major step up in terms of how such thing was done in the past games. - Gameplay improvements. I maintain this franchise isn't one for RPG combat, and if you really wanted to force it into mainline series there are better ways to do it, but the system that they have now is certainly much better than the one from the previous game. Moving to line up skills, balancing of said skills, difficulty curve all have vastly improved, so for instance you don't have to grind to have a chance against a boss.Now that that's done, let's start with the low hanging fruit. NG+ being locked behind DLC is absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and everyone should be very much up in arms about it. It's a feature that was already in the standard game, but was stripped away for extra cash. I understand wanting extra money for a pretty expansive product, but have the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ decency to feature actual extra stuff worth paying for instead of something that should've been packaged to the base product.Story at times is absolute garbage. Please, for the love of god, Yokoyama, never touch omnipresent, all-knowing factions again.  Like the incompetence is just astounding, these things took me away from the game outright, stuff was on par with rubber bullets.The combat. Look, it's better, it's an improvement over what it was in last mainline entry and in any other franchise it would be great, but it just does not work in terms of what Yakuza was. Brawler installments were always a good mix of building tension and letting you release that tension, whoever the bad guy was you could do some brutal maneuvers against them that i hope nobody had a chance to feel in real life. Sure, as time went on there were some outliers in this, like Akiyama's air combos or Majima's shadow clones in his fight, but they were still used sparingly or were otherwise intertwined with actual grounded stuff. You just don't get that with the RPG system - shooting ink from a squid, swinging a giant fish - none fit the game's aesthetic for anything more than a one time gag (though in all honesty it's even infected brawler games, like the agent gadgets in Gaiden, the card superpowers in Ishin Kiwami and flying cutlasses and whatnot in the upcoming Pirate venture). It being turn-based doesn't help - until you make your move opponents are going to be shuffling about and yelling stuff, but are forbidden from attacking you. I would be a lot more open to the idea of combat style shift from brawler if it was more like FF VI for instance, where your opponents do move while you're taking your time waiting or thinking about next course of action. Granted, with DQ being the inspiration and the thing Ichiban's schizophrenia sees it's wishful thinking to expect adjustments that would heavily deviate from the original formula, but a man can dream.The game is also plagued by missed opportunities. Now, i'm not going to bash the studio for not getting more voice actors from past games to do stuff in this game, i know voice acting work in Japan is serious business and the fact they got Yamadera to voice Akiyama again was probably pricey enough as is. Instead, I'm going to focus on both voiced and unvoiced content that we got.Memoirs were great for the most part. A lot of characters were mentioned that I didn't even expect to see brought up again, but there were a plenty that were missing - Bacchus or Miss Tatsu, especially considering we did return to our Yakuza 0 combat styles, Mikio from Yakuza 3 (who helped with orphanage a ton - you'd think they'd mention him a lot more), Watase and any single person aside from Hanawa from Gaiden. The last part is especially odd with how he pretty much owes Tsuruno's funds his life at that point in time and how stellar storytelling was with Shishido for his final fight.Something that sort of relates to memoirs, but should be done more IMO are more passive mentions of characters - whether it's some radio talk show mentioning last Shinada game or police banner PSA to report to Tanimura regarding any problem in the Little Asia area, stuff like that. One moment in chapter 8 where Tsukumo and Sugiura make an appearance with 0 voice lines was a sweet nod and we really could use more of those.We now have some dynamic intros that involve characters other than Ichi fighting which is appreciated, but everyone disappearing for substories is something i thought would be fixed with the new release and it's disappointing that we didn't get there. It wasn't a problem when it was Kiryu alone trying to fix issues or solve problems, but now that you have a team you fight with you'd expect them to chime in, offer help or insist the group takes on some issue in particular, especially considering Ichi, who knows only the most basic of basics of English language, is in Hawaii, so you'd have his local companions act as translators for instance, or letting them take care of it all.I really, really hope to see some of what i mentioned in future releases, but hope is also what I had for prior titles. Still, I will love this franchise for everything that it does so well. We can meme about asset reusing all we want, but this franchise is probably the best case for it, the most justified one for it.

_childDocuments_.review: So, first off, the locking of NG+ and difficulty selection because of that behind paid dlc is pathetic, and is a horrible decision. Story has its usual RGG/Yakuza game pitfalls at points, but is overall very strong. It has what is probably my favourite turn based combat in any game out there. It has a varied high quality soundtrack, the characters are greatly realised and their interactions feel natural. I finished my first completionist run at around 149 hours-ish, and am now working on the big swell, a dungeon which has group interactions in between each sector. Its nothing mind blowing, but the extra team content with all the members present is dumb fun. It is, sadly, not voiced. I think its an overall excellent game, which is taking bold strides forward and in a very positive way. If you enjoy JRPGs, turn based combat and excellent companions, I think its a must.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I had a heart as big as Ichiban's to handwave all the faults of this game's writing.Many good things can be said about Infinite Wealth - a story about influence, the danger of herd mentality, redemption, and how everyone should educate themselves on how to acknowledge a world champion at the hater Olympics. The charm, wit, and batsh*t energy that can carry any single bizarre plotline. The lovely salubrious aura that keeps these tales one foot on the ground while their head stays in the clouds. They dare to go over the top but never get irreverent, they shamelessly do callbacks and references but never get too indulgent, they aren't afraid to look corny because they are confident in their own corniness. Everything is still here, wrapping Infinite Wealth in their arms, as sweet as fresh strawberries in autumn.And yet by the time I concluded Infinite Wealth, all I felt was a strange nothingness that never happened to me in any Yakuza game before. The song this game sang reached the newest highs in a few notes - Kiryu's life links subverting his approach to society, the writing and characterization of Yamai, and Ichiban's reunion with his mother are easily the best parts of this woefully distracted tale that tells us very few new things about our hero and the spotlight characters that it promised to shed new light on. Ichiban's character arc feels like a flanderization, a result of RGG Studio huffing their own hype and memes about him being the overlord of the Golden Retriever Clan, and while the main storyline managed to contrasts him against a cult leader antagonist which just makes sense thematically, it never tried to break any barrier when it comes to portraying Ichiban in any way that he... isn't. His goodness influences people and gives him the strength to prevail against abstract forces like hate and twisted allegations. That's who he is, his puppy eyes, big heart, power of friendship, and an unreal amount of altruism gave him strength... which was already established and told in a much more heartbreaking and heart-touching way in Y7, and what Infinite Wealth did is simply confirmed Ichiban's traits against people who he mostly had no relation to, and I simply never got invested in his journey this time. For Kiryu, his actions actively kept coming up and bit him in the ass. For Yagami, his existence in a much more sinister world gave his character tons of weight. For Ichiban, his tales are rainbow colored fairy tales that simply want me to feel good. Ichiban is a great person and I want a friend like him in real life, but I am genuinely not interested in another story that just reconfirms to me that Ichiban is a great guy who can solve world threatening matters with his doofus mannerism. Everything you love about Ichiban is still here, it's just that they also took out the bitter feeling of a life taken away from him, while making all returning teammates the same goofy buddies that lift Ichiban and Kiryu up and didn't even bother to actually settle Ichiban x Saeko relationship by the end.Maybe you have to forgo infinite feelings and infinitely well written antagonists to get true infinite wealth.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 8 has many ups and downs, but overall, it is a good game. If given the option, try to get this game of sale, as the $70 is overkill.For those who started with Y7, this story is most likely NOT catered to you. While Ichiban plays a prominent role in the story, this game focuses on Kiryu and his journey. Sticking to the positives, Y8 only improves upon y7's combat system. The job system is more engaging, and the ability to move your character before selecting moves was a much-needed addition. Kiryu's move set is entertaining to play around with. However, the grind to unlocking Kiryu's full potential could be better, The characters introduced in Y8 are a mixed bag; new additions to the party, like Yomizawa and Chitose, play a fantastic role in the story and have strong personalities that are hard to dislike. The best addition to the series is Yamai, of course. Yamai makes sure every scene he's in is captivating. His story development is some of the best writing in the game, as moments when he wasn't present felt dull. For the returning cast, their new drink links further expand upon their personalities and how they're doing after the events of Y7. My favorite character, Zhao,  The way I feel about Zhao's developments is the same for the rest of the crew, even Saeko. The sudden interest in making Saeko the "love interest" was a weird shift in tone. However, people claiming this game was a character assassination are exaggerating; they most likely didn't even give her a chance or think of it from her perspective. The story for this game is mixed. I loved the beginning and the inclusion of Honolulu. The new characters greatly help move the story along and help get the player accustomed to Hawaii. However, half of the story feels very dragged. I never really fell in love with Honolulu as I did Onomichi; I can't pinpoint why. Hawaii is a nice change of pace, and as someone who's played all prior games, I was interested in seeing how they'd cross the English and Japanese language barrier. Their handling of the language barrier was poor. So much so that it feels like the game was meant to be played in English. Besides the occasional "Engrish" moments, they sometimes play into the language barrier or ignore it; side-quests are the most guilty of this. The ending of Y8 was underwhelming.  Y8 makes me appreciate just how well-written Y7 was and how they introduced so many lovable characters while still making a captivating story for new and returning players.  I have more to discuss. However, I'm getting bored writing this review, so I'll add more later. Chao!

_childDocuments_.review: It's definitely my new favorite Yakuza game, with a stupid amount of content, and a genuinely great story. Having Ichiban and Kiryu both be protagonists works super well, and switching between them each chapter reminds me a lot of 0, which is a good thing. Moreover, the new Hawaii setting is great, even though using dollars as a currency in a Yakuza feels cursed.The turn-based combat has been drastically improved since 7. At the point it'd make going back to 7 feel like so much is missing. Just being able to move characters around in combat makes such a drastic difference. The new jobs are great, and everything feels satisfying and punchy.The new side content is even better. The business mini game this time around is basically Animal Crossing and it's super fun and silly. Customising the island with ridiculous decorations to boost your sales is prime gaming. Catching fish/bugs to fill out compendiums, and upgrading your tools is also a blast. Beyond that, there's also a Pokemon side mode where you have to collect 4 badges from different elite trainers. But instead of Pokemon, you use local homeless crack addicts to fight for you.The new exclusive characters are also great, 3 new party members, and all the old ones from 7 return (excluding Eri but she was optional anyways). Moreover, the story does a great job at tackling previous plot points from across the series. Past characters from Kiryu's life appear in abundance.Speaking of Kiryu, they do an amazing job continuing his character. His appearance feels a lot different, featuring more as a prominent side character, and for the first time, exclusively operating with a group. Which narratively makes sense, as he finally replies to those around him when tackling new threats. Ichiban is also great as always, having some of the best moments in the series.I'm going to conclude this review early for everyone's sake, but really it's Yakuza at its highest point in terms of quality, and the fact not everyone has played it is criminal. Ichiban/10(PS. Yeah Sega is stupid and greedy for charging for NG+)

_childDocuments_.review: My history with the Yakuza series goes all the way back to the first entry on the PlayStation 2 in 2005. Since then, many more games in the series have been released, and about as many shirtless brawls atop of tall buildings have taken place.Now, almost 20 years later the time has come for the latest addition — Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth, and I was curious as to how it would stack up.The previous mainline game — Yakuza: Like a Dragon was one that I was skeptical of at first, as it changed things up in a big way, perhaps most notably going from real-time combat to turn-based combat, along with adding various things most typically associated with the JRPG genre. However, the game quickly won me over, and so I had high hopes for Infinite Wealth.Infinite Wealth uses the framework laid out in its predecessor, and improves on it in several ways. The combat feels even snappier and more engaging than before. One of my favorite additions ended up being a mechanic called Smackdown, which allows one to basically win fights instantly if you're so much more powerful than the opponent that having the fight play out normally would just be a waste of time. It's a smart way of speeding things up a bit, which is thankful seeing as how Infinite Wealth is a massive game which will likely take most players anywhere between 50-70 hours to get through.Another thing that has improved is the difficulty curve. This was the biggest issue a lot of people (myself included) had with the previous game, which featured an incredibly steep difficulty curve towards the end of the game that felt a bit like running into a brick wall. Infinite Wealth thankfully is a lot better with this, and has a much more even difficulty curve. In addition to this, the game will often let you know what the recommended level is for progressing through the story.Storywise the game is interesting in that, unlike the previous game, it features not just one, but two leads, one being Ichiban Kasuga, first introduced in the predecessor, and the other being the legendary Dragon of Dojima himself — Kazuma Kiryu who's been the lead in the majority of the Yakuza games. As the story goes on, the game alternates back and forth between the two, and does so in a good way where neither one feels like they are being sidelined. The game also features a brand new Hawaiian setting. This feels like a breath of fresh air, and really makes Infinite Wealth stand out from the other games in the series, all of which take place in Japan. The overarching story in the game is interesting, though, I did feel that it fizzled out a bit in the third act of the game, and that some of the characters felt a bit underdeveloped.The series is no stranger to having familiar faces from the past show up. Infinite Wealth cranks the dial up a bit further and includes several fan favorites that longtime fans of the series have been clamoring for. While seeing some of these characters again is definitely nice, I felt that it was a bit of a missed opportunity, as many of these encounters are small isolated sidemissions that don't factor into the bigger story. At times it felt a little bit too much like cheap fan service.True to the series, Infinite Wealth also features a plethora of different sidemissions and minigames, many of which are a lot of fun. One of the highlights for me was being able to visit the arcades where one can enjoy some classic Sega games of yore. Or how about Crazy Delivery, an insane minigame inspired by Sega's Crazy Taxi which sees Ichiban going around on a bike delivering fast food.While not without its flaws, Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth is yet another fantastic entry in the Yakuza series, and one that that I would highly recommend trying out.

_childDocuments_.review: It's really hard for me to talk about this game because it's the first Yakuza title I've been very excited to play. In fact, I believe this is the game I've been most hyped for since Portal 2. Due to this, some disappointments might be bigger than they would be otherwise, and I've definitely learned that watching trailers is a no-no for this series, considering they show stuff from final chapter without any care.That said, it's still a very good Yakuza game, likely in top 3, but I think I've enjoyed it less than Yakuza 7.It does a lot of things to be a better game, with more polished battle system and a ton of little QoL improvements that make playing it a blast. In particular, I've really enjoyed that exploration is somewhat tied into levelling up with the addition of overworld bosses - unique encounters that will grant good loot and good exp. If you like exploring but not grinding, they are a GREAT addition to RPG formula as just beating unique bosses will keep you on the level the game wants from you most of the time.The story is probably one of the most simple for a Yakuza title, completely ditching insane conspiracies of PS3 era and focusing more on interpersonal relationships. No other title in the series spends so much time on slice-of-life moments, and they were all fantastic. That said, while the story is easy to follow and has plenty of good characters (Yamai, for example, being my favorite, with a great performance by Japanese DIO actor), the plot is fairly badly paced. First off, it takes way too long to start free roaming. While you do unlock Yokohama within an hour or so, it's pretty much empty, and only by around hour 6 of the playtime will you be introduced to new mechanics and side-stories.The actual story also kicks into gear in chapter NINE. Before that it's relatively aimless, with characters looking for a person they can't find and just drifting from place to place meeting new people. Again, certain scenes are great, but overall story decides to be good only after the midpoint. I'd also argue it's not as gripping as Ichiban going after right-wingers in 7, but when the aimlessness subsides it's still a really good time!It seems to me that focus on relationships that's also been boosted outside of the main story with a TON of voiced content might've been the reason for what's likely my biggest disappointment with the game: the lack of substories.The reason for Yakuza's success in the west, the side quests are a staple of the series, but with increasing expectation and more voiced scenes it seems there could only be so many, and unfortunately there are way too few: only around 60.60 might not sound like a small amount, but there are a lot of them that are story-required or are a part of the chain of 4-6 stories. Some only exist to introduce a mini-game to you and can't really be called "stories". For example, Sicko Snap or Crazy Eats minigames have a "story" at the beginning, but it's only there to unlock a thing, and doing everything in those mini-games will not advance anything past "You've unlocked a thing". Overall, I'd say, there are only around 30 substories that are unique, contain an ending, and aren't part of a massive side activity.While some stories are among the best in the series (Let It Snow might be one of, if not the best substory in the franchise), there are also some that are just bad. The series has seen its fair share of problematic moral lessons, but I feel they've always been relegated to comedic stories. Sure, you did help a sex worker reconnect with her pimp, but it was over pizza as a delivery boy cheered, so it was clearly meant to be extremely ridiculous! Infinite Wealth, however, has hits such as "forced to work as a sex worker? Go to jail!" which is presented as a drama with a good ending. The chain of bonds Ichiban has with a few female NPCs might, however, be the worst side-content in Yakuza, effectively having 5 or 6 substories where Kasuga is raped. It's all very cartoony, sure, but it's still a tired old joke about a woman overpowering a man. What sucks is that quite a few of those characters are pretty good, so ending their quests just makes them into a rapist. Cool. I guess I can only be thankful weird mixed messaging about sexual abuse isn't a part of the main plot much like one other series SEGA owns now. It's especially weird considering similar quests were in 7, but aside from the somewhat cringey finale just hinted at normal consensual sex.Side stories might be my big problem with the game, but side content definitely isn't. The game features some of the best and most involved side activities of any Yakuza title, two of which could be complete games on their own with a bit more polish:Sujimon - a name for enemies in the game - have now received a complete Pokemon facelift, and you're now able to capture and battle them in separate battles. It's an involved chain that also unlocks a separate class that can use your tamed weirdos to do spells. Catching Sujimon can be achieved through normal random encounters, trainer battles, a gacha system, or raids: specific battles that appear around the map that will give you a chance to snag a leader of said battle;Dondoko Island is an Animal Crossing-like with you having to catch bugs, fish, collect stuff, craft, farm, build, and manage guests. Effectively every asset from the series is here to craft and decorate your island with to make it into a resort, and it's wild how much there is to it, and how different it is from the main game. I was glued for it for hours at a time, and thanks to its progresive rewards that raise any bug/fish's price every few times you catch one along with tons of in-game achiements and rewards it always felt like I'm doing something. If there's one thing I didn't really like is that there are very few assets you can decorate with that actually fit - most will just turn your paradise into Kamurocho 2.There are other minigames too, of course: MissMatch for example is a culmination of all things sleazy in the series, asking you to create and edit a profile on a dating site, pick responses, and get a date with a hot girl while they keep sending you feet pics for chatting well. Racing games, puzzles, a few arcade ports, a friend system, randomized dungeons - this game is full of stuff. It doesn't feature as much side-content as Yakuza 5 did, which effectively was 5 or 6 games in one, but I'd also argue it's not as boring on the main story-side as Yakuza 5 was.I will say, however, that this game is not a place to start on. It's not only Yakuza 7: Part 2, but also yet another apology for botched Yakuza 6 ending with how it finally gives closure to Kiryu's saga. Due to this you'll be assaulted with references and things that won't emotionally resonate throughout big chunks of the story. However, for any long-time fan all of this is a treat.It's not a perfect entry and is unlikely to end up being anyone's favorite, but it's an absolute blast aside from minor hiccups that likely were due to developers creating a whole new map and a ton of assets.

_childDocuments_.review: There's just so much about this game that I hated that I was relieved when I reached the final chapter because I couldn't bare to play any longer. In the first few chapters, you end up being forced into a bunch of minigames and side quests that aren't even remotely entertaining. The dialouge in general just seemed to drag on forever but I'm not sure if the pacing is affected due to the game offering two additional voice languages or if it's because of the stiff in-game cutscenes that has weird pauses and animations in-between dialouge. The enemy encounters during free roam were also completely unbalanced. You'd either bump into higher level enemies that are two attacks away from wiping your whole party out or enemies that are so low-leveled that you're just one button press away from defeating them within seconds using the "Smackdown" option. And lastly (and without spoilers), the ending was trash. Basically everything was left open-ended. It's easily got the worst endings in the franchise. The only positives I can think of is that one, the soundtrack is fire. I bop to the Baracudda battle music on an hourly basis. And the JP VA for Chitose has a voice of an angel. Honolulu City Lights is easily one of the best karaoke tracks in the franchise. Secondly, the combat system is a huge upgrade from the previous game. It's a lot more fun compared to the previous game. My only gripe was wishing Kiryu's beat 'em up mode would last longer the higher he levelled up.I feel like this game was definitely overhyped. It wasn't nearly polished enough to warrant it's AAA game price tag. (Why were only 10% of the cutscenes fully animated? Why's the lighting so trash at night?). If you really liked Yakuza: Like a Dragon, get this on sale. It's not worth paying full price.

_childDocuments_.review: Infinite Wealth takes every lesson learned from 7, retools and balances the RPG elements to present a more engaging, rewarding, and streamlined experience. So many quality of life changes that prevent this game from becoming the slog that 7 became at certain points. Hawaii is a wonderful new local and I look forward to RGG recycling it for at least the next 3 games and 2 spin-offs.The worst most stumbling part is the previous care that was awarded to the English dub in 7 falls by the wayside here. All performances for this game were great, I especially loved the two new party members and hope they carry onto the next game. But, Yong Yea should not have been given Kiryu as a role so early in his VA career. He can do fine work, but they should have considered maybe another person who can consistently nail such a beloved game character, because his performance goes from middling to lousy. Everyone else also suffers for it, the previously non-tuned karaoke performances from 7 have all been auto-tuned and ruined. There was no reason for the VA director to undo parts of 7 that worked.New features like Dondoko and the other mini-games need a little bit of ironing out if they're going to be introduced into the future games. As they really started to drag toward the end. I liked them, but they were dangerously outstaying their welcome by the time I was done with them. All for 100% completion. Finally, the story. This story goes to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ odd and incredibly overblown places. I feel like they got far too goofy and are going to pigeon hole themselves into not being able to one-up themselves for whatever Kasuga gets up to in LAD:9. The resolution to Kiryu in this franchise was appreciated, but even for someone who played the other games and loves Kiryu, his presence here felt unneeded and like RGG can't let go. The torch had already been passed at this point and this game continued to them trying to figure out when Kiryu could logically distance himself from the mainline. Ichiban continues to shine through as the new protagonist and in the end proves just how beautifully written a character he is, but to a story that tries to dodge around giving him the stage fully.A must for Yakuza fan's and people who have gotten into the series via LAD:7.

_childDocuments_.review: It's impossible to dislike the Yakuza series, they're the essential Japanese games anyone must play at least once in their lifetime and the newest in the series Like A Dragon Infinite Wealth would've been at the top of the food chain if not for some story beats that I really did not like. 👍 +Amazing cast of characters+Phenomenal soundtrack+Fantastic gameplay mechanics👎-The last few chapters and the villains of the story were pretty meh-A bit bloated in minigamesInfinite Wealth continues where things left off from Ichiban's previous adventure, and now he's searching for his mom in Hawaii. This time around we get two protagonists, Ichi and the main man from the previous Yakuza series, Kiryu. You'll get to meet up with all your favorite companions from the previous game as well as new ones. Having two protagonists isn't something new to the franchise, however, I think this time around, they kinda of messed up a bit by sidelining Ichiban in favor of fanservice which was a bad decision. Don't get me wrong, Ichi is still great in the game and you'll play more as him than Kiryu, however, this is in regards to the main story and the last bits of it. I cannot go into details because it would be a massive spoiler, but I will just say that the way things ended, left me with a bit of a sour mood. It's not a tragic ending or the end of things, but it's because things just ended like "whatever wait for another sequel" which is the opposite of how all Yakuza games ended.. To add more sourness to the main story, the villains were extremely uninspired especially the Hawaii one. The entire Hawaii main quest felt like a massive side quest only to be sidelined by Kiryu's main story which mostly takes place in Japan. Even the way they handled Kiryu's "issues" was pretty lame. If it weren't for the great cast of companions you meet and some funny/moral side quests this would probably be at the lowest of all Yakuza main stories. Story rating: 7/10Just like the previous Like a Dragon game with Ichi, the game is turn-based in combat and features a lot of fun and not-so-fun minigames that I'll talking in a moment, looting, crafting, and everything you'd expect from a JRPG. There are a few improvements done to the combat compared to the previous game, such as more control over your actions and where you aim your skills and more companion combos. Furthermore, Kiryu's style also brings new mechanics to the turn-based combat which I'll let you discover for yourself. The only issue with this is that if you want the best of him you can't change his default class. Speaking of classes, or jobs as the previous game called them, this time around you acquire a different class through a traveling agency. It's pretty much the same thing, a different naming convention. You'll find some of the old classes you're familiar with such as Breaker or Chef, but some new ones as well that fit well with the whole Hawaii atmosphere, such as the surfer. The new classes and their ultimate skills are just as cool and funny as the previous game, no complaints here. You'll also get access to the summons feature, which felt a bit underwhelming this time around, cinematic-wise anyway. Crafting, exploration, and equipment also has improved a bit, but not by much. Now let's talk about the minigames. The Yakuza series are famous and infamous for their minigames, some are fun, some are average, and some are bad. Infinite Wealth has all your classical minigames from the previous game and a few new ones. The two most important minigames are the Sujimon League and the Dondoko Island.The Sujimon League is as you probably guessed it, similar to pokemon, but instead of pokemon, you use the enemies you encountered in the game, the sujimons as Ichiban sees them. It has some depth to it, each sujimon has its own type as well as rarity, you fight against other trainers, you evolve them, and it's all pretty good. The problem with this minigame is that it won't give you many benefits in the actual game other than towards a specific class you can switch to which wasn't that great. The other main minigame, Dondoko Island, will be your main cash cow. The problem with this one is that is ♥♥♥♥♥ boring. You arrive, forcefully, at an island, it's filled with garbage and your task is to clean it up and build it up as a resort. It's basically like Rust but a much worse version of it. You smash rocks, garbage, and trees with your bat, you collect the stuff, you craft buildings and other things and you place them on the island. However this process takes a lot of time and to fully complete it and reap the monetary benefits, it would take around 15 hours or more. Not only that, if you instantly hate it, you can't go back to the main game and you're forced to do it for the first hours or so. While you gain a lot of money from it, it was a massive tedium. I hated it. I fell asleep during it. Gameplay rating: 8/10As always, if you play Japanese games with English dub, I'm going to call you a mo-ron, learn to read. The Japanese cast is amazing, everyone does an incredible job voicing their characters, especially Ichi and Kiryu. Yakuza games are also famous for their insane combat songs and oh boy does this game have some amazing bangers. The music is awesome, one of the best in the franchise, and I'll just leave it at that. Audio rating: 9.5/10The Dragon engine they're using is showing its age in a lot of lighting conditions, especially in the daylight. It worked well in Japan due to lots of neon lights and whatnot, but Hawaii is quite different and at times the lighting looks quite weird. It's not bad, but it needs some improvements. The character models and most effects are great though. That being said, this engine is one of the few that runs absolutely perfect without any performance-related issues so a huge plus for optimizing such a massive game. The level design is impressive, Hawaii is massive and has a lot of back-alleys and paths you can explore. Verticality is still an issue in Yakuza games, but c'est la vie. They have at least improved the quality of the Dungeons a bit, but they're still boring to explore.Graphics, performance and tech analysis score: 8/10The game is big, has a lot of content, a great cast of characters, an amazing soundtrack, and fun combat and while the story is not so good this time around, do not let that dissuade you from buying Infinite Wealth regardless of its price.

_childDocuments_.review: My second favorite Yakuza game (Yakuza 0 is still my favorite 10/10 fwiw). If you're a fan of the series, then getting this is a no brainer. If you're new to the series, I'd recommend playing Yakuza 0 first, even though combat is totally different, because if you don't enjoy 0's story and content structure, then I don't think the Yakuza games are for you. If you do enjoy Yakuza 0, then try Yakuza: Like a Dragon. If you enjoy Like a Dragon, then you will likely enjoy Infinite Wealth. Obviously, if you enjoy 0, you could try other games in the series first, but time is finite and burnout is real, so I'd recommend my 3 game order.8 out of 10.

_childDocuments_.review: A very bizarre case of a game having one of the weaker stories in the series, and still being among the best purely because everything else is done well. The combat's a massive improvement over the previous game and adapts even more beat-'em-up mechanics to turn-based combat, but still stubbornly refuses to give even a semblance of important numbers and instead gives generic light/medium/heavy amounts for ability damage, and nigh-meaningless arrows for buffs and debuffs. Hawaii's great and full of quality ♥♥♥♥ to do, but the story's a very mixed bag and a large portion of the game will only be enjoyable to people who've played the series in full.

_childDocuments_.review: Great storytelling game. You fall right in love with the characters and the game is actually funny. The graphics are always really good with Yakuza games. I think you will like it and even though it is turn based its done and executed the perfect way so it doesn't feel sluggish when taking turns. Its action packed. _childDocuments_.review: Living up to the hype started by the original Like a Dragon, which twisted the classic Yakuza games from action to JRPG, was a tall order, in which Infinite Wealth delivers in some aspects...and falls short in others.Kasuga's first adventure was a really simple JRPG with a combat system with many shortcomings, and Inifnite Wealth has improved it quite a bit. I would say it still lacks some complexity, but there are some fun new features and jobs. It would say that while there is room for improvement, it went a couple steps further than the original.It lacks a quite a bit, though, in the narrative department. The strongest point in Yakuza games, since their inception, was the story and characters it introduced, each brimming with either charisma, or goofyness...and Inifite Wealth suffers from mediocre pacing and lacking characters. The main story is mediocre at best and besides a couple of exceptions (mainly Yamai, and maybe Chitose), new characters, both allies and foes, never really spoke to me. Side stories never really caught my attention and felt like they were in the way more than anything. I would say, the last two chapters are full of action and feel like a notable Yakuza game, but the rest of the story doesn't make a great job to build up to a rather decent ending. Kasuga's first adventure felt way more epic than this one.Technically-wise, it lives up to the standard of the series. Sound and dubbing (I'm talking original JPN voices here) are great, and graphics, are a mixed bag - as usual, there are great models for main characters faces, but environments, animations, and NPCs definitely could use some work. It is also a blatant defect that RGG didn't take advantage of a setting such as Hawaii to bring us more varied and beautiful, natural environments. Aside from an underground cave (a very short sector) and Honolulu's beach, there isn't really anything that would catch my eye.As for lenght/replay value, it took me about 80hrs to complete this one, which is more than lenghty enough. I conquered both legacy dungeons (funniest part of the game despite their greyish design, something that could change in the future) and did most of side quests. Mini games are a mixed bag here - there is a Crazy Taxi-esque minigame which was short but fun. Hopefully they bring it back, bigger and better. They could have reused the racing game from the original but chose not to do so, which is a shame, because the main two minigames are rather dull...there is a pseudo-pokemon (sujimon) game which is a great idea on paper, but is so simple it gets boring after a while. The Dondoko Island minigame, I'm sure it will have its fans, but it was inmensely boring to me and I flew as soon as I could.Overall, I would rate this game similar to the previous Like a Dragon, but taking into account that that was the first attempt at something new, and despite polishing some details, I think this one is a little step back compared, hopefully something they can polish if they decide to male it a trilogy.Overall score? High 7, Low 8 from my perspective.

_childDocuments_.review: If you just want a side story where some of the characters from 7 meet in Hawaii for... reasons... Then you'll probably have a good time. The minigames and activities are good, claims of it having the best mini-games in the series are greatly exaggerated but they are fun. The Party Talk system (basically the skit system from Tales series) continues to be great and has a lot of funny dialogue that made me laugh and gave some goofy casual insight into the characters.The combat has some nice improvements over 7's very basic system, many attacks have knockback and you can knock enemies into the environment and each other, adding a little more thought and strategy to the basic attacks and allowing for more expression in combat. Enemies will now sometimes block, reducing the damage from all but the new grappling moves. Though this doesn't happen all that often it adds a bit more variety to encounters.If you were coming into RGG8 hoping it would continue the story of either Kiryu or Ichiban though, then you might be disappointed. It opens strong but as soon as it get's to Hawaii it all goes to pot. Characters introduced defeated and forgotten about like they're doing a crap villain speed run, barely coherent plot points that don't make sense and are never explained, terrible one dimensional villains and lame story choices (want a big focus on social media and a cult taken straight from scooby doo? no, me neither)Returning characters get no development, the party from 7 are just kinda there and don't have a meaningful role in the story. Older characters are barely there at all. Kiryu and Ichiban are the only ones that get any sort of development and they don't get much, ending in much the same place as they started. The new party members are fine and get a little development but ultimately the nonsense plot lets them down. New villain Yamai is a standout with a great little story that should have had a much greater focus, easily the best part of the narrative but there's not much of it here.Too much of the story is spent on awful plot points that go nowhere and mean nothing, the whole thing feels like filler in the end. It's a decent RGG theme park with a lot of attractions but a truly terrible continuation of either 7 or 7 Gaiden. If you're in it for the continuing story, you'll miss nothing skipping this and waiting for 9 when presumably, hopefully, they are ready to continue the story in some way.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros- Fixed most issues with combat- Finally get a way to get around faster using a segway, but you can't pick up items while riding- Music is great- Minigames are great. Arcade games are OK.Cons- Outfit changes only show up in combat. No way to change regular clothes -Combat still needs tweaking (forced to use field items on basic attacks if they're too close, attacking downed enemies that are getting up is 50/50, very easy to get overleved on accident and there's not really any level scaling or smart AI, so combat gets easy if you're used to rpgs.)- The only way to get all achievements is to pay for dlc. This is blasphemy and should be changed (but it won't)- Story is ok at best. The plot is convoluted, certain plot points are absolutely stupid, new villains are uninteresting for the most part and the aversion to gore or actual killing takes the impact out of certain scenes, even though the game is rated M. Overall, if you like the series you're gonna get this anyway. Even though the plot wasn't engaging, the gameplay and music were, so I kept at it. Solid 2.5/5

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who's a massive fan of the series, this is the first time I write a negative review about a Yakuza game...hell this is my very first negative review ever. My review may contain minor spoilers please be advised.PROS+- The gameplay is amazing. It's the same formula like in Yakuza 7 but on steroids, lots of QOL changes.- The setting, atmosphere, music, minigames. It's all there as you should expect it from a Yakuza game.- The new characters are fun, lots of good chemistry between them and the voice acting is top notch.CONS-- The story. This is probably my biggest gripe with the game. It starts off well but half way through it falls apart so bad I couldn't even believe it. After Yakuza Gaiden the bar was set so high for Kiryu's ending. For the love of God please let this man rest. Yakuza 7 did a great job asserting a new main protagonist, we don't need 4 more games of Kiryu's suffering. As for Ichiban's part this was the most unhinged story writing among all of the Yakuza games. There were so many good characters introduced within the first few chapters but none of them were explored even the slightest. The climax of  Ichiban's story was so hilariously bad, I was just sitting there telling myself "ok there has to be something more.....right?"- Putting a whole dungeon and NG+ behind a paywall. This is some next level greed for an offline game which I've never seen before.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth is, in my opinion, the best way that they could conclude the story of Kiryu Kazuma. Before you think I just spoiled the game for you, this is very apparent from the second you first encounter him within the story. The game is advertized as a goofy and fun game about Ichiban going to Hawaii, which it still of course is, but the plot itself is much thicker and deeper, and dare I say, Kiryu Kazuma himself is the main focus of it.Throughout the story, you end up switching between playing as Ichiban and Kiryu several times. They both have different parties, with Ichiban getting two new characters to the series within his. Kiryu's party though entirely consists of returning characters, which I believe thematically suits him. Kiryu's inclusion within the story is all about him coming to terms with his life, and remembering who he truly is. As I said before, I really don't want to give away too many plot details, as this story is both insane yet incredible, but if you've played all the other entries leading up to 8, then PLEASE pick this entry up, as it feels like a culmination of the events of each game. An issue regarding the story that I've seen come up is how 8 flanderized Ichiban as a character, making him too kind and empathetic, which to that.... i just don't get what it means. Ichiban's entire character arc in 7 is what leads to him being such a loving person, and of course he's going to have the same knowledge which he gained in the last entry in this one. Showing kindness is not weakness, and that's a huge message in 8 which I believe a lot of people need to come to terms with. Ichiban Kasuga is one of fiction's greatest example of someone being strong without always having to use force. You'll see what I mean as the story continues.Now, to talk about the story here is an entirely different thing. The story here is CRAZY, and I mean absolutely INSANE. The plots of the other games have all been relatively contained within Kamurocho and the various other cities, but 8 introduces an INTERNATIONAL THREAT. I honestly think that they pulled it off incredibly well though, and it didn't feel too pushed or edgy. It still felt like a Yakuza game, which I think is the most important part. Bravo RGG, you managed to make a Metal Gear type plot work in your series about Japanese men ripping their shirts off and beating each other up.In conclusion, this game is a must for Yakuza fans, and it's the perfect finale that we've been waiting for. The price tag is daunting, and I get why that would be an issue for people. As for me personally, I waited until it went on sale before buying it, but there's so much content within the game including a full on resort building game, a whole Pokemon esque system, TONS of substories, and so much more (yakuza 5 reference) that I think it's worth the full price.Bon Voyage.

_childDocuments_.review: The Dragon is dead; long live the Dragon.In terms of gameplay and pacing of content, Like A Dragon: Infinite Wealth is the best JRPG I've ever played, hands down, and I have played a lot of them.  My actual playtime was about 180 hours, and I earned 53 out of 64 non-postgame achievements.  I am having trouble believing this myself, but I don't feel like any of that time was wasted or boring.The game has more competition in the areas of story and character development, but that isn't a criticism.  It rubs shoulders with the greatest games of the largest franchises.  The highest compliment I can pay any media is to say, "I would not have done it differently," and LAD:IW earns that praise.Most importantly, it is a worthy entry in the acclaimed ten-game-long series, although it is very different than anything that has come before, including Yakuza: Like A Dragon.  If anyone thought that the movement of the series toward a goofier tone in Y:LAD was a one-off, LAD:IW puts those suspicions to bed.  This game is goofy.The Yakuza series has always been a little silly, but even in Y:LAD, it rarely interferes with the drama.  LAD:IW is something different.  This is a comedy game with a dramatic plot, not a dramatic game with comedic elements.That being said, though, one of my favorite things about the game is this: as ridiculous as the job list in LAD:IW is, it is remarkable how many of them Kazuma Kiryu has held over the course of the series.  So it must not be that ridiculous.The clear change in tone is not a bad thing, but I do think it marks the end of an era, which is both appropriate and bittersweet.For 20 years, the Yakuza series has had incredible, almost unprecedented, success.  I deeply respect the developers at Ryu Ga Gotoku for recognizing that it needed to change in both tone and content to be successful for another 20, and not only executing that change but doing so to critical and fan acclaim.  LAD:IW isn't about saying goodbye, it's about letting go and looking ahead.  Ichiban Kasuga is a hero who does that, and maybe now, Kazuma Kiryu can be as well.  He deserves it.This has been a payoff long in coming.  Yakuza 6, Y:LAD, Like A Dragon: Gaiden, and LAD:IW are almost one (very) long game in four parts, and that's discounting the importance of the earlier games to Kiryu's story.  You absolutely can enjoy LAD:IW by itself, but if you do not plan to eventually play all of these games, you are doing yourself a disservice.If I have any complaints at all, they are these:I wish the sujimon and Dondoko Island content was more fleshed out.  They are fine, but they could be so much better.  There are so many great sujimon that are uncatchable, and the battling has even more in common with rock-paper-scissors than its inspiration.Dondoko Island is honestly a bit disappointing.  Every game in the Yakuza series has been an asset flip -- that is part of their brilliance.  Ryu Ga Gotoku has always had an excellent sense of where to save development effort so that it can be spent where it is most needed.  Dondoko should have been a celebration of this fact, and instead it falls short.  Its implementation is clunky and incomplete, and it only just barely manages to be satisfying if you've purchased the supporting DLC.  Otherwise it is a slow grind.Like many more recent Ryu Ga Gotoku games, LAD:IW is so big that it takes a long time to get up to speed.  However, once it is there, the second half of the game flows like a dream.  Just the right alchemy of variety, complexity, and depth.  I really can't say enough about how good the pacing is for a game this size; I've never finished the side content of a Yakuza game at the same time as the main story before. The story also follows the recent trend of Ryu Ga Gotoku games in being unnecessarily convoluted, especially for its more light-hearted tone, but it never has its head as far up its butt as either Judgment game, or even some of the more political Yakuza games (all of which are still good).  Thank goodness the main character death count is so low; it is very hard to take these villains seriously when your best weapons against them are a surfboard, a floor buffer, and the ability to summon homeless people like pokemon.But all things considered, I prefer it this way.  Overall, LAD:IW does a good job of following what I consider to be the first rule of Yakuza stories: "Everyone cares about Akira Nishikiyama; no one remembers Kyohei Jingu."  Yakuza is at its best when it is about personal conflicts, not political intrigue, and LAD:IW hits that mark.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth is an enthralling game that takes players on an unforgettable journey through its immersive world. With its captivating storyline, strategic gameplay, and well-developed characters, it offers a gaming experience that is bound to leave a lasting impression. However, there are a couple of aspects that could be improved, including the English dub for Kiryu's character and the requirement to pay for New Game Plus.Positive Points:1. Immersive World: Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth presents a beautifully crafted world that is rich in detail and brimming with life. The cities are bustling with activity, and the environments are visually stunning. The attention to detail in the world design adds an extra layer of immersion to the gameplay experience.2. Gripping Storyline: The game's storyline is a rollercoaster ride of emotions, filled with compelling twists and turns. It delves into deep themes of friendship, loyalty, and personal growth, keeping players engaged from start to finish. The well-written narrative and memorable characters make the game a joy to experience.3. Strategic Gameplay: Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth offers a unique blend of turn-based combat and strategic decision-making. Players must carefully plan their actions, utilize their party members' abilities, and adapt to different enemy encounters. The combat system provides depth and satisfaction, ensuring that each battle feels rewarding.Negative Points:1. Kiryu's English Dub: Unfortunately, the English dub for Kiryu's character falls short of expectations. The voice acting lacks the emotional depth and authenticity found in the original Japanese version, which can be disappointing for fans of the series. While the overall English voice acting is solid, the portrayal of such a beloved character leaves room for improvement but lucky the is a mod to put in his japanese voice actor while still enjoying the rest of the dub.2. New Game Plus Cost: One aspect that will discourage some players is the requirement to pay for the New Game Plus feature. While New Game Plus adds replay value and allows players to carry over progress and items from their previous playthrough, it can be disheartening to discover that it comes at an additional cost. This paywall will hinder some players from fully enjoying the game's post-completion content.In conclusion, Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth offers an immersive and thrilling gaming experience with its captivating storyline, strategic gameplay, and vibrant world. However, the English dub for Kiryu's character and the need to pay for New Game Plus are notable drawbacks. Despite these flaws, the game still manages to deliver an enjoyable and memorable adventure that will captivate fans of the RPG genre.

_childDocuments_.review: It's an insanely fun Journey from Japan to Hawaii and the game improves upon the RPG turn based combat that was in the previous game, there is a lot more characters to play as in this game and the Story is very long but extremely enjoyable from start to end. The contrast between Ichiban and Kiryu makes the story a bit different from previous Yakuza games but also unique in a good way, the amount of content on display here is phenomenal and there is so much to do on this one that I can't list it all off. I really enjoyed the Sims/Stardew Valley/Animal Crossing Island simulation side game, as well as the Kiryu Bucket list and sub stories. I also really like the new dungeons and abilities that the characters can obtain which are extremely outlandish and fun, with the different jobs you can give to your party members. The size of the Hawaii map is huge it's definitely the biggest area in a Yakuza/Like a Dragon game and it doesn't feel empty for a second with all the sights to see, enemies to fight and secret items to obtain.My only gripes are that I wish that new game + wasn't being sold separately because it was a core feature of the old games and came with each release for free, but is now for some reason being sold as DLC. I also wish that there was more arcade machines in this game as there's only 3 different games to play with SEGA BASS Fishing which is iconic, Virtua Fighter 3tb and SpikeOut which are all great and slightly different from other games, but I want to see a huge collection of all the arcade games from previous Yakuzas all in one game. Also it's kind of baffling that they didn't include Crazy Taxi (original) as a playable game as they have a biking minigame with a similar name which is obviously in reference to it. I love rolling around on my Segway like Paul Blart and listening to classic SEGA music like Open Your Heart from Sonic Adventure 1 and the Daytona USA theme.I really love the humour is this game and the amount of cool special moves and classes along side the available special attacks that you can use when fighting enemies is amazing! Everything is bigger and improved upon from the previous Like A Dragon (as I said before), I also really like the fan service in the game though for long time players as there are a lot of references to characters and events from previous games that actually don't seem out of place. The devs clearly took a lot of time to make them contextually accurate and things are elaborated on in a well thought out and elaborate way so it's all in good taste. The game balances all elements very nicely and it isn't too grindy or too difficult either I get the sense that you could pick almost any job and use any combination of characters and with good enough gear and recovery items you could customise each playthrough however you see fit.It's extremely good and worth the asking price I just wish that new game + wasn't charged for separately that's really greedy (SEGA)...9/10 Extremely solid and fun game it's pricey but the amount of content and the fact that it's of serious triple AAA quality makes it worth it!

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:-	Loved most of the characters.-	Loved that they seem to actually hire native English speakers to voice English dialogue. Japanese anime can learn a thing or two from this. Voice acting was generally excellent across the board with the only exception being Bryce. I don't understand why he is the only one who speaks to barely intelligible English.  -	Turn based gameplay was fun and there is a myriad of skills to choose from to adjust to your play style. My one complaint is that enemies and allies keep walking about even though it’s not their turn making area of effect skills harder to pull off.-	They further developed on the Pokemon parody, Sujimon mini-game and added Sujimon battles and even gym battles instead of just collecting Sujimons like the last game. It was fun enough but I feel like I cheated as I mainly used the DLC Sujimons (your main party) who were stronger that any Sujimon you captured in the wild. Kinda wish the Devs did not overpower DLC characters to sell their DLC. Also wish there were more female Sujimons other than the DLC characters.-	They also developed a whole Gatcha system to draw new Sujimons fully based on in-game cash. It was fun to roll the Gatcha to get SSRs. Sadly, they made it so that draw animations for normal Sujimons cannot be fully skipped so playing the Gatcha got old really fast.  -	The Dondoko Farm mini-game was really good and I honestly got addicted to it and completely forgot about the main story, only returning to it after fully developing the Farm and finishing the Dondoko story.Cons:-	Incorporates 3rd-party DRM: Denuvo. Thankfully, they properly optimised the game so that Denuvo does not affect performance, as least for my system. -	When I started the game, I thought this was a sequel to Yakuza: Like a Dragon. Instead, it is more like a sequel to all the Yakuza games and IMO, should have been named Yakuza 8. I only played Yakuza 0 and 1 and only got halfway through Yakuza 2 so a lot of the Kiryuu segments felt like spoilers.-	Even though most of the side-stories are set in Hawaii, all characters in them conveniently speak Japanese. There’s this weird disconnect between the main story and side-stories where native characters would obviously speak English only in the main story. It feels like the Devs engaged a third-party to write these side-stories based on the last Yakuza games but forgot to ask them to account for the setting.  -	SO many plot contrivances, even more that the usual Yakuza game (spoilers).  Overall, 8/10. Really fun game set in the Yakuza universe despite some iffy bits. Just wish they did not have to ♥♥♥♥ on the story with the aforementioned stupid segment at the end of the Final Chapter. Will play through Yakuza 2-6 when I have time.

_childDocuments_.review: The sins of the yakuza are mine. And if I have to, I'll take on every last one.If Kiryu’s saga established the man as a legend inextricably tied to underground crime, Infinite Wealth is truly able to bind the man to his fate.Past games establish one point clearly: while he can hide all he wants, while he can even erase his name and wallow in regret, he cannot erase his name.If Ichiban’s previous game established anything, it’s making clear that you can truly rise up from any odds if you put your mind to it. Rehabilitation is possible, and if a washed-up 42-year-old former yakuza can take down the governor of Tokyo, so can anyone else.7 establishes this guy’s ideals, and rather than him simply follow the footsteps and mistakes of his predecessor, Ichiban’s natural familial lovingness and talent for leadership are given a purpose by Kiryu.The infinite wealth of experiences both we and Kiryu have gone through, the countless trials and tribulations, the visceral deaths and betrayals, it all defines who he is. Kiryu is deeply frustrated with who he’s become, but he can’t run away. He’ll take the sins of the yakuza with him, the lived experiences, the brutality, the violence. It’s his burden to carry, and it’s Ichiban’s to shape a better Japan in his stead.Infinite Wealth’s enormous berth of side content, extravagant set pieces, rock solid character writing, and sense of scale cement it as the greatest work RGG Studio has created. Some iffy pacing and rough edges cannot hold back the beautiful storytelling that wraps the story of one of the most inspirational protagonists of the genre in a bow.
