_childDocuments_.review: From the perspective of someone who has played the previous Yakuza/Like a Dragon titles, as well as the Judgement series:Like A Dragon: Infinite Wealth or Yakuza 8 is a great game that follows the story of Kasuga Ichiban after what has happened in Yakuza 7, as well as a farewell story for Kazuma Kiryu. The game features a story that'll get you hooked and a lot of fan service regarding the past titles of the game, including the Judgement Series. If I were being honest, I would love to recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a good story and pretty good turn-based RPG but there are just so many things you would miss if you didn't play the past titles so I encourage you to play the past few titles before diving into this one, the trip is long (and a bit painful) but it's so damn worth it imo (Especially Kiryu's side of the story).Now onto the actual review:Story: The story is pretty great, the game manages to make this grown ass man cry (twice). Both Ichiban as well as Kiryu's side of the story makes it already feel like the Journey of playing Yakuza 0 to 7 (as well as the Judgement series) oh so worth it. The Substories, Drink Links, Table Talk, and the likes are also great, they are hilarious and would usually encourage you to find out more just so that you could hear what other dumb things these guys have to say. With that said, there are some things that aren't great with the story. The villains is what I would like to call "forgettable", most of them just acts tough until you beat some sense into them, and then they start pissing their pants (heh). The only villains who I consider actually cool is Ebina and Yamai (for obvious reasons). I'd also love to hear more of how Chitose came to be, because I feel like they didn't do her enough justice in either story or drink links.Gameplay: The gameplay is turn-based and is a straight-up upgrade to the mechanics we previously had in Yakuza 7, so much so that I couldn't imagine myself playing Yakuza 7 anymore with just how much Yakuza 8 has spoiled me. All the attacks have details in them, if they are normal, grapple, or knockback. The area attacks now show how far it reaches or how it would attack. Back attacks are a thing. You can move your party in a certain area so you could efficiently use your abilities to its fullest. Kiryu's attacks and styles are super cool and unique from what we had previously. All the new jobs are funny but my gripe with it is that it outshines the past jobs that we used to have in Yakuza 7 so the past jobs were basically rendered almost useless. Honestly, in terms of gameplay, I have nothing but praises for it because of how unique it is. People might hate it or think differently than I do, but I kinda like the simple-ish turn-based combat mechanic they have and improved from Y7. 10/10Music: Damn did the music not disappoint at all. From battle music, karaoke, boss music, and the rest, RGG studio never fell at that aspect. Some people say that Y7 music has more better music than Y8, to that I say, fair but you can't argue if music is actually good, plus most of Yakuza games are just like that, they never really disappoint when it comes to music. Shoutout to 'Baka Darou', 'Honolulu City Lights', 'Barracuda', and 'Slugfest' for being absolute bangers.Graphics: I'm not really a guy who ponders with graphics, as long as the game doesn't look like absolute piss it should be fine. But damn do I love how the game looks. Can't give a detailed explanation about this because I ain't an expert, but go ahead and see it for yourselves.All and all, the game is amazing. In my heart, this game is a 10/10 and I might be a tad bit biased when it comes to stuff regarding Yakuza. But... we all know this game is not perfect, not only story wise, but the decision to put New Game + is kinda dumb and I do have to dock points for that. With that being said, the honest review I give this game:[8.5/10]Gatekeeping Notes (Ignore this if you don't really care):Please play the previous games before playing this one, istg most of the story wouldn't make much sense without playing the past game. ESPECIALLY KIRYU'S PART OF THE STORY. So for the love of God, just do as I say if you want a definite, real experience.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is good and is to Yakuza 7 what Lost Judgement was to Judgement. The gameplay has improved an insane amount and the overall quality of the game is undeniably the best it has ever been. Where the game severely falls short however is the story. It is a disorganized mess and needed a rewrite. Honestly it feels like they wanted to tell a story, then added hawaii in there for no reason and also added kiryu as a dual protagonist for no reason as well. The best parts of the game however is Kiryu's sections but again it doesnt mesh well with the overarching story and I feel like it would have benifited from being a Kasuga only game.This game does however give me hope the future. One big problem with RGG games so far is the lack of consistantly good character writing between games but this is something that I think was improved on massively here. Nanba, Adachi, Tomizawa, Chitose, Zhao, Joon-gi and Sonhee are all awesome and have great development and moments in the game.The Gameplay is awesome and the class system was massively improved. Unlike the previous game where you just spammed one ability that hit everything in the room, this time you actually have the strategise and use the tools the game gives you for a majority of the games run time. You can create custom movesets to create a unique way to play your characters and truely play the game the way you want to. Some moves are super op looking at you fire arrow from samurai.The issues come in the late game (level 45-50ish) where you become so digustingly overpowered it feels just like the last game where you just one shot everything with little to no challenge.

_childDocuments_.review: The game was fun but I'm so glad I waited for a sale. There's certainly more side content to do (Sujimon/Dondoko) but they sacrificed the quality of the sub-stories to make that happen. Most sub-stories were over within a couple of interactions compared to YLAD and they weren't as interesting. You also don't get that much exp, idk what people mean when they said they were over-leveled by the end of the story just from side content. I literally finished Sujimon and Dondoko as soon as I could, same goes for every sub-story and link/bonds, but by the finale I was level 47.I'd also like to question certain game design decisions for this game but one of my biggest gripes was the fact that certain bosses would have a recommended level but the final one had absolutely no warning. Don't get me wrong, I ended up beating it while being under-leveled but ♥♥♥♥ dragged on longer than it should've IMO. And for the people saying they were able to beat it at under level 46, I genuinely call cap on that. And was the point of giving me Joon-Gi at the end of the game? Seriously what the ♥♥♥♥ was that decision?? Granted he comes at an appropriate level and with decent gear but just let me carry around Nancy-Chan at that point cuz they're both not gonna be contributing anything useful to a fight anyway. Final gripe, which manager thought it was a good idea to introduce the job system half way into the game?? WTF give that ♥♥♥♥ to us from the beginning so we can level up jobs THROUGHOUT THE DAME STORY.The story itself was seriously.. not good. It took a lot of willpower not to skip a quarter of the cutscenes because they were just so unbearable to watch. My biggest issue was the fact that this whole thing was basically an anime, Naruto to be exact. ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Ichiban and his talk-no-jutsu and lets not forget that Golden Retriever personality of his that automatically forgives ANYONE as long as they show the slightest sign of regret. The whole mom situation was understandable, he made it very clear that he wouldn't know what to feel upon meeting her since to him, shes literally just a random woman aside from the biological connection. I'm not gonna go further into detail cuz thats spoiling but this story seriously left a lot to be desired.TLDR: Overall, YES there are a lot more things to do in this game than the previous but its a lot more shallow BECAUSE they were focused more on jamming in activities rather than the quality of these activities. _childDocuments_.review: Easy GOTY nominee, the game is absolutely fun and big in general but it does make some things better than others.The upgrade in the gameplay since Yakuza 7 is very notorious, now is a bit more strategic instead of just being a random mess were you basically try to bash the enemy with whatever you have near, at the same time they made the game a lot more easier, there's no more game over if you lose a fight in the story and also there's a lot of money and items that they gift you, personally this didn't harm my gameplay cause I'm usually on a rush when finishing story games but I think it's important to mention, besides I don't think these games should be too grindy, it's Yakuza after all, not Elden Dragon: Infinite Dark Souls.The characters introduced in this game have me in a 50/50, the ones in the ''good side'' are all amazing and pretty unique, the villains/bosses are not bad but there's like barely any of them, I mean sure, all the fights are incredible but when you have a game so big that it takes up to 2 countries and 2 different evil organizations I would've expected more unique villains, and that's without mentioning how pathetic most of them are at the end except for  and maybe .In contrary for what a lotta people say online I think the story was great, most of them are just forgetting the hype this game got was for the question ''Will Kiryu Survive?'' and when they got the answer to that they swept the game. The reason I think this game has a nice story it's because it manages to be engaging without resorting to constantly confusing the player with useless plot twists that later turn into nothing, in other words, because it's simpler than other previous games, same exact reason why I think the Judgment saga has the best stories in the Yakuza games, the way this saga generally tries to write stories (at least with the older ones) is by making them too complicated and tangled, which in the long run in my opinion doesn't add any points in "being a better story." Personally I hope RGG will continue creating stories like this.As for the music, as always, it bops. Although I expected a larger amount of bangers I can't state anything negative against it since it has Barracuda, Brutality -Rebuild- and The End of Denial, karaoke is cool too.Regarding the side content, it's most probably the best one yet, like, since Yakuza 7 this is the game I've struggled the most to follow the main story because of how many side stuff you have at your disposal. Except for obvious painful stuff like Mahjong and Shogi there's literally not a single bad or boring minigame in this. In respect of the finale, Final Opinion: Marvellous game, can't recommend it as an entry point to the series (although I've seen a lot of people do it), can't say anything that hasn't been said already about the DLC NG+ drama but I really hope that RGG won't get used to shamelessly put stuff like this as dlcs, I love hawaii!! _childDocuments_.review: I'm maybe half way through the game, so recommending it feels somewhat presumptuous. Even in recommending it's not a total recommendation and I'll try to explain myself.It's good. It's a better fleshed-out party-based RPG than Yakuza: Like A Dragon was. There's more to combat than there originally was; timing and positioning have an impact and that improves the experience from being mechanically like Dragon Quest. It's serviceable appearance-wise; the engine doesn't appear to be significantly different to the previous game, and that was built off the same engine as Yakuza 0 (so far as I know). The story plays out well - characters are fun and well rounded, and the story is paced well.That being said, it's also kind of bad. Dondoko Island is a slog to get through; it's optional but it's a way to generate money that's much slower than the older hostess club minigames. The biggest sin to me though is that it's starting to feel less and less Japanese compared to its predecessors. I don't know how much of this is playing to a Western audience but when I play a Yakuza game I actively want some cultural dislocation. I don't pick these games to have my own cultural prejudices reflected back at me, and it feels like the game is becoming international in a way that means this is going to be my last game in the series.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is truly one of the best games I have ever played. Like A Dragon: Infinite Wealth acts as the true passing of the torch from Kiryu to Ichiban.Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth's combat REALLY improves the Yakuza: Like a Dragon's combat. Here are the lists of the improvements that I have notice or saw during the trailers:The better version of permanent skills since it allows a diverse, and creative move set for everyone. Unfortunately it is locked behind bonds; thankfully, clubs exists and you can spend millions to achieve bond level 100.Kiryu's combat is more unique due to his unique style switching feature. Kiryu can switch between Dragon, Beast, and Rush with each styles having their own unique feature to them. Dragon style allows Heat Actions to trigger if specific requirements are met, and they can hit multiple enemies even if it shows one getting pummeled. Beast style allows Kiryu to pick up heavier objects and its object swings have orange trails now. Rush style allows Kiryu to attack normally twice. All of the styles also share unique proximity bonus attacks with Dragon being mostly just standard with a QTE to deal extra damage (even when awakened), Rush being a flurry of hits with a spam QTE to deal extra damage (awakened makes the animation longer), and Beast being VERY good since it turns it into a full circle AOE grapple move with a QTE to deal extra damage (even when awakened).Kiryu's Dragon Resurgence can be activated with the special infinity symbol (When as party leader only, if he isn't then it will give Dual Dragons), and allows Kiryu to become Like A Dragon and break the turn based system. Basically, Kiryu makes the game into a water downed beat em up, since enemies will not attack you and Kiryu only has access to his Yakuza 6 DOD Extreme Heat move set.Kiryu has gotten rusty due to his condition and age; thankfully by just viewing special memories of the past (Dragon Memoirs), he can wipe the rust off and become slightly stronger. Kiryu can also talk to a familiar friend who will try help Kiryu tie up his loose ends from the past. This mechanic is just like Ichiban's personality, but only with 3 personalities that relate to the 3 styles.The original cast of Ichiban, Namba, Adachi, Saeko, Zhao, and Joongi (excluding Eri) returns; however, the cast would be split between Hawaii and Yokohama. The New Cast would be introduced in Hawaii since none of Ichiban's buddies came over with him. This new cast would include Kiryu, , , and .  is another down to earth guys who had .  is . Finally  is .Ichiban's new home alongside his friends. The map is fully open, but with certain stuff missing like PCF's Dragon Kart Minigame; however, there is still a ton you can do in Yokohama.The newest map of the Yakuza Series ever since Yokohama was introduced 4 years ago in Y:LAD. The map is based off of Waikiki, Hawaii. The map is sadly fogged which I hate; however, it has a ton of new minigames and a ton of new locations. I also like how your Yen was converted into USD upon entry to Hawaii.After three years, Kiryu is back in Kamurocho as an actual map, and probably the last time we get to see Kiryu strolling around the city. There is really nothing notable about the city since nothing major has happened to it during the story, and too be honest it's rather barren, but it does contain the most Dragon Memories.I am surpised that RGG made two really good games so close to each other and filled them with so much content despite how scummy Y:IW's was to its DLC. In summary this game is one of the best Yakuza games out there, and I really recommend playing this game after playing Y:LAD first since this is basically a sequel to that and contains many spoilers from it. Kiryu would also have spoilers, but hey it is your choice to decide to jump into this game before or after playing the previous games.

_childDocuments_.review: This game saved my life.I am 37.My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and adopted our son together. They are now both 4 years old.When we were going through our separation, I found myself lost and miserable. I was self destructive. I got so mad one day from everything spiraling out of my control that I punched some concrete in a moment of overwhelming emotion. That caused me to break my 5th metacarpal in my right hand... my working hand... my games hand.. the hand that I held and carried my children to bed with.. The hand I desperately needed to make sure I could continue to provide.After learning of the severity of my self-inflicted damage, I was borderline suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man with no history of depression or anxiety. I have never had fits of rage, or been one to break down and cry, but I was in a low spot that just really buried me from being able to see the light on the other side.Having nothing better to do, I searched for a game I could play, ONE HANDED while I recovered. I somehow stumbled upon this game and read some of the reviews. I decided that it had to be worth a shot... I must admit, I didn't beat the game, or play nearly as long as some of you. In fact, I may have only played this game a day or two.. With that being said, after doing so, I had a new found joy and hope for life. I was able to put behind me the pain and suffering that had been cast over me. I was able to experience other peoples joy and happiness. I was able to see the fruits of my "labor". I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ing minutes to this music long enough to realize that I was going to be okay.After coming to that realization, I turned the game off, and I went back to work. It hurt my hand like hell but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so damn sorry for myself, and I became the father I needed to be in that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving as.Today, I am close friend with my kids mother. We don't fight, or argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents, and friends.I now have 3 kids. My third child is, wait for it, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my own separation, and we just stumbled in to each others life unexpectedly. We have been in a relationship for a year now, and are very happy together.Moral of the story, you never know what life holds in store for you, and if I would have given up when all the odds were stacked against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.Thank you.

_childDocuments_.review: This game seems to improve upon the last one in every possible way and then even more than that. From the combat to the minigames to sheer amount of engaging side content you can get lost in, this is a massive RPG with easily a couple 100 hours of fun content to get lost in. I'm still only on Chapter 6 so far, but I already want to recommend this game to anyone who likes RPGs, monster catching games, and/or games like Stardew Valley and Animal Crossing. This game has it all. All the RPG mechanics you'd expect from the last game such as elemental and different physical damage types plus weaknesses and resistances to go along with them are improved upon in this. Now the elemental damage of your weapon is often also applied to your skills. There's also the ability to move around and better position yourself in combat and clearer indications when you can do combo moves with your teammates. They've also expanded on and improved the weapon crafting and upgrading system to allow further customization of your characters' weapons for combat. All that on top of adding new jobs like the Sujimancer-a job that summons some of your collected Sujimon and has them join you in battle and do different moves based on that particular Sujimon. That is of course the name given to the different enemies in the game, a huge number of which can be captured, leveled up, combined with others of their same kind for further power boosts, and evolved. They also can be battled in a 3 on 3 battle against trainers with their own Sujimon scattered around the game's world map. You can collect Sujimon either by talking to one if it sticks around after you beat it in a fight, or after beating one of the many raids scattered around the map that pop up for a limited time before going away and then coming back after a period of time. There's an entire gacha system around them involving tickets you can win from beating trainers or getting just from walking up to the Sujimon spots where you level up and evolve them. You can also get master tickets for the Kiwami spins or Japan spins for even more Sujimon you can't normally catch in Hawaii. With at least 130 different Sujimon to collect and 5 types with different weaknesses and resistances to them for combat, there's a ton of work you can put into that side content if you so wish.You just might wish to do at least some of it cause there's also: Dondoko Island, your very own island resort you can build up into a 4 or 5 star resort. I just hit 3 stars and am working on 4 for the achievement for it before I go back to the main game in Hawaii where I left off. It's a lot of fun running around the island gathering resources and building decorations and facilities to improve the resort and make more people wanna come and spend money there. Most of it's kept to it's own Dokobucks currency that's relegated to buying upgrades or lodgings or clearing out new places to keep expanding your resort's buildable space-but with each new run of visitors and each new star rank you climb you get money to spend back out in the main game and it's raked in more money than I've probably collected the whole time I've been playing so far.Speaking of money, you're gonna need it. A decent amount of it. Hawaii's not exactly cheap and if you wanna experience the most of it-like unlocking all of your available jobs including the preordered ones-you're gonna have to spend money at the Alo-Happy tourist spot to unlock those jobs/classes and same with the returning Ounabara Vocational School you can take tests at to boost Ichiban's Personality traits.Those Personality traits feel even more important/useful and not just cause you need to be a certain level of it to unlock the Linebacker and Tennis Ace preorder classes, but you get resistances to debuffs and status effects like Fear or Rage that can potentially ruin an encounter for you if you're not able to heal Ichiban and he dies cause everyone's afraid or enraged and not eble to use items or skills. It also opens up more opportunities elsewhere in the game. I can't get into them cause I haven't stumbled upon them as far as I know yet, but in the last one I remember unlocking access to a gambling parlor when my Style reached a certain level so I imagine it's more things like that.They also expanded upon the Bonds and Drink Links from the last game and instead of just 5 levels to their Bond, you can gain 100 levels and they gain more abilities than they did before. I don't think unlocking potentially chained attacks on enemies knocked to the ground was in the last game. There are also more ways to level up those Bonds beyond just combat and eating at restaurants in the game. You can also give them gifts and find special walk and talk segments with them to unlock spots on their bingo card-which of course gives you huge boosts to their Bond when getting bingos and filling out the full card.They also made it better/easier to level up different jobs to further encourage you trying out different ones. Beyond unique items to boost job xp for specific jobs like a bone necklace for the Pyrodancers, there are free magazines you can find in stands around the map as well as potential drops in dungeons-although the dungeon drop ones are more specific in that they're not flat xp to gain for the job but a full level for it-like the preorder level up bonuses. In other words, those particular preorder bonuses are items you can find in the game and they're useful for unlocking skills to carry over between jobs. Speaking of-yeah-they improved that too. Now instead of just getting a selection of skills unlocked for leveling up different jobs that would all carry over, you get to build your own loadout from seemingly almost any skill unlocked from any job and as you level up your Bonds with your other characters, they can have more skills in their loadout.I think I'm about only a third of the way thru this game and in every way-in every new thing unveiled-it feels like this game has improved upon the last (and I already loved Ichiban's first game.) If you've never played a Yakuza game, don't let that put you off-at the start of the game, they do a good job of giving you opportunities to get caught up on Ichiban's story before sending you off to Hawaii where they really start showing you how massive this game truly is. This is a phenomenal game I would recommend to anyone who simply likes RPGs and leveling up their characters while exploring a world and either engaging with an interesting story or just going off and doing their own thing for hours or days at a time.

_childDocuments_.review: Infinite wealth is an awesome game that is absolutely jam-packed with content and just random ♥♥♥♥ you can do. There are so many mini-games, side activities and overall fun stuff to do that it is exhausting honestly. The combat is surprisingly fun, it seems that RGG studio really knew where and how to improve their turn-based combat from the previous title. It feels very dynamic and engaging due to all the interactions, button prompt actions and strategic positioning. It's kinda addicting actually.The soundtrack is filled with bangers and the game looks pretty decent, especially Hawaii. The story starts out pretty interesting but it really steers into the nonsensical and boring at the end. I am also kind of mixed on the whole Kiryu sendoff, I don't think it was bad but I expected something much bigger. I also really wish we had some more OG Yakuza characters in the party. Most of the party members are very one-note and kinda eeh while on the other hand, there are many more eccentric and fun characters (even new ones) available in the game. I mean Kiryu, Ichiban, Seonhee and Chitose were good but I was not a big fan of most of the other party members. It's disappointing to see Kiryu's sendoff title without some of the other Yakuza staple characters in his party. But still that is not a huge deal as the game overall is an extremely fun, very well-polished and varied experience.Honestly, there are only 2 huge negatives that I think must be mentioned about this game: 1 - Infinite wealth severely lacks enemy level scaling because it is very frustrating when you are unable to just play at your own pace with regards to how much side content you want to do because you can become overleveled very quickly and the game becomes piss-easy. And that is a shame because some of the most fun I had in this game was in the dungeons when I was close or slightly lower than the level of the enemies. In those cases the game was decently challenging and very very fun, so more of that please. Just add some scaling so that it doesn't get too out of hand. 2 - This one is on Sega and their scummy decision of putting a basic New game plus mode, a new end-game dungeon and most importantly for me ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ DIFFICULTY MODES behind a paywall. What the ♥♥♥♥? Every Yakuza game that I have every played I did so on harder difficulties because I know damn well that these games are pretty easy as it is and this was the first one where I was unable to choose my difficulty and that annoyed the living hell out of me. So I think Sega must be called out on this garbage as it feels like they are trying to take a steaming dump on an otherwise very good title.So overall, I recommend this game to all Yakuza fans even the ones who think that the turn-based combat is unfitting and too slow for this franchise as well as to newcomers but I suggest to go about it in smaller portions and try not to wear yourself out as this game is MASSIVE.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth? Adventure Across Continents Meets Controversy! (ฅ'ω'ฅ)"This game excels with its engaging narrative and dynamic combat across Japan and Hawaii, but is marred by controversial monetization practices, particularly the locking of difficulty levels behind a paid New Game Plus.""Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth" marks another ambitious chapter in the esteemed RPG lineage of the Yakuza series. The game brings together two iconic characters, Ichiban Kasuga and Kazuma Kiryu, in a narrative that weaves fate and dark undertones into a rich tapestry of storytelling. The emotional drama is palpable, as players navigate the lives of these two larger-than-life heroes, each grappling with their own demons and destinies. The journey is not just confined to the neon-lit streets of Japan but also stretches to the picturesque landscapes of Hawaii, offering a refreshing change of scenery and a sense of grandeur to the adventure.The game's combat system is a standout feature, offering a dynamic and strategic RPG experience that leverages the environment in innovative ways. The customization options and varied job classes inject a fresh layer of strategy, allowing players to tailor their party's abilities to their play style. The transition to a more refined turn-based system enhances the tactical aspects of combat, emphasizing positioning and timing for maximum impact. This commitment to evolving the combat mechanics keeps engagements thrilling and intellectually stimulating from start to finish."Infinite Wealth" excels in delivering an expansive adventure that stretches across the Pacific. The dual settings of Japan and Hawaii offer a rich tapestry of cultures, environments, and activities that ensure the journey is as diverse as it is engaging. From bustling city streets to serene beaches, the game offers a plethora of quests and side activities, providing a satisfying blend of storyline progression and leisure exploration. This diversity not only enriches the game world but also allows players to immerse themselves fully in the expansive universe the game creates.Despite its strengths, "Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth" faces criticism for its monetization strategies. This model, seen as diverging from traditional gaming practices, has been a point of contention, raising questions about the balance between profit and player experience. _childDocuments_.review: It's a fun turn-based RPG. This turn-based combat feels like playing pool where you line yourself up in front or behind an enemy and try your best to rebound the enemy into a wall, an arena hazard, into another enemy for combo damage, or towards another teammate for them to hit the enemy once more. You have bond meters to level up associated with your party members through various means, and as it progresses, you'll gain the ability to move yourself to other members before attacking and perform partner attacks (but the attack is mostly some goofy acrobatic missile maneuver) and also have a higher chance that a party member will do a free follow-up attack. Know that this bond meter is not leveled like Persona games where you have to make strictly timed decisions based on min/maxing calendar days. It's much more relaxed and it increases as you battle, play mini-games, progress from a list of accolades, etc.They've got something great with the combat, but I wish it had skill shortcuts. You'll kick-off battles where you and your enemies have a starting point: while you have your own zone to move around and then make your decision (Attack/Skills/Items/Defend) at the start of your turn, your enemies in the meantime can sporadically go from being grouped in a perfect 10-pin strike formation prime for an AOE move at the start of the battle to all over the place. If you had hotkeys / skill shortcuts, you could quickly execute what you want with out menu-ing to the 10-14 skills to navigate through. This personal issue I described isn't awful, but it's something to point out.You won't run into walls of main story level grinding or money grinding like Yakuza 7: Like a Dragon had. The game gives you frequent recommended level notifications and saves/heals before a series of mob fights or bosses.You'll get a chunky melodramatic story and deeply unserious side-quest humor. I have some personal issues with the overall narrative so my opinion is that it isn't perfect. There's quite a number of MacGuffins and it left the main character Kasuga Ichiban's narrative to be somewhat aimless. I found the golden eggs of enjoyment in this game from the gameplay, environments, humorous side quests, and nearly all of the main cast's characters/character arcs.Don't buy the DLC. It's a bad dungeon with empty character interactions and basic New Game Plus feature. It's not a NG+ that you want. I read it doesn't scale properly.If you want to jump right into this game, I strongly recommend watching a story retrospective of Yakuza 7 and LAD Gaiden: The Man Who Erased his Name to firmly understand the characters presented in Infinite Wealth. Even if you watch recaps, I do additionally recommend watching the ending sequences of those two games uninterrupted.

_childDocuments_.review: Hell yeah, I’ve been waiting for this one. It’s got everything I liked from the last game and more - more characters, more heart, more side-games that could have been entire games in their own right. I admit I haven’t finished it yet—which I’ll get to—but I’ve easily put down 80 hours already, and I’d consider a New Game plus down the line (even though it costs $20 to unlock, which is the most ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cashgrab I’ve seen in some time). I slowed down when I found myself doing the same things that slowed me down last time - feeling a need to full clear the side dungeons and fully upgrade each ultimate weapon, which require extremely rare ingredients - but that helped me reach an epiphany. If you really want to grind your way through everything Infinite Wealth has to offer, you can absolutely do that, and it’s likely more fun than Like a Dragon was to do the same thing. But you don’t need to do that to enjoy a great story and get a taste of some fun mini games - and I’ve played games where grinding is required. There’s still a few achievements I’d like to grab before finishing the story, but I should finish the game this year. I might just need to ascribe to the idea that I don’t need to 100% this game and it’s okay to just make a beeline for the main quest. If this game is anything like the last, a lot of that will be available in the postgame (and Kiryu’s story in particularly might mean a lot more to me once I’ve played the games where he’s the protagonist).

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon continues to be one of the best long-running Japanese series in the market right now. Infinite Wealth comes with important changes to the combat that completely fixes the flow compared to the previous game. The ability to move around during turn-based combat changes the dynamic quite a bit, and adds a layer of strategy in positioning your characters. Hawaii, as a setting, is also one of my new favorite Yakuza locales, right up there with Okinawa and Sotenbori. They put a lot of love into this game, and you can tell. The minigames are back! The "main" ones in this game is an animal crossing clone, and a simple pokemon clone. I didn't enjoy the pokemon clone all that much but the animal crossing clone is solid. Interesting characters, comfy gameplay, and a decent sub plot. Some people claim it's the best in the series, and I disagree. I still prefer the business minigame from 7 and the hostess club management from 2 and 0. But still, they're incredibly fun, and you can easily waste a ton of time with them. Now.... the plot. Let me just preface this by saying that the characters you love are still here, and they're the best they've ever been. The newcomers fit nicely within the group dynamic, and the party chats, the table talks, and all the other slice-of-life interactions are as loveable as ever. But.... the plot. The plot started up really strong, and I felt like they did a good job setting up intrigue and build up towards the middle half of the plot. But then it just completely floundered. Switching between 2 protagonists felt okay at first but it led to tonal upshifts and downshifts that give you severe whiplash towards the end. I was quite disappointed with the ending, and without naming any spoilers, I feel like some characters got the short end of the stick in terms of closure. But then again, the plot has never been the strong point of the Yakuza series. And as bad as it was, there are some worse endings in other Yakuza games. To summarize, if you've played Yakuza: Like a Dragon, then playing this game is a no-brainer. It is 100% a better version of Like a Dragon, (except for the plot).

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah when I bought this, I actually didn't know they locked both difficulty select and new game+ behind a $20 paywall. I think if I had a better understanding of what I was buying I would've not purchased this as it's both anti-consumer and also not a game good enough to warrant looking past that. It's about of similar quality to Yakuza: Like A Dragon (mainline entry 7). I liked 7. I feel Infinite Wealth gets a lot of smaller things right, while the main story in 7 is more compelling. Here certain aspects of the game are improved such as performance, gameplay balance, quality of life tweaks to game flow, and substory writing. Flip side is that this game does character assassinate who Ichiban was in 7 in service of getting the ball rolling on a new plot. I'm still not really over that. Beyond that, the plot following that is mostly lackluster, and is in essence a fanservice Hawaiian beach episode with mostly flat and predictable dramatic moments. Of course, most playtime is actually spent on mini-games and substories, and to the game's credit, for the most part, they're fun. It's just that comparative to other Yakuza entries, what's on offer isn't any more special than substories in other games so it doesn't really make up for anything.In writing this it feels like I'm completely glossing over the turn base combat, which would seem to be a core part of an rpg and this game in particular, but it's just not particularly engaging beyond spamming everyone's strongest single target or aoe moves. There are guard and guard breaks mechanics as well as elemental weakness and resistance mechanics, but they don't show up that often or meaningfully enough to make me switch party build or skills around. Base classes usually have tools necessary to work around stuff, so class changing is more for flavor. 7 was kind of the same way, but then I was playing it more for the story.I will comment on two of the bigger substory lines I think may have been shown in media, which is Sujimon and Dondoko island. Sujimon is pokemon but with the game's enemy mobs and inch deep stat and mechanical depth. It's kinda boring once you understand it. Dondoko island is actually more fun and depthful than I initially thought it would be as it's basically a set of smaller minigames and systems within a separate island game mode. For better or worse, it's a casualized progression treadmill in the vein of animal crossing or some city builder. I think love went into it considering it's length, but I was often at odds with wanting to engage with island customization and just placing down whatever new unlocks I was getting that increased island satisfaction more than what I had a minute ago. By the time I beat the Dondoko storyline, I kinda felt like half my unlocks were preset buildings I didn't really care for. Smaller stuff was nice, but by the time I beat it and was free of my pseudo-obligatory need to go for the much larger satisfaction objects, I didn't have a reason to do anymore building. It's a weird feeling of "I think this could've been done better" to walk away with, since I never really got that from pocket racers or any of the cabaret mini-games ever.Obviously this is an easy "don't buy" to anyone that didn't like 7 or the new turn based series direction. If you like the way this looks and haven't played 7, consider 7 or any of the other Yakuza games. To people that wanted more 7, this is technically more, but I'm leaning against saying this is a deserving improved sequel. I recommend saving your money and/ or finding a different game.Edit after completing mostly everything in the base game and tripling my playtime from ~50 hours to ~150ish: I definitely left this game on overnight sometimes so I don't know what my actual playtime is, but it's probably still 120+ hours. I also spent a lot of that in the first two deep dungeons leveling the different classes for the whole cast, which I really didn't super benefit from other than raw levels. I'd still consider that playing the game. Anyway, I think I was mostly right about everything I wrote in my initial review here. I would like to emphasize further that the main story here is terrible. Most of the time your driving motivation is solving mystery intrigue that does not pay off. The main story has a buckshot approach with connecting smaller plot-lines and nothing has a strong showing because most things don't have screen-time to develop, and the things that do have little consequence. This feels like a fanservice entry a lot of the time, but if you consider the main story in isolation it seems uninspired, by the books and like it's scrambling for things to pad that story with. Final thoughts: forget this entry like RGG forgot how to write a plot and like how they'll also probably forget this game as a whole.

_childDocuments_.review: I am nearing the end of yet another yakuza  * cough  * like a dragon title. This will make the 8th one i've completed and it is worth every penny. A full price top tier game right here. With ichiban kasuga returning as the main hero this time around. Bringing the humour back to the franchise 10 fold. Not saying the other games didn't have there funny moments but ichiban is certainly more humorous. What to expect : . Substories that some how make all the sense and are just as wacky as ever.. Likable characters all through the adventure. Mixed to good english voice acting you know what im referring to...  . The sound track is by far the best in the series to date. Seriously give the sound team a raise. . Good old turn based jrpg combat with stats  weapons and armor strategies all the fun ! ( this maybe off putting for some but give it a try ) . An excellent well written story that has shocks and omg moments at about almost every chapter. . Beautiful breath taking views. 3 large open world maps to explore including kumorochu because it's not a yakuza game without that. With that out of the way as an avid turn based rpg player my self i loved the switch over. rgg studio nailed the formula down to a t. There is actually some difficulty here where if you are not welcome in an area yet without some slick avoidance of enemy mobs you won't be able to explore said section until you are strong enough.The combat is just like the last like a dragon game with some added tweaks and ironing out. Kiryu for instance now has a move where you can freely move around the battlefield hitting people. I thought it was fun at first but you can basically just mash the button to win with that. It slowly charges over time so you can't abuse it.  There are new jobs to play around with which i won't spoil. The game wants you to explore the jobs and be creative with team setups. Theres no real wrong party setup. Just have fun and try all the jobs out. If i had to point out a draw back with this game... It has a slooooow start. You won't get to have any really fun with all the systems until it all unlocks so just play through the story regularly until that happens. Once everything gets unlocked and you are introduced to everyone it will pick up and slap you in the face. The maps them selves. If you've played all the yakuza games to this point then the only real new map is hawaii.You would have already explored injincho and kumorochu before. But each map looks just as great and even more detail through the land.  Kumorochu has changed a bit in this game but mostly everything is in the same spot. Or just just flat out blocked off so you can't explore that section anymore.  For example little asia. Yea thats just blocked off entirely Now for the english vo. Most of the cast sound great ! However the elephant in the room.... Yes kiryu.... Well i give credit to young yea for trying.... He just over stepped his bounds here. Most of the time kiryu sounds flat and bland. No emotion what so ever in most scenes even though there should be something there... They really shouldn't have cheeped out with the voice acting cast kiryu could have been a lot better. 10/10 game.

No idea why the studio tries to market this game as a good entry point since it follows up on the whole Kiryu saga and heavily references all previous games. So yeah, is it a fun game? Hell yeah? Should the newcomer pick it up? I don't think so. They should play through the whole saga first from 0, through Kiwami 1, Kiwami 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, Like a Dragon and Gaiden. _childDocuments_.review: It somehow beat Yakuza 7/Like A Dragon, and it's a damn near masterpiece.Infinite Wealth surpassed all my expectations and I'm so glad it lived up to the hype. It is beyond fun and the amount of content there is almost infinite. Definitely one of my favorite games ever made. However, there are some cons to the game, some nitpicking and others just downright annoying.CONS:-Sujimancer is very bad, for such a cool premise, even with strong sujimon, it is downright the worst job in the game. -Some of the jobs just suck and not worth investing into, but that's pretty much typical for a game in this genre.-New Game Plus priced as DLC, beyond stupid.-Some English va's should've been in the Japanese dub, for instance; Mendez is not voiced by Danny Trejo in the Japanese dub, like why? -Buying and upgrading materials is a damn chore, having to buy 1 material individually. WHY??-The 2 dungeons are just boring to go through?? I felt like there should've been more events to happen other than saving people and the boss battle at the end.-Minor nitpick but I really wish the level scaled with your party, being overleveled made the game just boring. But that's how RPGs work so that's on me for just playing the game too damn much.-Another nitpick; watching the trailer and just seeing  just ruined the surprise. -Really, REALLY wished we had the option to change time earlier in the game than in the final chapter, just annoying overall. I'm sure there's plenty more negative stuff out there but the positives just outshine everything.PROS:-The parties feel much more alive than before, there is so much dialogue that I had to give up looking for them. It's great, and each party members are amazing to each of their own. -Bond Bingo, as tedious as it was to go across the entire map, the conversations between Kiryu/Ichiban with their party members is fantastic. The finale of each bingo card is very sweet as well.-Revamped combat; being able to move within a circle is a godsend, plus other mechanics.-Akiyama, Majima, Saejima, and Daigo. -As much as I hate the "Power of Friendship" syndrome with every game, it really works here, especially with Kiryu.-Hawaii, such a fun map to walk around for the first time, if the series goes on, I really hope they keep doing this. By that I mean go out to other countries other than Japan. -Side content aka Sujimon/Dodonko Island/Crazy Delivery/Sicko Snap etc. I just REALLY REALLY wished that Sujimancer was better. Another complaint is that I kind of felt limited to Dodonko Island's placement of objects, as usual that's a nitpick. Overall it's a very nice "mini-game" to customize an island resort. -The story; I will definitely say that it isn't amazing, but when it hits, it really hits. It's a story carried by the characters, Like a Dragon stories are so ridiculously dumb you just have to set it aside and just play for the hell of it. It was great, I just wish one of the main villains wasn't so blegh compared to the other. They just felt like an afterthought?? imo.-Memoirs of a Dragon and Life Links; thank you for catering for fan-service, as Kiryu's "final" game it was nice to see old faces again. -Main Protagonists Ichiban and Kiryu splitting up into 2 parties. This might seem like an annoyance to some people but I actually liked this aspect of the game. It made none of the party members feel left out, except for Joongi which came in pretty late into the story (still ofc did Joongi things).-Kiryu's finale; I'm just relieved. It's a beautiful send off to him and I cried like a ♥♥♥♥♥. The entire ending is beautiful really. -Japanese dub, A+. There is so MUCH stuff this game does right and it's impossible to get into everything, but I'm glad it's a big upgrade from Yakuza 7.For 100hrs of content and completing almost everything, I definitely got my money's worth. Still not a fan of the new $70 trend but with so much to do, I hope the next game in the series surpasses even this one. Overall it's an amazing game, we finally got a proper send off to Kiryu and in doing so, passes the torch to Ichiban who is an awesome protagonist. 10/10 would cry again.

Even after 200+ hours in the game, I still haven't done everything.However, to get this out of the way, yes. New Game Plus AND the post-game content (The Big Swell) is locked behind the Deluxe Edition, an extra $15. Even if you do not care about NG+ as a feature, we should not condone this behavior and frankly while I am happy that RGG is seeing success, I can't help but worry that they'll view this monetary success as the gaming community supporting their DLC practices. Or worse, encourage them to charge extra money for OTHER features that should be in the base game, like Premium Adventure mode or something worse. Perhaps what irritated me most during the game was that the DLC Sujimon characters couldn't be used for Dondoko Island nor the Sujimancer job, as the DLC characters were the ones I used and leveled up throughout the Sujimon story. Wwithout the recognizable DLC characters I wouldn't care about playing the Sujimon game otherwise. (I did receive this game for free because an extremely generous family member and friend of mine pre-ordered the ultimate edition for me as a Christmas present, so I did try to take advantage of said DLC to not let their generosity go to waste.)Anyway, back to the game itself. If you found the turn-based combat of the previous game to be unbalanced or felt as though something was missing, I implore you to give Infinite Wealth a shot. The combat is much improved, with quality of life features like being able to control your characters' movement and positions during battle, as well as having indicators for where your AOE attacks will land. These two changes have made a HUGE difference in the battle system for me, which I was originally lukewarm on. Considering how rough the Dragon Engine's real-time beat-'em-up combat is (I've yet to have played Lost Judgement) I actually would prefer if RGG stuck to turn-based combat from now on, as at this point it feels more dynamic, engaging, and deep than real-time combat arguably ever has. To the point where I often forget Kiryu even has Dragon's Resurgence, and only use it as a way to finish off certain bosses.This game's story, meanwhile, is a bit mixed. Yakuza: Like a Dragon's story is definitely better, as it had better-written and more fleshed out themes and antagonists. Certain characters from the previous games have clearly taken a backseat and at times feel like they don't belong in the story. Newcomers like Chitose and Tomizawa, however, are really great and well-written additions to the cast. As much as I love these new characters though, I really wouldn't mind if they never appeared in any future entries. If this game is any indication, including previous characters in the party when they don't need to be REALLY drags the story down. If RGG just kept Saeko, Nanba, and Adachi around as core party members and swapped out the others in future games as they gain or lose relevance to the main plot, future entries would be better for it. As for side content though, oh man, it's incredible. ALL of the substories are bangers. This game easily has the best substories in the whole series. They're nothing if not funny, creative, and/or genuinely emotional. Infinite Wealth has set a new standard for the series in regards to substory content. I also enjoyed pretty much any content that involved raising bonds with your party members. A noticeable improvement from the last game is that bond level isn't locked behind a drink link like it was in Y:LAD, so even when you've unlocked a new drink link but haven't gotten to it yet, you can still further increase your party member's bond level. I've never been a HUGE fan of the drink links, I just find myself getting bored with all the sitting and talking for so long. Maybe I just have zoomer brainrot and my attention span is fried. But the smaller conversations you hear as you walk around the city and the "Table talks" you do at restaurants were quite entertaining.Lastly... The side stories/businesses. As Ichiban, you have Sujimon and Dondoko Island, and as Kiryu you have his bucket list/life links. I much prefer Kiryu's side story, if I'm honest. His bucket list is quite straightforward compared to Ichiban's content, and I honestly prefer it that way. Like I said before, I only did Sujimon because I could control the familiar DLC characters like Majima, Saejima, and Daigo. The Pokemon parody is amusing, but the battle system isn't all that enticing or fun. As for Dondoko Island, I'm still working on it, but to be honest the minigame just stresses me out. Having to manage my guests feels like a chore, and the building is tedious and my creativity is limited because the bonuses I get for the furniture/buildings I create for the island are only applied if near a path. While this would make sense, you have to make some pretty ugly-looking paths in order for a table with four chairs to work. It's nowhere near as fun as Animal Crossing.Perhaps the worst part of the larger side businesses in the recent Yakuza games is how they're forcibly interjected into the main plot. The game forces you to engage with what should be delegated as side content for 30 minutes, if not longer. The worst example is Clan Creator in yakuza 6 and kiwami 2 which is just an hour of yapping and a lame tower defense mobile game. Sujimon and Dondoko isn't QUITE that bad, but it's still really annoying if you'd rather see what happens next in the main plot and don't care for these minigames. It's easily my biggest gripe with the Yakuza series post-Yakuza 5 (in terms of release order) which is when they introduced this idea. I know RGG isn't going to listen to the pleas of a lowly gamer such as myself, but PLEASE, LET THE SIDE CONTENT BE SIDE CONTENT. QUIT FORCING IT INTO THE MAIN PLOT.TL;DR- Turn-based combat returns and it is MUUUUCH improved. The story is a tad bloated and some plot points/themes/characters are less fleshed out than others. The side content is amazing if not peak, but as per usual, some of it is hamfisted into the main story missions. The DLC practices (NG+ and post-game content is $15) are questionable. Overall one of my favorite Yakuza games, DLC aside.

_childDocuments_.review: I saw the game on sale and I thought "Well, I am a fan of the series" and so I bought the Ultimate Bundle. Be warned that it doesn't give you all the DLC, especially not the two DLC classes, and some DLC shouldn't be DLC at all. It gives you NG+ and hardest difficulty, which is disgusting to paywall, but then it gives you a bunch of nothing: the alternative outfits and the CDs may as well not exist for almost everyone. The Island plus Sujimon (read: not_Pokemon) stuff is cute but whatever, you certainly don't need it - and most importantly, it isn't worth spending an additional $20 to $40. Sigh.Including this installment, I've played every Yakuza game except for Dead Souls. I've beaten Amon in every single one of these games. This game has to be the most disappointed I've ever felt, and I'm including experiencing the transition from Yakuza Kiwami 2 to Yakuza 3 when I first started playing this series on my playstation quite a few years ago.Let me get this out of the way real quick: yes, the absurd way this game is priced is disgusting but I wouldn't have factored it in my review at all. In fact, I was going to recommend this game... until I beat the DLC dungeon where the final boss of it called out the consumers for "wasting time spreading malice across social media" - which is a fancy way of whining about how we're negatively reviewing the stupid price gouging the DLC is pulling off. Wowee... Sigh.Do we blame Yokoyama for this? Two years ago, Nagoshi and Sato both left RGG and Yokoyama took over and here we are.Anyway, I'm not going around hating this game for stupid reasons. I have gotten all achievements except the NG+ ones, so basically all of them. It isn't the turn-based combat that turns me off - after all, I enjoyed Y7. It certainly isn't the English dub - I kinda care about this but I ain't factoring it into my review. I just feel that the entire quality of the game and its plot is just bad; characters mishandled and the world making less on a fundamental level. Also, it is poorly paced and I discussed it with some people that there is a chapter missing; something bad must've happened in development and the game suffers due to it. I can promise you will be lost on what happened to one specific character.What kills this game for me is that the devs gave up trying to have a good plot. 90% of this game's plot is kicked off because of anime tiddies. You might be thinking "lol that's a joke," or "no way." Yes way, actually. Lemme be clear: anime tiddies in this game are so strong that they go up against the trio of legendary Tojo Clan Officers of Daigo Dojima, Taiga Saejima, and Goro Majima -> AND THE ANIME TIDDIES WIN! I hate what I just typed.An example: a tiny, remote island (that you can't find with satellites) that has with absolutely incredible signal and internet AT ALL TIMES! (obviously not talking about Hawaii)Another: the government passing a Five-Year Clause in response to Y7's Great Dissolution (and it isn't mentioned in Lost Judgement, so RGG made it up specifically for this game) that literally counters the Great Dissolution. Why do we all accept this instead of saying "this makes no sense." When you learn about it, I was like "this has to be a joke, right?" But here I am, alone and wondering why it is accepted.Since I bought that topic up, let me bring up tiddies from Yakuza Kiwami 1: there is a side quest where you meet a chick that has - and the game brings a ton of attention to this -> F-cup breasts. You're lured in to have a drink with her and the drink is very obviously drugged (you can see the bubbling in the drink). You can choose to accept it or you can choose to reject it. Accepting the drink screws you over, but you barge back in and fight to get your money back - meanwhile rejecting the drink skips straight to the fight. Note: you don't fight the lady, but the bartenders who are in-on-it.Why am I bringing this up? Here in whacky Yakuza 8 land, Ichiban gets drugged through drinks and stripped naked - this is the first trailer we see of the game. When the world opens up soon after that very event, there is a side mission with a pretty lady who is planning on drugging Ichiban (in a fairly obvious way tbh... like bruh) to take his money and stuff. You cannot refuse this. You can only infuriatingly watch as it happens.This is incredibly stupid and there is no excuse for this. I wanna meet Ichiban, get him drunk, rob him blind, stab him in the stomach, and immediately apologize -> then, when he believes me -> I'll stab him in the back. No more Homeless Jesus, or whatever RGG is trying with him (I wish I was kidding), and let's get a real character in for the next game, like Akiyama.On the topic of absurd things, this series is FULL of them. The peak used to belong to Y4's "Rubber Bullets" but Y8 has topped it, without side stories. I wanna say it topped it multiple times over and list them... but honestly, it's just lame. Absurd and lame at the same time - that's a new low.It sucks when a series you love has gone soooooo downhill that you're feeling that it is dead... where you've gotta move on and leave it behind... this sucks because this is my situation. Screw you Yokoyama for ruining this series. Yes, I'm blaming you since you're the director of RGG.If you're a big ol' fan of this series, then yeah, get it, maybe on sale. I don't recommend anything more than the basic version. Brace yourself for some stupid story telling that doesn't belong in this series. Despite all I've said, I haven't really spoiled anything.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth is the 9th mainline game in the Yakuza series, taking place in 2023, about 2 years after Yakuza: Like a Dragon. This game was one of the biggest hype points: The return of Ichiban Kasuga, Kiryu becoming a party member in turn-based combat, and a completely new locale in sunny Hawaii, what else could go right? And frankly, it was phenominal.For the shorthand, this game is an easy 9/10. There's still a lot of content packed into this game alongside a more fluid combat system that Yakuza: Like a Dragon had. If you've played previous Yakuza games, it's worth it. If you haven't, pick up 0 and play through chronologically, or pick up Yakuza: Like a Dragon first if you care more about Ichiban's story than Kiryu's.Graphically, this game is beautiful. Upgrades to the Dragon engine allows Honolulu to shine like nothing else the series has had. Instead of the grimy urban jungles of Kamurocho or the more dreary locale of Yokohama, instead we get a bright, sunny city jam packed with color. Whether it be daytime or nighttime, Honolulu has been the pinnacle of graphics in the Yakuza series thus far. The character models, whether it be enemies or party members, have also gotten upgrades visually, especially in certain contexts, such as party members running through water and part of their outfit gets drenched or how the trim on certain clothing pieces reacts with the light. Combat wise it's improved drastically. Like a Dragon was pretty good for a first attempt for a RPG, especially coming from a team who mainly did real time brawler combat, but there were glaring flaws such as not being able to see AoE radius, being unable to move your character to allow for weapon attacks, combat being sluggish even if you massively overlevel your opponent, and even a tedious grind centered mainly around fighting bosses or tracking down and farming vagabonds. Infinite Wealth addresses most concerns players had previously: You can now move your character in a radius to allow you to position for weapon attacks alongside being able to attack in new ways: Proximity ups the damage of your basic attack if you're close (and in some cases changes the attack) and back attacks guarantee they crit while ignoring the enemy's guard if they have it up, all classes gain MP from basic attacks now albeit at a lower rate than previous, if an enemy is way weaker than you you can skip the encounter at the cost of XP, attacks now have better descriptors as well as it tells you the AoE and type, such as radius or a line, and you can even see if a target is resistant to a type of damage before you launch the attack. Combined, this makes the combat more fluid and feel much closer to a RPG than an autobattler with a couple extra steps. Progression has also improved. It takes less XP to level up jobs and characters than before, meaning no more grinding for hours on end to get jobs to the minimum level needed for all inherited skills. On top of this, any skill can be inherited, but you can only inherit 5 normal skills and a Kiwami skill. Jobs not only have more variety, but are also much closer together power wise than in Like a Dragon, where only about one or two non-exclusive jobs were actually worth using over exclusive jobs. There are more ways to increase bond with your teammates, allowing you to see their story quicker and without having to farm for it specifically, such as repeating easy encounters or repeatedly eating at restaurants. Progression not only feels smoother, but also doesn't takes as hilariously long as Like a Dragon's did for max level.However, I do have some criticisms overall. First, it's still a tad bit too easy to amass wealth (the game's title has nothing to do with this). Starting at about chapter 6 I had ~$2mil/200mil Yen. Even spamming poundmates, I would almost always break even or profit off of encounters from there. The game also felt shorter than Like a Dragon from a story standpoint, as it feels like the plot is very slow starting off, only for it to start zooming by later on. The story also has holes in it that should've just been shown rather than inferred, especially for certain major plot points (i.e. in the first chapter, if you don't do the recap of the events of the last game, a certain story thread that was left loose isn't explained). There's also no real proper rewards for doing 100%, whereas other games would give rewards for things like completing all substories or finishing off a character's side story or training, instead the most reward wise you'll get is a couple of moves that Ichiban learns all the time and a weapon or two. Probably the biggest criticism that most players have is also to do with the DLC: the DLC of this game is overpriced and just hacks off content. If you don't get the master vacationer bundle, you lose out on New Game+, an endgame dungeon available in premium adventure, and you can't get every achievement as they're tied to that exclusive content (Steam, unlike Xbox and PS, doesn't isolate DLC achievements into their own category, meaning you have to do them in order to get 100% achievements.). Especially for $20, it's actual robbery that SEGA are trying to nickel and dime us, despite the fact this game is full priced at $70.Overall, this game is phenomenal. Great story, better combat, amazing voice acting, nothing better could be said. However, due to DLC practices and some glaring and odd issues, the game is somewhat held back from being perfect. In future, when this game is available for $20 everything included, it would be great. But for now, if you're going to gun for all the possible content, I'd advise waiting for a sale. If you don't care about achievement hunting or Post-game/NG+, you can just pick up the base game with no skin off your back.9/10. Easily could have been 10/10 if not for the amputation of content to be shoved into a $20 DLC.

_childDocuments_.review: ----- this story is all over the place and i was totally on board with the chaos and twists but personally i felt the ending fumbled a bit — it’s kinda hard to judge this game against previous ones cause it features two protagonists (i wouldn’t even call kiryu a protagonist he gets like 3 chapters as the main focus) so it has to make sure they’re both integral to the plot which dampens other parts… i absolutely loved ichi’s storyline and his final boss (though bryce felt a bit weak, i feel they could’ve done more) but ebina as a villain thematically?? makes sense??? but also he’s already so forgettable as a villain that it pains me that he’s kiryu’s most likely last boss. i understand they probably didn’t want to wear out the “brothers fighting brothers” trope if they assigned ichiban to fight ebina but it seemed like a weird pairing. i’m hoping ebina eventually grows on me the more i think about infinite wealth but for now i’m kinda iffy on him. in terms of characters introduced, though, holy ♥♥♥♥. almost every single new character was instantly admirable and complex (except maybe wong tou and eiji — will elaborate in a second) and they felt relatively fleshed out. yamai was a perfect addition to the cast and he was a pleasure to watch fight with us or against us, as well as understanding his backstory later in the game. tomizawa and chitose are lovely i love them both and akane oh my gosh i love that woman!!!! as perfect as you can get with wrapping up loose ends with kiryu's saga and giving him the appreciation he deserves in giving him back his name. i personally don't prefer infinite wealth's story to 7's, but with how much of a dream game this is it's kinda hard to compare the two as equals. the highs are the highest in the series and the lows are still better than yakuza 4 so hallelujah please go play it!!! _childDocuments_.review: From what I remember, I loved Yakuza 7’s changes of a new, lively protagonist, an interesting approach to turn-based combat, and expansive new minigames and activities. It seemed a great way to keep things fresh, as I actually felt the action beat-em-up stories of Kazuma Kiryu had worn out their welcome by then. Later however, I read into plenty of people’s complaints that these changes were only halfway there in terms of mechanical depth and party flexibility. I also do remember not loving level requirements that game would not warn you of, just to have you walk all the way to a boss to get inevitably crushed, forced back to grinding just to continue the story. As well as this, the minigames didn’t give you that much incentive to participate in them with interesting rewards, outside of pure novelty, which at least to a Yakuza veteran, usually isn’t there anymore.Infinite Wealth seemingly improves on just about … every issue I and many others had with that previous game, showing that while RGG does reuse assets, it’s definitely iterative over “derivative” game design changes that’s gone into making this.Combat is improved to give players more tactical control & options each turn, mainly by allowing manual positioning before initiating actions. You can line up area attacks precisely, prepare combos with your allies, and use more arena weapons strewn about the battlefield for all characters. Jobs don’t take ages to grind through the base ranks to earn all skills, including kiwami ultimates, and I’ve almost never found a “bad” combination of jobs to run my party with, having tried over a dozen. You can mix and match ANY unlocked skill with inheritance slots, earned by progressing Bond levels, allowing you to truly experiment with your personal favorites, for fun and functionality. Going into dungeons or large combat sequences, the game gives recommended level / equipment prereqs, even when necessary grinding outside the story is minimal. Even dealing with trash mobs in the late game is smooth, with “Smackdown” acting as instant wins. It’s honestly great. Adding the setting of Honolulu, Hawaii to the series has been fantastic, as the entire city is as large and detailed (if not more so) than Yokohama. As such, you can now fast travel directly via calling taxis (instead of having to run & find them), as well as a segway to glide around, all with an in-game playlist of Yakuza / SEGA game tracks! You’ll still be running around finding items and cash, greeting and beating up certain strangers along the way: the difference here being regularly rewarded with combat viable items. Party chats are back, alongside more personal walk & talks for individual characters & table talks at restaurants: both of which are encouraged with the greater emphasis on Bond levels in combat. Minigames & dungeons are introduced naturally, with plenty of classics and new additions (some quite literally being ENTIRE separate games at this point) all giving you opportunities to grind & earn unique rewards with usually a nice sidestory to boot. It’s genuinely good side content: stuff you don’t NEED to do to progress the story, but genuinely interesting & rewarding enough that people would want to stop and smell the roses on their own accord. The narrative I couldn’t help but walk away… very satisfied. The plot itself is, I want to say, as good as Y7, but not necessarily as thematically focused: the individual moments were the real highlight. Ichiban is still as lovable as ever, but I particularly enjoyed his character growth in communicating to those he  cares about. The choice to make Kiryu a party protagonist alongside Ichiban, was an interesting one, but they really did pull it off well. After all, it makes sense that a legend nearing his end of days, needs a couple friends to back him up now and then. Homaging his real-time beat-em-up style as a unique “Ultimate” of sorts, as well as his classic Soul, Tech, and Body stats being meshed into the newer RPG mechanics, just felt creatively well handled. The game does a very good job revering Kiryu’s legacy via his bucket list sidestories, rewarding it with stat boosts and summons if you do so.  As such, I always recommend Yakuza 0 or 7 as starting points not requiring any prior knowledge, and if you like those, continue the Kiryu saga at your own pace until then. It will make this chapter more worthwhile, believe me.I will say, the dub here is a lot more  than in 7. I definitely found myself jumping between English for Ichiban’s chapters and Japanese for Kiryu’s (as those characters and their accomplices I’ve come to know with those voices respectively the longest). YongYea’s version of Kiryu was just poorly miscast, and to have that be for Kiryu’s swan song, is truly a shame. Just a fair warning I couldn’t ignore.Lastly, however, I need to discuss the elephant in the room: DLC.  Personally, I never liked the single-use consumables being sold either. Unfortunately, I could see this coming as post Yakuza 7 (or even at the time for Japan), these practices were already in full swing, only getting worse by the time it reached internationally today. Personally, I wish SEGA would stop now before they waste the goodwill they’ve earned over their competitors, all on cheap short-term revenue. It will not last, as I’ve seen many veterans and interested newcomers drop this game entirely on this business practice alone. I understand that, but it’s a shame given how much improved this game is.

_childDocuments_.review: Infinite Wealth is the culmination of almost 2 decades of constant evolution, refinement, and passion. I can confidently say that no other game in the series respects your time as much as this; for long-time fans, the relatively short introductory chapters will feel like something worth celebrating just as much as everything else Infinite Wealth improves upon the established formula. Of course, like it's predecessors, the expected dark narrative tones are executed flawlessly - well enough to invoke memories of RGG's previous magnum opus, Yakuza 0 - and they have gone above and beyond cranking up the dials on the humour, sparing no time to make you laugh and never slowing down, except to leave room for the, often nostalgic, emotional scenes that tie this experience altogether. On top of this, even if you exclude the weirdly addicting, lawsuit-provoking minigames RGG has blessed this title with, the amount of content is still spectacularly overwhelming. Even with dozens of hours of playtime, there is always something new and enticing to experience that, more so than any other game in the series so far, truly serves to enhance rather than bloat.It shouldn't come as a surprise then that I consider Infinite Wealth to be RGG's new greatest accomplishment. Where Yakuza 0 utilised nostalgia to bring the 80s back to life, Infinite Wealth harnesses the nostalgia we all share for the 8 prior games worth of character development and world building to create one of the most important stories RGG has ever told. Combine this with the addicting, innovative gameplay and there is no doubt in mind that this is a title worthy of being heralded best in the series.
_childDocuments_.name: Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth is probably the greatest game I have played in my life. Yakuza is a series that I have loved for many years, and this entry has exceeded all expectations. The base game-play is incredibly fun. The open world of Hawaii is a bustling landscape with many interesting characters to interact with and places to explore. There are so many shops, stores, kiosks, and carts to visit. The world feels alive with various NPCs traveling around the map living life in Hawaiian paradise. Having a dedicated "Aloha" button was something I didn't know I needed. The bright shiny beach never gets old. The fights are dynamic and interesting, this game has one of the best turn based battle systems I have ever experienced. Your teammates can combo, follow up attacks, utilize various surrounding items as makeshift weapons, all on top of an amazing job system. There are also so many sidequests to take part in. The Suijimon quests and Dondoko island are almost entire games by themselves, the fact that they are just a small piece of this game is an incredible feat. All of these are positive areas are also on top of the top notch story which has twists and turns as well as an incredible voice cast. I'm not all the way through the story, but I know it will just continue to get better. I would recommend this game to anyone who likes video games. It is an incredible joy to play.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the 8th entry in mainline Yakuza games and everyone at this point knows what these games are. It is an open world with many activities to do, some very engaging mini-games and wacky side-quests. It's all here just like the games before it.Changes from the last game are most noticeable in combat, the positioning and combos make a lot of difference here and make for some pretty cool moments. Also makes combat faster which in turn makes the encounters more fun. I liked all the new jobs they introduced. No complaints from the gameplay part.Narrative wise I liked the main narrative. I think it had too many characters which makes the story a little bloated and convoluted, but it's not too big of an issue and the characters are cool so it didn't bother me that much. Though I would like them to reign it a bit in future games. Also, I think the substories are not that good this time around, it felt like I had already played them all before. It's disappointing as the substories were most fun in older yakuza games.Summary:I liked it better than the last game, the combat is faster and better and I liked the main narrative better.
