_childDocuments_.review: A great sequel to Yakuza: Like a Dragon and LaD Gaiden, albeit excessive at timesStory is good, carried by Kiryu's involvement and how much investment the player has in his storyline. Ichiban is great and so are the new cast additions; previous cast (with the exception of 1 returning character) gets very little development. 1 portion of the story is excellent while the other comes off as uninteresting.Game is constantly throwing new things at the player (i.e. minigames, side quests, checklists) until 2/3 into the game; a lot of the side content is great, but it can become overwhelming. It is best to enjoy at your own pace; you will have plenty of time to get through nearly everything.Combat is much improved, with many contextual actions being added to give more agency to the player (i.e. weapon attacks, combo attacks, tag team, positional adjustment). New jobs are overpowered, but it doesn't ruin the game.Visuals are great; lots of variety in the environment. Soundtrack is, as always, great. Hawaii is a treat to explore.Overall, it's a great game, especially if you enjoy the character of Kiryu.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth has shaped up to be one of the highest quality games in years. The game being jam-packed with so much content has shocked me because games these days charge a premium price but under-deliver in every way possible. I will acknowledge that I, admittedly, do not like the side games, but I love the main gameplay loop. The story is also good for the most part, albeit scenes can be dragged out at points. If you're looking for a brand-new video game that you will obtain a lot of mileage out of and have multiple weekends to spare, I recommend Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth. Be prepared to play as Kazuma Kiryu, a man with terminal cancer who somehow still has the ability to throw people across entire rooms like it's just another Tuesday afternoon, and Ichiban Kasuga, a guy who can befriend literally the entire world if he wanted to, because he's just that likable.

_childDocuments_.review: Once again, RGG Studio has delivered an absolute gem!If you loved the previous games in the Like a Dragon/Yakuza series, Infinite Wealth is a must-play. This game brings everything you’d expect and then some—an engaging storyline, great character development, and of course, that signature blend of intense drama and hilariously quirky moments.The length of the game is perfect, offering dozens of hours to get lost in side quests, mini-games, and the main story. Every chapter feels rich with detail, and the open world has tons to explore. The cast of characters is phenomenal, mixing the gritty with the heartwarming, and the writing really makes you care about each one of them.Gameplay-wise, it’s a joy. The turn-based combat is still fresh and fun, with plenty of wacky skills and unique enemy encounters. The mini-games and side activities, as always, add so much variety and charm. Where else can you go from high-stakes fights to managing a tropical resort or making friends with some of the strangest people you'll ever meet?All in all, Infinite Wealth is a blast from start to finish. Whether you’re a longtime fan of the series or just looking for an unforgettable RPG experience, this one is worth every penny.

_childDocuments_.review: Out of my 28.6 hours at time of review, I have spent about 10 of those playing the animal crossing riff, which takes place in a dilapidated locale called Dondoko Island. So I don't feel overly qualified to comment on the main game but the island part is pretty damn good.Just being smart: the main game so far has been pretty good, there's so much to do, tons of mini games, including a Pokemon game, of which I've barely scratched the surface. Honolulu is pretty well adapted, much better than other games I've played that take place in real world locations.The story is funny, and Kasuga does a few REALLY cringy things right off the bat (as expected!), but it otherwise has me intrigued and is keeping me guessing. There were a couple of what I would call intensely graphically violent scenes, which aren't my cup of tea. but they were over quick, just a bit too squidgy for my taste.Your team from the last game is with you in varying capacities in the beginning, which takes place in Japan, before you scuttle off to paradise. So far I have been joined by Kiryu and two of the new characters, Tomi and Chitose, who are decent enough characters. I find some of Tomi's battle lines to be grating, but he's certainly shown some good character development so far. Chitose joined me recently, but she is at the exact center of the intrigue I'm currently feeling in the main story. However, I did honestly get derailed in the beginning of chapter 6 because of the Dondoko Island activities (story? what story?).i think the fact that I'm enjoying the main game, and that a frickin mini game has distracted me so completely, the purchase has definitely been worth it for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Joking aside, yeah there's a ton of content here but the game is too damn expensive. The crummy DLC just makes it worse. I haven't bought it or played with it at all, but what it adds isn't anywhere near the price they are charging. It's all extra fluff, outfits and classes, but no additional story or challenges* are added.Much like Yakuza: Like a Dragon, we got another JRPG style game. I don't feel like writing another Yakuza: Like a Dragon review, so just know that gameplay-wise the game is VERY similar, just bigger.With gameplay out of the way, I need to talk about the story. This game does the two stories going at once approach, which the series has done before to good effect, but this time around I felt the story felt a little more "okay." It's hard to describe exactly what felt "okay" about it without going into too much detail, but Ichiban's villain was a little too crazy, even for me. Kiryu's situation since Yakuza 6 and LADG:TMWEHN is even less believable than the insane organization Ichiban is fighting.With the gameplay being more JRPG fights and the story being a little less than what I expected, hopefully the classic Yakuza time-waster minigames would have me hooked: and while I must admit there's a ton of effort and content here, I just found myself getting bored of them. One is a Pokemon parody game, and the other is a fully fleshed out Animal Crossing clone... Unfortunately I already own Pokemon and Animal Crossing, and these imitations were just slower, more grindy versions of those. Some people might absolutely love these, but I'm not really one of them.So from this review, it might sounds like I didn't like this game. Not true, I liked it a lot. But it's probably the most disappointing Like a Dragon game I've played since 5, which I also enjoyed! The scale of the game is enormous, the Hawaii environment is cool, and there's is tons, and I mean TONS of nostalgia bait going on in this game. A big fan of the series should absolutely get it!...Someone who is a little curious, maybe a casual fan of the series, I insist you buy it on sale, maybe 40 dollars, 45 dollars tops. But try to go lower if you can.*Edit: There is an additional dungeon in the DLC, along with New Game+ and Legendary difficulty... All things that were included in the base game in Yakuza: Like a Dragon. Scummy to lock them behind $20, and to be quite honest probably not even worth it unless you absolutely ADORED this video game.

_childDocuments_.review: 150 hours later and all achievements earned apart from those related to finishing NG+, I feel qualified to write this  review. My perspective will be particularly useful to those who got their start on the series with the previous mainline game, like I did. If I had to summarize the experience, I'd say it's quite good, while the previous game was awesome. Here's why: as a new fan, I felt able to play the previous game because it was a reboot with a new protagonist, and it was presented as an action RPG, a genre that engages me more than beat 'em up.Fast forward to Infinite Wealth, and suddenly the previous game was not a reboot at all. In fact, this is ironically the game that requires  knowledge about the Yakuza series. Why they would go this route is besides me, apart from some fan complaint about Kiryu being a bit player in the previous game. Well, one thing is for sure, he definitely shows up in this game, and in fact, a bit less than half of it is about Kiryu. The narrative goes in depth into all of the relatioships he built over the course of the games that starred him, and in spite of Infinite Wealth providing some token context out of pity to new players, it's impossible not to feel lost in that narrative.This would be eased if Ichiban was still the protagonist and we got to see events through his eyes, which would naturally call for greater explanations, but the events are split between Ichiban and Kyriu's parties, which cannot mix until late into the game and have fixed members. Worse, the regions each party acts in are also locked, so you will not be able to complete the side-activities and minigames from one or the other during certain chapters. Also, some playable characters get added to your party so late in the game that it is unexplainable.Overall, all of the above was disappointing, because what made the previous game so much fun was how you could go about it in an open manner while also following a grand narrative. Here there is a strange combination of open world and on rails that to me doesn't feel the same. So, why would I play the game for 150 hours? Well, it's still great whenever the convoluted and sort of pointless narrative isn't dragging it down. The story itself is actually interesting at its core, but the team clearly didn't know how to connect all of the dots, so most plot points fail to land.I'd still say you should play it due to the engaging battles, the minigames, the exploration of a brand new area, the likeable characters, and all of the good things that were already there, to be honest. You just need to adjust your expectations and patience in case you have not been following this series for decades or played the games in order at some point.

_childDocuments_.review: Infinite Wealth feels like it takes one step forward and two steps back (trying my best to be spoiler free)I think RGG have a real gem on their hands with how they've evolved the combat from 7. It feels dynamic, involved, and strategic. Sometimes, the way units position makes it feel like you have little choice in options but, most of the time, it's very enjoyable. Some of the boss fights are honestly the best in the series.I'll be honest, I think the story is a huge swing and a miss, miles worse than 7. It meanders for way too long and feels super bloated. Side content gets shoved in and interrupts main plot progression and takes you totally out of the moment. Some characters and plot elements are extremely undercooked or even idiotic. There's a major plot point that's meant to mirror 7, and the game honest doesn't earn the same emotional payoff because it's just dumped on you and barely expounded upon. However, one of the big highlights of this game are the Kiryu sections, especially with his special to-do list. That content was great and HOPEFULLY gives the man some much needed closure to finally exit the series like he's been trying to do for like 10 years.And, no, contrary to what RGG told us, playing Gaiden is not necessary in the slightest to enjoy this game. The side content is fine. I think they're neat distractions and things you can get a little invested in. Some of the substories are excellent, my favorites being the snow one and the one where a woman scams you, but some are just not interesting or flat-out badly written.Yet, ultimately, I will recommend this game. It's still very competently made and a fun experience, I just don't see it as my favorite (or even one of my favorite) Yakuza/LAD games. If I had to give it a number score, probably a 7/10 or something like that from me. I think RGG has a solid foundation on which to build a great LAD9, but we'll have to see in a couple of years or something.

_childDocuments_.review: Not saying it is a bad game...but...it feels disappointing that as a sequel this offer less content than the previous entry in the series. It didn't feel like it offered enough mini-games to keep moving around the cities interesting. A lot of the mini-games are brought back from previous entries (The Can collection one, and the Sujimon battles, for instance)But... no more Business management mini game, or the Kart racing, or even the RC races which is weird despite the fact that they make references to it, and show you that the place is still there, only to not have you play it anyway. They added a 'crazy taxi food delivery' mini game but... it feels really similar to the can collection one. They added another version of the pervy mini games where you text women and get rewarded with 'sexy pics' and then a soft core video of them....but they also added this joke into it where half of them are just fake people that show up into the room. Like, they make the same joke several times. The story is also not that interesting when compared to the previous entry. Taking a turn to a race for governor, discovering the new mafias of Yokohama, the social commentary with Bleach Japan, all that with a lot of twists that keep the story interesting made the previous game grip your attention throughout. But here? Well...there is a forced return of Bleach Japan but without any content to it...they spend time making a big deal of the dissolution in the past game only to walk that back in this one... there is a cult plot line that doesn't get explored at all. The story begins interesting with a social commentary on the difficulty that former Yakuza have in rejoining society, but it's dropped really soon. The plot about the channel that does exposes of people and cancel them had a lot of potential but then it really goes nowhere ... it was such a let down in comparison. It's cool that all your allies are back on your party, but then again, we are not really given many new characters to make it interesting. We only meet two new people (Chitose is really interesting, the taxi dude, not as much) plus making Kiryu a playable character. Also, some of the characters from before feel like they were added more as an afterthought, since they don't really interact much with the plot at all. In summary, it was a disappointing experience given the expectations that the first installment of the RPG version of LaD left on me.

_childDocuments_.review: In many ways it's better than LAD7. Combat is more strategic since it takes the attack positioning more into account, the difficulty curve is better and gives you more opportunities to challenge yourself, Hawaii is the largest and most detailed location in the series yet, and jobs are more fun to experiment with thanks to the skill inheritance system. I enjoyed Dondoko Island more than the business management mini game last time and if the game wasn't as long as it is I'd go back for more.Unfortunately the story, substories and minigames took a bit of a hit compared to 7. Not like 8 is a big fumble but looking back despite coming across as more ambitious, 7 feels grander since Ichiban goes on a big character journey, really starting from nothing and coming out on top. 8 in comparison tries to juggle two characters stories where Kiryu had a nice arc but with less screen time and Ichiban's is longer yet much of that time feels wasted. Maybe if Kiryu was the main character and had a larger slice of the substory, open world JRPG pie you'd recapture a lot of more of what made 7 stick out as a hero's journey, due to Kiryu's weakened position compared to past entries.Meanwhile crazy eats sucks compared to Dragon Kart, Sicko Snap sucks compared to the cinema, Sujimon collecting is novel but the battles themselves were boring. The academy is back and still fun yet it doesn't hit the same when Ichiban's done this before and maybe I was too good at the game but outside of one island guest I never felt pressured into raising his stats. Most other side activities boil down to going on a point on that map and listening to dialogue. The dialogue is still charming luckily and I enjoyed this more than the side activities themselves since they involve the great supporting cast.I would also like the next game to rely less on quantity over quality with the open world activities, put some more effort into substories that aren't just comedic but try to tell a good self contained story, and for the love of god so stop playing that same cheesy meloncholy song from 0.Now Dondoko Island which is the big business mini game, really clicked with me acting as Animal Crossing without being in real time and a bigger emphasis on attracting tourists. It's really addicting as more and more daily tasks pile on, making your own Yakuza city with iconic buildings is rewarding as your resort grows, they hit the right parts of your dopamine center with the sound effects and animations. If you've ever been grabbed by a game like animal crossing or Minecraft you'd probably enjoy this. Unlike the last game you don't need to do this either as it doesn't break the economy completely and the one in game paywall is nowhere near as expensive as last time, in fact I made the money from the mandatory battles before it.Despite the negativity it is a great game. Certain story moments hit hard and they did a good job on improving 7's issues, but it does feel like a Tears of the Kingdom situation where when you follow up a series revolution it isn't going to hit as hard the second time, and you can create new issues when you lose track of why you revolutionised in the first place. It sits well with the PS3 entries for me, another great installment but flawed and not a favourite

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth is the sequel to Ichiban's story, but this time, the story involves Kazuma Kiryu.I highly encourage you to play Yakuza:Like a Dragon before playing this game because Infinite Wealth sometimes heavily references the past, without going too deep into details.This game feels like a love letter to Kiryu's adventure and his passing of the torch to the new generation: Ichiban Kasuga, the Hero of Yokohama.The story is a bit weaker than its predecessor due to not being as dramatic as Y:LAD, but it is also a matter of bad plot twists that make you go:"Really? Again?". The action mostly happens in Hawaii where Ichiban meets his new team members. The game is structured so that you get a lot of characters, but you can use most of them, instead of just using 4 of them and the rest rotting away in the sidelines.The combat is a big improvement over the last game, implementing environmental attacks and moving in an area to aim your skills more effectively. The jobs are very fun, the accent being on new jobs, but the old classic jobs make a return as well, so you have complete freedom to play as the job you want. Also, a new feature allows Skill Inheritance, so you don't get your skill window bloated by the skills of all jobs, you only get the job's skills and the skills you choose to inherit (I believe 5 normal skills and an essence skill at bond level 100).The game itself was a blast, it felt amazing to play through with all the characters. I think this game is more about Kiryu understand the strong bonds of Ichiban and his friends. I wish there was a bit more development for Ichiban as a character as well, but I do understand that sharing the spotlight with the Dragon of Dojima, doesn't really give you time to shine. Kiryu's part of the story heavily relies on his past and accepting who he is and letting go of all regrets, I really loved his story and I believe it was the highlight of the game. The ending of the game was very satisfying, both Ichiban and Kiryu managing to finish their missions.The bonds were a huge part of the first game, and they're here as well. You have 5 heart events each team member where you get to find out more about them or have a deeper understanding of their motives. Now instead of having 5 bond levels, there are 100 bond levels, but it's easier to get bond levels when you fight, do bond bingos on the map, eat or simply have conversations randomly in the world. But for the last heart event for each character, you just need bond level 50, not 100. 100 is just for Skill Inheritance.Of course, it wouldn't be a Like a Dragon/Yakuza game without a crazy amount of minigames. The new ones include:-Crazy Deliveries which is crazy taxi but on bikes;-Miss-Match which is a dating app for raising Ichiban's personality;-Sujimon battles which is basically Pokemon Battles (this expands on the Sujimon idea from the first game where you were able to just collect them in a "Sujidex");-Dondoko Island which is Harvest Moon, being able to decorate, fish, catch bugs, fight baddies etc. I must say though, I hated the combat on Dondoko Island, it felt very clunky.New Game Plus felt a little bad to play at first because of stuff like when a new character joins the party, it's automatically equipped with a level 1 weapon which does no damage. It certainly feels like NG+ was an afterthought, for example, the only thing that scales in NG+ is character XP and job XP. The loot remains the same as in the base game. I think that, with a bit more attention to details, this feature would've been more enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's face the truth, this series has become Japanese/ Yakuza Saint's Row and it's not a bad thing.These games have always been a little zany in the mini games and side quests, which is why when you make the connection to being like saint's row in that it's serious stuff going in a dark criminal underworld but here's a minigame where you build a kooky island resort from the ground up and get rid of trash by destroying it with a bat.I have only played all like a dragons and yakuza 0. So, my opinion may not hold as much weight to some of the die hards of this series.I only have one real complaint. In the previous entries, there was always a major mini game to make money. I.e. real estate mogul or host club king. In this game's version of that, the money you make from that is a pitance by comparison to the money you wind up with just grinding out your levels/job levels in the dungeon. it made all the effort spent developing the island feel like a waste of time because what was the point other than oooo, look how pretty my island is and completing the minigame/substory for the achievement. The main character developed in the minor ways in this story. To some, it may seem like he didn't have any development but it's much more subtle, like any other regular superhero in a normal game. It's also important to remember this guy is in his 40's most people get stuck in their ways by then. But, I was satsified with this story and the way they told the story of everyone involved. I do worry about how the story would continue from here or what in the world could possibly happen from this point on to create another continuing entry but i'm still excited to play another one.

_childDocuments_.review: I think overall I can recommend this title but only for people who will take about anything RGG will throw at you. For anyone else, or people who have only played 7, I really don’t think there’s much in store for you. The RPG combat is intensely flawed with many baffling design choices (for example, having to wait for the other party members to randomly shuffle close enough together for your area of effect heal to actually work instead of just making it a standard group heal)You can’t walk into most any store throughout Hawaii, daytime looks atrocious as does when it rains, most locations of note are extremely far apart separated by countless empty buildings and you are berated by more enemies at a higher frequency than any other game in the series, all adding up to making open world traversal feel like you’re walking through drying concrete. most side content is fine but very surface level unless it’s Dondoko island (which you’ll hate if you’re not an animal crossing new horizons fan) or Sujimon (which you’ll hate will hate if you’re not a Pokémon fan, bizarre that they did this with two Nintendo games). Many side quests do suffer from being extremely boring, with most never ever hitting the emotional relatability of prior titles. A good way for me to describe this is prior LAD games will have a side quest open with wild characters in a weird as hell situation, but it turns out the weird people are suffering from deeply human issues and you take the time out of your day just to take the effort to make them happy. Often with this game that basic premise is there but the execution is just sort of off and most issues boil down to “I am being bullied by X group and can’t defend myself”. I’m confident to sit here and say the narrative is the worst in the series. I was HOOKED with the first couple of chapters, but the game really loses the plot and meanders for immense amounts of time, feeling like it’s actively going on tangents that are a total slog but feel like an overly busy mess when looking back on the narrative because it happens so frequently. This is the first LAD storyline I thoroughly dislike, and found myself extremely exhausted trying to push through. I’ve found plenty of bugs in the game that have been ironed out with time, but HDR is absolutely borked. I have an amazing OLED display that I’ve calibrated with the proper equipment and the HDR just cannot ever ever ever look right, and I don’t think it’ll ever be fixed. It’s a shame, because Gaiden just before this has great HDR, along with Lost Judgement. I could say a LOT more, but the game has honestly just exhausted me and kind of bummed me out. All of the joy has subsided and I’m left with what feels like a lopsided mess that doesn’t have a lot of the things I love about the series, or even things I loved about 7. Hopefully Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii will pull me back in again, because this game has me generally worried about where the series is heading next. I truly think there’s a great game buried in all of this, but it needed another couple of years in the oven, and the devs need to either learn how to properly make fun turn based combat or just drop it entirely because it REALLY really really took a lot of enjoyment out of this title (and again I am a big fan of 7 and many other turn based RPGs, Infinite wealth just has a laundry list of very annoying and sluggish design choices for combat).

_childDocuments_.review: Infinite Wealth is a fantastic game that builds upon the foundation set by its predecessor, making notable improvements to the battle mechanics and depth of side content. I had an enjoyable experience playing and I think anyone who enjoyed LAD 7 will enjoy this title as well. The story is weaker but still a banger and the side quests are great as always, same lovable RGG nonsense that we're all used to. My one gripe with the game (aside from wahh wahh SEGA bad shut up guys I know 90% of you never actually gave a ♥♥♥♥ about NG+) is that the transition between parties from Chapter 8 onward turns into a clunky experience. It's a small problem but it turns into a massive headache over time. I'll grind in the Hawaii dungeon for a few hours, finish the chapter, then realize my Japan party is underleveled and it's back to grinding. I'll be in Chapter 13 Hawaii and realize the 5* weapon I need for one of my characters' endgame 7* recipe is only obtainable in Japan -- great, guess I have to go into the final battle without it. Then I'll be playing with one party and think about my next move with one character until I realize that's only on my Hawaii party character. On one occasion I started a battle after getting into a new chapter and remember I forgot to re-gear because party gear is shared and there's no way to save equipment loadouts. Just really clunky and poorly thought-out. Endgame content also drops off heavy if you're not a Kiryu simp. 8.5/10 idk

_childDocuments_.review: As a westerner who generally finds JRPG's boring, Ryu Ga Gotoku did an excellent job with their titles.  The predecessor was excellent and very much in my top 10 list for story writing.  I quickly bought this sequel after completion of the former. My stance on Infinite Wealth is that it is still a solid sequel to it's predecessor; however, not too much has changed from the original and everything feels very familiar - just in a different setting.   I found myself getting exhausted nearing the end and wanted to just finish it.   There are some new additions that add some spice to the formula, but overall they do feel unnecessary and tacked on without any real reason to do them aside from breaking up the formula. The story itself is definitely not as compelling as its predecessor.  That being said, it is still very well written compared to 99% of other story based games on the market. Overall, it is a good sequel, but not a great sequel.  For me, it did drag on far longer than it should have.  I would have preferred a shorter, but sweeter sequel - but that is just my opinion.  8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 5, again.I've been playing these games for twelve years, and consider a few of them in my all-time favorites. After Gaiden, my expectations for Infinite Wealth's narrative were through the roof, and I'm sad to say it fell short of those lofty heights in a number of ways. IW tries to do a lot with too little time and ground. It's a long, long game, but not long enough to tell what basically amounts to three main stories; it shines in side content and substories, yet most of these do nothing to reinforce the main narrative. The changes and improvements it makes to Y7's base structure in combat are unmitigated achievements, yet challenge is sparse unless you delve into postgame content. So why do I still love it so much?Like Yakuza 5, the emotional highs trump everything else for me. I can forgive a lot of flaws if a piece of media wrings enough emotion out of me to make me cry, and Infinite Wealth, like Gaiden and Y7, manages to do just that. The sincere goodness in its protagonists' hearts tramples over every flaw I'd lay against the writing otherwise, because there are so few games I've played that read as genuinely tearful affirmations of humanity. Ichiban makes me wish there were more.

_childDocuments_.review: Pro:- huge story with many heartwarming characters, intriguing plottwists and many sidestorys to explore- big maps to discover for newcomers aswell as lots of added extras for returning yakuza players- lots of quality of life features like fast travel, auto battle, newly added transportation method with auto navi drive function, etc- many ways to play the game from equipment to unclock to classes which have different designs and animations for their attacks and finishers- huge amount of playable minigames from traditional card games to spin off minigames like crazy taxi or pokemon snap lookalikes with own reward lists and point systems for every minigame- lots and lots of dialogue to learn more about every characterCon:- the new dungeon system with random pattern layouts that get boring quick (I prefer the fixed dungeon layouts from the previous game more as even running through all the areas of all dungeons gave more variety as any of the random components in the new system can give you after beating any dungeon for whatever amount of times. In short: if you've seen one of the new layouts, then you've seen all of what the new dungeons have to offer optically, layout- and enemy-wise)- lots of old systems, locations, npcs aswell as their random dialogue has been copy pasted from the original, but there are some times you can find additional dialogue referencing the previous game or other conclusions to storylines from known characters and npcs, but a lot of the old maps contents are untouched and only the hawaii map has the all new content in gameAlmost as good as the previous game but new implemented features and mini games feel a bit shallower than before. The game has way more content than expected and feels like a big new story dlc for the original title and is just more of what I already love. But all in all it feels just like were getting more of what already worked with some added features that could've needed some more time to be fully fleshed out. Some of the features would even have the potential for another game to be made just by evolving the separate game modes even further.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely loved every moment I had with this game. Having played and beaten every mainline game in the series seeing Infinite Wealth filled with references from every game made me so happy. The combat was my favorite part of this game and made grinding so much fun. Getting to level 70 and the legendary weapons make you a god by end game. Tomizawa and Chitose were great additions to the story and added a lot to the party. My biggest problems with this game were the villains and overall story. The main villains were probably the weakest antagonists in the series which is weird since Yakuza bosses are among the strongest parts of the game.As for the story, they made a lot of odd decisions. This is really a Kiryu story. Character development? Kiryu. Personal stakes? Kiryu. There's really no relation between Kasuga and the main antagonist, just a villain of the week. The best moments were Kiryu memories. The most interesting character mechanics were Kiryu's. Not complaining since I love Kiryu, but Kasuga and his character progression were a second thought overall. All that said, I absolutely adore this game and you should definitely play it.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth totally knocks it out of the park! If you loved the last game, you’re in for a treat. The combat system has been seriously upgraded with awesome new job classes and abilities that make each fight more exciting and strategic. It’s way smoother and more fun to play.The game world is huge and packed with cool new places to explore. You’ll find yourself getting lost in the vibrant environments, and there’s always something interesting around the corner. It’s way more immersive and engaging than before.The story is a huge step up, diving deeper into Ichiban’s life and throwing in some pretty wild twists and turns. The new characters are fantastic, and the whole narrative feels richer and more gripping. You’ll really get attached to the characters and their journeys.And let’s not forget the side activities! The minigames and side quests are back and better than ever. Whether you’re into quirky mini-games or tackling challenging side missions, there’s tons of stuff to keep you entertained. It’s perfect for taking a break from the main story and just having some fun. The combat system is sharper than ever, with new job classes and abilities that make battles more strategic and exciting. Smooth animations and tweaks to gameplay make every fight and interaction more enjoyable. The game world is bigger and more diverse, offering tons of new places to explore and enjoy. There’s a great mix of minigames and side quests that add a lot of fun and variety to the game. The story digs deeper into Ichiban’s life with richer character development and engaging plot twists. Fresh faces and returning favorites bring new dynamics to the story. The twists and turns keep the narrative exciting and full of surprises. The graphics are improved, making the game world look even more immersive and vibrant. Stays true to the series’ unique style while adding new visual elements. Features a catchy and fitting soundtrack that enhances the game’s atmosphere. Top-notch voice acting that brings the characters and story to life. The graphics are improved, making the game world look even more immersive and vibrant. Stays true to the series’ unique style while adding new visual elements.Overall, Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth takes everything great about the last game and makes it even better. _childDocuments_.review: After getting into the series with Yakuza:Like a Dragon in March last year I am now back at the end with Ichiban again and I'm actually happy to have Kiryu in this game as well, but the game still managed to leave a bit of a sour note. Still an enjoyable game but not my favorite one of the series.Gameplay:They did a great job and managed to do what a sequel should: keep the basic gameplay and improve it. We get new cool jobs as well as the old ones. Kiryu and Ichiban get a special move later on, where Kiryus is a form of the old action combat format but just as a remnant. Still a nice idea.There are lots of Mini Games like always and the build up the Sujidex from the last game to a full monster battler, as well as a Sujimon Snap and Dodonko Island.Maybe that's a personal negative point, but I didn't need the auto battle function. Instead I would've liked the old short cuts for skills back instead. Dodonko Island wasn't my cup of tea as well, though that's probably because I never showed interest in Animal Crossing. Just seems like they put a lot of work into that one, which could've been used elsewhere. The "Essence-Move" you get as a reward was really boring. Just the same laser like in the last game with another colour.Story:One of the important aspects of Yakuza and here is where they fumbled the bag imo. We get a nice start to why Ichiban goes to Hawaii and meets Kiryu, it builds up to be interesting and ends pretty meh.That Ichiban is a loveable airhead who sees good in people is completely fine as a character, but instead of letting him grow to become better, they just ramp up the "is an idiot"-section to 100. Chitose and Tomi were redeemable characters but ♥♥♥♥ Eiji. In 7 Ichi was way better as a character and would've been a promising new Protagonist if they would build up on him instead of down.Kiryu gets finally some crumbs thrown his way to maybe get an rather quiet ending. Though it could've been handled better it was at least something. The Daidoji plot was all over the place like always. In one game they have so much money and control that Kiryu is reduced to nothing and can't do anything about it and here they have just 4 people to send to Hawaii with him and some nobody with a shaky camera can reveal his identity without them noticing anything.Daigo, Goro & Taiga get used as a muscle up as always while Kiryu trash talks them even though he wrote that heartfelt letter to Daigo in 6. The old "you're all responsible, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up while fixing it and need to fix it again"-spiel is pretty tiresome. Those guys deserve more respect imo. Though the fight itself was pretty awesome, especially the section where the combat action gimmick comes into play. Being surrounded with all the old pictures while punching it out was really nice.Best new character was Yamai. His story was one of the best things in this game and having Takehito Koyasu as his voice actor the cherry on top. Would be nice to see im again in the future as an potential teammate.Graphic and music was great as well while running smooth. Had no bugs or problem with this game.I just hope that they can get a better grasp on the situation and if they want to retire Kiryu or not. Also I hope they didn't pump to much budget into having people like Danny Trejo in the game. There is no need to get Hollywood stars into these game to gather more western attention. Instead they should stop hearing what a tiny minority of the western "gamers" have to say about certain aspects in japanese games. Especially localization should be better controlled so people don't bring in buzzwords or memes where they don't belong. Just like German Dubs, while pretty good, always had to add something like "dude" in sentences even though the original was completely different in some animes.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh boy, so let me start off by saying I really enjoyed the First like a Dragon and I really do wish I enjoyed Infinite wealth... I just don't.So to start off with the actually combat; it's functional however it's not much different from the first game. There are a few additions yes (Such as been able to position yourself before using a skill which does help hit additional enemies.) it's ultimately I found myself using the same set of skill with the same set of classes as I did with the first game. By the time I got to the end of the game I was actively avoiding battle just because I felt they were a slog to get through. Not hard just dullStory wise I found the game lacking, without spoiling it I called almost every single plot point at least a few hours before they were revealed in game where as the first game did take me off guard on more than a few moments. The new characters/ party members introduced I found very flat and lacking. Even after doing the side content to get to know them better (which is it's own can of worms of sheer boredom) I just didn't care unlike the first game.Ultimately without making this review 10 years long I'll brake it down like this. Infinite wealth is a bit like having too much of a good thing. If you've played the first game I wouldn't bother with this one unless you really want more of the same, even then I'd wait for a sale for it.I really, REALLY, wanted to like Infinite wealth but I just couldn't bring myself too in the end.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an absolute masterpiece!! The story is engaging and full of gripping character moments, the world has never felt so large and bustling thanks to how social Honolulu feels, and my GODD the music slaps. I love all of the new characters - Tomizawa, Chitose and Yamai are all so so much fun, and there are so many returning characters and it was awesome to check in with them allThis game presents such an interesting side to Kiryu. Due to his difficult situation, you see a lot more inner conflict than has been present in any previous Yakuza game. This game truly portrays Kazuma Kiryu at his most vulnerable, which is such an intriguing angle to approach him from. And going and revisiting all of his old memories felt truly nostalgic.As always, the side content is great in this game. I spent about 12 hours of playtime just on Dondoko Island alone because, when it opened up, I was so hooked that I played start to finish barely leaving the island. The Sujimon battling isn't as fun to me, but I appreciate how silly a gamemode it is. And, as always, the substories are incredible, with some being your typical goofy Yakuza substory and some being very... melancholic.After finishing the game today I'm so not thrilled that, for the next two or three years, that cliffhanger is going to have to sit in my head while I wait for Yakuza 9. But *that* pain just speaks to how truly great the plot of this game was. When you look over it as a whole it is maybe a little shallow but it's watching it unravel and experiencing the solid character moments that makes the game's plot feel specialIn conclusion: Play video game

previous game in the series, I can see how much  has been put into making this.The game is full with very well placed references, properly used fan service, not just because every other long running RPG series where each game is connected to the previous ones does it…but because the developers know how much the series matters to them, and of course, to us.And yeah, with Infinite Wealth here being one of the  (I’d say it’s bigger than Yakuza 5, and that game is pretty long), well I could only keep taking my sweet time and ponder about all the stuff that the series has gone through, and all these characters, and it’s so good, so, so well done, really.This is a PC review, though, so let’s throw in some Performance information here, shall we?On my , much like with LAD Gaiden, this game can doing the Kiwami remakes and later using Dragon Engine, but clearly Infinite Wealth here represents the peak of their animation, and hopefully they can continue with this level of quality in future titles.The  has some incredible pieces, especially for the , it really does sound like a trivial thing to say, since the series has some truly memorable pieces, but yeah the music in this game is overall pretty epic, quite happy with most of it, especially certain couple tracks in the latter chapters and the finale…damn. wise is where the biggest improvements can be instantly noticed, coming I find it still has room for even more improvements and tweaks, especially when it comes to certain status effects and debuffs but, overall, having played Infinite Wealth now…it’d be very difficult to go back to the previous game’s system, which was very basic. were, mostly, quite good, with excellent character bonding scenes, they were all very good, there’s a lot of camaraderie going around, lots _childDocuments_.review: This game did not disappoint whatsoever...it is just phenomenal. It does everything the first one did and improved on it in every way. From the characters, sub stories, settings, combat, music, and story, it is all so good. This is the type of game where if you don't do most or all of the stuff it offers to you, you truly haven't played this game correctly. I feel like I took a whole vacation in Hawaii after this game. The new classes in this one are really fun and the way they split stories gives you a chance to try out more classes at a given time now which is really great. You can think of this game as a trip down memory lane or a tribute to some extent with certain characters and if you have played the other Yakuza games, it hits hard.    They went to town on the Sujimon aspect of the game, and it is pretty much Pokemon but if Pokemon was done right honestly. You can spend hours just on that bit alone and I haven't even got every thing yet. Some of the major side games from the previous game come back which I didn't expect but a nice addition and the arcade games in this one are really great too. This music doesn't disappoint and there are plenty of CDs to get and listen to along the way.   Overall, not many games can captivate me from start to finish such as this one and I simply did not want it to end. You feel like you've been on a vacation by the time you finish and there will still be a lot more to do afterwards (if you are a completionist that is). All the new characters were great, even got new favorite ones like Yamai of all people. The performance of the game is great, ran better than the first, at least for me, even in most dense areas of the game. If you are a fan of turn based games as well, this game executes it very well and all the special moves you acquire make it enjoyable and fresh. Simply play this game is all I can say!

_childDocuments_.review: Negatives:-Once you reach level 20 the game significantly reduces how much base level and job XP you obtain, making the grinding at level 20 very tedious, even after progressing the story.-You only get an XP or job boost of 20% per accessory, with a max of 40% if you equip both. In Yakuza 7 each one gave 50% and if you had both of either equipped you would get 2 TIMES MORE XP, meaning that you get LESS THAN HALF as much XP in Infinite Wealth compared to Yakuza 7.-Smackdown which is the game's take on quickly killing weak enemies, is not fast enough; it still takes like 10 seconds to do it, for both the unnecessary animations and the result menu to finish.-Navigating the long list of menus is too slow and tedious, this problem is prevalent with armor, accessories, items and weapons, especially items.-They removed the feature to quickly use skills with keybinds that was in Yakuza 7, a game that is more than 2-years-old.-You can't change your character's job/class until chapter 5, which is almost halfway through the game.-The "Street Surfer" which is the electric scooter, can be completely missed if you never complete a specific substory.-Despite XP boost items helping, they still hinder how much MP you have by a lot, making fights a lot slower and painful.-Crafting the best weapon for each job requires you to find and fight a specific boss at specific points on the map in a specific city.-There's only like two weapons per star tier, which gets rid of the freedom of having multiple great weapons.-There's too many different recovery items, and the amount of space you have for each one is too little. This creates the problem of constantly scrolling through the item menu to recover your team's HP and MP outside of battle, and having to waste multiple minutes going to several shops on the map to restock.-The "Nostalgic sites" that you encounter as Kiryu later on literally just boils down to Kiryu saying "Ah I remember when that happened, those were good times..." which adds nothing to the story.-Sujimon battles are the most bare-bones turn-based Pokémon rip-off.-Enemies have a lot more HP, making grinding to level up a massive pain since it makes fights last too long and forces you to waste too much MP, use up too many items, and constantly upgrade everything. I understand that bosses as a whole and the enemies that appear in the story need to be strong, but outside of that, it becomes excessive.-The amount of items you get from enemies is too little, even when equipping multiple pieces of equipment that boost drops.-Dondoko island is a lot like a mix between Minecraft and Animal Crossing, but more tedious. I completed it, and it just boils down to spamming the attack button and choosing the buildings with the greatest satisfaction. You have little to no freedom to build what you want, since there's too little space to build and guests ask for too much.-Each Sector in Hawaiian haunt and the Yokohama dungeon has a big difficulty spike. Despite grinding each floor for so long, each new sector made my party feel extremely weak.-Both Hawaaian and Yokohama dungeons always place enemies in very small rooms which makes it impossible to run away from fights in most scenarios, unless you constantly use smoke bombs to escape.-Some rooms have obstacles in the way making it impossible to walk around enemies that are blocking your way. Other rooms have enemies continuously facing the entrance of the area they're blocking, which forces you to fight them.-The more simplistic layouts of the dungeons from Yakuza 7 are better than the procedurally generated ones because they don't lead to so many dead ends, and they are easier to navigate.-There are enemies inside two specific dungeons that give more XP (Transcendent Transient hobos), but instead of being easy to kill with the right skill like in Yakuza 7, this enemy ALWAYS gets their turn at the beginning of the fight and the first thing they always do is protect themselves and reduce like 80% of damage you do, just to run away on their third turn.-The safe rooms are mostly a waste of time since one out of two safes contain a boss that only gives basic enemy loot and one safe that gives the same loot you earn by just finding the exit of each floor.-Eventually both Kiryu and Ichiban separate into separate teams; the problem with this is having to grind both teams levels to progress the story since once they separate, they won't be getting back together for the entire game.-Another problem with your team separating is that you have a lot less freedom to choose your party members, since you only get two to one additional party member on both parties throughout the whole game.-Personality stats are just the game's way of locking good jobs behind tedious, repetitive grinding and boring trivia tests.-Sometimes in a fight, your characters will move away from the outline of the skill, so for example, it shows a skill that hits in a straight line, and you point it to hit as many people as possible, the attack will completely go in a different direction. This is even more common with tag team attacks that you unlock with drink links.-Three out of the four antagonists seem one-dimensional, lacking the complexity that makes characters feel human. It would be more engaging if the villains had deeper motives beyond generic desires for power and wealth.-The only well-developed antagonist in the entire game appears as the final one, having compelling motives and an excellent backstory. However, a significant drawback is that much of his background is only revealed during the final boss encounter, conveyed through an eleven-minute monologue.Positives:-The soundtrack, cutscenes, and animations are the best in the series.-Being able to move around in combat and the majority of skills having range to them, which incentivizes you to aim and strategize, made the combat much more engaging and fun.-Ichiban's eventual meetup with his mother was perfect and worth the buildup.-Being able to equip and unequip anything from both Ichiban and Kiryu's team at any time is an amazing quality of life feature. This also includes jobs.-This is the best-written version of Kiryu, so much of his personality shines a lot more, and the entire game makes him a lot more human.-Dragon of Dojima job is the best and most fleshed-out job in the series, especially since you don't need a weapon to use it, which also gets rid of the necessity of grinding to get a great weapon for Kiryu.-Weapon attacks (The ones you find on the floor) are much more common and easier to use, which adds a lot more interactions in most fights.-Kiryu's final dungeon is outstanding; it is a lot shorter but packed with so many engaging fights, great interactions and more engaging map design.-The final two chapters are the highlight of the story, easily being some of the best in the series.-It has more than double the amount of jobs.-The ending is one of the best in the series; it is very satisfying and uplifting.-Seeing Kiryu's interaction with some of the characters that he helped in past substories in other Yakuza games was short and sweet.-The eventual fight between Daigo, Majima and Saejima was even better than the fight in Yakuza 7 against Majima and Saejima.I liked the game's story and characters, but the grinding, lack of many qualities of life features, and lack of freedom to play how you want made me massively dislike the game.

Gameplay, amount of content and characters were great but I feel the wacky side content was concentrated between the two main side stories (island and sujimon) leaving not much outside of that. I did skip a ton of the standard mini-games throughout the world, but usually there's something aching to the cabaret club to hook me in these games side stuff, and the island wasn't it leaving me a little dissatisfied on that front.The main story I felt was among the weaker ones of all the Yakuza titles. Too many story threads, too many bad guys and some of the events were downright silly (and i mean the bad kind, not the wacky stuff we love like punching tigers). I would give this game an 8.5/10. _childDocuments_.review: Rating: ★★★★★Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth takes the classic RPG formula and catapults it into a realm of infinite possibilities. As a fervent fan of the franchise, I eagerly delved into this latest installment, and I can confidently say that it not only met but exceeded my expectations.The first thing that struck me was the game's mesmerizing graphics and attention to detail. The bustling cityscape of Kamurocho has never looked so alive and vibrant. The neon lights, dynamic weather, and meticulously crafted environments create an immersive experience that keeps you hooked from start to finish. The transition between exploration and combat scenes is seamless, making the world feel cohesive and interconnected.The narrative, as expected from the Yakuza series, is a rollercoaster of emotions. Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth introduces a fresh protagonist, compellingly portrayed by a talented cast. The story weaves together elements of crime, drama, and humor, providing a narrative tapestry that keeps players engaged and invested in the characters' fates. The script is witty, emotionally resonant, and at times, surprisingly poignant.Combat in Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth undergoes a revolutionary transformation, adopting a turn-based RPG system. The shift from the series' traditional brawler-style combat may initially raise eyebrows, but the execution is nothing short of brilliant. The tactical depth and strategy required in battles add a new layer of complexity to the game, keeping combat fresh and engaging throughout the entire playthrough.The character progression system is robust, allowing players to tailor their party members to their preferred playstyles. The job system offers a plethora of options, from traditional roles like "Hero" and "Mage" to more unconventional choices, such as "Idol" and "Chef." Experimenting with different combinations keeps the gameplay dynamic and ensures that no two playthroughs are the same.Infinite Wealth lives up to its title with an expansive array of side activities and mini-games. From managing a virtual business empire to participating in go-kart races, there's no shortage of ways to amass wealth and enhance your character's abilities. These diversions not only provide a welcome break from the main storyline but also contribute to the overall sense of immersion in the game world.In conclusion, Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth is a triumphant addition to the Yakuza series. It successfully blends the familiar charm of the franchise with innovative gameplay mechanics, stunning visuals, and a captivating narrative. Whether you're a long-time fan or a newcomer to the series, this game is a must-play for anyone seeking a rich, immersive, and endlessly entertaining RPG experience.

detailed_description: JOIN OUR DISCORD COMMUNITY About the Game GOT WHAT IT TAKES? Viewers at home, here's the news you've been waiting to hear: THE FINALS is accepting new contestants, and that means YOU! That's right, soon the world could be watching YOU tear apart our newest dynamic arenas and seize everlasting fame! As you know, THE FINALS is the world's greatest free-to-play combat game show! Our contestants plug in to our virtual world and join teams in escalating tournaments. They fight it out in our beautifully-rendered arenas based on real-world locations that they can alter, exploit, and even destroy. Sure, you can aim and shoot, but contestants that add our carefully curated virtual environments to their arsenal are more likely to advance, so do anything you can imagine in the name of victory! Burn arenas to the ground! Send wrecking balls crashing into your opponents! Don't just pull triggers - pull down buildings! Gather fans and fame as you craft a unique avatar with the help of our generous sponsors and dazzling customization options! GET FAMOUS This is the opportunity of a lifetime. Arenas based on iconic places, unparalleled destruction, and endless tactical possibilities await - make them your own, and the floodgates of fame will open. _childDocuments_.review: As a frequent player of FPS games, I was drawn to "The Finals" for its promise of innovative gameplay and dynamic destruction. Developed by Embark Studios, this game has many strengths but also some notable areas for improvement.Gameplay Mechanics: The core shooting mechanics are robust and satisfying. Each encounter feels significant, with responsive controls that reward skillful play. The highlight is undoubtedly the environmental destruction. It adds an intriguing strategic element, allowing players to reshape the battlefield in real-time. However, this feature can occasionally be a double-edged sword, as it sometimes leads to unpredictable and chaotic situations that can feel overwhelming.Visuals and Audio: The game's presentation is unique, blending a competitive FPS with a game-show aesthetic. The graphics are impressive, with destructible environments that are both visually and tactically engaging. The audio design is equally strong, with impactful sound effects that heighten the intensity of battles.Performance and Stability: Here lies one of the game's main issues. While I enjoyed smooth gameplay most of the time, I did experience high ping and occasional lag, which can be frustrating, especially in a game where timing and precision are crucial. This seems to be a common complaint among players and something the developers should prioritize addressing.Community and Multiplayer Experience: The team-based gameplay is compelling, encouraging cooperation and strategy. However, the matchmaking system sometimes creates unbalanced teams, leading to one-sided matches. The community is active and mostly positive, but like any competitive game, it can have its moments of toxicity.Verdict: "The Finals" is an ambitious and largely successful FPS that brings fresh ideas to the table. The environmental destruction and strategic depth are standout features, but the game is marred by technical issues like high ping and occasional matchmaking imbalances. I rate "The Finals" a 7.5/10. It's a game with tremendous potential, but one that needs further refinement to fully realize its promise.

_childDocuments_.review: » If there’s one genre that lends itself to boom or bust, it's the online shooter. For every success like Call of Duty, Halo, or Apex Legends, it seems like there are at least a dozen other games that have come and gone with barely a spark before they fizzle. With so many good competitive shooters in play, what makes one stand out? After dozens of hours, I’m beginning to see how  answers those questions: with an excellent gameshow-infused style and a brilliantly destructible playground.» There are currently two main modes: the first, Quick Cash, has each team vying to collect a vault of coins and deposit it at a designated spot on the map, which tends to result in the bloody convergence of all three squads at those points. This effectively keeps the action going, and because taking over the deposit doesn’t reset its progress, rounds move steadily and avoid momentum-killing stalemates altogether.Meanwhile, the Bank It mode focuses a bit more on direct PvP battles, but they also tend to be more scattered. Here, each player carries coins in their virtual pockets, all of which is gathered either from vaults around the map or by eliminating enemies. The on-the-fly strategizing of going for kills one second and then needing to deposit your loot before it all goes to waste the next is exciting, and it’s pretty fun to eliminate someone right in front of the bank so you can deposit all their coins yourself.Individually, both modes are well-designed and generally very fun. The fact that The Finals is limited to just those two options, however, is a red flag. If the player base starts to grow tired of these game types and there aren’t any other options, there is a real possibility of people moving on before too long. While I didn’t find that to be an issue during my time playing, that does present a potential concern for the long-term health of this community that I hope is addressed with new modes in future updates.Once you’ve played a few matches you’ll unlock tournaments, and this is where the competitive attitude of The Finals really shines. The primary tournament mode puts you and seven other teams in a bracket playing modified versions of Cashout. Two games of four teams each run simultaneously, with the top two squads from each game advancing to the second round. The top two teams from that game then face off in a direct 3v3 match to determine the overall winner. It does a great job mixing the high-stakes nature of actual competition with rounds that are fast and satisfying enough to elicit that “just one more game” feeling after each tournament. There’s a ranked version, where players can move up in leagues based on their performance.» You can choose from three different weight classes for your character, and they all play very differently from each other. The Light build, for example, focuses on mobility, trading stopping power for a grappling hook to quickly get to high or far places. The Medium, meanwhile, is an all-rounder and has abilities that focus on support, such as its healing beam. Finally, there’s the Heavy, which could have been taken straight from Rainbow Six: Siege, as it alternates between controlling the battlefield with heavy weapons and smashing through walls like the Juggernaut.There’s a solid variety of equipment for you to choose from before each match, and they can have a major impact on the battlefield if used properly. There are standard choices, like frag grenades and deployable cover, and those are tried and true options that do what you’d expect – but they hardly stand out when you can instead drop jump pads that launch you high into the air, or goo grenades that can seal large spaces with an expanding foam. Some options are universal, like the pyro grenades, while others are restricted to specific classes like the Medium builds’ defibrillator that instantly revives downed teammates.» Each character archetype also has a litany of cosmetics that can be unlocked through XP progression or by spending real-world money. There’s a pretty solid assortment to choose from right out of the gate, though the amount of time it takes to unlock good-looking items (without taking out your wallet) requires major retuning. After 20 hours, the best I could afford was some fanny packs and tights on one character, which makes getting the whole squad glammed up feel like a pipe dream.That slow progression is also true of VRs, the in-game “cash” you earn for playing that’s used to unlock non-cosmetic things like different abilities, weapons, and gadgets. I get that there needs to be a balance between giving you everything too soon, which can take away the joy of progression, and making it take too long to earn things, but right now The Finals skews a bit too much towards the latter. It’s hard to experiment with builds when all the pieces for each character are locked behind dozens of hours of matches.» The destructibility of each stage is the real star of The Finals. Sure, you can enter a room from the door or window. But taking the less obvious path of crashing right through the ceiling is a thrilling way to get the drop on unsuspecting teams, and you haven’t played The Finals until you’ve stolen the vault by blowing a hole in an upper floor and had it drop right in front of you. By the end of a tense match, the battlefield is often littered with debris from entire buildings beginning to collapse.There’s a lot more to that system than some cool rubble and an ad hoc door, too, as the strategic impact is huge. One map is high atop skyscrapers connected by sky bridges, and I sat in stunned silence the first time I saw a team destroy the section where a bridge met a building, causing the entire thing to collapse to the ground below. Split-second judgment calls when buildings fall around you about whether to jump off or ride the debris down can make or break firefights and create unforgettable moments – like when my entire team was dead in the final seconds of a match, and the only thing that stopped another team from stealing the bank for the win was the amount of rubble they had to dig through to reach it.» There will always be an element of luck in the quality of teammates you are matched with, which is a big part of why The Finals (as with most team-based shooters) is better across the board with people you know. It’s so much fun to coordinate an assault with friends or to seize the bank and then protect it with mines and defensive structures. It’s also a huge advantage to work together. A flamethrower wielding Heavy supported by a healing beam from a Medium can wipe an entire team, and the strategic element of choosing complementary builds and kits is very engaging. When someone dies, they leave an action figure behind that can be used to revive them, and scooping one up so you can find a safe place to bring them back is as useful as it is hilarious.» The Finals does a great job standing out from the competitive shooter crowd thanks to its fast-paced action, excellent environmental destruction, and gameshow-meets-squad shooter vibes. The way flying through the battlefield with a grappling hook or hulk-smashing through buildings mixes with its strict, objective-based modes is a breath of fresh air. It’s a concern that there are only two of those modes total right now, and it definitely feels like both in-game balance and the overall reward economy need some adjustments. But those are small critiques relative to the outrageous fun and breathtaking spectacle of buildings crumbling around you.» If so, please leave a rating. Awards are also greatly appreciated!

_childDocuments_.review: Video review: The Finals is a fast paced but equally strategic first person shooter that is entire free to play no strings attached. In my opinion it is a fad game that will eventually disappear but even so it is still very fun and is definitely worth your time.You play as a contestant of a game show. Your objective is to extract as much money as possible. You usually play in a team of three and you can choose one of three class types each with their own unique useful abilities. I'm not exactly sure why it's called "The Finals" but if I had to guess we are literally playing the championship match of a virtual tournament broadcasted for imaginary viewers every single time we play a new game.The Finals is a ton of fun because it's easy to get into but leaves a ton of room to improve and master your skills. The time to kill is very good in this, because the pace is like Call of Duty but the time to kill is more like Halo or Apex Legends, meaning you get a perfect balance of fast pace and strategy. Another benefactor to the overall pace of gameplay is the fact death is quite punishing and if your entire team gets wiped their is an additional penalty added to the respawn timer, and you respawn quite far away so even though the gameplay is fast you still want to plan your attack and make sure each life counts and has impact to the objective as to not waste precious time. The match length is also perfect, not too long or too short, and allowing time to be extended if your team is playing well and contesting the win condition.What I don't like about The Finals is how generic it's "skin" is. The bones of the game are incredibly strong, in fact some of the strongest of any first person shooter to date I would argue, but the skin covering it is basic at best. If you think of a game like "Team Fortress 2," every class has a unique flavor and personality to them, but here it's just "Light," "Medium," and "Heavy," and they're just literal regular people. The visuals are great but the sounds and overall theme of the game is cartoonish, meaning the guns and grenades don't actually have weight or impact to them because everything feels "floaty" or "like a dream," and my final issue is with some of the balancing, I feel the Heavy class is too powerful with no weaknesses, I'm a Light main using an SMG and I will just straight up avoid them now because an entire clip of my weapon won't bring them down regardless of range or accuracy, and I also low key despise melee weapons because you can't win against them in close quarters by default and they even have the ability to deflect bullets.The Finals is a ton of fun but it's hyper generic looking and sounding and will fade away one day I believe. This genre is highly competitive and while I do like it, there's a lot more FPS games of this nature I would recommend before this one.8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me preface this review by initially stating that my interest in multiplayer games has waned and withered over the years. But The Finals has managed to blend a level of casual play, competitive play, and overall fun that would even draw me back into the PvP market. Along with its mechanics and choice of weaponry and equipment to further push the boundaries of the inherent sandbox this game lays at your feet, there is a lot of potential to be had for this game’s future.For a Free-to-Play, this game does not skip a beat when it comes to a quality shooter. Developed by Embark Studios, who are comprised of some of the industry’s veteran game developers, comes a somewhat familiar feeling of casual/competitiveness paired with an incredible destruction system. The amount of destruction would put even Battlefield to shame. You can level entire buildings, create new sightlines, establish a well-fortified position, sabotage that fortified position by wrecking the foundations of a building, take advantage of a crane with a wrecking ball that will demolish just about anything in its path, etc. And the fact that the destruction runs generally well further illustrates the talent and competency of Embark Studios as the new underdog developer that’s up and coming in the industry entirely.To further note, if you’re looking for a game where you can simply one or two tap people, stray your sights elsewhere. This game is a pseudo-class-based shooter. For further context, you have three “Builds”: Light, Medium, and Heavy, and each has their own playstyle. You still craving a faster pace of play with some of the most powerful weapons and equipment in the game? Good at hit-and-run tactics? Good at isolating priority targets? The Light is what you may be looking for, though its tradeoff is a low health pool. Or how about playing support for the team? You want to play medic and heal teammates while they dish out damage? Or plant a turret and lay down an extra line of fire to preoccupy your targets? Add an extra level of mobility for the team and plant a jump pad for you and your team to gain an advantageous elevated position over your enemies? Try out the Medium, with an average health pool and moderate movement speed. Or to change up the game, how about becoming a master of destruction? Want to abuse an explosive arsenal that can render half a block into rubble? Want to charge at enemies and knock them back? Or even ground pound then into a pile of coins? How about utilizing heavy weapons to lay down suppression and an endless slew of bullets at your enemies? Heavy may be just what you are looking for. Obviously they will be slower than the other two builds but pack the most health.With what this game offers in terms of gameplay, it is strictly PvP as of the writing of this review. There are several modes of play, but all consistently have a similar theme behind them: 3v3v3. Three teams consisting of three players each fighting to reach the goal of the game. There is Cashout, the first mode you will be introduced to. This is basically the game’s bread and butter. The first team to reach $20,000 wins. A vault will spawn somewhere on the map and must be opened. Once opened, someone must bring it to a Cashout station, which will start a timer as to when the vault can be cashed out. The station can be captured by other teams so building a proper defense is key and strategy comes to mind here. You only really need to cashout successfully twice to win, but the maximum the game can go is four in case all teams are tied. Then there is Bank-It. This one is simpler but more chaotic. There are four teams of three in this mode (3v3v3v3) and works somewhat similarly to Cashout. However, instead of depositing a vault to a Cashout station and defending it for a period of time, you instead open vaults or kill players to obtain coins. These coins have value and must be deposited manually into Cashout stations. The more coins you’re holding, the longer a trail you leave behind to signify to other players the wealth you carry. Vaults will also spawn around the map and will offer a lot of coins when cracked open. Like Cashout, the first team to deposit enough coins wins. And for those seeking a competitive kick, there is a competitive category for your taste. There is Tournament and Ranked. Tournament is essentially Cashout, but you are locked in with the loadout you take, and you have limited respawns. So, a well-coordinated and warmed up team is encouraged. And Ranked? Well personally I can’t really say as I don’t push myself to that line but feel free to take a spin if you’re feeling up for it.Progression. It exists in this game. Each class has their own abilities, weapons, and equipment. Though some classes share several items of equipment universally. There is a progression currency called VRs, which are earned by completing matches. Unsure of how much you get as obtaining VRs after every match feels inconsistent. Abilities and guns are worth 800 VRs, but equipment is 1,000 a piece. All abilities, guns, and weapons also have their own progression. Every time you level up any in particular, you get a new skin for it. Though this is nothing too much to scoff at as all guns and equipment offer the same skin for each of the six levels to progress respectively. Abilities, on the other hand, offer different progression cosmetics like charms, stickers, sprays, etc. Though in terms of customization for weapons and equipment that alter their performance, it is nonexistent. No changing attachments or anything like that, you get what you get on your gun. Lastly, there is a Career rank for your account. Every time you level up, you get a new cosmetic for your character. As of right now, there are 49 rank rewards in total, though that may change over time.Live services exist in this game as well. There is a Battle Pass and microtransactions in this game. Even then, however, there isn’t a large plethora of cosmetics in the store for everyone’s pick. So, standing out from the crowd isn’t that much of an option at the moment. Though some cosmetics in this game are pretty fire. There is a Legendary skin for the Mac-11 that prints out a receipt every time you get a kill, which is funny.There are some problems with this game, as it is Free-to-Play, which doesn’t surprise me. As a class-based shooter, weapon balancing is a bit off. There are times where enemies melt your health away with an MP5 or a Mac-11, and using the same doesn’t feel as powerful in your hands. There are times where the matchmaking will pin you with a couple of Lights that do significantly worse than you as a Heavy and you will get pub-stomped by a well-coordinated team that dominates the game. Certain guns kick to the point where even if you’re controlling them efficiently, you still really can’t tell if the bullets are lining up with where you are aiming or not. This is very noticeable with the M60 and Lewis Gun. And since the Heavy has the smallest weapon selection of the three classes, the developers should at least throw an extra bone and buff some of the Heavy’s weapons. Either up the damage or reduce the recoil so the Heavy can stand more of a chance at mid to long distance combat. Or buff the Scar-H for the Medium as a 20-round mag, at times, isn’t enough to make-or-break a 1-on-1 with a Heavy. Or how a team of Light mains can decimate any team dynamic and completely break the game with glitch grenades, tasers, swords, MP5s, and cloak. The weapon and class balancing still needs some touching up.Other than the above, this game still has so much potential and can be so much more. It’s generally good for the competitive and casual crowds alike. It can’t hurt to give it a try since it is free, and you can test out each class in the firing range to see what gadgets and weapons suit your style. Take it as you will, hope this review was helpful.
