_childDocuments_.review: This was such a sweet story. I don't always play VNs but seeing one about games/online messaging really got my attention. I love those kinds of aesthetics/nostalgia. Once I started, I just could not put it down and had to see it to the very end in one sitting. VIDEOVERSE is a very sweet story about how the world is so small. The little things we experience across a vast ocean of people and interactions can stick with us for a very long time. People come and go, but fate may have a surprise sooner than we think. Overall, this was such a touching game and this little world felt like an actual pocket of someone's life experiences. They really pulled off an authentic internet with characters that felt real and relatable.
_childDocuments_.name: VIDEOVERSE

_childDocuments_.review: Where do I begin?Videoverse tales the story of Emmet, a user of the Kinoku Shark. Emmet spends his days playing Feudal Fantasy and chatting with friends on videoverse. How you reply and treat others on the site shapes Emmet's decisions, and ultimately the ending. I really enjoyed this game and the nostalgia it made me feel. Game can be beaten in around 4-5 hours, more if your a completionist. If you like games that tell a narrative, this is up your alley, if you want something more action packed, look elsewhere. Team Shark forever.
_childDocuments_.name: VIDEOVERSE

_childDocuments_.review: Can I get hooked on a visual novel whose story is good, but feels a little predictable at times? Apparently yes!VIDEOVERSE is a game where the way the story is told is more interesting than the story itself. You mostly play VIDEOVERSE by interacting with a fictional social media platform for a fictional monochromatic handheld videogaming system from the early 2000s. This is extremely cool!Playing the game feels very close to actually using social media in a way that's captivating. You read posts from people, leave comments in reply, send DMs, report abusive messages, and even get to make a drawing at one point. The social media platform is populated by a very wide variety of characters. There's a smaller subset that end up having big stories, but even among the minor characters, there's threads to follow.The actual story that ends up being told feels somewhat predictable, but was nonetheless touching and managed to bring me to tears, with certain parts feeling painfully relatable. All in all, VIDEOVERSE felt fresh and well worth experiencing, especially for those who have spent a considerable amount of time in an online community before.
_childDocuments_.name: VIDEOVERSE

_childDocuments_.review: An overall excellent experience that masterfully captures the feeling of socializing online in our hyper-digital age. The characters are exceptionally crafted, and uniquely this game allows you to choose how you personally relate to them with multiple different outcomes dependent on how you internalize the social landscape around the lead protagonist. As a player, you can choose how much you engage with the Videoverse, which interestingly, may result in different insights depending on what temperament you cultivate from its community.The story of Videoverse may be brief, but it illustrates multiple nuanced portraits that guide the player towards a thoughtful reflection that is rare in video games. After my first playthrough, I asked myself if I had truly made the most out of my experience with the fictional in-game fan community, and if I had brought out the best in the people around me. But more importantly is what this game may bring out of us as players.10/10. Masterpiece.
_childDocuments_.name: VIDEOVERSE

_childDocuments_.review: A feel-good narrative title that gorgeously evokes the online community's vibes in the early 2000s and the ways in which friendships can be forged, strengthened, and even frayed. _childDocuments_.review: I'm not sure whether I personally like this game, though it might be good for a certain type of person.  I like the idea of internet simulation games with a nostalgia aspect, and I like relaxing comfort zone games.  I'm fine with story driven games and interactive experiences.  I think what holds me back on this game is that the dialogue seems a bit boring to me.  The characters act more like an imitation of a teen JRPG character than what an actual teenager would sound like, and even then the dialogue seems a bit naive.  Maybe it's just me.  I'm not usually the kind of person that post comments of a flattering nature (ie "cool pic") or trolling just to be mean.  What would make this game work better for me would be a better grasp on what people were like during certain time periods with emphasis on interesting and unique personalities.  Hypnospace Outlaw was a great (and hard to follow) example because it's loaded with the kind of personalities that you would run into if you were a college student in the 90s, maybe someone you knew that was in Computer Science or working in tech support.   Just because people are nerdy or sciency doesn't mean they don't have personality quirks.  Then you have the older generations that don't trust what the kids are into...sometimes for good reason.  You really need to have a finger on the pulse of these attitudes and personalities if you want to make a good nostagia game.  For me the personalities in this game are more of an adults interpretation of what a kid sounds like....or maybe just not so good writing.  I also wish I had more freedom to write my own responses rather than rely on boring pre-written responses.  AI could make this possible in a game.  The game is a also a bit pricy for what it is.  I would be ok with the price if I connected better with the writing or the characters however.

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty good game. Where you choices seems to matter. This game reminds me a little bit of the emily is away games, in a good sense. _childDocuments_.review: I was never on miiverse, the most obvious inspiration, but Videoverse manages to evoke something communicative and universal all the same about the bonds we make online and what’s left unsaid at the end of things. _childDocuments_.name: VIDEOVERSE

_childDocuments_.review: This was beautiful. Easy recommendation.Mechanically, it plays like a visual novel version of Hypnospace Outlaw. There are lots of optional tasks you can do for other characters, but really it's all about getting absorbed in the game's world and story (at least, that's how I played it).The game did a great job of taking me back to being a teenager online in the early 2000s (players who weren't that age at that time will have plenty to relate to, too). For example, I felt genuine butterflies when waiting for the protagonist's crush to reply, after I'd just said something cringey that I feared may have messed up our relationship - all that good stuff! That's how real the bonds I made with the other characters felt.The game also deals with some meta themes, about the important role video games and online communities can play in some people's lives. These were explored beautifully. All in all, this one's well worth your time and money, if you like this kind of thing :)
_childDocuments_.name: VIDEOVERSE

_childDocuments_.review: Its a simple visual novel really but the framing device is like an old-school games console that had a very basic slice of the internet, with community boards and chat programs etc. Its quite nostalgic if you remember the early days of the internet. Story was engaging and quite poignant. Controls are simple; entirely playable with mouse which is unsurprising considering accessibility in games is one of the themes throughout.Seems like there is some conversation choices you can make which can effect the story-line in some subtle ways or at the very least lead to different achievements. So while the game is short there is some replay-ability.  Overall recommended if you want something chill and nostalgic
_childDocuments_.name: VIDEOVERSE

_childDocuments_.review: My impressions video: I'm not normally into visual novels, but take an interesting in one with unique subject matter and that aren't as focused on dating elements. I hadn't heard of VIDEOVERSE until the developer reached out to me, but I really enjoyed the premise of a time shifted gaming world, where the Totally Not Wii U (tm) and Totally Not Miiverse (tm) came out earlier than it did and had technical limitations more in line with the day.The story is about making and maintaining online friendships in an era where communication was not as instant, free or high fidelity as it is today. I first got on the Internet in 1994, when there was no video chat and most friendships were made through text with the occasional static image, during the brief periods of the day you could get online. If you got close to someone, levelling up your friendship at that time involved talking on the phone with obscene long distance charges. VIDEOVERSE's world isn't quite that primitive, but shares many of the same struggles.The gameplay is fairly typical visual novel faire. You have conversations, make choices and those choices can shape future outcomes. It's not possible to see every outcome in one playthrough, so there can be a good number of hours here if you want to see it all. The writing is sharp and doesn't waste words, which is in line with the communication standards of the day, but also means the story doesn't turn into a slog, like many visual novels can be for me. There are a number of different characters with different personalities, but there is no real romance here. This is a game about friendship, not dating.It also offers some light commentary on the games industry itself, and what it can mean to people when platforms go away, even less popular ones and how it's not easy for people to just move to the next thing to stay in touch. It's not preachy, but it does make you think.I enjoyed VIDEOVERSE, both for its subject matter and for the way in which it differs from many other visual novels. If the story concept does something for you, I think it'd be worth checking out.
_childDocuments_.name: VIDEOVERSE

_childDocuments_.review: A really sweet ball of early 2000s internet cringe (and i mean that in a good sincere way) tied to a good story and fun charactersThe mechanical side of things is a bit wonky in places - there were a few bugs (ie messages not coming through and locking me out of progress), a few times I'd pick choices I didn't mean to progress text, and due to its presentation, you can't really speed up text which makes things a little slow in places (especially if you reload after picking a choice you're not happy and have to redo stuff). Overall, this didn't affect my enjoyment too much though
_childDocuments_.name: VIDEOVERSE

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best games ive ever played. I expected to get something like Emily was away. A game that uses nostalgia to enhance its characters in a social media like setting. What i got was one of the most emotionally resonant games ive ever experienced. The writing is just so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ good. So many characters are well written the characters feel so human despite being just text. _childDocuments_.review: If you've ever been a part of a text-based online community, and built any connections with people online, then there is an extremely good chance that you're going to see something of yourself in Videoverse. Whether you built friendships on AIM, IRC, MSN or fan forums, exchanged tips and drawings with others on Miiverse, or still get involved in the latest discourse on Twitter/X to this day, there is something in Videoverse that you will surely recognise and appreciate.This game is unlike anything else out there. The concept of a fictional social network is pulled off fantastically, the interactions feel authentic, and there are many small touches and references to enjoy. It really feels like you're taking a trip back in time and are a small part of a dedicated community. Throughout, I felt like I was looking into a mirror to decades ago, experiencing parts of my online past all over again. It's funny, sad, joyful, exciting, emotional, nostalgic, all brought together in a stylish package. Big thumbs up for the console boot up sequences!I adored my time with Videoverse and strongly recommend it. It's easily one of the best games I've played this year.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing this game back to front, this is a well written story which connects the nostalgic themes of 'retro-styled' internet design with the formation of internet forums from the early days of the internet. It offers a transformative experience, capturing what it was like to experience the technical difficulties of the early days of the internet, yet subtly underlining the memories made from the connections you make during them.Very much like the early days of the internet, you find yourself doing a few things; chatting with friends and finding more people to connect through forums. Only, this takes those ideas and is jammed with creativity, and instead of making it into another visual novel, rephrases the visual-novel formula to transport the player as if they were back in those early days of forum chatting. From the simple forum design to the audio design in the notifications, I felt like I was transported back to the pre-windows 7 days, immersed in the game.And yet behind the firewall of these forum-MSN style design lies a mature story that examines the relationships of people who only knew each other from behind the screen. Characters that you speak to are well-grounded to the point these may be people you have actually met while using social media today. Kinmoku whisked together a mature and meaningful story that examined individual growth, underlining the growing concept of online relationships, the desire for accessibility and how you can make the internet a better place within a growing network.I enjoyed this game. _childDocuments_.review:
Relive the days of past social gaming networks in VIDEOVERSE, a decision-based narrative adventure focusing on character development, friendship and love, from the developer behind One Night Stand.

As Emmett, a young video game fan and aspiring artist, dive into this fictional video game era, where the Kinmoku Shark gaming system and its online social network, Videoverse, were still popular. name: Spirit Hunter: Death Mark II
detailed_description: The latest installment in the Spirit Hunter series. Spirit Hunter: Death Mark II is a suspense-horror game set at a prestigious academy. When rumors circulate about supernatural occurrences at the famed Konoehara Academy in Tokyo’s H City, it’s up to the head of the Kujou family, also known as the “Spirit Doctor,” to take on the case. Notices that announce people’s deaths, and students who aren’t what they seem. Through your investigation, it appears that a spirit called “The Departed” is the mastermind behind it all, and it looks like it wants something from you... This entry introduces a new side-scrolling function when traveling across different locations. Combined with the first-person perspective during investigations, the Spirit Hunter experience is more immersive and terrifying than ever. The partnering system has also been enhanced. The success rate of your actions during “Suspensive Acts” change depending on your partner of choice, further elevating the elements of suspense in this installment.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's just get this out of the way right off the bat: I really liked this game. That said, I had a lot of problems with it.It felt much more like DLC for the original than its own game deserving $50. The story is fun, the art is beautiful, and I enjoyed most of the puzzles, but there's just not that much going on. Much of the exploration is very repetitive, and feels like padding, especially considering the only proper location to explore is the school. I kept expecting to be lead somewhere new, to really get that sense of adventure I got from the first two games, only to be a bit disappointed that none (except one) of the promising new areas seen in the story were fleshed out at all. One of my biggest gripes was how little each of the "spirit of the week" stories was fleshed out. I kept finding myself thinking "that's it?" at the end of each chapter after the second. Chapters one and two were very long and fleshed out, and I felt satisfied by the information I discovered on the spirit's past, and the way they were "saved." Unfortunately, every chapter after was much shorter, and much less detailed, which is a crying shame, considering how fun uncovering those mysteries can be. The last big thing that bothered be was the collectibles. I love collectibles. I'm obsessed with them. If I know they exist I can't keep playing until I know I've found them all. Make sure you also play like this, because despite how optional the game makes them sound, I'd argue at least half are completely necessary to finish the game without relying on RNG to make it through the final scenarios. It's not a huge deal, but it certainly does upset the tension of certain scenes when you feel the need to backtrack to find every collectible before doing what the story wants you to do, which is usually a supposedly time-sensitive issue. I know I had a lot of pretty specific complaints, but I really do think anyone who enjoyed the first two Spirit Hunter games would also enjoy this one. That said, wait for it to go on sale. It's not worth $50.
_childDocuments_.name: Spirit Hunter: Death Mark II

_childDocuments_.review: Spirit Hunter: Death Mark II is like that awkward high school reunion where you see everyone’s aged a bit, but the drama is still as thick as the fog rolling in from the nearby graveyard. Set between the chilling events of Death Mark and the mind-bending nightmare of NG, this installment tries to recapture the magic of its predecessors, but ends up feeling more like a haunted hallway than a haunted house.The main storyline revolves around "The Departed," but don’t get too excited; unfortunately, most of the game feels like wandering the same halls over and over, a lot of the scenarios are repetitive, all happening within the same high school. Chapter 4, in particular, feels like it's just there to fill space—more hollow than a chocolate Easter bunny.The art style in "Death Mark II" has not changed from the previous two games, retaining the same eerie and atmospheric visuals. The artist, Fumiya Sumio, continues to deliver their signature style, which is both vivid and emotional. However, the overall CG quality feels less captivating compared to "Death Mark 1" and "NG." While the artist has certainly put in effort, the visuals lack the same haunting impact as the previous games. It’s like looking at a familiar face but realizing their makeup is a bit off. The limited setting of the high school, compared to the varied urban legends explored in the earlier titles, might contribute to this sense of visual monotony.The gameplay in "Death Mark II" has shifted towards a side-scrolling adventure game (AVG) format, reminiscent of the classic urban-legend game "Twilight Syndrome." While this nostalgic nod is appreciated, the system can be cumbersome, especially when fast-traveling. The "return to infirmary" button is handy but doesn’t quite cut it for quick navigation across major locations. Imagine needing to backtrack through a haunted house with only one shortcut—frustrating, right?A standout in this game is the new female protagonist, Michiho Kinukawa. This white-haired high schooler is as cute as a button, and her character development makes it worth unlocking the true ending. Otherwise, her fate remains less than desirable, and who wants that for such an endearing character? The extra chapter is a curveball,, but it cleverly ties into "NG" and sheds light on why Kaoru Hazuki, my favorite character of this whole franchise, looks the way she does in the sequel. It's a nice touch, but it also leaves you craving more. And then there's the ending. The words "Spirit Hunter... The End" after the credits felt like a punch to the gut. I'm hoping this is just a well-placed scare tactic, because if this is truly the final curtain call for the franchise, then the ghost writers of this series owe us a sequel to NG."Spirit Hunter: Death Mark II" is a mixed bag of thrills and chills. Despite its shortcomings, it offers enough intriguing elements to keep fans engaged. Here's hoping the series isn't truly dead and buried with its lackluster sales number on steam(2760 copies as of today)
_childDocuments_.name: Spirit Hunter: Death Mark II

_childDocuments_.review: In the first game and NG you really had to pay attention to what order you explored the rooms, as you were rewarded or punished for searching every room and interacting with most objects.This game outright tells you where to go next in bold colored text, while also littering the map with empty locations to explore and needless items to click on that point out the obvious, like that chairs in the room are stacked. In a game where you are suppose to search for clues, having dozens of pointless interactions bogs the game down.It's one thing to punish a player for exploring, but it's ill advised to have the player backtrack previously explored empty rooms for minor (clues) the player already knows from very obvious dialogue and story points in a earlier act. In the school on the second day you need to go to the student council room as the dialogue states. Though gives you the option to search 5 other rooms which state "no one is here right now," which is a needless choice. If the choice does not have a consequence (good or bad) then the story should just be continued VN style with scene transitions instead of forcing the player to run around to find the one something or someone the game forces them to find in the first place.Wasting the players time with needless mechanics does not enhance the experience, it's just tiring. Do I need to really search 9 different class rooms to learn that a character was bullied when it was literally written on the walls and even stated by the ghost that you were not a bully?Also, when deciding which clue to use during encounter there is a chance that using the clue will fail based on RNG. Not because you chose the wrong person, or wrong clue, but just because the RNG decided there should have to repeat the clue selection options to choose the same clue again for another RNG roll.The game introduces a side scrolling element that makes use of low detail anime style 2D art. If I had to guess, it was a cost cutting design choice. As in the first game and NG every frame was very detailed since you saw it in the first person point of view.Furthermore, in NG and DM1 all of the monsters were either frightening or disturbing in appearance with a few I did not want to look at due to their more disturbing features. Though DM2 went in a more PG direction with its monsters, where they have some "horror" elements, but also look cartoon-ish enough not to really be frightening when they walk toward you. The first monster made me think "a water balloon for a head, what a weird choice" and the second "The face isn't realistic enough to be scary, it's more like an alien," and the same ends up being true for all of the spirits as CH4's was just silly looking. They just are not scary when you see the full reveal.Having finished the game, I feel as though the story was underwhelming compared to the first game in the series. As the original starts with nothing but a mystery, which comes to a climactic conclusion with a plot twist that only really started to reveal itself toward the end.In SH 2, the plot twist is practically given away at the start. So the ending will not surprise at all. Not to mention the way some characters behave will just leave you wondering, "why did they even include this" because there are a fair few glaring moments in the story where content feels like it would have been better off cut from the game. This includes characters, dialogue, and even one of the spirits.(The game has a very rough start.)(A short and inconsequential chapter.)Though it might just be my personal taste, so I will just leave it at that. Anything more would just end up being spoilers.1. Cut out the RNG mechanics. The game would need a lot more game-play to justify having RPG mechanics, as adding RNG to choosing clues was an awful idea.2. Make the monsters frightening again, the spirits were the least frightening in the series. Though I will say,  curse was praiseworthy. Otherwise, all of the spirits were a disappointment visually.3. The cut-scenes should have been cut from the game, they did not even provide a good intro for the spirits.4. Heed all of the critiques made in this review.5. While returning characters can be nice, the game would have been better off focusing on the new cast like NG did. The returning characters are hardly more than interchangeable companions with flavor text, while the only returning character that had a meaningful part to play in the story was the detective. Instead the focus got split between a needlessly expanded cast of characters.All of the other returning characters just took away opportunities from the new characters to shine. As it is better to have a few meaningful interactions than to have many meaningless ones.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm giving this a thumbs up, since I overall had an enjoyable time with the game, but my actual feelings on it are a bit mixed. Even though Death Mark II does improve on some aspects of Death Mark I, such as giving more of an impression of the physical space the characters are traversing, using already built investment for bigger emotional stakes and having some CGs involving female characters that are actually scary (you know, like a horror game might do) rather than just blatant fanservice, I would overall call it the weakest of the 3 Spirit Hunter games released so far. Some of that is due to my own interests and preferences. Mystery and folk horror are my favorite genres, and so the game's attempt to veer into both ended up disappointing me all the more. The overall mystery was way too easy and the folk horror aspects were significantly more basic and shallow than what I was used to. I also found half of the ghost designs more funny than scary, and the other half utilised symbolism that didn't really connect to the story of the spirit. Plus, I'm not really afraid of insects.On a more "objective" note, though, basing your likelihood of getting a game over in big part on not skill or reasoning, but pure luck wasn't a good idea. I know that it's supposed to add tension, but when it fails it's not scary, it's just annoying and frustrating. And while I like the Adventure genre, the game never really utilised its new style for actual scares. There is a flashlight mechanic, but you can always see through the darkness anyway and there's never anything hiding there. Still, though, if you enjoyed the previous 2 entries (and maybe wait for a sale), there is fun to be had with this game. You can see what those characters you already know have been up to, enjoy their fun dynamics and slowly learn about a couple of unfortunate human tragedies in a somewhat spooky manner. If you haven't played them yet, though, I'd recommend you to just get NG instead.

_childDocuments_.review: As a big and long-time fan of the Spirit Hunter series, I was really happy with this addition overall, but I do have some complaints.I will now break down my thoughts into different categories in my review which will contain a lot of comparisons with the previous games in this series (Death Mark 1 and NG). And as this is my first-ever review I hope this is helpful to both old and new fans who are considering this game!I personally really liked the VN, point-and-click format in the previous two games and was slightly skeptical about the addition of the side scroll element in this one at first as I thought it would lessen the sense of dread and immersion during investigations, but I ended up liking it. Although what I feared did occur, the overall atmosphere is still as tense as ever, and adding the side scroll makes the exploration feel much more fun. They fixed up a lot of gameplay issues from the previous two games. From my memory, there were many times when I felt frustrated (especially with the decision-making logic) and found navigation difficult in the old games, but I didn’t feel any of that in this one! The exploration felt straightforward and clear, with a much more understandable logic in its choices.As for the system of battling spirits, this new approach is a little strange. It is cool to add the RNG element, but also annoying at the same time because what do you mean that the MC who is a teacher has a low success rate of reading out a passage? On top of that, sometimes you could still fail certain actions when the success rate is very high. The fact that you can keep retrying before your health runs out also makes the encounters feel less challenging. This format is a little silly to me, and although I got used to it later in the game, I preferred the old system where if you pick something wrong, then it’s an instant Game Over. I think the story was good overall with how engaging it was the whole way. It is a little unfortunate how the twist wasn’t that surprising, but at least they kept me second-guessing the whole way.As for the tales of the spirits, since the location is more strictly related to high school this time, I found some pretty cliche since this setting is overused. I understand it was a challenge to make them interesting, which they managed to do in most cases, but it didn’t quite hit for me. Although I still enjoyed them, I think that the spirits and their tales were more creative and memorable in the previous games (especially NG), so this was a slight letdown.They were a huge improvement from Death Mark 1. I really loved the original cast in Death Mark 1 but will admit that they suffered from the lack of characterization due to how many characters there are and how they didn’t have much time to shine due to the story’s structure. Although minimal as it is not the focus of the game, the old crew had so much more characterization this time around through their little comments during exploration and interactions with one another, making them feel more alive despite still not having a lot of screen time.As for the new characters, they were fun and quirky, but I honestly didn’t really care for them, which might be intentional for the player to focus more on the OG crew (and if that is so, it was successful). I wish we had a little more time with some of them, but considering how many characters there are, it is understandable that some, among the new characters, didn’t get as much spotlight as the others.As some may know, this game was crowdfunded and probably gave them way more budget to work with. The artwork in this series has always been one of its highlights, at least for an artist like me, and this game did not disappoint. I was really happy with the quality of the CGs and their consistency throughout the game, regardless of their significance level, which was most likely achieved by the extra budget they had this time around. The death CGs you get when you fail to bring a spirit to complete salvation were great! Death Mark 1 did not have any, so it was cool to see these CGs of the original crew. Of course, they are also exceptionally well composed and rendered; however, conceptually speaking, they are a step down from the ones in NG in my opinion. Maybe it is due to this game’s spirits’ nature, but I wish the CGs were as gruesome and violent as NG’s.As for the spirits designs, I preferred the ones in the previous games, but this could be due to my personal taste. In my opinion, I think this game’s direction went for more of a weird and bizarre vibe, whereas the previous games were more grotesque and disturbing. I was certainly more terrified of the previous spirits’ designs compared to the one in this game.Delicious. This series has always been really good with their sounds but I think this is another step up from the previous games and I am very impressed. Really kept up the suspense and tension all the way through each investigation. Again, bless the budget!!This game does not have a lot of voice acting, most of it being grunts, pants, and short voiced lines here and there, but considering how there was close to no voice acting in previous games, I am happy with it.Now this is something I never liked about this series. There are a number of CGs with partial nudity of underaged girls in suggestive poses. I was a little glad with NG where they reduced that from Death Mark 1, but Death Mark 2 seemed to go back to its roots. I think there are fewer in Death Mark 2 compared to 1, but I still can’t help but feel uncomfortable seeing them.—----------------TLDR; Despite all its faults, I would recommend it! A huge improvement from the previous titles (especially Death Mark 1) in many aspects, although there are certain things I still prefer in NG. The game is not as difficult or scary as the previous ones but I think it is still worth a shot. To a lot of people, I would say $50 is a bit much but as someone who appreciates the art in this game a lot along with the fact how this includes 2 DLCs (if I am not mistaken), I didn't mind.For newcomers, I think it is ok to hop into Spirit Hunter with this game, although I would still recommend playing Death Mark 1 first since this game is a direct sequel to that. 7.5/10 as a game, 9/10 for my heart

_childDocuments_.review: I'm mostly writing this review for people who played the previous two Spirit Hunter games, but newcomers might find this review useful, too.To give a quick recap, the previous games were pretty unforgiving. Make a wrong choice when facing a Spirit, and there's a good chance that it's an instant death. Also, you're on a timer, which kind of doubled as a health bar, so you better choose fast. Some choices require a bit of thought, and you might feel some self-doubt in the first playthrough, which was the main source of tension IMO. Basically the uncertainty of if a choice will kill you or save you.The first thing that stuck out to me as strange was that this game introduced  to choices. At first I thought the game was actually faking the randomness as a clever way to add tension, and correct choices were secretly 100% successful. But, nope, I overthought it, and it's exactly like it looks. So, even if you make the right choice, you can fail. Or, obviously, wrong choices can fail, so you can either  or . But, don't worry, because failure isn't very punishing at all. Besides the wasted action points you basically get a do-over. For example, once I tried to toss an item to a Spirit. With a ~70% success chance I failed, and the item just slipped out of the main character's hands. And the Spirit didn't do anything, just sort of waited there watching the main character look like a clumsy idiot until the second try.And, like I said, in previous entries wrong choices could kill you,  you're on a timer, but now each choice costs a few action/health points (they're called different things but they're the same), instead. So the less actions you take, the better. So, as long as you don't choose blatantly incorrect choices, you should usually be OK. And I  choose blatantly incorrect choices, letting my health get low. What I found was that you can die from just taking an action, which I discovered when choosing to sing a song. Imagine the main character being too tired to sing so he just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ dies.Anyway, I guess the random success rates and health consumption were strategies to still make choices tense. It doesn't really work IMO, and honestly gave me a chance to laugh at some of the things you can do, instead. I get that this change is probably better for a larger audience, but I think it does kind of lose something.But, with that out of the way, I think the artwork is just as horrifying and beautiful as the previous games, and the spirit designs are still unique and tragic. But some of the spirits look so strange that they kind of leave the realm of horror and end up just plain weird IMO. The music is great, and the story is fun and interesting, too.I'd rank it as about as good as the first Death Mark, and better than NG.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: After beating the game, and taking my sweet time to do it (I only play it at night pacing myself to no more than 1 chapter a night), I'd like to say that even though I still hold everything I wrote to be true, the story really starts to shines as it progresses to the point you'll have a great time in spite of all the bad decisions they incorporated into the gameplay. I can recommend it without batting an eye, but I hope they pull back a lot of the new things in the next installment. Fingers crossed for one!----------So I'm a big fan of spirit hunter series, and I'm giving this a positive review, but it has to be by far the worst title in the series. The good is they've introduced some quality of life updates which were all welcome. But that aside, the story is kind of weak, the monsters I've encountered so far don't look scary, in fact one looks goofy, they've destroyed exploration by making it into a side scroller, and they added a collect teeth to unlock extras thing which forces you to do the mind numbingly boring exploring. The side scrolling also kind of defeats any scary ambiance they manage to create because you aren't afraid of bumping into anything and you know nothing's gonna pop in on you, it also breaks the pace of the game. So all and all, I hate collecting teeth and side scrolling.Other than that the writing, art and sound design continues to be what you expect from these series so it's still a good time. But not a GREAT time. Anyway I'm giving it a positive review cause I want more spirit hunter games and I'll die on that hill even if it means enduring the mind numbingly bad side scrolling and teeth collecting.Oh and they added % of success to actions in time events. So even if you pick the right action it can fail. Ngl I kind of hate how they handled this change. Seems they put it in there so that you are forced to collect teeth to trade it in for stats upgrades that improve your % of success. I don't think anyone asked for any of this... its like trying to be more than a visual novel by incorporating rpg elements in a really bad fashion

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game, and the series, but I get the feeling this'll be the last one.But I feel like it's missing something.The story here is great, some magnificent psychological build up (the protagonist this time has character!) and it has some real great character moments. However, because of those character moments, a lot of other characters get sidelined, and the same applies to places in the school. If you think that setting looked nice, you'll never see it again. As someone who loved the art of the older games, Kazuhiro Oya's take was incredible. But I feel the design of the spirits have sunken in contrast to what we have here. The older spirits were horrifying, looked like a real grudge given form, like something I wouldn't even dare go near let alone want to see! yet here we have spirits that are like 'yea Also, i would like to comment on the brutality of the cgs. In the older games, we saw the most gruesome death you could imagine, genuine nightmare fuel that put any horror you've ever seen to shame, but now we get something that looks just a lil' spooky and doesn't feel like it fits in a horror game. Don't even get me started on the sexual cgs those are weird as hell. I want to be scared, I don't want to be horny.But the music is magnificent, something truly beautiful. The deduction them, and the theme of the school, both really capture the atmosphere, and it's super wondrous how it works, I genuinely feel oppressed when I feel like I'm being talked to in the school, thanks to the music. (the composer is Naoaki Jimbo and he is THE BEST composer, im just sayin' if he needs a kidney or two)And overall?I really enjoyed this game, I was there since the announcement trailer. I waited several years (since the release of NG) for another game, and they've delivered a great piece of art. (also the side scrolling mechanic is cool)I only bought the game because I'm a nut for this series, but if you're on the fence, just wait till it goes on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed playing the game, but it did have its some issues. While there's a lot to delve into about this game in comparison to its prequel, I'll keep it short. _childDocuments_.review: I love this series. I consider myself lucky to have stumbled across it and I'm definitely going to be helping Kickstart any future games. The mystery and tension didn't feel as high as the first game either, but from a mechanics standpoint, I enjoyed finding the collectibles and it was easier to navigate.If we end up with a game that has the stakes/tension of Death Mark 1, the vibrant characters of NG, and the mechanics of Death Mark 2...that would be one hell of an experience.As a side note: the game is a direct sequel to Death Mark 1, so you should definitely play that first. _childDocuments_.review: A good entry in the Spirit Hunter series, although still not as good as the original. The "new" "feature" of 2d side-scroller sections isn't really much of anything except a faster way to get between locations over the slow, manual, step by step method of previous entries.They've almost completely removed the creepy events that happen when you wave your flashlight around. There's a occasional ones when you interact with objects and rare ones in loading screens if you keep them turned on. So the atmosphere is less tense than previous games.I do appreciate the story though. Each chapter is a well-made story in itself, and the overarching plot is well-paced throughout the chapters, giving hints and warnings at each step so you never forget why you're doing what you're doing, or feeling like nothing's going on with it.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, it wasn't as good as the previous games. I liked the first game for the puzzles and battle system and I liked the second game for the story. But this game felt like a bit of a downgrade to what I liked about both of them. The difficult puzzles were what made the first game fun, but since the second game, they became a lot easier. The battle system also became less fun, I liked it when we had to make a combo move, it was more engaging. The second game made up for these losses with it's superior story, but this game didn't. The mysteries were, in my opinion, were way too obvious, and made the game lose its element of mystery for the most part. The story didn't seem to improve since the second game, and it still suffers from a lot of the same problems as the previous games.The lack of details is the main problem for all of the games. It was still pretty weak in this game, but it was an improvement from the first. Even though we has access to a lot of areas in this game, there wasn't much to explore. You couldn't find any interesting details in the areas you had access to, especially if it wasn't relevant to the main story. If it isn't relevant to the main story, it doesn't exist, that's what it feels like. The story treats normal living, like explaining things to people or driving to the school as unimportant, and just skips over it. But it would add to the story to know what it's really like to live in this world. And it would add to Yashiki's character to know how he explains things instead of just saying, "he told them the situation" or something along those lines. It may take up more time to explain things that we, the audience already know, but this line was used so many times and I feel like we don't really know who Yashiki is because we aren't allowed to see how he communicates. Letting Yashiki explain things would've been perfect for when he was teaching the students. Without little details like this, it makes the story feel incomplete and empty. Details like Yashiki putting enough sugar in his coffee until he's satisfied or Akira picking which drink he wants to get from the vending machine and getting to taste it make me way too happy when details like this should be expected. But yeah, the world building and characters are shallow because of the lack of details. These problems may have been lessened with the drama CDs, but sadly, that's locked behind translations for the English audience.But I have more complaints than this. Namely, the lack of horror in this game. It felt like compared to the rest of the games, they didn't put as much effort into the horror elements. There weren't any jumpscares like in the previous games. I had the jumpscares on, but I don't recall seeing anything in the shadows like in the other games, just a glitching screen and loud noises occasionally when I entered a new room or clicked on the menu option, so I just turned off the jumpscares near the end of the game because it was more annoying than scary.Another one would be the avoidable deaths. I understand that Yashiki's arc is about not being able to save everyone shouldn't stop him from trying his best, but you'd think at some point you'd learn the warning signs that someone is going to die. This is mostly with the hooligan. His death may have been  avoidable if they continued to search for him, but they didn't. It felt like Yashiki just wasn't learning from his past mistakes.I also feel like the way Yashiki gets answers for his questions is too clean and convenient, especially compared to the other games, unless if there's a reason for this.The spirits that Yashiki purified throughout the story felt more bland/not as memorable compared to the previous ones. That may have been because of the lack of variety in the settings, but I'm not really sure why, that's probably just my opinion.But if there was anything that this game did better than the previous ones, they made the protagonist better. Other than Yakumo Miroku, Yashiki is my favorite character. He's a kind person who has a great ability to sympathize with even the spirits he purifies, but the fact that he's a good person doesn't constantly get rubbed in your face like other stories I've seen: he's more subtle. In fact, he didn't even start out as a person that wanted to save everyone, he just wanted to escape the mark he was cursed with and found others with the same problem, which motivated him further, wanting to save everyone else as well. And with this game, they gave him a character arc. It made him more realistic and developed as a character when his guilt for not being able to save everyone follows him more compared to the first game, where someone dies and it's forgotten about it for the rest of the story.The main antagonist of this story is also interesting, though not as much as the others though because to me, they don't seem like they'll have as much relevance in future games as others but an overall good antagonist.Despite this game's flaws, I really do like it, and I look forward to the next game because I want to see it improve, so I recommend the series, it needs more love.

_childDocuments_.review: Only finished Chapter 1 for now and it's fun to see side-scrolling investigation (I hope I won't have to run and hide from dangers in Clock Tower-style haha), 10 running old men grunts out of 10. Previous games pixel hunting somehow gave more spooks and immersion tho, but I won't complain much about it, it's nice to have fresh mechanics.Also glad to see that now stats and items can actually have weight in gameplay, as well as success system gives more intrigue (but sometimes it feels a bit silly, I wish it could look more spooky).Will update the review after finishing the game! For now, I'm gonna reflect on cases and Some of things didn't turn out as I expected both mechanic- and story-wise, but overall I still enjoyed the game.I wish there were more engagements and surprises in side-scrolling part. Although I'm glad no one chased my ass, but something like hiding spooky spirits or someone slowly approaching you in the hallway so you have to run to the destination would be nice for extra pressure. Or more changes in enviroment as curses growing stronger or a bit more puzzles, perhaps?Speaking about jumpscapes, in DMII they feels cheap, wacky and more annoying rather than really spooky :( I love the way they were done in prequel, when you are scared to open a closet or move flashlight to a certain spot because you may find otherworldly presence silently staring at you and then disappearing in a blink of eye, as if making you question your own sanity.The spirits didn't feel so grotesque and disturbing as I expected and failed to make feel uneasy. Most time I laughed at their goofiness (still would not want to meet those guy IRL tho). I think the designs from previous games did a greater job in horror terms.The fights became much easier to go through and I wish they were much more challenging (random is kinda fun at first but overall this element feels wacky and doesn't make me tense my butt on the seat) and unforgiving for mistakes.And uuuh chapter 4 was totally unnecessary, in my humble opinion.......... And yet, I enjoyed the story and the growing tension despite the answer to a mystery being more obvious than I could expect. I also love to meet old crew and see more developments to their characters as well as engagements with each other. Also enjoyed bits of everyone's voices :)I would give a solid 7/10 because it was good, but it could be much better. Perhaps if there wasn't the unfortunate incident of losing a lot of development progress, the game could have all the things that it is lacking now :(Meeoo

_childDocuments_.review: I feel the need to review this game because I really hope this series gets another sequel. The game is certainly not perfect, but still very enjoyable. For the 2D aspect, while I did not mind it, I am not sure it added anything.For negatives of the game, there's a few. First, this game has less major spirit cases than the previous 2 games, likely due to focusing more on the the main antagonist spirit. I will say that I think this is the best main antagonist of the spirit hunter games, and that was helped by the extra effort into them. The true ending was enjoyable, but getting it was a little contrived in my opinion. I did enjoy the twist of the game. While I will say the price is a bit high, I certainly enjoyed it. _childDocuments_.review: I was really looking forward to this new entry in this series, as I loved both previous installments. While  was more like a side story, this one (as the title implies) is a full-on sequel to , so we get to play as the ‘Spirit Doctor’ once again. Unfortunately, I didn’t feel like this newest chapter could live up to its predecessors, but still, it wasn’t bad, either.The new gameplay elements include walking around in 2D environments, collecting and using stuff, sometimes with a companion who we can also interact with. This part reminded me of  games (without anyone actually chasing us), and was a great addition, in my opinion, as the whole thing started to feel more like a classic, old-school point ‘n’ click adventure game rather than simply a visual novel. More interaction in these types of titles is always a big plus for me. With that said, the atmosphere somehow wasn’t as creepy as in the previous entries, and I believe it was not a good idea that 90% of the main plot took place in one location and its direct surroundings. Running back and forth between the same rooms and buildings in each chapter became quite tedious for me after a while, and not even the jumpscares worked too well. Though I must admit, the evil spirits still look terrifying, and we get many brutal, gory scenes, some even depicting suicide, so keep that in mind.Overall, the story was OK, but the twists are not that surprising if you pay attention, and the puzzles are not that crazy difficult, either. It was nice seeing the old characters again, and some fun new ones. If you liked the series so far, give this one a try, but don’t expect anything too memorable.
_childDocuments_.name: Spirit Hunter: Death Mark II

_childDocuments_.review: If you like the other Spirit Hunter games you will like this.  If you haven't played the series before, this is certainly the one with the most forgiving game play with lots of nice QoL changes.I thought the move to 2D side scrolling was pretty good, though the school didn't really take advantage of it.  The forest really showed the potential of side scrolling though so I hope they will build on it in a sequel.Strong story as usual that really makes you want to try for the true ending.  They don't make you jump through too many hoops to get it (or anything else) which is nice though this does make the game shorter than the previous ones.  The extra case was cute but if you were expecting something meaty like in Death Mark 1 you'll be disappointed.Translation seemed fine.  Ran into one bug where I went into the Infirmary and my screen went black.  I could still move around though and once I exited the Infirmary everything went back to normal.Overall, I loved it and continue to love this series.
_childDocuments_.name: Spirit Hunter: Death Mark II

_childDocuments_.review: I love these games so much. I wish that they could go on forever. I love this game as much as the first two, but I do have some critiques.As always, the art is my favorite aspect of the series. I've always loved the skill of the artist with their rendering and the variety of people that they can design and draw. The monster designs have always been my absolute favorite part. That said, some of the monster designs in this game were either relatively dull compared to the rest of the spirits across all games, or the designs didn't make sense within the context of the spirit and its story. The good and true endings (I don't have the bad one yet) overstay their welcome. The need to tie everything up into such a neat package and/or give exposition on every single detail of the case is unnecessary in a game like this, and I believe that it's clumsy and awkward.The RPG-esque elements were interesting, but why the success/fail percentage? Aside from adding tension, it doesn't make sense and is only frustrating when you know you've chosen the right answer but it doesn't work.Even with those critiques, the only aspect of the game that truly disappoints me is the absence of Hyakki Yagyo. That's been a looming threat that's been mentioned in the first two games, and even if it wasn't the focal point of this game, I was hoping that there would at least be more build-up to it for a future game. Sadly, that wasn't the case. I hope that the Hyakki Yagyo plot hasn't been abandoned. I was/am very excited for it! I hope that there is a next game and that Hyakki Yagyo will be the focus! Also it would be amazing if Yashiki and Kijima team up like NG hinted!!!That said, the mysteries were very interesting, I was happy to see the Mark Bearers again, it was really cool to be in a single location instead of moving around and become familiar with it. The new traversal system is great (I liked the old way too, but this is certainly easier to navigate and the animated characters are more dynamic to watch), and THANK YOU for the quality-of-life gameplay design choices like [Q] to return to the Infirmary. The game would have been very tedious without that. It was SO COOL to have little animated movies at key moments! I loved it! Thank you very much for another marvelous game!!!

_childDocuments_.review: Spirit Hunter: Death Mark II is a top-tier VN horror game. I would recommend it 100%, with a 1000% for horror-enthusiast.The ghost stories are deeply engaging, complex and well-thought out with the main theme being LOVE BEYOND DEATH (twisted love, pure love, you name it the game has it all). I was constantly on the edge and glued from beginning to end, and given the nature of the game, I'd say they did exceptionally well in this regard. Obviously, I feel like the character interactions, puzzles and multiple choices are the biggest contributions as to why the guessing game in here is so damn good. Also, having played the previous entry (Spirit Hunter: Death Mark), I appreciate all the little details, references and the passion the devs poured into the game, which enriches the experience more. I believe in order to fully enjoy this outstanding sequel, playing the first game is highly recommended to understand the world of Spirit Hunter in regards to cursed dolls, spirits and events that lead to Death Mark II.To begin, the suspenseful, mysterious and tragic storytelling of Death Mark II coupled with our 'precious sensei' or Spirit Doctor, Kazuo Yashiki the MC is a prime example of how horror stories should be told. Yashiki ability to mesh with the rest of the cast and bring about their full quirky personality, as well as the way his relationships with the main heroines develop deserves praise. His reactions between hope and despair are priceless, yet despite the impossible odds, his determination and resourcefulness to save the living and the dead are what makes him truly unique (yes you need to save both to achieve the True Ending). This element of individuality adds weight and depth to his character, allowing the story to progress as it meant to be told. Adding to that, I really dig the 'feel' of the art designs for the ghosts, not to mention the eerie tracks on some areas which are the main reasons why I keep coming back to play Experience.Inc's games. And I really like the new characters (playful and teasing Michiho, shy and timid Douryou, yandere waifu The Departed, strict and stern Sakamoto, weird but helpful Abe) as well as returning ones (Satoru, Yasuoka, Daimon and Hiroo). Furthermore, the game has short movies in some chapters and I think its rare to see this in horror games, which is a delight to experience. Though, the 2D-side scrolling feels like a downgrade due to the fact that it made the horror sections i.e spirit interactions much 'cheaper' of an experience compared to the usual exploration in the previous entries, however it did manage to create a sense of adventure when you're collecting items to level your spirits and receiving area damage. That being said, the rest of the game are dreadfully fun since it focuses more on character stats and sacred objects to help you in your cases. As for jump-scares, you can turn it on or off in the settings, but having it enabled feels much more immersive imo since it can appear in a variety of ways even when you're chilling in the corner :). Now for the fan-service on the main heroines (which are likely made for the Japanese audience), they are tastefully done (in a weird way) and doesn't clash with the ghastly, macabre atmosphere at all, rather it serves to further entrap you with a sense of bizarreness and anxiety where death is your constant companion.In terms of technical issues, I believe there are some text errors here and there i.e Nakamura instead of Nakamatsu, Stoppping instead of Stopping etc. The controller support follows the Xbox control layout but so far I've faced no problems playing with a controller.Overall, I had massive fun and enjoyment playing Spirit Hunter: Death Mark II. The game is worth it (only when it's on sale, if ever). I consider it an unforgettable 9/10. It's just that good, I hope Experience.Inc will cook up another Spirit Hunter game and keep up their Japanese spirit, maybe focusing on Lovecraftian horrors next (fishing hamlet, otherworldly city and fish people in Japan) or European settings (vampires, witch-hunt, castle ruins) because I know they can make it happen. The sky's the limit, there are so many ways for this series to branch out and I'm excited to play its sequel.

_childDocuments_.review:
In the suburbs of Tokyo's H City is a private institution called "Konoehara Academy," which was established over 100 years ago. There were rumors that every 10 years, the dead would creep into the academy and spread a curse.

Around the end of summer, some students of the academy died an inexplicable death in the academy garden...

While a police investigation was unable to confirm the nature of the incident, many rumors spread among the students regarding their tragic death, such as "it was the work of the dead" and "they were summoned by spirits."

In order to regain a sense of composure within the academy, the chairman requested an investigation from the Kujou house, which has been involved in rituals since ancient times.

A strange and sullen middle-aged man able to "examine" the supernatural, the head of the Kujou house begins an undercover investigation as a temporary teacher in order to determine the truth of the rumors.

And to experience the terrible curse from the dead that has crept into the academy....

name: Capes
detailed_description: Digital Deluxe Edition About the Game Twenty years ago, the supervillains won. Since then, they’ve created a dystopian city where developing super powers is a crime. Nobody has managed to slow them down, until now. Capes is a turn based superhero strategy game where you build a team of heroes and fight to take back the city. Played across a series of campaign and patrol missions, choose to push forward with the story or take the time to explore the side missions and unlock more heroes, earn skill points and complete challenges, and learn more about your heroes lives. Recruit new heroes with a range of unique powers and abilities. Every hero plays differently, and requires a fresh approach to their powers and abilities. Learning and exploiting each hero's unique play style will build their power in combat allowing them to unleash their personal tide turning Ultimates. Exciting, heroic, turn based combat to test your strategic skills. Team ups and positioning matter, unlocking new ways to approach every enemy type and supervillain you encounter. Capes combat isn't based around random numbers or lurking behind cover. Power doesn't make you invulnerable, far from it. Your choices will make the difference between victory and defeat. Take up to 4 heroes to work together in each mission. Each hero gains a unique team up ability from each of their allies, allowing them to work together to take advantage of their unique powers. Level up your heroes to gain access to new abilities and powerful upgrades. Use Skill Points acquired from completing objectives and challenges to unlock their powers. Complete collections of hero specific challenges during missions to earn bonus Skill Points and unlock optional missions that give a deeper insight into each of the heroes.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to enjoy this game. I am a huge fan of the Superhero genre in general, have hundreds of hours in other games, as well as TTRPGs. The powers, characters, story, all good.My only complaint is that it feels very tactically restrictive. There doesn't seem to be multiple ways to handle a mission, and it feels more like solving a puzzle with a pre-determined solution than actually making tactical choices and reacting to the battlefield. It has all the foundations there, but I feel like unless you make the "right" decisions, then every battle is just a slog.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is pretty simplistic and basic.The UI is very bare bones and lacks detail both in terms of giving details to the player, and in terms of visual fidelity.  The audio is, by default, incredibly low.  Very weird.  I had to bump it up a ton.  Not the end of the world.  The voice acting is very hit or miss.  The writing feels like a first or second pass on writing and some of it feels like it was written by someone in high school or college (I find myself rolling my eyes a lot as people speak).  Characters are one dimensional and cartoonish versions of people (they don't seem believable or real).  The entire concept of the villains coming from an organization called The Company makes me want to throw up a bit.I have no idea where this game takes place.  Accents in the game are ALL over the place.  The main characters each have a completely different accent.  The enemies in the game have different accents.  The hero Weathervane and his father have very different accents where the father is clearly French and I just can't figure out what the voice actor for Weathervane is trying to do.  It's distracting.  A Chinese character with a New Zealand accent (I think), an Indian character, a British accent ... one of the villains sounds Scottish or something ... some of the people sound like they're from New York.  One of the heroes has a very generic American accent (like American with no regional affectation ... like neutral American).  One of the heroes is Nigerian. It's hard to tell what's going on with the people.There aren't nearly enough character models.  This is mostly an issue in cutscenes where you will see multiple of the exact same character (same outfit, same colors on those clothing, same weapons in hand ... exact same character .... stamped over and over into a given scene).  It sure would have been nice if there was ... some kind of variation.  Even just tints on clothing would add a lot.  Have 3 of the same model in a cutscene ... give one a yellow tint, another a green tint, another gets a black tint ... whatever.  Just try to avoid people wearing street clothing where lots of people bought the exact same T-shirt and pants in the exact same colors.  In other games characters have uniforms and an intentional unified look .. here it's just people in street clothes so you really should expect to see variation ... or they should have used uniforms and made the enemies seem less like random street thugs (literally wearing a t-shirt and jeans and holding a pipe for a weapon).The game has been out for about 2 months.  From what I can see online it looks like they've sold roughly 9,000 copies.  41 active players is the max number of active players in the last 24 hours (says steamdb).  Not 25K or whatever.  Just 41 people.  I'm 5 hours into the game and the achievements I'm getting are at like 28-44% of steam users.  So, 9000 copies sold (says vginsights).  41 players playing (peak).  And, less than half of the people who own the game have completed Act 1 yet (representing 4-5 hours of gameplay).The gameplay feels shallow.  It makes me miss Freedom Force (from 20 years ago).  I absolutely LOVE tactical RPG games and I'm a big sucker for the super hero genre of games.  This game should be an absolute slam dunk for me.I think for $15-20 this is a perfectly fine buy!  I got it on sale for $29 and I feel like overpaid. I'm not giving up on it!  But, it's taking effort for me to want to turn it back on and play the next mission.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that should be my love. I saw and loved Guardians: Agents of Justice at E3 and heartbroken when it canceled. I love Freedom Force to bits and was my all time favorite single player Supes RPG till Marvel Midnight Suns. I also played and still from time to time play City of Heroes. This game should be a new fav, you can level up, the voice acting and story are decent, but one thing just did this game in for me. The missions are structured to be puzzle like, think Breach. If you like that game, you might enjoy this. I just couldn't enjoy that or this in the end. For a few hours gaining powers eases the puzzle aspect, offering you a sense of growing control of tactical options to solve missions. Till Mid act 2, you lose any ability to deal with the situation tactically with waves and waves of reinforcements and a objective that has many HP you have to do the perfect response to both puzzles to achieve. This ended my journey, I like tactical games, not puzzle games where you repeatedly die and replay over and over till you figure out the "trick"!Its a shame, i thought for a minute this started out restrictive, and will build and upgrade into your powers overcoming the puzzle. That would have worked. This just wasnt for me....

_childDocuments_.review: The tactics aren't fun. The cast is a diversity quota checklist, not actual characters. The game's tone is all over the place. I don't want to play it, and I don't want to watch it for its story either. In both gameplay and story, the game acts like a derivative of a derivative of a derivative. There's no soul here, nothing interesting. It's like a superhero game made by people who hate superheroes.The game also does a scummy thing of making it look like you have alternate costumes to equip, but trying to equip them instead takes you to the Steam DLC page to try charging you $11 for it. That's screwed up. That's mobile game crap. I lost a lot of good will for the devs when I saw that.The missions have BS in them that tactics games shouldn't have. Like objectives you don't know about until partway through the mission, which would have dictated the whole way you run it. They're contrived, and don't feel natural. I was putting up with it until one mission that was too annoying for me to continue playing.I stopped at the mission where you kidnap the streamer girl atop the skyscraper. It's an escort mission. To get her to follow you, you have to be ahead of her. You have to run her onto this elevator so she can escape. But to do that, you also have to be on the elevator. You also need to escape. Why don't you take that elevator? You've already got at least one character on the elevator to get the NPC escort there.there is no reason. It's just a contrivance to make the mission harder. You instead have to run to a totally different area while enemies spawn infinitely in your path.Also I heard no music during the missions. All I had were the same canned statements with atrocious accents.The characters are really bad. They went out of their way to combine multiple something abnormal about everyone. Everyone has a thick accent, but they're all different accents.- The African Tank is supposed to be a lawyer, in his last year of law school, but he talks like an idiot. You'd expect someone with multiple years of law school to at least be able to use words to describe what they see or their feelings.- As a Tank, he has a Taunt power, which would be a great place to include clever insults or good wordplay, as you'd expect someone with most of a law degree & ostensibly a high verbal IQ to do. But no. All of his taunts are utterly childish statements- Backstabbing lesbian rogue naturally backstabs people both in her life and in the game's mechanics. She's rewarded for it. She's obviously the dev's favorite because she's way more fun to use than the other characters. She has both massive mobility and massive damage output. The African Tank feels like he barely moves or acts at all by comparison. - Crippled Indian telekinetic who gets around the crippled part by just levitating himself everywhere. He plays a pity party card about being judged and bullied a lot (by whom???) and so doesn't want to judge or bully others... but when you play him, you can hear him getting off on making people weak and then hurting them. Sorry not sorry, I'm not falling for that. You can hear the voice actor giggle like he's getting sexual pleasure each time he makes people get brain problems and then makes them suffer. You expect me to have any sympathy for this character?None of the other characters mention this.- Brazilian (?) American football player who controls lightning and wind. His ultimate power involves him screaming in pain for a solid 5-7 seconds. It's an extremely long animation and scream. What a nightmare that would have been to play before the devs introduced a speed up button.- Asian speedster. Not much to say about her.If there are more characters, I'm not going to see them, because I don't care to play this game again.The tone is so inconsistent that I can't get a read on what the game expects. Sometimes people are throwing around swear words in every sentence, and other times they talk like G-rated comic book goons. The game shows the bad guys shooting people to bloody death but nobody mentions how your heroes are killing a lot people too.The evil people are The Company and The Government. That's literally what they're called. It couldn't be more bland and lifeless if they tried.

_childDocuments_.review: Can't recommend.Capes will get compared to X-Com, but really it's more like the spinoff Chimera Squad. There's a linear storyline and combat takes place on smaller maps and you worry a lot about turn order. The problem is that while other games give you a neat set of tools and a sandbox in which to play with them, the Capes levels are very narrow in their acceptable path to winning. Any deviation from that path means you fail, often spectacularly. Honestly I don't know how they playtested some of these levels, because a lot of people with many hours in other turn-based tactics games are bouncing off Capes' levels. The level design is a big part of this - Capes typically wants to overwhelm the player with twelve or more opponents at a time - sure you've got a squad of four heroes, but it's easy to get surrounded. Just when you think you've got a handle on something here come another half-dozen thugs. I suppose if you're playing optimally this is all fine, but it's a complete train-wreck if you're not.There are some great ideas in here - for example each hero has a unique team-up power with another hero. Sure, most of Weathervane's team-up powers are about adding Push to another hero's attack, but then Facet boosts Mercurial and she leaves an entire wall of crystal when she dashes across the map.If you're on the fence, I'd wait a few months and see if they can fix the balance issues. Right now it's a mess, which is a shame.

_childDocuments_.review: Right now you can get both Into the Breach and Marvel's Midnight Suns for less than the price of this, and I'd recommend doing that. If you want something retro, you can throw in the Freedom Force games and still come out ahead. Each of those are individually more fun, so getting all of them for less than the asking price is a no-brainer. I wanted to love this game, it has such a cool premise, but there's so many issues with it, ranging from the writing being atrocious, to having to grind the same missions ad nauseam to get any XP. The biggest problem is it doesn't feel like there's any customization - every map is small and feels like it has a fixed solution, so there are objectively "right" ways to build your heroes, rather than bringing in your own strategy. It ends up just feeling kind of boring, because you're literally doing the same moves and missions over and over, with no reason to ever deviate.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a huge fan of tactics games. I get hooked on all sorts regardless of quality. This one, however, is rough. I can overlook the annoying characters and B tier voice acting. I don't mind the graphical simplicity. The mega generic world with awful writing doesn't really matter to me. What matters to me is the gameplay and this one just doesn't hit the mark at all. It's bland, it's irritating, and worse than that, it's limited in what you can do. Sure, every character has a handful of neat abilities and you got a bunch of characters to select from, but you know how you level them up? Skill points that are ONLY earned by doing "optional" objectives within premade missions. That means there is NO freedom at all. You don't get to experiment like in other tactics games. You go into these premade missions, you do exactly what the optional objectives require in order to get skill points, and that's that. Over the last few years there has been a resurgence of tactics games. Phoenix Point, Shardpunk, Lamplighter's League, Othercide, Battle Brothers, and several others. They all have their problems but they're all FUN. They allow you to mess around. To experiment with your units, their abilities, and still let you progress accordingly. Capes doesn't do that. You either experiment OR you level up and progress as intended. I can't recommend this game at all. Go play the few others I listed, or the incredible XCOM franchise for the millionth time. Seriously, Lamplighter's League had problems but it was such a fun time in a really cool setting. Shardpunk is a super low budget indie with rat hordes and steampunk gadgets. Othercide is stylized with a cool world. Go play those instead. They all deserve your time and money far more than this mess.

_childDocuments_.review: I picked this game up thinking I was getting an X-Com super hero game; but instead what I got was Into the Breach.  What I mean by that is this game is more of a puzzle-game than it is a turn-based strategy game.  If I had known that I likely would not have purchased it.  So far it also seems like there are no "random" missions which could allow the player to freely experiment with how to use their powers either.Sadly this is one of the few negative reviews I've posted; but hopefully it can help others make the right decision on rather or not they want to purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: I was very hyped for Capes. The idea of a turn based superhero game sounds great, in theory. But to be honest, I don't really feel anything for this game. Some might say that only 3 hours of play is a bit too little to judge, and that's fair enough. I'm giving this review now to give you some perspective. So let's start with the positives:- The heroes designs are pretty cool! I like the old school X-men costumes and I do get that kind of vibe from these Capes.- Controlling your heroes is pretty easy. I have miss clicked on things a few time's, but I think that's more my problem than the games.- The game itself runs well. Not had any kind of issues, technical wise.The negatives (here is where I might be a bit harsh):- The writing is average at best and cringe at worst. This goes for the voice actors as well. I get the impression that they are doing their best with the material they have, but good lord... Sometimes it's pretty bad.- The XP system is a bit strange to me.  For context, you gain 1 experience for a beginner mission, which sounds reasonable. The problem is. getting from level 2 to 3 requires you to gain at least 15 XP. There are higher difficulty missions, but it presents the same issue. It will take far too long to level up your heroes. If it was something like X-com where you gained XP for each bad guy you knocked out or assisted with KOing, that would make sense.- The combat does start to get tedious after a while. I like doing combos with other heroes, but even that starts getting old pretty fast.I might update this if and when I get round to playing more. As of right now, I'm not really compelled to do so. Again, if you think it's unfair to criticise after only a few hours of game time, fair enough. As I said, I'm giving this review now so you have a rough understanding of what to expect.If I could give an average review I would. But it's a thumbs down for now.
