_childDocuments_.review: Note: I did not finish the game but I did put in almost 50 hours.Overall, I think this game is a mixed bag. If you like really challenging gameplay that forces you to make very few mistakes, you might like this. If you want to experience a superhero power fantasy or a modern X-Com like experience, I would suggest looking elsewhere. It plays far more like X-Com Chimera Squad than X-Com 2.The general gameplay puts you and a team of up to four relatively underpowered heroes in a small arena against a horde of mooks, sometimes with more elite (and interesting) forces. While there are some tools and interesting power combinations to help deal with these issues... sometimes... sometimes the forced combination of heroes and the arena prevents this.What the developers I think missed was the power fantasy that is heroes (while respecting this as a tactical game that does need to challenge the player) and the progression that tactical games provided. In X-Com, you develop your squad vs stat boots at leveling, researching new equipment, and selecting new abilities at level up. Here, the only betterment of your heroes is spending points that you need to grind for (although, with achievements, there do seem to be a decent amount of them). Leveling up your character only lets you buy more abilities, but provides no other aid.The story it seems tries to be a little grey, with secrets between the older, former heroes, but the tale never truly grabbed me. You also have to buy that the federal government would let a corporation just take over a city and violate human rights on the daily instead of sending their Superman equivalent to just clean them out.Overally, the gameplay just wasn't fun, with forced/unfair stealth, stacked odds against the heroes, overreliance on hordes of mooks/reinforcements, and supeheroes who are too underpowered to feel like... well superheroes.I give the team (I believe it was only 4 people, just incredible) credit for their efforts. But what they created and what I prefer were ultimately two different beasts and I just can't find enough in it to recommend it to others.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish that Steam had a "neutral" rating, because for this game I have things I like and things I don't like, but if I have to choose between Yes or No I reluctantly choose No. A pity, because I played the demo when it was first released and liked it so much I wishlisted the game and bought it almost as soon as it was out. Please note there will likely be spoilers, but I will try to keep them vague.Things I liked:* Characters being able to combine their attacks or powers* Being able to disarm enemies or knock them off ledges* The evolution of powers and abilities as time goes on (e.g. Rebound being able to hit more enemies, Weathervane being able to knock enemies further)Things I didn't mind:* What some people call inconsistency with the accents etc I just chalked up to the city being pretty metropolitan, with all sorts of people living there. I myself know people who speak English with a pronounced accent but whose kids speak with American accents due to picking up the language via media or Filipino accents due to having teachers or caretakers who spoke that way. Things I disliked:* Some of the option missions weren't very fun, and trying to do some of them in one go could get frustrating.* The characters. This specifically is why I haven't gone back to continue the game. The 8 deadly words (i.e. "I don't care what happens to these people"). I at least didn't mind the first few characters we meet like Rebound or Facet, and how they bounce off of each other. But as the game went on, we start running into characters or find out more that eventually caused me to actively dislike them. As an example, one character is portrayed as hot-headed and angry, and at one point insists on visiting home despite being warned this is a bad idea. They're then furious that his family is put at risk, when it's their own damn fault for insisting on going. Another character is introduced as being someone with a chip on their shoulder, and in a conversation straight up states they actively want to make people angry. I instantly developed a dislike of them, but got the impression we'd be forced to make use of them for story reasons. That a number of prominent characters ostensibly on the side of our heroes are unpleasant at best made me lose interest in seeing things through. * The story. At first, I kind of liked the idea of a city where villains run things and heroes are underground, but by the time the game came out I was kind of sick of the whole "oooooh, what if the villains won and killed off or drove heroes into hiding?" thing done in places like Marvel or DC or even Transformers of all places. In addition, as the story progressed I got the impression it would lead to a "as it turns out, the heroes weren't all that heroic after all." twist, which is again something I'm a bit weary of seeing. It was enough that I didn't care enough whether to see if I was right or not. As you can see, I mostly enjoyed the gameplay but because I began to actively dislike the characters I just lost interest in playing through to the end. I won't claim I was scammed or anything, as the demo's gameplay was what sold me on this game in the first place, but it's a bit of a shame that it's stuff late in the game that may cause you to lose interest like I did.

_childDocuments_.review: I like the art, the game play, and the story, but it's just too hard.  Each mission is just a puzzle, and I'm just not able to solve them, so I can't go any further.  I'd rather play an actual game than solve a series of riddles, where if you can't think of the answer you're just stuck until you do.  The last level I played had 35 enemies on the field at once.  Each of them did at least 1 damage per attack, one of my heroes only has 3 HP, (apparently for the entire game) and once she goes down you have to start over.  Super frustrating, and not fun - you definitely don't feel like a powerful superhero.  Not to mention it's hardly fun watching 35 enemies all take the turns in order, even with the new "fast forward" button they've added.  The level I stopped at has about that many enemies walking in patrols, and you're supposed to sneak through them without being spotted.  I've tried at least 50 times, and if there is a way through, I expect it's only for one specific set of heroes, with only one specific sequence of 30-50 moves and actions.  There are no hints, there are no alternative strategies, or ways to proceed - if you can't come up with that one solution, the game is over for you.  I don't know why the developers thought we'd want to guess the single solution they thought of, or brute force our way through thousands and thousands of combinations to it, but this just sucks to play.EDIT: Since posting this, I've read a lot of other reviews that do a better job at phrasing the same issues that I had.  I didn't start the game until after the recent update, so I don't know what changed, but my impressions here are based on the current version.  For example, the stealth mission I mentioned above is called "Don't Meet Your Heroes."  And sure - if you're spotted, it's not a hard 'game over.'  You just fail the primary objective of the mission, you don't get the XP award for doing it, and you now have to fight an overwhelming number of enemies, likely with your team starting in awkward positions because you were trying to avoid the fight.  From the developer's response to this review, it sounds like it used to be a 'hard stop,' and now it's it's only a 'soft stop' because you're technically allowed to keep going, but being allowed to progress despite everything in the game making it clear that I've failed what is supposed to be a stealth mission just isn't appealing.  Who would want to keep going, if you feel like you failed the mission?  I don't think that's what people in these reviews have meant when they've said missions should have more than one solution.In the other mission I mentioned in my initial review, you fight a supervillain that hits everyone on your team for 2 HP each round.  Some heroes only have 3 HP, so you're dead right away unless you disarm him every round - but he takes 4 tries to disarm each time, and each of the four heroes you can bring on the mission can only use the Disarm action once per turn.  That wouldn't normally leave you with enough actions each turn to make progress against all the henchmen shooting you, or to actually damage the boss on top of just disarming him.  Except - SOME heroes in your roster have actions that cause 2 disarm at once.  Great!  But you have to bring those specific heroes, and use those specific actions each round.  There's nothing in the game that warns you about this, and you're free to try and fail the mission with your favorite heroes, the ones you actually want to play as, or to fail it by using the attacks that you think are more fun.  The gameplay here hinges on spotting those problems and figuring out the solution - it's essentially a puzzle game, with a very small number of solutions to each mission.  That's not fun for me, even though I was really enjoying the story and characters and setting.

_childDocuments_.review: My opinions about Capes are complicated. It reminds me of everything I like about both Gloomhaven and Freedom Force. The combat mechanics are well-designed and show off a remarkable amount of depth without being overly complex. The characters each have a unique feel and the synergistic "team-ups" add an extra layer of depth to team construction. The encounters are varied, with different tactics required for each fight and a wide variety of objectives. And yet, the actual gameplay leaves me frustrated. I don't think I ever felt properly challenged while playing Capes - the difficulty was always either trivially easy or overwhelmingly difficult. I don't think the gameplay loop of "just barely make it through the encounter once and then come back and breeze through it later for extra points" works. The initial playthrough of each level includes feeling like a screw-up for missing secondary objectives and then being surprised by weird changes in primary objectives (e.g. a level where you have to escort an NPC to an elevator, only to then have to run the rest of your team to another elevator on the other side of the zone). My save file got corrupted from a system crash (trying to load back in just put me back in the main menu), and so I think that concludes my experience with Capes.

_childDocuments_.review: Tactical superheroes is an underserved genre, and particularly after the updates the game has received, this is a welcome entrant. It's got issues, but I think, at least on sale, it'll be worth your time if you enjoy the genre.Strengths Include:* The game gets pretty challenging as you progress, but after the patches, I think it manages to mostly avoid the "puzzle" vibe many complained of at launch, and is a proper tactics showdown. It's not XCOM, but it's not Hard West, either.* While not all of the heroes are great (see weaknesses below), there's enough options with enough upsides to each that I found myself often having to stop and consider just who to bring on any given mission.* While it can take a bit to get the right advancements, some of your more offensive heroes evolve into satisfying, mook-legion wasting unholy terrors.* "Team Ups" are a neat gimmick, where heroes in close proximity to one another can utilize modified versions of their powers, bolstered by their companion. Having each hero not be standalone but also a source of mobile powerups adds another layer to positioning and helps give each character a bit more mechanical identity.* Another mechanical widget I found novel is disarmament; enemy weapons, as well as certain boss and miniboss big moves that take time to wind up, can be "disarmed", which can make your life *much* easier when applied well. Heroes vary significantly in their effectiveness at this, so depending on what you anticipate facing and how disarmable it might be, this will be a factor in who you pick out of your roster.* As Tactical Breach Wizards has illustrated to us all recently, defenestration is a must for the genre, and I was pleased to see it offered here in abundance.* It's a neat little thing to me, but you can replay previous missions to try to perfect them, and some of the dialog differs based on who you bring to the party. This includes heroes you wouldn't have had access to when running the mission initially, which is a cute touch!Weaknesses:* The enemy variety is ultimately a bit lacking.* Even post-patches, a few of the heroes are pretty lackluster. "Facet", one of your starting characters, is a good example; pretty much a pure tank with near nothing offensive power, but doesn't really have the durability to do that, either. Most of the characters are in a decent place, but when a mission demands that you bring along one of the stinkers, you really feel it.* On a similar note, other than Facet, the next two characters you get are the squishiest in the game (3 HP, when attacks typically do 1-2), and they're all you get for a while. It's probably educational to have to learn to be very, very careful with your positioning, avoiding greed and the like, but it's also not a gentle introduction.* Advancement is... odd. You earn a small amount of Skill Points from completing missions, but the lion's share of them come from completing optional side objectives. These SP are spent to unlock upgrades and new moves on any hero. Characters also get XP and level up from going on missions, but all this does is raise the tier limit on what upgrades can be bought with SP. You don't have to pursue that side SP if you don't want to, particularly if one seems very annoying, but they're not wholly ignorable either. Neglect them entirely, and you'll eventually start feeling underpowered. As stated above, you can go back to earlier missions to try to score those side objectives (and do so with heroes and upgrades you've unlocked since), but I did get bogged down at a few points where particularly difficult main missions had me going back and hunting down spare SP wherever I could to try to bolster my odds. * The writing is... bad. Very bad. Seemingly still an earnest labor of love, but a bad one. Mood and tone whiplash all over the place, characters are flat and sometimes inconsistent, and the plot demands a lot of idiot ball holding.Lastly, because apparently this is *the* controversy for the game: there's a lot of histrionics over the involvement of Sweet Baby Inc, "DEI", "wokeness", and so on. The cast of heroes *is* very diverse, and most of them don't have much going for identity outside of that... but that is, again, because the writing is bad. In other timeline, instead of flat, dull intersectional heroes, we'd have a team of flat, dull, mostly white ones. Just completely missing the forest for the trees, because they're apparently the wrong color. Whining about the one bit of character detail they do manage to have, when even that apparently needed outside consultation to get, is the only thing more cringy than the writing itself. To sum up: this probably isn't a Buy At Full Price title, but provided you enjoy the intersection of genres and think you can stomach routine eye rolling, there's a good bit of fun to be had here.

_childDocuments_.review: Lots of fun. The game feels quite tightly balanced on hard, at least until the very later missions (arguably too easy). The powers are interesting and there's a fair amount of utility in the heroes's kits, and each hero has a pretty distinct style and feel.From reading other reviews, there seems to be a complaint about how 'puzzle-like' the game is. This is somewhat true, but it only really holds early on, when there are a limited set of heroes and thus powers to operate with. Especially on hard, the first few missions really do play like puzzles as you have to play in a very specific manner to get all of the SP achievements in a single go. Later on, however, there are a lot more options and many more ways to approach the problem. Sure, certain heroes have advantages with certain objectives, but that's the whole point of having a diverse set of skills. I'd almost say the latter missions are too easy because of that, compared to the early ones - there are many ways of handling the problems once you have all the heroes leveled up decently.Also, I don't really understand the complaint about having to grind. There's basically zero forced grinding in this game. While XP is used for gaining levels, levels by themselves don't actually increase your power directly; levels only control what talents you can learn, and you need to spend SP to actually learn and upgrade powers. So while you can get XP by re-running a mission, you are primarily limited by the SP availability, which is quite finite as they can only be earned once by doing achievements in the missions. You can get all the SP you can get from a mission in just one run. While there are character specific non-mission achievements you can theoretically grind, I never felt like I was behind the curve power-wise by simply doing each mission once to get the SP achievements. It's also a fairly hefty game given the missions are all hand-made. This is both good and bad since it does mostly limit replay value (it's linear, though some of the dialogue seems to change depending on your team comp) but it's a good deal of content given the nature of the missions.The game is really more Fire Emblem than X-Com in terms of the tactics, though it's also much more utility focused than either. Also, as the missions are set pieces, you should expect to reload a couple of times on the harder ones until you find a good strategy for approaching it. Straight damage is not really the focus (though damage is good); instead, positioning and utility abilities tend to be much more important considerations. The numbers and map sizes are small, yes, but I don't see that as being a downside; instead, it keeps the focus on maneuvering and precise actions rather than trying to deal with blobs.The game is not a grand strategy and it's not massive in scope; it's a small-unit TBT with strong focus on CC and movement. Within those lines, it does a good job and it's pretty well tuned in terms of challenge.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game and I did get enjoyment out of it but there's just one major issue I can't get over.The optional objectives. Firstly, they're not all that optional, if you consistently miss them you won't have enough SP to properly upgrade your heroes as the game increases in difficulty. Secondly you are forced to play the game in a very narrow way because of it. On almost every level I could have beaten it far faster and more effectively, but to get the optional objectives I had to be slow and inefficient with my moves; Leaving enemies alive so I could disarm them instead of simply killing them etc. It's a really obtuse way to increase difficulty and forces you to hold yourself back from what you're really capable of. A system like this forces you to play the level in the way the developers intended, with the heroes they wanted you to use. It removes player choice and creativity from all the levels at least the first time you play them, and due to the puzzle like, deterministic nature of this game (Which I actually like) there is no incentive to play the level again once you've beaten it the *right* way.I would fix this by making every level give you bonus SP for beating it in as few rounds as possible instead, as that would incentivise efficiency while still allowing a lot of player creativity. I'd also just get rid of XP completely, all character trees being unlocked from the get go, allowing you to spend SP more freely, giving you even more agency over your personal playstyle. This would also make replaying the game more interesting, as last time you may have fully invested in your favorite hero and used them to smash every mission, but what if you challenged yourself by not using that hero this time? It would make every level feel like a totally fresh puzzle.Also, I think team based turns like Xcom are better. I just wanted to tab through my team to see all their options instead of having to delay them, which is mostly fine when they're all lined up in the que, but gets messy once initiatives start getting mixed up. I understand why they chose to do it this way, because initiative is one more lever to pull, I just don't think it adds enough to be worth the sacrifice. This one is a minor gripe though.Also, Rebounds ultimate targeting enemies randomly, especially in a deterministic game like this, is a shockingly strange and very frustrating choice. I wasted so much time save scumming it to get the outcome I was looking for. Someone really dropped the ball on that one.

_childDocuments_.review: What it is:A squad level turn based tactics gameA system based on simple premises that generate interesting decisionsCheesy superhero actionWhat it isn't:A custom hero creatorTop end graphicsA literary prizewinnerI enjoyed the demo plenty when it was released and have been looking forward to the game ever since. The thing that sold me on it was the combat system. There are some simple ideas (Heroes gain modified versions of their moves when within 3 spaces of another hero) that generate a lot of options and create competing rewards. The UI is clean, it's easy to see what a move will do and to predict how enemies will act and react. The optional objectives that produce level ups being present each mission creates a tension between the best move to win the mission and the best move to further the objective. I'm a gameplay first kind of a person, so the core gameplay loop being interesting and good is what sold me on the game.As far as the demo went, the team are listening to fans and making improvements too. There are a bunch of small things in the game that iron out kinks that were reported during the demo. A really simple example: The indicator at the top of the screen showing how many parts a mission is in. Previously it was possible to blow an ultimate to make sacrifices to complete objectives before a level was over, only to find that there's a lot more level left and you could have done the objectives later more usefully. Now it's clear how much mission is left. These sorts of things are never going to be the big things that make or break a game, but that sort of attention to detail makes the game smoother to play and it's nice that the demo was a tool to improve the game rather than just a marketting gimmick. Gives faith in the devs.If you're a graphics first rather than gameplay first kind of a player this may not be your cup of tea. They're plenty servicable, but they're noticably dated, the videos and screenshots on the store page give a pretty accurate impression of what you're in for. Similarly if a character builder is a deal breaker for you this game doesn't have one, I think that was a great decision, since it means that the characters can all have very different skills and niches without needing to worry about having them fit some generic 'ability builder' template. It's the price of having all of the characters be different and interesting.I can't speak to value for money yet. I tend to figure on wanting at least an hour out of a game for each pound I spend on it - less if the game's a work of art, more if it's grindy - but until I see the end credits roll I won't know if there's enough game for that or not. If you're reading this review a year later you can compare my total playtime to the game's price and see what you think.Overall, based on the demo and the first few levels, it's a thumbs up from me.

We've seen plenty of those the last few years, but none has managed to get even close to the overall 'feeling' and experience that X-com gave us.So now we have this game, Capes, yet another part of the "throw enough sh-t at the wall and some are bound to stick".  Sadly, this really isn't the next X-Com game/clone one might've hoped for.Sure, it's not "fair" to compare it X-Com or whatever.   But it's impossible not to.The story is...mediocre.   You really *really* dont give a flying rat's behind about the story. It's yawn-inducing at BEST.Graphics are ..dumb.  I'm personally not too picky with graphics, not every game has to look super realistic or whatever.  The graphics in this game is also, mediocre.   The artstyle is some weird mix between cartoon and clay.  That's the best way I could describe it.     The animations in some of the so-called 'cutscenes' are also wonky sometimes, where certain moves they make are just weird, as in sudden superspeed in a motion.  And no i'm not talking about superheroes with superspeed. Just the normal animation of two people talking, one guy might do half a facepalm, but the animation for it is cranked up to 400% speed.  That's just one of MANY examples.    You can look past one or two weird animations,  but after witnessing several, in a row, you can't help but notice every single weird thing/animation.The voice acting is...well, not bad, but far from good.  Around the mediocre ranking for this as well.So, graphics are alright, but mostly dumb, animations sometimes looks like it was made with stop-motion, using clay figures..  Story is terrible, boring, and puts me to sleep.   Cutscenes are boring.So...what about the cream then, the combat, the action? The "super powers" and all that fun stuff?Combat is...take a guess?mediocre at best.There's no depth to the combat.    The way it SEEMS to be made by the devs, is that there's ONE way to complete each encounter/mission, and one way only.  It's up to you to play this guessing/puzzle game of which way to attack or approach.There's really no tactics involved.  Do the mission the only way it's possible, the way it's coded, forget even using your brain and come up with some sweet combos and masterful tactics.   Your plan could be amazing, but unless it's the way the devs thought this mission should be played, then forget it.    So you're left with just trying to see what the devs was thinking when they made this mission.Sounds fun eh?   Why would we want to play a game like this, with our own brain and smarts, trying to immerse yourself in the combat and story.  Nah,  forget that, there's no room for you to plan or be 'smart' in this game.  Only way for you to be smart, is to, as I said, play it the *exact* way the devs imagined the mission when they created it.Several 'superheroes' in your party (only starting out with 2 but more join later), with their own 'unique' skills and powers.  Sounds kinda cool eh?   On paper it is, before actually playing the game, it all sounds amazing. Superheroes, and X-com-ish kinda game? Sign me up!      Well, in my opinion, do not sign up,  instead, run away.  Put those money into another game instead.  This game is very much overpriced.This game was, to me, a disappointment.   I dont think even a 7yr old would enjoy this for more than 10 minutes, MAX.You are literally better off playing X-com instead.   Despite being pretty old today,  X-Com still plays better, is more fun, keeps you interested, AND actually looks better.  There was some whining about "woke" and stuff surrounding this game.  I dunno. as I personally dont care, as long as they dont force feed me this "DEI" stuff.   All I can and will say, is that you start the game with 2 characters.  A dark skinned male. And a lesbian girl.  And the supervillain is a white male.  You draw your own conclusion.This isn't a game that's in Early Access, with tons of improvements and changes to come, so I could say "wait til it gets more content".  This is a finished product, for almost €40,  and the only thing that could change in this game is that perhaps they'll add more missions, probably thru DLC.     And if the game is boring now, it will forever and ever be boring, because the game needs a compelte overhaul to become FUN and interesting. And that's never gonna happen.  Maybe in the future we'll get "Capes 2"  maybe that one will be worth my time and money.I'm gonna ask Steam real nice if I can refund this game.   Because when I quit the game it said 118minutes of gameplay, but then 5 seconds later, ticked over to 2hrs 1minute.    So 1 minute over the 'allowed' refund time.  So...wish me luck, and pray that I can refund this ...thing.In short:   Not worth the money. Boring story. Combat has zero depth and barely gives you any leeway of your OWN tactics.  It's pretty  boring overall. And not even visually interesting.  Characters and voice-overs are also both bland.  You would think a game about super heroes, would have some fun and interesting characters eh?   I'm almost tempted to suggest you go play Midnight Suns instead.  Overall that game really IS better.  As it's a game I've finished myself.  But it's also a tedious game, so I wont recommend it.    But compared to Capes,   Marvel's Midnight Suns is waay better.     Still, for the best, go back to X-Com, even after all these years, not a single game is even close to achieving what Xcom did.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good little tactical hero game. It won't scratch your FFT or XCOM itch, but since one of those comes out every decade or so, it's a good way to pass the time in between.Imagine something like XCOM: Chimera Squad. You've got 4 man squads, unique abilities for everyone, and a lot of fiddliness like disarming weapons, pushing enemies off ledges, individual initiative counts, buffs, debuffs, environmental hazards, and all that sort of thing. The missions are a bigger than a single Chimera Squad room, and generally (but not always) smaller than an entire Chimera mission. One difference is that they all take place on a single map and you don't get automatically repositioned between phases. You can sometimes find yourself out of position, but you'll never be forced out of position by a cutscene.One caveat is that the beginning of the game feels very puzzle-y, like Into the Breach. Less heroes, less enemies, smaller maps make every fight feel like a very angry closet, but once you get your fourth and fifth hero (thus opening up the possibility of different team comps for a given mission), the possibility space opens up considerably. You're still dealing with small, XCOM-like numbers (you never get more than Facet's starting 5 HP on hard, for example) but there's as many ways to win later levels as there are players.

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost: TEMPER YOUR EXPECTATIONS. This is an indie game. It did not have a triple-A budget. The core design team was four guys. They did not have the luxury of endless iterations based on expensive market testing. There was no way Capes was ever going to be "XCOM 2 but superheroes." If that is what you were hoping for, you will be disappointed. This is an indie title and should be evaluated as such.The Freedom Force ancestry is hard to miss, so if you loved that game, there's a good chance you'll enjoy Capes.It's a little cheesy, but in a more modern way than FF. The characters are interesting and diverse, and the anti-corporate vibe will resonate with a lot of players. Mechanically, the freshest aspect of Capes is that every hero has a unique team-up combo with each other hero in the game. As you might guess, this adds a lot to the team composition decisions and tactical planning.Incidentally, that is why you can't make your own custom hero. There would be no way to give your own guy such well-thought-out, tailor-made combos with every single other hero on the team. It's well worth the trade-off, in my opinion.If you don't care about superheroes, it's probably not for you, but Capes is an easy recommend for anyone who likes comic books and tactical RPGs.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not X-Com. If you want X-Com, don't buy it. It needs to be said because so many people somehow expect a game like X-Com as soon as they see grid based tactical games. What this game is instead, is a turn based tactical game that goes more into a puzzle direction. You can compare it to the likes of Hard West 2 or Miasma Chronicles. Every attack and ability always hits and deals a fixed amount of damage (if any). Every character is pre-made and has a distinct and very specific skill set. So the question every turn becomes - given the action points and tools I have, how do I make progress towards my objectives with taking as little damage as possible?There are optional objectives in every stage too that require even more planning and often specific characters to get all of them in one attempt. You can consider that complete mastery over a stage. Character progression is tied to achieving optional objectives over the course of the game but you'll earn enough skill points even without mastering all the stages. I've read criticism that this puzzle nature forces you into a specific play style. There is some truth to it, but I think there is enough flexibility in the system too. The main objectives will be obtainable with many different party compositions and you'll be more and more flexible as you go through the game and aquire new characters and skills. And the optional objectives can be unlocked objective by objective too. It's not too hard to get an objective when you focus on one specifically. Only getting all the optionals in one attempt requires super specific solutions. This is fine in my book.I should also mention that the game is not easy, even at the default difficulty. I've hit a roadblock or two where I had to restart a stage a couple of times. And that can happen pretty early in the game too. But I figured out a solution for every one so far and felt all the more accomplished for it. The devs already said on the forum that they might tweak some things to make them more accessible to more players. So if you are afraid of getting stuck, wait a patch or two. But the game is solvable as it is.I'm having a great time.P.S. for a developer team this small and this kind of game, the game is remarkably polished. I've never even seen a wiff of a bug.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid B to B+; if you're fine with puzzle fights/stealth segments, you can probably bump it to an A-, but I don't know if I'd go that far. Still, we've been lacking a good evolution of Freedom Force to the more depressing/darker era of comicdom, and this was a good fit. I will admit -- there are a few too many stealth missions/gimmick maps that you'll probably wipe once to learn the next phase, which is part of why I can't get this up to an A. Still, I'm glad to have played it, and if they make a sequel, I'd be there.It's silly and over the top at times, but silly and over the top in a dark way. You're not a guy calling himself Minute Man fighting a Russian guy named Nuclear Winter -- but it's still fun. Drop it down to a C or D if you're not a fan of grid based RPGs, because that's really it's main selling point, and if you don't like that, you're not going to like this.

_childDocuments_.review: I think a lot of the negative reviews are coming from a misunderstanding of what this game aims to be.This is not XCOM with superheroes. It is much more into the breach with superheroes. Most levels are more like a puzzle to complete, with lots of different possible ways of doing it, but still a puzzle. Personally, I'm really enjoying it. On the steam deck it is the perfect 10 - 15 minute blast. It runs really well, the powers of each hero are interesting and the enemies all have their own little quirks.The story is very simple, with the twists and turns coming a mile off. The characters are all written like they're from a bad 80s movie. But neither of this is the focus so it's fine by me. The main bad point is that the XP is very limited, so quite often you have to grind through replaying levels you've already done to level up a hero. This is exacerbated by when you get a new hero, they are level 1 so require levelling up. However, since i generally enjoy the gameplay loop this is fine by me.£30 is a bit steep for most people for this game, but I'm happy and am enjoying the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm giving it a thumbs up, with some reservations. If I could give this game a Neutral rating, I would. Capes has an interesting enough premise, being a turn-based-strategy featuring young superheroes rebelling against an evil corporation (bit on the nose, but whatever). But unfortunately, it falls short because of a number of flaws that can be summed up in two words: It's SLOW. The story is slow. The gameplay is slow. Progression is slow. And in terms of games, slow is one short step to "frustrating" and "boring." The story, like I said, has an interesting enough premise, but the story events progress so slowly that the stakes didn't feel real, which meant that I had no real investment in the story. There were attempts to build up the characters with side missions and dialogue between them in the hub, but it didn't feel like enough to give them more than two dimensions. The gameplay really felt sluggish, and looking back, I realized that just the overall tone did not help. There was very little sense of urgency to anyone's actions, and missions would frequently pause to allow lengthy dialogue in the middle of a combat scenario, which, again, does nothing to underline what's at stake. Heck, even the animations of the characters moving looked more like they were just quickly walking than running over to hit the bad guy. On top of that, even the more basic enemies had frustratingly high health, making fighting them a slog. And progression was frustratingly slow, because of the way it was implemented. There are two tracks to progressing: XP, which is earned by participating in missions, levels up your characters and allows them to unlock new skills, but doesn't give them any new abilities. That comes from completing side objectives in missions to earn skill points, which are added to a collective pool. The issue is, the way that side objectives were set up, it meant that missions often felt more like puzzles with one correct solution rather than missions where you could experiment with new abilities, combos, and strategies. (They did kinda fix this in a later patch, but it still left a bad mark, and it's still, to my mind, an overly and unnecessarily complicated method of progression)As it stands, Capes isn't an out-and-out *bad* game per se, but it's definitely not a great one. In fact, I'd hesitate to even call it a good one. It might click with some of you, but for me, it was a solid 5/10 and while I had some enjoyment of it, there are other guys that I have a lot more fun with. I'm perfectly content to let it languish on my back shelf until I get bored enough to try it again.

_childDocuments_.review: This game drives only on the "super hero" theme without bringing anything new to the table and even drops components that are not expected for the genre. If anything it feels like a watered down X-com with only combat.Other than distributing points on a very limited character sheet, the game has no other management component. There is no HQ management or equipment management, no character creation, you are just railroaded through a series of storyline missions and optional missions. You basically pick a scenario from a list and then you fight it out, rinse and repeat. The hero design is interesting but their writing is is very basic and cringy. I was really looking forward for this game but I have been left disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a cautious recommendation.There are missions where everything clicks and I see a clear way to achieve all the optional objectives, there are others where I realise an hour in that I went the wrong way on my opening round. That said, when I do hit the existing target, I get a brief moment to feel smarter than I probably am. I really like the characters and the interactions they all have. I like the way their power sets all feel unique, and overall, I think the devs have done a great job.I was a fan of both Chimera Squad and Midnight Suns, and this scratches that same general itch.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm torn on this game, but I sadly have to lean towards a negative review.tl:dr - The game is good, but the main story is lacking, the character-stories are mostly unresolved, the heroes are heroically unbalanced, and the game just isn't hard.The long version.1. There's a number of personal character plots throughout the game where you follow one particular character and then sculpt a team around them. I really enjoyed this in concept, but the personal quests were definitely not created equally. In my opinion we have:- Full Stories: Fractal, Mercurial- Full, but unsatisfying: Kinetic- Partial Stories: Mindfire, - Barely a Story: Rebound, Ignis, Hyde, WeathervaneWhile everyone gets something, for half the roster you're left with 1-2 missions that barely introduce a theme (Or even don't introduce a theme; looking at you, Rebound) and definitely don't resolve an arc for the character. It's disappointing and I ended the game feeling like I needed another 10-20 hours of story to actually feel like the story had ended.2. The game is short. I played the game on Hard mode, completing every 'All In One' objective on my first time through the game, and it took me 26 hours to complete the game. On a lower difficulty with less focus on trying to max out my characters, I can't see this game having more than 10-15 hours of content.For a £30 game, that's not great value for money. I haven't completed all of the challenges or gotten every achievement, but they all feel like extra 'tasks' to complete, not interesting goals.For many games a 10-20 hour runtime isn't the worst thing to complete the main story, because you can play the game again. However, this is the point where the 'Puzzly' style of the game comes back to bite itself. I can play the game again, and it will play out exactly the same every time which leaves little enjoyable replayability. I'd just be covering the same ground again. Which is unfortunate; with a little variety to the levels starting conditions, the different hero combinations should give plenty replayability, but it just doesn't right now.3. The storyline itself ends just a little too quickly. Act 1 and 2 are reasonably paced with interesting points raised throughout. Act 3 comes down to 4 main missions and accelerates the story a ridiculous amount. It really feels like the budget of the game had ran out at this point and it just needed to be completed. I honestly feel that Act 3 needs to be twice as long and that would give it more time to build upon my first problem where character personal quests are ignored/unresolved.I understand that the game developers were trying to leave open some plot holes for a sequel, or at least that's my assumption. But too much seems to have been taken away from the end of this game and it makes the ending unsatisfying.4. Content. This falls in line with point 2 and 3 somewhat, but it was a real shame to realise that there isn't actually enough XP to level up all your characters in one run-through. Yes, you can replay missions to get more XP, but I don't find that enjoyable. Throughout my run I was careful to not waste any XP. Once a character hit level 5, I stopped using them. Despite that, I still finished the game with 4 heroes at level 4, somewhere between 50% and 75% to levelling up. This meant that when I completed the final mission using subpar heroes who were poorly suited to that mission, I was 'rewarded' with the realisation that there was no reason to do that at all. The game was over. This was a sour feeling. It shouldn't be a guarantee that you'll hit max level by the end, but it should be possible without replaying missions. More content means more XP. It should be made that by following the Recommended Heroes option on every level in the game, you'll complete the 2nd-to-last mission with the last of your Heroes levelling up to 5. This would let you pick your favourites for the final mission and it'd feel more complete and satisfying.As a side note... why does Mecurial need less XP to hit level 5? She's the only one and it felt strange. 5. Difficulty. I played the game through on Hard mode, attempting to complete all 'All In One' missions on the first run through of the level. As you'd expect, this would make things more difficult.Oddly enough, it was very inconsistent. Some missions were surprisingly easy. Others were  difficult, requiring multiple re-tries (Double-Damage, City Surveillance, and Tech Support are the ones that come to mind). I actually have no issue with the extreme difficulty of those three. Rather, it was the relative ease for the others that was my issue. The final 3 boss battles in Act 3 were all incredibly easy, if tedious. I'd like a higher difficulty with less tedious objectives, (Basically all Disarm Missions, especially on Primax) and instead more interesting objectives (Old Debt's objective was  for a challenge.My suggestions for the final boss battles would be:- - Generally, more interesting objectives and less "Do X action Y number of times.". The Disarm and Ultimate objectives are just a chore, not a challenge. 6. Hero Design. There also needs to be some rebalancing of Heroes. Rebound is basically good in every single mission as a high damage, high survivability character. Kinetic, on the other hand, is garbage until you level him up enough to be taking extra turns. Then he's . And then there's Fractal who is a liability most of the time. If there isn't an NPC you need to keep safe, then you're actively better off just picking someone else every single time. - Ignis is a worse Weathervane. - Hyde is a better Fractal.- Mecurial has her Niche- Mindfire can fit into most missions effectively, but does most things worse than others.- Kinetic and Rebound ultimately end up being strong enough to fit into every mission. Rebound from level 1. Kinetic from level 4. But getting him to 4 is a chore.I'd like to see maybe double the number of levels (10 instead of 5) and the power spikes more evenly ironed out so that the progression feels natural and all characters feel good to play. Kinetic taking 4 levels to get usable, but Rebound increasing her total damage from 4->5 at level 2, then her Strike from 2.5->3 at level 3 is just very strong when the breakpoint for standard enemy health is 3hp, 5hp, or 8hp.7. AI and Abilities. This is more a quality of life thing. The AI of 'allied' characters in the game is dreadful. Freedom Crossing comes to mind with Grindstone just charging headlong into enemy attack ranges despite being perfectly safe if she'd not moved. This was frustrating.Rebound's Ultimate. Oh... this one really annoyed me. If a single instance of an attack from Rebound's Ultimate should kill an enemy, she should not be able to attack them 5 times. All other Ultimates in the game are satisfying to use (Except maybe Fractals). Rebound, however, is pure RNG in a game about tactical play. I found just not using itI've said a whole lot of negatives, and ultimately that's because I wanted this game to be more than it actually is. It's  to being a very good game, but it just falls shy. Another 10 hours of story-focused gameplay, some balance between the characters and a focus on interesting objectives and this review would be a resounding success.As it is, unfortunately, Capes is just not quite good.

_childDocuments_.review: A little turn based tactics game with a super hero theme, made by a tiny 4 person dev team.The gameplay is actually good and fun. The different heroes have unique styles, and that, alongside the team up abilities (enhanced version of a hero's ability based on who is nearby), allow for various fun situations.Like in Chimera Squad, Mutant Year Zero, and Showgunner there are no random maps. This means that each mission can play a bit like a puzzle, as you try to figure out the optimal play to achieve all optional objectives. As they can all be replayed though, you can also try out different approaches for fun.But yes, it is a tiny dev team, so don't expect XCOM 3.And no, you don't make your own heroes - there are specific, story based heroes.

_childDocuments_.review: This game never claimed to be an XCOM 2 clone, so it's rather odd to see people complaining that it does not have things like "strategy layer" base building or custom hero creation (things never claimed to be features here). If anything, it's more like Chimera Squad as a timeline-based and close-quarters tactical scenario game where pre-determined characters unlock more options to offer new tactics.I absolutely love the setting, depicted in a stylized comic book presentation. The art style might not be to the taste of some, but it lends itself to looking like a comic artist's aesthetic. The characters are a nice range of personalities, with a little depth beyond the basics. (more if you go into optional Dossiers, a welcome change for those not a fan of the Midnight Suns relationship grind)As for the plot: Familiar superhero world, with a less-often-done dystopian twist. Superheroes get persecuted on sight, like when the X-Men are fugitives. Not much of a deeper story than "Evil Corp is evil!", in case you were hoping for hours of worldbuilding or were dreading any "culture stuff".Do levels feel like "puzzles" rather than strategies sometimes? Yes, and that is the one complaint that I will agree is a fundamental flaw with the game. But the range of heroes and abilities you get represent a nice toolbox in trying to figure out just how to (eventually) pull out a flawless win with all side objectives. Turn-based strategy games always have a puzzle component, but here it does go a little too restrictive on what it takes to succeed.
_childDocuments_.name: Capes

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, if you scan through these reviews, you'll notice that a sizable proportion of negative ones highlight that the game is bad because it's "woke." If you're a remotely mature individual, you'll flag that to mean "has a plurality of characters that are female, non-white, or queer, and doesn't ridicule them for being female, non-white or queer." The game *does* feature a number of female, non-white and queer characters, but the game and its story aren't about those qualities at all: it's about superheroes fighting bad guys. It's a meaningless critique if you're a normal person... so, moving on.As for the game itself: it's good. Is it the masterpiece we'd hoped for? No, not quite, but it's a good time.The characters are varied in interesting ways: each member of your squad brings a completely different set of tools to any fight, along with distinct strengths and weaknesses. Given that variety, the tactical play is pretty complex. The characters also feel really authentic to the genre: the powers, personalities and appearance of each could easily fit into a print comic series. The story and setting(s), too, are well written, and the voice acting is solid. It's an atmospheric adventure that draws you in.Downsides, for me: one, it's not a visually polished game. To be clear, I'm not talking about budget, technical resources or man-hours: I'm talking about smart aesthetic choices. Portions of the game are rendered with semi-animated 2D illustrations, and frankly, those are great: it's not technically sophisticated stuff, but the characters are stylish and looks good. Other portions, which include cutscenes and actual play, are rendered in clunky 3D models which would have felt dated 15 years ago and simply weren't a good choice. There's a version of "Capes" where the devs made better decisions based on their budget, focusing on a 2D art style that didn't try to emulate pricier games. What we have instead is a little distracting.Finally: the linear mission construction and the limited roster lead to missions that feel less open-ended and more puzzle-like, giving players the sense that there are limited ways to approach a given battle and emerge victorious. The frequent comparisons to XCOM will frustrate anyone enamored of that series' dedication to randomly-generated arenas and enemy placements, where the paths to victory feel endless.All in all, I've been having a lot of fun with "Capes," and I appreciate what it's up to. It may not be the Holy Grail tactical superhero game we're hoping for, but it'll hold me over for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to say this outright - do not get this game if you're expecting XCOM/XCOM 2 levels of character customization or mission variety. This is not XCOM. This is more like XCOM Chimera Squad, except it's even more on the rails. There is no base-building, there's not really any character customization, and it's very tactically restrictive - Both in how you build your characters and in the mission design. Each character, from what I could tell, is extremely specialized, and they're not good for much outside their very specific niche. I also have issues with the costume design in general - It's... Pretty goshdarned bland, all things considered. Like, I get why that'd be the case - The conceit of the plot's that superheroes had to go underground because of the Man - But it is pretty boring. In terms of the actual missions you get, well, in my very subjective opinion those are also pretty restrictive. I'm really not a fan of extended unskippable tutorials in the games I play, and that's pretty much the case for like, the first five missions I wound up playing in this game. It feels like the game goes out of its way to hold your hand and walk you through how various characters and mechanics work for an irritatingly long amount of time. I'm really not a fan of this, but YMMV on this front. Do get this game if you're interested in turn-based tactical superhero battles. That is something this game does provide. Do also get this if you're into camp and cheese, because this game does also lean on the superhero tropes pretty hard which can be entertaining. I just don't think it's worth $40 though. And personally, I refunded this game because it ran pretty poorly on my system even though I met the recommended performance specs. I was getting framerate drops out the butt even after turning down the settings which made my gameplay experience pretty miserable. Would I recommend this game at $40? No. Would I pick it up and give it a second chance if it went on sale at 25-50%? Probably. I think there's potential here, but the start was seriously off-putting for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:* It is what I was told it was: X-Com with superheroes. It lacks a lot of the depth of x-com, but it hits that core strategic gameplay style.* It's challenging enough that you won't just walk through it and the enemy AI makes decent strategic decisions at all levels.* There are a decent variety of battle maps with elements which keep them from feeling too similarCons* The writing is just straight up bad. I want to say that more kindly but it's just really not good. The heroes are basically devoid of personality and the villains are horrible and obvious. The dialog is... bad. Just really bad.* As I mentioned, the gameplay itself is kinda thin. Hero development is slow and frustrating with absolutely zero customization. Also, there's no outside game activities other than leveling up your heroes along their upgrade rails, so when the combat is as mediocre as it ends up being, the game has nothing to fall back on.* Visuals are unimpressive and occasionally irritating. The character art makes me think of what someone who doesn't read comics thinks comic books look like. Also the weird 'bounce' motion the characters make during conversations is incredibly annoying, especially when one relies on subtitles and the tail of the text bubble moves in a distracting and irritating fashion.Listen, I want to like this game, but it's just not good. Get any x-com game or go play final fantasy tactics: the war of the lions.

_childDocuments_.review: Calling this game a Second Freedom Force feels unfair - any superhero game with a few key aesthetic choices is gonna draw that comparison. But Capes really does come across like a successor, trying to encapsulate how comics felt in that era and let you feel like you're in the midst of that action!The tactical layer is solid. There's more challenge here than a lot of turn based tactics games I've played in the past - every hero has a broad ability suite, and you won't normally just think about 'what does more damage?' - knockback and status effects are pretty important. You also have team up effects with the other three heroes on your team - letting you use either a new action, or enhanced versions of your current actions. That makes positioning vital - if you want these team up moves, you'll need to keep your heroes close together.It's not quite faultless. It feels kinda clunky to enforce a strict initative order; you can't pick what hero takes a turn when, which limits some combos you might want to perform. But that's a nitpick to me - the combat's really fun in practice.The game's story and feel is probably its weaker aspect. The VA is a little hit and miss; the main characters are usually solid, but some of the secondaries are... not well done. Writing wise, it's struggling to make its heroes stand out - the characters have strong mechanical identities, but in conversation the main person who stands out is Rebound (team snarker). I was thinking Facet would be similarly unique, the idealist of the team, but a lot of the other characters are also somewhat idealistic. Even Rebound is a pretty clear cut hero type - her background has her as a morally neutral underground figure who was almost forced into this, but we keep seeing her care about both people in general and her team mates.But the story works. It's fun in practice so far; a team of young superheros getting to learn the ropes fighting an oppressive super-villain company. The villains, now dominant, snipe at each other in cutscenes. You feel outmatched - so many missions throw a ton of goons at you, to the point it's an exact balancing job. Your heroes aren't so strong that they can all just wade in and take all of that. Someone like Mindfire can take, like, three punches. Speaking of your heroes, while I stand behind Rebound as the most clearly characterised member of the team so far, the other heroes aren't unlikable; they just don't really have enough to distinguish themselves. The team's absolutely tried to make the cast unique, we see secondary characters who interact with them, individual arcs after or before they've joined the team. There's just a lot of material to manage and it's tough to make this many characters feel clearly distinct.So to sum it all up... yeah, Freedom Force in the iron age. I'd say it's stronger than Freedom Force mechanically, a bit weaker in the thematics, absolutely worth your time. I can see some negatives here, but I don't get the negative reviews - the positives clearly outshine them for me.

_childDocuments_.review: It’s a tactical rpg kinda like Xcom, but you control a team of superheroes. Took me about 30 hours to complete. Fights weren’t super difficult, but completing all the bonus objectives was at times.  Overall, if you like the xcom style tactical genre, I think this brings something new to it with team ups between all the heroes. The fact it’s an Indy game really shows through in the animation and some of the voice acting. The animation in cutscenes is stiff and loops a lot. The voice acting is surprisingly good at times for the main characters, but also cuts corners in some places. The writing is actually pretty good. The villains are all billionaire supervillains who won some 20 years ago through treachery and capitalism. So taking them down always feels pretty good. There’s some good writing surrounding the means vs ends of taking them down (especially towards the endgame). 6 of 8 superheroes you recruit throughout the game are some kind of minority. Always good to see representation in games; especially when it’s not shoved in your face like some major plot point and it just exists. Overall would give the game 4 of 5 stars. Rough around the edges from what are clearly budget constraints, but I think they nailed all the core ideas.

_childDocuments_.review: Those calling this XCom for heroes have it wrong. In Xcom and its clones, you can figure out a general set of tactics which you can reapply for each mission with a few tweaks and generally steam roll every map. That is not how capes works though. Each mission is a very tightly choreographed puzzle if you want to fully unlock all the bonus objectives. For me, that was incredibly fun; I enjoy working out the right strategy and experimenting to beat each map. The game is challenging even on easy difficulty and I love that about it. This is not a game were you assemble your favorite characters and stomp through enemies easily though. The margin of error to fully hit every objective is very thin and will take brain power. If you are looking for a challenging experience which calls for thoughtful planning and working out the right unique hero combo for every challenge, then I recommend this game.

So, save yourself the headache, do the objectives that you can and move on the the all in one bonus in the simulator. Especially with the levels that introduce tutorials in them later on. When this is cleared, I freakin love this game! Its campy in the writing, sure. BUt the gameplay shines bright and you can combo your way out in a very satisfying manner. Its similar to the Midnight Suns game in vibes, where the main story is really grim, but the urgency gets toned down with the dialogues. The writing could be improved, but its bearable. Its a charming game however. Get on sale if you are on the fence. A good time, if not on the more difficult kind.

_childDocuments_.review: Capes:~~~~~ Twenty years have passed since the Supervillains won the battle against the Superheroes and took control of King City. A deal was struck between the Secret Government and the Supervillains entity known as the Company. As life has become a little more peaceful in the streets of King City since the peace breakthrough, the powerful Company is providing its members with better food and medical supplies than the rest of the citizens. But recently, they have been scooping those citizens with superpowers off the streets, and none of them have been seen since. An old Superhero, Doctrine, who has been hiding since the treaty, has taken a group of young Supers under his wing to take up the fight against the evil Company. Do you have Superpowers? Then join the Capes Now! Capes is a superhero turn-based strategy game developed by Spitfire Interactive and published by Daedalic Entertainment on the 30th of May 2024 on the Steam platform. The game is also available on PS4/PS5, Xbox One, Xbox Series X|S, and Nintendo Switch.Capes has a lengthy solo campaign, as far as I can see after having played 25 missions, including the main story and side missions.  With 28+ hours of game time, I am still on the second act. It is pretty impressive, and I am genuinely enjoying the game.   You start with two superheroes, Facet and Rebound! As you progress throughout the story, you'll unlock another six supers, each with specific powers. Facet's ultimate power can stop all enemies within close proximity for one turn, while Rebound can go on a frenzied attack and damage all enemies within a particular area. What has become obvious to me since the first mission is the importance of your character’s movements so they can combine their powers each turn to maximise an attack or a defence action. It’s also important to charge each of your character's ultimate powers as often as possible during each mission. Facet will gain a recharge point each time an opponent hits him, while Rebound will charge her ultimate power by stabbing enemies from behind. You can see the various team-up combinations for all the heroes when you are at the hidden base between missions.For each mission, you can have up to four heroes, whom you can choose before the mission starts or press the recommended tab to nominate heroes for that mission.  Missions have three difficulty levels: easy, medium and hard. Each mission will also have specific objectives to achieve, with skill points attached to each objective. There are three to five objectives per mission, and you'll bank all the skill points of the objectives that you successfully complete. Then you can use these points to upgrade your character's powers and other actions. A few of your Supers have additional abilities to unlock, which you need skill points to acquire. Experience points are also given when you successfully finish a mission and are automatically passed onto the characters you use in that mission. These points also help your character to level up, giving access to upgrade the character's powers and actions. Each character can level up five times. You might not have many issues completing the easy missions, even if you haven’t successfully completed all the objectives. But be ready to replay medium and hard missions several times before you beat the level - they are challenging missions, let me tell you! In terms of the gameplay, well, it is a typical turn-based tactical strategy, and as mentioned, movements and combining heroes' powers are the key to your success. You have to make sure that your characters are close to each other so they can combine their powers, while at the same time keeping your distance from attacking enemies, as some of your heroes don't have many life points or any defence whatsoever. It can be tricky. Also, it is easy to revive a fallen hero as you usually have only two turns to revive them if fallen. If one of them has fallen three times, it’s game over. In terms of the design, levels are mostly compact, but some are of average size. In regards to the enemies, as you progress through the game, not only will the enemies keep coming in more waves, but new and more challenging opponents will make their entrance to spice up the difficulty level. I have faced off against two of the main Company bosses, and they were a struggle, especially Alpha, who kept duplicating himself.The story is fun and cheesy, and I thoroughly enjoy the cartoony illustrations before each mission, which have good voice-overs, too. I also appreciate that the developers have worked on elevating the relationship between heroes. As you progress through the game, you’ll unlock cut scenes of conversations between characters, which you can find on the dossier tab at the base.The graphics, soundtrack and voice-overs are excellent. I experienced a few frame-rate drops here and there, but apart from that, there is nothing significant to report. The game provides a good difficulty progression, and it is challenging and addictive. The game has been translated into ten languages and offers full controller support. But if you’re like me, you might prefer using your mouse and keyboard.Positives:~~~~~~~ +	Fantastic graphics and comic-book-style illustrations+	Lengthy campaign+	Fun, cheesy story +	Good voice-overs+	Eight different heroes and superpowers+	Good variation of enemies+	Fun and challenging gameplay+	Achievements and trading cardsNegatives:~~~~~~~~ -	A few frame rate drops here and thereCapes is an excellent, addictive, lengthy and challenging turn-based strategy game with a cheesy story and epic fights on small and well-designed levels. Capes are my new favourite Superheroes!8/10 Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I enjoyed the game and would recommend it to those that like superheros and/or turn based tactics. I don't think there are enough out there with the superhero theme and do it as well as this one does.  I think that it has been mistakenly compared to some other games in (or near) the genre along with some misconceptions, so I will tackle a couple of those after I share what I liked about the game, along with one minor disappointment.The bottom line is that Capes is about superhero battles and the game does that really, really well, both in mission and superhero character design. The super heroes themselves and their powers are varied and interesting,  While I gravitated towards my favorites, every one of them was fun to use, especially as their powers grow.   A really nice touch is the team-ups that tie two character's abilities together.   The scenarios are likewise unique and provide differing challenges without being time slogs.  I actually found it a breath of fresh air that it didn't have procedurally created missions that I find get repetitive and uninteresting.As I mentioned to start, there are a couple of misplaced comparisons about this game.   It's less X-com and more Chimera Squad.   Freedom Force was a real-time with pause while this is turn-based.   While some people would argue Marvel's Midnight Suns is a better buy, this game has far less repetitive battles, doesn't involve a relationship simulator, and does a better job with the actual tactical battles and super hero abilities in the game (even though I found both fun).Of the three biggest complaints or critiques I see about the game, two are flawed and one is dead on.The first critique I think is flawed is the lack of an ability to make your own character.   While I could see this turning people off, the heroes are varied enough that you'll probably find one that you just like the best.   I also think that in both the last two games I played where I could create a superhero (Marvel Midnight Suns and Sentinels), my created character was the least interesting in all respects.  So, if this is stopping you, I'd encourage you to give it a go.The second critique that is flawed is the idea that this is a puzzle game.   It is not.   A couple of tutorial missions and maybe one or two missions may have that feel, but there are multiples methods and a myriad of ways to complete the rest.   I wouldn't be surprised if people are completing missions in ways and with combinations of characters the devs didn't dream of.The critique that I agree with  (and disappointment I mentioned earlier) is regarding simulator missions (playing missions you have already succeeded) and secondary objectives, key aspects of the game to help level your characters.  It has been said these are optional and you could complete the game without them, but that would be really tough.   Besides missing out on points to level up the characters you want, every character has required missions that are either optional patrols or key campaign missions.   If you just ignore a character, or even a couple, it will make those missions a lot harder.   Sometimes I wanted to replay missions to get a cool new ability for my favorite characters, other times I felt forced to do so in order to level up a character to complete  certain mission in the game.I don't that should stop anyone from getting the game (it's certainly a lot less annoying than Midnight Suns' relationship simulator or other menial tasks that you have to do to build up characters in that game), but it is one area I'd like to see improvement in for what will hopefully be either expansions or sequels.

_childDocuments_.review: I knew what I was getting into when I bought this. I supported the developers anyways in spite of knowing many of the games issues. Including the "puzzle" like nature people are complaining about. I don't really view the game as a puzzle per se, what I will say is for a superhero game it is a pretty poor power fantasy. You see Marvel movies or even play games and you feel like a proper superhero. Here, even towards the mid-game and later you are facing many waves of enemies and you never really feel like a superhero. It advertises as a hero game but you feel more like a mercenary squad because you heroes are incredibly squishy. They can easily be killed by normal humans so never did I get into that power fantasy you would expect. I hope the Devs read this for their next game. It is fine to throw massive waves of enemies at you but at least make them as you'd expect having ever watched any superhero movie or played a game. You should effortlessly be able to take out normal enemies. In Capes, it is a struggle at all times. Not very "super". I did enjoy the game in spite of this, but again, I knew what I was buying and getting into.

_childDocuments_.review: So this game is ok.  Not great but ok.  It's generally fun to play around with super powers and upgrading them.  The combat is decent, but some of it feels more like puzzle solving than strategy at times.  The designs though are all over the place.  The character models look like bad action figures that move, but the cutscenes use some 2D flat static designs for the characters and they look very different, almost like two totally different design teams worked on them. The difficulty spikes are rough though.  At times you will replay sections over and over again (hint use the quick save feature to help).  It can take some time to learn the best approaches to use.  It also doesn't allow a lot of mixing of characters, as some areas really require certain types.  Occasionally story will fix certain characters to each mission, but otherwise you have to use the recommend button almost every time to see what the best characters are for that mission.  Overall the budget price of the game makes it worth it.  I think the small team and lower budget brings the potential down on this game, as it has some good elements to it.  I really hope they keep trying and perhaps make even better games in this world in the future.  Yes, it follows a lot of story elements from existing comics but I don't think those are bad stories and enjoy playing them.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is an easy recommend now after the patch.  Fixed most of the issues that were holding this game back.PROS:  -  Combat itself is fun,  *Patch fixed this.- Synergies between party members feels great.- Different abilities between party members is unique so each character has a distinct identity- Usually I hate when games use the "multiple waves of enemies" for a challenge, but this one pulls it off without feeling too obnoxious.- Like any good tactics game, feels very satisfying to see your combos get pulled off as planned.CONS:-  *Patch now allows for ffwd during ultimates, thank the lord!- .  *Patch adjusted the objectives to be more attainable/flexible and no longer feels as restrictive as it was originally.-  I wish there was better indicators of enemy intent.  In general, the closest ally will be the one attacked, but sometimes that's not the case and there's no indication of who is going to be attacked.  In a tactics game, I feel like the player should have complete awareness/knowledge of what damage is incoming so they can strategize accordingly.  This leads to unnecessary frustration from attacks you didn't anticipate because you simply didn't have any indication.Overall, this game is a fun time now.  Story still isn't that strong, but the gameplay itself is a ton of fun and now is a lot more flexible in how you can approach missions.EDIT:  Just adding that this game works on steamdeck out of the box so that's a big plus.

Even with picking recommended heroes for each mission, it became easier.After beating the game, I went back in some missions to just go wild. _childDocuments_.review: After fully beating the game on hard and getting all the bonus objs, I can give a more detailed review.Pros: the story is quite good. Nothing amazing but I was invested throughout the whole thing and it has its moments. The Overall gameplay was also pretty good. Each character has their own strengths and weaknesses,  They have different synergies with each other, and you can have quite a diverse team and can do missions differently depending on who you take.Cons: I wished there was a bigger enemy variety. Theres a decent amount but they all felt somewhat similar near the end. Think they could have added a different enemy or 2 to mix things up a bit more. Ive encountered a few bugs as well as one of my saves getting corrupted. The few bugs either softlocked me or made the missions harder. Either through not being able to have one of my characters go before another for some weird reason, or through the mission just not proceeding forward. Only happened twice but it is something to consider. The corrupted save sucked but thankfully one of the devs was able to fix it.Another small con I have are the side objs. You can play with any group you want, and you can for the most part get most of the side objs by just playing normally, but IMO it seemed like certain charaters made getting the side objs much easier and were just more useful in general, and they give you a ton of resources in upgrading your characters. I think it would have been fine if you got more for just completing the mission and less for each side obj.At the end of the day, I give this game a 7/10. Nothing amazing, but I did find the game worth my time and money.

_childDocuments_.review: Good, fun game that I enjoyed immensely. Is it the best game in the world? No, the graphics could use some work in some places and there are some bugs - but this is also the first game made by this developer, and it makes up for it with it's fun characters, writing, and general charm. It scratches that turned-based itch and provides the player with some actually challenging levels where you have to stop and think about what you're doing (which is why I really appreciate the quicksave/checkpoint feature - makes going back when things go wrong or trying something out easier). It's also nice to have a superhero game that isn't from Marvel or DC. Had a great time playing, hope to see more from these developers (and potentially more in this game's universe) in the future

_childDocuments_.review: Like a lot of other people, i really wanted to enjoy this game. It's just very... bland. And I know that there's bound to be superhero stereotypes, but there's very little that had me interested in the team members. The gameplay was fine, but I would have liked a few extra options on how to use the characters, something like a "normal" attack rather than using their powers. Facet seems like he'd be able to punch, but he can only do one single push attack? I didn't experience any graphical or audio glitches while playing - that was all fine and good. It just just don't feel like a "me" kind of game. SRPGs are my jam and what I spend most of my time playing, so maybe this could be good for someone just trying to get into the genre? There's definitely potential behind the concept.
