Often you could be making moves very quickly, then realise a situation was brewing which you had to carefully map out before engaging. _childDocuments_.review: Shogun Showdown is one of the most clever roguelikes I've played recently. It has satisfying controls, tight and engaging combat, a great variety of encounters and weapons (even in Early Access), and some of the best overall visual design I've seen. Every encounter feels like a dance, as you weave your way through and around the web of enemy attacks, finding the right time to prepare and the right time to strike. Moving around feels great - this game can be played with only a mouse, with movement bound to the scroll wheel, and it works so elegantly it's a wonder this hasn't been done before. I've sunk many hours into the various demos and prototypes for this game, and I plan to play this for many more hours to come. If you like turn-based roguelikes, but you want something completely new and different from what has come before, you owe it to yourself to check this game out.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love this game. I racked up well over 10 hours on the old build/demo versions, and expect I'll be getting into 100+ hours in the official release. Which is especially impressive as I'm not a big gamer like I used to be.It's all about the combat system. The movement and tile system is easy to understand, and after a few runs you'll be able to memorize how each enemy behaves. If I have anything bad to say it's that in early runs, you may be confused as to how certain bosses and their abilities work. But since the game is meant to be ran through over and over, you'll understand quickly.Using different tiles and upgrading them in various ways scratches that itch for deck building/drafting. The predictability of the enemies keeps you from feeling like things are ever unfair. It's a perfectly FAIR game. That is, when you die it never feels like it's unreasonable. It's always the player who could have done better. Either because of a major misplay or because you just haven't been keeping the whole run tight. Some deck building rogue-likes like Slay The Spire for example. (I still love that game) sometimes just give you awful runs: you get bad cards, run into unreasonable obstacles. If you want a more consistent, skill-testing experience, Shogun Showdown is for you. Of course RNG still matters in Shogun Showdown; some tiles are really good in a ubiquitous fashion, like the spear, and some are difficult to use like traps. But every tile has a home in some sort of build, optimized or not.Part of the satisfaction also comes in the ability to process and play quickly. There is no time limit, but there are achievements and goals to play faster. It can be extremely satisfying to execute a plan, thinking several steps ahead of the AI.Is it a perfect game? Almost. I certainly can't think of any major flaws. This is an anomaly and the creators should be beyond proud. The aesthetic and sound design are just the cherry on top. I still had a blast when the graphics were simpler, and the sound design more primitive, but in the full release everything feels snappy and satisfying. This is one of those rare games where I really can't criticize much. The only thing I wish was present would be a popup when hovering over abilities which show their description during combat.
_childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.review: Early impressions after first (Day 1) win. Shogun Showdown takes a relatively simplistic gameplay loop and adds layers of complexity to it to create an addicting and satisfying combat system. Combat is easy to understand but takes time to master, even at the easier levels. The additional weapon and skill tiles you unlock in between runs presents enough variety (at least through the early game) to make each run feel different, even if you find and tend to stick to a couple of your favourites.My biggest concern at this point is that the gameplay loop will start to feel repetitive or the difficult increases between ascensions (days) will feel unbalanced but at this point, I’m hooked enough that I want to play more and experiment with the different unlockable characters and combos to try to conquer the more difficult ascensions and achievements. So far, I think Shogun Showdown is a very fun and well-made game that I would recommend to fans of tactical and card-based games, like Slay The Spire and Into The Breach. The game scratches the same itch as some other titles in those genres but is uniquely its own.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the kind of game that I wish I had made. The mechanics are so tight, so interwoven with each other, and the execution is so clean and fantastic. I do think it could stand to be a tad more difficult. I beat the game on my first run (I did play the demo a bit). Felt like it should be a bit more challenging.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my favorite game.Shogun Showdown is nothing short of a masterclass in strategic gameplay, offering an experience that is as exhilarating as it is challenging. From the moment you dive in, the game welcomes you with a vibrant world full of rich detail and engaging mechanics that make every session a unique adventure.One of the most captivating aspects of Shogun Showdown is how each run feels distinctly different. The game's clever design ensures that no two runs are ever the same. The diverse array of weapons and the unpredictable difficulty days add layers of excitement and challenge. Whether you’re grappling with the swift and deadly moves of The Wanderer, harnessing the precise strikes of The Ronin, or employing the elusive tactics of The Shadow, every character brings a unique playstyle that keeps the game fresh and thrilling.The enemies you face are as varied as the characters you control. From the relentless Ashigaru to the strategic Yumi Snipers and the imposing Shadow Chargers, each foe is designed with unique abilities that test your strategic thinking and adaptability. The bosses, like Daisuke the Dasher and The Shogun, are not just formidable—they’re captivating, each bringing their own flair and challenge to the battlefield. These boss encounters are the heart-pounding moments that make every victory feel earned and every defeat a learning experience.Exploring the game’s regions is like embarking on a journey through a beautifully crafted world. Each region, from the tranquil Bamboo Grove to the eerie Forsaken Grounds and the majestic Shogun's Castle, is meticulously designed, offering new challenges and enemies. The game’s music, with its 8-bit Japanese-inspired soundtrack, perfectly complements the visual and thematic elements of each region, creating an immersive experience that draws you deeper into the game.The thrill of Shogun Showdown comes from the perfect blend of strategic depth and dynamic gameplay. The ever-changing weapon drops, the intensity of the difficulty days, and the cool, challenging enemies make every run a new adventure. The game encourages you to think on your feet, adapt your strategies, and savor each hard-fought victory.Playing as different characters—The Jujitsuka with her graceful moves or The Chain Master with his versatile attacks—adds another layer of excitement. Each character’s special abilities offer a new way to approach the game’s challenges, making it a joy to experiment and find your preferred playstyle.Shogun Showdown isn’t just a game; it’s an experience that combines strategic depth with exhilarating action. The emotional highs of defeating a tough boss, the satisfaction of mastering a new character, and the joy of discovering new regions make every moment spent with this game memorable. It’s a title that rewards your time and effort with endless fun and a genuine sense of accomplishment. If you’re looking for a game that challenges you and keeps you coming back for more, Shogun Showdown is an absolute must-play.10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.review: There's a LOAD to like about this game! I downloaded the demo (you should too), played for a while, then bought the damn thing (you will too).You can play this for a long time, or a very quick moment. It's flexible and addictive, and you don't need to carve out some 'gaming time' to enjoy a hit of this fun, tactically goodness! But if you have time, you'll find you are kicking yourself for not thinking that last move through, and starting again, and again. But not in frustration, just in enjoyment. You do an action, your opponents do. You hit them, they (hopefully) don't hit you. You win and move onto the next round. See? Simple. You don't think far enough ahead, you get hit. You don't think properly about the move you were planning or the move they are planning (which you always get to see), you get hit. Then you die. See? Challenging.I love when a game is incredibly well designed in its CHALLENGE, but simple in the EXECUTION of how you play it. This is that game. Easy to pick up. Easy to get the concepts. Hard to get right. But not annoying. HIGHLY worth playing. If you think strategically you will definitely love it (and do better at it than me...).Oh, and while it's too short and therefore repetitive, the music is an earworm...The game is definitely compatible on steam deck and plays well. I do not like the control layout they've assigned. I click the wrong buttons some times and get annoyed at myself. BUT... that isn't a criticism of the devs. At the bottom right it shows you what each button will do, so my confusion is easily fixed with me just double-checking. I just don't find the default layout intuitive and can't be bothered mapping out an alternative.   From a performance perspective, battery life, graphics, size of game files etc, it's all a big 2 thumbs up for Steam Deck play,  which is always a bonus!

_childDocuments_.review: Shogun Showdown was sick, and genuinely kept me absorbed as my main Steam Deck squeeze for almost a month. A fresh take on 2D turned based strategy that was both really easy to learn and very tricky to finally wrap my melon around.The only downside seemed to be after a certain point, the strategy ended up being the same for almost every run. Difficulty didn't matter much, and the character you chose didn't matter much. The uniqueness of the combat definitely contributed to how limited it was and it just didn't have the pull of other, better roguelikes to keep me chasing playtimes in the 50+ hour range.Still, $15 should get you easily a 30 hour run before you start to get bored and believe be you will be completely hooked until that point. If not for Balatro, this would be the best indie game of the year for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Shogun Showdown is.. interesting. It's a good roguelike overall, the first 10 or so hours were extremely fun - some of the best I've had out of any game. Completely worth the price tag and the unique aesthetics are also amazing.Each character feels suitably unique and weapons show a somewhat clear progression line as you advance more. Some flaws do start to appear when you get into the later days and beat the game more, the game is not.. difficult. It punishes you for being hasty but that's about it. It feels like a super simple system where it devolves into 3 questions:1. Is the enemy attacking me?2. Are there are any ranged enemies?3. Are enemies going to spawn behind me?Pretty much it, any level is solvable if you think about those for a second. Even the Shogun can be beat in a few turns if you take a couple minutes out.Another thing is that there isn't enough variety, understandable considering the state of the game. Playing the same level over and over to get back to the same levels to fight the same enemies, it just feel stale after some time. Unlike other strategy or roguelikes games, the experience tends to be the same throughout.The weapon system is fairly nice, I love some of the weapon modifiers and while some things can be balanced more there isn't really much I can complain about here. Shops have a lot of different upgrades too. Items are extremely helpful when you need them, the shield can save a flawless run if you put yourself under an unstoppable attack. Combo chains and attacks are wonderful as well.Bought it on sale therefore it is definitely worth to me, may not be for everyone, keep that in mind.

_childDocuments_.review: It is a really creative and cute game, but at it's current state I don't think I can recommend it.I definitely can't declare myself an expert of the game, but I think this roguelike game has a huge "run variety" issue.It's a turn based game, where "queue up one skill", or "using all of the queued skills (up to 3)" **each takes one turn**,  which implies your efficiency of turns is determined by the power level of the skill you are using (since using "good" skill and "bad" skill both takes the same amount of turns),  which further implies, the game strongly encourages the player to upgrade only one to two damaging skill during a run, upgrading their damage and cooldown speed as much as possible and keep using them over and over again, to maximise your turn efficiency.So the best strategy for each character, is just to upgrade their starting skill over and over again, instead of counting on the random skills you can get in your early shops. Plus, the strategy for each "main" skill is, in a way, fixed, there are certain support skills you would want for certain damage skill, which ends up really restricting the variety of the game.So they can add as many skills and items as they want to the game, but most of them wouldn't matter for most of the run for the current structure and design of the game, because you just better off using your starting skill (or if you are lucky, finding other synergistic damaging skill combinations in your early shops/rewards).And I'm not having the motivation to trying to reroll again and again utilising all the different skills the game has to offer, which is a bit sad.

_childDocuments_.review: Even though it's still very early on (It's version like 0.5.7 or something like that as of writing this) it already feels very polished. Haven't encountered any bugs yet,  and the strategy involved in the combats and deckbuilding is very satisfying; there's a decent amount of tiles and passive abilities so far (and I'm guessing more to come) and you have a lot of options in terms of how you want to build out your character on each run. The 3 available classes feel surprisingly varied too; my favourite is the Shadow, who's all about quickly weaving back and forth in and out of enemy range. The aesthetic is also gorgeous, with some of the music tracks especially being total earworms. My one suggestion is if you're playing on Steam Deck, make sure you spend some time fiddling with the controls; the control stick with the default mapping has a tendency to accidentally trigger a double move. I wound up remapping the W A S D keys to the control pad and haven't had any issues since then.

_childDocuments_.review: Into the Breach but in a single dimension with a great balance between depth and accessibility. Tactical games are as good as their combos, so Shogun Showdown makes sure that combos is the name of the game. With a few dozens abilities, the total number of combos is astronomical (N ^ 3). so I always come across a new way to obliterate a level. Some combos are more effective than others, and sometimes it takes a single tile to reach a combo, but so far I have not had two runs relying on the same combination of tiles.I recommend the game to all fans of turn-based tactics (XCOM, Into the Breach etc.) or chess puzzles who value precise calculation over story and button mashing. So far it is my personal game of 2024.Pros:1. The game is tight. The difference between killing or being killed is a single click, and with 10 HP it takes 5 regular enemy attacks (hence, 5 mistakes) to GG.2. Despite having a single dimension (from left to right), space varies from 5 to 9 tiles, forcing you to be a jack of all trades to an extent. Bosses and some enemies employ environmental attacks and explosives, making terrain a foe of its own.3. An immense variety of tiles (=abilities) and enemies. The latter range from a standard set of close range - medium range - long range to quite creative specimen. For instance, some enemies can steal your ability and turn them against you.4. You and enemies share the same abilities. Unlike most games where the hero is absurdly overpowered, the only difference between you and enemies is intelligence and HP pool. Yes, enemies can also heal, create shields, apply vulnerabilities and build combos.5. Movement and space manipulation trumps direct damage. Clearly inspired by Into the Breach, the game emphasizes the importance of positioning and playing enemies against each other. So much so that the key difference between four characters is their mechanical ability (swaping / pushing / phasing / throwing).Suggestions (a lot of spoilers ahead):1. The game is too easy. I managed to beat the highest difficulty with all characters without dying even once.2. HP potions are overpowered because they restore 30% while I'd put it at 20%.3. Poison potions are a wolf in sheep's clothing because they can get you out of a tight spot but are so chaotic that prevent any combos.4. I always find it difficult to distinguish various types of elite enemies and get frustrated when my combo relies on moving an unmovable enemy or hitting twice a shilded enemy.5. The final boss is fully predictable and barely presents a challenge after a few runs.6. The player should see the number of health points of any boss.7. All shops offers a health potion for sale, which I would personally randomize. 8. Abilities are almost always stronger than tile upgrades. so I find it useless to place upgrade options in shops.9. All environmental hazard (arrows, traps, corruption etc.) is created by units, but it would be exciting to toy with the idea of purely external forces (e.g. falling debris, earthquakes, spreading fire, kicking enemies off the board)10. Abilities from the combo shop are all but useless against bosses.11. Although there are no bugs as such, some tiles should not be working so literally. For instance, Lighting should hit the boss instead of the summoning statue in because, being invulnerable, it can not be considered an intended target.12. Freezable bosses can be killed trivially with Freeze + Cooldown. That is, a tile that can apply frost every 3 turns can keep a boss frozen permanently. I suggest reducing the duration of frost on bosses from 3 turns to 1 turn.

_childDocuments_.review: Samurai Showdown is a pixel art masterpiece with combat that makes you use your brain as much as your blade. The art alone had me trying to draw pixels myself, and then quickly remembering I’m no artist.Combat is all about strategy—enemies politely broadcast their moves in advance, and instead of planning, I usually panic and regret everything. But when you get it right? It's like solving a sudoku. The game ramps up difficulty smoothly, so you’re never just smashed by a random spike.I’m only 80 minutes in, and I can’t stop. Every battle is a new puzzle, and even when I’m sure I’ve been dealt a bad hand, there’s always a clever way out. My only gripe? Let me see how much health (in numbers) the boss has left! I need to know if my last-ditch effort is going to finish it off.In short, play Samurai Showdown. It’s challenging, beautiful, and seriously satisfying.
_childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.review: Come for the complex but easily-readable mechanics and the gorgeous pixel art style. Stay for the dynamic, on-the-fly strategizing and the soundtrack of wall-to-wall bangers.One modest critique: Why can't I know how much health (numerically) a boss has? In a game that hinges on knowing how much damage you need to do, why deny this information in a critical moment? Too often in a boss fight I'm left crossing my fingers, hoping the damage I'm about to do is enough to kill the boss without being certain.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game...Until you realize how frustrating the ability upgrade system is.I think the game would be better if there were no upgrades that only change the cooldown / damage as the player ends up focusing on upgrading one skill only.Currently the game relies too much on the upgrade system where you win or lose based on the amount of "+ damage" and "-cooldown" upgrades regardless of player skill. shop purchases seem trivial in comparison to a flat "+2 damage" meaning the money is better spent re-rolling the upgrades, even most abilities are better off refunded for upgrade re-rolls.  I would prefer if there were no upgrades and instead I got more abilities. (upgrades that change the weapon mechanically are great, those can stay)Combos are fun to do but gameplay punishes you for doing them by spawning the next wave instantly, no fun allowed I guess.Horrible "new shop" got introduced that allows player to pay grind coins to win making the victory feel cheap if that shop is used.Can't bring myself to play the game exclusively due to the upgrade system, did not get your main ability to do "+5 damage" on a short cool down? Too bad, you lose.

_childDocuments_.review: Stepping into the world of "Shogun Showdown," I immediately felt the adrenaline and precision of a ninja's life. The turn-based combat is ingeniously paired with a swift execution mechanism; just a press of the space bar, and a series of meticulously planned actions play out in a heartbeat. This combination ensures that, with experience, every battle unfolds with lightning speed, capturing the essence of a ninja's deadly efficiency.The depth of strategy demanded by this game is remarkable. As I upgraded my tiles and honed my combos, each choice became an integral part of my journey towards confronting the Shogun. But it's not just about the combat. The replayability here is exceptional. Every new playthrough brings fresh challenges, characters, and skills to the table, ensuring a unique experience every time.Considering this is still in its alpha stage, the potential "Shogun Showdown" showcases is immense. If you're seeking a game that offers a blend of strategy, swift action, and the thrill of mastering every encounter, then this is well worth the full price tag.5/5 - Dive in and embrace your inner ninja! Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Frustratingly repetitive puzzle game that requires next-level chess abilities to think way too many moves ahead when you get past day 1.  The elite abilities, especially the one that makes an enemy get a shield after taking damage, are way too punitive to deal with for the average player.  Game is fine on day 1, but there's no crazy overpowered run you can get here, you just get a very good easier run because you got good luck with damage/cooldown upgrades and dumped them all on your starting skill.  Why is the classes starting skill the best in the game?  Why do I even want to unlock other skills, other than the utility ones for moving around?  It's very poorly designed, every run will be the same as the last, the skills (relics from slay the spire) are not build-enabling they're just a nice-to-have sort of thing.  It's just so aggressively mediocre, the first 5 runs or so are great, then you've seen everything the game has to offer.

_childDocuments_.review: Shogun Showdown is an excellent blend of simplistic mechanics with tactically challenging gameplay. The game's core designs are elegantly simple; Music, art style, combat, and progression are all easy to understand and appreciate.This quaint little side-to-side turn based fighting game leans heavily into Japanese aesthetics. Ninja, Shinobi, Shoguns, Samurai, and all their specific weapons are used to create this pleasant roguelike experience. The gameplay itself is simple, every action progresses the turn, enemies announce the attack they intend to use, and then announce when they are attacking. You are challenged to defeat your foes using the same limitations. Progression after each encounter is simple, one or two rewards will be offered and they can effect your weapon cooldowns, damage, special effects, or even give you new weapons to work with. By the end of a run you might be using 6 different weapons, all with widely different stats than when you picked them up.The weakest aspects of the game is its difficulty. The game is surprisingly easy and doesn't challenge the player significantly until about the midway point of any given run. Sometimes early game runs are grindy, or boring, because of the lack of challenge and further lack of equipment that can spice up the encounters. Bosses are simple, initially, and lack enough diversity to avoid that feeling of grind. However, that all said, halfway through a run certain zones and bosses really amp up the difficulty and can significantly challenge any player depending on the route you take.Shogun Showdown is an excellent game to accompany those who have enjoyed Slay the Spire, Hades, Sekiro, or XCOM. The turned based gameplay feels quick and responsive, the aesthetics are wonderfully pleasant, and the long term progression is good enough to support a decent amount of replayability.

_childDocuments_.review: What Shogun Showdown manages to do is remarkable: while being a roguelike and (sorta) deckbuilder, the unique mechanics set it apart from the greats that typically overshadow the genre and let it stand in its own light. What's even more impressive is that the turn-based, one-dimensional board you play on with a limited number of actions somehow makes you feel more like a badass martial artist than just about any other martial-arts themed game I've played.It's weird to write as I didn't know this is what I was getting into when I picked it up, but once you get the hang of it this game delivers on the emotional experience of being your favorite out-manned action hero better than just about anything else. As the combo-kills rack up and you explore the different move sets and their enchants, it all just flows.10/10 would recommend to anyone who:+ likes games like Slay the Spire, Monster Train, etc.+ Wants to feel like John Wick, Jackie Chan, or Neo

_childDocuments_.review: Fun, snappy gameplay tied up in good art and music. Each wave of enemies is a puzzle to solve – how to get past everything while taking as few hits as possible (hopefully zero, if you've prepared well)? Not all options are equal, but a single bad tile or upgrade roll won't kill your run, and a good one might turn a middling run good – or a good one great.Runs are about 15-30 minutes, depending on the difficulty level, the upgrades and skills you find, and on how quickly you can plan out your turns.
_childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.review: This game is honestly great, i was looking for card battling rouge like games and i stumbled across it, even got a discount for it. Only paid 7 USD for this game and i must say, its breathtaking. I love the graphics and how simple the game is, yet how difficult it can get once getting deep into the game. Its a really good game but i can see a few flaws, mainly how it can use more content but other then that its pretty good. Would recommend to anybody who wants a fun rouge like game to pass the time.
_childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.review: it's 5:41am, I bought this cute little indie roguelike thinking it would help me get to sleep and instead I am dancing to the music and "Just One More Running" across a hellscape of islands hell bent on murder. I did not expect it to be this good.Edit: the music is a bop, the stages are short enough that any one song does not wear out its welcome. The stage's theme matches the music perfectly and just adds to everything. 5/5 game. I went back for one last run, it's now 6:43 am...
_childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.review: once I finally wrapped my head around its controls on keyboard, Shogun Showdown revealed itself to be an incredibly satisfying tactics game where the battles contain such a cathartic thrill when you absolutely rip through one of its battles without taking a single tick of damage. the pixel art is also very delightful.for more thoughtful recommendations of the best games on Steam, check out my curator, .
_childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun and innovative implementation of a turn-based combat system. Each action being a turn is such a difficult concept to implement. The conceptual problems were all solved by the attack queuing system, which allows players to queue up to three attacks before attacking. Note that each queuing action also takes a turn. This is also reflected in enemy design, where they also need to take a turn to queue up attacks.Once you get the flow down, it is such a satisfying game to master. A true shining diamond in the recent rough sea of mediocre roguelikes
_childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.review: Despite still being early access, this game is great and mechanically feels pretty complete. It will provide a pretty touch challenge on the later days, but you'll feel like a god once you get the hang of it. You will really have to familiarize yourself with all the enemy movesets, bosses, and different cards, powerups, characters, etc. I very much recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.review: It's cool and fun but not that fun, the potential for super strong and interesting builds is so low because of how short the full gameplay loop is. The art and music are good or decent, this is just a personal thing, I don't think it's that fun.This game made me realize I just dislike roguelites in general, despite loving roguelikes, so, that's a plus. _childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best new Rouge-lites I have played. If you like Into the Breach or turn-based strategy games, this game will scratch that itch. Its a game thats simple to learn, hard to master. Simple mechanics with so many variety which makes it complex. Since this is early access, the game will only get better but even right now theres a lot to love. Props to the developers for making a really good game
_childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely incredible game! Just when you think every turn-based roguelike is going to be a copy of the rest, a game like this comes out of nowhere.If you like the positioning shenanigans of Into The Breach, I would imagine you will love this game. The deck building element is rather lite, to be honest, but with so many games so heavily emphasizing that part (Slay The Spire, Monster Train, etc... which I played through all the ascension levels of each) the emphasis on positioning and movement here is extremely refreshing!They just put out a road map for adding more islands, difficulty levels, and imminently, controller support (although I played it on Steam Deck fine even without this, just using the trackpad). This will make the game even better. It's clear it doesn't have quite all of its content yet, but you can absolutely enjoy it a ton right now. I've been hooked since finding it!10/10, Do not miss!
_childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.review: One day I'm flailing a spiked ball around the field, and finishing all wounded enemies in an instant, and the next day I'm shoving them around like they weigh as much as a feather, cursing them and poisoning them as I do so.If you like to take the time to think your moves out, and want to be a super cool ninja, then this is the game for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy turn based thinky games or rogue-things you'll probably enjoy this.  Even if those aren't your favorite I'd say give it a try, it's got a lot of depth but it's in a simple cozy package so you don't have to get lost in paralyzing decision fatigue unless you really want to. _childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.review: It's a simple (in a good way), strategic, turn-based, tile game. Very unique, but excellent! Where a non-speed run will take 30-40 minutes. _childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.review: Half-puzzle, half-roguelite deckbuilder that has very few RNG mechanics. If you are tired of RNG-based deck builders that often punish you because your build is too weak, this game will become a breath of fresh air. You always control the situation - all of your "cards" are always at your disposal and you can use them in any order, at any time, without any mana costs. You always have the needed tools to get out of a tricky situation, you just have to use them wisely. If you get hit, it means you either made a mistake, or decided to tank some damage to perform a devastating combo. The build-making systems feels satisfying and balanced, you always have an option to upgrade one of your abilities or buy some new ones. There are some interesting status effects like Freeze (stun for a couple of turns), Curse (doubles next damage received), or Perfect Strike that resets the cooldown of your card if it killed an enemy by dealing an exact amount of damage needed.Overall, this game is a shining example of a nice idea and a near-perfect implementation. Even if you are not a huge fan of deck builders or roguelites, this game will surely be able to entertain you for 10-20 hours or even more.
_childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.review: I actually found the combat in this game to be very well balanced. It took me a lot of hours to learn how to take advantage of certain tiles and upgrades, but this game gets really fun (and really challenging!) when you figure out some really creative combos on the toughest enemy hordes. I highly recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.review: I've been waiting for this game to drop for the longest time. The demo was amazing and I'm happy early access finally dropped. This was worth the wait and it's so addicting. I wish I had the time to play a lot more but this game is what I look forward to after a long day of work.Update: After about 9 hours of play I've unlocked all available tiles and characters. I've beat the Shogun on each character once or more but find myself getting stuck towards the end of Day 2 on my runs. I really find that my runs lack synergy and very rarely get enough coins for perks & upgrades. My critique is that this game is extremely fun and addictive however I would love to see more synergies between tiles and perhaps have a way to reduce the RNG for the tiles you want in a run (especially if you have all of them unlocked already). This game is hugely underrated and needs more people talking about it. Excited to see what the devs have in store for this!
_childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.review: It belies its true intentions with its slick and simple systems; it wants you to be patient despite them. You on the other hand, or I at least, want to proceed quickly-- action, action, action-- but it punishes you for that, for failing to see the folly in aggression, for not looking at the next guy in the chain and his intentions towards you. It forces you to focus layers deep, like any good strategy game would do. But it's not so punishing as to keep you from ever learning the way. And the way is quite satisfying when you do.

_childDocuments_.review: This roguelike doesn't have a lot of moving parts and is comparatively short for a roguelike (by the time of this review i've beaten last boss on highest ascension on one of characters), but the parts that it has are polished to their peak and overall experience is super high. _childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.review: Shogun Showdown will not bore you with eye candy or narrative. You start the game and go through some rather strategic turn-based action in which you have to survive waves of foes while using a variety of various abilities and weapons. It's actually rather surprising given how basic the game appears on the surface but how much complexity there is already in the strategy section. You must truly consider what you want to achieve and how you intend to engage your next foe. Because they do take damage from one other, you can even use their skills against them depending on the type of character you choose. The game is enjoyable for around 30-60 minute periods as a way to pass the time, but I couldn't see myself sitting through longer than that, not because it isn't enjoyable, but because it's more of a game to play in small bursts when you want to play strategy. Reasonably priced too for what you get.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a new player, I highly recommend this game. But my gaming experience is terrible.It has fatal bugs if you have savadatas of older version. The game freezes in many situations: starting for the first time, choosing a class, defeating a general... You can select the Nth day in the departure UI, and N can be a negative number... _childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.review: This is a solid second-tier roguelike that works as a great intro to the genre. Sort of a 'baby's first roguelike'. The decision space is very narrow, but as your progress the battles get increasingly complex. Pulling off complex combos is quite rewarding. There's also some nice, albeit relatively small, variation between characters that helps make repeated runs interesting.However, its strength is also its weakness. The decision space is so narrow that much of the game, particularly on early levels, is very same-y and ultimately becomes tedious. Part of the problem is that there are too many levels in between meaningful choices.  Part of the problem is the super limited 2D battle space. Again, strengths are weaknesses and vice versa. Also, I have to mention the clever/annoying controls, which after 50+ hours still result in unintended moves and deaths.But if your are into turn-based roguelikes it's easily worth the money and will be addictive for a solid 20+ hours. Just don't go into it with the expectation that this is the next Into to The Breach, Slay the Spire or Monster Train and you'll be fine.

_childDocuments_.review: While early impressions are pretty strong, I eventually found this game way too repetitive. No matter what character or build you have, it feels like that you are basically doing the same things every run. Try to get one or two position manipulation tiles, move out of the way of melee attacks, combo finish ranged attackers, drink a shield potion if you can't avoid taking damage, etc. Bosses have the same attack patterns every time you fight them, so if you have remembered their patterns you will never lose to them. Runs are long enough to where I get bored of my current build before I finish them. There is very little difference between most of the playable characters (their special move and starting two tiles).It's a shame, because I usually enjoy turn-based combat systems that focus on position manipulation. This one doesn't seem to have enough variety to keep me engaged. I can tell that the developers tried their best, but none of the content feels all that meaningfully different. Maybe the combat system is too restrictive.

_childDocuments_.review: SPOILER WARNING FOR THOSE WHO HAVEN'T BEATEN DAY 7This might be the king of all strategy games, the absolute peak of it's genre. Everything from music, art and gameplay is fine tuned into this enthralling experience that is worth playing over and over again. Games like these don't come around often, so when they do it is an absolute treat. The only negative thing I have to say about this game is the final boss. And I'm not talking about the shogun. The week 7 final boss is complete bull in a lot of aspects, requiring you to have either the most broken build of all time, or an absolute giga mind to efficiently and narrowly escape death. Ranged weapons are essentially required for the fight, and not having any just feels like a forced reset. This is without mentioning that you have to actually still BEAT the shogun before facing it, while only having 2 shield potions, assuming you didn't already WASTE them in the shogun fight itself. This final boss is so hard in fact, that the devs even give you credit IN the credits for beating it at all. Other than that, the game is fantastic. I genuinely can't wait to see what DLC or spinoffs this game gets because of just how much fun this one is. HIGHLY RECOMMEND!

_childDocuments_.review: Shogun Showdown is an indie turn-based combat game with roguelike and deck-building elements. It is similiar to Slay the Spire and Into the Breach, and like in these games movement and positioning are critical. Attacks and abilities, each with different ranges and effects, are powered by a limited energy resource that must be carefully managed. Success hinges on learning enemy behaviors, managing resources, and adapting strategies to the ever-changing game environment.When I was buying it I knew that SS is difficult, and to be honest, it often feels unfair. If you don't get good upgrades in the very first stages, your run is essentially doomed. Unlike other roguelikes/roguelites, there is no progression here. There's nothing to make future runs easier, aside from unlocking additional weapons and skills. The gameplay also becomes repetitive very fast, with the best strategy seeming to be maxing out your starting cards. This game is promising, but at this moment there is not enough variety or content (no diffrent paths for example) especially at the start of each run. I quickly hit a wall and found myself unable to progress further. Overall, I found it more frustrating than fun.Can't recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to be very critical about this game and it's the first time I give a negative review, but with the "overwhelmingly positive" reviews so far I reckon the game can survive a negative one. The game costs less than 10 quid, so buy it away if you know what you 're getting. I played the Prologue first so I knew what I was getting but I got it anyway because it's so cheap.The tl;dr of it is that I found the game more frustrating than entertaining, and while I keep coming back for the elegant simplicity of its design, the game punishes me with boredom instead of rewarding me with enjoyment.First, the game. You play as one of three characters. You start as "The Wanderer", and there are two more characters that have to be unlocked. So far I have unlocked one other character, "The Ronin". The two characters I've seen have different starting "tiles" (moves they can make) and different specials. The Wanderer can move through enemies, while The Ronin can push enemies back.To unlock The Ronin and the other character you have to defeat a boss for each. Defeating "The Twins" unlocks The Ronin and to unlock the third character, whose name I don't know because I haven't unlocked it, you have to defeat "Nobunaga the Wicked". I am going to go out on a limb and say that "Nobunaga the Wicked" is the final boss, but I've only reached to "The Statue", one boss after "The Twins", so I don't know. Maybe the final boss is Eren Yeager.The game loop is a turn-based fight in essentially two dimensions. Each level consists of a few squares that can be occupied by one character or enemy at a time. Movements are to the right or left only, but some moves can effectively teleport a character through multiple others, sometimes striking them in the process. Besides moving you can fire off attacks and special moves by choosing a "tile" (like a card). Tiles are placed on a Last-In-First-Out stack and the stack resolves (hint hint M:tG hint) with the press of a button, at which point all the tiles in it are executed without interruption.When you kill an enemy, they might drop some coins or potions. Potions give you temporary power ups or heal 3 HP (you start with 10). The healing point is... edamame. WhaAfter every fight you find a sort of idol where you can upgrade your current tiles, or two pedestals offering you one of two new tiles. You can spend coins to reroll the offerings of the idol or the pedestals. You can also spend coins in shops you find on your way through the "overland" map that takes you from fight to fight.When you die you lose all the coins, potions and tiles you had gained. Some fights are boss fights and defeating a boss gives you some number of "skulls" that you can spend to buy new tiles at the start screen. If you do, those tiles have a chance to appear on a pedestal in your next runs. You can also spend skulls to upgrade shops by adding more slots where items appear. If you die before defeating any bosses you get no skulls.The idea of a linear, turn-based fight where you can only move and strike in one dimension is simple and elegant and is what keeps me coming back for more, but the rest of the game is a chore.One big problem is that fights are very inconsistent. I don't like to whine about "the RNG" but I will have three or four runs where I fail to make it past the first boss, "Daisuke the Charger".  Then I'll have one run where I'll make it three bosses later to "The Statue".  I don't know what's past The Statue (OK, I suck, OK?). What's really frustrating with all that is that every time I lose, I'm taken back to the beginning and I have to do all of the same things over, and Over and OVER again. That's mind-numbingly boring, like a game of snakes and ladders.I get it, the game is a roguelike. I play Nethack, right? I die all the time in Nethack. But, in Nethack you have 13 classes (as of version 367) and a garbanzillion of items. Every time I die in Nethack and start a new game, it's a different game. Every time I die it's in a different way. In Shogun Showdun (hereafter, Sho-Sho) every time I die it's in the same way (bloody pikers), and every time I start a new game, it's the same game, with the same character, with the same tiles, with the same special, on the same map, and facing the same enemies in the same way.  Even the different tiles you can find do not add much variety after all because the majority are rather narrow in scope and I find myself selecting the same few ones all the time:  Swirl, Arrow, Spear and maybe once in a while a dash or a curse. So there's no variety there either.  That's ===> b o r i n g <===That boring is a direct consequence of the "elegant simplicity" of the game that I note above, so I don't know what can be done about it, and I apologise to the devs that I can't offer any more constructive criticism. I really have no idea how this game could be made more interesting. Add more starting characters? More varied tiles at the start? More diverse enemies?I mean, if I've played the game 50 times (I think I have, in 4.4 hours of play) shouldn't I get to see _something_ changing every time I start it?Despite my negative review, the game is cheap and still in early release so there's plenty of time for the devs to do better. Maybe they're focusing on stability and efficiency etc, and leaving gameplay for later, which I would say is a wise move. If you're interested in turn-based fighters, roguelikes or card games, buy it because it's an interesting take on all three. Oh, also: the graphics are cute, the music is chiptune cool and I could see no bugs.EDIT: One of the developers has replied to my review. Apparently comments can't be longer than 1000 characters, so I'm basically going to reply here. The developer, Thomas, gave a kind and patient reply! I have to say he is much better than me in dealing with negative feedback on his work (I got better; I'm a researcher, and negative feedback means my papers don't get published, which hurts a lot and not just my ego!).I thought about changing my review to "recommended" since I really don't want to hurt Sho-Sho's :) chances to be recognised and well received. I was going to do it, but I saw that the rating jumped again to "overwhelmingly positive".  I think the momentary drop of the rating from my comment was the result of only having a small number of reviews, positive or negative, so far (662 at the time of writing). As more people play and review the game, the score will become normalised and, if the current trend lasts, you can expect the overall rating to be "overwhelmingly positive", certainly for "All reviews" but also for the recent ones. So don't worry about it too much. I still think Sho-Sho can survive one (and more!) negative review.I think I should leave my review as negative for the purpose of indexing it, especially for people like me who go straight to the negative reviews to figure out whether a game is for me or not. I do that a lot and I believe it has saved me a lot of frustration with games I didn't want to play after all, even if it seemed like I did at first. I think this is good not only for the player, but also for the developer: I'm guessing developers don't want players returning their game after they throw the keyboard/ controller in frustration! I hope the ceveloper can accept the possibility that my negative review not only doesn't hurt Sho-Sho's prospects, but even improves its reception a bit, by helping those who don't want to play it, avoid playing it then being grumpy about it and leaving more negative reviews. Of course there is the Prologue for that, but I'm hoping this kind of review is an extra bit of buffering between unfairly negative reviews from people who didn't have the time to finish the Prologue.OK, end of character limit for this review, also :P

_childDocuments_.review: Game is way too easy, I have a crazy amount of hp and I find hp potions constantly. Enemies barely do any damage and have little to no health. The most amount of hp I saw an enemy have was like 5-6, which is nothing. There are "6 days", in other words 6 increments of difficulty that increase every time you beat the final boss. I guess this could've made the game harder but after beating day 2 final boss I was already disinterested in the game.I know its early access, but game is too short. I would've been interested to see my build refined even further, and fight against really strong enemies with it.Overall I had a lot of fun the first hour of my playtime, and I think its because I was still getting used to the mechanics and so the game was more challenging. I liked the upgrading system, I liked how you could increase the max level of a card, and the enchantments. The scaling of cards was fun, but could've been more if game was longer. But there was no incentive to make a strong build because my mediocre build was already plenty to beat the game. I was haphazardly going through the levels and upgrading cards without much thought and I beat the final boss twice.Reply to the developer:It shouldn't be expected of players to slog through the boring parts of the game to unlock the fun part of the game. It's not that the progressive difficulty wasn't going too fast for me, its because the baseline difficulty was too low to begin with.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not worth more than $10.00.And I would have recommended it if I didn't feel like the developer/publisher unjustifiably increased the base price by 50% earlier this year.The game-play is cool to me; you can try the demo and feel it for yourself.  However, the game screams cheapness and lack of polish (which is why I contend it's not worth more than $10.00):For one, there are lack of helpful tooltips, especially for a 1.0 launch.  Even for a $10 game (which again is overpriced to $15), I think it's fair to expect to see a tooltip when you hover over the little skull-icon in the corner of the screen, with a little blurb explaining what they're used for. Another example of cheapness and lack of polish can be seen when you return to camp to spend those mysterious skulls on new "tiles" or cards.  When you hover over your options of new cards to purchase, you are only given the name of the card and a message saying, "once unlocked, you may find this tile in future runs." Unless you've already memorized the card's mechanics (/sarcasm), you have to close that menu and open a completely new menu to find your three cards and evaluate them from there...and the cards may each be on different pages that you have to scroll through to find.  This is so irritating that it actually serves as the impetus for this review, more so than the price-hike.A third example of cheapness and lack of polish can be seen in the fact that the hit points of bosses are hidden.  They have an HP bar, but the exact number of hit points is not seen.  So, imagine, 90% of the time I'm calculating all my moves to eliminate these waves of enemies as efficiently as possible, but when it comes to the boss fights I have to guesstimate how much damage I need to do to him/her/it.  It's a travesty of simplicity.Lastly, and probably the cheapest thing about this game: the world map.  It's very disappointing to have binary choices in a roguelike more than 6 years after slay-the-spire.  I actually felt like I was playing Donkey Kong Country ONE again, but in a cheap way.So, with all this in mind, I've drawn two conclusions:1) Roboatino and Globlinz rushed a 1.0 launch and capitalized on positive reviews with an unjustifiable price-hike.2) If you're on a budget, I don't recommend spending more than $10.00 for this game; there are plenty of games in the Steam.

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah, this game is overrated. It's frustrating and boring. I hate when games with a cool concept introduce "cards" or "deckbuilding". Deckbuilding/card style removes organic interaction and reduces everything to discrete actions, which is inherently limiting. A shogun game becomes just a card game, a spaceship game becomes just a card game, etc. It twists the genre into just another card game, which is oversaturated. There is nothing satisfying about using a weapon here like there is in FTL. It's all about positioning, it's a puzzle game, and that isn't fun for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Watch this dev team. They are up to no good.This is a fun game, but devs arbitrarily decided to raise the price for no real reason, claiming the content they now have matches the price. I disagree, as with 15 hours I have experienced everything the game has to offer outside of grinding RNG for achievements.This game is fun and executed well, but I cannot condone the devs raising the price. This is not something that early access games should do while still in early access. This sets a terrible precedent and has caused me to lose any faith I had in this company.Edit for dev response:"We took the time to tell you why we wanted to raise the price, put a sale so you can still grab it at 9,99 so we don't get you by surprise. We stand by the fact that we think the game is worth $15 even in it's current state ; 4 characters with an alternate build and 5 ascension levels to play each (which I doubt you did in 15 hours), and more to come (as you can see on the roadmap)."Nothing that you have said here changes the fact that raising the price of an early access game before its complete is a terrible practice. The sale is irrelevant. You are setting a bad precedent. Will you go on sale the next time you raise the price? What about the time after that? Will you raise price again when the game is complete? These are all legitimate yet unanswered concerns. In fact, the dev responding outright disregarded them.As far as the dev's doubts about what I've done in the game, I have indeed played all 4 characters and their alternate builds, though I did not take the time and play through each ascension, which is just an incremental difficulty increase that provides no new content, hence why I stated that I have experienced everything the game has to offer."Also, it does not concern you since you already bought the game? I'm not sure why you're reviewing negativelyI know I won't make you change your mind, and that's fine, but we do think rising the price of $5 was not that much of a big deal that "sets a terrible precedent""This is very selfish of you. Do you review products for your own good or do you review them with other consumers in mind? It takes a special kind of person to completely disregard and dodge the concerns raised by someone else.You've missed the point completely. This is a not recommended from me because by raising the price in this early access game, you have established the precedent. It's not about "oh its just $5" as you make it out to be, it's about an incomplete game with an uncertain future trying to squeeze as much money as they can out of consumers. It's very simple.If you really wanted to raise the price, you should have waited for full release.

_childDocuments_.review: I really, really hate games that have class-based ascension systems. It is such a *massive* pet peeve of mine in this genre. Why on EARTH would you restrict higher floors to the one class you've gotten up with. What if I want to keep climbing, but try with another class? Or just to mix it up? I now have to start over and climb from a lower difficulty. Ugh... You are locking out a ton of your content for those of us looking to climb. It's not like each class has very many class-oriented unlocks. Everything is mostly purchased from the shop. It's demoralizing to see this. It takes my drive away from wanting to play because I want to play other classes but I don't want to start over.I'm downvoting the game purely on this pet peeve. _childDocuments_.review: This is a recommend but with a caveat. The game is great, and the systems in the game are really fun. Each encounter is like a mini puzzle, as you try to manoeuvre yourself around the enemies manipulating your positioning to take out foes as efficiently as possible. However the games greatest strength is also its weakness. There isn't enough variation in the skills and ways to interact with the enemies to keep it fresh. Every class' special ability is just a slightly different way of moving across the 5-10 tile encounter maps, or ways to move the enemies around. I had a lot of fun with the game for about 40 hours, but then it got stale, and I had no desire to chase the various challenges in the game. So if you're ok with a roguelike that you may not be able to play endlessly, then definitely try it. For the time I played it, it was totally worth the money!

_childDocuments_.review: A perfect rogue-lite that feels very rewarding as you progress. The turn-based combat and tile system is very intuitive. Enemies, skills, abilities, and items all function uniquely and add a layer of depth that keeps this game feeling fresh. Some battles are challenging, but when you defeat a boss with your last HP and a properly planned combo it will feel zen-like. To top it off, the themes of this game are great: charming character design, a sound direction that is classically familiar yet not passé, and backdrops that all flow together with their theatrical scenes. Ultimately, this is a very fun game that's easy to pick-up and put-down, but you'll feel that itch to play one more run. Highly recommended for fans of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: If you’re looking to lose a few hundred hours of your life in the most satisfying way, Shogun Showdown has you covered. This game is the ultimate time-sink, where every run is different, the replayability is endless, and each turn feels like a tiny tactical masterpiece. It’s got pixel samurais, clever combos, and just enough strategy to make you think, 'One more round!' (or twenty). Seriously, it's super addictive—highly recommended if you’re ready to outsmart the Shogun and lose track of time in the best way possible!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an absolute masterpiece, and deserves a place in the pantheon of GOAT rogue-likes/deck-builders/RPGs.It has a bit of a steep learning curve, in time you slowly begin to understand the core mechanics and intricacies of: waiting, movement, cool downs, attack tiles, synergies, enemy behavior, abilities, consumables, and so on.Shogun Showdown has a scaling difficulty in terms of Days 1 through 7 that unlock as you beat the final boss of the previous day. These difficulties add a slight variation in terms of consumable drops, enemy/boss behavior, HP and so on. Just as a side note the spike difficulty of day 6 and 7 are not for the faint of heart but are extremely rewarding once you finally see that glorious VICTORY screen, you got this I believe in you.The variety of quests/achievements are awesome and I love that these can be completed in Day 1, since you can go for fun combos and not sweat these out in the later difficulty levels. Some of these achievements/quests include: -Speed running.-Strategist (beat the game in the least amount of turns).-Combo-kills.-Taking the least amount of hits.-Beating all the difficulties (Day 1-7).My current playtime is 93 hours, as I just finished my last no-hit run and completed all the achievements. It was an absolute blast, thank you to the developers and everyone who has worked on this absolute gem of a game. Please do yourself a favor and play this game. Stick with it, I promise it'll be worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: My first hour of Shogun Showdown, I didn't quite get it. I clumsily stumbled around the battlefield, walking into enemy attacks, facing the wrong way when using my own attacks, spending a turn adding an attack to my queue while a spearmen was ready to stab me in the face. But then you have a moment where everything clicks, and the elegance of the gameplay really begins to show. Shogun Showdown is a careful dance of setting up the perfect attack while managing the enemies around you. The game feels heavily inspired by Into the Breach, but it makes the brilliant decision of reducing the 2 dimensional grid to a 1 dimensional one. You can move left and right and that's it. Moving also does not turn your character around, changing direction is it's own action that takes a turn. The claustrophobic arenas combined with the many systems to consider at any moment completely remove the need for Into the Breach's cities. In that game, the ability to freely move in two dimensions makes the enemies' telegraphed attacks pretty toothless when used directly against the player's units, a problem that's solved by having "city" tiles the player must defend at all costs. Here however, there is almost nowhere to run. And often, the only direction you CAN run will put you face to face (or back to face if you don't have time to turn around) with more enemies. The game gives you an impressive arsenal of tools for dealing with these situations, I've only played a few hours and I'm already floored by the variety and simplicity of the different attacks, but the lethality of the enemies must always be respected. This is a pretty spectacular strategy roguelike that builds a lot on established genre conventions expertly, while introducing its own twist.
_childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting mechanics, and plays really well.It's not super complicated, but you still mess up now and then. "Obliterating" your opponents is very satisfying. (Flawless Victory)Weapon upgrades are pretty vague and boring, but does offer some possibilities for different synergies. However, there's many different weapons to unlock with permanent progression. (It will off course dilute the pool and force builds to be more diverse)Classes and their starting weapons are different enough to change your playstyle. Looking forward to try the third class.
_childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.review: I love the aesthetic but the game play looked very simple from watching the trailers. I figured this game was over-hyped and there was no way something that looks so simple could deserve an overwhelmingly positive rating unless people were making joke reviews or they hadn't played many roguelites.I've never been so happy to be wrong.The mechanics are simple but the strategy is surprisingly deep. Anyone can move and attack. But can you plan multiple moves ahead and put together devastating combos? Can you adjust when a new enemy spawns in a less than ideal location? Can you adapt when the next run throws new enemies into the mix and gives familiar enemies new buffs? Will you rage quit when you become complacent then make a stupid mistake and lose a run because you just weren't paying attention to that one enemy that was primed to attack as soon as the enemy in front of them fell or will you learn from your mistakes and do better on the next run?Shogun Showdown is incredibly addicting, easy on the eyes, and very fun. In a sub-genre where it seems almost every game is trying to follow in the footsteps of Slay the Spire and focus on synergies, Shogun Showdown offers up a wonderful mix of movement, planning, and combos. It deserves every bit of praise.

But I open mouth cackled at the moment where I used two upgraded smoke bombs and a big ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mace to samurai style slice between three enemies and instakill each of them in one turn.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a big thumbs up from me. Great game, lots of fun. They really captured a "ninja" feel to the gameplay: dash around, reposition yourself and/or enemies to dodge attacks, move out of the way to make them hit each other, set up combos, it really embraces the feel of it in a satisfying way. There are characters and new tiles (actions) to unlock as you progress and difficulty levels increase.While there are five characters, there is only one tile set, so there are no unique moves for any character. They do each have a unique special move though. This isn't a bad thing, but it does make it feel a little bit limited. On the other hand, I think there's a ton of room for expansion content, both in terms of expanding the existing ideas and adding new mechanics.Overall this is well worth the $15 price point.

_childDocuments_.review: Very unique roguelike that kept me going to the end, but there is a lot of room for improvement. The progression system is just ability unlocks that all character share, and there is no way to manage that or customize, so the more you unlock, the less of a chance for weapons/abilities you want. For me it came down to just using one of the characters (shadow) that seems way better that hte other chars, and kind of using cheap tactics to beat the end game. Overall a positive rec if you enjoy rougelikes, but don't expect any sort of intresting builds or sotry.

_childDocuments_.review: Never have I played a game that so effectively rewards your skill by making you feel like an untouchable anime protagonist. This roguelike is incredibly well-designed and polished, rivaling that of Into the Breach and Cobalt Core. All combat is turn-based, so you have as much time as you need to make a decision, but there is no undo or rewind button to be found. The combination makes the game both highly fair yet highly punishing. One big mistake at the end can cost you a run, but virtually every mistake I've made playing this game has come as a result of not properly thinking through the order of operations. Every enemy is predictable, such that you can learn their movement patterns and predict what they will do even before seeing the turn preview. The exception to that rule is bosses, which require a bit more effort to learn their AI and how to counter it. Turn previews themselves only tell you what enemies will do on their turn, meaning it is up to you to calculate what will happen after you make your move. The game has no shortage of difficulty for people looking to prove their skill at the game. The Ascension system is based around a 7-day calendar, with each day being unlocked after completing the previous one and increasing the difficulty. If you only want to play casually, you can simply stick to day 1 and unlock everything that way until it starts getting too easy for you. With 5 playable characters in total, you'll need to beat the game at least 35 times in order to get 100% completion. Each run takes 30 minutes to an hour, so you can sink quite a bit of time into the experience. Your primary means of combat are the various weapon tiles you obtain over the course of a run. The variety of those weapons helps keep each run feeling distinct, especially in combination with the character variety and increasing difficulty. There are also a whole host of achievements, with a good mix of easy and difficult ones.I highly recommend this game for all fans of strategic roguelikes. One of my favorite games of the year.

_childDocuments_.review: Personally really enjoyed Shogun Showdown a ton, wanted to give my perspective as someone who has finished 100% forsomeone who just generally enjoys roguelikes. TL;DR at the end if you don't wanna read my rant.To give a quick TL;DR of that this game is: You go through various battles, you fight in them, get new "tiles" which are move actions that you can use to defeat enemies. Tiles are your bread, with the upgrades and modifiers you add to them being the butter. You have skills which are kinda like Slay the Spire relics/ Monster Train artifacts. There's also nice variety in the different characters in the game with each of them having their own cool-down based "signature move" that can be used as a sort of "oh I'm kinda cornered, lemme just move over here or move you away instead of letting you attack me thx"The game is not super hard (I completed a large majority of the challenges I attempted in fewer than 2-3 runs), but does allow for some very calculated decision-making when running the challenges or playing at the higher difficulties. Notably the RNG never really felt consistently or excessively "unfair" at any point (though ofc there are going to be random exceptions here and there. Until I learned about those and then like got good and then stopped dying to that unfair thing). You often can make routing/pathing choices based on what enemies you are good at fighting, or what types of shops you want to visit to fish for certain skills/upgrades. Rerolling rewards vs saving for buying something better. Keeping potions to account for bad rng in combat vs selling them to get a skill that might avoid that in the first place. Potions in this game can be thought of as an alternate currency/resource you can exchange for money or to save health. As you start to become more familiar with the systems, you can chain together some insane plays like killing the whole screen at once with two moves with a good setup. Thinking like "oh hey I should get a movement tile to help dodge that one annoying attack the upcoming boss can do."Now for the fun part: Stuff I don't like about the game (oooo how dramatic :0)Tbh its not much really.I don't like that in some fights you can kinda just stall out enemies and move back and forth and they can kinda just like not hit you at all since they are melee. The game stops spawning enemies if there are too many on the map, but I kinda wish a tiny bit that they would start just adding on more pressure to punish you for stalling. The game has a solution for this mainly in that there are some ranged enemies that will immediately attack once you take out the front-line enemies. You have counter-play to this though by setting up a combo move that takes out both the melee and ranged blokes. Also late game there are some tanky front-line ranged enemies, but the game doesn't have a solve for this in the early game as much, which leads me into the next bit.The early game is kinda just too easy. It fairly repetitive because you only start with two tiles and the enemies aren't that varied. Though once the game adds elite enemies with higher difficulties (regular enemies but with special buffs) then it gets quite interesting. Also if you start with random tiles that makes it fun too.Also the twins mid-way through the game are kinda just. Really like too easy to cheese. Almost always end up perfecting their fight.I honestly wish there was more difficult/advanced late-game challenging mechanics. Don't get me wrong Day 7 (the hardest difficulty) can be quite brutal but I kinda just wish there was a little more like (Lets go insane god mode and just destroy everything). But honestly that's not the type of game this is. It's more of a (okay how so we surgically deal with this?)TL;DR: Play this game if you like roguelikes. It is a very unique roguelike concept that's executed extremely well. Idk in what case you wouldn't like this game? Maybe just if you really don't like repetitiveness to any extent but that's roguelikes in a nutshell.

_childDocuments_.review: It's like Slay the Spire, but instead of standing still you can dodge attacks and fling the enemies around. The enemy and boss variety here is really good, and it gets even more expansive on the higher difficulties. While it's still a rogue-like, it doesn't feel as luck dependent to me as many other games in the genre. Every build I've had in this game has felt viable to an extent, and victories feel earned just as much as the defeats feel justified. Runs are pretty quick to complete (about 30-40 minutes for me depending on difficulty and how good my build is), and there's plenty of weapons and skills to unlock to spice up future runs. I've only really sunk time into 3 out of the 5 characters, and while they all draw from the same weapon pool, each character's unique skill is enough to make them all feel unique from each other. Outside of the 7 difficulty modes for each character, there are plenty of achievements to go for, like beating a run in X amount of time, or beating a run without taking damage, so for completionists there is a lot to like here.Also the soundtrack ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ SLAPS

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to recommend this over Into the Breach for a no-luck tactical roguelike. I love both games, but this one does such a good job of letting you feel powerful and powerless at the same time. Aesthetics aside (which are all great), the gameplay in this is only rivaled by Into the Breach. It feels unfair at first while you're learning the game, but it gives you so many tools and encourages you to push past your own nearsightedness to use the game's systems against it. If at first you lose, stick with it. This game wants you to win and gives you many tools to learn how over time.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best turn based roguelites I've played in a long time. Similar to StS with the relics system and deckbuilding, those systems are pared down making room for tactics 8 spaces horizontally. Each action - setting up an attack card, moving, turning, executing stacked attack cards - takes one turn. And again, like Spire, one sees enemy intents. Though you can only lineup 3 cards max from your hand, the game still  allows for crazy combos and synergies based on your relics, deck, upgrades (attack damage, lowered colldowns, upgrade slots, elemental magic), enemy type and positioning. The moment to moment combat is where this game really shines.Again, I have to say how simplified SS feels in comparison to something a little weightier than StS, and yet, Shogun Showdown has complexity and charm all its own. Regarding artstyle and music that conveys this period I'm Japanese history, it's all beautiful. The soundtrack kicks ass!Highly recommend this game for roguelites turn based lovers with a love of tactics. As far as indie games like that go, this is one of the best of recent releases and one of the best, period.
_childDocuments_.name: Shogun Showdown

_childDocuments_.review: Very satisfying fine-tuned tactics - pulling off a perfect combo that saves your bacon / kills a ton of baddies is a good feeling. The art and music do an alright job setting that mood, but neither are especially great.I wish there were more interesting choices to make on the map - the choice of which shop to visit is really all there is. Choosing between "fight" nodes are only meaningful in which stores you can access after. Choosing between islands is only meaningful in the same way - the types of enemies and bosses add some variety, but I never felt like I was choosing based on my build, or building my tiles based on the upcoming islands.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a masterpiece, and it's like no other I've ever played. If you enjoyed turn-based strategy titles like Slay the Spire, Into the Breach, or Darkest Dungeon, you're sure to enjoy the precision and diversity on offer in Shogun Showdown, while also enjoying the ways in which the game steps outside of deckbuilding and tactics genre conventions. Quit waffling or waiting for a sale—just buy it already.In Shogun Showdown, play feels like a dance, with elegant combinations of movement and action rewarded much more than brute force. There is excellent progression both in player abilities and enemy challenge throughout each run, as well as a perfect balance of varied builds available without making players feel overwhelmed by options.And a note on the visuals: the animations are punchy, and the background art is unspeakably beautiful. Pixel artists everywhere, look no further for your references—this is what you should aspire to!Thank you, Roboatino, for such a gorgeous entry. I look forward to many fun-filled hours to come!
