_childDocuments_.review: The One Piece of RPGsIt is definitely hard to get into this game, but just about everything for an interesting game experience is here. The story is really great if you work for it and probably a little better if you are familiar with past SaGa entries. The Final Emperor, Mr. S and Macha are pretty important figures in other SaGa games, for example. But the combat is also really rewarding, but a slog, especially if you are relying on trades rather than trial rewards. It is also missing some quality of life features that the "prequel" game (Scarlet Grace) provided, like being able to move to the end of the timeline with L1/R1, speeding up animations by pressing X/A, faster paced combat and animations in general, et cetera. On the other hand, the combat has been improved a lot from that game, with combos that are easy to activate and can turn the tide of battle easier, showstoppers that prevent a battle from snowballing too easily, first aid roles that easily heal up LP and are standard for every (non-ephemeral) character (you used to need really slow methods for LP recovery in Scarlet Grace) and two new types of skills which although I rarely use them, make it even easier to manipulate the timeline and prevent too many unfair situations.The main characters are amazing in this game too. They really change the experience of playing the game more than the characters in SaGa Frontier. Ameya gets a lot of help making her potentially much more powerful than your other characters if it is your first or second playthrough or something. Siugnas can get insane amounts of LP that he can spend for useful skills and he also can interact with his team members in interesting ways. Tsunanori Mido can power up his puppets with a lot of unique easily acquirable roles that make his team very powerful in early game, but require a lot of work because of the Mimicry skill learning of Kugutsu.  Diva can switch her mech body, giving her potential to gain some permanent benefits that other mechs can not get, and she also gets Wednesday and the plant girl who are very useful and rare types of party members. Bonnie and Formina barely have anything (that I know about), but they do get to start with three "monsters", which are another potentially great companion for early game. I think Siugnas and Mido are the best protagonists and sadly Ameya only seems to get better when you nearly 100% the game. That brings up another important point - this game is based around many playthroughs. Ameya is basically the worst character to do multiple playthroughs with until you meet all of the conditions. Mido is so good that you might want to just play with him 5 times as your first character. Siugnas has a lot of great story and might unlock content for the worlds. Bonnie and Formina seem to learn about the core plot points of the game, but so does Mido. Diva seems the least worthwhile so far in terms of payoff.Anyways, if you are bored with straightforward and tropey games and you also are a fan of grinding a great combat system, this game is perfect. However, like games of old, this game is much better if you take a lot of breaks rather than trying to binge and see all of the content quickly.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: You may have already played a SaGa game if you played any of the Final Fantasy Legend games on the Game Boy (with the mutants, robots and all that stuff). Those games were SaGa games rebranded since FF is more well known.If you are tired of regular RPGs, this one has:- A combat system where every turn is a different situation. You're not just pressing A and occasionally healing (there's no healing from what I've seen), you have to strategize and combat often ends with one party member standing at low HP.- Comeback mechanic for when you get rolled. In Scarlet Grace (the game this is an iteration upon) sometimes you could end up in hopeless situations. Emerald Beyond has Showstoppers which allow a lone party member to do several attacks in a row.- Many different races of characters with different mechanics. Robots, cats, plant-people and of course, humans.- Comedic tone with the occasional melodrama.- Freedom. When I played Mido's story I was surprised at how many quests I was able to turn down.- Kick-ass soundtrack.What this game lacks:- Exploration. I don't consider this to be a bad thing but exploration is an RPG staple. If you like towns and dungeons, this game doesn't have them.- Cinematic storytelling. Story scenes are quick slideshows instead of long, drawn out cutscenes. I personally prefer this since I read really quickly (so cutscenes actually really annoy me), but cinematic storytelling is a modern RPG staple so you ought to know ahead of time that this game doesn't have cutscenes.I recommend this game and the series it is from for people who are tired of regular RPGs where you mash the A button and occasionally heal. I'm not saying those games are bad (I play and enjoy them myself) but sometimes you just want something different.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: The SaGa games always make it hard to give an easy thumbs up or thumbs down.  Square's commitment over the years to a franchise with constant mechanical experimentation, obfuscated information and systems, and difficult combat is admirable, but also mean that they're not games for everyone.  Emerald Beyond falls into that tradition, while being somewhat of a funhouse mirror version of Scarlet Grace. The combat system is incredibly strategic and in-depth; positioning, turn order, status effects, timeline manipulation, damage types and formations all play into a deep and satisfying combat system, where you can pull a victory out of a hat at the last possible moment.  In a lot of ways it's a refinement to the system from Scarlet Grace, but has some wrinkles, like a complete inability to heal within combat meaning that defensive techniques and smart strategies are mandatory.  The downside is that there's no such thing as a short battle in Emerald Beyond, so even if you're outmatching your opponents, you can't just mash through the fight.  There's also comparatively little overall variety in enemies, so you'll see most of them and learn their combat capabilities in relatively short orderIn contrast to Scarlet Grace's extensive and branching story campaign, Emerald Beyond is more of a Choose Your Own Adventure RPG.  Each of the five campaigns (and six protagonists) have an overarching story and plot, but you'll spend a majority of your time going through a grab-bag of themed worlds; if you go through multiple campaigns you'll see some of them multiple times, though they won't necessarily play out identically (due to inherent RNG and/or different choices you may make yourself).  It's nice to have variety as you go along, though the stand-alone nature of each one means that the whole game tends to take on an episodic feeling and you might get tired of some worlds if they keep showing up in your runs.  It all lends itself to a very story-light and casual RPG feel, though the protagonists are varied and amusing both mechanically and in terms of personality.  The game even has the different campaigns potentially play out differently on a replay, with some characters potentially not even fighting their final boss on the first run.I can't recommend Emerald Beyond to folks not already onboard with SaGa titles, but if you've played some of the other titles in the franchise and want something that feels more bite-sized instead of a 40+ hour campaign, EB is worth a look.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of my favorite turn-based battle systems ever. Manipulating the timeline by choosing abilities with different speeds, counter attacks, follow up attacks, and so on is as fun as ever, and the new combo system is a nice change up to Scarlet Grace's untied attacks. The different forms of character progression for humans, monsters, robots, ephemerals are a lot of fun to play with. I've played through Diva's story (took about 25 hours, though I was slow and thorough) and had a blast. It's goofy kitchen-sink B-movie science-fantasy, but it's a lot of fun if you enjoy that type of thing. I'm currently playing Ameya's story and enjoying it as well. Some of it reminds me of the old choose your own adventure books I read growing up -- you never know where a choice will lead, and it's fun to go back and try other choices. There's really a lot of variance in how things play out on each of the games various worlds. If you're looking for a traditional JRPG storyline, you may be a bit disappointed, though. Similarly, while I enjoy the pop up book presentation of the worlds and designs of the characters, the low budget definitely shows. While I love the combat system, it can punish mistakes harshly and requires a fair bit of thinking for every turn, which I can see being a turn off for some. My best advice is to play the demo and see if it interests you. There's a bit of learning barrier, and you have to be willing to go with the flow, so it may not click right away. Regardless, it's a bit early to say for sure, but Emerald Beyond is shaping up to be my favorite game in the franchise and maybe even earning a spot of my overall favorites list. There's a lot of things I could complain about, but, when it comes down to it, there's nothing else out there doing what Emerald Beyond does, and I think it's doing something special.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: While the game has a very simplistic visual presentation, the essence of what makes SaGa SaGa is very much there. If you know what to expect with the series and especially the the previous entry, I don't think you'll be disappointed. If you're a fan of SaGa, then this title is very easy to recommend IMO. The battle system and sound track are excellent. As for the story, so far it has kept my interest in a good way. If it can continue doing so, that only raises this title higher. Great game so far.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: A weird JRPG as most Saga games tend to be. The game is kinda a fusion of Saga2's (FFL2) world, story and races, and the Saga Scarlet Grace's great turn-based battle system. Clearly made with a small budget.Edit: Now that I have played Saga Frontier, I would add that that game also was clearly inspiration for this.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: I write this after having finished Diva no. 5's scenario. I think beating one character is enough to get a feel for what this game is all about.I'm a long-term SaGa fan, since I first played SaGa Frontier back on the Playstation One. It has remained one of my favorites. This detail is relevant because Emerald Beyond definitely brings back some elements from Frontier, such as the wacky Sci-fi/fantasy setting, different worlds, and the different races. Otherwise, the game is functionally quite similar to SaGa Scarlet Grace.This game, I would say, is one of the smoothest and most comfortable SaGa games that I've played. The menus, tutorials, and design are all made for a pretty enjoyable experience. However, there are the usual SaGa elements such as steep difficulty curves and having to figure out all the nuances of the battle system so that you can beat difficult encounters (how about that final boss of Diva's scenario, eh? No joke...)SaGa games can be quite difficult to get into, but if you've played Scarlet Grace, you should feel at home with this game. There are some changes they've made that put Emerald Beyond above Scarlet Grace, in my opinion. It has mainly to do with the setting, worlds, and focus on dialogue. Emerald Beyond has probably the most dialogue and characterization of any SaGa game, and I've found it very enjoyable. The stories are bite sized and also still have all the SaGa quirks, good and bad, but I have thoroughly enjoyed this new focus. The battle system has proven to be deep and nuanced, even if it has been streamlined a bit since Scarlet Grace, and some may not like the changes. But I love the higher focus on combos. Later on, you will be having combos on top of combos on top of interrupts on top of conditionals. It can get pretty crazy. Generally, the battle system they've created for Scarlet Grace and Emerald Beyond is one of the best turn-based battle systems ever created. The only issue is that the game is very combat focused, so after a while it's good to take a break and come back the next day or two. I definitely recommend people to try the game. SaGa is one of my favorite weird little obscure RPG series, and Emerald Beyond is definitely in true form for the series. It's also pretty accessible this time around, at least comparatively for the series. The game is, however, relatively low-budget, and this is pretty obvious. But they did a great job doing all they could to make the game true to the series while also being accessible for newcomers. This is just the nature of the series, as it is quite niche.I spent hundreds of hours replaying characters in SaGa Frontier, so I wonder how many hours I'm going to sink into this game, with all its multiple endings and branching paths. I'm also looking forward to chaining overdives beyond 2. That sounds kinda crazy.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve been a SaGa fan since playing the first Final Fantasy Legend game as a kid, before I even knew the series was called SaGa.  While it’s definitely different from previous entries, it’s a very fun game with challenging combat and an interesting approach to exploration.  The game doesn’t just benefit from playing multiple times, it requires it to see the full extent of the worlds and the story.  I’m still making my way through it but I’ve finished one run with every character so far and I’m really enjoying the subtle changes that are building from run to run.  Definitely worth a try for any SaGa fan, and for any RPG fan that’s looking for something different.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: A very fun take on the SaGa formula with a very rich and engaging combat system. The linearity and small worlds system is a little off putting for people more used with traditional JRPGs (or even with other SaGa games, such as Frontier), but it works quite well and reminds me of the Gameboy Color SaGa games. Lots of replay value as the worlds themselves change quite a lot across playthroughs (even with the same character) though!
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: So, while I acknowledge that this game has some flaws, I have to rate it pretty highly. SaGa Emerald Beyond is a highly ambitious and unique game, even by the standards of the SaGa series. This game is not your standard JRPG. The visuals aren't stellar, there's no real exploration, and the story is extremely non-linear. During your first couple of playthroughs, you might even wonder what the story even is. You're expected to play this game multiple times, if you only play it once on any character, you've barely experienced any of what the game has to offer. There are 17 different worlds to travel to, and on any given playthrough, afaik, you can only travel to 11 worlds. The thing is, these worlds have branching paths depending on several factors. You have the power of the emerald waves, which shows you lines leading to different places/events in the game. Due to this, exploration is virtually nonexistent, everything is a choice given by the emerald waves. You might think that this makes the game linear, but I think it just makes the game much more accessible without guides. It's a positive thing in my books.The events of the worlds can play out in different ways depending on the order of which you follow the emerald waves, but also depending on the past events of your previous playthroughs. If you've played the world on other characters first, it'll be different than if it was your first visit on any character, for the most part. If you played the world repeatedly on the same character, it will be different as well. The amount of replayability is very high, and the fact that the community still has not figured out many details about the game is testament to that.Perhaps the best part about this game is the battle system. It is mostly an improvement on Scarlet Grace's combat system in every aspect. The combo system, while I felt it was very RNG at first, is pretty reliable once you understand it. You try to link up your allies on the timeline, which will create a combo. Each attack will increase the combo rate by a certain amount, less if the enemy blocks, more if it is a critical attack (targets a weakness). If you get over 150% combo rate, you have an RNG chance to enter overdrive, and if you get over 200% the overdrive is guaranteed. When you enter overdrive, some or all of the party members that participated in the combo will attack again. The attacks in overdrive are somewhat random, sometimes the attacks will mess up the timeline which can cause unexpected results, like breaking your own combo or giving an enemy showstopper. Showstopper is when a character is isolated on the timeline by two spaces, and they use all their remaining BP(battle points)+1 to do attacks. When a boss gets a showstopper, your party can get absolutely decimated. However, when you use it, you're able to make clutch victories sometimes in the face of defeat. In general, compared to Scarlet Grace, it's far less punishing for characters to die and sometimes it can even be used strategically with showstoppers, since the timeline is less populated making it easier for characters to be isolated. The game is pretty challenging overall, but generally not to an unfair degree because of battle rank system. Basically, encounter difficulty is scaled to how you approach the fights and how many fights you do. Also perhaps by how strong you are relative to the encounter. If you're breezing through the fights, the game will get harder, and if you're struggling the game will still get harder but not as much. I think the game handles it pretty well, and the endgame fights are extremely challenging and will probably take multiple runs using the same characters to get strong enough for.One of the main negatives I'd like to highlight about this game is the slow menuing. Specifically trading and battle challenges between fights is pretty annoying to do between battles, though you can trade sparingly and set the battle challenges to auto order, it's not really optimal. However it is more convenient so I'd recommend it. The way the menu is set up for looking at your equipment and upgrading it is pretty inconvenient as well.Overall I'd recommend this game if you're looking for a game you're willing to sink your teeth into. I briefly went into the combat system, but I just scratched the surface and there's even more to it like formations, weapon properties, learning spells, glimmering etc. It's pretty rewarding learning it, and the story isn't too bad if you give it a chance to unfold.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: I could literally write a thesis on why this game is great. But the tl;dr is that it takes the genius of Scarlet Saga Graces in terms of providing a strategically complex, yet fair, battle system, and removes or tones down almost every aspect of Scarlet Saga Graces which was needlessly frustrating. If you want a game where almost every battle is very strategic, this game is it right here. I do feel that the stories in this game are very uneven though. For the best experience, I strongly recommend playing Siugnas. You can tell there was much more effort put into his story than some others, like Bonnie and Formina.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: About as weird as SaGa gets and full of complex and deep combat mechanics, I think the short individual stories combined with the branching paths give this one a lot of potential replayability. I'm not the biggest fan of the visual novel look and the pop up storybook style it's inherited from Scarlet Grace but overall I think it's a better game and Scarlet Grace is a pretty good game. Worth a look if you're interested in getting in to SaGa, though you might want to look at the Romancing SaGa games or Frontier if you want something a bit more traditional (at least on the surface).
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: A blend of design decisions from SaGa Frontier and from Scarlet Grace. TLDR: Buy it if you are a fan of Frontier and/or Scarlet Grace or if you are just craving for an extremely engaging and challenging turn based combat system.This is the crunchy game mechanics JRPG. The visuals are not going to please everyone and the overworld is very similar to what Scarlet Graces did, but with a twist.From Frontier:+Many worlds (17 in total) with their own look, characters and plots.+Characters come from different species, in this case Human, Vampire, Thrall, Mech, Ephemeral, Kugutsu (Puppet) and Monsters. Each species has its own unique features.+Techs can combo into a powerful group attack.From Scarlet Graces+Overall aesthetics, with a visual novel style of vignettes for dialogue and story progression and moving around the map to interact with encounters which could be either puzzles, dialogue choices or combat.+UI with tooltips and structure of encounters from Easy, Normal, Hard and Brutal.+Formations, character menu and party wide BP. Scarlet Grace has the best turn based combat in any JRPG I have ever played and Emerald Beyond refines that and adds some more layers on top of that excellent combat system.New features from Emerald Beyond+Combat now has layers as not only you need to take a look at the damage types, resistances, conditionals, interrupts but now also chain attacks, pursuits, combos, showstoppers and overdrives. +Weapons now have subgroups. For example, the "one handed melee" includes broadswords, fleurets, knives and axes. Some techs can be used by all weapons within that group but some are exclusive to their specific subgroup, meaning, some techs can only be used by fleurets, for example.+Replay value galore! with 17 worlds and 5 main scenarios with their own unique characters, the many species with their unique features, and the worlds themselves having the same multiple outcomes depending on the choices made like Scarlet Graces, even replaying the same scenario can lead to a different playthrough. For example, I played through Ameya's scenario twice and I've gotten to visit different worlds and meet different characters, but, when I got to one of the worlds that I already had visited with Ameya, but this time I went with Diva No.5, the storyline for that world went in a different direction, even being able to recruit a different character than I did with Ameya.It is still unknown how that system works but we know so far that at some point you can eventually unlock a door that leads to a choice of any of the other worlds. Whereas on a normal playthrough you would have a choice of a few worlds that are designated at random, so your first and even your second time going through each scenario, you may not even get to see all the worlds. It looks like the devs really focused on replay value and a more "roguelite" style of SaGa game, where you are meant to pick a scenario main character and run through a handful of worlds and then import your save to play again with that same main character or pick another one.The game has a lot of heart and you can tell there was a lot of passion put into this project. SaGa games have always been a niche and I hope this isn't our last main SaGa series entry but if this is the swan song for the series, then Kawazu made sure it went out with a bang. Buy this is you are a SaGa: Scarlet Graces fan, this game follows a lot of the same winning formulas from that game. Buy this if you liked Frontier's worlds and different species as this game draws inspiration from those systems. Buy this if you are a turn based JRPG fan that wants a combat system that is deep, robust, engaging and challenging. Buy this if you are a JRPG fan that wants to try something new. I strongly recommend this game,
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: I don't understand how this is supposed to be a SaGa game. This isn't a turn-based JRPG, it's a poorly written visual novel with combat as an afterthought. It's hard not to compare this with older games in the SaGa franchise, which had interesting story elements, a strong battle system, and thoughtful world building. Instead I'm beginning the game with a fetch quest to find cats that raise my stats. Huh? The world is an ugly mash of 2D spritework and copy pasted "buildings", with about as much space to explore as my kitchen pantry. Is this the same franchise that brought Romancing SaGa 3? And SaGa Frontier 1 & 2?Plus this game doesn't even have stasisdrive, or a giant ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ battle roulette wheel, that's an automatic 1/10.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: Try this game if you played SaGa Scarlet Grace Ambitions and liked it. It uses the same battle system as that entry along with some new ones that make it a new take on the battle style of the previous game. It is an enriching experience if you take your time and enjoy the worlds as well as build up your parties.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: SaGa: Scarlet Grace was an experiment in rethinking what an RPG could be by cutting away elements to create something that felt entirely new.SaGa: Emerald Beyond keeps that foundation, but it adds complexity and variety in a way that's uniquely SaGa. It offers more types of party members, an even more complex battle system, and more diversity of scenarios by offering many small and strange worlds instead of one large world map. Both approaches have their merits, and I'm not sure which one I'll prefer in the end. But I'm glad Kawazu and the SaGa team are still taking big risks. It's not for everyone, but it's definitely for me.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: For fans of the series there is a lot that is familiar, but like always there are plenty of new approaches.  Each protagonist scenario is full of decisions, and will change on repeat play throughs.  You can burn through most in around 10ish hours, or you can take 30+ exploring each nook and cranny.  There are 6 protagonists, with 2 as a duo that each have their unique reason for adventure.Combat is strategic, and a refined version of Scarlet Grace.  Some fights get pretty rough, but you usually have the tools to win with a little luck or change of strategy.I've have had such an excellent time playing this game, I suggest the demo if you are uncertain.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: This is a pretty cheap feeling and looking game with frankly some of the worst click economy I've seen in its UI in any RPG I've played in like the past decade. The base combat system is actually pretty fun imo but I'm not incredibly big on the way Interrupts/Quells work because it basically turns combat into a guessing game every time ??? shows up on the timeline. It took me a while to even understand the ins and outs of this mechanic owing to SaGa's characteristic but not really appreciated poor tutorializing and even when I did get it, I still don't like it? I just think it's bad for tempo which is already pretty sluggish.So that's kind of a strikeout on most fronts of an RPG there. The visuals don't wow me (since this game had to be made to accommodate smartphones, which is a devil's bargain), the combat system has a spark of fun but has quirks I just don't enjoy. This would only leave the story which is kind of hurt by the game's visible lack of budget so nothing can really stand out, there's a ton of repeated dialogue/character portraits stringing things along from beat to beat.sorry SaGa sickos, this isn't the one that's going to convince the masses. It has convinced me I might like one of the games in this franchise that had more budget than three pennies and a ham sandwich, though?
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah, it's a pretty good SaGa game. Probably the best one ever made. They found a good formula with Scarlet Grace and expanded on it. Started from the demo and there is lots of combat, although in the first world a lot of it is optional. The graphics are not that bad and are better than Scarlet Grace probably, although that is not saying much. I don't know if newcomers to the series can enjoy it. They should probably start with an earlier SaGa game (like Frontiers) that had random encounters. But I suppose the advice would be not to worry too much about things and just choose attacks based on what you like. Surprisingly, after the fifth battle you'll start getting the hang of the complicated but satisfying battle system, and there will still be new things to pick up even after a very long time.The story is ridiculous and quirky. I couldn't believe it when playing the demo, but somehow they managed to pull it off and made me laugh at the ridiculous situations, but also made it compelling and make me want to explore more or regret options that I didn't take. All in a few sentences. "There are some researchers that have been gone for a long time and we need you to check up on them. Oh forgot to mention that there are some cursed tomes down there and because they are researchers and couldn't help themselves they read them. They are all probably cursed. Well, good luck!" Genius writing (because it somehow feels natural in this crazy world)! It was hard to pick this option over the quantum cats quest though. I'm sure you've seen the other reviews. But the bottom line is that it is probably the best SaGa game. New players to the genre will probably hate it, but will start liking it after around the five hour mark, and become fans by the end. Typical. The caveat is that I only played this particular one for five hours so far (with the demo included).
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a game of RPG exploration so much as a string of combats, and the combat is... good, but not great, and not enough to make wanting to continue playing it worthwhile.SaGa Frontier Remastered, the SaGa collection, and The Secret of Varonis are right over there and definitely better purchases than this.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: Before I get to the review, this title should  be priced at $50.  $30 would be appropriate, $40 would be a stretch, but at $50 the game simply doesn't have enough to it for that price tag to be reasonable.  With that for context, the game is a significant improvement for the series - a lot of the more questionable design decisions will make a ton of sense if you're familiar with Unlimited SaGa, the game that until now I thought would be the death of the franchise. This game is built just about entirely on its combat system - and that combat system (along with a couple of other improvements to deal with long-standing series issues) really does carry the experience.  Not to a $50 price tag, unfortunately, but it comes close enough to be worth waiting for a sale.Story: This is a SaGa title - like most of the games before it, EB has story that can best be described as 'minimal'.  Plots are more or less confined to single individual Worlds (basically the Regions from Frontier but with extradimensional travel instead of boats), and at least three of the five protagonists are world-hopping in search of their own specific maguffins.  Most sections are therefore designed to work identically regardless of who you pick, with at most interstitial scenes at the start and end.  In terms of actual storytelling things are very, very light - just a bit ahead of Romancing SaGa 3, but thinner than the first Octopath Traveler.However, unlike Octopath Traveler things move at a fairly brisk clip, and the game can (and often is) quite charming in how downright odd things can get.  Presentation: This is a _very_ mixed bag.  Positives: -Solid character designs, decently modeled.-Soundtrack ranges from 'good' to 'absolutely wonderful'.-The overworlds have a low-fi pop-up book quality to them that feels intentional enough to be charming.-English and Japanese voiceacting.Cons: -All story events are presented in the style of a Visual Novel.  This is a hold-over from Unlimited SaGa, and if these segments had good art it would honestly work well enough.  Unfortunately, everyone looks like the character models were screencapped, and then that image was run through a Photoshop filter.  Everyone has a weird, dead-eyed quality to them - it works really well for Diva but everyone else is right in the uncanny valley with her.-Voice acting is used quite sparingly, and the Japanese voice acting is only really a positive because the English VAs are exactly what you'd expect.Mechanics:The combat system is essentially a beefier Unlimited SaGa's, but with the god-awful Reels removed and things like Interrupts and Follow-Ups to take their place.  Each round of combat involves carefully planning out a series of actions based on a time line - link characters together to create combos, use counter-attacks and follow-ups to keep enemies from doing the same to you, and use guns to stop enemies from using their own counter-attacks and follow-ups.All of your characters pull AP from a single pool - this pool starts at a smaller value but increases either with each round or via other actions, all based on one of several formations your party is in.  Formations can also be used to reduce skill costs, usually based on actions taken in the previous turn.This whole thing results in an incredibly complex puzzle-box of a combat system, where fights tend to take a good amount of time, but are also challenging and satisfying (and they don't generally get ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hard unless there's an easier alternative to take).Outside of combat, decisions have been made to streamline things:-There are no maps besides the 17 regions and the Interdimensional oubliette that links them. -Combat encounters are opt-in, often repeatable, and will tell you what monsters will appear provided you've seen them before.  They also come with a 'difficulty' that lets you know how rough things will be.-The game lays out where all events on the map are, complete with pointers to them and colors to show what type of event they are.-Stores and money do not exist; all equipment is either dropped or traded for, and then upgraded using the game's fairly simple crafting system.While some people are likely to find the way events are handled to be a bit too hand-hold-y, personally I think this is far better than previous entries' 'have a guide open or have no clue what you're doing' approach.  The end result of all of this is a game that feels like its primary reason for existing is as a battle system, secondary systems designed purely to support it, and then a loose context that was cobbled together to be draped over it.  The result  a lot of fun, but that low-budget quality set against the $50 price tag probably has a lot to do with the mediocre reception.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: I'll give a concise review.  If you've ever played a SaGa game before (Romancing Saga, Minstrel Song, SaGa Frontier, Scarlet Grace, etc.), then just ask yourself if you liked any of those games, and you'll probably like this game about as much.  If you hated any of those games, particularly Scarlet Grace, then you probably won't like this game.  That's okay.  You don't need to force yourself to play it if you don't like it, even if the diehard SaGa fans are telling you something is wrong with you.  It's a game series that people tend to either love or hate.  If you're unsure if the SaGa series is for you, then I would sum it up as, if you're a JRPG veteran and like JRPGs but find that the traditional gameplay mechanics of the genre start to get stale, then this is the series for you.  Everything is innovative, often to the point of being overly cryptic, and fans will tell you that's the schtick.  It has a special indie charm despite coming from Square Enix themselves.  If you're wondering if Emerald Beyond is a good series entry point- yep, it's a great place to start.  I'm not going to tell you that you need to play the other games in the series first and in which order to do that.  This is a review for this game.  If you want reviews for the other games, then go read those reviews.  I'm updating this review after having beaten the game with three of the five protagonists.  In the first playthrough, the story is ridiculous, borderline "so bad it's good."  It isn't until you replay the game that you start to realize how brilliant the story is.  The story isn't great because it's some sweeping timeless epic, it's great because of the sheer volume of variations you can get in each subworld that makes it a treat to see what changes you'll notice each time you replay a world or replay a protagonist.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: A SaGa game for SaGa fans. The short worlds accommodate quick pick-up-and-play style if you're into that. The worlds and characters are charming, though character acquisition is a bit hard on your first few playthroughs. The soundtrack is amazing as usual, and the battle system is in my opinion the best in the series, it's very addictive.The game is meant to be replayed as doing so unlocks more scenarios for each protagonist and for each world, which leads to different outcomes. The worlds you get each playthrough are somewhat picked at random, so you get a different experience each time. Each protagonist (except Bonnie & Formina) has a unique mechanic to them, so even if you're visiting variations of the same worlds, you get something different. The scenario length also varies by character.I want to emphasize the fact that this game is meant to replayed, if you're looking for something to play once, this game might not be for you. Though having said that, a few of the scenarios are 20~ hours long if you take your time with them. If you're curious, you can try the demo which lets you see a few worlds, and you can carry that save over for the main game.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: This is the single best turn-based battle system ever put in an RPG, combined with a wholly new gameplay and campaign structure that expands and evolves over the course of 10+ playthroughs.  The plot and world change in fascinating ways, and each protagonist interacts with NG+ in their own interesting and unique ways.There's a load of UI issues unfortunately and a few irritating bugs, as well as an overall game speed that is a bit slower than Scarlet Grace's unlockable Fast mode.  It needs a patch. Cheat Engine with the Speed Hack option solves a lot of this, but I don't know how to review a modded game like this.  EDIT: Some of the UI issues have been addressed in multiple patches, but there's still room for a few more critical changes.   The UI is enough of a barrier that the game is not getting recognized as the absolute masterpiece that it is.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: It's not like the old saga system, no wp/jp. It's got the scarlet grace system of attacks. The overworld is cheaply done but I have a feeling it's due to how expansive the world is, as I'm starting to see even repeat plays of protagonists change a bit. The story isn't terrible by any means though some protags may be worse than others. I may update later because I intend to play them all at least twice over. They put a ton of effort into the combat system; difficulty is clearly optional. Doing brutal fights right off the first world felt a bit hopeless but I think that depends entirely on how you explore to maximize your encounters before doing a first world brutal encounter.. like Tsunanori can get in about 5 fights before you choose to fight a giant flying squirrel that will make you hate life. The fight felt like I just needed to screw around with things a bit to get a handle of the boss but I guess that will be for another run. Every brutal fight 2nd world onwards has been manageable and you can get some grinding time in to make them easier if you really want to put the effort in.Despite the lack of effort in graphics for overworld and dialogue I still appreciate everything about the game.. then again I'm the one idiot who loves Unlimited Saga so there's that. I think that's probably the one big negative for a lot of people as it seems like they get lazier with every new release since the ps2 era.Edit: This game is indeed 100% all about combat. The story's alright for a once over but the game is quick enough that you can beat a protagonist in under 4hrs and start transferring stuff over for a more prepared run.If you're new to saga I'd strongly recommend you follow the recommendation from the game (Green Icons) for your 1st-2nd run while starting a new game and bringing over your previous run gear (Don't carry over your battle rank in new protagonist runs; this WILL make the run insanely hard) then start exploring outside of the hand holding path. This will ensure you aren't severely underpowered going into new runs and in repeat protagonist runs that you'll have some useful skills to work with.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: SaGa Emerald Beyond, offers players the choice of six protagonists, each with a unique storyline, set across multiple worlds.Pros:- Diverse Protagonists and Storylines: Players can experience six distinct narratives, each offering a unique perspective and enhancing replayability. - Strategic Combat System: The game features a deep and engaging combat system that rewards strategic planning and adaptability. - Rich World-Building: The multiple interconnected worlds provide a vast and immersive setting for exploration and adventure. Cons:- Steep Learning Curve: Newcomers to the series may find the game's mechanics complex and challenging to master. - Inconsistent Visuals: Certain graphical elements appear outdated compared to modern standards. - Pacing Issues: The narrative pacing can be uneven, with some storylines progressing slower than others. In conclusion, "SaGa Emerald Beyond" offers a rich and varied experience for fans of the series and newcomers alike, despite some areas that could benefit from refinement.Score: 7 out of 10 glimmers—A shining addition to the SaGa universe.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game so much. I had to delete a 20+ hour save because the route I chose (Diva) is nearly impossible for a new player to do without careful planning throughout the route or doing it on NG+. The communication of key mechanics is nonexistent. Random encounters have gains so minimal they're barely worth doing, and then they raise the difficulty of bosses with each one you do. The difficulty curve is a chaotic mess of peaks and valleys with no rhyme nor reason. To get the best ending of some routes requires careful precision along unsignposted flags to land just right. Until you're on NG+, you'll get about one round of equipment upgrades for the entire route. Things meaningfully change on every run of every route along with whether you've done other routes. I cannot recommend this game to anyone.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: Most of the negative reviews and refunds could have been avoided by trying the demo for 30 minutes to an hour. I dinnae wot they think they're doing just jumping right in there without doing any research, love. Would say this has been a real treat as a more gameplay and mechanics driven SaGa fan. Though you visit the Steam forums here before April 25 and see a common trend in players that absolutely did not like the demo(s) to downright horrified, disgusted, and even insulted. If by the end or during the demo, you aren't entertaining the possibilities of your team, formation, gear, roles, and what to learn next and how the outcome of a given world could have been - you'll have saved yourself the purchase, the additional time, and the emotional damage.Some things that I've enjoyed about the game:1. The voice acting (English and Japanese both) and ability to change the text language in-game without any external hurdles2. The combat depth3. The facets to develop your party4. The music5. The overall amount of transparency6. The potential for replayability even for the same character7. Ability to have short play sessions and still make sizeable progress8. Nods / homage to the series that warms my heart as a long-time SaGa fan9. Feels like a blend of SaGa Scarlet Grace, Final Fantasy Legends II / SaGa 2, and SaGa Frontier 1 in ways.10. I find that I don't mind the more contained world exploration though this can easily be a con for players looking to get lost and find more tangible secrets and random battles11. Built-in controller support (at least on PC), support for mouse and keyboard, and if you realllly had to, touch screen (tablet computer)Things I don't like:1. Occasional gaps in story logic, though not as big as most of the earlier SaGa games2. The still 3D models for storytelling given how well playable characters can animate in battle by comparison3. Potential large gaps in voice acting when you're on a role in the intro breakfast, then it's text and sometimes you forget what the VA sounds like or haven't heard one yet to imagine the dialogue4. The price - but I also rationalize that I got 200+ hours out of SaGa Scarlet Grace and this builds on most of the things I liked about that game, so I can't go wrong - but you aren't me and you absolutely can still go wrong.5. Lack of Playstation or Switch glyphs on PC, Xbox only (which is less an issue for me, but hurts when I'm recommending the game)I digress, Very fulfilling to me so far. Would probably have bought sooner instead of delaying the purchase several days after launch.

_childDocuments_.review: So look, I get it. SaGa Emerald Beyond can't stand toe-to-toe with more beautiful games like Dwarf Fortress or Minecraft. That's okay. Sometimes we have to accept that games aren't aesthetically pleasing. Not every game can look as good as Monaco or Caves of Qud. But hey, a game is not a Grateful Dead poster, you know? We're meant to enjoy playing it rather than enjoy staring at it for six straight hours while tripping on acid with our neighbor Sean, listening to "Friend of the Devil" on loop, wondering how we got here and what life is truly about. So yeah, Emerald is a little ugly.But heck, bud, SaGa games have always been a little ugly.And sure, I know it can be upsetting when a game flubs the localization. Why is my cartoonishly stereotypical cowgirl character speaking with a cartoonishly stereotypical cowgirl accent instead of like an authentic high-pitched waifu straight out of Osaka? Or worse. How come my bean-shaped murderbot is speaking with a melodic Scottish accent instead of like a nice, homely high-pitched waifu from Hokkaido? And heck, don't get me started on Mido! No one talks like that, bud!But seriously, long-time fans might have a bit of trouble getting into this one. Long gone are memorable characters from previous SaGa games, like the Slime from SaGa Frontier who joins up with you inside the innards of a giant monster. Instead we have lame characters, like Byaku, a slime who joins up with you inside the innards of a giant monster... but talks! Heck!This game has flaws, for sure. Some of them are intentional designs, some not so much (I'm looking at you, sluggish menu). But there is something magical and charming in SaGa.I think when I approached Emerald Beyond, my hope was that we'd be getting Scarlet Grace again, but this time with all the aesthetic bells and whistles you'd expect from one of the twelve Final Fantasy Sevens. Instead, we got... another SaGa. But new. It has the beating heart of a SaGa, the blood of an established JRPG franchise, the soul of invention, and the budget of Stardew Valley.And you know what? This game is fun as all heck (excuse my language).Many of the SaGa games have toyed with ideas of needing subsequent playthroughs to experience everything, but Emerald Beyond takes it into a new direction. Story content, alternate paths, and optional characters are unavailable unless you do NG+ runs. It's like a long-form roguelike, in a way, but you actually learn more about the game the more you do it. Plus, there are so many things to explore just in the battle system—something I can rarely say about a good mainline JRPG. What's fascinating is that this mechanic of repetition is not projected by the plot. You aren't Groundhog-Day-ed into the past, you aren't warned that "next time it'll be different-er".The game trusts that you'll have the curiosity to do it all again, and then rewards you for doing so.Well, heck. This may not be for everyone, but it's for me.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing SaGa games for 30 years, starting with FFL1 / SaGa1 on the brick gameboy.This is my favorite one. I like the sci-fantasy SaGas the best, and I never expected to get such a lovely SaGa in that genre in 2024.I'll write more when I'm done, but one thing before I go: I really didn't like Scarlet Grace, but I love this. If you disliked that game and are concerned about this one for that reason, you might be pleasantly surprised.If you are unfamiliar with the SaGa series and looking for something that feels more like a traditional jrpg with serious writing, you will probably be confused by this game. However, as long as you like the combat aspect of JRPGs, I think you'll find something to entertain you here: the battle system is incredibly fun.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: Pared down to its core, Emerald Beyond is a bunch of wildly unbalanced and swingy combat encounters strung together in a dull, repetitive, and grindy loop. The story is negligible, the crafting system is clunky and overly reliant on RNG to get materials for, and let's not even talk about the environment design or the art. As along time SaGa series fan, this was a disappointment through and through. Can't imagine how this would feel as an entry point to the series for new players.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely incomprehensible, unplayable mishmosh.If you managed to play more than an hour of this, you really must have TRIED to like this. A classic example of style over substance, SE once more proves that they have long since ceased to make games and are just interested in coasting on the reputation their IP's have rather than on actually having people enjoy their products.I must've been spoiled by the great games we got in 2023, because this just let me down. The last time a SaGa game disappointed me THIS much was Unlimited SaGa, and now US has a contender for the absolute worst. Square: Don't give me a wall of text and expect me to just pick up and run with a game. The GOOD games show, they don't tell. BG3 is incredibly complex and all it takes is going through the Nautiloid "tutorial" to figure out how to play it.Dont give me static, cardboard characters with text, show me some scenery, don't just thrust me in front of a character and expect me to like them just because they look a certain way, character design alone cannot make a good game, you need to make me interested in your worlds and lately, you guys have been halfassing it. You're Square Enix! In the 90's, I would've paid anything to try out what you had in store! Nowadays, you guys have lost that magic you once had. This is far from being worth 50 bucks. Try harder.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who's only played Romancing Saga Minstrel Song Remaster, and having only played about an hour, I'm obviously not fully qualified to speak on the qualities of this game, but man it just put me off that hard. The game looks like it's straight from the PS3 in some of the worst ways possible. It looks like the modelers did a good job but then someone threw weird compression and filters on every texture so it all looks muddy and annoying. The menus instantly give away that this is a game you can play on your phone, and that is a bad thing when I'm playing on a 2K monitor. The menus feel like they go all over the screen. The combat and general gameplay loop might be fine, but the opening presentation is so bad, and the story is already kinda meh, on top of there being basically no exploration for the first hour (started as Mido, maybe that's why), that I just can't be bothered for 50 dollars when Sand Land is right there. I still have a lot of playtime left in Romancing, let alone Frontier, I think I'm good. I see no reason to play this over those games, unless you just really really really like how loud and bright everyone dresses and you're fine with mobile game UIs.

_childDocuments_.review: This game bring really the fun in the NG+. Why the heck can´t every game do the same with NG+ liuke SaGa does. If you finish your first play round and go into NG+ you will find new Stories, new Items, new Friends.The Battle Function is for a firstime a litrtle bit confusing, but becomes later a big COMBO WOMBO spectacle, where your Characters bring epic Combos into Battle.Also the whole steal Monster Abilites is also fun. The story come with every run closer too the Mainpoint, means you need NG+ too understand why did the villian do this and what is more behinde it.Imagine you would play Dark Souls and NG+ gives you more Story, new Bosses, new Weapons.

_childDocuments_.review: Summary: SaGa Emerald Beyond is a quirky RPG with a deep combat and an emphasis on replayibility weirdly seen in the genre. And it is one of the best games of the year.I orginally started playing SaGa Scarlet Grace a few years ago and I didn't get into it. I did not grasp the system, the story was functional and simple, but it was one of those games that I wanted to like and give a chance.Then, before release of Emerald Beyond (on Switch, mind you) and at first I did not get into the game... 2 hours later I got hooked in and ended up loving the battle system, the diversity of the cast, how every "race" has its own mechanics regarding combat and growth... How the narrative is relatively to the point and does not takes too seriously. It clicked to me and I enjoyed it as if I were playing a quirky PS2 / GBA game. And the duration of arout could be up to 10 hours, and in a world of long games, this feels like a blessing.Nonetheless I think is a title you should give a chance, but take into account a few things:* I recommend to Start with Tsunanori. It has a simple and short campaign and quite to the point. I played it, I think I got a premature ending but... so what? It is part of the journey, and this game has a lot of emphasis in replayability* If you fail a combat... Wait and think about what happened. Jot it down, converse online, change formation, your retinue and even equipment and try again, no battle is impossible.* If you are on the fence... Try the demo, for real, if you like it, you will enjoy the game (though it can be hard post demo)It is a weird game, the kind of weird game that after a few years you think about and remember the struggle and the funny bits.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: I took down my negative review because it wasn't quite how I truly felt about it, but the more I play it, the more I enjoy it. I still wish I hadn't preordered bc it was very expensive for me, but I highly recommend. The combat is the meat of this game and it is excellent. I guess Romancing SaGa 2 remake got all the budget, but it doesn't diminish how good this game is. I think people won't appreciate this game for years to come with hindsight. I've certainly played worse games before.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun SaGa game.It was a little easy compared to most of the others, but still impossibly enraging sometimes.The variation in how the stories of each world play out really eats away at your mind, wondering why things were different this time, if you influenced that with your choices, and how much different they can be on subsequent playthroughs.I don't know why, but I enjoy the leveling system of the SaGa series more than traditional JRPG experience points.I had to abandon a 20-hour playthrough because I couldn't beat the final boss. But it was because I didn't understand the combat system well enough. After completing more protagonist stories, I understood it much better and was able to beat the final bosses. Not with ease, not on the first try, but with proper strategizing and a little luck.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Emerald Beyond

name: Classified: France '44
detailed_description: Classified: France '44 Editions Classified: France '44 Overlord Edition The Overlord Edition of Classified: France '44 contains: Classified: France '44 Classified: France '44 - Season Pass The Season Pass Includes: All content to be released in 2024. DLC 1 - Guerrilla Pack (Out Now) DLC 2 - Agent Pack (Out Now) DLC 3 - Talon Pack (Out Now) DLC 4 - Devils Pack (to be released) Each DLC contains: Two new Special Ops missions Two new weapons or weapon variants One new clothing set Classified: France '44 Deluxe Edition The Deluxe Edition of Classified: France '44 contains: Classified: France '44 Base Game Guerrilla Pack Expand your arsenal and take the fight to the enemy with new Spec Ops missions and a brand new map in the Guerrilla Pack The Guerrilla Pack contains: New Map – “Church” Two new Special Ops missions: • Tomb Raiders • Time to Kill Two new weapon variants • Bren “Ambush” • Thompson “Boa” New Clothing Set • Female Resistance “Guerrilla” About the Game Classified: France ‘44 is a new turn-based strategy game, set in World War II during the desperate months leading up to the Allied invasion of France in June 1944. Take charge of a special-ops team of Allied commandos and French resistance fighters. Recruit elite operatives to build your squad, then engage in a sweeping campaign of sabotage and destruction. Deal with competing factions to build the resistance network and strike at German targets deep in occupied territory. However, the more chaos you cause, the more you’ll draw the merciless attention of the Gestapo secret police. In exciting missions inspired by the exploits of the Allies and French, the game expands on turn-based tactical concepts, bringing authentic World War 2 combat to life. The campaign allows for multiple playthroughs that are different each time. For those who really want to test their skills, our rich Mission Creator tool allows players to create, share and download custom missions. Every Shot Counts. In Classified: France ‘44’s unique morale system, every shot taken affects you or your enemies. Suppress and break your opposition, giving you a brief window to flank your cowering targets and finish them off. Shape the Battle. Use stealth tactics to eliminate key targets and start the fight on your terms. However, the more kills you make, the more enemies will begin to suspect that something's wrong, so be ready to unleash your ambush before they sniff you out! Build your Team. An authentic and characterful mix of heroes will be yours to choose from, each with their own story to tell. Train, customise and equip them with your growing arsenal of skills and weapons. Raise the morale of your team by spending time around the campfire, and learning about their lives as they fight across the war-ravaged fields of occupied France. Experience History. Complete challenging objectives in over 45 missions supplied to your team by the French forces. Choose which missions suit your strategy to grow the resistance and support your ultimate goals. Manage your team by sending them on strategic operations. Built to Last. Updates and expansions will grow the world of Classified: France ‘44, bringing new and exciting elements to your freedom fight. Our Classified Mission Creator and the modding tools ensure there will always be player-created content to explore. On to Victory. Classified: France ‘44 is full of challenge. Work out the optimum grand strategy while deploying the best tactical play and discover the game's multiple endings. What will your D-Day look like?

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, this game is.. it's okay. I just finished one playthrough on normal-difficulty ironman. It took me 21 hours, I now have 60% of the achievements, and I won a major campaign victory (but not quite the greatest possible victory, I wonder what that looks like?). Everyone talks about how it's XCOM in WWII but let's ignore all that and talk about how it's  XCOM.First, XCOM2 (like Rimworld) has good random generation figured out and leads you to fill in gaps with your own storytelling. Somewhere along the line I realized this game is very handcrafted in comparison, with focus on replayability. (I don't plan on replaying it myself, but I still appreciate that!) There are 12 named, written, voiced, and modeled/drawn soldiers, of which you can recruit 8 per campaign and deploy 4 per mission. The missions themselves must all be designed by people, not generated, and therefore finite - a few felt very deliberate and I found myself recognizing more and more of the locations shown in loading screens.Soldiers cannot die. If you let them hit 0 HP, you're punished with reduced max HP, and if you let the horror of combat turn them into a frozen huddled mass, they'll break down under pressure more quickly next time. This sort of has this unfortunate side effect where, if a soldier is innately weaker mentally or physically, that's the side of them most likely to give, deepening that same flaw/counter in future missions, snowballing into more injuries or mental breaks... I can't tell if that's intentional game design? These permanent character debuffs stack up and can be fixed by taking a slap on the wrist in the management side of the game (some resources spent and two missions out to heal).The fact I played on ironman at all is a testament to the stability of the game - that beats out XCOM for sure. This thing just came out! No crashes!! Very rarely did I feel cheated by the game: indicators worked nearly flawlessly, and a couple times I was warned and given a chance to abort before breaking stealth (like if I clicked on a space that looked clear, but spotted someone watching that area on the walk over). The only time I felt dumb and wanted to reload because of BS or unclear indicators was because it looks like you can hide behind adjacent bushes, like low cover, but you cannot, you must hide inside. They just look over the bush and start shooting.I like the system of movement and actions, it's unique, just be prepared to do a lot of quick 1-16 arithmetic. In D&D and Fire Emblem, you get to move some as part of your turn, it's free. In XCOM you have to spend one of your two actions to move at all, which always feels bad if you just need to shuffle a little to the side. In this game (F44? Is there an acronym?), everyone can move 12+/-a few spaces, an inch at a time if you want, in any order to swap places easily if you want. Doing other things like reloading, opening doors, or healing friends costs some of that movement. Be sure to save enough to shoot or overwatch, otherwise you feel stupid. There isn't an indicator of when you'll accidentally walk too far to shoot.D&D progression is very horizontal - tiny stat bumps are hard to get but new abilities flow freely. Fire Emblem and RuneScape progression is very vertical - you get the next level or tier of thing and some numbers go up but fundamentals don't change. XCOM has mostly horizontal progression with soldier abilities, but vertical progression with weapons and armor, just in distinctively big chunks - getting laser weapons early isn't an incremental upgrade, that's a pretty big deal! This game feels very incrementally vertical. There are lots of cool abilities in a large tree with 4 different capstones to pursue per class, but that tree is packed with more generic stat-boosting upgrades. 2 max health, 1 damage reduction, 1 more damage with this weapon. Meanwhile, enemies start stacking up armor too, much more than my own guys by the end. The end result was.. mostly, fighting each type of enemy felt about the same throughout the whole game. Was it expertly balanced? Was it tracking my strength and scaling up to match? In both cases, why is this better than just keeping numbers the same? An arms race to the top to reward good management, maybe, but the curve seemed both not harsh and yet impossible to get ahead of.Part of those incremental upgrades come with gear, which uses the lootbox/battle royale color-tier-scheme of rarity and goodness that's become a thing the past several years. It's weird to see here, but I think it helps with keeping so many little numbers digestible at a glance. You find and buy bits soldiers can equip based on nationality and gender, all with minor stat increases that all add up to so eloquently have no net effect after enemies get more buffs, unless some poor soul's still got an early-game gun that can hardly hit through armor now.The music is not enough. I had to mute it eventually and put my own on. It's fine, it fits, I don't think I could hum a single song from it right now, and there needed to be way more variety.The characters are interesting. There's, like, random Fire-Emblem-style support conversations? One happens between a seemingly-random pair of camp members in-between each mission. Keeps characters from becoming too one-note by hearing some banter and learning some random and irrelevant things about their likes, hopes, and fears.Finally, that led me to my last question, which I still have: are these real people? At some point I started googling, "Tom King WW2," seemingly nothing. Some Americans, a book published in 2017. I figured they're just historical fiction characters and pushed it out of mind until I beat the game and it gave me Fire-Emblem-style epilogue cards at the end, including each character's ultimate fate and year of death. They were all weirdly specific: some died in war in like the 50s, some lived til the late 2000s. Are these characterizations and voices an homage to specific people? Was Willard really involved in operation market garden? I would like to know, so, if you do, um, tell me. It's a weird way to be immortalized, to have words and sass put in your mouth, but so many died to have all forgotten besides their name... I think I would like it, at least. But they're probably just characters.Thanks for reading, this took like an hour to write, and for what? If you made it this far, I guess for you. Yeah, you. Have a nice one now.

_childDocuments_.review: Played 2 campaigns, done every achievement except the hard difficulty campaign, and it was actually the second campaign that turned this from a positive experience to a negative experience. If i could, i would leave a "neutral" review because the first play through was OK, but frustrating.First up, the pro's. The turn based combat works fine, the stealth system is solid for the most part, and the morale system is possible revolutionary? I can't think of any other games that has such a good and concise UI showing the result of shots in terms of damage and suppression, i love the spray mechanic, and the line of sight lines are great.Unfortunately, the cons outweigh the pro's.First up, the stealth system and the ambush turn. I love the stealth system, makes great sense for the fact you are a commando/resistance team who doesnt want to be detected. The ambush turn should be a meter you build up then you can  to "go loud". It makes no sense that a silent stealth kill will alarm every guard across the map and instantly give away the position of every team member because it happened to be the "third kill" or whatever the case may be for that map. This could have been a turn-based Commandos (great games from the 90's), but the enforced go loud kill limit ruins this.Secondly, difficulty scaling. End game is dragged out by stacking armour and HP on enemies. This limits the possible buiilds on each character and forces you into building moral busting and armour penetrating builds. There is an illusion of choice in the skill tree, but realistically, half of it is junk due to the way the game scales. The game becomes "each enemy has 20hp and 5 armour, you have 4 squad members, enemy will have 16-20 members, ad infinitum".Thirdly, "class locked weapons". I hate, in fact I , the fact that certain class types are locked to certain weapons. Particularly the shotgun, which is in almost all ways subpar compared to all other weapons, and yet a full third of all possible characters are locked to this weapon type. At the least, every class should be able to select semi-automatic rifles. This is exacerbated by being locked to a 4 man squad from mission 1 through mission 25.Fourthly, and the most negative of the lot, re-playability. Or more accurately, . It was during my second campaign i realised that the missions are . The order in which you play them, the characters you use, and the skills your team has will change with each play through, but every map has the same enemies doing the same patrols with the same objectives, every time you run the mission. This means, in effect, this is chess. It will be possible to plan out a route for every map that is identical every play through to give an "optimal" clear. The lack of dynamic random missions, coupled with the locked in objectives and mission routes meant i could cherry pick the missions to suit my squad and know what i was going in to each mission, as well as being able to specifically remember certain maps and enemy wave spawns, etc. kills all challenge in play through #2.There are solid bones here, but it needs some serious overhaul to make this a game i ever come back to. For the price, going in blind on 1 campaign it's a slightly above average squad based tactical game that drags in the third act, and is probably a good enough experience for most. But there is zero longevity in the game as it stands.

_childDocuments_.review: All around a very good game so far. I'll edit this review as I get further if anything dramatic changes my opinion, but in 2 hours of play here's what I've noticed:It's impressively bug-free, feels feature-complete, and is easy to dive into after the brief tutorial.  Core gameplay is rewarding--enemy AI isn't brilliant but they aren't brain-dead. Getting hit is downright lethal in most missions though, so where the AI don't checkmate you the sheer challenge of the lethality makes for a tense time! Sounds are mostly great, but some guns sound more like bass hits than gunshots. The music is great--in-mission music often reminds me of the old Medal of Honor WW2 game soundtracks by Giacchino. Graphics are sharp and good looking, and it runs smoothly except for some minor lag on certain enemy turn moves. Campaign has good depth so far, and the mechanics to balance aren't surprising but they're good, and I imagine it'll have some good replayability (especially as you tackle Elite difficulty or Ironman), but overall some of the extreme levels of campaign customization/depth that XCOM 2 laid out are not there. So maybe not AS much replayability as XCOM 2.  Still, for the price this game punches above its weight, and the devs aren't getting XCOM levels of game dev budget, so I'm actually more impressed than not.Only gripes I have so far? Sometimes enemies don't make the most of flanking/positioning and they just sit and fire. Not being able to tab over to your next soldier during move animations or reload animations for other soldiers feels slow-paced in an unrewarding way, and my BIGGEST issue is that getting 4 stealth kills in certain mission types means guaranteed reveals.  I failed a "do not get detected" objective because I was *too* good at stealth? Because after killing my 4th target quietly, one of my guys shouts "ALRIGHT WE'VE GOT THE JUMP ON EM!" and we go loud?  Feels arbitrary. Oh and as of the time of this review, go into Options and crank up your Camera movement speed way way up--thank me later. (Though they may change the Default speed in a patch, so test it first).I'm really excited for community mission-making and modding tools--the devs already have people signing up in their discord, ready to make maps/missions. Campaign replayability will surely be helped by community modders making their own missions+narratives, and the room left over for DLC stories is promising. The setting of this game is delightfully original (I'd never heard of the Jedburghs until now!) and the devs were clearly passionate about WW2 history, as you get presented historical facts and choices based on the real-world lead-up to D-Day in 1944.  There are some other little things that I believe might be easter eggs too, like one particular character often using the voice like "YOU WANT ME??!" which makes me think one of the devs was a big fan of the beautifully complex character Kevin Leggett from Brothers in Arms.  This game oozes with attention to details that I didn't expect.  This is not just some WW2-based XCOM clone.Overall this game is exactly what we need more of in gaming:  Ambitious ideas developed and delivered in a ready/finished state, by passionate devs. This is a strong entry to the tactics game genre.  I think it's worth the purchase and I'm eager to see what expansion content they add, what the community comes up with, and what the devs move on to next.

_childDocuments_.review: Reflecting on over 30 years of gaming, I can confidently say that this title has evoked the most negative emotions in me. Not because it’s a bad concept—far from it. The concept and most of its elements are excellent. It has the potential to be a standout in its genre, which for simplicity, I'll refer to as the "XCOM formula." I love these types of games, and initially, this one seemed very promising.However, after a few hours, the flaws in some design decisions and level builds become glaringly obvious, particularly in terms of balance and tactics. This initial enthusiasm quickly turns to frustration. I've never yelled at a game as much as I have at this one. I usually never rage quit, but this game had me doing it repeatedly, only to come back hoping for better luck and ending up even more upset.There are too many issues to address comprehensively, but here are some key points:1. **Poor Scaling**: Typically, you earn one improved gun per completed mission. However, what good is one gun for a team of eight heroes? The upgrade from 4 to 5 damage is a mere 2.5% improvement overall. Imagine if in XCOM, you invented a laser gun, but only one soldier could use it while the rest were stuck with basic weapons. That's what playing this game feels like. You might also get some “impressive-looking pants” that add a few points to morale, but overall, the game’s scaling is terrible. Even when you get new firepower, the game just scales up the difficulty with tougher enemies and more reinforcements. It's very discouraging.2. **Frustrating Mechanics**: The need to reload and retry missions constantly is incredibly frustrating and feels like a waste of time. Reinforcements can be announced just one turn before they arrive, and unlike XCOM, characters here can barely run any distance. The action point system is very restrictive—you can only move about the length of a house if you do nothing else, with no "double run" option to escape tight spots. Soldiers can move and shoot much more efficiently than you. If enemies appear unexpectedly close, it's almost impossible to escape. They can pin you down easily, even shooting around corners. The ready action feature is poorly implemented, often resulting in ineffective shots taken at the first possible moment rather than when the enemy is in a better range.Other bizarre design choices include:- Getting stabbed through walls.- Explosive satchels that are ineffective because the environment isn’t destructible.- Having to down an officer twice or he revives, forcing you to expose yourself unnecessarily.- Limited stealth kills before forced confrontations, which makes many stealth skill tree abilities useless.The game bombards you with encounters that feel largely luck-based rather than tactical. The Germans have superior numbers, skills, and equipment, which might be realistic for a resistance scenario, but it doesn’t make for an enjoyable game.So, do I recommend this game? Despite its potential, the significant balancing issues overshadow the graphics, bugs, and overall design. The mechanics themselves are mostly fine, but they lose purpose when the odds are so poorly balanced. Tactics and strategy take a backseat to luck, which is not satisfying for this genre. Therefore, despite wanting to love this game, I have to give it a thumbs down.Oh - before the comment field goes bananas: I DO understand that some smocks out there will have found the game easy and "can not  possibly understand what my struggles/gripes are". I would suggest reading-glasses. This review is not that the game is hard to beat pr say. It is more about the enjoyment while beating it is not on par with what I want it to be. I think/know it COULD be great. But if they keep the formula as is -*I* did not find it a good formula :) I would say try it after a few patches (in the hopes that they DO realize the shortcomings) and buy it on sale if you LOVE it. It is good for a few hours of fun before it all goes pearshaped.
