_childDocuments_.review: I desperately wanted to like this game, but after about five hours, I realized that it was only getting worse, and it wasn't going to get better. Since I'm past the point of getting a refund, I guess leaving a bad review is my only outlet.Classified starts very well. It introduces a few new mechanics to the XCOM formula that seem interesting and has decent voice acting and graphics for a game of this price, although pretty bad animations throughout. The basic gameplay consists of dodging German viewcones in stealth sections and playing out turn-based battles after being detected. I think the word for how stealth works here is non-ludonarratively diagetic, as soldiers conveniently ignore the bodies of their slain comrades and only hear loud screams of, "Mein leben!" from three inches away. You can stand behind an enemy and braid his hair for him and he will not notice you, so long as you do not break a window within six tiles of him or step in the single pixel of his vision.Evading vision cones is the most primitive form of stealth gameplay. It is the bare minimum. And it's basically all Classified has. Unlike a game such as Partisans 1941, though, here you get to do it in agonizingly slow turn-based sequences, where you're forced to watch each enemy and each ally walk to and fro while hoping the German you want to melee execute looks in the right direction next turn to speed things up a little. It is very slow.Classified has a problem with slowness. XCOM is also sometimes slow, but one of the things those games do to alleviate the tedium of having to watch each unit run around the map after receiving an order is that--you aren't forced to watch each unit run around the map after receiving an order! If you have five squaddies to move from A to B, they can move more or less simultaneously.Not in Classified. Here they go one at a time. In fact everything is one at a time. Have two soldiers side-by-side, ready to synchronized takedown to Nazi soldiers? I'm afraid that isn't allowed. A lot of XCOM-likes struggle with enemy variety. After five hours, this game's is among the worst. Each new type of soldier looks identical but has some new gimmick that makes him agonizing to encounter. Why can't I stealth kill grenadiers? Why do officers need to be double tapped? Why do heavies have so much health? Why are bombadiers exploding when I shoot them at point-blank? And why, FFS, are these melee guys dodging five 97% shots from my entire team on a turn? How exactly am I meant to deal with an enemy who I can't shoot, but can down one of my guys in a single attack?These aren't fun to deal with. They don't have interesting counters. They're just tedious. When I calculate my movement AP and run to flank a bombardier, but it turns out I'm one tile within the 8-mile blast zone that he randomly emits using the Martyrdom perk upon death, it just feels like Activision is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with me again. It doesn't feel like I'm being challenged by the designers in a meaningful way. Tedium is the name of the game. Stealth sections are not hard, but they are very, very tedious. Skipping out on them is even worse, though, because you'll be morale drained by enemy machine gunners (and thus forced to lose HALF of your action points!) spraying and praying from across the map within seconds of going loud, while your poor squad members, of whom you only get FOUR (+1 often), miss again and again and again. The morale system does seem cool, but you aren't going to have enough men or ammo to effectively suppress the vastly superior numbers you're facing down without thinning them first. Reinforcements? They come from seemingly random entry points, for no narrative reason, whenever an objective is completed. You often only have one turn to react. They aren't hard to deal with, mostly. But they're so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ tedious, esp. when your units move very slowly. Can we not have infinite reinforcements on every mission? Please? All in all, you will be forced to reload constantly, and thus endure more repetitive animations, for no reason, while stumbling through boring and uninteresting stealth sections, so you can complete basically decent but not really very good XCOM-clone combat. And all in service of... a ticking clock down to D-Day. The characters are extremely basic national stereotypes, and while not horribly written, there's nothing more interesting to the narrative than that. Really, for a game like this, they should have gone full XCOM and let us make the PCs ourselves: instead, they've met us halfway, with a story that isn't character driven or engaging, overworld mechanics that are extremely half-baked, and a clock that I don't care about at all. After three hours I had completely lost interest in any of the narrative, in part because it's not meaningfully tied to the gameplay. How are the missions progressing our goal? What's the plot?There isn't one. Just tickle the Germans until Eisenhower comes to save the day. This game has an amazing premise. Its constituent parts are not horrible. There are a lot of good ideas, and some good implementations. I might give it another try. But I doubt it. I was wondering why I'd never heard of this game despite it being in my favorite genre, but I know now. In two words, it's not fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this, as "XCOM but it's WW2 commando stuff" is a very easy sell for me. I wasn't expecting it to be as tight or polished as XCOM, and would've been more than happy with a few rough edges and fumbled ideas. Unfortunately, it's mostly just that.It's less a WW2 XCOM-style game and more a recycled set of WW2 game tropes bent crudely into shape to fit on a fairly poorly-observed XCOM clone that feels at odds with itself. It's about being outnumbered and relying on stealth and cunning, except you can't rely on stealth because I suspect the devs realised you could just knife your way through most levels and added the arbitrary stuff like the stealth kill limit that alerts the entire Wehrmacht instantly, or the enemy types that can't be stealth killed and respond to being stabbed by alerting the entire Wehrmacht instantly. I suspect that the fact that there are no suppressed weapons is that it threw off the balance completely. Frankly, if you're going to ignore a whole raft of weapons that were designed specifically for the type of situation your game is supposed to be about because it is difficult to balance, you've got a fundamentally unsound basic design.The combat is a pretty barefaced attempt to copy XCOM's homework, but without the extremely tight, well-balanced rules and clear, concise delivery of information. I never felt like I was getting screwed by XCOM, because I could always tell why things were going badly and had a clear enough idea of the rules that I could immediately think of multiple ways to deal with it. In Classified, everything feels chaotic, and not in the way I think they intended. The basic premise of being constantly outnumbered and under pressure is compelling enough, and the idea that suppressing and pinning the enemy down can be just as useful as killing them outright is great. However, instead of a tense, taught experience where you're trying to control key ground and force a numerically superior enemy to fight on your terms while you complete your objectives and escape, instead you're just trying to tread water with limited options against what are often endless waves of enemy troops. Once things start to go wrong (such as only having four attacks and five enemies), you end up with a cascade of failures. I'm not averse to games about managing bad situations, but something about Classified feels scrappy and unsatisfying, like you're just the victim of a bad dice roll than an active participant.Probably the thing I like the least (aside from the extremely uninspired music; for god's sake we've had like 25 years of every WW2 game soundtrack being a low-effort Saving Private Ryan or Band of Brothers rip-off) is how often it's just XCOM with a paper-thin WW2 reskin. For example, one of your classes have shotguns, because XCOM had a shotgun class, also they only fire twice between reloads, because XCOM, and also there's an enemy shotgunner class, because XCOM. There are probably more shotguns in this game than were actually used in WW2. Rather than look at the historical inspiration and try to figure out how to translate that into a game, the devs pulled the standard move of just bending the setting to fit over the shape of player expectation, much like how the Battlefield games dredge up rare prototypes to fill familiar weapons classes instead of basing the gameplay around the weapons that were actually used. Another example of this in Classified is the fairly pointless collectible weapons: you're rewarded with different versions of the same guns, except this one is better because it's blue or purple. It's just stuff put in the game because that's what you're supposed to put in the game. Frankly I'm amazed there wasn't a crafting system.I will give points for the devs pointing out that the French resistance were not a homogeneous organisation though. I was genuinely pleased that balancing relations between the various political tendencies was a gameplay mechanic, even though it's a implemented in a fairly insubstantial manner. Ultimately the most disappointing thing about Classified is that there was room for it to be much more interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Hm, it is a turn-based strtategy title, and certainly a rather good one. Even at first glance, Classified: France '44 has a lot to offer, and I don't just mean the nice graphics. You lead a group of elite soldiers who fight alongside the French Resistance against the Nazis in the months leading up to the Normandy landings (on June 6, 1944) in order to fulfill strategic objectives and weaken the German occupiers. Depending on the success of your missions, the actual landing will be a great success or a massacre like the landing in Dieppe in 1942. You play both the individual missions in turn-based battles, as well as a strategic part in which you set up and train your team and select the next mission.The game attempts to create a semi-authentic gameplay when simulating the battles. This means you dramatically increase your chances of success by using real-world military tactics, such as forcing enemies into cover while another team member attacks from the flank. The battles are the heart of the game. They are turn-based. First you place your soldiers, which allows you to start from a favorable position if you choose your position wisely. Your enemies will not all see you from the start (in certain missions), so you can hide and possibly eliminate the first enemies inconspicuously before the rest have even noticed you. Both the range of vision of the enemies and the volume of your actions play a role here. In special "stealth" missions, you can theoretically eliminate all enemies one by one without making a sound.Each of your soldiers has action points, and different actions (movement, attack, use of special abilities) consume different amounts of them. Unused action points allow your units to go into "overwatch" mode - so they automatically open fire when enemies enter their firing range. Cover reduces the probability of your enemies hitting you. When health drops to 0, your soldiers go down. After three rounds, they are ready for action again, but if they are hit again, they flee the battle. This is not as brutal as the (often sudden) death in X-COM. If you have medics with you, you can also treat injured comrades during the battle. You can also hit enemies in cover with snipers. A special feature of Classified: France '44 is its morale system. Just like in real life, soldiers react to bullets whizzing around and take cover. You should take advantage of this to quickly position your own men in a strategically favorable position or to eliminate enemies crouching in a corner for a short time. Enemies with less than 50% morale have fewer action points, shoot less accurately and cause your units to lose less morale.Complex turn-based tactics game in which you control your units on the side of the Allies against troops of the German Reich in preparation for D-Day, the Allied invasion of France. The different missions are linked in a dynamic campaign, and the outcome of the missions leads to different game endings. There's nothing to complain about in terms of graphics and user interface, so if you're looking for historical war games with gameplay reminiscent of X-COM, Classified: France '44 is just the thing for you.

_childDocuments_.review: ► The CAMPAIGN is a story-driven affair designed to finish on D-Day after conducting x25 out of x45 possible missions. Some are binary, which means those not chosen will be missed. Others are not. There is no free map roaming.► TIME-LIMITS are present within mission objectives, reinforcements and even dictate the length of the campaign forcing gameplay,  reducing leeway to choose alternate strategies.► REPRISAL SQUADS bring jeopardy to the strategy map, ensuring the need to periodically counter damaged sectors or stall Gestapo [et al]. Keeping these in check are the repair TASK or deployment of Free French (FFI) assets.► MISSIONS have good variation as layouts are mostly unique. Objectives are a variation upon a theme. Assault, Ambush and Stealth types play out loud, in partial stealth or at full stealth. The multitude of factors that go into design make only a very few missions feel over-engineered. Lacks a deployment phase.► Unique and shared skills of the x4 CHARACTER classes makes them role oriented, which are defined by their own special actions and solitary weapon type. Characters cannot be generated. A total of x8 characters from x12 can be recruited.► The SKILL TREE makes for versatile character progression. Each one is divided into x4 sections of which x2 can be fully specialised if max level is reached. There are a good range of passives to raise stats. Skills that augment mechanics or provide actions make a big difference in missions.► INVENTORY loadouts are chosen between missions and are fixed. Weapons can only be exchanged for those of better quality, through mission rewards or trader purchases. Era themed clothing assigned to x3 slots is a great addition. They buff stats while changing the appearance of operatives to match. Ammo capacity is unlimited, but abstracted.► AP makes TBT COMBAT feel more JA, despite mission design being like X-COM. There is no sequence. Attacks include: melee, explosives and aimed or hip fire. Without certain skills and leaders, only one attack is permitted per turn. Crits are vital especially against enemies in armour which stunts nades. Overwatch and friendly fire tend to be more lethal than regular shooting.► COMBAT ROLLS are more consistent than in X-Com 2. Low hit chances tend to favour the enemy. There are inconsistencies such as missing at point-blank range with 50% and no morale issue.► The wealth of COMBAT MECHANICS makes combat really involving. POSITIONING and, COMBAT and MORALE STATES applied from weapons, shooting or skills provide a breadth of options which must be maximised due to the limited attacks of the squad. The use of stationary MGs may not cost any AP, but are underwhelming.► The MORALE system is mostly good, deducting amounts when attacked. The loss of AP means even a miss can be effective. Loss is countered by small doses of auto-recovery. Not losing morale when flanked or facing fewer enemies seems an oversight. Nor gaining any after enemy kills or completing objectives.► OVERWATCH provides flexibility when choosing to use it or not, though not the order. Useful to opt out when there is friendly fire. Can be lost when suppressed. Interlocking fields of fire makes it deadly. Can only be used once per turn without skills.► When in stealth the AI is rigid with scripted patrol patterns. In combat enemies use cover, fire in the attempt to suppress or damage, and then move to flank. It uses its numbers to overwhelm, but retreats infrequently. Uses overwatch and class skill(s) intermittently.🔶 ACCESSIBILITY - Has a x2 mission tutorial. New concepts are explained with pop-up windows when first encountered. These are collated within a training manual. A real lack of tooltips can slow gameplay down.🔶 DIFFICULTY - On normal diff the squad is always at a disadvantage. The design to have one attack per turn that uses up remaining AP diminishes enjoyment while making the game harder.🔶 BALANCE - Standard missions felt balanced. Many elements such as; missing the few attacks per turn, not having a semi-realistic injury system that affects enemy targeting make brutal and lethal missions unbalanced.🔶 PACING - Is fairly on point. Mission times deduct from the D-Day time-limit consistently. New and enough encounters come routinely. The strategic layer does not detract from mission focus.🔶 SCALING - Tends to rise in conjunction to operative capability, apart from when tougher soldiers are introduced. Of the x25 missions faced x3 were taxing. New gear becomes available at a good rate, as long as region reputation is raised promptly.🟨 REPLAY VALUE - Binary missions, different approaches to province control and alternate recruitment options bring higher than expected replayability. Unhistorical campaign variant would have added to this.🟨 LONGEVITY - Designed to be replayed at least twice. Some achievements require multiple playthroughs. Its possible to fail D-Day. Included is a editor for one-off missions.🟣 QUALITY - Well made with a good amount of polish. A low number of bugs have been reported and some design issues with mechanics have been questioned. ** More in the FULL REVIEW **🟣 STABILITY - No crashes experienced.🟣 STEAM - A mix of organic and missable achievements. Cloud saving. Screenshot capture. Almost full controller support.🟣 OPTIMISATION - Runs at 45-60 FPS in missions. Slows during transitions. Gfx card runs a little loud at high settings.

_childDocuments_.review: Another review where I wish I had a neutral button - but since I am refunding the game - I figure I have to lean on not recommend and explain why.This is a strange game where a lot of the pieces are here and I can see how this could be enjoyable for some people. The primary problem I have is that I have pretty high expectations of this genre. For the VERY small amount of time that I played this and engaged with the basic mechanics, I just couldn't get over the fact that I'd rather be playing XCOM or Phoenix Point. This is hardly fair to the game, I only played the tutorial and did one of the scenarios that the devs provided. However, during the scenario the pace of the game and the way the conflict worked just felt off to me. The enemies are hilariously unaware during the stealth phase of the combat. There is no real tension in the stealth phase and you can act with impunity.The pacing of the turns also felt really clunky and awkward. This is a nit-picky complaint, but your units move slowly through their movements and you cannot queue concurrent movements up for routine movements on the field. The combat itself introduces an interesting enough idea with "every shot counts" and morale, but something about it just didn't connect very well for me. It may come together later, but I found myself too disinterested to move forward with it.Finally - the thing that I really hated the most is the nerve of launching this game with three DLCs: A season pass, cosmetic pack, and mission pack. Launching a game and pay walling content on Day 1 is a scummy practice and it needs to be called out as such. To restate - I am neutral - read favorable comments that can more capably describe the experience. I do not have a good grasp on what this game has to offer. The best thing I can say is that this game rekindled my desire to play what I feel is a better game.

_childDocuments_.review: "It's Dad-Com," I said."What's that?" "It's X-Com for dads.""What is?""This game, Classified France '44. Not a great title, I guess. But like, you know how dads are obsessed with World War Two? And they like simpler, slower things? A little less flash, you know? A game where they can take their time, not aggravate their carpal tunnel. Maybe a game that throws WW2 facts and stories at them that they can breathlessly tell their family about at dinner. And it's basically just X-Com. So, Dad-Com.""Who the hell are you? Get away from me."But I'm already gone. Evac'd the second my feet hit the zone.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommending this game comes with a few caveats but if you can get around a few design choices and bugs I'm wagering are being ironed out, it's hard not to like this. I've gone through the campaign four times and have two achievements left to go and I honestly find myself coming back to it. I DO recommend it, though. Keep in mind this is a game where you are trying to keep your presence hidden, not the front line of the ground forces. Kills aren't what you're trying to achieve (they're just a fun perk). Getting in and out quickly is the point of your actionsPros: Great voice acting, interesting and distinct characters, wonderful narrative cutscenes told through a sketchbook, unique weapons and clothing bonuses, the absolute joy of having Killzone on a heavy with a large magazine and letting them dumpster anything that moves in their massive overwatch cone, information on operations and facts in the sixty days leading to D-Day on their rough date in the lead-up to the landings at the beaches, killing nazis, alternate outcomes for D-Day and how much you influence it, many unique maps with only a handful re-used (to my eyes) for other missions in the campaign (you will need at least two playthroughs to see all possible missions), usually no penalty for taking as many turns as you need (some missions to have objectives that need to be completed before X amount of turns pass). After your initial 4 characters you will have options to recruit 4 more from a pool of eight so that you can add a another of a particular class from a pair on offer.Middle Ground/Player Dependent: The D-Day timer means you have roughly 30 or so missions you can undertake before you reach the final mission- some played abhor this kind of thing but I don't honestly find it that stifling as someone who generally doesn't like time limits. The ambush system can feel both arbitrary and also extremely useful (see below). XP is awarded not by kills but by objectives (so you can't farm XP) which means some missions can be completed without needed to kill a single enemy if you proceed smartly and are patient. Supplies are not overly bountiful so you do have to consider if you want to buy that shiny rifle from one of the factions or if you want to save for costs needed for training, region repairs, recruiting FFI units, retaining, aiding a particular faction, or sending someone to get their wounds taken care of. There is no perma-death for your characters but a stacking wounds penalty (to health if downed and morale if broken in combat) and effectively only one down per mission (the second down removes the character from the mission entirely and halves their XP gained from the mission). Cons: Sometimes running into a soldier immune to stealth kills can feel like running into a brick wall (especially when they're entirely unarmored), some sub-optimal pathing that can require some step-by-step maneuvering around diagonal moves through hidden squares in order to maximize AP to distance moved, some pathing that will outright run through enemy vision in stealth (but not actually break stealth, thankfully), some skills seem objectively like must-haves which might make it hard to branch out from the more powerful builds, enemy levels and armor essentially causing grenades drop off in efficacy swiftly after a point in the campaign (and some grenade options feeling objectively worse than others), sometimes bonus objectives feel like a bit more trouble than they're worth. Some timed objectives feel like they are absolutely designed so that you will have exactly one turn before you can complete them (difficulty doesn't seem to affect these timers). Some mechanics/information I'm still not entirely sure about like obscuration (being within foliage), I could not tell you how much of a cover bonus this provides (but scouts can spec to have 50% damage reduction when in this kind of cover though not every mission will let you make use of this where other 'final' skills in their tree will be effective in every mission). It seems enemy heavy gunners have a much better version of suppressing fire that sweeps a broader area where nothing I've seen in the heavy gunner kit lets you sweep such a large range with the suppressing fire skill- this could just be part of the challenge in some encounter design.Now I get wordy,Some points of contention:- The D-Day Timer: Some people really hate time limits and will absolutely not buy this because of the timer so it's best to get that out of the way because if this is a deal-breaker for you then you know now. (60 days, each mission takes 2 days with some factors depending so roughly around 30 missions you can do in that time frame)- Ambush System: This is both useful and frustrating. I can understand the balance behind it and the ambush turn is actually very useful (especially when paired with the regional ability to do 50% bonus morale damage on the ambush turn). This effectively lets you choose when to go loud and get a free turn when you do but it can feel like the number of stealth kills you're allowed before you are forced to go loud is very limited in some missions while in a few you'll need to go out of your way to make sure you can fill the kills needed to set up the ambush turn. I kind of wish you could just initiate the ambush turn with any number of stealth kills (or even just a couple).  There ARE missions with unlimited stealth kills and they feel very satisfying to skulk through.Another wrinkle here is how you begin to run into more and more enemies who cannot be stealth killed. No matter how deep you have a scout specced into melee damage there are units flat-out impossible to stealth kill and this can be equal parts frustrating and interesting. It can force you to adapt a new strategy on the spot or it can just be annoying. I understand the balance reasons around this- some of these units make it so that you need to consider your approach but it always feels a little annoying when you can't stealth kill a grenadier in bulky armor but also can't stealth kill an officer in just a uniform. Again, this could honestly cause some missions to be entirely too easy or eliminate a need to consider your approach beyond carving a direct line with stealth kills. An additional note: Bodies of enemies do not cause any reaction on the enemy's behalf and while this removes an element of planning when and where to shank an enemy it would also require the ability to move bodies and it's entirely possible this was something the devs wanted to do but just didn't have the resources. It requires some suspension of disbelief but it's also a video game so it comes with the territory.- Reprisals and FFI: At a point into the campaign the enemy will begin deploying special units that move around the board and their presence increases the time a mission takes by an additional day (3 total) unless you have taken full control of the region that negates this. Reprisals are not hard to come back from but getting FFI units to temporarily disable these enemy units takes about two missions worth of time (so you may end up with someone just spending all their time doing FFI recruitment). Reprisals demolish a section of controlled areas but this damage can be repaired in the span of one mission's time if you have the supplies and a free soldier (you will always have someone to spare for that). They feel a little frustrating but it's an element of the game but I do wish the importance of FFI were more emphasized.- Enemy Strength Ramping: It feels as if enemies rather swiftly begin stacking up armor (and making grenades begin to feel more and more lacking in the same measure) and it can just be frustrating at how much damage you can put out and how much gets mitigated. Suppression and breaking help but it still feels annoying to see how little damage some enemies can take because of a lack of armor penetration on weapons. It just feels a bit too quick.(More in comments)

_childDocuments_.review: Logbook Entry - Operation: ShadowfireDate: June 6, 1944Location: German-occupied NormandyMission Objective: Sabotage enemy communication infrastructureClassified: Eyes Only0600 Hours:Jumped out of the plane with my unit, bound for German-occupied Normandy. The night sky was alive with the sound of aircraft engines and the distant thunder of artillery. Luck wasn't on our side from the get-go. Lost one comrade during the jump, fate unknown. The other landed nearby. Will ascertain status later.0200 Hours (D-Day):Landed safely amidst enemy territory. Ground reconnaissance revealed an old farm used by the Germans as a base. Proceeded cautiously, maintaining silence and cover.0300 Hours:Encountered two members of the French Resistance. They offered invaluable support for future operations.0400 Hours:Received orders to destroy a vital enemy radio tower. Executed the mission with the assistance of Resistance fighters. The game, so to speak, guided me through optimal strategies.0500 Hours:Missions vary from retrieval of crucial documents to elimination of high-ranking officers. The scope is wide, including bridge demolitions, safeguarding supplies, and liberating imprisoned Resistance members.0600 Hours:Navigating through the intricate web of factions resisting the German occupation. The Resistance comprises diverse groups: criminals, nationalists, and even communists, each with unique agendas for France's future. Building trust among them is paramount, earned through successful missions.0700 Hours:Despite initial distrust, gradual progress in gaining favor with the factions. More missions completed, more allies gained. Equipment upgrades crucial for enhancing soldier effectiveness. Acquisition of resources through mission looting enhances gameplay depth.0800 Hours:Overall assessment: a commendable game experience. Offers a realistic portrayal of the challenges faced behind enemy lines. Opportunities for strategic thinking and resource management abound. A few minor flaws noted, but they do not detract significantly from the overall experience.End of Logbook Entry

_childDocuments_.review: This game's difficulty curve is quite frankly, insane. The first 5/6 missions or so, there is a clear and sustainable progression that is quite rewarding, providing enough challenge but missions can be cleared with only minor issues to deal with across the squad.Then suddenly, the next set of missions you entire squad will get wiped out within less than 6 turns. No matter what you do, the enemy will always outnumber you, outmanoeuvre you, and seemingly will never miss their shots. For example, on one of these missions (assault type), you spawn in completely surrounded on all sides. It takes all 4 of your squad to kill a single enemy on the first turn. By turn 2, your entire squad is dead with literally nothing you can do about it. Restart, maybe play defensive. Doesn't matter, enemy moves forward, shoots and hits without fail, all 4 members of your squad is dead on turn 2 again. And because of how the game is designed, you are now stuck in a negative feedback loop as your squad is injured to the point of being useless (cannot just recruit new members to replenish fatigued and injured squadmates just as a temporary buffer) so every mission from then on becomes not only insanely difficult but impossible.Shame, because the first few couple of hours of this game showed promise. But the ridiculous level of difficult spike makes it an extremely frustrating and unenjoyable experience

_childDocuments_.review: As a x-com like games fan, I wanted to give a shot at this game. Although it has potential, it felt like a copy of a copy of a copy. namely lamplighters league copy, which is xcom copy, which is ufo: enemy unknown copy. I believe this game is not released as complete, I always had the feel they introduce something but only as a poc/mvp but never fully implemented it. let's get into it: Strategy map: I was pretty disappointed in this. there is really not much you can do here. after every mission, you listen to some dialogue between characters to get in game bonus (?!), then change loadout if you got some better rewards and improve characters with gained xp. lastly you choose tasks and a mission. Tasks:for me the tasks or only money sink, seemed to be there only to prevent you from getting the best gear. one of the most frustrating parts is you can only do 1 at a time. so you can't heal 2 of your injured (emotionally or physically) squad members at the same time. you have to do it 1 by 1. It also takes by default more time then a mission to heal one, so do the math, you need to get less then 1 character wounded/broken each mission. same with FFI, so you can't stack them. so you have to use instead repair region, each of these punish you without any reward. I would have expected here some Gear modification task which lets you add mods to your gear, which seemed like a natural thing to do, having all these different modded items, but no, not possible.Loadout:Another frustration for me. you are limited to pre-scripted gear you get from missions and pre-scripted items from faction stores. no randomness, no luck, your gear progress is railroaded. of course once tasks start punishing you, using the store becomes impossible, because you can't earn money by selling old gear or by any other means than doing pre-scripted/fix amount missions. so no grinding to get perfect gear, which some of us completionists expect. I understand the countdown to DDay and the theme of limited time etc, but this is not an excuse. Characters: your characters are from a fixed pool. they are all named and they CAN'T DIE. This is similar to lamplighters league and phoenix to have special characters but at least there they CAN die. another, weird thing is, you have a couple of choice missions where you decide whom to take additional to your starting 4. not sure how they get selected, but for me, I didn't get any snipers, no americans and only one female, which causes issues on loadout because your "armor" is only wearable by a specific gender and country citizen. I had literally 10 american hats, for just 1 guy. It wouldn't be much of a problem if I could just SELL them. but no, you're stuck with them, knowing you can never use them. Missions:A couple of things that bug me on missions. in the beginning there were a couple stealth missions but I think last 80% of the game there were 0 stealth missions. why? noone knows. it's 80% ambush and 20% assault. so you don't really have much of a choice of going silent and stealthy really. apart from that there are usual AI issues, they go around doing nothing. get scared of your overwatch and stay put etc. I also noticed most missions you can't skip, you have to do all of them unless they tell you it's one or the other type of mission, which really takes away the surprise/luck factor, you are railroaded into which missions to do, which gear to use and which characters to choose. too much control and you feel it. I'm already tired complaining but last thing is character development, they as usual have classes, each character has 1 unique talent, rest you select. BUT each class has maybe 10% unique talents, rest is common among all classes. so much for diversity among character abilities. I finally finished the game today with "minor victory" even though i did all the missions perfectly, had only once reprisal, and prevented the rest. not sure how you can get better. but oh well, at least i didn't loose assuming that's even possible with immortal characters.

_childDocuments_.review: **EDITED in 05/08/24Just recently I found that the DLC's add nothing to the campaign, so I had to change my review from thumbs up to thumbs down. I was already bothered by the lack of communication from the team, especially by not clarifying the requirements to win the game, so finding out that I spent (a lot of) money on the Overloard version that delivers nothing for the campaign was the cherry on the cake for me. ****Original review**The game is very well made, but I need to start with an important caveat. "Classified: France '44" has the worst thing about the XCOM 2's legacy: you'll always be highly outnumbered, overwhelmed against much stronger enemies and with (almost) infinite reinforcements waves.In general, your four-members squad will face an average of 12 to 15 enemies per mission, plus various reinforcements waves released as soon as an objective is reached. There is an incentive for stealth, but it can be considered illusory because in ambush missions there is a limit on stealth kills allowed, and there are also many enemies that cannot be killed stealthily (in other words, you'll have to go loud).The main innovative combat mechanism presented is the morale system "every shot counts": even if the shot is missed, it reduces the enemie's morale, which can result in suppression or breakdown. However, when you are 4 against 15, it is more likely that you will have your soldiers broken, so it is common in the most difficult battles for you to skip one or more turns because all your soldiers are broken, making them sitting ducks.On the other hand, the storytelling is engaging and the artwork, especially in the cutscenes, is beautiful. If you're ready for the XCOM 2 style - that is, a game designed for you to suffer - you've come to the right place. If you prefer a fairer and less overwhelming experience, look for another title (I would suggest Jagged Alliance 3, for me the best and most balanced turn-based game).

_childDocuments_.review: Possibly a bit mean to give this the thumbs down after getting 25 hrs play. But ultimately this was a disappointing game that seemed to full of promise. XCOM style tactical WW2 game? i`m in! But - much like one of those enticing tourist trap restaurants you find on holiday- once you are in and realise this games failings it too late. This is a broken and souless gaming experience that is sorely lacking in certain areas and could have be so much more. On the plus side it has a good starting premise with decent graphics and interesting historical notes. Build up a team and make tough choices. But as things progress it becomes clear that the pacing and gameplay balance are badly off. Most frustrating in later stages are the bullet sponge enemies that just wont die. I think that even if I had borrowed advanced Xcom weapons they still would shrug off a full mag . The ineffectiveness of your own upgrades and tactics gives the impression that the game cheats just to make the game a challenge. But its a challenge that quickly gives way to frustration and many many restarts of a level. Honesty, some of the "super soldiers" you met can shrug off a full machine burst at point black range from behind. In later levels I had to hit enemy 3 times and then stab to kill. All whilst fending off an endless swarm. Still I made it to the end somehow after many restarts. At yet- despite not failing a single mission- I still failed my overall objective. Really not sure what more I could have done. There is a randomness to the game at times in terms of characters and events. But the time deadlines can be so tight and the strategy map, just like the tactical battles, needs perfect choices every time. Overall this feels like a missed opportunity. Its very clearly designed with console focus. Some annoying bugs and glitches. Tight timescales. Not enough people to cover all of France, build up factions and take down waves of Terminator T-800 modelled Nazis. Healing takes 4 days. If you pick any option that brings forward D Day then its likely game over. This could have been a much much better game had it taken a more hardcore realistic style of combat or been better play tested. And I definately felt the AI cheats as enemy soldiers instantly shrug off that supressed status and lobs a grenade from sniper range and further than anyone on my team. In the end this game just became a chore to get to the end. And for which I received the poorest of ending. If you want to play a decent WW2 resistance game try Partisans 1941 instead. Much more fun.

_childDocuments_.review: this game is really dull. there aren't any interesting character abilities and there's very limited synergy between characters (edit: after finishing the game, i did find some characters work well together e.g. support's hollowpoint ability with the heavy's unlimited overwatch ability). i think i'm about 1/3 of the way through and have zero investment in the characters or what they're trying to do.the weapon implementation is also really dull. weapons are limited to be used by certain classes. OK fair enough that the marksman is limited to using rifles and the heavy class is limited to LMG but why should the leader/scout/support class be limited to their respective weapons? it would be way more interesting if anyone could use any weapon. the clothing options are also really annoying because they are restricted to nationality.the game is slooooow. especially during the stealth phase when your units walk extra slow. pathfinding is cooked - your units will jump over two walls instead of taking the equidistant path around them, and they do it soooo slooooowly. you can't tab to another unit during movement. you're even forced to watch the reload animations. at the end of turn, the camera pans to some random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ which you're forced to watch for a few seconds for no apparent reason e.g. it will focus on an enemy unit that was already visible. the action cam is also slow which would be OK if it weren't so anticlimactic. it would be way better if this only happened on kills. thankfully you can turn the action cam off. sometimes it will trigger even on misses. the post-mission 'debrief' takes so long too with slow and unskippable dialogue boxes. enemy actions also take ages. you'll be waiting a second or two for an enemy to rotate 30 degrees or just go into overwatch without even moving. put on a youtube video while you play 'cause you'll need something to do while you wait. i don't like to whinge about difficulty because usually, being ♥♥♥♥ is my own fault but the hardest difficulty is just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. the enemies can just wall bang you with pinpoint accuracy through every wall of an entire house and will just sit there and keep doing that even when there's no way they would have line of sight. they never need to approach your overwatches. the normal difficulty feels just a smidge too easy. there's also an annoying bug where enemy health bars disappear. you can still see hit percentage but you wont know what kind of attack to use. ultimately, you just  have to waste AP to ensure you score a kill.this game needs some QOL fixes at the very least. until then, it's probably only worth finishing for fans of the genre (edit: after finishing the game, i would not even recommend this to fans of this genre. it's a very forgettable experience and my hours are only so high because i alt-tabbed waiting for the enemy to make their turn then forgot to come back.)

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I'd give this game a 3/5. If you enjoy turn-based tactical games like XCOM, then you'll probably like this game, but not love it.I'm going to compare Classified: France '44 a lot to XCOM2, since I really loved XCOM and it's quite similar. There will be mild spoilers for both games, but nothing major.There are a few reasons this game isn't a 5/5:The first is that there is this looming timer of when D-Day is coming. This makes sense from a historic standpoint, but isn't great from a gameplay standpoint. Something I loved about XCOM was that, while there was a looming "timer", you always had ways to delay that to ensure you won the game. Here, if anything delays your gameplay at all, it affects your ability to win the game and there is absolutely nothing to be done. So if you lose 2 days for some reason, it may be literally impossible to properly win, no matter what you do, even if that occurs very early on in the game.Another issue is also related to the win condition. There are multiple levels of winning that you can achieve. This is personal preference, but I really prefer games to have a win versus not winning. A place where this issue "shines" is trying to get enough points to get a full victory. In my playthrough, I needed one type of mission to achieve this, but 6 times in a row didn't have it as an option. So just by luck, with literally nothing I could do, I achieved a 95% victory instead of a 100% victory (no way to delay the timer, and no way to force the game to give me an option to win).An issue I had with XCOM is that, towards the end of the game, it was annoying to assign gear to your squad (mass unassigning, assigning gear piece by piece, etc.). Classified: France '44 makes this a bit worse, unfortunately, in having gear that can only be equipped by specific characters (only if you're French, only if you're a woman, etc.), which really feels like a step in the wrong direction. It's interesting to have gear unique to certain people, but I'd prefer it remain strictly cosmetic (and have gear with actual stats be assignable wherever).You can also get away with just having one real squad that you use for missions (maybe cycling one person out), and having everybody else doing "admin" work and such behind the scenes. While I really enjoy the voice acting and character development, I think it fed into this problem. Characters don't die (only retreat), so even if a mission is truly botched, you can still keep using that same squad and not really being punished for it. So I had a character who was very low level at the end of the game because I had them doing assorted other tasks the entire time, and I was never punished for that.Edit: One additional thing I forgot, the ambush system is a bit infuriating at times. You may be stealthily doing a mission very well, but a character will shout "Ambush!" and have everybody break stealth after so many kills. It feels way too forced, and you actually have to back away and tactically make decisions based off somebody screaming for no reason. It feels very frustrating.There are a few smaller things, like there being too many status effects, the action point system, and I'm a bit uncertain about the morale system, but those could just be personal preference.I'm only leaving such a detailed review because I really think the game had much more potential than this. I really love WW2 history, and I really enjoy turn-based tactical games (like XCOM), so I was really hoping this would hit the mark for me, but it didn't. I'd still recommend it overall, but it's just not quite what I wanted it to be.For any future games in this series, I'm hoping for a change to the victory conditions. Maybe something that isn't perfectly fixed in history, so there's no timer nor set way it "should" go. Maybe the Germans or Japanese invade the US, and you have to build up a resistance to take back the country. I'd also like something less personal for the characters. It made them more interesting, but I think made it impossible for them to be killed off, so every fight felt "meh" because there was no real risk if I failed to make a correct decision.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a turn-based that allocates action point resources to actions like shooting, reloading, moving, and special commands (i.e., giving orders, medic abilities, sniper abilities, close-combat abilities, etc.).  The game has a timer to 'D-Day' and your objective is to prepare France for D-Day through the use of primarily French Partisans assisted by various allied nations.The Positives:- World War 2 Setting with a focus on French Resistance.  The story delves into facets of the French Resistance and conversations between the characters between missions give you insight on their motivations.  Little conversations like the French-Speaking Canadian soldier from Ontario that is finally seeing where his ancestors immigrated from and interacting with the French Resistance members was interesting to me. - The 'Action-Point' system.  The system works well, particularly when you find combinations that "unlock" renewable action points, extending your turn and making the later missions easier.  Such as the close-combat ability to regain six action points upon melee kills.  If you see a string of weaker soldiers together, you can take them out in one turn if you send in the character with that skill.  Using the 'Order' command to clear a stretch of ground and set up flanks is also very rewarding.- The Mission Types.  There are three different mission types 'Ambush / Assault / Stealth' and each feel very different.  'Assault' reminds me of 'X-COM' whereas 'Stealth' reminds me of Commandos and avoiding sight-lines.- The Load Out System.  It consists of a Skill Tree, equipment load out, and weapon choices.  The skill tree options are not too restrictive in the points you are allowed to allocate at Max Level and makes a significant difference in the play style. Equipment and Weapons vary only slightly, but I appreciate that they use historically accurate firearms.  I find the satchel charge almost useless as it take two turns to detonate and the enemy will prioritise avoiding the blast zone, perhaps there is a use for it that I haven't discovered.- Fatigue system is interesting and encourages you to rotate team members between missions.Minus:- Unclear Overall Objective.  You are preparing France for 'D-Day' and there is a meter that shows the allied strength and enemy strength at the top of the map screen.  I "assume" I need to completely fill the allied strength, but you are on a timer and enemy forces will damage regions and allied strength as you play.  How best to fill the meter is unclear, it appears to be through securing regions but there are other bonuses for securing some regions more than others.  I still have 18 Days to 'D-Day' so I am unsure if there are different 'endings' based on how filled the allied strength is by endgame.  A bit more explanation was required to the strategy for the map section as players may focus on filling the wrong territories.  It should be something that is re-explained by the commanders as you progress, or at least, you could find the explanation somewhere.  I'd hate to win every mission but then lose the game because I did not secure the correct map sectors in order.- Difficulty.  I am playing on 'Normal' and find the game challenging but rewarding.  I don't have issues with the difficulty but I can understand those that would because completion of the secondary objectives are almost mandatory as you will desperately need that additional XP and Supplies Bonuses.   I would also recommend avoiding team members getting wounded if possible to deter having to allocate supplies to healing.  Hold out spending supplies only on the top tier faction store options, but do use supplies for tasks (i.e., aid faction, recruit FFI, training).  If you don't do this, you might struggle near the end game and that isn't exactly clear from the outset.-Graphics and animations.  Some of the environments and enemy graphics are great, but some of the animations such as the troops marching to a mission are incredibly awkward. _childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy X-com, you may well like this game.  It is a bit thin on the ground because once you've played campaign a couple of times there's not much incentive to keep going.  It has a lot of elements common to most squad based tactics games. There's basically one type of shot (hip shot) which you will primarily use - unless you're a sniper and you get aimed shot.  Additionally there is a rather rudimentary skill system, but that's not necessarily a bad thing as games of this nature can sometimes over-complicate things.  There's no research or base building either, which simplifies things as well.  Since it's a historical game, researching (for example) an Uzi 9mm would be a bit out of place, so that's fair enough but I do miss that aspect of the game.  You can get weapon upgrades from the Black Market, however.Unlike X-Com however, your team can only comprise of eight pre-determined members of five different classes (Leader, Shot-gunner, Scout, Sniper and Heavy Gunner).  You start with four and recruit another four as the mission progresses.  I would have liked to have seen more people to choose from, because it blunts replayability value when you have to use the same team over and over again.  Hopefully this will be addressed in the season pack.ProsI enjoyed the subject matter and tying into historical events made it enjoyably realistic.  You do feel immersed in the events going on around you.  The different guns you get from different factions are realistic and have different traits.A good mix of British, French, Canadian and American people to recruit, rather than just Americans with a token Frenchie.  The aforementioned french characters are also diverse - from different races and sexes. Morale System so even if you miss it lowers enemy morale causing them to panic or freeze up entirely.  They also become more prone to critical hits when panicking.Reasonable variety in missions - hold an area, assassinate someone, get to an extraction point, kill everyone in the building, etc, etcConsVery few team members to recruit.  As far as I can tell, there are only two of each class to recruit max.  On top of that Each class has the same template of skills to pick from, so in theory your two scouts can be given identical skills.  The characters only have limited interactions and so you don't really see them as individuals, they're rather vanilla.Faction screen has flags on it but it isn't immediately obvious you can click on the flag and then buy gear from them.  They should put a storekeeper in front of the flag to click on.  I went half way through the game before realising you could actually click on the flag and buy things.  Update !  They've put "Store" on the flags now and so fixed that problem.  Well done, developers !Not enough stealth missions in Campaign to choose from.  They seem to be mainly ambush (limited stealth) and assault (no stealth whatsoever)A glitch at the end that incorrectly calculated the number of missions my team had been on.The expansion packs seem largely bereft of content.Things I'd like to see ...1) More characters to choose from.  2) IF an expansion pack, somewhere like Norway so you could have snow terrain3) The scoring system - despite not failing a single mission and controlling over 80% of France, I scored slight victory 91% - wtf ?!?!!?4) New Game plus so you keep all your acquired loot  5) Maybe individual challenges for each team member, which reward you with medals or something to keep playing as a character beyond the first campaign.6) A reason to play Spec Ops Missions.100% Completion rating - Might be tricky on Elite level, so realistically you're looking at 90%Overall, I enjoyed playing the game but after completing it I don't feel like there's much more to do.  It did take me upwards of 30 hours to do one run through (although I was afk for a good bit of that) so maybe you consider that value for money.Finally, consider waiting for a sale before buying - Low replay-ability coupled with (from what I can see) A single spec ops mission and two weapons seems poor return for an expansion pack.

_childDocuments_.review: So far, I have played 19 hours on medium difficulty and most tactical fights/scenarios are still challenging. I am on mission 15 or so and about halfway through the count down to D-Day. I like the Factions, RPG, etc., adding better weapons/clothes that add better stats and leveling up the characters by adding Skills. The tactical battles are quite challenging. However, this is not Wartales, XCom, etc., and while it has the tactical battles, it is not an open sand box but more like chess matches where you have to figure out how to beat the map. There are three types of missions (Ambush, Stealth, etc.) and from one to three skulls (level of difficulty). You can save frequently (and it has quick-save and auto-save, so I tend to save each mission at start and then quick-save through the fight, and it I don't like the results of my latest move I can roll it back (save scumming). I think the game would be super challenging on iron man, as you wouldn't gain enough supplies to pay for upgrades to heal, buy, support, etc., your regions, units, etc.I have run into one or two freezes and a few times and also I can't understand why some of my units have movement left after one of their actions, but all I can do is end my turn (this might be a game mechanic and not a bug), but with all the frequent auto-saves these weren't a big deal. The keybindings are changeable, which is very helpful.The positives way outweigh the negatives (which are minor and few). I personally prefer an open world sandbox game more like War Tales and Battle Brothers (I have over 450 hours in both), but this is still quite a good game and worth it on sale. I also bought the two DLC's to support the Developers. It has a scenario builder and users can add scenarios, so I am looking forward to some community added scenarios. I think this game is an easy buy on sale for those who like tactical team-based isometric shooters, WW2 games, etc.UPDATE: After 36.7 hours of game play, I completed all 24 missions, all with 5 stars (replayed maybe 2, and only the last did I get a wounded soldier and only 4 stars) and on easy/medium difficulty, I only got a "Stalemate Victory" meaning the D-Day troops got bogged down on the beach. Not sure what that means but it sounds pretty average, lol. I guess you have to do it on higher level of difficulty or get all 5 star victories to get better than Stalemate? As I passed certain missions when you have to choose, I did not see all possible characters that can be hired nor did I do all missions available, so I think there is a few replays after the initial run. I  found the SA Riflemen Leaders and the SMG Scouts the most useful (usually getting two shots per turn), followed by the SG medics and then the HMG Heavies. Anyway, it was quite engrossing and I really enjoyed and would recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Band of Brothers & Inglorious Basterds meets Wasteland 3 & XCOM. Incredibly satisfying to play.  This game is loaded with pleasant surprises. The first thing that caught my attention was the moral system, which is a great addition to this sort of game where missing a target happens frequently (I'm looking at you, XCOM, and your 95% missed Sniper shots), With the moral system, even if you miss, enemies take moral damage. They can become suppressed (half AP, reduced accuracy, do less Moral damage to you) or even broken (skipping their turn). It's a fantastic extra layer to the combat system that most turn-based games like this don't employ. It adds to the strategy, giving the player more options for neutralizing enemies. Maybe you can't kill that heavy gunner this turn, or even the next turn, but you might be able to CC them for a couple turns, and that's just as good. Additionally, the combination of stealth approach, ambushes, and "Go Loud" combat is incredibly satisfying. Every mission feels like an episode of Band of Brothers. There's a beginning, middle, and end, with various escalations along the way, culminated in a nail-biting extraction. And after every mission, you'll get a little historical context, with an artistic vignette that tells you what was happening outside the bubble of your little resistance as we march toward D-Day. Then there's the base camp side of things. Sometimes these features can be a bit boring, but here the developers have done a great job making the game feel immersive in the WWII setting. There's a chance after every mission to listen in on a couple of your soldiers and learn something about them, while also providing Moral boosts. And these little interludes are worth listening to not only for the story, but because the voice acting is great. The soldier classes are fun and I really liked the skill trees. Also, it's very cool how you start the game with only a couple soldiers and then go about doing missions to recruit more people to your team. It gives the game that Inglorious Basterds feel and I absolutely love it. I also liked the way the factions worked in concert with the gear. As you do missions you'll earn supplies, which you can spend at the faction stores to purchase upgraded equipment. Improve your reputation with a given faction and get access to better gear. Some of this equipment is specific to a nation, too, like France or Britain, so only the appropriate soldiers can wear those pieces of gear. I absolutely loved that. It reminds us all that WWII was a multinational effort, and I liked seeing those little details here. Finally, I'd be remiss if I didn't mention this, but there are big machine guns setup in some missions, and you can actually fire them, and good lord it's glorious to watch those things spit lead. About my only complaint is that the animations for crawling through windows and some other maneuvers play out rather slowly. But that's such a minor thing I almost don't care. The game is great. I'm thrilled it exists.

_childDocuments_.review: I saw a lot of reviews comparing this to XCOM, and while I understand the desire to do so, it seems somewhat unfair. Cover-based attacking always has that time when a 10% hit chance turns out to be a fatal critical.. or vice versa on your 90% hit chance, which can be discouraging, and the game doesn't explicitly explain the objectives clearly, so you can get some unintended mission results. _childDocuments_.review: Soviet Union didn't directly contribute troops or resources to Operation Overlord (D-Day), but indirectly played a crucial role in the success of D-Day, not by participating in the operation itself, but by significantly weakening Nazi Germany's military capabilities on the Eastern Front. By the time of D-Day, the Red Army had been engaging a major portion of the German military might in fierce battles. This relentless pressure forced Germany to divert troops, resources, and attention away from Western Europe to counter the Soviet advances. And the fact that during the narration the Red Army is remembered only once, and then in the context of competition ("while we are smoking here, the Soviet Union will capture Berlin") seems strange to me, to say the least.But otherwise I really liked the game. It was a great 32 hours.The game is easy, I completed it in terminator mode on the first try on the highest difficulty, although I could not get the best ending (it is not at all obvious that “+4 to resistance forces” affects the end of the game like this). I went into the last battle with the weakest squad, thinking that even more difficult battles awaited me ahead... These were the most intense 16 turns...The game is more similar to the old Comandos series, the new Desperados 3 and Hard West 2. In a limited (but comfortable) time, you need to take the most advantageous position, silently eliminating no more than N enemies, and then shoot the remaining ones, simultaneously completing several additional objectives.There are 8 characters with 4 classes in the game - leader, sniper, heavy and medic. Each of them can develop in 4 directions, although by the maximum level 25 they will have mastered 2/3 of all (3/4 useful) skills and become unsurpassed death machines. Classes limit the list of available weapons, characters have a nationality and gender that limit the list of available equipment. Unlike skills, resources to purchase weapons and equipment are always in short supply, so while your sniper is running around in his best uniform, the rest of the team can show off in their underwear. At the beginning of the game, all classes are equal and have their own features, but towards the end, frankly unnecessary characters appear who cannot penetrate enemy armor, while your sniper is able to shoot an enemy tank in two turns.By choosing different characters, goals on the world map and missions, you can feel some non-linearity and influence on the game world. But this does not add replay value - you don’t want to crawl after enemies on your belly a second time.If you like not very difficult tactical one-off games with XCOM mechanics in the style of Hard West 2 - don't pass it up!

_childDocuments_.review: If you are a TB squad tactics fan, I don't really get why you wouldn't enjoy this game.It's quite deep and there seems to be a fair amount of branching and RNG in terms of missions and loot.There are 5 core classes with 4 subclasses each and a freeform skilltree. You are allowed a lot of freedom in how you build your characters.The characters are pre-written like Jagged Alliance and each has a unique perk, but you can build them how you want. Weapons are restricted by class, while clothing is restricted by nationality (the idea being non-nationals wearing national colours will be considered spies -- and more importantly, for balance).This is not a stealth game primarily, and they bend over backwards to prevent you from stealthing most missions. However! There are three mission types and one is "Stealth," which is indeed a puzzle-like stealth affair.The other two mission types, Assault and Ambush, are pure combat and a hybrid type, respectively. In Ambushes, you will be forced out of stealth after a certain number of stealth kills, so choose your targets carefully and be sure you're in position when the fighting starts. (Not sure why people complain about this; it's great.)If anything, the devs were a bit too kind in some respects. Downed allies can be revived with a wound, and if they go down a second time or are injured while downed, they will "retreat." This leads to dumb strategies like sacrificing 3 team members who complete the objectives and "die" ("retreat") and then leaving one character behind at the exit to secure the win. There are penalties for this (wounds), but it is a bit silly. Maybe I'll grow to like it.I also think the game would have benefitted from stances like Jagged Alliance -- at least stand and prone. The morale system is interesting, but it doesn't really make sense for a guy with broken morale to just stand there and do nothing out of cover. It would make more sense if suppressed and broken characters went prone and wasted their turns that way instead.Overall, it's a deep map-based tactics game with several layers to it and some unique ideas on the tactical layer. I don't really understand why someone would review it poorly unless they just don't enjoy this type of game.

_childDocuments_.review: A good turn based tactical game similar to Jagged Edge but without the whimsical sense of humor. A lot of the beginning of each fight is based around stealth and positioning. And you almost always have to use stealth, you can't just stroll into the fights and expect to win. Which is good and true to the theme of the game. The interface is easy to use. The game's difficulty increases at a suitable pace compared to character progression. There is also some larger strategic decisions to be made between each mission/fight, which gives flavor to the game. The only negative I can think of is that after enough character progression you will have unlocked all skills on the slate for each character. Progression would have been more interesting if I couldn't possibly unlock all skills eventually. But this works! I'm enjoying the game!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great. The combat system is fantastic, and I wish they'd make more games like this. I really enjoy the suppression mechanics, so no shot ever feels wasted. It also makes machine guns actually feel different from semi-automatic rifles and submachine guns. The friendly fire and suppression mechanics give you a reason to move your guys and avoid bunching up. The active abilities of your soldiers are super useful, and you'll wish you had some more AP to do more of them. The perks you gain from leveling up often give huge bonuses.If anything, I'd like to see the campaign map fleshed out just a little more. Sending people on jobs is neat, but it'd be cool to be able to do two missions simultaneously by splitting your forces and best equipment. It does feel a little weird to have your guys switching around magical pants before missions.

_childDocuments_.review: Sorry guys, unfortunately not yet. Got this on the recent sale and thought, give it a try, although the critics were mixed. The game reminds me most of "Phantom Doctrine", but of course also in parts of the current versions of "Wasteland", "Jagged Alliance" and the old-timer "Breach & Clear", the latter primarily because of the somewhat narrow combat distances, although the maps are quite large and very nicely drawn.The game is also fun and when you have completed a mission after several reloads because suddenly the best shooter can no longer hit from roughly 3 meters or the Wehrmacht sniper must have been a magician in civilian life who goes through walls like his bullets in the war, it is also entertaining if not rewarding. The whole structure around it with provinces, factions, rewards, missions, etc. is rich, seems to make sense in itself and the combat values such as HP and morale also seem logical in themselves, although I didn't fully understand the effects of morale on the enemies or found them to be consistent.The problem, however, is that the fine-tuning in the combat missions is definitely lacking in pretty much everything. If not the rough polishing in some areas before that too. The controls are nervous, mouse-over is too often wrong or confusing, differences in height when scrolling across the map are automatically only compensated upwards, character selection with the mouse is tedious, etc. etc. In the fight itself, the cover seems to be non-existent, especially vertically. I noticed this particularly in a mission with trenches, where everyone can understand in reality that a shot wouldn't work from that angle. Or that when monitoring an area, if the enemy leaves cover and wants to shoot and therefore stands up, no reaction is triggered, but if he moves sideways half-crouched in the trench - including the probability of landing a hit - it is?!? So why do soldiers dig trenches at all? The same applies to half cover on the same level, where the graphics at least show the character crouching behind cover. It is quite unrealistic to get hit in a position like that, no matter if the shooter stands ten or five meters away. Unless of course the shooter was a magician.In addition, the battle model unfortunately seems a bit simple to me. By that, I don't mean damage points from weapons and how that works, but the course of the battle. What happens if an action doesn't work or doesn't succeed, for example a shot misses for whatever reason. It seems to me that as a result going onward, nothing works for you and everything works for the enemy. Just like if the first move in chess is successful, the probability seems higher that the next moves will work and the opponent's won't, and vice versa if the first move doesn't work or you make a mistake yourself. This kind of balance or momentum, while true for a relatively simple game like chess, probably doesn't come very close to the circumstances on a battlefield and is especially annoying when the outcome of the initial action seems somewhat RNG.Conclusion: Not recommended at the moment (June 2024).

_childDocuments_.review: As a fervent enthusiast of both World War II history and tactical strategy games like XCOM, Classified: France '44 has left an indelible mark on my gaming experience. Stepping into the shoes of Allied commandos and French resistance fighters during the tumultuous period preceding the Allied invasion of France in 1944 is an exhilarating journey.One of the game's standout features is its impeccable attention to detail, both in historical accuracy and gameplay mechanics. The clandestine operations, sabotage missions, and intricate network-building with resistance factions mirror the covert struggles of that era. The looming threat of the Gestapo adds a palpable sense of urgency, brilliantly balancing risk and reward with each daring move.The strategic depth of Classified: France '44 is truly commendable. The recruitment of elite operatives, coupled with the dynamic campaign structure, ensures that no two playthroughs are alike. Whether meticulously planning every move or embracing the chaos of guerrilla warfare, the game accommodates diverse playstyles flawlessly.Moreover, the stealth mechanics in Classified: France '44 are a revelation. Sneaking past enemy patrols, setting up ambushes, and executing precise strikes evoke a sense of tactical satisfaction rarely found in other titles. The gradual learning curve ensures that even newcomers to the genre can immerse themselves fully, while veterans will relish the strategic nuances woven into every encounter.The character development in the game is another highlight. Each member of your squad feels distinct, with their own strengths, weaknesses, and personal stories. Engaging with these characters adds an emotional depth to the gameplay experience, forging a bond that transcends mere pixels on the screen.Furthermore, the Mission Creator tool extends the game's longevity exponentially. The ability to craft, share, and download custom missions ensures that the community remains vibrant and the replay value remains sky-high.In conclusion, Classified: France '44 stands as a testament to the prowess of turn-based strategy gaming. Seamlessly blending historical authenticity with gripping gameplay, it delivers an unforgettable experience for fans of World War II history and tactical enthusiasts alike. If you're seeking a meticulously crafted journey through the clandestine operations of WWII, look no further than Classified: France '44. It's a masterpiece that deserves every accolade it receives.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this type of game. Macro strategy with tactical turn-based mission game play. XCOM2/WOTC and Battletech are two of my favorite games. As a history buff I was naturally interested in this game. I played the demo and watched some footage via The Mighty Jingles and was very happy to pick up the full game. I'm currently 25 hours in and still loving it.The macro side of game play is satisfying. You have to balance influence, enemy forces, and decide what regions (i.e. upgrades) you're going to pursue and protect. All the while with the ticking clock of D-Day. Once thing that I find challenging is that you can only have so many agents so you have to decide what types you are going to double up on and which ones you can make do with only one of. I'm also running into challenges with balancing my supplies as you really have to use them wisely or you'll run out quickly.On the tactical side, I love how missed shots still have an effect. You really have to plan out your routes and tactics or you can find yourself in hot water really fast. I'll confess that I hate to lose so I really appreciate that the game has 3 autosaves that it rotates through plus a quick save feature. I love working out the best way to approach the missions and get as many of the secondary objects as possible.Long story short, I have gotten fully sucked into this game and already thinking about how I'm going to try to handle things in a second playthrough.On a important note - I have been playing on my LCD Deck. It plays well, looks great (both native screen and docked), and I've got the controls set up in a way that I like them. You can find my control setup as DC's Classified '44 Custom Layout

_childDocuments_.review: So, fun game. I enjoyed playing, and the second world war trivia was interesting. Pros: Gameplay entertaining. 'Stealth' kills were by far the most fun. Cons: So, possibly this is my gaming laptop being a couple of years old now, but the loading seemed to take forever sometimes, and occasionally just failed and hung. There were occasions when the game just lagged badly or outright crashed for me. The morale failures could occasionally get annoying when an enemy fired at you from miles away, didn't come close to hitting you, and you still ended up panicked. _childDocuments_.review: An excellent tactical combat game. Feels more like xcom than other similar games but differs in interesting ways. This is a no-brainer yes, even at full price.There are a couple combat mechanics that I thought were done really well. The first is that there are two types of damage: Physical (HP) and Morale. Weapons deal both types of damage and only the physical damage can be avoided if the shot misses. Morale damage occurs regardless. Weapons differ in relative physical vs morale damage, making for some interesting choices. Even a low percent chance to hit can be useful against an enemy behind cover since the morale damage will still occur. If morale goes below half the character is "suppressed" and loses half their action points, but morale recovers a bit each round and there are leader abilities that can help recover more.The other interesting combat mechanic is spray fire. Every gun has a "spray zone" that extends in a cone around the selected target. Each weapon has a "spray accuracy" in addition to the normal, primary target accuracy and can deal full damage to targets in the spray zone if hit. Like morale damage, spray zone size and accuracy are different for different weapon types and loadouts.There are mechanics that I know some people hate, like mission timers, but please know that the timers that do exist are very lenient. Not all missions have them (less than half I'd say) and they give you PLENTY of time. They are very reasonable, and you can retry missions easily from the menu (plus there's a quicksave) if you struggle with it at all. Not all the timers result in full mission failures either, some just prevent completion of side objectives.I did encounter a few mostly visual bugs, but these were cleaned up either by rotating the selected character or reloading a save game. Nothing that impacted my ability to play the game or my enjoyment of it. As someone who is generally picky about bug severity/quantity in games, I was happy with the state of this one.
