_childDocuments_.review: A more detailed video review can be watched here: From the perspective of someone who played most classic Turn Based Tactics games alongside modern XCOM, Classified: France '44 does a lot of things right. It didn't just blindly attempt to copy Firaxis' XCOM, instead it mixed it with things old-school Turn Based Tactics games did right [Action Points are still the superior way to handle turns imho] and added its own mechanics. The result is a streamlined yet very competently designed experience.My only gripe is that it's on the easy side, but I think a regular player will find it pretty well balanced. It's not very replayable, since missions are hand-made [and very well-made I might add], but you can play again if you want to have access to different companions and their bits of dialogue.This is the debut title of a small studio, but the end result is very impressive.

_childDocuments_.review: The most positive aspect is the historical context.  It was the 80th anniversary of D-Day this year and for anyone interested in that history this game would be fun to play through at least once. Although not historically accurate, it does feel authenticate. The setting of a behind the lines group working to destabilize the Germans before D-Day was done well.Unfortunately it is let down by the slowness and repetitiveness of the game. Each mission has a great back story but they can be frustrating slow to play. For example you have to wait for each of your troops to finish moving before you can move the next one. You also have to wait for each of the enemy troops to finish their moves, which they take one at a time at a slow stroll pace. The stealth mechanic at first was fun but quickly became very tedious. Tip toeing around the map while you wait for gaps in the enemy sight lines before you move meant that some turns you couldnt move at all. So you sit and wait while each enemy one at a time moves.  The actual combat is ok I liked the morale system where troops can be left unable to act as they are "broken" from being under fire. I also liked that each weapon had a line of fire and anyone caught in it took damage. You have to think carefully about positioning. I thought the enemy AI was pretty good at giving a good tactical challenge. I enjoyed the first play through mainly because of my interest in D-day and the fact that my recent XCOM campaign ended so heart breakingly catastrophically I couldn't face taking on Advent again...at least not for a while. Looking for an alternative this game was good at first but it is hard to fully reccommend. I wish there was more cutomization available, I wish there were more interesting skills and abilities, I wish each character had a wider variety of weapon types. Most of all I wish the pacing was better both tactically and strategically.
_childDocuments_.name: Classified: France '44

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty solid tactics game. Not without its issues, as some other reviews have mentioned. Some of the gameplay choices can seem a little restrictive, particularly missions that have limited numbers of silent take-downs before alerting enemies across the map. Also enemies that are simply unable to be killed silently. I understand this is probably designed as a balancing measure, or differentiating mission types, but for those who like the sneaking aspects, it can be frustrating.The randomness and accompanying frustration are still here from the lineage of games like XCOM. Frustrating to miss a shot at 91%, but hey, it's a game. There has to be some element of randomness, otherwise we're just playing chess.The combat is generally good. I do really like the morale system, which opens up new tactical elements by pinning down enemies without necessarily killing them outright. The strategy view of France is also well done. Satisfying to undertake missions, complete areas of control, and unlock those regions' abilities. Although a bit of a bummer that I got the tracking meter to 82% and that was only good enough to allow the Allies to fight D-Day to a Stalemate. And then the game made fun of me for being bad. Whatever.The game is well-made. I came to really like the graphics, sound work, voice work. Didn't encounter any bugs, stable through my whole play-through.So, I think worth the price of admission if you like the general tactics gameplay, the setting, and willing to forgive some of the shortcomings.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is decently fun, but it has a handful of pretty serious issues. The animations are HORRIBLE. Distractingly so. Your characters hold the guns so awkwardly, and they don't move like humans at all.The game is ugly. Not a huge deal to be fair, but it's just not nice to look at at all, and that can weigh on your enjoyment of a game more than you might think. It looks like a PS3 launch title. They could have stylized the graphics in some way so it could look good while not being like photo-real cutting edge graphics, but they didn't.You don't get random characters that you can heavily customize like XCOM for example. Your guys are set in stone named characters. They talk to each other and stuff in the camp, but it's pretty boring and I don't care about them at all. You can change their clothes, but each piece has stats and stuff, so if you purely wanted to play dress up, you'll have to sacrifice your stats. I wish they would have gone for a more XCOM style of character customization and let you change their nationality and their gear and everything. Kind of a personal gripe that some players won't care about at all, but whatever.The skill trees in the game give buffs that are so small, you'll literally probably forget how you built your characters from time to time. The progression is not nearly meaningful enough.The game is fun enough, but doesn't do much of anything to stand out from other XCOM style games, even with the World War 2 setting. I have wanted a WW2 XCOM game for years and years, and I finally got it with this game, but I still haven't finished it yet because it's just so whatever. The game is just bland and ugly. I don't want to go into extreme detail about how bland the gameplay is because this review is long enough already, but playing this game is like eating a sandwich with Kraft singles for cheese and no sauce.If I could get a "maybe" or "meh" review instead of a flat out negative one, I would.

_childDocuments_.review: Classified: France '44 is a turn-based strategy game set during World War II and focused on the resistance  agents operating in France. I came into it expecting a WWII XCOM or Battletech, which is more or less what it is. You usually have a squad of four operatives and have to achieve a limited set of objectives against a much stronger German army. As a big fan of turn-based strategy games and WWII history, this is a game I immediately wanted to try when I first heard about it. If I was ranking it under a percentage system, I would give it a 77%. Overall, it's an okay turn-based strategy game, but it's encumbered by some odd mechanics such as an odd stealth system on some maps that forces you out of stealth even when you're successful, a large but ultimately meaningless set of skill trees for the various character classes, and a shallow meta game involving liberating territories on a map and building relationships with different factions. The small studio that made it clearly had some big ambitions for the game that ultimately feel under baked in the finished product. If you're a fan of turn-based strategy games and the World War II setting, I think you'll find something to like in Classified: France '44 if you go into the game with tempered expectations.

_childDocuments_.review: Trying to be unique in this world that XCom popularised is tricky, but I think CF44 does a pretty great job at giving players who are familiar with the genre a lot of common ground to start from; while expanding it with their own flavours to make it their own. I assume anyone reading this has already seen some screenshots, or understands the premise. You get a small squad to accomplish a variety of objectives, and you're generally always outgunned. So far, so X-com with reskinned bad guys. Starting with positive ways it distinguishes itself: - The campaign timer is a really nice way to make decisions seem important. You can't just fly around the map endlessly, waiting to gear/ train everyone up to max level; you have a clock to beat and an invasion to prepare for. Similarly, giving you the sliding goal of preparing for the invasion of Europe is a really nice way to distinguish between 'you did well at the mission', and 'you did well at the campaign'. - While most attack actions tend to end your turn, I do like the breakdown between weapons. Shotguns and SMG's only take 1 action point (and you generally have about 12 to play with), encouraging a playstyle with those units of being fast flankers, while heavier guns tend to require more planning and execution. It's a subtle change to the 'two actions, one to move and one to attack' system which I think lends itself really well to making the classes distinct. - I alluded to this earlier, but I like the mission variety. Ambush, stealth, and assault missions change up play styles and keep missions feeling fresh. That said, missions are very much prepared ahead of time and it lacks the sort of endless procedural configurations you get in other games of a similar style. I don't entirely mind as each map feels like it's own well thought out puzzle to crack; but it does hamper repeated playthroughs when you know precisely where you need to stand to deal with the incoming wave, etc... - Honestly, I like the 8 characters they chose. I think you get a little history which adds a little more color to the game and theme, and I enjoyed seeing how they interacted with one another (both in mission and in camp). Voice acting's good, and the characters seem as well written as you can get for something as surface level as the game is willing to go (you're not going to get Fire Emblem style relationships, but that's not really the point). With the positives out of the way (and genuinely, it's a solid game which I've really enjoyed), there are a few negatives. - I would not recommend anyone try the ironman version of this game. Not because of difficulty or 'gotchas' which may throw a curve ball; but because there are clearly some UI issues which need to be addressed. Things like how I would click on a menu option but the game would think I was clicking on a tile so the character I had selected (in the background of the menu) would then go running. Or how many times I'd try to choose my next character to go and wind up moving someone. If I were seriously playing an iron man run, these accidents would be infuriating. Maybe you'll be a far more precise player than I, but that was a sore point for me. - I really like the morale system in the game, but I think it's a little over powered. In most games, being able to stun an enemy is a really big deal; and CF44's morale system basically means you can stun anyone if you throw enough attacks at them. I dig this conceptually, but when combined with the cone of damage/ suppression that weapons deal; it's entirely possible to stun lock entire waves before they get to act. I think a good middle ground might be to only allow a 'broken' status to be inflicted if the target would receive more morale damage after being at 0 morale (and otherwise they get to be suppressed). It makes the stun condition a little more valuable (often I'd stun targets that were already broken anyway), and means you really have to commit to locking someone down. That's just my opinion though, so your mileage may vary.- A really minor gripe, but I'd really like to see us move beyond Normandy. Maybe this could be a first iteration, and we get some similar campaigns for other theatres of war, but Normandy has been retread so many times. Yes, it was heroic and all that; but how about a campaign for other nations and their various war fronts?Overall; CF44 is a great game. If you're a fan of the isometric tactical squad based genre, this is a fantastic entry into that style of game. I actually think that while XCom is the easy comparison for mechanics, I'd point to something like Valkyria Chronicles for theme in that sort of 'grim romance of WW2'. As someone who loved both games, CF44 is a very easy recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: I am really disappointed in this game. The actual mechanics are clunky and I have had way too many game freezes (always on enemy turns, for some reasons, but my main gripes are really more about the absolutely ludicrously unrealistic aspects of the game play itself. The combat stats are nuts, You can give an enemy a full burst from a BAR at point blank range and see him survive what would blow any human being into bloody rags.   The medic rules are sheer fantasy, Characters can get shot down to one health stat and healed enough to get back in the action over and over and over again. If they do get reduced to zero health, they don't die, they just "retreat," that is, they miraculously vanish from the  map, even if surrounded by enemies, and reappear after the mission is over. I guess you could call it "permalife," and it takes away a lot of the tension that any combat game should have. There's also a medic trait that allows the healer to return full health points to every friendly character on the map regardless of their distance from the medic. This isn't just unrealistic, it's downright magic.   I am a huge fan of turn-based combat games, but this one is so unlike actual combat that I really regret buying it and will definitely not be playing it again.

_childDocuments_.review: BLUF: Way too expensive for what you get. Buy it at the $10-$15 price range.I love XCOM2. This is not XCOM2 (which has been out for 8 years). It's not even a pre-D-Day window dressing over top of XCOM2. It's just not that deep. In fact, if you really have to scratch the turn-based itch with a WWII flavor, look up Soldiers at War--a game that came out over a quarter century ago and frankly has about as much depth as this game.Here are my gripes with this game:-The AI is abysmal. It sometimes runs to flank you, and other times runs off the screen into the fog of war. Especially if you have it surrounded, it can't seem to make up its mind about who to go after and instead waffles back and forth.-The enemy view area is absurdly truncated--these German soldiers need to seriously get their peripheral vision checked. The location each enemy can see is depicted in bright red on the map as to make the game even less challenging.-There is no randomness to the German movements when they aren't alerted, which makes it incredibly easy to get into position. If that wasn't enough, there's a little arrow on each soldier that shows you where they are moving next turn.-The weapons upgrades and clothing just aren't interesting. They really only bolster basic stats. XCOM2 is so much more interesting.-The interface is awful. I can't find where to adjust the scroll speed (it's super slow). Every time character does something, the screen jumps, and it always moves right when you click to move a different character, meaning they go to the wrong spot. When you use an ability on another character, the screen literally jumps back and forth between them four times before settling back on the original character. It's just not well thought out, which is unfortunate because this has already been smoothed in other similar games.-They really try to sell you on emotional connection with the characters, but it's just not happening. For example, at the end of the game, they give you a little post-war history for each person (a la the last episode of Band of Brothers), but it's super contrived because a) they aren't historical people and b) there's not really a "story." There are intermission conversations between characters, but the only reason to do them is because they restore mission-related abilities. It's just not interesting.BLOB: A game that's digestible at $10-$15. Certainly not the $35 when it was released.

_childDocuments_.review: Classified France 44 is a game about positioning. The stealth mechanics do not exist to allow players to take out an entire maps worth of enemies, they exist to give you a chance to position your units correctly before you attack. The knee jerk reaction to knife the first few enemies you see is something to be overcome, not something to embrace. The combat is a puzzle and you must use your limited stealth kills to open up cover positions rather than as "free kills" at the start of the match.Take your time, explore the maps, flank the enemy before engaging them and rain hell down on their heads in two or three turns of actual combat. Flank and Fire tactics are the name of the game. This game was made with the real military tactics of World War 2 baked into the design. If you want to get better at the game, to feel like you're not trial-and-erroring your way through the levels, pick up a military training manual and employ real maneuvers to control the battlefield. Staying still will get you killed. Hiding behind cover, popping shots may work in XCOM but it's not going to work here.I actually think the comparison to XCOM is doing the game a disservice. It's a far more thoughtful game than XCOM. You're not tentatively poking mist till you fall into a firefight like in XCOM, you're deciding how the firefight is about to happen. You're gathering information and planning your next move, watching, waiting. It's about using one unit's actions to open up more options for another unit, working as a cohesive whole instead of a set of individual super soldiers.It's also painfully historically accurate. Every outfit, weapon and cutscene is lovingly recreated from reference material. It has a story to tell and your characters need to survive to be a part of that story. Again, the XCOM comparison hurts the game. If you're looking for a brutal experience where you have to restart the entire game because your team got wiped, XCOM has you covered. If you're looking for a story based experience where you are expected to press ahead through your mistakes, not write off your save file, Classified is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: An XCOM like set in the infinitely more interesting setting of a Jedburgh team behind enemy lines in France 1944. It's clear from the start that the developers took great care translating actual history of the setting into gameplay which is commendable. It's not just the structure of the game (objectives of your team, main mission, factions you deal with) but also the characters you have. At first glance they might seem stereotypical and the dialogue is a bit tongue and cheek here and there, but when the Moroccan and French Canadian talk about their experience in the base camp, you know some real history lovers went all out with the 1944 France setting and it's not just the same old story again. I haven't met the major antagonists yet but have high hopes. The gameplay itself is solid and tries to distinguish itself from other games in the genre and also, again, trying its best to translate the setting into game play.EDIT After first playthrough: All my points from my early review still stand. This is a game from history buffs who didn't feel the need to dress up the already incredible story of the Jedburghs. The mission variety throughout the campaign is great both in terms of game play as well as objectives. The gear and build progression is very flexible. Overall, a very pleasant surprise with a great ending.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game, a solid 8 or 9 out of 10. People who like X-Com will love this. Excellent graphics and sound. Solid, thoughtful game play on excellent tactical maps that look great. Managing health/morale and movement points, soldier classes, items and also soldier perks as you level them up on the tacticla layer. With growth and perks and friendly factions, along with choice of missions, healing soldiers, stopping enemy police raids etc on the strategic level. I am eagerly waiting for a DLC already!You have soldiers of differing classes who will level up and use skill points to gain additional skills, perks, passive bonuses etc. Classes can use different weapons and do different jobs on the battlefield. You outfit your team with various weapon types depending on class, plus 3 types of clothing(head/body/legs), dagger, grenades and pistols all with their own stats.The combat is like X-Com and Commandos all rolled into one. A grid of squares that enemy soldiers patrol/watch/guard, can be a town, a bunker, rocket site, tank factory, coastal guns, submarine docks etc. You will need to think about how to get your mission done, like a puzzle, using your soldiers skills and items against the enemy. Maintain stealth or go loud, cut your way through a fence and sneak up to a good shooting position, or rain grenades on the enemy.Mission types are assault where you are attacking or defending, ambush where you can stealth kill a few enemy before opening up on them and pure stealth where you can sneak and stab your way through (or just shoot everything that moves, your choice!) So the missions are varied and interesting and fun to play.The strategic layer has you increasing resistance cells in France, adding territory that may have a bonus (faster healing, extra xp etc). With 3 factions you can buy items from or complete missions to earn items. All up an excellent game.

_childDocuments_.review: You might like this, if you like Jagged Alliance 3, Gears Tactics, Hard West 2, and Showgunners.I just finished the campaign, and must say I am truly enarmored with this game. It could have used a tiny bit more polish here and there, but the game mechanics are probably the most well thought out, I have seen in the last years.Tactical RPGs are currently my favorite genre. I wouldnt say I am super advanced at them, but truly enjoy them. And I especially like it, when they dont overwhelm me with a convoluted skill system (like WH40K: Rogue Trader), instead we find this beautiful skill system similar to Gears Tactics, where each single skill point has significance for gameplay immediately, and all the skills are easy to understand from the get go.I also enjoyed, that the meta-layer was small. XCOM tends to overwhelm me with all the options. And I play these games mainly for the tactical combat, not for the strategic layer.But my favorite part were the characters classes and how they were laid out. That was just sooo good! Once I had understood how each class is supposed to be played, it became so much fun and such a cool tactical puzzle. Games like Jagged Alliance really missed, with Snipers for everyone basically being the cookie cutter alpha strike build. But here: *chef's kiss* This was really a labor of love of some people who have dug really really deep into tactics games, identified common flaws, and made a truly elegant design!Some more points: * No random abstract timers, but always anchored in the mission design - really cool.* Morale system - worked surprisingly well for me. Alwas considering, do I want to kill them or can I at least break them? :-) Only in the end did I notice, I could interrupt many enemies just by overwatching.* Having named characters is always a plus in my book. I prefer that sooo much over a random recruits like XCOM. It's fun to customize the first squad, but everyone afterwards just ends up forgettable for me.* I loved that we can find uniform parts and weapons we can equip our characters with! Had a good pace of progress, where most pieces felt meaningful. (only in the last few missions I would no good weapons anymore from missions.Keeping the classes simple with their skills, having just the right amount of progression to still have varied gameplay every mission. By the way, those had some really neat designs. Good sized missions that didnt overstay their welcome.I am surprised this game scored only 74% on Steam. And probably didnt sell all that well with about 500 reviews. Always makes me sad that TRPGs dont sell that well. I hope the developers make enough money still, so it is worthwhile to keep making them. I did buy all the DLC, when I realized how much I like the game, just to show my support to the studio.Maybe the game could have used a little bit more polished with the graphics, UI and sound. I would have liked to see bigger characters faces in the game, and make the characters sihouettes and voices more recognizable. Even after 30 missions I am still kept confusing Tremblay and Belanger. :-P And I heard a little to many "en movement"s ;-)There were a handful of UI bugs, and the sound kept switching from very loud to very quiet sometimes. Especially funny, when my Support would silently lay down an explosive and then yell their confirmation so loud, the whole map would be able to hear them. ;-)I feel grateful to the studio for giving me this great experience and am looking forward to their next game very much. :-D

_childDocuments_.review: Classified: France '44:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Your name is Captain Willard Cassidy. You and two other daredevil soldiers have been parachuted into Picardie, France, in 1944, deep behind enemy lines. Your first goal is to contact the French Resistance. Then you and your men, with the help of the Resistance fighters, must create havoc across the North of France to the German army and installations. Your team must confuse and weaken the enemy so they are on the back foot when Operation Overlord is launched two months from now. Good luck, Captain; we count on you in Classified: France '44.Classified: France '44 is a turn-based strategy game developed by Absolutely Games and published by Team17 on the 6th of March 2024 on the Steam Platform. The game is also available on PS5 and Xbox One Series X|S. What an elaborate strategy game Classified: France '44 is; I was sucked in from the start. Why elaborate? Well, there are a number of things you can do in the planning before launching a new mission. I also like the moral character attributes within the combat phase, which can determine how much pressure your characters are under and their effectiveness in combat. But before you do that, you must choose which of the three difficulty levels you'd like to play the game in. I strongly recommend starting with the regular difficulty, which is how the game is supposed to be played. You can also add the Ironman option, but you won't be able to quit or restart a mission or manually save your progress. Then, you'll have a great introduction through live sketching accompanied by great voiceovers. These illustrations will reappear after completing each of the missions, where the story of these men unfolds from Captain Cassidy's perspective. The first mission will be a solid and comprehensive tutorial before you get to the Northern France map.The map is a significant aspect of the game. There are ten regions, and each is divided into three parts. Each region will be occupied by one of the three resistance cells: the Criminals, Gaullists and Radicals. Each region will have a specific ability, and every time you complete a mission in that region, the tie with that resistance faction will increase, and you'll also be able to receive additional benefits from that part of France. For example, in the Nord Pas-De-Calais, there is a hospital. If you acquire one out of the three areas, it might take four days to heal a character's injuries, but if you have all three areas, it will take only two days. Each region has a specific ability to unlock, and yes, you must have all three areas in each region to acquire these benefits. After a few missions, German figurines will appear on the map. At first there’ll be one, but as you progress, you’ll find four figurines scattered around the map. These units will eliminate the connection with the resistance faction that is operating within that specific area. The only way to counter this is to send an FFI (French Forces of the Interior) unit to stop their progress. To be honest, it will be tough for a while because you need to complete a specific mission to be able to recruit these units. Although some missions will have an FFI token as a reward, reaching the highest relations with each Resistance group will also give you a free FFI token. But to be honest, that won't be enough, as it will only sideline each German unit for three days. Ongoing FFI recruitment will be needed as soon as they are available to you. The basecamp tab is where two of your characters will chitchat, adding more substance to the story and giving you more insight into your characters. It will also boost the morale of both characters and heal one fatigue point.The loadout tab is where you can swap weapons, customise outfits and upgrade skills for your characters. After each successful mission, your team will receive supply and experience points and rewards, including weapons and uniforms. The maximum level your characters will reach is level 25, and they will slowly progress toward it. There are usually one or two levels per mission, as long as you have selected them. Even if you have eight characters on hand, you can only select four at a time for each outing, leaving the others to perform alternative operations on the map. The skill tree per category unit is cool, with four paths to follow and 36 skills upgrades each. For the marksman category, you get to decide if that specific unit will become a sniper, huntsman, veteran or defender unit. It’s the same for the leader, scout, support, and heavy units, but with four different paths. Most skills cost one point, but some of them cost two experience points. The last tab is for the three resistance factions, and as your relationship grows with each faction, you'll be able to purchase more weapons and gears with better combat values. Remember that anything you do or anything you purchase will require supply points. On top of that, events will happen here and there, requiring you to choose what to do. In terms of the gameplay within the missions, it’s typical of the game genre, and I particularly enjoyed the morale aspect that can interfere with each of the characters during battles. So, let's say you are shooting at an enemy that takes cover behind a tree trunk. If your character is positioned in front of the trunk, you might not hit him, but the fact that bullets are hitting the trunk will unsettle his morale gauge, and if the gauge is fully depleted, the enemy won’t be able to do anything the next turn. It's well done. I think that the difficulty progression of new enemy units onto the battlefields is pretty fair on the regular level of difficulty. I also like that you can plant bombs on tanks, planes, brides, V1 launch ramps and armoured vehicles, but I am a bit disappointed that buildings can't be destroyed during combat.  There are three types of missions: ambush, assault and stealth. Ambush will allow you to kill from three to eight soldiers with stealth ability – melee weapons. During the assault mission, you will be in combat immediately, and in the stealth mission, you'll be able to sneak and kill most of the soldiers on the map until one of your units is detected. The maps are small to medium in size, which is fine. Positive:~~~~~~ +	Great Graphics and voiceovers+	Good character skill tree+	Good character customisation+	Implementation of difficulty progression in combat is fair+	Three levels of difficulty+	Good tactical implementation in map and combat phases+	Excellent game encyclopedia +	AchievementsNegatives:~~~~~~~~ -	Few issues with screen flickering and one crash after loading a saved game-	The screen went black for a few seconds while moving the camera in one mission-	 No trading cards as yetClassified: France '44 is well-presented and provides good tactical pre and in-mission gameplay. It is dangerously addictive and shouldn’t be missed by the fans of the genre.8/10  Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: For you if you like: squad turn-based combat, modern setting such as WWII, an immersive story surrounding the combat, and you are happy with AA as opposed to AAA production values.  I like it, for the above reasons.  The developers have put a lot of thought into this game.  They seem to have saved money where money should be saved, such as the cutscene conversations are not motion capture or extensively animated and the graphics are not AAA.  In this game you don't just run and gun. Cover matters.  Stealth matters. You don't even just 'kill', mental states (morale) matter also.  The game's design mitigates the frustration of a missed shot by a missed shot nevertheless having a morale effect (e.g., unnerves the target)--I like that.  Yet, the game's design encourages you to be brave by sometimes you just move the max you can to move and shoot and finish off that enemy.  My context is while I have loved fantasy turn-based tactical games, I'm now looking for more realistic and modern settings.  The developers have said they aimed to be 'historically authentic' rather than 100% 'historically accurate', meaning stay consistent with history as much as possible but allow some modification to make a better game.  I'm happy with the result.Some modern QoL features that I like are save anywhere, and there's no need to press a key to advance a conversation to the next thing to be said in a dialog.  For me, the save anywhere allows me to experiment as I am learning the game.  For example, I can try out 'what happens if I do this' and then reload if the game mechanic didn't work as I expected (but I learned something).  Some of you may not like that style of play, but I find it more enjoyable and relaxing (and makes the learning curve at the start of a game less stressful).

_childDocuments_.review: It's a nice game. I'm a big fan of XCOM2 and this is the closest you can find on the market right now.After completing a campaign, I would describe Classified: France 44 as a "small & forgiving Xcom2".If you're coming from xcom2, you'll find yourself at home:- turn based with ambush system: similar to stealth + alpha strike.- square grid: similar movement & line of sight.- loadout: clothing for "armor perks", 1 primary, 1 secondary, 1 explosive & 1 melee per character.- Tree & level: a 4 ways tree per classes, 4 (or 5?) classesWhat's good: - stealth is less tedious, because you get the intent of the enemy patrol (rotating or direction for the next turn). LoS are way less cracked than xcom2, which is less frustration, but tend also to ease the game (map are smaller in classified: France 44 tho).- Overwatch: you decide if you wanna shoot or not on enemy getting inside your locked area. It's extremely great, if you have 2 targets getting in, you can decide to leave the first one, but take your shot on the second. This has been very frustrating in xcom2 sometimes.- Throwable: grenade are more simple to deal with (in Xcom2 it would be sometimes a pain to land them properly).- Spray: every weapon have a spray. It's super satisfying in packed area and its tactically interesting.- Stragegy: on the strategical map, you have some kind of "TW à la shogun" style actions. It feels close to xcom2 WTOC, you're getting pressured & hunted by the enemy, breaking your logistic or modifying mission condition. It's great. It's another small level of play, but a nice one. Also, like xcom2, you have an explicit time counter, each days should be used best. You know "when" the campaign will end, & it gives you an incentive to move fast.What's meh:- explicit morale management. Basically, if you miss your shot, you will contribute to demoralising your enemy until he get fully suppressed, reducing their action points. I don't know about this one. It feels kinda easy (I completed the campaign in normal, but without major struggle after my great deal of pain in legendary on xcom2). "I miss the shots, but I'm safe because the enemy cannot move the next turn" mechanics is a bit weak. I like the suppression mechanic, but it should be exclusive to LMG class. Because the morale is visible (yours and theirs) you have to think way less in case of missed shot. It really ease the whole tactical thinking. So again, very forgiving mechanics. For instance, I was buggued when i realized most of the melee combat would be harmless because of the moral effect: If you hit a target with your knife, moral go instantly to zero (on most enemy). So you'll sit there next to him, waiting for his turn to do nothing while you are juggling with your knife for your next turn... its a bit goofy.- LMG class is really imba. Its way too strong atm. Restriction should apply like ""only one LMG" per mission. I did my run with 2 lmg, and keep using them even with fatigue penalty accross mission. The build tree is way too strong because of one ability.- Building tree are meh. Its a bit exciting to discover them, but unlike xcom2 where you had only 2 per class. with fewer level, each choice were extremely impactfull and game changing. Here, I was building without thinking too much, its small perks, and small bonus and sometimes a big ability. I think for the scale of the game (20H, small map) it would have been nice to get a smaller tree, but more impactfull on each choice. Also you will end up with too much points... so at the end it's very forgiving.No perma death:- This was really bad for me. Your people will get down once, then revive by themselves, and then, ultimately "retreat" instead of dying. You'll find them waiting for your for the next mission. It's very very forgiving and it doesn't add this tension on roster management.AI: not the best.Scaling: It comes from balance in your own classes, but enemy are getting really tough on the 3 last missions.Diversity: because classes build are somehow meh, and enemy AI behaviour diversity not the best either, you will feel repetitive gameplay toward the end of the campaign. Conclusion: "A very nice, smaller & forgiving Xcom2 in a WW2 landscape".I closed the campaign in normal, not sure, i'll do it in harder difficulty. I hope they will do more game, because here the execution s flawless, full of potential.

_childDocuments_.review: Classified France 44 is a turn based tactical combat game with a light overlay of strategic activity.Set, as the title suggests, in France during spring of 1944. The goal of the game is to harass and disrupt Nazi activity in France and build up resistance capability to support the allied invasion in DDayThe more successful you are in your mission the easier it is for the allied to breakthrough.The tactical game is very similar to Xcom2 and Warhammer 40k Chaos gate. You are in command of a squad of 4 (sometimes 5) soldiers or resistance fighters and have an objective to complete before the mission ends.Missions come on three stylesStealth, Ambush and Assault.In stealth mode you can and should kill as many of the enemies as possible without being detected. As the game progresses, new enemy troop types are introduced, some of whom can’t be killed by stealth so they need to be avoided if possible.In ambush mode a certain number of stealth kills are allowed before an ambush is triggered (essentially a free turn). There is a counter so you know exactly when this will happen and it pays to think about where your troops are before this happens so that you can  take full advantage.In assault mode there is no mucking about. It’s just a straight up shoot out though sometimes the objective is to attack /destroy and others to defend.In between the tactical missions the broader strategic options play out These aren’t as complex as the strategic elements in similar games (Xcom2, chaos gate, BattleTech) but they are vital if you hope to succeed fully.Mission selection influences what resources you gather and which of the three competing French resistance factions is bolstered. You need all three to be maxed out to "win".Additionally, you can rest, heal and train your troops between missions though that does take them off roster for at least one and often two missions.Each region of the map belongs to a faction and completing missions which benefit that faction allows you to set up a resistance cell in an area of the map. There are three subareas in each region, and setting up cells in all areas of a region activates benefits (eg reduced healing time, more 'victory points') which adds to the strategic depth.As the game progresses, the Nazis respond to your success and they start to fight back, launching reprisals which pacify the areas you have successfully recruited, so another call on your resources is undoing this.Lastly you can and must spend resources recruiting Free French allies which can be directed against the marauding nazi police forces and gestapo, temporarily preventing reprisals.Compared to the base/ship management in other games of its type the strategic elements feel quite lightweight but to “win” the game at the highest victory level I suspect they are crucial.As you might expect from this type of game your troops gain experience when completing missions which can be used to increase stats and learn skills specific to their class (leader, scout, sniper, support, heavy).Better weapons/clothing which enhance stats or provide special effects can be acquired as mission rewards or bought from the resistance factions. The quality of equipment available scales with the level of support provided to that faction.The maps are varied, as is the difficulty level and the AI is smart enough to target weakened troops in the same way that a sensible player would so the battles are challenging but winnable. I did find myself restarting missions once or twice after making horrendous choices early on. In terms of play style, its very much of its type with the action point system governing fire and movement. Choosing when and if to shoot or use a ‘special’ action makes a huge difference to how a mission plays out as does the use of stealth . A well time ambush can make all the difference.The most novel feature in this game is the morale system (which works for both player and opponents). Any time a character comes under fire it reduces their morale. Characters with low morale have fewer action points, characters with morale of 0 cannot act at all, so the game effectively introduces and executes the idea of covering fire even when there is 0% chance of actually causing harm. This is very helpful if all you need to do is grab an item and run away, or buy time to close in or outflank opponents. It works both ways though so having a leader character who can bolster team morale is essential in most missions.Overall, it’s a pretty well-balanced game. Given the variety of options repeatability should be high particularly if, like me, you gained only a partial success by the time D-Day swung around on your first play through.I hope that DLC is added to this in due course, whether in the form of new missions or new theatres of war. I can see how it could be adapted for resistance in Italy for example though that would be a chunky bit of redesign.Until then I’m going to dive back in to France 44 and see if I can do better for the boys on the D-day beaches second time around.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is okay. I would give it around 6.5/10. If you like turn based tactics and enjoyed games like X-Com or Silent storm this might be your cup of tea. Tactical gameplay is decent but lacks some important options. First of all you cant shoot through cover if your soldiers cant see the enemy. Secondly the morale mechanic (enemies remain passive if their morale is broken) is extremely overpowered and hence pretty cheesy. All you gotta do is focus fire on an enemy and pretty much regardless of strength you will render him help- and defenseless. Also the skills your soldiers can acquire feel rather underwhelming. The only good skill being the ability to movbe after an attack. All in all I would still recommend C:F44 simply because you get a decent game with working mechanics on a tactical combat and strategic ressource management level. _childDocuments_.review: I would give this game a B-. With the caveat that it is  perfectly in my sweet spot for genre (I am basically a WW2 and turn based tactics junkie). If you are less than enthralled with this combination, I believe you will get significantly less mileage and it will be a C or less, depending on how Type-A you are.The game is reasonably entertaining. It tries to do a lot of things that are worth doing. It doesn't dramatically fail at many of them, but nor does it dramatically succeed at many of them.  So comparing it to a rock star game like X--COM would be bold indeed. Yes it has action points and a campaign. It has gear and you level up and get new skills. But the execution  under those surface bullet points is just worlds away in terms of sophistication and depth (from X-COM). And worst of all for the hard core gamer, replay-ability will have to be rated at quite low with the small, fixed number of scripted missions on non-random maps. By the third time through you are going to have seen all the missions, maps and bad guys. And even at a very leisurely pace a play through took me 30 hours -ish on Normal difficulty.  The fact that the DLC has ONE new map for 7 bucks (Canadian) tells you what you need to know on this score ...So, no big complaints from me. I got my money's worth and as a WW2 tactics obsessed gamer scratched my scratchy-est itch. But only for three weeks / 57 hours. Feels like if they tried a little harder they could have had a really good game. Not great, but good.

_childDocuments_.review: Dear Absolutely Games,You have made a real tactical gem here; please let me actually play it. Your assault missions are an absolute blast, and if your game was 50% assault missions, I would love it. With it being 75%+ ambush and stealth missions where none of your innovations shine, I find it deeply frustrating to play.When Classified: France 44' is working, it's tons of fun! Lining up an angle for your heavy to break the morale of multiple enemies at once, allowing him to shoot again, and setting up your sniper to pick them off is tons of fun. Choosing between polishing off the last few reinforcements from wave 2 or setting up a kill zone for wave 3 is similarly enjoyable.More Pros: The classes feel both unique and quite balanced. On the hardest difficulty, enemies are tough, threatening, and yet still manageable with strong tactics. No permadeath makes the game forgiving, while injuries make me care about playing well up to the last turn. I enjoyed choosing my path through the broad skill trees, and the strategic layer was a bit shallow for my taste but reasonable.The Cons: About 66% of gameplay is spent in stealth, which is a totally different, much worse game inside the game. The only apparent solution seems to be doing just enough stealth to make the mission possible before going loud, but it's extremely difficult to know when that would be.I would pay for a Assault Mission Pack DLC, but as it stands, I am throwing up my hands and quitting this game halfway through.

_childDocuments_.review: While the game isn't perfect, it's a blast to play and any fan of X-Com type games should love it. IMHO it is well worth the price! You'll find yourself taking low % shots because even a miss can be a big help if it pins down a tough opponent. If there's ever an X-Com 3 I hope they implement something similar. The strategic layer is by far the weakest part of the game. I think I won my first campaign, got an 87% score on medium diff, but it was just barely enough? D-Day was successful at least but the bar is set pretty high for a "good" victory where you feel like your team made a big difference. And I have no idea how I could have improved my score, think the game should give more guidance on how to make the most of your missions. And purchasing gear is kind of annoying too, wish it was more streamlined and less gamey... Why can't a Brit wear French trousers or hats? A minor annoyance, I'll admit. _childDocuments_.review: I'll draw a parallel between this game and xcom since they share some similarities. For context I only played xcom 2 and I'm about 18 missions in in CF44. This game is superior to xcom on many levels imo.The action and mouvement system especially has more granularity and is miles ahead here. Xcom is very rigid in that regard, almost boardgame like. You move and take an action or sprint. In CF44 you can move, take some actions, move again and go on until you run out of action points (AP) or you're doing some turn ending action. This means there is a great range of skill you can unlock and then use during your missions, some being more AP hungry than others.When a mission goes poorly in xcom I often feel a bit robbed. Because of the rigidity of the system it often comes down to the luck of the hits. While in CF44 you always feel like you could have optimised your movement and your skills usage better thanks to the granularity of the system. It feels like a puzzle you're trying to solve in the most efficient way.The moral mechanic in CF44 also plays a role into that. When shooting at an enemy you automatically apply moral damage whether you hit or not. It adds more consistancy since it's not luck based and you don't feel as awful as in xcom for missing. It also adds another layer of strategy and player agency which is great. Of course it also works against you so you need to be careful.Outside of the missions xcom is superior tho. The map in CF44 doesn't have many interesting choices for you to make compared to the ship in xcom. I also find the story and writing more appealing in xcom. Longevity might also be an issue in this game, the campaign seems a bit short and due to the ww2 setting the enemy and equipment variety is not on par with xcom.Overall a great experience. I definitely recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Finally a turn based tactics game set in WW2 - I know there are a few others out there, but so far in the time I have played it, it seems to have been done right.  Enjoying it thus far and I plan to play this to the end.  If you're a history/WW2 buff and enjoy turn based, this should appeal to you.  You could always try the demo first like I did.I have only had one issue which was during an enemy turn, the game seemed to have stopped and stuck on the enemy's turn - had to exit out and lost my progress, which sucks because it was a lengthy stealth mission - oh well, hopefully a patch can fix that.  Otherwise, fun game and I don't think I have scratched the surface of it yet.  Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: At the moment I only have 2.5 hours into Classified: France '44, but I am just so impressed by this game and especially its improvements to the familiar tactical systems I'm used to seeing in games since XCOM.The main thing I would cite is the improvement in overwatch, after placing a soldier on overwatch you get to choose which moving target you want to shoot at or even to not shoot at all if the options are too low probability which is just something that needs to become standard across the turn based tactics genre. I can't tell you the amount of times I've been annoyed about an XCOM soldier wasting an overwatch shot because the first enemy to move was the hardest one for them to hit instead of another unit that had to move later in the turn.The suppression system is also an important innovation in giving you a reason to take shots that are low percentage too and getting benefits even from missed shots. I like the stealth, I like the art design, I like the sense of the era, so far I just think it's excellent.I've only played a handful of missions and I don't know yet if the characters are more likely to grow on me or if I'll find them annoying by the time I finish the campaign. At the moment it is a game I can see playing through multiple times and that is something that I find myself saying very, very rarely(I still haven't finished Jagged Alliance 3 for instance)The one thing I would say against it is that I don't know how well it's optimized for less powerful computers, my laptop struggled with the demo and I've been using GeForce Now to play the full game, so I don't know if the optimization problems have been addressed since the demo. But if you have a computer to handle it or the connection to stream on GeForce Now, then I simply can't recommend it highly enough.

Classified: France '44 is a new turn-based strategy game, set in World War II during the desperate months leading up to the Allied invasion of France in June 1944.

Take charge of a special-ops team of Allied commandos and French resistance fighters. Recruit elite operatives to build your squad, then engage in a sweeping campaign of sabotage and destruction. Deal with competing factions to build the resistance network and strike at German targets deep in occupied territory. However, the more chaos you cause, the more you'll draw the merciless attention of the Gestapo secret police.

In exciting missions inspired by the exploits of the Allies and French, the game expands on turn-based tactical concepts, bringing authentic World War 2 combat to life.

_childDocuments_.review: As a lifetime fan of this genre & this series, I've played this game to death for the last twenty years, starting with the GameBoy Advance handheld version & then moving onto the big screen with emulators. This has always been the best  Double Dragon game, only being held back by its lack of local co-op due to it being a link-up GBA game (something emulators struggle to emulate), an issue that has finally been resolved with this new version.While recent games in the series like Double Dragon Neon & Double Dragon Gaiden are lots of fun, they never attempted to recreate the feel of the original arcade game, whilst modernising the mechanics & ironing out the issues expected in a game made back in 1987. in 2003 Atlus did just that, with what could be considered an Extended Edition remake of the original Arcade game. They just took everything that was great about the original Arcade game & married it with extra levels, enemies, weapons & moves introduced in later sequels, the NES home versions & Super Double Dragon. The result is what to me has always felt like the definitive Double Dragon experience.The graphics may look a lot more rough than modern beat em ups but the sprites are huge & dynamic. Gameplay in beat em ups hasn't hugely evolved in the last twenty years & you'll struggle to find a game in this genre with tighter controls than DD Advance. The fighting mechanics & button layout may appear strange at first, but unlike most beat em ups that rely on single button combos & special move buttons, DD Advance has a deep, engaging & highly versatile variety of moves for every situation. While it lacks the visual flashiness of recent beat em ups, it more than makes up for it with highly-efficient combat mechanics. Skilled players can really put on a show with the fighting moves on offer here. Probably the only beat em up I've played that really makes you feel like Bruce Lee.There's some improvements that could be made. No online multiplayer, survival mode is only single player & at the end of the day it is only a port of the GBA game, but for the price point you can't argue with it. Arc need to patch this as the Scoop Moto billboard on Stage 1 has been greyed out (presumably for copyright reasons) when they could have literally replaced it with a picture of a different car. Anything would look less ugly & lazy than a grey box.So a must-buy if you're at all a fan of beat em ups. If you know the game well you'll be happy to finally play it co-op without the restrictive GBA link-up, & new players will get introduced to a far more accessible & fun version of the most influential beat em up of all time. Now if only Arc Systems can release the 2011 iPhone game, or Double Dragon Zeebo.
_childDocuments_.name: Double Dragon Advance

_childDocuments_.review: Double Dragon Advance is the best Double Dragon game ever made. If ArcSys was smart, they'd iterate on this for any future sequels. It's the pinnacle of sandbox brawlers. Freeform combo systems without a reliance on canned dial a combos (which never work well in games vs mobs) , environmental interaction/manipulation, and enemy behavior changing up so that no run is the same, and you can get them to take each other out means the game is fresh across countless replays. Add in the survival mode, and there's tons of gameplay to be wrung out of this game. In terms of the overall package, it's still a GBA game at the end of the day, but you can bump up the resolution to 1080p and add in scanline options to take the edge off some of those giant pixels. Minor quibble on these options for me is the game wasn't designed for a CRT, rather a dim LCD panel, so an overlay that better approximated the true design intent behind the game would be nice as well. Three aspect ratio options are offered with one of them being fill meaning there's only two useful options. Audio options are weird. You can opt to crush the highs or the lows if you want. (Simulating covering the GBA speaker with the palm of your hand or something?) The enhance audio option is very welcome however since the base GBA audio is on the scratchy side. In all, its a functional albeit spartan package supporting an excellent game that's well worth getting if you like beat 'em ups at all. Note: As of the time of this review, the game runs at an uncapped frame rate, so you will have to cap the frame rate to 60fps if your monitor has a refresh rate higher than 60hz. Annoying, but fixable with quick tweaks in your respective GPU's control panel.

_childDocuments_.review: I never played this on the GBA but I'd heard it was good, so I got it on sale. To me, who grew up playing the original NES game and the arcade version, this feels basically like a middle point between those two versions. It looks and plays a bit more like the original arcade game, but it kind of feels sort of clunky like the NES version. I dug it, it was a bit of nostalgia-fueled fun, for sure.
_childDocuments_.name: Double Dragon Advance

_childDocuments_.review: I remember this game from coin-ops, dreamt of being able to play it on my Atari 65XE, what was impossible, obviously. I remember how disappointed I was when I saw a C64 version (?), that did not look like coin-op version at all. I remember being able to play it on PC using MAME. So, from this point of view this is a great game, bringing back tons of memories and I definitely recommend it for players like me. On the other hand, the game is ancient - ancient graphics, ancient animations, ancient mechanics, very short also. It IS a legend but not a game to play today, there are many much better fighting games and I doubt that anyone used to playing modern games will have much fun with Double Dragon today.
_childDocuments_.name: Double Dragon Advance

_childDocuments_.review: For over three decades, both the Double Dragon Advance and Super Double Dragon have been hailed as the epitome of the Double Dragon series. Fans can buy the six-in-one Double Dragon Collection physical box for Switch, containing the following classics: Double Dragon, Double Dragon II: The Revenge, Double Dragon III: The Sacred Stones (all in English version), as well as the currently available Double Dragon IV.

name: Beat Slayer
detailed_description: Beat Slayer is a roguelite hack n’ slay game like no other. Instead of just being in the background the music takes centre stage. Join Mia, a badass music lover and crafty tinkerer, as she battles hordes of robots in a dystopian 90s-inspired Berlin. There’s only one rule: Fight to the rhythm! Every move you make has to match the rhythm of the soundtrack. Fail to do so and you’ll pay the price. No button mashing, no frantic inputs. Only smooth and skillful gameplay will lead to your victory against the waves of different enemies and imposing bosses! Show them your moves! Leverage Mia’s nimble move set and decide within seconds which of your moves you should use. Dash to engage or disengage? Attack to build up your drive bar or spread your status effects? Kick your enemies against walls or into each other? The choice is yours! Slay it your way! Each run plays differently and is influenced by your playstyle and your thrill for risks, but also by your starting weapon, your chosen upgrades and your growing skill set. Berlin Attitude Rely on your unconventional team of rebels as you navigate through a robot-controlled and corrupted Berlin. Discover the city's diverse locations, from underground bunkers to towering rooftops, while your allies assist with weapons, upgrades, and valuable insights. Get in the flow! Put on your headphones, sync with the beat and dive more and more into the action to enter the “flow state”. Don’t think and just play. Let the music guide you and create your own symphony of destruction round, after round, after round!

_childDocuments_.review: Every round in BeatSlayer is a truly amazing experience. There is just something in rhythm games that's keeping me on the edge of my seat, hopefully hitting every beat, repeat after repeat. Okay, sorry about that. This game really is a lot of fun though, albeit being a tad bit short due to a smaller budget. Yet, instead of putting more meaningless content into BeatSlayer just to make it last longer, the focus was put on polished animations, sound and fluidity. Evil music mastermind Dietrich is sending his brain wave radio from the Berlin Tower ─ The Fernsehturm ─ to control every citizen, literally making them dance to his tunes. One of his captives, Toni, is the brother and closest family to our heroine Mia, who is desperately trying to free him from Dietrich's evil clutches. Between her and the tower-top crawls, flies and drives an army of evil robot henchmen, determined to put Mia down. I love this setting. Choosing urban Berlin as a rhythm playground feels both unique and fresh. Seeing the subway driving through Friedrichstraße while smashing some robot faces is just priceless. Being from Germany myself, I laughed along the punchlines, but I acknowledge that not knowing anything about German pop culture makes some jokes feel rather pointless. Still, the writing is pretty clever, repeatedly using musical catchphrases that serve the general theme. Frankly, you either love or hate the gameplay, there isn’t much room in-between. You move, hit, slice and kick to the groove, hopefully chaining enough beats together to enter a state called Tanzrausch. Once entered, your damage improves and many abilities offer increased potential. If you’re not able to feel the rhythm, the whole game could become a chore. Sure, there are plenty of accessibility options like a metronome, a rhythm bar and other useful features but if you’re having trouble staying in , BeatSlayer turns into an immensely hard game. Buildwise I found myself sticking to damage-over-time abilities and shield regenerates, due to the fact that raw damage attacks were hard to apply in more hectic combat scenarios, especially the final boss. That’s not to say that other routes weren’t viable but I felt that letting the dots do most of the work also helped with staying on the beat. If you want to explore different ways to finish, you can. Easily. As it is common for other rogue-lites, unlockable talents improve various aspects of Mia. Here however, the player is able to increase the chance in-category, guaranteeing the likelihood of for example, Virus Power-Ups throughout the run. I love how this makes changing playstyles less of a gamble and respects the players time. The soundtrack is amazing. It feels like there are only a handful of different tracks but they all come in variations, mirroring both the stage you’re in and the intensity thereof. 80s synthwave and straightforward kicks clash with EDM, guitar riffs and even live orchestration to keep your head bumping and axe swinging respectively. If you want to check it out, this is my favorite track:BeatSlayer offers quality over quantity with a rough game time length of 8-14 hours, depending on your skill level and need to unlock all achievements. The gameplay feels tight, responsive and rewarding, alongside a kick-ass soundtrack. If you’re using a bluetooth headset, I recommend following the game’s advice to adjust the latency accordingly to avoid frustration though.Personally, this has become one of my favorite rogue-lites of recent years, both in terms of replayability and entertainment factor. Sure, there isn’t as much of a story compared to genre-giant Hades but Mia still got the moves like Zagreus.

_childDocuments_.review: Byterocker's best game so far. Played it on the gamescom 2023 and 2x during the SteamNext Festival and super enjoy it. Its a rhythm game that feels like Hades and Hi-Fi Rush made baby... (but with a much smaller project budget, obviously). For me, it is the perfect game to play in between. Pros:Addictive game loop, great voice acting, EDM, Berlin setting, Currywurst, Roguelite, rhythm, art style, good progression system.Cons: Unfortunately there seems to be only one song so far, "rhythm feedback" could be a bit more "omnipresent" in the game.Overall, though, highly recommended to anyone who likes rhythm and indie hack and slay games. While playing I thought this would be a perfect game for the Steam Deck, but so far I have not tried it on the deck. (@Devs is it playable on the Steam Deck?)

_childDocuments_.review: Beat Slayer is an instant classic and something you should pick up immediately. It's a bit like Hades meets Hi-Fi Rush in what I hope is a blossoming A"Rhythm Action" genre where rhythm gaming is continuously added to more and more other genres. It's a game that feels fair, balanced, and scrappy as hell, and it deserves your attention.
_childDocuments_.name: Beat Slayer

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game for $13 during the Steam Rhythm Game sale.Overall, I enjoyed my time with the game. It took me just under 8 hours to complete the story (5 loops total).If I had to compare this to another game, I would call it Rhythm Hades. The gameplay is very responsive and feels good, the music is great (but limited), and the story is enough to get you by. The upgrade choices during a run and outside of a run aren't super deep, but they were enough to keep me interested.I don't know how long the devs plan on supporting this game, but if they make any updates, I would love to see more stages, more songs, and deeper upgrade paths. I'm definitely going to keep an eye on them in case they make a sequel to this game. This game has great bones and has a lot of potential to grow into a spectacular game.
_childDocuments_.name: Beat Slayer

_childDocuments_.review: Game is the good kind of addictive, you may fail often, but you just wanna keep on going and get better. Playing to the beat is a lot of fun, especially because the music is great. If you love electronic music, this is a must buy. Roguelite, action hack'n'slay and rhythm is a great combination of genres and I don't understand why nobody ever tried it before.
_childDocuments_.name: Beat Slayer

_childDocuments_.review: What a great game!It really dragged me in and I didn't want to put the controller down. At first I thought the story wasn't for me, but the characters are so well written, voiced and illustrated that I really enjoyed it. The cinematic hooked me immediately and Mia is just very likeable!The gameplay is also really fun. The combination of rhythm-combat and roguelike works well and I kept finding myself wanting to start another run and another run ^^Several times I had a strong power fantasy when I got my favourite skills and ended up destroying a bunch of enemies.I can really recommend it! Try it out and see for yourself!

_childDocuments_.review: Great game - for those on steam deck this runs great at 60 FPS!Couple of critiques that I had throughout my time that detracted from the experience I just want to share so hopefully these can be implemented in future:- There definitely feels like some memory leak exists as game gets choppy after 45 min- In game controller customisation is not a thing (have to commit to a workaround)- Game concepts and options are not explained very much in terms of further details - need a show more details button to showcase damage scaling, tick rate etc- The permanent upgrade options feel very one dimensional - "do 5% more damage with basics" and lack of build defining changes will hurt the games long term replayabilitySo far I am definitely enjoying the game and hope these changes are made to make the entire experience even better!

_childDocuments_.review: Love the beat. I am terrible at roguelike games. I always miss the beat. (But I still enjoy it. and will keep playing it.)The story is simple & so are the characters but since the gameplay loop is pretty memorable and nice and the music gets me carried away I absolutely recommend it.What I particularly like is the game's attention to detail. There are LOTS of construction sites, graffitis, trash, kebab shops and late night kiosks (all things that can be seen very often in Berlin) and I immediately felt at home :D

_childDocuments_.review: Great experience. Soundtrack feels great, controls and feel are okay, you have interesting characters to talk with at the base. You'll eventually get 3 weapons to choose from. This and the variety of different power-ups allows for the combat to feel fresh most of the time.If you want to get the good ending though, you'll have to play some additional content. And I wish it was a tad easier. Robots at the very end have too much hp, which makes fights feel more slow and boring when compared to before. Also If after 'main' gameplay I felt incredible about the game, my emotions got more washed out the longer I played. Had additional content for the best ending been a bit shorter - it would've been better.

_childDocuments_.review: Beat Slayer is a combination of rhythm game and roguelite that feels like a blend of Hades and Crypt of the Necrodancer. If you are a fan of games of this genre then you'll likely enjoy trying out this game!The rhythm mechanics of the combat took a little bit to get used to, but the game does a pretty good job introducing different techniques and skills. I personally played it using keyboard and mouse without any issues, so I'd say it's up to your own preference whether you play using controller or keyboard and mouse. Something to note though is that you should make sure to calibrate your audio/video input to adjust for any delays.Overall, I've been enjoying this game a lot. The music is lovely and the gameplay loop is pretty addicting. If any of the stuff I've mentioned catches your attention then I definitely recommend picking up this game (or at the very least try out the demo)!
_childDocuments_.name: Beat Slayer

_childDocuments_.review: Some of the best fun I've had in a long time. Best way to describe this is if Hades had a baby with Metal Hellsinger. The combat is super intuitive and most importantly, fun. My Fiance who has zero rhythm even managed to pick the game up and keep her Tanzrausch (Dance Frenzy) going, so don't let the fact of needing to keep rhythm put you off. 10/10 would recommend
_childDocuments_.name: Beat Slayer

_childDocuments_.review: Beat Slayer is an amazing game. Its Berlin backdrop pulses with electronic music, graffiti and interesting choices. The rhythm-driven gameplay? Addictive. Quality seeps from every pixel and keeps you in a constant flow-state Berlin awaits, and the beat never stops. 🎵Verdict: 9/10 – If you are into infused rhythmy-based games and rogue-likes, Beat Slayer is totally for you 🎶Tip: Make sure to calibrate your audio/ input / video in the menu first - to make sure you really hit the beat.
_childDocuments_.name: Beat Slayer

_childDocuments_.review: I love rhythm games but previously did not like roguelikes. Well guess that was because I had a bad start - Beat Slayer is motivating and fun every time, even though the harder difficulties are no jokes! The weapons are all unique and fun, randomized upgrades all feel great and when combining them, it makes you feel really powerful. This game mastered both making you feel good after a really tough stage and making you feel good when you are overpowered and just having a run crushing hundreds of robots to pieces. Also, I like the theme and the characters you meet between runs are all likable and have plenty of dialogue so you don't get repeated phrases all the time. Minor complaint: The game could use a few more permanent upgrades. It might make you overpowered though so not sure what I would like to see that would not make the game unbalanced.Oh and... almost goes without saying as it's the basis for everything but the soundtrack of this game is great! Absolutely worth listening to for dozens of hours.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice roguelike with a good balance of difficulty, short but interesting story and characters and satisfying gameplay. 2 things that could be impoved. 1) Main character lines repeat a bit too much since she is saying them at the start of every fight.  2) would be interesting to see moreweapon specific upgrades

_childDocuments_.review: Great Vibe and Game Idea with a couple of hickups. I will definitly keep on playing.Two things I noticed right from the beginning:1. Although there is a calibration option for users with bluetooth headsets, the range is not enough at all. You can adjust timings from -50 to +180ms. My headset usually has around +200-300 ms delay, so it is just not playable with bluetooth headsets2. The second boss is a lot harder than other bosses, also later stages. What makes this especially hard is its ability to have shields and its short time span to actually do damage while still moving away. I don't know if the actual health is more, but it definitly feels like it because you are held up 50% of the time killing bots during your attack phase

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommend this game.Have not finished the game yet, and if anything changes then i will let you know.TLDR: For now amazing Rogue Like with Hades/Diablo style combat that you have to play on a rythme. I played the demo very early in. Where I had a bunch of complaints of the game. Especially the feel it had. Problems with the timing where very noticable. Buttons for keyboard play felt weird and abonormal.ALL, litterally every single one of my complaints is fixed. The timing is now incredibly good to do, even if you have like timing issues you can change the timing of the music to fit for you ears. I noticed that i tend to press it consistently a little early so I just fixed that with the calibration settings. Great quality of life feature.The voice acting is amazing. Love the characters their very diverse and interesting.Setting is in distopian germany, right after the fall of the wall during the cold war.But then in a steampunkish setting with a bunch of robots that you have to fight.Love the artstyle too.Combat feels great, Have several weapon options you slowly unlock.Also bunch of fun achievements added, that are very reachable for even casual players which is a surprising change of pace for me. Music is great, no complaints there. Very nice beat its great to press buttons on.I do wish, they added a bit more variety. Most of the music feels very samey. (btw there is quite a bit of music its just all the same vibe/style)Have also the same issue with the maps. Technically this makes sense since its all in distopian berlin. But i would have loved to see like more biomes even within the city setting. And within those biomes a larger variety of music. Especially within a rythme game. I hope they keep expanding this game for a bit add a bit more dept to itThe game has potential for an DLC or 2 to give me just more to do.The only big critism/Con i have:I wish i could change my button settings to things i prefer.I would love to use my side mouse buttons for example to make things just a bit easier to execute. Perhaps change the dodge button to spacebar see how that feels for me etc. Just play around.Especially within rythme games its very important controls feel comfortable allow players to just set their own stuff. I ended swapping to controler, Which plays amazing no complaints there. But still also would have liked to swap certain buttons around. Would have liked the ultimate to be on RB for example rather then the Y button. All in al absolutely great indie game.100% worth the 20 bucks absolutely worth the price.If you enjoy Rythme games GET THIS GAME you will love itIf you enjoyed Hades GET THIS GAME you will love itIf you are a more casual player this games difficulty isnt insane so its also for you very playable!(PS. it aint easy its not an auto play game. But its very doable once you start grasping the controls)

name: Road 96: Mile 0
detailed_description: Road 96: Mile 0 is a Narrative-Adventure game with a musical component created by DigixArt, the French studio behind the successful Road 96, 11-11 Memories Retold and 5 Pegases Awards winner. Published by Ravenscourt, players will alternate between the roles of Zoe and Kaito, two teenagers with different backgrounds and beliefs. They live and explore White Sands, a luxurious condominium where Petria´s elite reside and where Kaito´s parents work. Zoe is one of the characters of Road 96. She comes from the rich side of the city and her father works for the government. Kaito, a character from Lost in Harmony, lives in the less privileged area. They're good friends, but that could all change quite soon. Their journey in Road 96: Mile 0 will challenge their friendship and everything they believe in. They say money doesn’t buy happiness, nor friendship. These teens are dreamers and they are going to learn where they belong. Will they remain friends? Road 96 World Understand the previous event of Road 96 and what made Zoe flee from her home. Play as Zoe and Kaito to shape the evolution of their fate. Besides this, you will run into many of the colorful characters from Road 96. Get to experience another side of the troubled country of Petria. It's All About Friendship This is a story about conflict and difference of opinion between two friends. Zoe and Kaito come from two different worlds, but they are unified by a powerful friendship. They will face many challenges, can they overcome them? Musical Rides The musical segments of the game are a real emotional experience that put you into inner worlds of Zoe and Kaito. You will have to make choices and ride and dodge to find your way through these beautiful psychedelic trips.
