_childDocuments_.review: A worthy successor to the previous game, reiterating on the formula by introducing a rougelite twist akin to the last game's DLC. However, the humor falls flat compared to the first game, akin to the modern Marvel "well, this is awkward" and "I TALK LOUD SO I'M FUNNY" type. The soundtrack is great, the gameplay is responsive although sometimess the aiming seems somewhat off, the final boos fight/late game stretch is a slog where a mistake or two sends you back quite a ways. Troony toons propaganda showed in nonsensically, appearing even in the final boss. However, there's some irony in Turnip Boy fighting and defeating the extraterrestrial last boss that shoots necromorph lasers, which probably gave me a chuckle along with one sidequest where a character sends a response to another one in a letter on which only "based" is written. Other than that, there's barely any humor to be had in a game that takes itself none too seriously.

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting followup to the first game, going from metroidvania-like to rogue-like, but still maintaining a similar feel. Expect a similar amount of content with the same kind of cute/amusing tone-deaf humor/seriousness of the first game. This might have been meant to be played with mouse/keyboard because joystick controls are somewhat awkward, but playable. The game loop is kind of addicting, but with weird pacing and quick ramp-ups in how quickly you earn money (probably to prevent it from overwhelming the turnip boy style as a sequel). This makes sense, because it is by no means a serious roguelike, but an adventure game like turnip boy but with a rogue-like twist. The way familiarization with the map factors into gameplay is kind of cool, and questlines are honestly not bad. Short and sweet again!

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, similar to the first Turnip Boy game but the story is continued from the ending and it's now a roguelite. Generally, the game is very good, it has all of the elements of a basic roguelite with the funny writing and characters, and it's generally a very short game, which is what I expected (I 100% the game in 6.5 hours) but it's still an important note. The downsides are that it doesn't have much variety to the runs in ways that really makes roguelikes shine, so in that way I think it's slightly worse than the first game simply based on the genre not quite matching what they were going for. I ended up getting tired of the gameplay near the end of the game, so it's good that the game is as short as it is. It feels like the game itself was only made to last until exactly until the end of the game, it doesn't overstay its welcome and by the end of the game you feel like you're kind of done with playing it, not very many games can accomplish that imo. Most games I either constantly want more of after the game is over or are too long and I get tired of them before I beat it, so compared to those, this is a fairly perfectly paced game for what it is. Personally, I don't think this game is quite worth $15, so I would wait for it to go on sale (like I did when I bought this a couple days ago), I just think that the game doesn't have quite enough content for $15 for me. On the other hand, buying the game at full price supports the developers more by giving them more money, so if you're wanting to do that, feel free to ignore my advice lol

_childDocuments_.review: Short and sweet. My boyfriend and I had a good time playing through this together. Each quest was charming and characters never got stale. I was a little frustrated that there was no way to guarantee finding the last specific elevator rooms. but it wasn't a hassle and it isn't like the necessary parts of the game were locked behind certain elevators. It took me less than 8 hours to 100% this game on a completely casual playthrough with plenty of tom♥♥♥♥ery, while on the harder difficulty (which was much more fun to play on since it gave my lack of skills an actual challenge!). I noticed a review that mentioned that one of the quests that requires you to kill a number of the cops in the game was too cumbersome and took too long. This doesn't really make sense because the enemies spawn really consistently once the timer hits 0, and it was no issue during my playthrough, and took no additional time to complete.Tl;dr- Cute art, creative writing, and decently engaging gameplay. Was honestly really fun to 100% and perfect if you're looking for a game to play through casually. Not much replay value, but I don't really think the first game was selling that point, and neither is this one.

_childDocuments_.review: It's good! I really didn't enjoy the ending but honestly it didn't take away from the fun of the rest of the game. The music slaps and is just kinda awesome. Big gaming.My main complaint is that there doesn't seem to be any obvious way to replay the game without messing with some files. Sometimes I find myself wanting to replay the game for funny, but there's no clear way to do that. Maybe it's just a limitation, or the devs just didn't want you to replay it, but with how short the game is, I would like to be able to go back and replay it every once in a while.That's kinda another thing. I don't regret my purchase or regret playing the game, but without a way to go back through the game, the endgame feels pretty stiff and unremarkable, which kinda sucks when there's no way to go back to a point before the endgame without messing around with your files or something. I really enjoyed the gameplay, but without the ability to clear your save and play the game through again, you don't really get to enjoy it all that much before you're stuck in the endgame.Also, thematically I think this game is definitely weaker than the theming in Turnip Boy Commits Tax Evasion. (Pretty major spoilers for both games ahead. Skip this part if you don't want spoilers for both games.) All that being said, this is not a negative review. There are soo many things I really enjoyed about the game that I just can't really remember specifically since I forgot to write my review right after I finished the game. _childDocuments_.review: Pros:-Adorable graphics and art style-Directly follows the previous game (Turnip Boy commits Tax Evasion)-Story is fun and silly but also unexpectedly deep-Different weapons offer different play styles-Fun little arcade style game that's easy to pick up and play at any point-Focuses much more on the combat portion than the previous game, making it more action packedCons:-Some missions are tedious to complete due to the randomness of the elevators. It could takes multiple runs just to find the one room you need to turn in a mission-You can dismantle weapons you find to provide additional weapons that you can take into the bank with you, but there's not that many so it only takes like an hour or two to max it out-Could just be a me problem but it took a while to learn the layout and not get lost all the time-Focuses more on the combat than the previous game, so if you don't like that then you may not enjoy this as muchTL:DR;Great game, really enjoyed all of it. Art style and characters are adorable and charming, and the randomness/arcade style of the game makes it super easy to pick it up and play it for a few minutes or hours. If you liked the previous game (Turnip Boy commits Tax Evasion) then you're sure to enjoy this just as much if not more.

I'm quite a newbie when it comes to these types of games and felt a bit anxious about it involving guns and the game play seemed a bit more difficult to me compared to the first game. However, this sequel did not disappoint. If you are quite new to games like this, I do recommend to start out with Turnip Boy Commits Tax Evasion and then play this game. They are great starter games, they are not too difficult and don't have a steep learning curve. This game also has a lot of humor and it was a joy with lots of funs and giggles for me to play. The music during the final boss battle was terrific, just like it was in the first game and it's so nice that as you progress, the music playlist keeps expanding. If there would be a third installment of the Turnip Boy games, I'd definitely buy it because of how enjoyable these games are. Both Turnip Boy games are the first game I 100% completed and I would recommend this game to all types of players (mostly to newer gamers, but I think more experienced gamers will enjoy these games as well).

_childDocuments_.review: As the description implies, this is a sequel to "Turnip Boy Commits Tax Evasion". The game is set after the events of that game, so go play that one first if you haven't. Where Tax Evasion is more of just a humorous adventure, Robs a Bank is more of the same but in a roguelite-style. The basic gameplay loop is this:- Rob the bank to earn money- Buy upgrades which allow you to survive longer, do more damage and explore more areas- Find boss whilst robbing the bank and beat it- RepeatThe game isn't particularly hard. I don't play games like this often, to for me, most of the difficulty was just getting used to the controls. Despite that,  the exploring, funny quest lines and dialogue, trying out lots of weapons, and more Turnip Boy was a lot of fun. Like the first game, it's as long as it needs to be and fun almost all the time. If you were disappointed by Payday 3, try this game that doesn't take itself too seriously and is also about heists (but also a Turnip Boy).

Even on MAX difficulty-Side characters really dont matter at all, you can ignore almost all side characters and still go trough the game which can feel like its all added to expand the runtime unlike the original where some NPCs were needed to continue the game-As side from the insanely easy gameplay, the bosses are also all a joke, even was able to beat them with starter weapons on my first try which seems a bit disappointing and makes you not really feel good about defeating them, They just feel like another basic enemy.-Without spoilers, the end boss is incredibly disappointing -A lot of the NPCs are so much more boring than the original that I felt like not even caring about anything they said, just waited for the quest to pop up and moved onIn conclusion, should you buy it?For a really watered down version of a dungeon crawler it can be a nice introduction for people who are just starting to play games in this genre.Or it can be nice as a relaxing experience overall if you are looking for something in this genre but just want to relax at the same time.If you are looking for a challenge, this game is not for you as its laughably easy no matter the difficulty Compared to the first game I definitely think the original was way more goofy, funny and an experience compared to this one, this one is more of a brain off, just play kind of game.Either way I recommend the game if its on sale, if not then wager if this kind of game is for you.As for myself, I wish I could pick a mixed button for the recommendation, I don't necessarily recommend it to anyone nor would I not really recommend it. _childDocuments_.review: While it couldn't quite recapture the pure shock and glee of Turnip Boy Commits Tax Evasion, Turnip boy Robs a Bank is a delightful, surprisingly well-crafted roguelike with fantastic music and cute art. Fetch quests can get a little tedious with the randomly spawning doors, and the final boss should definitely skip the dialogue at the start if you die, but a good core loop and some challenging boss-fights make for a solid skeleton to put bits of meme flesh onto. The writing is where I'm underwhelmed - while you may get a chuckle or two from the occasional well-crafted joke, there's not really a ♥♥♥♥-your-pants reveal like the last game, and the fact that all the characters are a few lines of dialogue and a sprite means that very few actually have satisfying narratives alongside their ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. With the shock of the prequel already established and no infinite dungeon for post-game, robbing a bank just isn't as noteworthy as tax evasion, but it's by no means a bad game, and I do hope we see more from this team - just maybe not more turnip boy.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr, this game is very fun, and I recommend it to people who enjoy a cutesy artstyle sprinkled with weapons of mass destruction and a semi-serious storyline.TBRB embraces the silly-yet-dangerous inclinations of our boi and savior Turnip Boy, and throws them into a game where you must cast morals out of the way for the sake of money...only to realize the bank you were trying to rob was the friends you made along the way.On a more serious note, this game is simple to learn, and the roguelike element is injected into this game in a very interesting way: the map never changes, but the many fixed doors to other rooms or dimensions do.That makes it so you have to actively move around the map and engage in the different areas to find what you're looking for. And while that can be a hassle if you're trying to find the one room that helps you 100% the game (*cough* me *cough*), it helps the game not get old, and always keep you looking around and remembering the fixed door points across the entire map.I beat this game in 8ish hours, and I think it was worth the play. Will you?Go on, rob a bank and find out.You won't.

_childDocuments_.review: It's an alright game, very different from the first in a lot of ways. This outing is more focused on being a roguelite than a zelda like, which I can respect - however it's also not very big or long. There is decent variety in weapons, but you're forced to recycle your weapons in order to get new starting weapons unlocked. Both a good and a bad thing from an experimentation standpoint, but I just chose a favorite early on and did my best to never lose it.I liked the gameplay loop up through the second boss, but the third area being a dark zone was more than a little irritating to see. Couple that with the fourth giving you so much cash that you can instantly max all your cash based upgrades almost the moment you step foot into it, and you've got me going from having fun robbing the place to me questioning why the cash based upgrades have no balance. I went from buying 2 main categories of them, being time and bag size, to maxed on all in a run. Really devolved into a boring mess at that point, I was already strong due to the mechanic of my favorite weapon but getting the cash shops maxed quickly made me far too overpowered on the harder difficulty.Speaking of messes, the side quests can fall into this category. See, every major zone in this game has 2 Elevators, with more kinds of rooms the elevators can be unlocking as you progress. One issue is some side quests require certain variants of certain rooms, so if you aren't checking them regularly and eating up precious time, you're bound to miss some. There's also a massive issue with certain ones - the dialogue in this game is horrendously slow, causing mashing to be a good strategy. The problem with that is if you mash too fast with any quest that has multiple steps, you can lose items permanently. This has happened to me - I've 100%ed the game, but I'm 2 Achievements short due to the Rock Collecting side quest. You get 8 rocks from other side quests throughout the game and turn them in to someone in an elevator room - if you mash through turning in multiple rocks at once, you lose the rock but don't get the progress. I lost 2 rocks this way, and my save file is permanently locked out of full completion due to it.It's got the makings of a decent game, and I'll say I had fun. I still prefer Turnip Boy 1 over it though, the bugs in this hampered my enjoyment between permanently losing out on 100% and having some soft locks that I had to quit out of. The final boss is also a bit of a gimmicky mess. It's a solid game that I think deserves a Mixed rating, but that isn't a thing on Steam. A bit too ambitious and small at the same time in my eyes - it doesn't have the replayability that Roguelikes and Roguelites thrive on, and it definitely needs some more time in the oven. I personally will not recommend it but don't let that stop you if you like Turnip Boy - the humor is still spot on and the characters are enjoyable, I just think that its side quest issues need fixed before I can recommend it in earnest.

_childDocuments_.review: I looooved Turnip Boy 1. To me it was quirky zelda type game with a short playtime, but a ton of character.Turnip Boy 2 is great, but it's different. You will need to attempt going further and further into the bank, bring more money every time, spend the money on upgrades or equipment, allowing you in turn to go even farther, until you get to the end of the game.But i loved it. It's longer than Turnip Boy 1, but i finished it in 6 hours. There were still a couple of secondary tasks to complete. And the ambience is very much in line with the first one.One weird thing : the game only plays in 4:3 aspect ratio. This is on purpose (look at the screenshots), this is their design choice. I'm not sure it makes sense, but you get used to it don't worry about it too much.

_childDocuments_.review: Worth the price! As a fan of these kinds of shooters I have nitpicks below but overall, get it if you liked the original. Everything you liked about it is here and more.Mechanically, it's ok. Turnip is a fast guy, but often you're getting stuck on terrain, or your bullets are hitting said terrain instead of enemies. There's also *heavy* auto-aim, such that your bullets are just zipping right at enemies off the screen. I looked around the menus and it's off, so it must be baked in somehow. Enemies lock on and fire almost before you see them, but health drops are plentiful so you shouldn't be dying much (just kind of frustrating). There's exactly one melee weapon that's worth messing around with, the rest will just get you shot for not much DPS. There's even a dummy in your base for DPS checks so I'm not sure how that happened.There also may be a slight imbalance in the progression systems. I had already unlocked all the weapons and items you get in base, which was the most fun thing to do imo, but the game just kept on going. With the light sense of meta progression gone, really the only thing left to do was complete the tasks, which CAN be fun, but often isn't. Many of the tasks require you to roll specific elevators to find the NPC you need to talk to, which makes it so you can't REALLY blast through all your shortcuts and get to the good zones, you have to check all the elevators to make sure you don't miss the one you need. Several other quests are just grindy kill counts that force you to stay after the time is up just to slay guards as they come down the ropes. I don't think I would have minded as much if there was anything left to grind for. Great ending though :)

_childDocuments_.review: The story continues 2 days after the final boss in the last game (so if you haven't played the last game, I suggest you play it for some context) where apparently a "war" happened and those who survived aren't lucky (I guess: it's not as important as it should've sounded). The leader of the Pickle Gang (from the last game, please play it) recruits several characters plus Turnip Boy to rob the Botanical Bank (Loaded with money and gold) in a rouge-lite/like style of gameplay as opposed to the first game's 2D Zelda style. The elevators are randomized every run but for the most part, quests, bosses, are kinda in the same location. Permanent upgrades make things a little easier. There's a bit of a grind but it wasn't too unbearable (by the time I reached the fix the bridge part, I'd had all the upgrades). Dying will cause you to lose all looted items and if that's too much for you, there's God Mode: which you'll be using on the final segment of the game.The final segment (I'm not calling it a final boss because it isn't a boss that you actually fight) spams enemies, projectiles, and has instant kill attacks (I got hit once and I lost half my health. Max is 6 hearts), cranked on God Mode and finished the game. "Final Segment" not withstanding, the soundtrack is a nice listen plus Bill Collectors Extended, so that's a plus. I'm not a fan of Rouge-lite/like and I'm gonna be honest: this game while I recommend it (with a couple of changes), didn't make me change my mind on Rouge-lite/like Games.Timer thing also kinda blows as it's something I didn't enjoy from Majora's Mask: I don't work well under pressure.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely doesn't have the EXACT same chill vibe as the first game, but it's far more enjoyable in gameplay.There's a timer (I'm sure there's an accessibility option to disable it) for your roguelike-esque runs through the Bank. You essentially get to choose what you prioritize. Want to do nothing but optimize your looting paths and memorizing dungeon layouts? Go ahead, there's no limit on HOW MANY runs you do! Zero timer in that respect.Want to run around and chat with all your foodfolk pals across the bank? Go nuts! No restriction there.There are pretty obvious bosses/obstacles for progression and there's tons of time-saving and headache-preventing features worked into the tasks/progression system. Very easy, very intuitive. I've barely noticed it so far; that means it's working perfectly.I wish there was a more specific branch for researching SPECIFIC weapons (i.e. looting automatics for automatics, shotguns for shotguns etc.) but that would lock down the player into looting enemies for SPECIFIC guns, which would suck. Having it be an XP based system is a necessary evil, in order to make the gun progression feel satisfying.Overall fun!

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10Turnip Boy Robs a Bank is a great sequel to Turnip Boy Commits Tax Evation. It builds on successful concepts and both aexpands and experiments with new ones. However, not everything lands and there are some things I would have liked differently. Let us get into it.Turnip Boy Robs a Bank is a proper sequel. It takes the story and lore from the first game and continues it here, with Turnip Boy choosing to help The Pickled Gang robbing a bank (do not worry, they have a good cause). You run, trip, use fantastically fun weapons and laugh at the world and its inhabitants. This time, however, it is a rogue-lite."A rogue-lite??? But the last game was some sort of Zelda-inspired game", I hear you say. Yes, that is the biggest difference between the games. Each run you go in, cause chaos, get money, progress various objectives and get out before a timer reaches zero. With the money you buy upgrades to make your time in the bank easier and the easier it is the further you progress and unlock new upgrades as well as story-parts. The loop is fun, each run is short and full of whimsical joy.The story is not the most important part here. It is still silly and baseless, with a lot of jokes being grounded in memes or generic tropes. I find it very cute and fun, but it might not resonate with everyone. However, the pace of the game is so hectical due to the timers and action-packed gameplay (sometimes it can feel like a bullet-hell type of game) that I cannot really focus on the story and dialogue. I often find myself scrolling through the dialogues and instantly forgetting what was said due to my focus being required elsewhere (shooting enemies and dodging bullets). You can rarely just stop and appreciate what is around you, and that is a shame.The variety of weapons is impressive. It is so much fun to pick up and experiment with all the silly weapons that are offered and everything feels cool and fresh. Not all weapons are good, and that is okay, that is the point. Maybe you want a challenge, maybe you are desperate and need to make due with what you find. It enables a lot of variety and fun when it comes to tackling obstacles.The soundtrack also slaps hard, sometimes too hard. THe composer gets a big applause from me, great job in making such a great soundtrack for a game like this, it matches the action very well!All in all, this is a three hour game that will net you a lot of fun. It is not perfect but it does not need to be, for what it is I can absolutely recommend it for the price it costs. You will have fun, you will laugh and you will feel challenged by the gameplay. Great job in making this, devs!

name: graveyard keeper
detailed_description: This is an ancient and interesting merge type game Players need to merge three tombstones (or zombies) with the same shape into a higher-level tombstone When all the squares on the chessboard are full, the game ends and you will get a gold coin reward according to the points If you encounter difficulties and cannot merge, you can try to use the round universal merge, or use a bomb. At present, the game is offered to fans as a free product. Therefore, the option to buy gold coins in the game is unlimited (cheating). If you are confused about the difficulty of the game, you can directly buy gold coins in the game for free, and then use gold coins to buy props for customs clearance. In addition, we have retained some 'back doors' of the game 1. Using the right mouse button in the chess board of the game can directly upgrade the object pointed by the mouse 2. Press keypad 1, and then press the left mouse button to automatically generate a zombie 3. Pressing keypad 2 and then the left mouse button will blow up the object pointed by the mouse 4. Pressing the L key on the keyboard will delete all the contents on the chessboard You can also try to use this series of commands to construct an 'interesting' level. Ten years ago, we were trying to make independent games. Unfortunately, the environment was poor at that time, and piracy was rampant. After the game came out, the prison break version was soon released, and the free version was overwhelming. So the game died. Ten years later, after a lot of things, the game has seen the light of the day again. In order to give back to our friends who insisted on supporting us in those years, and to leave footprints in the dusty past, this commemorative version of the game is specially launched for pure commemoration. The comments on this game will be taken into account in the subsequent reproduction products. This game is developed with unity3d 3.5.6, and written with ngui and uscript plug-in visual programming. Now the plug-in has disappeared, and this work is also the masterpiece of this plug-in.

name: Enotria: The Last Song
detailed_description: 'Enotria: The Last Song' is a thrilling Soulsike set in a sun-lit land inspired by Italian folklore and filled with danger. The world has been gripped by the Canovaccio - a twisted eternal play that keeps everything in an unnatural stasis. You, Maskless One, are the only one without a given role and master of your destiny. Defeat the fearsome Authors that created it and free the world from stagnation, by harnessing the power of Ardore. Become the Mask of Change. Summer Souls 3 Main Regions, 40+ hours, more than 100 different enemies Enotria is a beautiful sun-lit land inspired by Italian nature, that hides dark secrets behind its bright facades, and it is up to you to unravel the mysteries of this stunning world. Many Masks, One Face 30+ Masks Don your fallen foes’ Masks to take on their roles, enabling new ways to play, each with its own strengths and weaknesses. Swap between up to 3 customisable Loadouts at any time. Path of Innovators 68 Skills (Unlockable PERKS), with 150+ milions different build combinations Expand your playstyle options through a unique pool of talents in the Path of Innovators. Slot talents into Masks to create custom builds on a single screen, experience a unique system that makes theorycrafting and altering playstyle for each situation easier than ever. Unparalleled Flexibility 30+ aspects to alter your main statistics dynamically Choose strategically which Mask will face the dangers of Enotria and swap between up to three custom loadouts at any time. Each loadout allows you to try out a new playstyle, without the burden of a respec. Alter Reality 3 different type of Rifts Channel the power of Ardore to dynamically alter reality. Swap strategically between environmental states to solve puzzles, reveal secrets, traverse a decaying world and gain a strategic edge in battles. Awaken your Potential 100+ weapons, 7 different weapon classes, 45 spells, 8 parry modifiers Break an enemies posture to enable a devastating riposte attack, which grants you the mighty Awakened buff. Chain kills and swap between Masks to alter the boons you receive to best match the opponent. Key Features: ♦ Wield Ardore to alter the world around you ♦ Stay on the offensive with quicksteps and chainable parries ♦ Strike foes to charge powerful magical Lines ♦ Strategically swap between up to three Loadouts at any time ♦ Break an enemies posture for a devastating attack, granting you a mighty Awakened buff ♦ Reveal the secrets of Enotria to gain Inspiration & unlock new perks in the Path of Innovators

_childDocuments_.review: I highly recommend this game... just not right now. I have been following the development of this game closely for roughly 2 years now, and it was my most anticipated game of 2024. It delivered a bloodborne x sekiro combat system that I absolutely love, along with a good story, interesting lore, and a gorgeous world that I want to explore more of. However, with my bias now being addressed, this game isn't worth the $50 price tag. This is the devs first game, and that unfortunately really shows. The game lacks polish. Features that should have been included in the game on launch day were pushed onto a road map to be released in increments throughout the next year or so. The first big patch on this roadmap is a quality of life patch releasing in November with items that should have been in the game to begin with, and the polish patch is estimated to be released in January. Yes. January of 2025. Then the final planned patch to be released is a moveset expansion and voice actor patch, because for some reason, the game shipped with only 2 or 3 NPCs having voice lines. I don't now why the game was released this early when it should have been released next year. With that being said, I still love this game, but if you are on the edge about it, give it a year and come back to it. I think by then the game will be polished enough (hopefully) to be worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: Most of these positive reviews were probably written during the first area, Quinta. I would recommend that game at that point, honestly. Decent showing. But once you get to the 2nd area, (sunny Greek isles), combat and build variety falls apart as the game forces you into parrying everything 10x or more just to survive.Spells are useless and weak, and the enemies will stagger and stun you to no end unless you're using a fast weapon. There's no way to deal with ranged enemies so you just have to endure them until you can walk up to them (who thought this was fun?), and platforming is a mess. Boss fights in the 2nd area are also a lot clunkier (save for the main story boss). I recommend waiting until you reach that point in the game before you drop a review.I'm at the 3rd region now which is not as bad as the 2nd region and I'm close to finishing the whole game. I can tell you that the game isn't as varied as most early game players think when it comes to combat especially when it just forces you to parry and stack up HP during mid to late game. At $50 I honestly expected less jank and more voiced dialog or at the very least, the ability to change controls. Animations are awkward and feels like early access. Bugs are also aplenty, I even got soft-locked from starting the 3rd region because an elevator bugged out. I also can't seem to disable motion blur even if it's turned off in the settings. It's still there.

_childDocuments_.review: I would love to recommend this game.First, the good:The artstyle is terrific and I love the era and the inspirations. 15th/16th century Italy is not something we get to see pretty much ever in gaming, so seeing that brought to life in a dark soulslike is really cool!The mask idea essentially creating different loadouts is very cool as well, and I like the fact that your mask changes everything about your character. Boss design is also very strong, with interesting style and some very fun situations (I ended up beating up a giant winedrinking monster with a wine bottle sword).Now, the bad:Optimization. I was having constant lag issues on an RTX 4080, on high settings. Even medium still had these issues. This is frankly insane - I can understand having dips now and then during intensive sections, but this was just standing there! Now this is something that can be improved, and I hope it will be in the future.Animations. These are janky, to say the least. Attack animations are serviceable overall, but are often interrupted by themselves or are otherwise weird - attacks will hit when it seems out of reach, or vice versa - and overall the game just feels clunky - forcing you to use faster weapons or else get locked into a stun fest.Enemy consistency. Enemies will sometimes get staggered by attacks, sometimes not, with seemingly very little rhyme or reason for it. It's frustrating, because it means every fight is extra stressful - will this attack be interrupted by my attack, or not? It's a guessing game in the worst way.Quality of Life. So this is a bit of a lump thing, but some other things I found bothersome: The tutorial is...rather awful. It's a very short span of time that absolutely spams you with information and terms, most of which you have no idea what it means. It means you don't end up retaining much of that information, and it feels...frustrating!The second boss is an awesome design - but he's so big his attacks become really hard to see! And knowing where to stand in order to actually get the stagger attack off is a bit of a guessing game. If they had done it like Lies of P, where it actually shows you, it would've been much better.Customizable keybinds. I played on controller, which is fine! But not being able to customize keybinds on release is not acceptable. I'm glad they'll be adding this in soon, but it just makes me confused as to why this wasn't in from the get-go.Overall, I think most issues can be resolved, especially optimization and quality of life. The big issues are the enemies feeling so inconsistent and plain not fun to fight. I'll probably give this game another look in a few months to see if things have improved! _childDocuments_.review: I spent 8 hours playing the demo and now just getting settled into this game. Everything I loved about the demo is here and improved upon.I was a huge fan of Lies of P, and that's what this game reminds me most of (maybe some Dark Souls 3 as well). Combat is smooth, customization is almost infinite like a From Software game, and the lore is very compelling -- makes me want to continue playing to learn more about the world.Relative to the demo, there are opened up new areas even in the first part of the game, so lots of content, lots of side paths and secrets to discover.Graphics are 10/10, and I'm getting 120fps at ultra on a 4090 with DLSS quality. If you're a fan of Lies of P or Dark Souls, you're going to love this game. A long'ish shader compiling like Wukong takes place up front, so I never saw any stuttering.As a side note, it gave me the option to continue from the demo, but the character didn't seem to work, so you'll be starting fresh in all likelihood, which you'll want to do anyway because a bunch of things in the first area were locked off or not there in the demo.EDIT: I completed the game in just under 20 hours, but I clearly didn't get the best ending. Ending was a twist, overall a very very fun game for any fan of the genre so eager to start my second play through.  People reporting bugs are way overstating it IMO. I crashed out over 5x during my first 20 hours of Wukong, and I think I had two crashes here. I got soft locked in Wukong a few times, didn't ever get soft locked here.  Like any 1.0 build it's not perfect, but as good as Wukong was if not better. If you're a fan of Lies of P and DS3, just buy it, you'll love it as this game was made for you.

_childDocuments_.review: I think that this is a very high quality game when you take into account that it is coming from an indie dev team. I feel like folks who are coming to this title from other bigger budget titles might be setting their standards and expectations a bit high, and it is fine if they want to do that. From my perspective, I think it is important to acknowledge that Jyamma has not made a game of this scale before (seriously look up some of the other games that they have made), they are not From or NCsoft, and arguably different standards should be applied when evaluating games from this developer. Why? Well, if they have potential and a supportive fan base, maybe they will make bigger and better things in the future.Why am I recommending this game? Well, first and foremost, I think that they have done a great job with world building, and I find the game's art style to be rather unique and impressive. I also think that the scope of the world from a purely visual perspective is pretty amazing (even if in actuality the game is not necessarily massive in scale). I think that this also makes exploration more engaging. The combat in this game is also significantly better than what you could find in many, if not most, first attempts at making a soulslike game. However, I will acknowledge that the complexity of the animations and some aspects of the parry system are not on par with what you can find in AAA+ titles. I also think the mask system, elemental damage types, and skill loadout systems are relatively unique even if they are not fully breaking the genre's mold.As far as critiques go, I can understand why people do not appreciate the limited move sets (each weapon of a particular type is basically the same with very few exceptions), enemy hit tracking, enemies commonly holding off their attacks, and the amount of bosses that are simply knights. These are all things that happen to be in the game, and it is up to you to determine whether or not you can live with them.**Edit: I will add that there is pretty much no animation canceling, e.g. you cannot attempt a full combo and cancel out of the third hit to parry. This is likely why many folks feel that slower weapons are not viable and part of why folks feel that the combat is clunky. I will agree that this is somewhat irksome because it detracts from the fluidity of the combat and makes it more difficult to focus solely on offense, but it does not ruin the game for me.**There are also a number of critiques that are simply inaccurate. Maybe there are points in the game that feel like a "parry simulator," but I feel like saying that this is all the game is after the second area is an exaggeration. Even if it was true, I can think of at least two games that have been well-received that lean more heavily on the parry mechanic. I also think that heavy weapons are viable, but you might have to be familiar with attack frames and spacing or be good at parrying and/or dodging to use them; it is definitely not the case that long sword is the only viable weapon type. Lastly, performance is great on my PC, and I have worse specs than most of the people complaining about it (who have i9s and RTX 40XX GPUs). Lastly, I will just point that it is incredibly easy to respec your stats and invest in passives that do not relate to your current build, many of the hardest enemies seem like they are optional and/or are meant to be fought after exploring other areas, and a key remapping feature is on the way. Anyway, sorry for rambling. Hope you enjoy the game. If you don't refund it.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: shallow Lies of P style soulslike, decent enough if you want to scratch that itch and get it when on sale.  - combat is decent, very similar to Lies of P with a big focus on parries and stace breaks. - the soundtrack of the game is quite good and never gets annoying, also the ambiance effects you can hear in the background are very well placed and even funny in some instances. - besides some fps drops/stuttering in some specific areas the game runs well on my quite dated by now rig even on ultra settings. - the major areas are huge, easy to get lost in and get very repetitive very fast. - there are a gajilion weapons in the game but every last one of them has the same moveset  based on their weapon category. - the game is really bad at telling you were you should go next and gives you no clue whatsoever on what "quest npcs" want from you most of the time. - the difficulty scaling is all over the place, most enemies are quite easy to deal with untill you get randomly thrown against an incredibly frustrating fight... and then back to joke enemies for another 10hrs. - Heavy weapons are only useable for doing the finisher after you stance break an enemy, also elemental (status?) weapon are way stronger than their non-elemental counterpart;yes even against enemies that resist your weapon element. - there are tons of bugs still in the game, some of the most glaring ones:you can break most bosses ai just by interrupting their "phase change" with a posture break, making bosses walk onto breakable items also does the same thing;game crashing/quitting during a boss fight will respawn you into the boss arena without the boss nor a way to exit, if you are out of "return to checkpoint" items you're hardlocked and have to restart the whole game.Overall the game is decent, you can have fun with it but it pales in comparision to other competing soulslikes.The price tag is way too high for the current state of the game and i wouldnt hold high hopes it will get much better in the future due to some fundamental design flaws.Overall it's a 5.5/10, decent enough to scratch the soulslike itch but i wouldnt advise spending more than 10 bucks for it

_childDocuments_.review: So, after about 30 hours of gameplay and a full cleared game in NG (I'm in NG+ now) this is my review.Graphics and visual design: as everyone says, they're really remarkable, I don't know what else to say... some uncertainty in the distances or secondary details but overall I'm really satisfied.Sounds and music: apart from some repetition, overall very well structured, characteristic, unique and dense.Narrative and themes: if you are cognitively capable of following the plot, it is told really well, deeply and is even worthy of interest. Nothing overly innovative, I admit, but the emotion with which the characters experience things is truly transmitted and shared (incredibly the sort of encyclopedia provided not only doesn't ruin the immersion but allows you to keep track of the quests and the acquired plot notions).Game mechanics: here are the flaws. It took me an hour to get used to it and it was not easy. At the beginning I even had a bit of motion sickness from the camera (I come from 700 hours on multiple accounts on Elden Ring, I wasn't expecting this). The animations of certain attacks/deaths/movements/etc are somewhat sped up x10 and sometimes they either reset or are uncertain, in short not as fluid as any mob you would find on Elden Ring. HOWEVER, after this first hour in which I got used to the game by bending to its rules a bit... I started to have fun. This fun increased from mini boss to boss further and further on until the Final Boss which for me was the most enjoyable of all. I had so much fun that I will do a NG+ for the other ending and the quests that I did not complete.The level design is really well done. Clear, intricate enough, interesting.The overall balance seems well done (using all the game's tools such as masks, items and various weapons). If an optional boss is too strong just go back later (happened once).Playability: in my opinion acceptable and appropriate, it took me 25 hours for the first NG in which I cleaned all the maps and now having done the non true ending I am encouraged to replay it since it's not an endless game, the major and minor boss fights are many and adequately located along the path and it is nice to try different masks/abilities/weapons.These are my two cents.

_childDocuments_.review: Great visuals, thoughtful level design, cool enemies, awesome music... but I can't recommend this. Unlike the Souls games, which value expressive play, this game is highly prescriptive; you need to do the exact thing they want you to overcome each challenge. The optimal way to play is to stand still and time your parries and i-frames perfectly, until you get the chance to deliver a crit. Don't use your attack button in boss fights, it's a trap.Despite all that, the parry window isn't too bad, and this game would still work as a mislabeled rhythm game if the bosses didn't hit for 75-90% of your health most of the time. When did it become illegal to survive two hits in Soulslikes?

_childDocuments_.review: Wait for a small sale. If an OK thumb option existed on steam I would use it. But it is just up or down, for now I'll pick down.Even if my review below is somewhat harsh and critical I want to convey 1 thing. I do hope these devs keep creating, given that this is their first game. Some of them even first game out of university. They have talent for sure and hope they keep going! It is not BAD but I do think games such as Lord of the Fallen or the Surge do things a lot better. I am somewhat enjoying it still but not a game I am wanting to get back to every day. I will finish it but not at a rapid pace.Some pros and cons:Pros: - Looks great, but you have read that 150 times here. It is true though. From textures to lighting, well done. - Runs great actually. Better than most games coming out lately. - This game has HEAL CANCEL. That is too good. More souls likes should implement this. - Level design seems above average. loads of wraparounds and shortcuts.- Atmosphere and art direction (not talking graphics) are pretty interesting and unique in this space. Well executed.- Controls bad? No, they are good. Maybe they are bad on keyboard and mouse but on controller they are as expected for this type of game. Dodge is B like in most other souls-likes. IDK what people are complaining about. No remapping is a problem maybe but not a big deal. Cons:- Enemy animations are just not refined enough. Some are a bit too shaky or glitchy and not smooth at all. Like they did not properly refine them. Reminds me of Dark souls 2 somewhat.- The whole element weakness and strength system is more annoying than fun. Why should my weapon that i invested heavily in be useless against some (often important/strong) enemies? Developers should stop trying to innovate on this idea. - Enemies seem too tanky. Some basic skeletons for example take way too many hits in my opinion. Bosses are also way too tanky for how (un) interesting they are so far. They feel more like endurance fights than actually hard.- THIS is the biggest for me: The parry system and dodging. While good as a general mechanic (feels good enough to do), it falls apart because you still take damage when deflecting... WHY!? And dodging is practically useless in this game. Either make the dodge better as an alternative or make deflecting better. As it is now both are too punishing. - Definitely prefer a traditional armour system over the mask stuff. Not convinced. The passives system being not general passives but "skills" you put in your loadout is also something I do not like. - All the Italian naming of effects and elements are a nice idea but half the time I have no idea what I am looking at (skill issue probably)- EDIT: You have 0 poise or hyper armour, so you constantly get stunned when you want attack or move. It is extremely frustrating with heavier/slower weapons. There is a reason why Hyper Armor was implemented in these games, at least for the big slow weapons. It just works.If this was a 30-35 euro game or so, I would be a bit more lenient, but for 45 it is in the end kind of a tough pill to swallow.

_childDocuments_.review: Switching my review to positive after the most recent update (Oct 3 2024)Increasing attack speed really made the game feel better. They also reduced (heavily in some cases) the number of parries it takes to stagger certain bosses and enemies. This is a huge relief, some late game enemies took dozens of parries to stagger which was incredibly boring and frustrating. Feels much better now without being too easy (though the game is overall still on the easy side).Bugs are still present, but the major progression blocking ones are gone. I expect further tweaks down the line but for now things feel pretty good. The only big problem is the Armonia flask (estus) is bugged, being extremely weak until it's leveled up so high that the game is practically over. I expect this to be fixed in the next update.Again exploration is exceptional. Level design rivals that of Dark Souls 1. Areas are vast and beautiful, with great use of verticality. Combat is now also up to snuff as I said earlier, everything is faster and the game feels more fluid. All weapon types are now completely viable, whereas before the big weapons were not useable in some niche situations due to their slowness.They also increased the rate at which mask lines (spells) charge up, which IMO made a huge difference. You can now use spells from the start of the game to pretty good effect, and they get better as you progress.Basically every aspect of the game was improved, feels much closer to a finished product now. Not all the way there, but far enough along that I don't mind that much. $50 is still a lot of money, but I'm really enjoying the game so to me it's worth it. Will probably play through again after the next major update.Pro tip - if you can get away with it, don't use frame generation. It increases latency which throws off parry timing. It's worth getting less FPS for lower latency IMO.

_childDocuments_.review: A great acting/theatre focused Italian themed Souls-like with great visuals and sounds great.I think this is probably the first ever souls-like that I cannot recommend (yet) as it really lacks polish, and while some "jankiness" is fine and tolerable, when the lack of polish is just very global it's very hard to recommend to anyone. Some of this ranges from just some textures and models being off and positioned incorrectly and lacking collision, to some animations on both the player and enemies just feeling extremely off, to the point of affecting gameplay. And I'm not talking about an enemy with a huge axe having an instantaneous sudden strike in the middle of a huge windup and well telegraphed combo - I mean just lack of attention to enemy animations such as the riflemen just standing there aiming without a single reload animation or a recoil animation or anything, so you just have to time 4-5 seconds in your head on when you need to dodge/block their shot as there is absolutely no other way to tell when they will shoot. This is a minor example, sure these riflemen die in 1-2 hits anyway, but this type of thing is just sprinkled all around the game.The aesthetics, the soundtrack, the visual and themes - all of that is excellent. The combat is decent, though with very high highs and VERY low lows. There is a lot of love here, and you can see a lot of passion and love for the project for sure, if that makes it worth your time is up to your to decide though. I have played half way though NG+ and while a recent patch made it a lot better, there are still very much the same issues present. Going through the game again made me notice the lack of polish even more, again with animations primarily. The invulnerability on enemies from them standing up is also very different for different enemies, while some can take 5 seconds to get up and be invulnerable during the whole thing, others can take 3 seconds but be already hit-able half way through. Not to mention the "get up" animation is it, there isn't a transitional animation from it, the very SECOND this get up animation ends the attack is already coming out, to the point of your own character's parry animation being barely fast enough to dodge out of he way of the enemy's attack as it already recovered from it's own downed animation (specifically on crawling/ground enemies). Then the reuse of enemies and bosses being enemies is also a very big pain point, to the point that literally the second you leave a new boss arena, right around the corner, is the boss as a regular enemy. Then there's the repeated music. Don't get me wrong that incredible battle theme is definitely VERY good, but when it's the only battle theme that plays for every single mini-boss it does get a bit tiring.I really want to like this game, even to love it, but in its current state it is aggressively mediocre, and definitely cannot recommend it at £40Makes me wish half the marketing/promotion money was spent on polishing the game instead.

_childDocuments_.review: In a static world caught in the clutches of the Canovaccio—a ceaseless play starring every living soul—you awaken as the Maskless One, the only being outside of the script, and the only one capable of destroying the enigmatic figures behind each twisted scene. An incredibly inviting and novel intro, no doubt; however, the main plot never really escapes it, so quickly revealing itself as fractionally more than 'go to the place; stab the thing' until you've gone to enough places and acquainted enough things with the business end of your stabby stick. Coupled with a collection of somewhat extraneous side quests playing out mostly in the lore compendium and often ending just as soon as they begin, Enotria's central narrative doesn't inspire a great deal of curiosity.Yet, as is so often the case with soulslikes, what came before in Enotria's Italian-themed world is infinitely more alluring than what lies ahead. From a gorgeous Venetian city torn down by the very eldritch knowledge and insatiable avarice that raised it to a once grand coastal empire ravaged in the crossfire of feuding gods, each of the three major locations has a captivating story to tell, drip-fed paragraph by paragraph through scattered lore collectables everywhere you look. They're told non-linearly, too, but it's all very digestible; later logs in the timeline find context in the fractured, crumbling landscapes around you, leaving you not lost or confused but rather more deeply enticed by what on earth could have happened in the intermediary chapters.Unsurprisingly, between the staple light and heavy attacks, a dodge step and roll, and the classic Estus-style healing flask, most of the usual Souls suspects are front and centre in the Maskless One's combat capabilities; however, it's here Enotria also departs most from the standard formula. Those light and heavy attacks can be mixed and matched, resulting in a much-needed and relatively wide range of combos for the otherwise limited weapon pool; that dodge is little more than a repositioning tool, left by the wayside almost entirely in favour of a responsive, stance-breaking parry; and complementing all that out are the Mask Lines, a huge selection of chunky, encounter-defining active spells and abilities with often lengthy cooldowns proportionate to their power.As far as soulslike movesets go, the impact, fluidity, and overall satisfaction of this one leaves very little to complain about; your opposition, unfortunately, isn't so lucky. Generally, the bigger an enemy is, the more bizarre they are to fight: boss battles, in particular, are so frequently memorable not for their spectacle or narrative significance, but rather their janky animations awkwardly snapping from one goofy attack to the next, limited movesets often playing those same actions over and over, and delayed strikes held so long you may as well reply to a few emails while you wait.These encounters are still largely a good time, superbly scored and, despite some fairly questionable balancing on both ends of the spectrum, won't leave you thinking anything much worse than 'that was a bit of a missed opportunity'; yet, they  missed opportunities, and Enotria's various build systems leave a similar impression. Masks are supposedly the centrepiece of any given setup, allowing the *checks notes* Maskless One(?) to indefinitely don the visage of select fallen foes; however, they don't grant power comparable to the complete change in physical appearance they provide, but rather effects more in line with your typical soulslike ring. We're talking '+10% this', 'slightly more resistance to that'—boons that could well be completely bugged and I'd genuinely have no idea.Whether it's the substantial skill tree inexplicably allowing only six of its perks to be wielded at a time or the irritating stat requirements for , there's plenty more dubious design in Enotria's build systems, and I could honestly be here all day; yet, I think nothing encapsulates it all quite like the finer details of your Mask Lines: their charging speeds are written in Italian terms typically used to denote tempo in classical music, and while that's all very thematically appropriate, there's no in-game guide for what these words mean. It's easy enough to infer where something like presto fits, but allegro, on the other hand, directly translates to cheerful, requiring further Google searches to find out it indicates a high BPM but not as fast as presto and oh my god why am I on a Wikipedia page for musical notation to figure out how to play a video game properly?There's rarely anything inherently wrong with any of Enotria's build systems—bash your head against them long enough and they'll eventually start making sense—however, between hordes of proper nouns, rushed, overly complicated tutorials you'll only ever see once, and the general prioritisation of style over accessibility, fashioning a decent, cohesive build is a tremendous uphill battle. Coupled with relatively low difficulty across the board, there's ultimately very little incentive to take a setup any further than the first few things that catch your eye, and although a nice big bonk stick and a handful of fancy Mask Lines just about satisfied my monkey brain over the fifteen to twenty-hour runtime, new game plus isn't exactly calling my name.On paper, Enotria's world is something of a mixed bag. It's considerably more linear than your typical soulslike, enemy variety is on the slimmer side, and it's broadly held together by somewhat abrupt 'press X to travel' prompts; however, it's a more streamlined experience done well, fully leveraging the satisfying ease of generally simple, mentally mappable level design though not sacrificing any of the sense of discovery so critical to the genre. There's still a generous helping of secret side routes and hidden rewards, but they're never particularly winding or far off the beaten path, and that mental bandwidth otherwise desperately keeping track of where you have and haven't been is, instead, completely free to soak up the stellar art direction and the excellent stories nestled within.Beyond that, each area feels complete: take a certain side passage in an early-game town and you'll quickly find yourself traversing the rooftops, and that coastal empire from before takes you everywhere from its shores to every inch of the city above. There's an efficiency and consideration of the space, too, not just in the looping paths and classic doors that 'can't be opened from this side', but atop the tallest towers so proudly flaunting the trials and tribulations of the last few hours, and, above all, in the sense of place, history, and purpose behind each destination along the way; you won't find any random poison swamps for the sake of having a soulslike poison swamp, and the world is all the better for it.Enotria: The Last Song is scrappy, it's certainly not your new favourite soulslike, and never have I ever seen a game of this size so brazenly post an 'improvements roadmap' full of QA and QOL features that should never have missed the launch window. However, its innovations are as novel as they need to be, it doesn't royally screw anything up, and, in a genre renowned for its ridiculous, almost comical range of quality, sometimes just good is good enough.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not complete. Yes, you can start the adventure, beat the bosses, collect the weapons and the special abilities. You can wear different masks, you explore the worlds, you can fight things, and you can play the game, but it is not a complete game. It is 90% of a game.There are fundamental, amateurish, straight up mistakes in this game that cover its environment all the way to its mechanics. There are a few broad problems and a lot of smaller issues that stack up to be a thousand little pricks of frustration that erode any real pleasure that this game creates. POINT 1: The mask system. This system exists to give this game characteristics that are different than other souls experiences. But it comes at a great costs, which is the loss of true customization of your character, which, in an RPG (ROLE-PLAYING GAME) Is pretty important. You do not have true agency in how your character looks. Not to mention, fundamentally, there is no reason to switch masks on the fly, which renders the entire mechanic completely irrelevant to a "normal" souls experience. Most souls games, you commit to a build that you find resources and put experience points towards, making that build as OP as possible in order to mount the challenges that the game presents. This game has committed far too much to a mechanic that has no purpose. Furthermore the entire design of the world, enemy encounters, and navigation through the levels do not in anyway motivate the player using this system that clearly a lot of thought went into, except of course the thought, that it is pointless and probably diverted too much attention away from other aspects that need more polish, such as the environment and the feeling of the combat, as well as the very important boss encounters. POINT 2: The boss fights. Easily the biggest draw of any souls game, is how cool the boss fights are. Enotria does accomplish one thing, in that it occasionally introduces and entertains with the boss encounters early on, but soon it is proven that the attack patterns, hit registry, and general flow of the combat during boss battles reduces itself to a mind numbing game of slap and parry. The move sets for the bosses get less and less interesting, as you play more of the game. Many of the top tier boss fights, turn into mindless slap fights where spamming parry, and then smashing your melees end up being the strategy that wins the day. There is very little spectacle or deeper strategy necessary to defeat 99% of the boss encounters. At one point, the rock/paper/scissor mechanic with the different elements, became so irrelevant I didn't even need to switch any attribute in my character to overcome a challenge that was being thrown at me. This flaw in design is paired with a flaw in the execution of its animations and hit detection, which is a prominent issue throughout the game, but shows itself the most when fighting a furious boss that is supposed to be dominating you with a furious bellow of blows, only to swing their sword over your head and miss you completely while you sit there and spam the block button, hoping that when one of these attacks actually lands, you'll be lucky enough to land a parry. SO a unnecessary amount of the fights end up being random flails of shiny swings, only to end up being massive strike outs and undermining the intensity of the battle itself. This does not include the moments where certain bosses will have their ai bug out, rendering them stoic statutes that offer zero challenge. A lot of the boss fights towards the end also were simply reskinned enemy types that were scaled up, so to my count there are 3 instances of giant crab boss, 2 instances of giant stone colossus, and 3 instances of poison dancing lady, that were all the same fight, and led to a disappointing, cheaply made, scam feeling, that for 50$ I deserve some more unique things within a 15 hour playthrough. POINT 3: There's too many cracks in the walls. I don't mean this as in there's too many cracks drawn as a texture on the walls of a crumbling Colosseum, I mean that whoever was building the environment didn't put the pieces of the walls close enough together, and there are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ GAPS in the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ WALLS, where there should be a solid surface. I noticed in more than a dozen locations, instances where the staircases have cracks in them from mis-aligned pieces (stock assets mind you, from unreal engine) which should never happen, on the main path in a game they are charging 50$ for.I accept some problems like this in games where the landscape is sprawling, but this game is not nearly large enough to merit the numerous amount of shoved together structures done in such a lazy and sloppy way, that it becomes an issue of concern for me, while I"m trying to enjoy the act of exploring an environment. POINT 4: The game has inadequate guidance to help the player understand where they are supposed to go. This is a bit convoluted to explain, but I will try. A lot of the navigation in the game is dependent on where you find new shiny things to pick up, and often times you will push down a path, collect all the shiny, and not remember where you've been, after you've hit a dead end, and then you end walking back down the path you came, only to then end up in a weirdly circular dead end and you were supposed to have remembered after 2-3 hours of exploring, this one path that you didn't take earlier in order to go forward. So for a game with a lot of diverging paths to explore, being solely dependent on your ability to remember small facets of a new environment, while also balancing learning the language of the game and its mechanics the game does a piss poor job reminding you or guiding you towards the right path. As a result, there were more than one occasion where I lost 1 hour of my life, wondering where the ♥♥♥♥ is the right path forward, running in desperate circles, cursing my choice to play this game, and wondering why it is so hard to simply nudge me in the right direction, with either good level design, or an elegant mechanic that simply whispers to me if i'm getting hot or cold. they mention in their improvements that they will make the navigation "Better' but I find it atrocious that I would have to wait 6 months after release to be able to navigate this game without the assistance of external walkthroughs. tl:dr navigating sucks and they dont' have any mechanics to help dumb people like me remember when they forgot to go down a hallway. POINT 5: This game is not optimized. I have a PC with a 3060ti, and an i7 10 it is not top of the line by any means, but is more than the recommended and yet I was struggling to maintain a 60 fps while locked at 60fps, AND using DLSS on PERFORMANCE. There are multiple locations that struggle to maintain their frame rate, and a certain boss fight that made my frame rate tank to the point where I had to play the rest of this game on the LOWEST GRAPHICAL SETTINGS to get a smooth experience. BY comparison I played the entirety of SPACE MARINE 2 which boasts incredible on screen numbers of enemies and a variety of effects rendering in real time simultaneously and I was able to get phenomenal performance even with my computer being below par on the rec specs. So even in potato mode which dramatically reduces the fun factor of this game, it struggled, and I found that completely unacceptable.SummaryThis game is promising, but clearly was rushed out to generate revenue for this "small" studio. for an independent production I applaud their ambition to make a game on the same scale and scope as the coveted Dark Souls genre. BUT, that does not really excuse lazy, corner cutting, and under developed games being sold at market price. 50$ should be much more polished and put together than this game. If I had to put this in a pile, this would go right in with Steel Rising, Lords of the Fallen (at release).

_childDocuments_.review: I REALLY want to like this game but unfortunately I have to leave a negative review, at least until it gets fixed.  You can tell a lot of love and care went into the world and the devs clearly had a lot planned with how many features there are, but unfortunately everything just feels sub-par and it lacks the polish for a game with a $60 price tag.- While not unplayable, it's buggy and I had a lot of technical issues. My frame rate would absolutely tank in certain areas and I got stuck in elevators on multiple occasions. AI would just break at times and enemies would stand there doing nothing. It runs, but it is far from perfect.- Weapons overall are seriously lackluster. There are about 6 or 7 weapon types in the game ranging from polearms to colossal hammers. This in itself isn't a problem, but every weapon of that class shares the same moveset. Are you using a curved sword? Well when you find one... that's it. There's no point in experimenting because you already know what they all do, so you just go with the highest damage option and call it a day. And this game doesn't have weapon arts or skills of any kind, either. So essentially, every weapon functions exactly the same apart from stats and elemental/status effects. Speaking of those:- Elemental damage and status effects are cool conceptually but I just didn't feel a need to play around them at all. Raw damage from weapons and Lines (Enotria's versions of spells, basically?) was enough to get me through all of the game without much effort. And I've read from other people that some bosses are basically resistant to all effects anyway! Again, the idea there is cool, the developers clearly had a "trump" system in mind where Effect 1 > Effect 2 and so on, but it all just feels so unnecessary.- The game's locations ranged from perfect to, you guessed it, lackluster. Quinta is the first major area you tackle and it's wonderful. Tons of hidden items, puzzles (or at least platforming), lots of things to do, there's nothing bad you can say about this area. Fast forward to one of the later areas (which I'll just call "Lit" to avoid spoilers) and things are a lot more linear by comparison. Lit also has a lot of ridiculously frustrating design choices, and I think this is where the devs started to phone it in. See that roof over there next to the platform you're on that you can clearly reach with a jump? Well haha, you're stupid, there's an invisible wall there, now you fall into the water and die. See that little pier down there with boats leading around the corner? Well you can jump on the pier (and can't get back up) but when you jump on the boats, you phase through them and fall into the water and die. It's all so frustrating especially when the first area was SO good.  This is just how Enotria was for me overall, unfortunately. The opening moments were STRONG and offered such a fun and unique experience, but the game peters out massively midway through and never finds its way back.  Enotria should not have been released in it's current state. This is a late-stage Early Access game. I paid $60 for this game and now I have to wait a year for the developers to complete their roadmap to get the "full" version of Enotria, and that's simply not fair.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, this is very hard to review, I think I'll have to make a dedicated video about this game. No, it's not polished, at all., Yes, it has some glaring design issues (on top of execution issues) BUT... there is just something that keeps me coming back at this, took me 57 hours to reach the end (in part due to a game breaking bug that happened to me when I reached the final third of the game, which forced me to restart the whole game) so I'd say it's about a 30 hour experience. Main issues: 1. Parry/Deflect hybrid: this is possibly the biggest thing holding the game back, it has a timed block mechanic, which is not like Sekiro's deflect, and it's not like Dark Souls' parry. The timing is not as generous as Sekiro's, but not as tight as Lies of P, the problem, is that in order to land parries, you need to anticipate them. You need to hit the parry button at the end of the enemy's wind-up (like in Dark Souls) instead of when the hit lands (like in Sekiro) now, this works in Dark Souls, because 1 or 2 parries at most, gets you a critical attack... Not in this game. here you're expected to consistently nail parries (as if they were Sekiro deflects) but with half as much benefits.  Unlike Lies of P there is no blocking here, also Lies of P's perfect guards are also more like Sekiro's deflects, as in, you have to start when the attack is just about to land. This is a huge difference, because it changes parrying from a reaction (you see an attack, you parry the attack) to an anticipation (you have to have seen the attack first, multiple times to figure out when to hit the parry button) - the issue is that, if parrying is such an integral mechanic, it should be a lot easier to pull off, and it should be more reactionary (i.e. like Sekiro, or even Lies of P) if parry is a tactical choice, a high risk vs high reward move (like in Dark Souls) then it's something you'll not be doing all the time. 1.5. Dodging is awful. There is a weird start-up delay to the iframes or even to the dodge animation itself, you get used to it after like 30 hours in the game, but it never feels great. Compared to like, Black Myth Wukong, the doge here is basically useless. Which on an RPG with such build variety, is a complete shame. 2. Lackluster movesets: probably the main reason why this game is still sitting on "Mixed" instead of even "Mostly Positive", is this. The enemies have so few moves, from mobs to the final boss, you'll be lucky if an enemy has more than 5 attacks, some bosses easily get stuck in a loop of repeating the same 2 moves over and over again (like Giangurgolo or even Spaventa, or the many giant crab bosses that have literally 2 attacks, and sometimes a breath attack they won't do if you stay close to them)  There is an absurd amount of re-used animations between enemies and bosses, some enemies straight up use the same animations as the player's, the enemy variety seemed good at fist, that is until you realise so many of them just share the same animations, which effectively just makes them reskins of each other. 3. Lack of polish in animations: this may be less obvious, and most gamers will just say "doesn't feel good" and can't put their fingers on why. The issue is the lack of polish in the animations, you can really tell what is almost raw mocap data, vs what is painfully handkeyed, many animations have overdrawn wind-ups with super long anticipation poses, and extremely fast (like 2-3 frames) swings, yes over time you get adjusted to it but it just doesn't feel good to fight, because enemies will go from moving in molasses to being The Flash in the span of 0.05 seconds.  it's hard to describe in writing, this lack of polish and animation that has very obviously just been sped up or slowed down, it really isn't great for a game in a genre that relies so heavily on polished animation.4. Lack of weapon variety: this may seem weird because the game has a good amount of weapons. but here's the issue. All weapon within the same class, use the same animations. This means the difference between each individual weapon, are the stats, the 3D model/textures, that's it. This makes the weapons into nothing but stats sticks, some weapons become completely useless because there is another weapon in the same class with better scaling, so the other weapon is a better option in 100% of cases. I understand that making animations is expensive, so instead of having "different weapons" with a limited budget of maybe 5 animation sets, then just make the individual weapons cosmetic only, and then allow us to chose what scaling/affinity we want. 5. Camera: this game has possibly the worst camera of any soulslike, it will often stay at the same height of your character's butt and pan up to try and see the enemy, which ends up (in many cases) with your character's silhouette blocking the enemy view, which triggers the mesh to become semi-transparent. I shouldn't even have to explain why this is terrible, but it is, the camera should be translating up, and tilting down, so you have a clear view of yourself and what you have locked on, especially with most of the characters in the game being around the same size as you (or slightly bigger) - yes you get adjusted to it, but it's awful, it makes parrying projectiles even worse because most enemy projectiles (especially magic ones) will track you and become hidden by your character, so you've now any of telling when to press the parry button cause you can't tell how far they are. 6. Various visual glitches, none of this is game breaking, but for example every time you go back to idle from the end of an attack, the character's arm will glitch and swing the sword around like it's completely weightless. Or when you jump, even if are carrying around a column that you use as a weapon, you'll go in the default falling pose and you'll see the colossal weapon move across the screen like it's not there. All of this is just at odds with how LONG the anticipation for your attacks are, I mean, this game has really high commitment and long wind-ups, hyper-armor only activates once the swing goes (so you can very easily get locked out of every attack, regardless of weapon) so when the attack animations are telling me a story, that the guy is wielding around a super heavy object, but then some glitch like that happens, and the object no longer has weight, it just pulls you out of any immersion you may have had, and reminds you that this is a AA game., So, why would I recommend this game?  It really is a case of the whole being greater than the sum of its parts, I can't quite place my finger on it, it's like a really really rough gem, it has some charm to it, besides the absolutely stunning art, unique setting and just everything else, you can tell there is a good game here if you like the genre and you adjust to the jank. The level design is probably the strongest aspect of the game, and yeah it's not perfect, but I can't say I didn't have fun. Overall, if they fixed a few things, this game would be a solid 8/10, but right now it's more like a 7/10. I'd say it's MUCH better than Lords of the Fallen (the 2nd one) and Steelrising and Mortal Shell. But it's nowhere near Lies of P, Dark Souls 3, Sekiro, and Bloodborne.
